input: Dawa Norbu argues that modern Chinese Communist historians tend to be in favor of the view that the Ming simply reappointed old Yuan dynasty officials in Tibet and perpetuated their rule of Tibet in this manner. Norbu writes that, although this would have been true for the eastern Tibetan regions of Amdo and Kham's "tribute-cum-trade" relations with the Ming, it was untrue if applied to the western Tibetan regions of Ü-Tsang and Ngari. After the Phagmodrupa Changchub Gyaltsen, these were ruled by "three successive nationalistic regimes," which Norbu writes "Communist historians prefer to ignore."
rewrite: Dawa Norbu contends that contemporary Chinese Communist historiography commonly advances the interpretation that the Ming dynasty merely reinstated former Yuan officials to perpetuate its governance over Tibet. He acknowledges this characterization may apply to the eastern regions of Amdo and Kham, which maintained tributary and trade relations with the Ming. However, Norbu asserts it is inaccurate for western Tibet (Ü-Tsang and Ngari), which, following Phagmodrupa Changchub Gyaltsen, was governed by what he terms "three successive nationalistic regimes"—a fact he states Communist historians typically disregard.

input: The study of genocide has mainly been focused towards the legal aspect of the term. By formally recognizing the act of genocide as a crime, involves the undergoing prosecution that begins with not only seeing genocide as outrageous past any moral standpoint but also may be a legal liability within international relations. When genocide is looked at in a general aspect it is viewed as the deliberate killing of a certain group. Yet is commonly seen to escape the process of trial and prosecution due to the fact that genocide is more often than not committed by the officials in power of a state or area. In 1648 before the term genocide had been coined, the Peace of Westphalia was established to protect ethnic, national, racial and in some instances religious groups. During the 19th century humanitarian intervention was needed due to the fact of conflict and justification of some of the actions executed by the military.
rewrite: The study of genocide has predominantly emphasized its legal dimensions. Formally defining genocide as a crime initiates a prosecutorial framework that treats it not merely as a profound moral transgression but also as a matter of legal accountability in international relations. In general terms, genocide is understood as the deliberate annihilation of a specific group. However, it frequently evades judicial proceedings, largely because such acts are commonly perpetrated by state authorities or those in positions of power. Prior to the coining of the term "genocide" in 1948, the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 established principles intended to protect ethnic, national, racial, and, in some cases, religious groups. During the nineteenth century, humanitarian intervention became necessary due to widespread conflict and the justifications provided for certain military actions.

input: New Haven was the host of the 1995 Special Olympics World Summer Games; then-President Bill Clinton spoke at the opening ceremonies. The city is home to the Pilot Pen International tennis event, which takes place every August at the Connecticut Tennis Center, one of the largest tennis venues in the world. New Haven biannually hosts "The Game" between Yale and Harvard, the country's second-oldest college football rivalry. Numerous road races take place in New Haven, including the USA 20K Championship during the New Haven Road Race.
rewrite: New Haven has hosted several notable sporting events, including the 1995 Special Olympics World Summer Games, which featured an opening address by then-President Bill Clinton. The city annually hosts the Pilot Pen International tennis tournament at the expansive Connecticut Tennis Center. It is also the site of the historic Yale-Harvard football rivalry, "The Game," held biennially. Furthermore, New Haven stages numerous road races, such as the USA 20K Championship within the New Haven Road Race.

input: The conversion rate of omega-6 DGLA to AA largely determines the production of the prostaglandins PGE1 and PGE2. Omega-3 EPA prevents AA from being released from membranes, thereby skewing prostaglandin balance away from pro-inflammatory PGE2 (made from AA) toward anti-inflammatory PGE1 (made from DGLA). Moreover, the conversion (desaturation) of DGLA to AA is controlled by the enzyme delta-5-desaturase, which in turn is controlled by hormones such as insulin (up-regulation) and glucagon (down-regulation). The amount and type of carbohydrates consumed, along with some types of amino acid, can influence processes involving insulin, glucagon, and other hormones; therefore, the ratio of omega-3 versus omega-6 has wide effects on general health, and specific effects on immune function and inflammation, and mitosis (i.e., cell division).
rewrite: The production of prostaglandins PGE1 and PGE2 is primarily governed by the conversion rate of the omega-6 fatty acid dihomo-γ-linolenic acid (DGLA) to arachidonic acid (AA). Omega-3 eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) inhibits the release of AA from cell membranes, shifting prostaglandin synthesis away from pro-inflammatory PGE2 (derived from AA) and toward anti-inflammatory PGE1 (derived from DGLA). This conversion of DGLA to AA is mediated by the enzyme delta-5-desaturase, whose activity is hormonally regulated, being upregulated by insulin and downregulated by glucagon. Dietary intake of carbohydrates and certain amino acids influences these hormonal pathways. Consequently, the balance between omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids exerts broad systemic effects, with specific implications for immune function, inflammatory responses, and cellular mitosis.

input: The university first offered graduate degrees, in the form of a Master of Arts (MA), in the 1854–1855 academic year. The program expanded to include Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Civil Engineering in its early stages of growth, before a formal graduate school education was developed with a thesis not required to receive the degrees. This changed in 1924 with formal requirements developed for graduate degrees, including offering Doctorate (PhD) degrees. Today each of the five colleges offer graduate education. Most of the departments from the College of Arts and Letters offer PhD programs, while a professional Master of Divinity (M.Div.) program also exists. All of the departments in the College of Science offer PhD programs, except for the Department of Pre-Professional Studies. The School of Architecture offers a Master of Architecture, while each of the departments of the College of Engineering offer PhD programs. The College of Business offers multiple professional programs including MBA and Master of Science in Accountancy programs. It also operates facilities in Chicago and Cincinnati for its executive MBA program. Additionally, the Alliance for Catholic Education program offers a Master of Education program where students study at the university during the summer and teach in Catholic elementary schools, middle schools, and high schools across the Southern United States for two school years.
rewrite: The university initiated its graduate education offerings during the 1854–1855 academic year with the conferral of the Master of Arts (MA) degree. In subsequent early expansions, the curriculum was broadened to include the Master of Laws (LL.M.) and Master of Civil Engineering, prior to the establishment of a formal graduate school. Initially, these master's degrees did not require a thesis. A significant structural change occurred in 1924 with the formalization of graduate degree requirements, which included the introduction of Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) programs. Presently, all five constituent colleges provide graduate instruction. Within the College of Arts and Letters, most departments confer PhDs, alongside a professional Master of Divinity (M.Div.). All departments in the College of Science offer PhDs, with the exception of Pre-Professional Studies. The School of Architecture grants a Master of Architecture, while each department in the College of Engineering offers PhD programs. The College of Business administers several professional programs, including the MBA and Master of Science in Accountancy, and maintains facilities in Chicago and Cincinnati for its executive MBA. Furthermore, the Alliance for Catholic Education program provides a Master of Education, wherein students undertake summer coursework at the university and fulfill two academic years of teaching in Catholic K-12 schools across the Southern United States.

input: Illustrated humour periodicals were popular in 19th-century Britain, the earliest of which was the short-lived The Glasgow Looking Glass in 1825. The most popular was Punch, which popularized the term cartoon for its humorous caricatures. On occasion the cartoons in these magazines appeared in sequences; the character Ally Sloper featured in the earliest serialized comic strip when the character began to feature in its own weekly magazine in 1884.
rewrite: Illustrated humour periodicals gained prominence in nineteenth-century Britain, beginning with the brief publication of *The Glasgow Looking Glass* in 1825. The most influential was *Punch*, which established the modern usage of "cartoon" for satirical drawings. While often single images, sequential cartoons also emerged; the character Ally Sloper is recognized as the first serialized comic strip upon gaining a dedicated weekly magazine in 1884.

input: The Gold Standard Act of 1900 abandoned the bimetallic standard and defined the dollar as 23.22 grains (1.505 g) of gold, equivalent to setting the price of 1 troy ounce of gold at $20.67. Silver coins continued to be issued for circulation until 1964, when all silver was removed from dimes and quarters, and the half dollar was reduced to 40% silver. Silver half dollars were last issued for circulation in 1970. Gold coins were confiscated by Executive Order 6102 issued in 1933 by Franklin Roosevelt. The gold standard was changed to 13.71 grains (0.888 g), equivalent to setting the price of 1 troy ounce of gold at $35. This standard persisted until 1968.
rewrite: The Gold Standard Act of 1900 formally established a monometallic gold standard, defining the dollar as equivalent to 23.22 grains (1.505 grams) of gold, which fixed the official price at $20.67 per troy ounce. Concurrently, silver coins remained in production for general circulation. This issuance continued until 1964, when silver was eliminated from dimes and quarters, and the half dollar's silver content was reduced to 40%; the final circulating silver half dollars were minted in 1970. In 1933, Executive Order 6102, issued by President Franklin Roosevelt, mandated the confiscation of gold coins. Subsequently, the gold standard was redefined to 13.71 grains (0.888 grams), raising the official gold price to $35 per ounce, a valuation that remained effective until 1968.

input: Worldwide prosperity changed dramatically with the onset of the Great Depression in 1929. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 served to punctuate the end of the previous era, as The Great Depression set in. The Great Depression was a worldwide economic downturn starting in most places in 1929 and ending at different times in the 1930s or early 1940s for different countries. It was the largest and most important economic depression in the 20th century, and is used in the 21st century as an example of how far the world's economy can fall.
rewrite: The onset of the Great Depression in 1929 precipitated a dramatic reversal in global prosperity. The Wall Street Crash of that year starkly demarcated the conclusion of the preceding era. This worldwide economic downturn commenced in most regions in 1929, persisting through the 1930s and into the early 1940s with varying national conclusions. As the twentieth century's most severe and significant depression, it remains a paramount historical benchmark for the potential depth of economic decline.

input: Rawski writes that Altan Khan's conversion to the Gelug "can be interpreted as an attempt to expand his authority in his conflict with his nominal superior, Tümen Khan." To further cement the Mongol-Tibetan alliance, the great-grandson of Altan Khan—the 4th Dalai Lama (1589–1616)—was made the fourth Dalai Lama. In 1642, the 5th Dalai Lama (1617–1682) became the first to wield effective political control over Tibet.
rewrite: Rawski interprets Altan Khan's adoption of the Gelug tradition as a strategic effort to enhance his authority against his superior, Tümen Khan. This Mongol-Tibetan alliance was solidified when his great-grandson was recognized as the Fourth Dalai Lama (1589–1616). Subsequently, the Fifth Dalai Lama (1617–1682) achieved effective political dominion over Tibet in 1642.

input: Aposematism, where organisms are brightly colored as a warning to predators, is the antithesis of camouflage. Some organisms pose a threat to their predators—for example they may be poisonous, or able to harm them physically. Aposematic coloring involves bright, easily recognizable and unique colors and patterns. For example, bright coloration in Variable Checkerspot butterflies leads to decreased predation attempts by avian predators. Upon being harmed (e.g., stung) by their prey, the appearance in such an organism will be remembered as something to avoid. While that particular prey organism may be killed, the coloring benefits the prey species as a whole.
rewrite: Aposematism, characterized by conspicuous coloration that signals unpalatability or danger to predators, stands in direct contrast to camouflage. This defensive strategy employs vivid and distinctive patterns to advertise an organism's capacity to harm, such as through toxicity or physical defenses. Empirical evidence, including reduced avian predation on brightly colored Variable Checkerspot butterflies, supports its efficacy. When a predator experiences a negative encounter, such as a sting, it learns to associate the warning coloration with an adverse outcome. Consequently, while the individual prey may be lost, this mnemonic avoidance confers a selective advantage upon the species as a whole.

input: A sound generated on any instrument produces many modes of vibration that occur simultaneously. A listener hears numerous frequencies at once. The vibration with the lowest frequency is called the fundamental frequency; the other frequencies are overtones. Harmonics are an important class of overtones with frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental. Whether or not the higher frequencies are integer multiples, they are collectively called the partials, referring to the different parts that make up the total spectrum.
rewrite: Any musical instrument produces a complex sound comprising multiple simultaneous vibrational modes, which are perceived as numerous concurrent frequencies. The lowest of these is the fundamental frequency, while the others are termed overtones. A significant subset of overtones, known as harmonics, consists of frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental. Collectively, all higher-frequency components are called partials, denoting the constituent elements of the complete acoustic spectrum.

input: In response to these hardware flaws, "Nintendo Authorized Repair Centers" sprang up across the U.S. According to Nintendo, the authorization program was designed to ensure that the machines were properly repaired. Nintendo would ship the necessary replacement parts only to shops that had enrolled in the authorization program. In practice, the authorization process consisted of nothing more than paying a fee to Nintendo for the privilege. In a recent trend, many sites have sprung up to offer Nintendo repair parts, guides, and services that replace those formerly offered by the authorized repair centers.
rewrite: In response to these hardware deficiencies, "Nintendo Authorized Repair Centers" were established throughout the United States. Nintendo stated this authorization program aimed to guarantee proper repair standards by supplying replacement parts exclusively to enrolled shops. However, the authorization process effectively entailed merely remitting a fee to Nintendo. Recently, numerous independent sites have emerged, offering repair parts, guides, and services that supplant those previously provided by the authorized centers.

input: On the next day, December 18, protests turned into civil unrest as clashes between troops, volunteers, militia units, and Kazakh students turned into a wide-scale confrontation. The clashes could only be controlled on the third day. The Almaty events were followed by smaller protests and demonstrations in Shymkent, Pavlodar, Karaganda, and Taldykorgan. Reports from Kazakh SSR authorities estimated that the riots drew 3,000 people. Other estimates are of at least 30,000 to 40,000 protestors with 5,000 arrested and jailed, and an unknown number of casualties. Jeltoqsan leaders say over 60,000 Kazakhs participated in the protests. According to the Kazakh SSR government, there were two deaths during the riots, including a volunteer police worker and a student. Both of them had died due to blows to the head. About 100 others were detained and several others were sentenced to terms in labor camps. Sources cited by the Library of Congress claimed that at least 200 people died or were summarily executed soon thereafter; some accounts estimate casualties at more than 1,000. The writer Mukhtar Shakhanov claimed that a KGB officer testified that 168 protesters were killed, but that figure remains unconfirmed.
rewrite: On December 18, demonstrations escalated into widespread civil unrest, marked by confrontations between military personnel, volunteers, militia units, and Kazakh students. This conflict persisted for three days before being brought under control. Following the events in Almaty, further, though smaller, protests occurred in several cities including Shymkent, Pavlodar, Karaganda, and Taldykorgan. Official estimates from the Kazakh SSR authorities reported approximately 3,000 participants in the riots, while alternative assessments suggest a significantly larger scale, citing between 30,000 and 40,000 protesters, with around 5,000 individuals arrested and an undetermined number of casualties. Organizers of the Jeltoqsan movement have asserted participation exceeded 60,000. According to government accounts, the unrest resulted in two fatalities—a volunteer police officer and a student, both from cranial trauma—with approximately 100 detainees and several sentences to labor camps. However, sources referenced by the Library of Congress indicate a substantially higher toll, alleging at least 200 deaths or summary executions, with some estimates exceeding 1,000 casualties. Author Mukhtar Shakhanov has cited an unverified claim from a KGB officer stating 168 protesters were killed.

input: Washington University supports four major student-run media outlets. The university's student newspaper, Student Life, is available for students. KWUR (90.3 FM) serves as the students' official radio station; the station also attracts an audience in the immediately surrounding community due to its eclectic and free-form musical programming. WUTV is the university's closed-circuit television channel. The university's main student-run political publication is the Washington University Political Review (nicknamed "WUPR"), a self-described "multipartisan" monthly magazine. Washington University undergraduates publish two literary and art journals, The Eliot Review and Spires Intercollegiate Arts and Literary Magazine. A variety of other publications also serve the university community, ranging from in-house academic journals to glossy alumni magazines to WUnderground, campus' student-run satirical newspaper.
rewrite: Washington University sustains four principal student-operated media organizations. These include the student newspaper, *Student Life*; the official campus radio station KWUR (90.3 FM), whose diverse programming also engages the local community; and the closed-circuit television channel WUTV. The primary political publication is the *Washington University Political Review* ("WUPR"), a self-identified multipartisan monthly magazine. Undergraduate students also produce two literary and arts journals: *The Eliot Review* and *Spires Intercollegiate Arts and Literary Magazine*. Additionally, the community is served by various other publications, from internal academic journals and polished alumni magazines to the satirical student newspaper *WUnderground*.

input: In the United States and elsewhere in the world, there has been a marked rise in the evangelical wing of Protestant denominations, especially those that are more exclusively evangelical, and a corresponding decline in the mainstream liberal churches. In the post–World War I era, Liberal Christianity was on the rise, and a considerable number of seminaries held and taught from a liberal perspective as well. In the post–World War II era, the trend began to swing back towards the conservative camp in America's seminaries and church structures.
rewrite: A pronounced global shift has occurred within Protestantism, characterized by the expansion of exclusively evangelical denominations and the contraction of mainstream liberal churches. Following World War I, Liberal Christianity ascended, with many seminaries adopting its perspective. However, in the post–World War II period, a reversal emerged, as theological conservatism regained influence within American ecclesiastical and seminary institutions.

input: Utrecht is the centre of a densely populated area, which makes concise definitions of its agglomeration difficult, and somewhat arbitrary. The smaller Utrecht agglomeration of continuously built up areas counts some 420,000 inhabitants and includes Nieuwegein, IJsselstein and Maarssen. It is sometimes argued that the close by municipalities De Bilt, Zeist, Houten, Vianen, Driebergen-Rijsenburg (Utrechtse Heuvelrug), and Bunnik should also be counted towards the Utrecht agglomeration, bringing the total to 640,000 inhabitants. The larger region, including slightly more remote towns such as Woerden and Amersfoort counts up to 820,000 inhabitants.
rewrite: Defining the agglomeration of Utrecht, a densely populated regional center, presents challenges due to the somewhat arbitrary nature of concise delineations. The core contiguous built-up area, encompassing Nieuwegein, IJsselstein, and Maarssen, contains approximately 420,000 residents. A broader definition, incorporating proximate municipalities like De Bilt and Zeist, raises the population to about 640,000. Extending further to include more distant towns such as Woerden and Amersfoort defines a larger region of roughly 820,000 inhabitants.

input: Turner Classic Movies is available in many other countries around the world. In Canada, TCM began to be carried on Shaw Cable and satellite provider Shaw Direct in 2005. Rogers Cable started offering TCM in December 2006 as a free preview for subscribers of its digital cable tier, and was added to its analogue tier in February 2007. While the schedule for the Canadian feed is generally the same as that of the U.S. network, some films are replaced for broadcast in Canada due to rights issues and other reasons. Other versions of TCM are available in Australia, France, Middle East, South Africa, Cyprus, Spain, Asia, Latin America, Scandinavia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Malta. The UK version operates two channels, including a spinoff called TCM 2.
rewrite: Turner Classic Movies is distributed internationally across numerous nations. In Canada, carriage commenced in 2005 via Shaw Cable and Shaw Direct. Rogers Cable introduced the channel in December 2006 as a complimentary preview for digital subscribers, subsequently adding it to its analogue tier in February 2007. Although the Canadian schedule largely mirrors the United States feed, select films are substituted due to licensing restrictions and other considerations. Additional regional versions of the channel are available in Australia, France, the Middle East, South Africa, Cyprus, Spain, Asia, Latin America, Scandinavia, the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Malta. Notably, the United Kingdom iteration operates two channels, one of which is a spinoff service branded as TCM 2.

input: A person's self-report is the most reliable measure of pain, with health care professionals tending to underestimate severity. A definition of pain widely employed in nursing, emphasizing its subjective nature and the importance of believing patient reports, was introduced by Margo McCaffery in 1968: "Pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, existing whenever he says it does". To assess intensity, the patient may be asked to locate their pain on a scale of 0 to 10, with 0 being no pain at all, and 10 the worst pain they have ever felt. Quality can be established by having the patient complete the McGill Pain Questionnaire indicating which words best describe their pain.
rewrite: The most reliable measure of pain is an individual's self-report, as healthcare professionals often underestimate its severity. A foundational definition in nursing, introduced by Margo McCaffery in 1968, underscores pain's subjective nature and the imperative to accept patient accounts: "Pain is whatever the experiencing person says it is, existing whenever he says it does." Assessment typically involves evaluating intensity, often via a numeric rating scale from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst imaginable pain), and quality, frequently determined using instruments like the McGill Pain Questionnaire, which catalogs descriptive pain terms.

input: Though still predominantly green, post-2004 series incorporate other colors to better distinguish different denominations. As a result of a 2008 decision in an accessibility lawsuit filed by the American Council of the Blind, the Bureau of Engraving and Printing is planning to implement a raised tactile feature in the next redesign of each note, except the $1 and the version of the $100 bill already in process. It also plans larger, higher-contrast numerals, more color differences, and distribution of currency readers to assist the visually impaired during the transition period.
rewrite: Post-2004 U.S. currency series, while remaining primarily green, have integrated additional colors to enhance denomination differentiation. Following a 2008 accessibility ruling in favor of the American Council of the Blind, the Bureau of Engraving and Printing will introduce raised tactile features in the forthcoming redesign of all notes, excluding the $1 bill and the $100 bill already under production. Further planned accessibility measures include larger, higher-contrast numerals, increased color variation, and the distribution of currency readers to aid visually impaired individuals during the transition.

input: In Sand Springs, an outdoor amphitheater called "Discoveryland!" is the official performance headquarters for the musical Oklahoma! Ridge Bond, native of McAlester, Oklahoma, starred in the Broadway and International touring productions of Oklahoma!, playing the role of "Curly McClain" in more than 2,600 performances. In 1953 he was featured along with the Oklahoma! cast on a CBS Omnibus television broadcast. Bond was instrumental in the title song becoming the Oklahoma state song and is also featured on the U.S. postage stamp commemorating the musical's 50th anniversary. Historically, the state has produced musical styles such as The Tulsa Sound and western swing, which was popularized at Cain's Ballroom in Tulsa. The building, known as the "Carnegie Hall of Western Swing", served as the performance headquarters of Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys during the 1930s. Stillwater is known as the epicenter of Red Dirt music, the best-known proponent of which is the late Bob Childers.
rewrite: The outdoor amphitheater "Discoveryland!" in Sand Springs serves as the official performance venue for the musical *Oklahoma!*. Ridge Bond, a native of McAlester, Oklahoma, who portrayed "Curly McClain" in over 2,600 performances of the Broadway and international touring productions, was featured with the cast in a 1953 CBS *Omnibus* television broadcast. Bond played a key role in establishing the title song as the Oklahoma state song and is depicted on a U.S. postage stamp commemorating the musical's fiftieth anniversary. Musically, the state is historically significant for styles such as western swing, popularized at Tulsa's Cain's Ballroom—a venue known as the "Carnegie Hall of Western Swing" that housed Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys in the 1930s—and the Tulsa Sound. Additionally, Stillwater is recognized as the epicenter of Red Dirt music, most notably championed by the late Bob Childers.

input: But Hanover is not only one of the most important Exhibition Cities in the world, it is also one of the German capitals for marksmen. The Schützenfest Hannover is the largest Marksmen's Fun Fair in the world and takes place once a year (late June to early July) (2014 - July 4th to the 13th). It consists of more than 260 rides and inns, five large beer tents and a big entertainment programme. The highlight of this fun fair is the 12 kilometres (7 mi) long Parade of the Marksmen with more than 12.000 participants from all over the world, among them around 5.000 marksmen, 128 bands and more than 70 wagons, carriages and big festival vehicles. It is the longest procession in Europe. Around 2 million people visit this fun fair every year. The landmark of this Fun Fair is the biggest transportable Ferris Wheel in the world (60 m or 197 ft high). The origins of this fun fair is located in the year 1529.
rewrite: Hanover is distinguished not only as a preeminent global exhibition city but also as one of Germany’s principal centers for marksmanship. The Hanover Schützenfest, the world’s largest marksmen’s fair, is an annual event held from late June to early July (specifically July 4th to 13th in 2014). The festival comprises over 260 rides and concessions, five major beer tents, and an extensive entertainment program. Its central attraction is the Marksmen’s Parade, a twelve-kilometer procession featuring more than 12,000 participants worldwide, including approximately 5,000 marksmen, 128 musical bands, and over 70 wagons, carriages, and festival floats, rendering it the longest such procession in Europe. Annual attendance reaches roughly two million visitors. The fair’s landmark is the world’s largest transportable Ferris wheel, standing sixty meters high. The event traces its origins to 1529.

input: In 1943, at the age of 16, Elizabeth undertook her first solo public appearance on a visit to the Grenadier Guards, of which she had been appointed colonel the previous year. As she approached her 18th birthday, parliament changed the law so that she could act as one of five Counsellors of State in the event of her father's incapacity or absence abroad, such as his visit to Italy in July 1944. In February 1945, she joined the Women's Auxiliary Territorial Service as an honorary second subaltern with the service number of 230873. She trained as a driver and mechanic and was promoted to honorary junior commander five months later.
rewrite: In 1943, at sixteen years of age, Elizabeth made her inaugural independent public appearance during a visit to the Grenadier Guards, a regiment to which she had been appointed colonel the preceding year. Nearing her eighteenth birthday, Parliament amended legislation to enable her to serve among five Counsellors of State during her father’s incapacity or overseas absences, such as his July 1944 visit to Italy. By February 1945, she had enlisted in the Women’s Auxiliary Territorial Service as an honorary second subaltern (service number 230873). There, she trained as a driver and mechanic, attaining promotion to honorary junior commander within five months.

input: By the early 1940s, the company was concentrating on lower-budget productions that were the company's main staple: westerns, melodramas, serials and sequels to the studio's horror pictures, the latter now solely B pictures. The studio fostered many series: The Dead End Kids and Little Tough Guys action features and serials (1938–43); the comic adventures of infant Baby Sandy (1938–41); comedies with Hugh Herbert (1938–42) and The Ritz Brothers (1940–43); musicals with Robert Paige, Jane Frazee, The Andrews Sisters, and The Merry Macs (1938–45); and westerns with Tom Mix (1932–33), Buck Jones (1933–36), Bob Baker (1938–39), Johnny Mack Brown (1938–43); Rod Cameron (1944–45), and Kirby Grant (1946–47).
rewrite: By the early 1940s, the studio had shifted its primary focus to lower-budget productions, which constituted its core output. This repertoire consisted predominantly of westerns, melodramas, serials, and sequels to earlier horror films, the latter now relegated exclusively to B-picture status. The company systematically developed numerous film series, including action features and serials such as *The Dead End Kids* and *Little Tough Guys* (1938–1943), the comedic *Baby Sandy* adventures (1938–1941), and comedies featuring Hugh Herbert (1938–1942) and The Ritz Brothers (1940–1943). Its musical series starred performers like Robert Paige and The Andrews Sisters (1938–1945), while its westerns featured a succession of leads from Tom Mix (1932–1933) to Kirby Grant (1946–1947).

input: A number of universities in London are outside the University of London system, including Brunel University, City University London, Imperial College London, Kingston University, London Metropolitan University, Middlesex University, University of East London, University of West London and University of Westminster, (with over 34,000 students, the largest unitary university in London), London South Bank University, Middlesex University, University of the Arts London (the largest university of art, design, fashion, communication and the performing arts in Europe), University of East London, the University of West London and the University of Westminster. In addition there are three international universities in London – Regent's University London, Richmond, The American International University in London and Schiller International University.
rewrite: Several institutions of higher education in London operate independently of the University of London federation. These include Brunel University, City, University of London, Imperial College London, Kingston University, London Metropolitan University, Middlesex University, the University of East London, the University of West London, and the University of Westminster. The latter is noted as London's largest unitary university, with a student population exceeding 34,000. Other significant independent entities are London South Bank University and the University of the Arts London, the largest European university specializing in art, design, fashion, communication, and performing arts. Furthermore, London hosts three international universities: Regent's University London, Richmond, The American International University in London, and Schiller International University.

input: On 26 February 2012, The Sun on Sunday was launched to replace the closed News of the World, employing some of its former journalists. In late 2013, it was given a new look, with a new typeface. The average circulation for The Sun on Sunday in March 2014 was 1,686,840; but in May 2015 The Mail on Sunday sold more copies for the first time, an average of 28,650 over those of its rival: 1,497,855 to 1,469,195. Roy Greenslade issued some caveats over the May 2015 figures, but believes the weekday Daily Mail will overtake The Sun in circulation during 2016.
rewrite: Launched on 26 February 2012, The Sun on Sunday succeeded the defunct News of the World, incorporating several of its former staff. The publication underwent a redesign in late 2013, adopting a new typeface. Circulation data indicates an average of 1,686,840 copies for March 2014. However, by May 2015, The Mail on Sunday achieved higher sales, surpassing its rival with an average of 1,497,855 copies compared to 1,469,195—a lead of 28,650. While analyst Roy Greenslade noted qualifications regarding these May 2015 figures, he projected that the weekday Daily Mail would exceed The Sun's circulation within 2016.

input: Incandescent light bulbs consist of an air-tight glass enclosure (the envelope, or bulb) with a filament of tungsten wire inside the bulb, through which an electric current is passed. Contact wires and a base with two (or more) conductors provide electrical connections to the filament. Incandescent light bulbs usually contain a stem or glass mount anchored to the bulb's base that allows the electrical contacts to run through the envelope without air or gas leaks. Small wires embedded in the stem in turn support the filament and its lead wires.
rewrite: An incandescent lamp comprises a sealed glass envelope containing a tungsten filament. Electrical current is supplied to this filament via contact wires connected to a conductive base. Typically, a glass stem or mount, sealed to the base, allows these electrical connections to penetrate the envelope while maintaining its airtight integrity. This stem also incorporates supporting wires that physically hold the filament and its associated lead wires in place within the bulb.

input: Compact Disc + Graphics is a special audio compact disc that contains graphics data in addition to the audio data on the disc. The disc can be played on a regular audio CD player, but when played on a special CD+G player, it can output a graphics signal (typically, the CD+G player is hooked up to a television set or a computer monitor); these graphics are almost exclusively used to display lyrics on a television set for karaoke performers to sing along with. The CD+G format takes advantage of the channels R through W. These six bits store the graphics information.
rewrite: Compact Disc + Graphics (CD+G) is an audio compact disc variant that incorporates supplementary graphics data alongside standard audio content. While compatible with conventional audio CD players, specialized CD+G players can decode and transmit a graphics signal, typically to a television or computer monitor. This functionality is predominantly utilized to display song lyrics for karaoke performances. The format employs the six subcode channels R through W, which are reserved for encoding the graphical information.

input: The term "Sumerian" is the common name given to the ancient non-Semitic inhabitants of Mesopotamia, Sumer, by the Semitic Akkadians. The Sumerians referred to themselves as ùĝ saĝ gíg-ga (cuneiform: 𒌦 𒊕 𒈪 𒂵), phonetically /uŋ saŋ giga/, literally meaning "the black-headed people", and to their land as ki-en-gi(-r) ('place' + 'lords' + 'noble'), meaning "place of the noble lords". The Akkadian word Shumer may represent the geographical name in dialect, but the phonological development leading to the Akkadian term šumerû is uncertain. Hebrew Shinar, Egyptian Sngr, and Hittite Šanhar(a), all referring to southern Mesopotamia, could be western variants of Shumer.
rewrite: The designation "Sumerian" is the conventional term applied by the Semitic Akkadians to the ancient non-Semitic inhabitants of Sumer in Mesopotamia. The Sumerians identified themselves as "ùĝ saĝ gíg-ga," phonetically /uŋ saŋ giga/, which translates literally to "the black-headed people," and called their homeland "ki-en-gi(-r)," or "place of the noble lords." While the Akkadian "Shumer" likely reflects a dialectal geographical name, the phonological evolution to the term "šumerû" remains unclear. Related terms such as Hebrew "Shinar," Egyptian "Sngr," and Hittite "Šanhar(a)," all denoting southern Mesopotamia, may constitute western variations of "Shumer."

input: During the Franco-Prussian War and the Siege of Strasbourg, the city was heavily bombarded by the Prussian army. The bombardment of the city was meant to break the morale of the people of Strasbourg. On 24 and 26 August 1870, the Museum of Fine Arts was destroyed by fire, as was the Municipal Library housed in the Gothic former Dominican church, with its unique collection of medieval manuscripts (most famously the Hortus deliciarum), rare Renaissance books, archeological finds and historical artifacts. The gothic cathedral was damaged as well as the medieval church of Temple Neuf, the theatre, the city hall, the court of justice and many houses. At the end of the siege 10,000 inhabitants were left without shelter; over 600 died, including 261 civilians, and 3200 were injured, including 1,100 civilians.
rewrite: The Prussian bombardment of Strasbourg during the Franco-Prussian War and its subsequent siege was a deliberate strategy to undermine civilian morale. This assault resulted in extensive cultural and infrastructural devastation. On August 24 and 26, 1870, the Museum of Fine Arts and the Municipal Library were destroyed by fire. The library, housed in a former Dominican church, lost its unique collection of medieval manuscripts, including the renowned *Hortus deliciarum*, alongside rare Renaissance books and archaeological artifacts. Significant damage was also inflicted upon the Gothic cathedral, the Temple Neuf, the theatre, the city hall, the court of justice, and numerous dwellings. The siege concluded with approximately 10,000 residents rendered homeless, over 600 fatalities (261 civilians), and 3,200 injuries (1,100 civilians).

input: In Northern Germany, Netherlands, northern Poland, Denmark, and the Baltic countries local building stone was unavailable but there was a strong tradition of building in brick. The resultant style, Brick Gothic, is called "Backsteingotik" in Germany and Scandinavia and is associated with the Hanseatic League. In Italy, stone was used for fortifications, but brick was preferred for other buildings. Because of the extensive and varied deposits of marble, many buildings were faced in marble, or were left with undecorated façade so that this might be achieved at a later date.
rewrite: In regions such as Northern Germany, the Netherlands, northern Poland, Denmark, and the Baltic states, a scarcity of local building stone coincided with a robust brick construction tradition. This gave rise to Brick Gothic, termed "Backsteingotik" in Germany and Scandinavia and often linked to the Hanseatic League. Conversely, in Italy, brick was commonly employed for most structures, while stone was reserved for fortifications. Due to abundant and diverse marble deposits, many Italian buildings were either clad in marble or constructed with plain façades to allow for future marble application.

input: Neptune's orbit has a profound impact on the region directly beyond it, known as the Kuiper belt. The Kuiper belt is a ring of small icy worlds, similar to the asteroid belt but far larger, extending from Neptune's orbit at 30 AU out to about 55 AU from the Sun. Much in the same way that Jupiter's gravity dominates the asteroid belt, shaping its structure, so Neptune's gravity dominates the Kuiper belt. Over the age of the Solar System, certain regions of the Kuiper belt became destabilised by Neptune's gravity, creating gaps in the Kuiper belt's structure. The region between 40 and 42 AU is an example.
rewrite: Neptune exerts a profound gravitational influence on the adjacent Kuiper belt, a vast circumstellar disk of icy planetesimals extending from approximately 30 to 55 astronomical units from the Sun. Analogous to Jupiter's dominance over the asteroid belt, Neptune's gravity has sculpted the dynamical architecture of this region. Over Solar System history, resonant gravitational interactions with Neptune have destabilized specific orbital zones, clearing pronounced gaps within the belt's population. The conspicuously sparse region between 40 and 42 AU serves as a direct observational example of this destabilizing process.

input: The formal study of adolescent psychology began with the publication of G. Stanley Hall's "Adolescence in 1904." Hall, who was the first president of the American Psychological Association, viewed adolescence primarily as a time of internal turmoil and upheaval (sturm und drang). This understanding of youth was based on two then new ways of understanding human behavior: Darwin's evolutionary theory and Freud's psychodynamic theory. He believed that adolescence was a representation of our human ancestors' phylogenetic shift from being primitive to being civilized. Hall's assertions stood relatively uncontested until the 1950s when psychologists such as Erik Erikson and Anna Freud started to formulate their theories about adolescence. Freud believed that the psychological disturbances associated with youth were biologically based and culturally universal while Erikson focused on the dichotomy between identity formation and role fulfillment. Even with their different theories, these three psychologists agreed that adolescence was inherently a time of disturbance and psychological confusion. The less turbulent aspects of adolescence, such as peer relations and cultural influence, were left largely ignored until the 1980s. From the '50s until the '80s, the focus of the field was mainly on describing patterns of behavior as opposed to explaining them.
rewrite: The formal academic investigation of adolescent psychology originated with G. Stanley Hall’s seminal 1904 publication, *Adolescence*. Hall, inaugural president of the American Psychological Association, characterized this developmental period primarily as one of inherent turmoil and upheaval, a concept he described using the term *sturm und drang*. His theoretical framework was informed by two then-novel paradigms for understanding human behavior: Darwinian evolutionary theory and Freudian psychodynamic theory. Hall posited that adolescence recapitulated the phylogenetic transition of human ancestors from a primitive to a civilized state. This perspective remained predominant until the mid-twentieth century, when scholars including Erik Erikson and Anna Freud advanced alternative theories. While Anna Freud emphasized the biological and culturally universal foundations of adolescent psychological disturbances, Erikson centered his analysis on the conflict between identity formation and role confusion. Despite theoretical divergences, these foundational figures collectively reinforced the notion of adolescence as a period of inherent disturbance. Consequently, less turbulent dimensions, such as peer relations and sociocultural influences, remained largely unexamined until the 1980s. From the 1950s through the 1970s, the field focused predominantly on describing behavioral patterns rather than elucidating their underlying mechanisms.

input: Hunting big game typically requires a "tag" for each animal harvested. Tags must be purchased in addition to the hunting license, and the number of tags issued to an individual is typically limited. In cases where there are more prospective hunters than the quota for that species, tags are usually assigned by lottery. Tags may be further restricted to a specific area, or wildlife management unit. Hunting migratory waterfowl requires a duck stamp from the Fish and Wildlife Service in addition to the appropriate state hunting license.
rewrite: The harvest of big game animals generally necessitates the acquisition of a specific "tag" for each individual. Tags, which are purchased in addition to a standard hunting license, are typically issued in limited numbers per hunter. When applicant numbers exceed the established species quota, tags are commonly allocated via a lottery system. These tags may also be restricted to a designated wildlife management unit. For migratory waterfowl, a federal duck stamp from the Fish and Wildlife Service is required alongside the relevant state license.

input: West founded the record label and production company GOOD Music in 2004, in conjunction with Sony BMG, shortly after releasing his debut album, The College Dropout. John Legend, Common, and West were the label's inaugural artists. The label houses artists including West, Big Sean, Pusha T, Teyana Taylor, Yasiin Bey / Mos Def, D'banj and John Legend, and producers including Hudson Mohawke, Q-Tip, Travis Scott, No I.D., Jeff Bhasker, and S1. GOOD Music has released ten albums certified gold or higher by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA). In November 2015, West appointed Pusha T the new president of GOOD Music.
rewrite: Established in 2004 by Kanye West shortly following the release of his debut album *The College Dropout*, the record label and production company GOOD Music was founded in partnership with Sony BMG. Its initial roster featured West, John Legend, and Common. The label’s subsequent artists have included Big Sean, Pusha T, Teyana Taylor, Yasiin Bey (Mos Def), and D'banj, alongside producers such as Hudson Mohawke, Q-Tip, Travis Scott, No I.D., Jeff Bhasker, and S1. GOOD Music has issued ten albums certified gold or higher by the RIAA. In November 2015, West appointed Pusha T as its president.

input: Many early immigrant groups traveled to America to worship freely, particularly after the English Civil War and religious conflict in France and Germany. They included nonconformists like the Puritans, who were Protestant Christians fleeing religious persecution from the Anglican King of England. Despite a common background, the groups' views on religious toleration were mixed. While some such as Roger Williams of Rhode Island and William Penn of Pennsylvania ensured the protection of religious minorities within their colonies, others like the Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony had established churches. The Dutch colony of New Netherland established the Dutch Reformed Church and outlawed all other worship, though enforcement was sparse. Religious conformity was desired partly for financial reasons: the established Church was responsible for poverty relief, putting dissenting churches at a significant disadvantage.
rewrite: Numerous early immigrant groups journeyed to America seeking religious liberty, especially following the English Civil War and contemporaneous conflicts in France and Germany. Among them were nonconformists such as the Puritans, Protestant dissenters escaping persecution under the Anglican monarchy. Despite shared origins, these communities exhibited divergent approaches to religious toleration. Certain leaders, notably Roger Williams in Rhode Island and William Penn in Pennsylvania, instituted legal protections for minority faiths within their settlements. Conversely, colonies like Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay maintained established churches. Similarly, the Dutch colony of New Netherland officially sanctioned only the Dutch Reformed Church, prohibiting alternative worship, albeit with inconsistent enforcement. This drive for religious conformity was partly economically motivated, as the established church typically administered poor relief, thereby marginalizing dissenting congregations.

input: Persistent heavy rain and landslides in Wenchuan County and the nearby area badly affected rescue efforts. At the start of rescue operations on May 12, 20 helicopters were deployed for the delivery of food, water, and emergency aid, and also the evacuation of the injured and reconnaissance of quake-stricken areas. By 17:37 CST on May 13, a total of over 15,600 troops and militia reservists from the Chengdu Military Region had joined the rescue force in the heavily affected areas. A commander reported from Yingxiu Town, Wenchuan, that around 3,000 survivors were found, while the status of the other inhabitants (around 9,000) remained unclear. The 1,300 rescuers reached the epicenter, and 300 pioneer troops reached the seat of Wenchuan at about 23:30 CST. By 12:17 CST, May 14, 2008, communication in the seat of Wenchuan was partly revived. On the afternoon of May 14, 15 Special Operations Troops, along with relief supplies and communications gear, parachuted into inaccessible Mao County, northeast of Wenchuan.
rewrite: Rescue operations in Wenchuan County and surrounding regions were severely impeded by persistent heavy rainfall and consequential landslides. Commencing on May 12, initial efforts involved the deployment of 20 helicopters to deliver essential supplies, including food, water, and emergency aid, while also facilitating the evacuation of casualties and conducting aerial reconnaissance of earthquake-affected zones. By 17:37 China Standard Time on May 13, the rescue force, comprising over 15,600 personnel from the Chengdu Military Region, including troops and militia reservists, had been mobilized into the most severely impacted areas. A field commander in Yingxiu Town, Wenchuan, reported the location of approximately 3,000 survivors, with the condition of the remaining estimated 9,000 residents yet to be ascertained. Approximately 1,300 rescue workers arrived at the epicenter, with an advance contingent of 300 reaching the seat of Wenchuan County around 23:30 CST. Partial restoration of communications at the county seat was achieved by 12:17 CST on May 14, 2008. Subsequently, on the afternoon of May 14, 15 Special Operations Troops parachuted into the otherwise inaccessible Mao County, northeast of Wenchuan, carrying vital relief materials and communications equipment.

input: Following the defeat of the German empire in World War I and the abdication of the German Emperor, some revolutionary insurgents declared Alsace-Lorraine as an independent Republic, without preliminary referendum or vote. On 11 November 1918 (Armistice Day), communist insurgents proclaimed a "soviet government" in Strasbourg, following the example of Kurt Eisner in Munich as well as other German towns. French troops commanded by French general Henri Gouraud entered triumphantly in the city on 22 November. A major street of the city now bears the name of that date (Rue du 22 Novembre) which celebrates the entry of the French in the city. Viewing the massive cheering crowd gathered under the balcony of Strasbourg's town hall, French President Raymond Poincaré stated that "the plebiscite is done".
rewrite: In the aftermath of the German Empire’s defeat in World War I and the Kaiser’s abdication, revolutionary factions in Alsace-Lorraine unilaterally declared an independent Republic, absent any prior referendum. Subsequently, on 11 November 1918—Armistice Day—communist insurgents in Strasbourg proclaimed a “soviet government,” emulating the contemporaneous actions of Kurt Eisner in Munich and elsewhere in Germany. French military forces under General Henri Gouraud entered the city triumphantly on 22 November, a date now commemorated by a major thoroughfare, the Rue du 22 Novembre. Observing the vast, celebratory crowd assembled before Strasbourg’s town hall, French President Raymond Poincaré declared that “the plebiscite is done.”

input: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat had a mother who was a dark-skinned Nubian Sudanese woman and a father who was a lighter-skinned Egyptian. In response to an advertisement for an acting position, as a young man he said, "I am not white but I am not exactly black either. My blackness is tending to reddish".
rewrite: President Anwar Sadat of Egypt was the son of a dark-skinned Nubian Sudanese mother and a lighter-skinned Egyptian father. In his youth, replying to a casting call, he described his complexion by stating, "I am not white but I am not exactly black either. My blackness is tending to reddish."

input: Madonna released the Material Girl clothing line, which she designed with her daughter, Lourdes. The 1980s inspired clothing line, borrowed from Madonna's punk-girl style when she rose to fame in the 1980s, was released under the Macy's label. Madonna also opened a series of fitness centers around the world named Hard Candy Fitness. In November 2011, Madonna and MG Icon announced the release of a second fashion brand called Truth or Dare by Madonna to include footwear, underclothing, and accessories. She also directed her second feature film, W.E., a biographic about the affair between King Edward VIII and Wallis Simpson; it was co-written with Alek Keshishian. Critical and commercial response to the film was negative. Madonna contributed the ballad "Masterpiece" for the film's soundtrack, which won her a Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song.
rewrite: The Material Girl clothing line, collaboratively designed by Madonna and her daughter Lourdes, was launched under the Macy's label. This collection drew inspiration from the 1980s, specifically Madonna's own punk-influenced style from that era of her rise to prominence. In a separate venture, Madonna established a global chain of fitness centers under the name Hard Candy Fitness. Subsequently, in November 2011, Madonna and MG Icon announced a second fashion brand, Truth or Dare by Madonna, encompassing footwear, lingerie, and accessories. That same year, she co-wrote and directed her second feature film, *W.E.*, a biographical drama focusing on the relationship between King Edward VIII and Wallis Simpson. Despite negative critical and commercial reception, the film's soundtrack included Madonna's ballad "Masterpiece," which earned a Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song.

input: Operation Torch also served as a valuable training ground for Eisenhower's combat command skills; during the initial phase of Generalfeldmarschall Erwin Rommel's move into the Kasserine Pass, Eisenhower created some confusion in the ranks by some interference with the execution of battle plans by his subordinates. He also was initially indecisive in his removal of Lloyd Fredendall, commanding U.S. II Corps. He became more adroit in such matters in later campaigns. In February 1943, his authority was extended as commander of AFHQ across the Mediterranean basin to include the British Eighth Army, commanded by General Sir Bernard Montgomery. The Eighth Army had advanced across the Western Desert from the east and was ready for the start of the Tunisia Campaign. Eisenhower gained his fourth star and gave up command of ETOUSA to become commander of NATOUSA.
rewrite: Operation Torch functioned as a critical formative experience for General Dwight D. Eisenhower’s development as a combat commander. Early challenges, including some disorganization introduced during the initial German advance into the Kasserine Pass and initial hesitancy in relieving Major General Lloyd Fredendall from command of U.S. II Corps, revealed areas for growth. Eisenhower subsequently demonstrated increased adeptness in high-level command decisions. In February 1943, his role expanded as Supreme Commander of the Allied Force Headquarters (AFHQ), with authority extending across the Mediterranean theater to include the British Eighth Army under General Bernard Montgomery. This army, having advanced from the east, was poised for the Tunisia Campaign. Concurrently, Eisenhower was promoted to the rank of full general, relinquishing command of the European Theater of Operations, U.S. Army (ETOUSA) to lead the North African Theater of Operations, U.S. Army (NATOUSA).

input: Both the vertical and dipole antennas are simple in construction and relatively inexpensive. The dipole antenna, which is the basis for most antenna designs, is a balanced component, with equal but opposite voltages and currents applied at its two terminals through a balanced transmission line (or to a coaxial transmission line through a so-called balun). The vertical antenna, on the other hand, is a monopole antenna. It is typically connected to the inner conductor of a coaxial transmission line (or a matching network); the shield of the transmission line is connected to ground. In this way, the ground (or any large conductive surface) plays the role of the second conductor of a dipole, thereby forming a complete circuit. Since monopole antennas rely on a conductive ground, a so-called grounding structure may be employed to provide a better ground contact to the earth or which itself acts as a ground plane to perform that function regardless of (or in absence of) an actual contact with the earth.
rewrite: Vertical and dipole antennas are characterized by structural simplicity and modest cost. The dipole antenna, a foundational design in antenna theory, operates as a balanced component. Equal but opposite voltages and currents are applied to its two terminals via a balanced transmission line, or through a balun when interfacing with a coaxial line. In contrast, the vertical antenna constitutes a monopole. It is typically connected to the inner conductor of a coaxial transmission line or a matching network, with the cable shield grounded. This configuration allows the ground plane or any extensive conductive surface to function as the second conductor of an equivalent dipole, thereby completing the circuit. As monopole antennas depend on a conductive ground, a dedicated grounding structure is often utilized. This structure either enhances electrical contact with the earth or itself serves as an effective ground plane, fulfilling the required function irrespective of direct terrestrial contact.

input: In 2012, Madonna performed at Super Bowl XLVI halftime show, visualized by Cirque Du Soleil and Jamie King and featured special guests LMFAO, Nicki Minaj, M.I.A. and Cee Lo Green. It became the then most-watched Super Bowl halftime show in history with 114 million viewers, higher than the game itself. It was also revealed that the singer had signed a three-album deal with Interscope Records, who would act as the distributor in partnership with her 360 deal with Live Nation. Her twelfth studio album, MDNA, was released in March 2012 and saw collaboration with various producers, most notably with William Orbit again and Martin Solveig. The album was well received by music critics, with Priya Elan from NME calling it "a ridiculously enjoyable romp", citing its "psychotic, soul-bearing stuff" as "some of the most visceral stuff she's ever done." MDNA debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 and many other countries worldwide. Madonna surpassed Elvis Presley's record for the most number-one album by a solo artist in the UK. The lead single "Give Me All Your Luvin'", featuring guest vocals from Minaj and M.I.A., became Madonna's record-extending 38th top-ten hit on the Billboard Hot 100.
rewrite: The halftime show for Super Bowl XLVI in 2012 featured a performance by Madonna, with creative direction by Cirque Du Soleil and Jamie King, alongside guest appearances by LMFAO, Nicki Minaj, M.I.A., and Cee Lo Green. This spectacle attracted 114 million viewers, establishing it at the time as the most-watched Super Bowl halftime show in history, surpassing viewership of the game itself. Concurrently, it was disclosed that Madonna had entered a three-album contractual agreement with Interscope Records, which would serve as the distributor in conjunction with her existing 360-degree deal with Live Nation. Her twelfth studio album, *MDNA*, was released in March 2012. The record involved collaborations with multiple producers, most prominently William Orbit and Martin Solveig. Critical reception was favorable; for instance, Priya Elan of *NME* described the album as "a ridiculously enjoyable romp," noting its "psychotic, soul-bearing stuff" constituted "some of the most visceral stuff she's ever done." *MDNA* achieved a debut at number one on the U.S. Billboard 200 chart and on numerous international charts. This success enabled Madonna to surpass Elvis Presley's record for the most number-one albums by a solo artist in the United Kingdom. The lead single, "Give Me All Your Luvin'" featuring Minaj and M.I.A., extended Madonna's record to a thirty-eighth top-ten entry on the Billboard Hot 100.

input: Genomes are more than the sum of an organism's genes and have traits that may be measured and studied without reference to the details of any particular genes and their products. Researchers compare traits such as chromosome number (karyotype), genome size, gene order, codon usage bias, and GC-content to determine what mechanisms could have produced the great variety of genomes that exist today (for recent overviews, see Brown 2002; Saccone and Pesole 2003; Benfey and Protopapas 2004; Gibson and Muse 2004; Reese 2004; Gregory 2005).
rewrite: Genomes possess emergent properties beyond their composite genes, enabling analysis through measurable traits independent of specific genetic details. Comparative studies examine characteristics including karyotype, genome size, gene order, codon usage bias, and GC-content. These investigations aim to elucidate the mechanisms responsible for the extensive diversity observed among contemporary genomes (e.g., Brown 2002; Gregory 2005).

input: As of the census of 2000, there were 197,790 people, 84,549 households, and 43,627 families residing in the city. The population density was 3,292.6 people per square mile (1,271.3/km²). There were 92,282 housing units at an average density of 1,536.2 per square mile (593.1/km²). The racial makeup of the city was 38.3% White, 57.2% African American, 0.2% Native American, 1.3% Asian, 0.1% Pacific Islander, 1.5% from other races, and 1.5% from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino of any race were 2.6% of the population.
rewrite: According to the 2000 census, the city had a population of 197,790 individuals, residing within 84,549 households and 43,627 families. The population density was 3,292.6 persons per square mile (1,271.3/km²). Housing units totaled 92,282, averaging 1,536.2 units per square mile (593.1/km²). Racially, the composition was 38.3% White, 57.2% African American, 0.2% Native American, 1.3% Asian, 0.1% Pacific Islander, 1.5% from other races, and 1.5% from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino individuals constituted 2.6% of the population.

input: The Times Magazine features columns touching on various subjects such as celebrities, fashion and beauty, food and drink, homes and gardens or simply writers' anecdotes. Notable contributors include Giles Coren, Food and Drink Writer of the Year in 2005 and Nadiya Hussain, winner of BBC's The Great British Bake Off.
rewrite: The Times Magazine includes columns addressing diverse topics ranging from celebrity culture, fashion, beauty, cuisine, and domestic life to personal essays. Its contributors feature notable figures such as Giles Coren, the 2005 Food and Drink Writer of the Year, and Nadiya Hussain, a champion of BBC's The Great British Bake Off.

input: The unlicensed clone market has flourished following Nintendo's discontinuation of the NES. Some of the more exotic of these resulting systems have gone beyond the functionality of the original hardware and have included variations such as a portable system with a color LCD (e.g. PocketFami). Others have been produced with certain specialized markets in mind, such as an NES clone that functions as a rather primitive personal computer, which includes a keyboard and basic word processing software. These unauthorized clones have been helped by the invention of the so-called NES-on-a-chip.
rewrite: Following Nintendo's termination of the original NES, a market for unlicensed clone consoles has proliferated. Certain distinctive systems within this category have expanded upon the original hardware's capabilities. Examples include portable units featuring integrated color LCD screens, such as the PocketFami, and devices tailored for niche applications, like a clone incorporating a keyboard and rudimentary word-processing software to function as a basic personal computer. The development of these unauthorized replicas has been facilitated by the advent of consolidated "NES-on-a-chip" technology.

input: Capacitors, especially ceramic capacitors, and older designs such as paper capacitors, can absorb sound waves resulting in a microphonic effect. Vibration moves the plates, causing the capacitance to vary, in turn inducing AC current. Some dielectrics also generate piezoelectricity. The resulting interference is especially problematic in audio applications, potentially causing feedback or unintended recording. In the reverse microphonic effect, the varying electric field between the capacitor plates exerts a physical force, moving them as a speaker. This can generate audible sound, but drains energy and stresses the dielectric and the electrolyte, if any.
rewrite: Certain capacitor types, notably ceramic and historical designs like paper capacitors, exhibit microphonic effects by converting acoustic vibrations into electrical signals. Mechanical displacement of the plates alters capacitance, thereby inducing an alternating current, with piezoelectric properties in some dielectrics contributing further. This interference is particularly disruptive in audio systems, risking feedback or spurious recordings. Conversely, the inverse microphonic effect transforms electrical signals into mechanical motion, as the varying field exerts force on the plates, producing audible sound. This process dissipates energy and imposes stress on the dielectric and any electrolyte present.

input: The early track record of the CIA was poor, with the agency unable to provide sufficient intelligence about the Soviet takeovers of Romania and Czechoslovakia, the Soviet blockade of Berlin, and the Soviet atomic bomb project. In particular, the agency failed to predict the Chinese entry into the Korean War with 300,000 troops. The famous double agent Kim Philby was the British liaison to American Central Intelligence. Through him the CIA coordinated hundreds of airdrops inside the iron curtain, all compromised by Philby. Arlington Hall, the nerve center of CIA cryptanalysisl was compromised by Bill Weisband, a Russian translator and Soviet spy. The CIA would reuse the tactic of dropping plant agents behind enemy lines by parachute again on China, and North Korea. This too would be fruitless.
rewrite: The Central Intelligence Agency's initial performance was markedly deficient, as it failed to furnish adequate intelligence regarding several critical Soviet actions: the consolidation of control in Romania and Czechoslovakia, the Berlin blockade, and the atomic weapons program. A particularly significant failure was its inability to foresee the intervention of approximately 300,000 Chinese troops in the Korean War. Compounding these shortcomings were severe security breaches. Kim Philby, the British liaison officer and a Soviet double agent, compromised hundreds of CIA-coordinated airdrops behind the Iron Curtain. Concurrently, Arlington Hall, the agency's cryptanalytic center, was infiltrated by Soviet spy Bill Weisband. Subsequent attempts to employ similar parachute insertions of agents into China and North Korea proved equally ineffectual.

input: The terms used to define Greekness have varied throughout history but were never limited or completely identified with membership to a Greek state. By Western standards, the term Greeks has traditionally referred to any native speakers of the Greek language, whether Mycenaean, Byzantine or modern Greek. Byzantine Greeks called themselves Romioi and considered themselves the political heirs of Rome, but at least by the 12th century a growing number of those educated, deemed themselves the heirs of ancient Greece as well, although for most of the Greek speakers, "Hellene" still meant pagan. On the eve of the Fall of Constantinople the Last Emperor urged his soldiers to remember that they were the descendants of Greeks and Romans.
rewrite: The criteria for defining Greek identity have historically been fluid and have never been exclusively contingent upon citizenship within a Greek polity. From a Western perspective, the designation "Greek" has conventionally encompassed all native speakers of the Greek language across its historical phases, including Mycenaean, Byzantine, and modern. During the Byzantine era, Greeks self-identified as *Romioi*, asserting political continuity with Rome. However, by the twelfth century, educated elites increasingly also claimed the heritage of ancient Greece, whereas for the majority of Greek speakers, "Hellene" retained its pagan connotations. Notably, on the eve of Constantinople's fall, the final emperor exhorted his troops to recall their dual descent from Greeks and Romans.

input: An exhibition game may also be used to settle a challenge, to provide professional entertainment, to promote the sport, or to raise money for charities. Several sports leagues hold all-star games to showcase their best players against each other, while other exhibitions games may pit participants from two different leagues or countries to unofficially determine who would be the best in the world. International competitions like the Olympic Games may also hold exhibition games as part of a demonstration sport.
rewrite: Exhibition games serve multiple purposes, including resolving challenges, offering professional entertainment, promoting the sport, or fundraising for charitable causes. Leagues often organize all-star exhibitions to feature their top athletes, while other matches may involve competitors from distinct leagues or nations to unofficially assess global supremacy. Furthermore, international events such as the Olympic Games may incorporate exhibition contests as demonstration sports.

input: If the data to be compressed is analog (such as a voltage that varies with time), quantization is employed to digitize it into numbers (normally integers). This is referred to as analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion. If the integers generated by quantization are 8 bits each, then the entire range of the analog signal is divided into 256 intervals and all the signal values within an interval are quantized to the same number. If 16-bit integers are generated, then the range of the analog signal is divided into 65,536 intervals.
rewrite: In the compression of analog data, such as a time-varying voltage, quantization is first applied to digitize the signal into discrete numerical values, typically integers, through analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion. For instance, employing 8-bit integers divides the full analog range into 256 discrete intervals, with all signal values within a given interval assigned the same quantized number. Utilizing 16-bit integers increases the resolution to 65,536 distinct intervals.

input: Contract law covers obligations established by agreement (express or implied) between private parties. Generally, contract law in transactions involving the sale of goods has become highly standardized nationwide as a result of the widespread adoption of the Uniform Commercial Code. However, there is still significant diversity in the interpretation of other kinds of contracts, depending upon the extent to which a given state has codified its common law of contracts or adopted portions of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.
rewrite: Contract law governs obligations arising from agreements, whether express or implied, between private parties. In transactions involving the sale of goods, it has achieved substantial nationwide uniformity through widespread adoption of the Uniform Commercial Code. By contrast, significant diversity persists in interpreting other contract types, contingent upon the degree to which individual states have codified common law principles or incorporated elements of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

input: The console was first officially announced at E3 2005, and was released at the end of 2006. It was the first console to use Blu-ray Disc as its primary storage medium. The console was the first PlayStation to integrate social gaming services, included it being the first to introduce Sony's social gaming service, PlayStation Network, and its remote connectivity with PlayStation Portable and PlayStation Vita, being able to remote control the console from the devices. In September 2009, the Slim model of the PlayStation 3 was released, being lighter and thinner than the original version, which notably featured a redesigned logo and marketing design, as well as a minor start-up change in software. A Super Slim variation was then released in late 2012, further refining and redesigning the console. As of March 2016, PlayStation 3 has sold 85 million units worldwide. Its successor, the PlayStation 4, was released later in November 2013.
rewrite: First officially unveiled at E3 in 2005, the PlayStation 3 launched in late 2006. It was distinguished as the first gaming console to utilize the Blu-ray Disc format for primary data storage. This generation also marked a significant evolution for the PlayStation brand through its integration of online social services, most notably the introduction of the PlayStation Network. Furthermore, it pioneered remote connectivity features, enabling control of the console via the PlayStation Portable and PlayStation Vita handheld devices. A redesigned Slim model, characterized by a reduced form factor, a revised logo, and updated software initialization, was introduced in September 2009. This was followed in late 2012 by a Super Slim variant featuring further refinements. Global sales reached approximately 85 million units by March 2016. The console was succeeded by the PlayStation 4, which launched in November 2013.

input: Estonia's land border with Latvia runs 267 kilometers; the Russian border runs 290 kilometers. From 1920 to 1945, Estonia's border with Russia, set by the 1920 Tartu Peace Treaty, extended beyond the Narva River in the northeast and beyond the town of Pechory (Petseri) in the southeast. This territory, amounting to some 2,300 square kilometres (888 sq mi), was incorporated into Russia by Stalin at the end of World War II. For this reason the borders between Estonia and Russia are still not defined.
rewrite: Estonia shares a 267-kilometer border with Latvia and a 290-kilometer border with Russia. The 1920 Treaty of Tartu originally established Estonia's eastern frontier, extending beyond the Narva River and the town of Pechory (Petseri). This territory, approximately 2,300 square kilometers, was annexed by the Soviet Union under Stalin following World War II. Consequently, the formal demarcation of the Estonian-Russian border remains unresolved.

input: There is confusion currently as to the name of the eldest Vinaccia luthier who first ran the shop. His name has been put forth as Gennaro Vinaccia (active c. 1710 to c. 1788) and Nic. Vinaccia. His son Antonio Vinaccia was active c. 1734 to c. 1796. An early extant example of a mandolin is one built by Antonio Vinaccia in 1759, which resides at the University of Edinburgh. Another is by Giuseppe Vinaccia, built in 1893, is also at the University of Edinburgh. The earliest extant mandolin was built in 1744 by Antonio's son, Gaetano Vinaccia. It resides in the Conservatoire Royal de Musique in Brussels, Belgium.
rewrite: Scholarly discourse reveals uncertainty regarding the identity of the eldest Vinaccia luthier who originally managed the workshop, with proposals citing either Gennaro Vinaccia (active c. 1710–1788) or Nic. Vinaccia. His son, Antonio Vinaccia (active c. 1734–1796), crafted an early extant mandolin in 1759, held by the University of Edinburgh, as is a later 1893 instrument by Giuseppe Vinaccia.
