However, the earliest surviving mandolin was constructed in 1744 by Antonio's son, Gaetano Vinaccia, and is housed in the Conservatoire Royal de Musique in Brussels.

input: Within hours of the UK and France declaring war on Germany on 3 September 1939, the RAF bombed German warships along the German coast at Wilhelmshaven. Thereafter bombing operations were against ports and shipping and propaganda leaflet drops. Operations were planned to minimize civilian casualties. From 15 May 1940 – the day after the Luftwaffe destroyed the centre of Rotterdam – the RAF also carried out operations east of the Rhine, attacking industrial and transportation targets. Operations were carried out every night thereafter.
rewrite: Following the British and French declarations of war on 3 September 1939, Royal Air Force aircraft targeted German naval vessels at Wilhelmshaven within hours. Initial operations subsequently focused on maritime targets and the dissemination of propaganda leaflets, with efforts made to limit civilian harm. Commencing 15 May 1940, in the aftermath of the Rotterdam bombing, the RAF extended its campaign to strategic targets east of the Rhine, conducting nightly raids against industrial and transportation infrastructure.

input: John's position in France was considerably strengthened by the victory at Mirebeau, but John's treatment of his new prisoners and of his ally, William de Roches, quickly undermined these gains. De Roches was a powerful Anjou noble, but John largely ignored him, causing considerable offence, whilst the king kept the rebel leaders in such bad conditions that twenty-two of them died. At this time most of the regional nobility were closely linked through kinship, and this behaviour towards their relatives was regarded as unacceptable. William de Roches and other of John's regional allies in Anjou and Brittany deserted him in favour of Philip, and Brittany rose in fresh revolt. John's financial situation was tenuous: once factors such as the comparative military costs of materiel and soldiers were taken into account, Philip enjoyed a considerable, although not overwhelming, advantage of resources over John.[nb 6]
rewrite: The victory at Mirebeau substantially consolidated King John's position in France. However, these gains were rapidly undermined by his subsequent conduct toward his captives and his ally, William de Roches. John's disregard for de Roches, a powerful Angevin magnate, caused significant offense. Furthermore, his harsh imprisonment of rebel leaders resulted in the deaths of twenty-two. Within a nobility bound by close kinship ties, such treatment of their relatives was deemed intolerable. Consequently, William de Roches and other regional allies in Anjou and Brittany defected to Philip II, and Brittany erupted in renewed revolt. Compounding these political setbacks, John's financial position was precarious. When accounting for comparative military expenditures on materiel and personnel, Philip held a considerable, though not decisive, resource advantage over John.

input: The Wagner tuba, a modified member of the horn family, appears in Richard Wagner's cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen and several other works by Strauss, Béla Bartók, and others; it has a prominent role in Anton Bruckner's Symphony No. 7 in E Major. Cornets appear in Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's ballet Swan Lake, Claude Debussy's La Mer, and several orchestral works by Hector Berlioz. Unless these instruments are played by members doubling on another instrument (for example, a trombone player changing to euphonium for a certain passage), orchestras will use freelance musicians to augment their regular rosters.
rewrite: The Wagner tuba, an adapted brass instrument within the horn lineage, features notably in Richard Wagner's *Der Ring des Nibelungen*, as well as compositions by Anton Bruckner, Richard Strauss, and Béla Bartók. Cornets are employed in works such as Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's *Swan Lake*, Claude Debussy's *La Mer*, and Hector Berlioz's orchestral pieces. When these specialized parts are not covered by regular orchestra members doubling on secondary instruments, ensembles typically engage supplementary freelance musicians to perform them.

input: In the British West Indian islands (and also in the United States), the majority of enslaved blacks brought across the Atlantic came from West Africa (roughly between modern Senegal and Ghana). Very little of Bermuda's original black emigration came from this area. The first blacks to arrive in Bermuda in any numbers were free blacks from Spanish-speaking areas of the West Indies, and most of the remainder were recently enslaved Africans captured from the Spanish and Portuguese. As Spain and Portugal sourced most of their slaves from South-West Africa (the Portuguese through ports in modern-day Angola; the Spanish purchased most of their African slaves from Portuguese traders, and from Arabs whose slave trading was centred in Zanzibar). Genetic studies have consequently shown that the African ancestry of black Bermudians (other than those resulting from recent immigration from the British West Indian islands) is largely from the a band across southern Africa, from Angola to Mozambique, which is similar to what is revealed in Latin America, but distinctly different from the blacks of the West Indies and the United States.
rewrite: Within the British West Indian colonies and the United States, the predominant source of enslaved individuals was West Africa, spanning approximately from contemporary Senegal to Ghana. Bermuda’s early Black population, however, largely originated outside this region. The initial significant arrivals were not directly from West Africa but consisted primarily of free Blacks from Spanish-speaking Caribbean territories, supplemented by Africans recently enslaved by Spanish and Portuguese forces. Since Spain and Portugal predominantly acquired enslaved peoples from South-West Africa—the Portuguese via ports in present-day Angola, and the Spanish through purchases from Portuguese and Arab traders centered in Zanzibar—this shaped Bermuda’s demographic origins. Consequently, genetic analyses indicate that the African ancestry of Black Bermudians, excluding recent migrants from other British West Indian islands, derives mainly from a broad region across southern Africa from Angola to Mozambique. This ancestral profile aligns more closely with patterns found in Latin America and is distinctly different from those observed among Black populations in the West Indies and the United States.

input: On October 25, 1989, the Supreme Soviet voted to eliminate special seats for the Communist Party and other official organizations in national and local elections, responding to sharp popular criticism that such reserved slots were undemocratic. After vigorous debate, the 542-member Supreme Soviet passed the measure 254-85 (with 36 abstentions). The decision required a constitutional amendment, ratified by the full congress, which met December 12–25. It also passed measures that would allow direct elections for presidents of each of the 15 constituent republics. Gorbachev strongly opposed such a move during debate but was defeated.
rewrite: On October 25, 1989, the Supreme Soviet voted to abolish constitutionally guaranteed legislative seats for the Communist Party and allied organizations in national and local elections. This action responded to significant public censure that such reserved positions were fundamentally undemocratic. Following vigorous debate, the 542-member body passed the measure 254 to 85, with 36 abstentions. Ratification as a constitutional amendment occurred at the full congress from December 12–25. Concurrently, measures enabling direct popular election for the presidents of all fifteen constituent republics were approved, a move opposed unsuccessfully by General Secretary Gorbachev during deliberations.

input: Social predation offers the possibility of predators to kill creatures larger than those that members of the species could overpower singly. Lions, hyenas, wolves, dholes, African wild dogs, and piranhas can kill large herbivores that single animals of the same species usually don't dispatch. Social predation allows some animals to organize hunts of creatures that would easily escape a single predator; thus chimpanzees can prey upon colobus monkeys, and Harris's hawks can cut off all possible escapes for a doomed rabbit. Extreme specialization of roles is evident in some hunting that requires co-operation between predators of very different species: humans with the aid of falcons or dogs, or fishing with cormorants. Social predation is often very complex behavior, and not all social creatures (for example, domestic cats) perform it. Even without complex intelligence but instinct alone, some ant species can destroy much larger creatures.
rewrite: Social predation enables predators to collectively subdue prey that exceeds the capacity of any individual member of the species. This cooperative strategy is exemplified by species such as lions, hyenas, wolves, dholes, African wild dogs, and piranhas, which successfully hunt large herbivores typically unassailable by a solitary predator. Furthermore, it facilitates the capture of agile prey through coordinated tactics; chimpanzees, for instance, prey upon colobus monkeys, while Harris's hawks collaboratively eliminate escape routes for rabbits. In some instances, this behavior involves interspecial cooperation and role specialization, as seen in humans hunting with falcons or dogs, or employing cormorants for fishing. Notably, social predation constitutes complex behavior not universal among social animals, such as domestic cats. Even in the absence of advanced cognition, instinctual cooperation allows certain ant species to overcome significantly larger organisms.

input: The task of organizing the U.S. Army commenced in 1775. In the first one hundred years of its existence, the United States Army was maintained as a small peacetime force to man permanent forts and perform other non-wartime duties such as engineering and construction works. During times of war, the U.S. Army was augmented by the much larger United States Volunteers which were raised independently by various state governments. States also maintained full-time militias which could also be called into the service of the army.
rewrite: The organization of the United States Army began in 1775. For its first century, the regular Army remained a modest peacetime institution, garrisoning forts and conducting non-wartime duties like engineering. During major conflicts, it was supplemented by the substantially larger United States Volunteers, raised independently by state governments. Additionally, states maintained full-time militias that were also eligible for federal service.

input: From January 18–20, 2010 a national conference on Tibet and areas inhabited by Tibetans in Sichuan, Yunnan, Gansu and Qinghai was held in China and a substantial plan to improve development of the areas was announced. The conference was attended by General secretary Hu Jintao, Wu Bangguo, Wen Jiabao, Jia Qinglin, Li Changchun, Xi Jinping, Li Keqiang, He Guoqiang and Zhou Yongkang, all members of CPC Politburo Standing Committee signaling the commitment of senior Chinese leaders to development of Tibet and ethnic Tibetan areas. The plan calls for improvement of rural Tibetan income to national standards by 2020 and free education for all rural Tibetan children. China has invested 310 billion yuan (about 45.6 billion U.S. dollars) in Tibet since 2001. "Tibet's GDP was expected to reach 43.7 billion yuan in 2009, up 170 percent from that in 2000 and posting an annual growth of 12.3 percent over the past nine years."
rewrite: A national conference concerning the development of Tibet and Tibetan-inhabited areas within Sichuan, Yunnan, Gansu, and Qinghai provinces was convened in China from January 18 to 20, 2010. During this conference, a comprehensive plan for the advancement of these regions was formally promulgated. The proceedings were attended by the full membership of the Political Bureau Standing Committee of the Communist Party of China, namely Hu Jintao, Wu Bangguo, Wen Jiabao, Jia Qinglin, Li Changchun, Xi Jinping, Li Keqiang, He Guoqiang, and Zhou Yongkang, thereby underscoring the high-level commitment to this initiative. The outlined plan establishes objectives to elevate rural Tibetan household income to the national average by 2020 and to provide free education for all rural Tibetan children. Since 2001, state investment in Tibet has totaled 310 billion yuan (approximately 45.6 billion U.S. dollars). It was reported that Tibet's Gross Domestic Product was projected to reach 43.7 billion yuan in 2009, representing a 170 percent increase from the year 2000 and an average annual growth rate of 12.3 percent over the nine-year period.

input: The Saint Helena Constitution took effect in 1989 and provided that the island would be governed by a Governor and Commander-in-Chief, and an elected Executive and Legislative Council. In 2002, the British Overseas Territories Act 2002 granted full British citizenship to the islanders, and renamed the Dependent Territories (including Saint Helena) the British Overseas Territories. In 2009, Saint Helena and its two territories received equal status under a new constitution, and the British Overseas Territory was renamed Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha.
rewrite: The Constitution of Saint Helena, enacted in 1989, established a governance structure comprising a Governor and Commander-in-Chief alongside an elected Executive and Legislative Council. The British Overseas Territories Act 2002 conferred full British citizenship upon the island's inhabitants and redesignated the Dependent Territories, including Saint Helena, as British Overseas Territories. A 2009 constitutional revision granted equal status to Saint Helena, Ascension, and Tristan da Cunha, renaming the territory accordingly.

input: About 98% of Antarctica is covered by the Antarctic ice sheet, a sheet of ice averaging at least 1.6 km (1.0 mi) thick. The continent has about 90% of the world's ice (and thereby about 70% of the world's fresh water). If all of this ice were melted, sea levels would rise about 60 m (200 ft). In most of the interior of the continent, precipitation is very low, down to 20 mm (0.8 in) per year; in a few "blue ice" areas precipitation is lower than mass loss by sublimation and so the local mass balance is negative. In the dry valleys, the same effect occurs over a rock base, leading to a desiccated landscape.
rewrite: The Antarctic continent is predominantly covered by the Antarctic ice sheet, which averages over 1.6 kilometers in thickness. This sheet contains approximately 90% of the planet's glacial ice, equating to roughly 70% of its freshwater reserves. Its complete melting would result in an estimated 60-meter rise in global sea levels. Precipitation across the continental interior is exceedingly low, often less than 20 millimeters annually. In certain "blue ice" regions, sublimative mass loss exceeds precipitation, creating a negative local mass balance. A similar process occurs over bedrock in the dry valleys, producing an arid, desiccated landscape.

input: A database management system (DBMS) is a computer software application that interacts with the user, other applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze data. A general-purpose DBMS is designed to allow the definition, creation, querying, update, and administration of databases. Well-known DBMSs include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, Sybase, SAP HANA, and IBM DB2. A database is not generally portable across different DBMSs, but different DBMS can interoperate by using standards such as SQL and ODBC or JDBC to allow a single application to work with more than one DBMS. Database management systems are often classified according to the database model that they support; the most popular database systems since the 1980s have all supported the relational model as represented by the SQL language.[disputed – discuss] Sometimes a DBMS is loosely referred to as a 'database'.
rewrite: A database management system (DBMS) is a software application designed to facilitate interaction between users, external applications, and a database for the purpose of data capture and analysis. As a general-purpose tool, it enables the definition, creation, querying, updating, and administration of databases. Prominent examples include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle, and IBM DB2. While databases are typically not portable across different DBMS platforms, interoperability is achieved through standardized interfaces like SQL, ODBC, and JDBC, allowing applications to operate with multiple systems. DBMSs are frequently categorized by their underlying data model, with the relational model—exemplified by SQL—being the dominant paradigm since the 1980s. Informally, the term "database" is sometimes used synonymously with DBMS.

input: In 1961, writer-editor Stan Lee revolutionized superhero comics by introducing superheroes designed to appeal to more all-ages readers than the predominantly child audiences of the medium. Modern Marvel's first superhero team, the titular stars of The Fantastic Four #1 (Nov. 1961), broke convention with other comic book archetypes of the time by squabbling, holding grudges both deep and petty, and eschewing anonymity or secret identities in favor of celebrity status. Subsequently, Marvel comics developed a reputation for focusing on characterization and adult issues to a greater extent than most superhero comics before them, a quality which the new generation of older readers appreciated. This applied to The Amazing Spider-Man title in particular, which turned out to be Marvel's most successful book. Its young hero suffered from self-doubt and mundane problems like any other teenager, something readers could identify with.
rewrite: In 1961, writer-editor Stan Lee initiated a significant shift in superhero comics by creating characters intended to engage a broader, all-ages readership, moving beyond the medium's traditional focus on child audiences. This approach was exemplified by the debut of Marvel's first superhero team in *The Fantastic Four* #1 (November 1961). These characters deliberately subverted contemporary comic book archetypes through their interpersonal conflicts, persistent grudges, and public celebrity, rejecting the convention of secret identities. Consequently, Marvel comics cultivated a reputation for emphasizing nuanced characterization and addressing more mature themes than was typical in earlier superhero narratives, a quality valued by an emerging generation of older readers. This was particularly evident in *The Amazing Spider-Man*, which became Marvel's most successful title. Its adolescent hero grappled with self-doubt and relatable mundane problems, fostering a strong sense of identification among the audience.

input: There are several other important art museums in Montevideo. The National Museum of Visual Arts in Parque Rodó has Uruguay's largest collection of paintings. The Juan Manuel Blanes Museum was founded in 1930, the 100th anniversary of the first Constitution of Uruguay, significant with regard to the fact that Juan Manuel Blanes painted Uruguayan patriotic themes. In back of the museum is a beautiful Japanese Garden with a pond where there are over a hundred carp. The Museo de Historia del Arte, located in the Palacio Municipal, features replicas of ancient monuments and exhibits a varied collection of artifacts from Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia, Greece, Rome and Native American cultures including local finds of the pre-Columbian period. The Museo Municipal Precolombino y Colonial, in the Ciudad Vieja, has preserved collections of the archaeological finds from excavations carried out by Uruguayan archaeologist Antonio Taddei. These antiquaries are exhibits of pre-Columbian art of Latin America, painting and sculpture from the 17th and 18th century mostly from Mexico, Peru and Brazil. The Museo de Arte Contempo has small but impressive exhibits of modern Uruguayan painting and sculpture.
rewrite: Montevideo hosts several additional art museums of considerable significance. The National Museum of Visual Arts, situated within Parque Rodó, holds the most extensive collection of paintings in Uruguay. Founded in 1930 to commemorate the centenary of Uruguay's first constitution, the Juan Manuel Blanes Museum is dedicated to the artist renowned for his patriotic themes. Adjacent to this museum lies a notable Japanese Garden, featuring a pond inhabited by numerous carp. Housed in the Palacio Municipal, the Museo de Historia del Arte displays replicas of ancient monuments and a diverse array of artifacts from Egypt, Mesopotamia, Persia, Greece, Rome, and pre-Columbian Americas. In the Ciudad Vieja, the Museo Municipal Precolombino y Colonial preserves archaeological materials from excavations conducted by Uruguayan archaeologist Antonio Taddei, exhibiting pre-Columbian Latin American art alongside 17th- and 18th-century painting and sculpture primarily from Mexico, Peru, and Brazil. Finally, the Museo de Arte Contempo presents a compact yet noteworthy collection of modern Uruguayan painting and sculpture.

input: It is common to classify wood as either softwood or hardwood. The wood from conifers (e.g. pine) is called softwood, and the wood from dicotyledons (usually broad-leaved trees, e.g. oak) is called hardwood. These names are a bit misleading, as hardwoods are not necessarily hard, and softwoods are not necessarily soft. The well-known balsa (a hardwood) is actually softer than any commercial softwood. Conversely, some softwoods (e.g. yew) are harder than many hardwoods.
rewrite: Wood is conventionally categorized as either softwood or hardwood. Softwood originates from coniferous trees, such as pine, while hardwood derives from dicotyledons, typically broad-leaved species like oak. This terminology can be misleading, as the designations do not consistently reflect physical hardness. For instance, balsa, classified as a hardwood, is notably softer than commercial softwoods. Conversely, certain softwoods, including yew, exhibit greater hardness than many hardwoods.

input: Asthma as a result of (or worsened by) workplace exposures, is a commonly reported occupational disease. Many cases however are not reported or recognized as such. It is estimated that 5–25% of asthma cases in adults are work–related. A few hundred different agents have been implicated with the most common being: isocyanates, grain and wood dust, colophony, soldering flux, latex, animals, and aldehydes. The employment associated with the highest risk of problems include: those who spray paint, bakers and those who process food, nurses, chemical workers, those who work with animals, welders, hairdressers and timber workers.
rewrite: Occupational asthma, induced or exacerbated by workplace exposures, is a frequently documented occupational illness, though many cases remain unreported or unrecognized. Current estimates suggest that 5–25% of adult asthma cases are work-related. Several hundred causative agents have been identified, with the most prevalent including isocyanates, grain and wood dust, colophony, soldering flux, latex, animals, and aldehydes. High-risk occupations encompass spray painters, bakers and food processors, nurses, chemical industry workers, animal handlers, welders, hairdressers, and timber workers.

input: The Victorian era of the United Kingdom was the period of Queen Victoria's reign from June 1837 to January 1901. This was a long period of prosperity for the British people, as profits gained from the overseas British Empire, as well as from industrial improvements at home, allowed a large, educated middle class to develop. Some scholars would extend the beginning of the period—as defined by a variety of sensibilities and political games that have come to be associated with the Victorians—back five years to the passage of the Reform Act 1832.
rewrite: The Victorian era in the United Kingdom spanned the reign of Queen Victoria from June 1837 to January 1901. This epoch was characterized by significant national prosperity, fueled by wealth from the British Empire and domestic industrial advances, which facilitated the expansion of an educated middle class. Some academic perspectives propose an earlier commencement around 1832, with the passage of the Reform Act, to account for the emergence of cultural and political sensibilities subsequently defined as Victorian.

input: Except for the five species of monotremes (egg-laying mammals), all modern mammals give birth to live young. Most mammals, including the six most species-rich orders, belong to the placental group. The three largest orders in numbers, are first Rodentia: mice, rats, porcupines, beavers, capybaras, and other gnawing mammals; then Chiroptera: bats; and then Soricomorpha: shrews, moles and solenodons. The next three orders, depending on the biological classification scheme used, are the Primates including the humans; the Cetartiodactyla including the whales and the even-toed hoofed mammals; and the Carnivora, that is, cats, dogs, weasels, bears, seals, and their relatives.
rewrite: With the exception of the five monotreme species, which are oviparous, all extant mammals are viviparous. The majority of mammalian species, encompassing the six most populous orders, are placentals. The three most speciose orders are Rodentia (e.g., mice, rats, and beavers), Chiroptera (bats), and Soricomorpha (e.g., shrews and moles). Subsequently, depending on taxonomic scheme, are the orders Primates (including humans); Cetartiodactyla (whales and even-toed ungulates); and Carnivora (e.g., felines, canids, bears, and pinnipeds).

input: In the 17th century, the Somers Isles Company suppressed shipbuilding, as it needed Bermudians to farm to generate income from the land. Agricultural production met with limited success, however. The Bermuda cedar boxes used to ship tobacco to England were reportedly worth more than their contents.[citation needed] The colony of Virginia far surpassed Bermuda in both quality and quantity of tobacco produced. Bermudians began to turn to maritime trades relatively early in the 17th century, but the Somers Isles Company used all its authority to suppress turning away from agriculture. This interference led to the islanders demanding, and receiving, the revocation of the Company's charter in 1684, and the Company was dissolved.
rewrite: During the seventeenth century, the Somers Isles Company actively restricted shipbuilding in Bermuda, insisting colonists focus on agriculture to derive profit from the land. This policy achieved limited agricultural success; notably, the Bermuda cedar containers used to export tobacco were often said to exceed the value of the tobacco itself. With the Virginia colony producing superior tobacco in greater quantities, many Bermudians shifted toward maritime trades earlier in the century. The Company, however, employed its full authority to curb this diversification away from farming. Such persistent interference ultimately prompted islanders to successfully demand the revocation of the Company’s charter, leading to its dissolution in 1684.

input: In the mid-19th century, Serbian (led by self-taught writer and folklorist Vuk Stefanović Karadžić) and most Croatian writers and linguists (represented by the Illyrian movement and led by Ljudevit Gaj and Đuro Daničić), proposed the use of the most widespread dialect, Shtokavian, as the base for their common standard language. Karadžić standardised the Serbian Cyrillic alphabet, and Gaj and Daničić standardized the Croatian Latin alphabet, on the basis of vernacular speech phonemes and the principle of phonological spelling. In 1850 Serbian and Croatian writers and linguists signed the Vienna Literary Agreement, declaring their intention to create a unified standard. Thus a complex bi-variant language appeared, which the Serbs officially called "Serbo-Croatian" or "Serbian or Croatian" and the Croats "Croato-Serbian", or "Croatian or Serbian". Yet, in practice, the variants of the conceived common literary language served as different literary variants, chiefly differing in lexical inventory and stylistic devices. The common phrase describing this situation was that Serbo-Croatian or "Croatian or Serbian" was a single language. During the Austro-Hungarian occupation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the language of all three nations was called "Bosnian" until the death of administrator von Kállay in 1907, at which point the name was changed to "Serbo-Croatian".
rewrite: During the mid-nineteenth century, Serbian intellectuals, foremost among them the autodidact writer and folklorist Vuk Stefanović Karadžić, alongside the majority of Croatian writers and linguists associated with the Illyrian movement under figures such as Ljudevit Gaj and Đuro Daničić, advocated for the adoption of the most widely spoken dialect, Shtokavian, as the foundation for a shared standard language. Karadžić systematized the Serbian Cyrillic script, while Gaj and Daničić standardized the Croatian Latin alphabet, both reforms grounded in vernacular phonemes and the principle of phonological orthography. This cooperation culminated in the 1850 Vienna Literary Agreement, wherein Serb and Croat signatories formally expressed their commitment to linguistic unification. Consequently, a complex bi-variant language emerged, officially designated as "Serbo-Croatian" or "Serbian or Croatian" by Serbs, and as "Croato-Serbian" or "Croatian or Serbian" by Croats. In practice, however, these envisioned common standards functioned as distinct literary variants, primarily differentiated by lexicon and stylistic conventions. The prevailing description of this arrangement was that Serbo-Croatian constituted a single linguistic entity. Under Austro-Hungarian administration in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the language common to all three constituent peoples was termed "Bosnian" until the death of Administrator Benjamin von Kállay in 1907, after which the official designation shifted to "Serbo-Croatian."

input: One of the most important developments that the Enlightenment era brought to the discipline of science was its popularization. An increasingly literate population seeking knowledge and education in both the arts and the sciences drove the expansion of print culture and the dissemination of scientific learning. The new literate population was due to a high rise in the availability of food. This enabled many people to rise out of poverty, and instead of paying more for food, they had money for education. Popularization was generally part of an overarching Enlightenment ideal that endeavoured "to make information available to the greatest number of people." As public interest in natural philosophy grew during the 18th century, public lecture courses and the publication of popular texts opened up new roads to money and fame for amateurs and scientists who remained on the periphery of universities and academies. More formal works included explanations of scientific theories for individuals lacking the educational background to comprehend the original scientific text. Sir Isaac Newton's celebrated Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica was published in Latin and remained inaccessible to readers without education in the classics until Enlightenment writers began to translate and analyze the text in the vernacular.
rewrite: A principal contribution of the Enlightenment to the scientific discipline was the systematic popularization of knowledge. This process was propelled by an expanding literate populace, whose demand for education in both the arts and sciences stimulated the growth of print culture and the wider dissemination of scientific learning. This rise in literacy was itself facilitated by broader socioeconomic improvements, including enhanced agricultural productivity which alleviated subsistence pressures and freed resources for educational pursuits. Popularization aligned with a core Enlightenment tenet: to render information accessible to the greatest possible number of individuals. Growing public fascination with natural philosophy in the eighteenth century created new avenues for professional advancement, as public lecture series and popular publications offered both peripheral amateurs and established scientists opportunities for remuneration and renown beyond traditional academic institutions. Furthermore, more formal works increasingly incorporated explications of complex theories for audiences lacking the specialized background to engage with original texts. The inaccessibility of seminal works, such as Isaac Newton's *Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica*—published in Latin and thus restricted to classically educated readers—was progressively mitigated through vernacular translations and analyses produced by Enlightenment writers.

input: By design, it is difficult to insert a USB plug into its receptacle incorrectly. The USB specification states that the required USB icon must be embossed on the "topside" of the USB plug, which "...provides easy user recognition and facilitates alignment during the mating process." The specification also shows that the "recommended" "Manufacturer's logo" ("engraved" on the diagram but not specified in the text) is on the opposite side of the USB icon. The specification further states, "The USB Icon is also located adjacent to each receptacle. Receptacles should be oriented to allow the icon on the plug to be visible during the mating process." However, the specification does not consider the height of the device compared to the eye level height of the user, so the side of the cable that is "visible" when mated to a computer on a desk can depend on whether the user is standing or kneeling.
rewrite: The design of the Universal Serial Bus (USB) interface intentionally prevents incorrect insertion of the plug into its receptacle. According to the official specification, the mandatory USB icon must be embossed on the plug's topside to facilitate user recognition and proper alignment during connection. This specification further indicates that the recommended manufacturer’s logo, depicted as engraved in accompanying diagrams though not explicitly mandated in the text, is positioned on the opposite side. Additionally, the standard stipulates that an icon be placed adjacent to each receptacle, with receptacles oriented to ensure the plug’s icon remains visible during mating. However, the specification does not account for the relative height of the device versus the user’s eye level. Consequently, whether the cable’s marked side is visible when connected to a desktop computer can vary depending on whether the user is standing or kneeling.

input: Motorcycles are also commonly used, particularly in locations that a car may not be able to reach, to control potential public order situations involving meetings of motorcyclists and often in escort duties where motorcycle police officers can quickly clear a path for escorted vehicles. Bicycle patrols are used in some areas because they allow for more open interaction with the public. In addition, their quieter operation can facilitate approaching suspects unawares and can help in pursuing them attempting to escape on foot.
rewrite: Motorcycles are frequently employed, especially in areas inaccessible to cars, to manage public order incidents such as gatherings of riders and to perform escort functions by rapidly clearing routes. Bicycle patrols are utilized in certain jurisdictions to foster greater public engagement. Furthermore, their silent operation enables covert approaches to suspects and aids in pursuits of individuals fleeing on foot.

input: The exact causes for the development of a particular sexual orientation have yet to be established. To date, a lot of research has been conducted to determine the influence of genetics, hormonal action, development dynamics, social and cultural influences—which has led many to think that biology and environment factors play a complex role in forming it. It was once thought that homosexuality was the result of faulty psychological development, resulting from childhood experiences and troubled relationships, including childhood sexual abuse. It has been found that this was based on prejudice and misinformation.
rewrite: The precise etiology of sexual orientation remains undetermined. Extensive research into genetic, hormonal, developmental, social, and cultural factors suggests a complex interaction of biological and environmental influences in its formation. Historically, homosexuality was erroneously attributed to pathological psychological development, stemming from childhood experiences such as dysfunctional relationships or abuse. Contemporary scholarship has discredited this perspective, identifying its foundations in prejudice and misinformation.

input: Director Sima Urale is an award-winning filmmaker. Urale's short film O Tamaiti won the prestigious Best Short Film at the Venice Film Festival in 1996. Her first feature film Apron Strings opened the 2008 NZ International Film Festival. The feature film Siones Wedding, co-written by Oscar Kightley, was financially successful following premieres in Auckland and Apia. The 2011 film The Orator was the first ever fully Samoan film, shot in Samoa in the Samoan language with a Samoan cast telling a uniquely Samoan story. Written and directed by Tusi Tamasese, it received much critical acclaim and attention at film festivals throughout the world.
rewrite: Director Sima Urale is an acclaimed filmmaker whose short film *O Tamaiti* received the Best Short Film award at the Venice Film Festival in 1996. Her debut feature, *Apron Strings*, opened the 2008 New Zealand International Film Festival. She co-wrote the commercially successful feature *Siones Wedding*, which premiered in Auckland and Apia. Notably, the 2011 film *The Orator*, written and directed by Tusi Tamasese, holds distinction as the first feature filmed entirely in Samoa in the Samoan language with a Samoan cast, presenting a uniquely Samoan narrative. It garnered significant international critical acclaim at festivals worldwide.

input: Bell's patent 174,465, was issued to Bell on March 7, 1876, by the U.S. Patent Office. Bell's patent covered "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically ... by causing electrical undulations, similar in form to the vibrations of the air accompanying the said vocal or other sound" [N 16] Bell returned to Boston the same day and the next day resumed work, drawing in his notebook a diagram similar to that in Gray's patent caveat.
rewrite: U.S. Patent 174,465 was granted to Alexander Graham Bell on March 7, 1876. It detailed a method and apparatus for telegraphically transmitting sounds by generating electrical undulations analogous to accompanying atmospheric vibrations. Bell returned to Boston that day, resuming work the following day by drafting a notebook diagram resembling the illustration within Elisha Gray's earlier patent caveat.

input: The phrase "[A] hedge or wall of separation between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world" was first used by Baptist theologian Roger Williams, the founder of the colony of Rhode Island, in his 1644 book The Bloody Tenent of Persecution. The phrase was later used by Thomas Jefferson as a description of the First Amendment and its restriction on the legislative branch of the federal government, in an 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists (a religious minority concerned about the dominant position of the Congregationalist church in Connecticut):
rewrite: The metaphor of "a hedge or wall of separation between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world" originated with Baptist theologian Roger Williams, founder of Rhode Island, in his 1644 work *The Bloody Tenent of Persecution*. It was subsequently invoked by Thomas Jefferson in an 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists. Jefferson employed the phrase to articulate his interpretation of the First Amendment's restriction on federal legislative power concerning religion, addressing the Baptists' concerns regarding state ecclesiastical favoritism.

input: The City of Charleston Police Department, with a total of 452 sworn officers, 137 civilians, and 27 reserve police officers, is South Carolina's largest police department. Their procedures on cracking down on drug use and gang violence in the city are used as models to other cities to do the same.[citation needed] According to the final 2005 FBI Crime Reports, Charleston crime level is worse than the national average in almost every major category. Greg Mullen, the former Deputy Chief of the Virginia Beach, Virginia Police Department, serves as the current Chief of the Charleston Police Department. The former Charleston police chief was Reuben Greenberg, who resigned August 12, 2005. Greenberg was credited with creating a polite police force that kept police brutality well in check, even as it developed a visible presence in community policing and a significant reduction in crime rates.
rewrite: The Charleston Police Department, comprising 452 sworn officers, 137 civilian personnel, and 27 reserve officers, constitutes the largest law enforcement agency in South Carolina. Its operational protocols for addressing drug-related offenses and gang violence are frequently cited as exemplary models for other municipal departments [citation needed]. Notwithstanding this, data from the 2005 FBI Uniform Crime Reports indicate that Charleston's crime rates historically exceeded the national average across most major categories. The department is currently led by Chief Greg Mullen, formerly the Deputy Chief of the Virginia Beach Police Department in Virginia. He succeeded Reuben Greenberg, who resigned on August 12, 2005. Chief Greenberg was widely recognized for fostering a professional police culture that minimized incidents of brutality while simultaneously enhancing community policing visibility and achieving a substantial reduction in criminal activity.

input: According to some historians, Bismarck adroitly created a diplomatic crisis over the succession to the Spanish throne, then edited a dispatch about a meeting between King William of Prussia and the French ambassador, to make it appear that the French had been insulted. The French press and parliament demanded a war, which the generals of Napoleon III assured him that France would win. Napoleon and his Prime Minister, Émile Ollivier, for their parts sought war to solve their problems with political disunity in France. On 16 July 1870, the French parliament voted to declare war on the German Kingdom of Prussia and hostilities began three days later. The German coalition mobilised its troops much more quickly than the French and rapidly invaded northeastern France. The German forces were superior in numbers, had better training and leadership and made more effective use of modern technology, particularly railroads and artillery.
rewrite: Scholars assert that Chancellor Bismarck deliberately precipitated a diplomatic crisis regarding the Spanish succession. He subsequently altered the Ems Dispatch, an account of a meeting between King Wilhelm I of Prussia and the French ambassador, to present the communication as a calculated insult to France. This provocation inflamed French public and parliamentary opinion, which demanded a military response, a course of action confidently endorsed by Napoleon III’s generals. Both the Emperor and his Prime Minister, Émile Ollivier, perceived a war as a means to resolve domestic political divisions. Consequently, the French parliament declared war on Prussia on 16 July 1870, with hostilities commencing three days later. The Prussian-led German coalition achieved a significantly more rapid mobilization, swiftly invading northeastern France. Its forces proved superior in numerical strength, training, leadership, and the strategic application of contemporary technology, notably railroads and artillery.

input: Napoleon turned his focus to domestic affairs after the war. Empress Joséphine had still not given birth to a child from Napoleon, who became worried about the future of his empire following his death. Desperate for a legitimate heir, Napoleon divorced Joséphine in January 1810 and started looking for a new wife. Hoping to cement the recent alliance with Austria through a family connection, Napoleon married the Archduchess Marie Louise, who was 18 years old at the time. On 20 March 1811, Marie Louise gave birth to a baby boy, whom Napoleon made heir apparent and bestowed the title of King of Rome. His son never actually ruled the empire, but historians still refer to him as Napoleon II.
rewrite: Following the conclusion of the war, Napoleon shifted his attention to domestic concerns. The continued absence of a biological heir from Empress Joséphine prompted anxieties regarding the imperial succession. Consequently, in January 1810, Napoleon dissolved the marriage and sought a new consort. To solidify the Franco-Austrian alliance via dynastic union, he wed the eighteen-year-old Archduchess Marie Louise. On 20 March 1811, she bore a son, who was immediately designated heir apparent and granted the title King of Rome. Although this son never exercised sovereign power, historical convention acknowledges him as Napoleon II.

input: During the First Opium War, the British navy defeated Eight Banners forces at Ningbo and Dinghai. Under the terms of the Treaty of Nanking, signed in 1843, Ningbo became one of the five Chinese treaty ports opened to virtually unrestricted foreign trade. Much of Zhejiang came under the control of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom during the Taiping Rebellion, which resulted in a considerable loss of life in the province. In 1876, Wenzhou became Zhejiang's second treaty port.
rewrite: During the First Opium War, British naval forces overcame Eight Banners troops at Ningbo and Dinghai. The subsequent Treaty of Nanking (1843) designated Ningbo as one of five treaty ports for extensive foreign commerce. The Taiping Rebellion later placed much of Zhejiang under Taiping Heavenly Kingdom control, causing significant provincial mortality. Wenzhou was established as Zhejiang's second treaty port in 1876.

input: The most recognizable icon of Mexico City is the golden Angel of Independence on the wide, elegant avenue Paseo de la Reforma, modeled by the order of the Emperor Maximilian of Mexico after the Champs-Élysées in Paris. This avenue was designed over the Americas' oldest known major roadway in the 19th century to connect the National Palace (seat of government) with the Castle of Chapultepec, the imperial residence. Today, this avenue is an important financial district in which the Mexican Stock Exchange and several corporate headquarters are located. Another important avenue is the Avenida de los Insurgentes, which extends 28.8 km (17.9 mi) and is one of the longest single avenues in the world.
rewrite: The preeminent symbol of Mexico City is the golden Angel of Independence, situated upon the grand Paseo de la Reforma. Commissioned by Emperor Maximilian and inspired by Paris’s Champs-Élysées, this nineteenth-century boulevard was constructed atop the continent’s oldest known major roadway to link the National Palace, the seat of government, with the imperial Chapultepec Castle. Presently, it forms a vital financial district housing the Mexican Stock Exchange and numerous corporate headquarters. Another significant thoroughfare is Avenida de los Insurgentes, spanning 28.8 kilometers and ranking among the world’s longest continuous avenues.

input: In December 1978, Gaddafi stepped down as Secretary-General of the GPC, announcing his new focus on revolutionary rather than governmental activities; this was part of his new emphasis on separating the apparatus of the revolution from the government. Although no longer in a formal governmental post, he adopted the title of "Leader of the Revolution" and continued as commander-in-chief of the armed forces. He continued exerting considerable influence over Libya, with many critics insisting that the structure of Libya's direct democracy gave him "the freedom to manipulate outcomes".
rewrite: In December 1978, Muammar Gaddafi relinquished his position as Secretary-General of the General People's Congress, declaring a strategic shift toward revolutionary rather than administrative duties. This move underscored his policy of formally distinguishing the revolutionary apparatus from the state. Despite holding no official government office thereafter, he assumed the title "Leader of the Revolution" and remained commander-in-chief of the military. He retained substantial control over Libya, with critics arguing that the nation's system of direct democracy afforded him broad latitude to manipulate political outcomes.

input: Feathers being critical to the survival of a bird, require maintenance. Apart from physical wear and tear, feathers face the onslaught of fungi, ectoparasitic feather mites and birdlice. The physical condition of feathers are maintained by preening often with the application of secretions from the preen gland. Birds also bathe in water or dust themselves. While some birds dip into shallow water, more aerial species may make aerial dips into water and arboreal species often make use of dew or rain that collect on leaves. Birds of arid regions make use of loose soil to dust-bathe. A behaviour termed as anting in which the bird encourages ants to run through their plumage is also thought to help them reduce the ectoparasite load in feathers. Many species will spread out their wings and expose them to direct sunlight and this too is thought to help in reducing fungal and ectoparasitic activity that may lead to feather damage.
rewrite: Feathers are essential for avian survival and thus require consistent maintenance. In addition to physical deterioration, they are susceptible to fungal infections and ectoparasites such as feather mites and birdlice. To preserve feather integrity, birds engage in preening, frequently employing secretions from the uropygial gland. Bathing behaviors, including water immersion and dust bathing, are also common; aquatic and aerial species may dip into water bodies, while arboreal birds utilize dew or rainwater accumulated on foliage. In arid environments, birds often use loose soil for dust bathing. Another notable behavior is anting, wherein birds facilitate ants moving through their plumage, a practice believed to mitigate ectoparasite loads. Additionally, many species sunbathe by spreading their wings in direct sunlight, which is thought to suppress fungal and ectoparasitic activity that could otherwise damage feathers.

input: The world's first institution of technology or technical university with tertiary technical education is the Banská Akadémia in Banská Štiavnica, Slovakia, founded in 1735, Academy since December 13, 1762 established by queen Maria Theresa in order to train specialists of silver and gold mining and metallurgy in neighbourhood. Teaching started in 1764. Later the department of Mathematics, Mechanics and Hydraulics and department of Forestry were settled. University buildings are still at their place today and are used for teaching. University has launched the first book of electrotechnics in the world.
rewrite: The world's first tertiary institution dedicated to technology is the Banská Akadémia in Banská Štiavnica, Slovakia. Established by decree of Queen Maria Theresa on December 13, 1762, and opening for instruction in 1764, its original purpose was to educate specialists in silver and gold mining and metallurgy for the region. It subsequently founded departments for Mathematics, Mechanics and Hydraulics, and Forestry. Its historic buildings remain in use for education, and the academy produced the world's first published textbook on electrical engineering.

input: A study published in the Neuropsychopharmacology journal in 2013 revealed the finding that the flavour of beer alone could provoke dopamine activity in the brain of the male participants, who wanted to drink more as a result. The 49 men in the study were subject to positron emission tomography scans, while a computer-controlled device sprayed minute amounts of beer, water and a sports drink onto their tongues. Compared with the taste of the sports drink, the taste of beer significantly increased the participants desire to drink. Test results indicated that the flavour of the beer triggered a dopamine release, even though alcohol content in the spray was insufficient for the purpose of becoming intoxicated.
rewrite: A 2013 study published in *Neuropsychopharmacology* demonstrated that the taste of beer alone can induce dopamine release in the brain, thereby increasing the desire to drink. The research involved 49 male participants who underwent positron emission tomography scans while a computer-controlled apparatus administered minute quantities of beer, water, and a sports drink to their tongues. Compared to the sports drink, the taste of beer significantly heightened the participants' craving. The data indicated that this flavor-induced dopamine response occurred despite the administered spray containing an alcohol concentration too low to produce intoxication.

input: The human brain is not fully developed by the time a person reaches puberty. Between the ages of 10 and 25, the brain undergoes changes that have important implications for behavior (see Cognitive development below). The brain reaches 90% of its adult size by the time a person is six years of age. Thus, the brain does not grow in size much during adolescence. However, the creases in the brain continue to become more complex until the late teens. The biggest changes in the folds of the brain during this time occur in the parts of the cortex that process cognitive and emotional information.
rewrite: The human brain remains underdeveloped at the onset of puberty. Significant maturation occurs between ages 10 and 25, with notable behavioral implications (see Cognitive development below). While the brain attains approximately 90% of its adult volume by age six, indicating limited growth in size during adolescence, its cortical folding continues to complexify until the late teenage years. The most substantial changes in these gyral patterns take place within cortical regions dedicated to processing cognitive and emotional information.

input: On 17 March 1883, she fell down some stairs at Windsor, which left her lame until July; she never fully recovered and was plagued with rheumatism thereafter. Brown died 10 days after her accident, and to the consternation of her private secretary, Sir Henry Ponsonby, Victoria began work on a eulogistic biography of Brown. Ponsonby and Randall Davidson, Dean of Windsor, who had both seen early drafts, advised Victoria against publication, on the grounds that it would stoke the rumours of a love affair. The manuscript was destroyed. In early 1884, Victoria did publish More Leaves from a Journal of a Life in the Highlands, a sequel to her earlier book, which she dedicated to her "devoted personal attendant and faithful friend John Brown". On the day after the first anniversary of Brown's death, Victoria was informed by telegram that her youngest son, Leopold, had died in Cannes. He was "the dearest of my dear sons", she lamented. The following month, Victoria's youngest child, Beatrice, met and fell in love with Prince Henry of Battenberg at the wedding of Victoria's granddaughter Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine to Henry's brother Prince Louis of Battenberg. Beatrice and Henry planned to marry, but Victoria opposed the match at first, wishing to keep Beatrice at home to act as her companion. After a year, she was won around to the marriage by Henry and Beatrice's promise to remain living with and attending her.
rewrite: On 17 March 1883, Queen Victoria sustained a fall upon a staircase at Windsor, resulting in a lameness that persisted until July. She never regained her full physical capacity and subsequently endured chronic rheumatism. The death of John Brown, her personal attendant, occurred a mere ten days following her accident. To the dismay of her private secretary, Sir Henry Ponsonby, the Queen commenced work on a eulogistic biography of Brown. Both Ponsonby and Randall Davidson, the Dean of Windsor, having reviewed preliminary drafts, counselled strongly against its publication. They cautioned that such a work would likely fuel extant rumours concerning a romantic relationship between the monarch and her servant. Consequently, the manuscript was destroyed. In early 1884, Victoria did publish *More Leaves from a Journal of a Life in the Highlands*, a sequel to her earlier volume, which she dedicated to her "devoted personal attendant and faithful friend John Brown." The day after the first anniversary of Brown's death, a telegram informed the Queen of the passing of her youngest son, Leopold, in Cannes, whom she described as "the dearest of my dear sons." The subsequent month, at the wedding of her granddaughter, Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine, to Prince Louis of Battenberg, Victoria's youngest child, Princess Beatrice, met and developed an attachment to the groom's brother, Prince Henry of Battenberg. Although Beatrice and Henry intended to marry, Victoria initially opposed the union, desiring her daughter to remain as her companion. After approximately a year, she acquiesced, persuaded by the couple's pledge to continue residing with and attending her.

input: Madonna's Italian-Catholic background and her relationship with her parents are reflected in the album Like a Prayer. It was an evocation of the impact religion had on her career. Her video for the title track contains Catholic symbolism, such as the stigmata. During The Virgin Tour, she wore a rosary and prayed with it in the music video for "La Isla Bonita". The "Open Your Heart" video sees her boss scolding her in the Italian language. On the Who's That Girl World Tour, she dedicated the song "Papa Don't Preach" to Pope John Paul II.
rewrite: Madonna’s Italian-Catholic upbringing and parental relationships are thematically central to her album *Like a Prayer*, which serves as an exploration of religion’s influence on her artistry. This is evidenced through Catholic iconography, such as the stigmata, in the title track’s video. Further religious references include wearing a rosary during The Virgin Tour and dedicating “Papa Don’t Preach” to Pope John Paul II. Additionally, Italian linguistic elements appear, as in the “Open Your Heart” video where her employer reprimands her in Italian.

input: In the early 20th century, many anthropologists accepted and taught the belief that biologically distinct races were isomorphic with distinct linguistic, cultural, and social groups, while popularly applying that belief to the field of eugenics, in conjunction with a practice that is now called scientific racism. After the Nazi eugenics program, racial essentialism lost widespread popularity. Race anthropologists were pressured to acknowledge findings coming from studies of culture and population genetics, and to revise their conclusions about the sources of phenotypic variation. A significant number of modern anthropologists and biologists in the West came to view race as an invalid genetic or biological designation.
rewrite: During the early twentieth century, numerous anthropologists endorsed and disseminated the doctrine that biologically discrete human races corresponded directly to distinct linguistic, cultural, and social groupings. This perspective was popularly applied within eugenics, a practice now recognized as scientific racism. Following the Nazi eugenics program, racial essentialism declined in mainstream acceptance. Anthropologists specializing in race were compelled to integrate insights from cultural studies and population genetics, thereby revising their conclusions regarding the origins of phenotypic variation. Consequently, a substantial proportion of contemporary Western anthropologists and biologists now regard race as an invalid genetic or biological category.

input: However, several de facto standards for tag formats exist. As of 2010, the most widespread are ID3v1 and ID3v2, and the more recently introduced APEv2. These tags are normally embedded at the beginning or end of MP3 files, separate from the actual MP3 frame data. MP3 decoders either extract information from the tags, or just treat them as ignorable, non-MP3 junk data.
rewrite: Several de facto standards govern tag formats, with ID3v1, ID3v2, and the more recent APEv2 being the most prevalent as of 2010. These metadata containers are typically embedded at the start or end of an MP3 file, distinct from its audio frames. Decoders may parse this information or simply disregard it as non-essential data.

input: UNFPA provided aid to Peru's reproductive health program in the mid-to-late '90s. When it was discovered a Peruvian program had been engaged in carrying out coercive sterilizations, UNFPA called for reforms and protocols to protect the rights of women seeking assistance. UNFPA was not involved in the scandal, but continued work with the country after the abuses had become public to help end the abuses and reform laws and practices.
rewrite: During the mid-to-late 1990s, UNFPA supported Peru’s reproductive health initiatives. Following revelations that a Peruvian program had implemented coercive sterilizations, UNFPA advocated for procedural reforms and protective protocols to safeguard women’s rights. Although not implicated in the abuses, UNFPA maintained its engagement after they became public to assist in terminating these practices and reforming relevant laws and policies.

input: The Guardian Council comprises twelve jurists including six appointed by the Supreme Leader. The others are elected by the Iranian Parliament from among the jurists nominated by the Head of the Judiciary. The Council interprets the constitution and may veto Parliament. If a law is deemed incompatible with the constitution or Sharia (Islamic law), it is referred back to Parliament for revision. The Expediency Council has the authority to mediate disputes between Parliament and the Guardian Council, and serves as an advisory body to the Supreme Leader, making it one of the most powerful governing bodies in the country. Local city councils are elected by public vote to four-year terms in all cities and villages of Iran.
rewrite: Composed of twelve jurists, the Guardian Council includes six members appointed directly by the Supreme Leader. The remaining six are selected by the Iranian Parliament from candidates nominated by the Head of the Judiciary. This body holds the authority of constitutional interpretation and can exercise a legislative veto. When parliamentary legislation is judged inconsistent with either the constitution or Islamic law (Sharia), it is returned to Parliament for amendment. Disputes between Parliament and the Guardian Council are mediated by the Expediency Council, which also functions as a key advisory institution to the Supreme Leader, rendering it a highly influential governing entity. Separately, local city councils are publicly elected to four-year terms across all Iranian municipalities and villages.

input: iPod batteries are not designed to be removed or replaced by the user, although some users have been able to open the case themselves, usually following instructions from third-party vendors of iPod replacement batteries. Compounding the problem, Apple initially would not replace worn-out batteries. The official policy was that the customer should buy a refurbished replacement iPod, at a cost almost equivalent to a brand new one. All lithium-ion batteries lose capacity during their lifetime even when not in use (guidelines are available for prolonging life-span) and this situation led to a market for third-party battery replacement kits.
rewrite: iPod batteries are not intended for user removal or replacement. Nevertheless, some individuals have successfully opened the casing, typically guided by instructions from third-party battery vendors. This issue was exacerbated by Apple's initial refusal to replace depleted batteries, instead directing customers to purchase a refurbished iPod at a cost nearly equal to a new device. Since all lithium-ion batteries experience capacity degradation over time, even when idle, a market for unofficial replacement kits consequently emerged.

input: France's major upscale department stores are Galeries Lafayette and Le Printemps, which both have flagship stores on Boulevard Haussmann in Paris and branches around the country. The first department store in France, Le Bon Marché in Paris, was founded in 1852 and is now owned by the luxury goods conglomerate LVMH. La Samaritaine, another upscale department store also owned by LVMH, closed in 2005. Mid-range department stores chains also exist in France such as the BHV (Bazar de l'Hotel de Ville), part of the same group as Galeries Lafayette.
rewrite: France's principal upscale department stores are Galeries Lafayette and Le Printemps, each maintaining flagship locations on Paris's Boulevard Haussmann alongside national branches. The nation's inaugural department store, Le Bon Marché, established in Paris in 1852, is presently owned by the LVMH conglomerate. Another LVMH-owned upscale store, La Samaritaine, ceased operations in 2005. Mid-range chains also operate, including the BHV (Bazar de l'Hotel de Ville), which belongs to the same corporate group as Galeries Lafayette.

input: Federalism has a long tradition in German history. The Holy Roman Empire comprised many petty states numbering more than 300 around 1796. The number of territories was greatly reduced during the Napoleonic Wars (1796–1814). After the Congress of Vienna (1815), 39 states formed the German Confederation. The Confederation was dissolved after the Austro-Prussian War and replaced by a North German Federation under Prussian hegemony; this war left Prussia dominant in Germany, and German nationalism would compel the remaining independent states to ally with Prussia in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71, and then to accede to the crowning of King Wilhelm of Prussia as German Emperor. The new German Empire included 25 states (three of them, Hanseatic cities) and the imperial territory of Alsace-Lorraine. The empire was dominated by Prussia, which controlled 65% of the territory and 62% of the population. After the territorial losses of the Treaty of Versailles, the remaining states continued as republics of a new German federation. These states were gradually de facto abolished and reduced to provinces under the Nazi regime via the Gleichschaltung process, as the states administratively were largely superseded by the Nazi Gau system.
rewrite: Federalism possesses a deeply rooted historical tradition within the German context. This is exemplified by the highly fragmented structure of the Holy Roman Empire, which encompassed over three hundred distinct territories circa 1796. A significant consolidation occurred during the Napoleonic Wars (1796–1814). Subsequently, the Congress of Vienna (1815) established the German Confederation, comprising thirty-nine states. Following the Austro-Prussian War, this confederation was dissolved and succeeded by the North German Federation, which existed under Prussian hegemony. Prussian dominance, coupled with rising German nationalism, prompted the remaining independent states to align with Prussia during the Franco-Prussian War (1870–71). This alignment culminated in the proclamation of King Wilhelm I of Prussia as German Emperor, founding the German Empire. This empire consisted of twenty-five states, including three Hanseatic cities, and the imperial territory of Alsace-Lorraine. Prussia exercised overwhelming influence, controlling sixty-five percent of its territory and sixty-two percent of its population. Following the territorial reductions imposed by the Treaty of Versailles, the states persisted as republics within a new federation. However, the Nazi regime effectively abolished these states through the *Gleichschaltung* process, reducing them to mere provinces as their administrative functions were supplanted by the Nazi *Gau* system.

input: The 1981 film Fort Apache, The Bronx is another film that used the Bronx's gritty image for its storyline. The movie's title is from the nickname for the 41st Police Precinct in the South Bronx which was nicknamed "Fort Apache". Also from 1981 is the horror film Wolfen making use of the rubble of the Bronx as a home for werewolf type creatures. Knights of the South Bronx, a true story of a teacher who worked with disadvantaged children, is another film also set in the Bronx released in 2005. The Bronx was the setting for the 1983 film Fuga dal Bronx, also known as Bronx Warriors 2 and Escape 2000, an Italian B-movie best known for its appearance on the television series Mystery Science Theatre 3000. The plot revolves around a sinister construction corporation's plans to depopulate, destroy and redevelop the Bronx, and a band of rebels who are out to expose the corporation's murderous ways and save their homes. The film is memorable for its almost incessant use of the phrase, "Leave the Bronx!" Many of the movie's scenes were filmed in Queens, substituting as the Bronx. Rumble in the Bronx was a 1995 Jackie Chan kung-fu film, another which popularised the Bronx to international audiences. Last Bronx, a 1996 Sega game played on the bad reputation of the Bronx to lend its name to an alternate version of post-Japanese bubble Tokyo, where crime and gang warfare is rampant.
rewrite: Several cinematic works have employed the Bronx’s austere reputation as a narrative backdrop. The 1981 film *Fort Apache, The Bronx* derives its title from the colloquial designation for the 41st Police Precinct in the South Bronx. Released in the same year, the horror film *Wolfen* utilizes the borough’s dilapidated landscapes as the habitat for supernatural creatures. A later example, the 2005 television film *Knights of the South Bronx*, presents a biographical account of a teacher instructing disadvantaged youth. The setting also features prominently in the 1983 Italian B-movie *Fuga dal Bronx* (alternately titled *Bronx Warriors 2* and *Escape 2000*), which gained notoriety through its inclusion on *Mystery Science Theatre 3000*. Its plot concerns a malevolent corporation’s scheme to depopulate, demolish, and redevelop the borough, opposed by a resistance group aiming to expose these plans. The film is notable for the recurrent directive, “Leave the Bronx!” though much of its filming occurred in Queens, standing in for the Bronx. Internationally, the 1995 Jackie Chan action film *Rumble in the Bronx* further disseminated the borough’s image. Beyond cinema, the 1996 Sega video game *Last Bronx* appropriated the Bronx’s notoriety to name a dystopian, crime-ridden version of post-bubble Tokyo.

input: After repeated efforts by the Samoan independence movement, the New Zealand Western Samoa Act 1961 of 24 November 1961 granted Samoa independence effective 1 January 1962, upon which the Trusteeship Agreement terminated. Samoa also signed a friendship treaty with New Zealand. Samoa, the first small-island country in the Pacific to become independent, joined the Commonwealth of Nations on 28 August 1970. While independence was achieved at the beginning of January, Samoa annually celebrates 1 June as its independence day.
rewrite: Following sustained advocacy by the Samoan independence movement, formal sovereignty was conferred by the New Zealand Western Samoa Act 1961, enacted on 24 November 1961, with effect from 1 January 1962. This date terminated the Trusteeship Agreement and was followed by a bilateral friendship treaty with New Zealand. As the first Pacific small-island state to gain independence, Samoa subsequently acceded to the Commonwealth of Nations on 28 August 1970. The nation commemorates independence annually on 1 June, rather than the January effective date.

input: The Buddha's death is seen as an illusion, he is living on in other planes of existence, and monks are therefore permitted to offer "new truths" based on his input. Mahayana also differs from Theravada in its concept of śūnyatā (that ultimately nothing has existence), and in its belief in bodhisattvas (enlightened people who vow to continue being reborn until all beings can be enlightened).
rewrite: The Buddha's death is regarded as illusory, as he persists in other realms of existence, thereby permitting monks to propose "new truths" informed by his ongoing guidance. Mahayana further diverges from Theravada through its doctrine of śūnyatā—the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena—and its emphasis on bodhisattvas, enlightened beings who vow to undergo rebirth until all sentient beings attain enlightenment.

input: This meant that nearly one-third of the U.S. lending mechanism was frozen and continued to be frozen into June 2009. According to the Brookings Institution, the traditional banking system does not have the capital to close this gap as of June 2009: "It would take a number of years of strong profits to generate sufficient capital to support that additional lending volume". The authors also indicate that some forms of securitization are "likely to vanish forever, having been an artifact of excessively loose credit conditions". While traditional banks have raised their lending standards, it was the collapse of the shadow banking system that is the primary cause of the reduction in funds available for borrowing.
rewrite: Consequently, approximately one-third of the United States' lending capacity remained immobilized through June 2009. Analysis from the Brookings Institution indicates that, as of that date, the traditional banking sector lacked the requisite capital to bridge this shortfall, noting that "a number of years of strong profits" would be necessary to generate sufficient capital for supporting such additional lending volume. The authors further suggest that certain securitization practices, characterized as artifacts of excessively lax credit, may permanently disappear.
