input: Most modern air defence systems are fairly mobile. Even the larger systems tend to be mounted on trailers and are designed to be fairly quickly broken down or set up. In the past, this was not always the case. Early missile systems were cumbersome and required much infrastructure; many could not be moved at all. With the diversification of air defence there has been much more emphasis on mobility. Most modern systems are usually either self-propelled (i.e. guns or missiles are mounted on a truck or tracked chassis) or easily towed. Even systems that consist of many components (transporter/erector/launchers, radars, command posts etc.) benefit from being mounted on a fleet of vehicles. In general, a fixed system can be identified, attacked and destroyed whereas a mobile system can show up in places where it is not expected. Soviet systems especially concentrate on mobility, after the lessons learnt in the Vietnam war between the USA and Vietnam. For more information on this part of the conflict, see SA-2 Guideline.
rewrite: Contemporary air defence systems are predominantly characterized by a high degree of mobility. Even substantial systems are typically trailer-mounted, engineered for rapid deployment and breakdown. Historically, this was not the norm; early missile systems were often cumbersome, reliant on extensive fixed infrastructure, and frequently immobile. The evolution and diversification of air defence capabilities have since placed a significant premium on mobility. Modern systems are generally either self-propelled—with armaments integrated onto a truck or tracked vehicle—or readily towable. Complex systems comprising multiple components, such as transporter-erector-launchers, radars, and command posts, achieve mobility through integration onto a fleet of vehicles. A fundamental tactical principle underpins this shift: fixed installations are vulnerable to identification and destruction, whereas mobile systems can deploy unpredictably. This emphasis is particularly evident in Soviet and successor-state doctrine, which strongly prioritizes mobility, a lesson underscored by experiences in the Vietnam War. For further analysis of relevant historical developments, one may consult sources on the SA-2 Guideline system.

input: The Strumica Carnival (Macedonian: Струмички Карневал, translated Strumichki Karneval) has been held since at least 1670, when the Turkish author Evlija Chelebija wrote while staying there, "I came into a town located in the foothills of a high hillock and what I saw that night was masked people running house–to–house, with laughter, scream and song." The Carnival took an organized form in 1991; in 1994, Strumica became a member of FECC and in 1998 hosted the XVIII International Congress of Carnival Cities. The Strumica Carnival opens on a Saturday night at a masked ball where the Prince and Princess are chosen; the main Carnival night is on Tuesday, when masked participants (including groups from abroad) compete in various subjects. As of 2000, the Festival of Caricatures and Aphorisms has been held as part of Strumica's Carnival celebrations.
rewrite: The Strumica Carnival (Macedonian: Струмички Карневал, rendered Strumichki Karneval) has been documented since at least 1670, when the Ottoman writer Evlija Chelebija, during a visit, recorded witnessing masked individuals moving between houses accompanied by laughter, shouts, and song. The event assumed an organized structure in 1991. Subsequently, Strumica joined the Federation of European Carnival Cities (FECC) in 1994 and hosted its XVIII International Congress in 1998. The Carnival commences with a Saturday masked ball, featuring the selection of a Prince and Princess. The primary procession occurs on Tuesday, involving masked participants, including international groups, who compete in various thematic categories. Since the year 2000, the Carnival festivities have also incorporated the Festival of Caricatures and Aphorisms.

input: In 1955, with both the United States and the Soviet Union building ballistic missiles that could be utilized to launch objects into space, the "starting line" was drawn for the Space Race. In separate announcements, just four days apart, both nations publicly announced that they would launch artificial Earth satellites by 1957 or 1958. On July 29, 1955, James C. Hagerty, president Dwight D. Eisenhower's press secretary, announced that the United States intended to launch "small Earth circling satellites" between July 1, 1957, and December 31, 1958, as part of their contribution to the International Geophysical Year (IGY). Four days later, at the Sixth Congress of International Astronautical Federation in Copenhagen, scientist Leonid I. Sedov spoke to international reporters at the Soviet embassy, and announced his country's intention to launch a satellite as well, in the "near future". On August 30, 1955, Korolev managed to get the Soviet Academy of Sciences to create a commission whose purpose was to beat the Americans into Earth orbit: this was the de facto start date for the Space Race. The Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union began a policy of treating development of its space program as a classified state secret.
rewrite: The commencement of the Space Race was formally precipitated in 1955, as both the United States and the Soviet Union developed ballistic missile technology with the latent capacity for orbital launch. Within a span of four days, each nation issued public declarations of intent to deploy artificial Earth satellites by 1957 or 1958. On July 29, 1955, U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower’s press secretary, James C. Hagerty, announced plans to launch “small Earth circling satellites” between July 1, 1957, and December 31, 1958, as a contribution to the International Geophysical Year. Subsequently, on August 2, at the Sixth Congress of the International Astronautical Federation in Copenhagen, Soviet scientist Leonid I. Sedov addressed international reporters at the Soviet embassy, declaring a similar objective for the “near future.” The competition was institutionalized on August 30, 1955, when Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secured the establishment of a commission by the Soviet Academy of Sciences with the explicit aim of preceding the United States into orbit. This date effectively marks the operational inception of the Space Race, after which the Soviet Council of Ministers classified all subsequent space program developments as state secrets.

input: In the 16th century, Count Hieronymus Schlick of Bohemia began minting coins known as Joachimstalers (from German thal, or nowadays usually Tal, "valley", cognate with "dale" in English), named for Joachimstal, the valley where the silver was mined (St. Joachim's Valley, now Jáchymov; then part of the Kingdom of Bohemia, now part of the Czech Republic). Joachimstaler was later shortened to the German Taler, a word that eventually found its way into Danish and Swedish as daler, Norwegian as dalar and daler, Dutch as daler or daalder, Ethiopian as ታላሪ (talari), Hungarian as tallér, Italian as tallero, and English as dollar. Alternatively, thaler is said to come from the German coin Guldengroschen ("great guilder", being of silver but equal in value to a gold guilder), minted from the silver from Joachimsthal.
rewrite: In the sixteenth century, Count Hieronymus Schlick of Bohemia initiated the minting of coins termed Joachimstalers. This name derived from Joachimstal (St. Joachim’s Valley, now Jáchymov, Czech Republic), the source of the silver, with "Thal" (modern "Tal") meaning "valley." The designation was subsequently abbreviated in German to "Taler." This term disseminated widely, evolving into forms such as "daler" in Scandinavian languages, "daalder" in Dutch, "tallér" in Hungarian, "tallero" in Italian, and ultimately "dollar" in English. An alternative etymology suggests "thaler" originated from the "Guldengroschen," a silver coin equal in value to a gold guilder, which was also minted from Joachimsthal silver.

input: Communal shelters never housed more than one seventh of Greater London residents, however. Peak use of the Underground as shelter was 177,000 on 27 September 1940, and a November 1940 census of London found that about 4% of residents used the Tube and other large shelters; 9% in public surface shelters; and 27% in private home shelters, implying that the remaining 60% of the city likely stayed at home. The government distributed Anderson shelters until 1941 and that year began distributing the Morrison shelter, which could be used inside homes.:190
rewrite: Communal shelters accommodated no more than one-seventh of Greater London's residents at any time. The peak utilization of the Underground as a refuge reached 177,000 individuals on 27 September 1940. A census in November 1940 indicated that approximately 4% of residents sheltered in the Tube and similar large shelters, 9% used public surface shelters, and 27% relied on private domestic shelters. This suggests about 60% of the population likely remained in their homes. The government issued Anderson shelters until 1941, when distribution of the indoor Morrison shelter commenced.

input: Extending across the north and south side of the Alps in west-central Europe, Switzerland encompasses a great diversity of landscapes and climates on a limited area of 41,285 square kilometres (15,940 sq mi). The population is about 8 million, resulting in an average population density of around 195 people per square kilometre (500/sq mi). The more mountainous southern half of the country is far more sparsely populated than the northern half. In the largest Canton of Graubünden, lying entirely in the Alps, population density falls to 27 /km² (70 /sq mi).
rewrite: Situated astride the Alps in west-central Europe, Switzerland exhibits pronounced geographical and climatic diversity within its confined area of 41,285 km². Its population of approximately eight million yields an average density of roughly 195 inhabitants per km². Settlement patterns are highly uneven, with the more mountainous southern half being significantly less populated than the north. This disparity is exemplified in the alpine Canton of Graubünden, where density declines to approximately 27 inhabitants per km².

input: At about the same time, Charles Coffin, leading the Thomson-Houston Electric Company, acquired a number of competitors and gained access to their key patents. General Electric was formed through the 1892 merger of Edison General Electric Company of Schenectady, New York, and Thomson-Houston Electric Company of Lynn, Massachusetts, with the support of Drexel, Morgan & Co. Both plants continue to operate under the GE banner to this day. The company was incorporated in New York, with the Schenectady plant used as headquarters for many years thereafter. Around the same time, General Electric's Canadian counterpart, Canadian General Electric, was formed.
rewrite: Concurrently, Charles Coffin of the Thomson-Houston Electric Company consolidated several competitors, securing their essential patents. The General Electric Company (GE) was established in 1892 via the merger of the Edison General Electric Company of Schenectady, New York, and the Thomson-Houston Electric Company of Lynn, Massachusetts, facilitated by Drexel, Morgan & Co. Incorporated in New York, GE long maintained its headquarters at the Schenectady plant. Both original facilities continued operations under the GE banner. Approximately during this period, its Canadian affiliate, Canadian General Electric, was also formed.

input: In Alghero, the IEC has adapted its standard to the Alguerese dialect. In this standard one can find, among other features: the definite article lo instead of el, special possessive pronouns and determinants la mia ('mine'), lo sou/la sua ('his/her'), lo tou/la tua ('yours'), and so on, the use of -v- /v/ in the imperfect tense in all conjugations: cantava, creixiva, llegiva; the use of many archaic words, usual words in Alguerese: manco instead of menys ('less'), calqui u instead of algú ('someone'), qual/quala instead of quin/quina ('which'), and so on; and the adaptation of weak pronouns.
rewrite: In Alghero, the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) has modified its standard to accommodate the Alguerese dialect. This adapted standard incorporates several distinctive linguistic features. These include the definite article *lo* in place of *el*, specific possessive forms such as *la mia* and *lo sou/la sua*, and the consistent use of the intervocalic -v- (/v/) in the imperfect tense across all conjugations (e.g., *cantava*, *creixiva*). It also employs numerous archaic terms common to Alguerese, like *manco* for "less" and *calqui u* for "someone," alongside adaptations of weak pronouns.

input: Before the release of iOS 5, the iPod branding was used for the media player included with the iPhone and iPad, a combination of the Music and Videos apps on the iPod Touch. As of iOS 5, separate apps named "Music" and "Videos" are standardized across all iOS-powered products. While the iPhone and iPad have essentially the same media player capabilities as the iPod line, they are generally treated as separate products. During the middle of 2010, iPhone sales overtook those of the iPod.
rewrite: Prior to iOS 5, the integrated media player on the iPhone and iPad utilized the iPod branding, mirroring the combined functionality of the iPod Touch's Music and Videos applications. With iOS 5, distinct "Music" and "Videos" applications became standardized across all iOS devices. Although iPhones and iPads possess media capabilities equivalent to dedicated iPod models, they are positioned as distinct product categories. Notably, iPhone sales surpassed those of the iPod by mid-2010.

input: With an estimated population of 1,381,069 as of July 1, 2014, San Diego is the eighth-largest city in the United States and second-largest in California. It is part of the San Diego–Tijuana conurbation, the second-largest transborder agglomeration between the US and a bordering country after Detroit–Windsor, with a population of 4,922,723 people. San Diego is the birthplace of California and is known for its mild year-round climate, natural deep-water harbor, extensive beaches, long association with the United States Navy and recent emergence as a healthcare and biotechnology development center.
rewrite: As of July 1, 2014, San Diego had an estimated population of 1,381,069, ranking as the eighth-largest city in the United States and the second-largest in California. It forms part of the San Diego–Tijuana conurbation, the second-largest transborder metropolitan area between the U.S. and a neighboring nation after Detroit–Windsor, with a combined population of 4,922,723. Recognized as the birthplace of California, the city is distinguished by its temperate climate, natural deep-water harbor, extensive beaches, longstanding naval presence, and growing prominence as a center for healthcare and biotechnology.

input: The War of 1812, the second and last American war against the United Kingdom, was less successful for the U.S. than the Revolution and Northwest Indian War against natives had been, though it ended on a high note for Americans as well. After the taking control of Lake Erie in 1813, the Americans were able to seize parts of western Upper Canada, burn York and defeat Tecumseh, which caused his Indian Confederacy to collapse. Following ending victories in the province of Upper Canada, which dubbed the U.S. Army "Regulars, by God!", British troops were able to capture and burn Washington. The regular army, however, proved they were professional and capable of defeating the British army during the invasions of Plattsburgh and Baltimore, prompting British agreement on the previously rejected terms of a status quo ante bellum. Two weeks after a treaty was signed (but not ratified), Andrew Jackson defeated the British in the Battle of New Orleans and became a national hero. Per the treaty both sides returned to the status quo with no victor.
rewrite: The War of 1812, representing the second and final military conflict between the United States and the United Kingdom, proved less strategically successful for the U.S. than its preceding Revolutionary War and Northwest Indian War. Nevertheless, the conflict concluded with several significant American achievements. Following the pivotal American naval victory on Lake Erie in 1813, U.S. forces seized portions of western Upper Canada, razed York (present-day Toronto), and defeated Tecumseh, thereby dissolving his Indigenous confederacy. Despite subsequent British counteroffensives, including the capture and burning of Washington, D.C., the U.S. regular army demonstrated its professional competence by repelling British invasions at Plattsburgh and Baltimore. These defensive successes compelled British negotiators to accept a status quo ante bellum treaty, previously rejected. Although the Treaty of Ghent was signed in December 1814, news arrived belatedly; two weeks later, Andrew Jackson’s decisive victory at the Battle of New Orleans elevated him to national hero status. The treaty ultimately restored pre-war territorial boundaries, resulting in a conflict without a clear territorial victor.

input: The library system of the university is divided between the main library and each of the colleges and schools. The main building is the 14-story Theodore M. Hesburgh Library, completed in 1963, which is the third building to house the main collection of books. The front of the library is adorned with the Word of Life mural designed by artist Millard Sheets. This mural is popularly known as "Touchdown Jesus" because of its proximity to Notre Dame Stadium and Jesus' arms appearing to make the signal for a touchdown.
rewrite: The university's library system comprises a central facility alongside individual college and school libraries. The primary structure is the fourteen-story Theodore M. Hesburgh Library, erected in 1963 as the third building to serve as the principal repository. Its façade features the *Word of Life* mural by Millard Sheets. Colloquially termed "Touchdown Jesus," this name derives from the mural's location near Notre Dame Stadium and the depicted gesture of Christ's arms, which resembles a football touchdown signal.

input: The primary motivation for migration appears to be food; for example, some hummingbirds choose not to migrate if fed through the winter. Also, the longer days of the northern summer provide extended time for breeding birds to feed their young. This helps diurnal birds to produce larger clutches than related non-migratory species that remain in the tropics. As the days shorten in autumn, the birds return to warmer regions where the available food supply varies little with the season.
rewrite: The principal driver of migration is typically food availability. For instance, hummingbirds may forgo migration if provided with winter sustenance. Furthermore, the extended daylight of northern summers affords breeding birds more time to gather food for offspring, enabling diurnal migratory species to raise larger broods than their non-migratory tropical relatives. With diminishing autumn daylight, birds return to warmer climates where seasonal fluctuations in food resources are minimal.

input: A staple for consumers in the city is the omnipresent "mercado". Every major neighborhood in the city has its own borough-regulated market, often more than one. These are large well-established facilities offering most basic products, such as fresh produce and meat/poultry, dry goods, tortillerías, and many other services such as locksmiths, herbal medicine, hardware goods, sewing implements; and a multitude of stands offering freshly made, home-style cooking and drinks in the tradition of aguas frescas and atole.
rewrite: The municipal market, or "mercado," constitutes a fundamental urban institution. Each major city district contains at least one such borough-regulated facility. These established markets provide essential goods, including fresh produce, meat, dry staples, and tortillas. Furthermore, they offer diverse services, from locksmiths and herbal medicine to hardware and sewing supplies. A central feature is the array of food stalls serving traditional, freshly prepared meals and beverages like *aguas frescas* and *atole*.

input: The first phase of neoclassicism in France is expressed in the "Louis XVI style" of architects like Ange-Jacques Gabriel (Petit Trianon, 1762–68); the second phase, in the styles called Directoire and "Empire", might be characterized by Jean Chalgrin's severe astylar Arc de Triomphe (designed in 1806). In England the two phases might be characterized first by the structures of Robert Adam, the second by those of Sir John Soane. The interior style in France was initially a Parisian style, the "Goût grec" ("Greek style") not a court style. Only when the young king acceded to the throne in 1771 did Marie Antoinette, his fashion-loving Queen, bring the "Louis XVI" style to court.
rewrite: The initial phase of French neoclassicism is exemplified by the "Louis XVI style," as seen in the works of architects such as Ange-Jacques Gabriel (Petit Trianon, 1762–68). A subsequent phase, manifested in the Directoire and Empire styles, is typified by Jean Chalgrin's austere, astylar Arc de Triomphe (designed 1806). In England, the first phase is represented by Robert Adam, and the second by Sir John Soane. Domestically, the early French interior style was the Parisian "Goût grec," distinct from court fashion. It was only after the king's accession in 1771 that Marie Antoinette introduced the "Louis XVI" style to the royal court.

input: The strictest definition of "plant" includes only the "land plants" or embryophytes, which include seed plants (gymnosperms, including the pines, and flowering plants) and the free-sporing cryptogams including ferns, clubmosses, liverworts, hornworts and mosses. Embryophytes are multicellular eukaryotes descended from an ancestor that obtained its energy from sunlight by photosynthesis. They have life cycles with alternating haploid and diploid phases. The sexual haploid phase of embryophytes, known as the gametophyte, nurtures the developing diploid embryo sporophyte within its tissues for at least part of its life, even in the seed plants, where the gametophyte itself is nurtured by its parent sporophyte. Other groups of organisms that were previously studied by botanists include bacteria (now studied in bacteriology), fungi (mycology) – including lichen-forming fungi (lichenology), non-chlorophyte algae (phycology), and viruses (virology). However, attention is still given to these groups by botanists, and fungi (including lichens) and photosynthetic protists are usually covered in introductory botany courses.
rewrite: The most precise taxonomic delineation of the term "plant" is restricted to embryophytes, or land plants. This group encompasses seed plants—gymnosperms (e.g., pines) and angiosperms (flowering plants)—as well as the free-sporing cryptogams: ferns, clubmosses, liverworts, hornworts, and mosses. Embryophytes are multicellular, photosynthetic eukaryotes characterized by life cycles exhibiting alternating haploid and diploid generations. In their sexual haploid phase, the gametophyte, the developing diploid embryo (sporophyte) is sustained within gametophytic tissues, a relationship maintained even in seed plants, where the gametophyte is itself nourished by the parental sporophyte. Historically, botany also included the study of bacteria, fungi (including lichen-forming species), non-chlorophyte algae, and viruses, now distinct disciplines. Nevertheless, botanical inquiry often retains a focus on fungi (including lichens) and photosynthetic protists, which are routinely addressed in introductory botany curricula.

input: On September 6, 2006, Sony announced that PAL region PlayStation 3 launch would be delayed until March 2007, because of a shortage of materials used in the Blu-ray drive. At the Tokyo Game Show on September 22, 2006, Sony announced that it would include an HDMI port on the 20 GB system, but a chrome trim, flash card readers, silver logo and Wi-Fi would not be included. Also, the launch price of the Japanese 20 GB model was reduced by over 20%, and the 60 GB model was announced for an open pricing scheme in Japan. During the event, Sony showed 27 playable PS3 games running on final hardware.
rewrite: On September 6, 2006, Sony announced a delay of the PlayStation 3 launch in PAL regions until March 2007, citing a shortage of components for the Blu-ray drive. Subsequently, at the Tokyo Game Show on September 22, 2006, the company disclosed several specifications for the 20 GB model, confirming the inclusion of an HDMI port while omitting features such as a chrome trim, flash card readers, a silver logo, and integrated Wi-Fi. Furthermore, Sony reduced the Japanese launch price for the 20 GB unit by over 20% and announced an open pricing scheme for the 60 GB model in Japan. The event also featured 27 playable PS3 titles operating on final hardware.

input: Chopin's music is frequently played with rubato, "the practice in performance of disregarding strict time, 'robbing' some note-values for expressive effect". There are differing opinions as to how much, and what type, of rubato is appropriate for his works. Charles Rosen comments that "most of the written-out indications of rubato in Chopin are to be found in his mazurkas ... It is probable that Chopin used the older form of rubato so important to Mozart ... [where] the melody note in the right hand is delayed until after the note in the bass ... An allied form of this rubato is the arpeggiation of the chords thereby delaying the melody note; according to Chopin's pupil, Karol Mikuli, Chopin was firmly opposed to this practice."
rewrite: Chopin’s compositions are often performed with rubato, defined as the expressive practice of deviating from strict tempo by temporarily altering note values. Scholarly debate persists regarding the appropriate degree and manner of rubato in his works. As Charles Rosen observes, most notated rubato indications appear in Chopin’s mazurkas. Rosen suggests Chopin likely employed an earlier form of rubato, crucial also to Mozart, wherein the right-hand melody note is deliberately delayed against the bass. A related technique involves arpeggiating chords to delay the melody; however, according to Chopin’s student Karol Mikuli, the composer strongly opposed this practice.

input: Exclusive Jurisdiction is a concept whereby only one Grand Lodge will be recognised in any geographical area. If two Grand Lodges claim jurisdiction over the same area, the other Grand Lodges will have to choose between them, and they may not all decide to recognise the same one. (In 1849, for example, the Grand Lodge of New York split into two rival factions, each claiming to be the legitimate Grand Lodge. Other Grand Lodges had to choose between them until the schism was healed.) Exclusive Jurisdiction can be waived when the two over-lapping Grand Lodges are themselves in Amity and agree to share jurisdiction (for example, since the Grand Lodge of Connecticut is in Amity with the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Connecticut, the principle of Exclusive Jurisdiction does not apply, and other Grand Lodges may recognise both).
rewrite: Exclusive Jurisdiction denotes a principle within Freemasonry stipulating that only one Grand Lodge is to be recognized within a defined territorial area. Should multiple Grand Lodges assert authority over the same region, other sovereign Grand Lodges must select which claimant to recognize, potentially resulting in divergent allegiances. This is illustrated by the 1849 schism within the Grand Lodge of New York, which produced two rival bodies each claiming legitimacy and forcing external Grand Lodges to choose between them until reunification. However, this principle may be set aside when the overlapping Grand Lodges themselves share a formal bond of Amity and mutually consent to shared jurisdiction. Consequently, as with the Grand Lodge of Connecticut and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Connecticut, other Grand Lodges are permitted to recognize both bodies.

input: Timely's first publication, Marvel Comics #1 (cover dated Oct. 1939), included the first appearance of Carl Burgos' android superhero the Human Torch, and the first appearances of Bill Everett's anti-hero Namor the Sub-Mariner, among other features. The issue was a great success, with it and a second printing the following month selling, combined, nearly 900,000 copies. While its contents came from an outside packager, Funnies, Inc., Timely had its own staff in place by the following year. The company's first true editor, writer-artist Joe Simon, teamed with artist and emerging industry notable Jack Kirby to create one of the first patriotically themed superheroes, Captain America, in Captain America Comics #1 (March 1941). It, too, proved a hit, with sales of nearly one million. Goodman formed Timely Comics, Inc., beginning with comics cover-dated April 1941 or Spring 1941.
rewrite: Timely Comics' inaugural publication, *Marvel Comics* #1 (cover dated October 1939), featured the debut of Carl Burgos's android superhero, the Human Torch, and the first appearance of Bill Everett's anti-hero, Namor the Sub-Mariner. The issue achieved substantial commercial success, with its initial and subsequent printings collectively selling approximately 900,000 copies. Although the content was initially produced by the external packager Funnies, Inc., Timely established its internal editorial staff within a year. The company's first official editor, writer-artist Joe Simon, collaborated with the prominent artist Jack Kirby to introduce the early patriotic superhero Captain America in *Captain America Comics* #1 (March 1941). This title also attained significant popularity, reaching sales of nearly one million copies. Subsequently, publisher Martin Goodman formally incorporated the entity as Timely Comics, Inc., with comics bearing cover dates from April or Spring 1941.

input: In Kazakhstan Russian is not a state language, but according to article 7 of the Constitution of Kazakhstan its usage enjoys equal status to that of the Kazakh language in state and local administration. According to estimates from Demoskop Weekly, in 2004 there were 4,200,000 native speakers of Russian in the country, and 10 million active speakers. 63% of the population was fluent in Russian in 2006, and 46% used it as the main language with family, friends or at work. According to a 2001 estimate from the World Factbook, 95% of the population can speak Russian. Large Russian-speaking communities still exist in northern Kazakhstan, and ethnic Russians comprise 25.6% of Kazakhstan's population. The 2009 census reported that 10,309,500 people, or 84.8% of the population aged 15 and above, could read and write well in Russian, as well as understand the spoken language.
rewrite: In Kazakhstan, Russian is not designated as a state language. However, Article 7 of the Constitution grants it official status equal to Kazakh within state and local administrative bodies. Demographic data illustrate its widespread use: a 2004 estimate indicated 4.2 million native Russian speakers and approximately 10 million active speakers. By 2006, 63% of the population demonstrated fluency, with 46% employing it as a primary language in domestic, social, or professional contexts. A 2001 assessment suggested 95% of residents possess conversational ability. Substantial Russian-speaking communities persist in northern regions, and ethnic Russians constitute 25.6% of the populace. The 2009 census further reported that 84.8% of individuals aged fifteen and above, totaling over 10.3 million, possessed proficiency in reading, writing, and comprehending spoken Russian.

input: On 18 June 1948, the National Security Council issued Directive 10/2 calling for covert action against the USSR, and granting the authority to carry out covert operations against "hostile foreign states or groups" that could, if needed, be denied by the U.S. government. To this end, the Office of Policy Coordination was created inside the new CIA. The OPC was quite unique; Frank Wisner, the head of the OPC, answered not to the CIA Director, but to the secretaries of defense, state, and the NSC, and the OPC's actions were a secret even from the head of the CIA. Most CIA stations had two station chiefs, one working for the OSO, and one working for the OPC.
rewrite: On 18 June 1948, the National Security Council promulgated Directive 10/2, authorizing covert operations against the Soviet Union and other hostile foreign entities, with provisions for plausible governmental denial. To implement this mandate, the Office of Policy Coordination was established within the nascent Central Intelligence Agency. This office possessed a singular administrative structure: its director, Frank Wisner, reported not to the CIA Director but directly to the Secretaries of State and Defense and to the NSC itself. Its activities were so compartmentalized that they were concealed even from the CIA's leadership. Consequently, most CIA stations operated with dual chiefs—one for the Office of Special Operations and one for the OPC.

input: The invasions brought new ethnic groups to Europe, although some regions received a larger influx of new peoples than others. In Gaul for instance, the invaders settled much more extensively in the north-east than in the south-west. Slavic peoples settled in Central and Eastern Europe and the Balkan Peninsula. The settlement of peoples was accompanied by changes in languages. The Latin of the Western Roman Empire was gradually replaced by languages based on, but distinct from, Latin, collectively known as Romance languages. These changes from Latin to the new languages took many centuries. Greek remained the language of the Byzantine Empire, but the migrations of the Slavs added Slavonic languages to Eastern Europe.
rewrite: The migratory incursions introduced new ethnic populations into Europe, albeit with significant regional variations in the scale of settlement. In Gaul, for example, the extent of settlement was far greater in the northeast than in the southwest. Concurrently, Slavic peoples established themselves across Central and Eastern Europe and the Balkan Peninsula. These demographic shifts precipitated linguistic transformations. In the former Western Roman Empire, Latin gradually evolved over many centuries into the distinct Romance languages. Conversely, while Greek persisted as the language of the Byzantine Empire, the Slavic migrations introduced Slavonic languages to Eastern Europe.

input: The Muslims took control of the Island in 904, after decades of fierce fighting, and the Emirate of Sicily was established. Muslim rule on the island lasted for about 120 years and was marked by cruelty and brutality against the native population, which was reduced into near slavery[clarification needed] and Christian churches across the island were all completely destroyed.[page needed] Palermo (Balarm during Arab rule) displaced Syracuse as the capital city of Sicily. It was said to have then begun to compete with Córdoba and Cairo in terms of importance and splendor. For more than one hundred years Palermo was the capital of a flourishing emirate. The Arabs also introduced many agricultural crops which remain a mainstay of Sicilian cuisine.
rewrite: The Muslim conquest of Sicily culminated in 904 following protracted conflict, leading to the establishment of the Emirate of Sicily. This period of governance, lasting approximately 120 years, was characterized by severe subjugation of the indigenous population, who faced conditions akin to servitude, and by the comprehensive destruction of Christian ecclesiastical structures. The administrative capital was transferred from Syracuse to Palermo (known as Balarm under Arab rule). Palermo subsequently emerged as a major cultural and political center, rivaling the prominence of Córdoba and Cairo, and served as the thriving capital of the emirate for over a century. Additionally, Arab rule introduced numerous enduring agricultural innovations that continue to fundamentally influence Sicilian cuisine.

input: Ganondorf then revives, and Midna teleports Link and Zelda outside the castle so she can hold him off with the Fused Shadows. However, as Hyrule Castle collapses, it is revealed that Ganondorf was victorious as he crushes Midna's helmet. Ganondorf engages Link on horseback, and, assisted by Zelda and the Light Spirits, Link eventually knocks Ganondorf off his horse and they duel on foot before Link strikes down Ganondorf and plunges the Master Sword into his chest. With Ganondorf dead, the Light Spirits not only bring Midna back to life, but restore her to her true form. After bidding farewell to Link and Zelda, Midna returns home before destroying the Mirror of Twilight with a tear to maintain balance between Hyrule and the Twilight Realm. Near the end, as Hyrule Castle is rebuilt, Link is shown leaving Ordon Village heading to parts unknown.
rewrite: Following his resurgence, Ganondorf is confronted by Midna, who utilizes the Fused Shadows to facilitate the escape of Link and Princess Zelda from Hyrule Castle. Despite her efforts, Ganondorf prevails, crushing the Fused Shadow helmet as the castle collapses. A subsequent mounted confrontation ensues between Ganondorf and Link, who is aided by Zelda and the benevolent Light Spirits. Link successfully unseats his adversary, leading to a final sword duel. Link emerges victorious, striking down Ganondorf and sealing his defeat with the Master Sword. Upon Ganondorf's demise, the Light Spirits restore Midna to both life and her true, original form. After a solemn farewell, Midna returns to the Twilight Realm and shatters the Mirror of Twilight to permanently sever the connection between worlds, thereby preserving balance. In the aftermath, with Hyrule Castle undergoing reconstruction, Link departs Ordon Village for an undisclosed destination.

input: In 1982, the US Mint began minting pennies coated in copper but made primarily of zinc. With the new zinc pennies, there is the potential for zinc toxicosis, which can be fatal. One reported case of chronic ingestion of 425 pennies (over 1 kg of zinc) resulted in death due to gastrointestinal bacterial and fungal sepsis, whereas another patient, who ingested 12 grams of zinc, only showed lethargy and ataxia (gross lack of coordination of muscle movements). Several other cases have been reported of humans suffering zinc intoxication by the ingestion of zinc coins.
rewrite: In 1982, the United States Mint initiated production of pennies with a copper coating but a predominantly zinc composition. These zinc-based coins pose a risk of zinc toxicosis, a potentially fatal condition. Documented cases include a fatality from gastrointestinal sepsis following chronic ingestion of 425 pennies (over 1 kg of zinc), contrasted with a patient ingesting 12 grams of zinc who exhibited only lethargy and ataxia. Additional reports confirm human zinc intoxication resulting from the ingestion of zinc coins.

input: Unlike many other MP3 players, simply copying audio or video files to the drive with a typical file management application will not allow an iPod to properly access them. The user must use software that has been specifically designed to transfer media files to iPods, so that the files are playable and viewable. Usually iTunes is used to transfer media to an iPod, though several alternative third-party applications are available on a number of different platforms.
rewrite: In contrast to most MP3 players, merely copying files to the device via standard file management does not enable an iPod to recognize them. To ensure playback functionality, dedicated software is required for proper media transfer. While iTunes serves as the primary application for this purpose, various third-party alternatives are also accessible across multiple platforms.

input: Airports are divided into landside and airside areas. Landside areas include parking lots, public transportation train stations and access roads. Airside areas include all areas accessible to aircraft, including runways, taxiways and aprons. Access from landside areas to airside areas is tightly controlled at most airports. Passengers on commercial flights access airside areas through terminals, where they can purchase tickets, clear security check, or claim luggage and board aircraft through gates. The waiting areas which provide passenger access to aircraft are typically called concourses, although this term is often used interchangeably with terminal.
rewrite: Airports are segmented into landside and airside zones. The landside encompasses public zones such as parking facilities, ground transportation access, and roadways. The airside comprises all operational areas for aircraft, including runways, taxiways, and aprons. Transition between these zones is strictly regulated. Passengers on commercial flights proceed from landside terminals—where ticketing, security screening, and baggage claim occur—to airside boarding gates. The enclosed waiting areas facilitating aircraft access are formally termed concourses, a designation frequently used synonymously with terminal in common parlance.

input: The power of parliament to pass bills was often thwarted by monarchs. Charles I dissolved parliament in 1629, after it passed motions critical of and bills seeking to restrict his arbitrary exercise of power. During the eleven years of personal rule that followed, Charles performed legally dubious actions, such as raising taxes without parliament's approval. After the English Civil War, it was accepted that parliament should be summoned to meet regularly, but it was still commonplace for monarchs to refuse royal assent to bills. In 1678, Charles II withheld his assent from a bill "for preserving the Peace of the Kingdom by raising the Militia, and continuing them in Duty for Two and Forty Days," suggesting that he, not parliament, should control the militia. The last Stuart monarch, Anne, similarly withheld on 11 March 1708, on the advice of her ministers, her assent from a bill for the settling of Militia in Scotland. No monarch has since withheld royal assent on a bill passed by the British parliament.
rewrite: The authority of Parliament to enact legislation was frequently obstructed by the monarchy. King Charles I dissolved Parliament in 1629 following its passage of motions criticizing and bills aiming to curtail his arbitrary use of power. Throughout the subsequent eleven-year period of personal rule, Charles engaged in legally questionable actions, including levying taxes without parliamentary consent. Following the English Civil War, a convention emerged that Parliament ought to be convened regularly; however, monarchs commonly persisted in withholding royal assent from parliamentary bills. In 1678, Charles II denied assent to a bill "for preserving the Peace of the Kingdom by raising the Militia, and continuing them in Duty for Two and Forty Days," asserting his prerogative, rather than Parliament's, over militia control. Queen Anne, the last Stuart monarch, similarly refused assent, upon ministerial advice, to a bill for settling the militia in Scotland on 11 March 1708. Since that date, no British monarch has withheld royal assent from a bill passed by Parliament.

input: Former Soviet states, as well as countries that used to be satellite states or territories of the Warsaw Pact, have numerous minority Slavic populations, many of whom are originally from the Russian SFSR, Ukrainian SSR and Byelorussian SSR. As of now, Kazakhstan has the largest Slavic minority population with most being Russians (Ukrainians, Belarusians and Poles are present as well but in much smaller numbers).
rewrite: Nations of the former Soviet Union and the former Warsaw Pact host significant Slavic minority populations, predominantly originating from the historical Russian, Ukrainian, and Byelorussian Soviet republics. Presently, Kazakhstan possesses the largest such minority, chiefly composed of ethnic Russians, with substantially smaller numbers of Ukrainians, Belarusians, and Poles.

input: Christianity is the most widely practised religion in Galicia, as it has been since its introduction in Late Antiquity, although it lived alongside the old Gallaeci religion for a few centuries. Today about 73% of Galicians identify themselves as Christians. The largest form of Christianity practised in the present day is Catholicism, though only 20% of the population described themselves as active members. The Catholic Church in Galicia has had its primatial seat in Santiago de Compostela since the 12th century.
rewrite: Christianity, introduced in Late Antiquity, remains the predominant religion in Galicia, having coexisted with indigenous Gallaeci beliefs for several centuries. Approximately 73% of the population currently identifies as Christian, predominantly within the Catholic tradition. However, only 20% describe themselves as active practitioners. The Catholic Church's primatial seat has been established in Santiago de Compostela since the 12th century.

input: Meanwhile, Kerry's staff began their own investigations and, on October 14, issued a report that exposed illegal activities on the part of Lieutenant Colonel Oliver North, who had set up a private network involving the National Security Council and the CIA to deliver military equipment to right-wing Nicaraguan rebels (Contras). In effect, North and certain members of the President's administration were accused by Kerry's report of illegally funding and supplying armed militants without the authorization of Congress. Kerry's staff investigation, based on a year-long inquiry and interviews with fifty unnamed sources, is said to raise "serious questions about whether the United States has abided by the law in its handling of the contras over the past three years."
rewrite: Concurrently, staff under Senator Kerry initiated an independent inquiry, culminating in an October 14 report that revealed illicit operations orchestrated by Lieutenant Colonel Oliver North. The report detailed how North had established a private network utilizing entities within the National Security Council and the Central Intelligence Agency to channel military equipment to the Nicaraguan Contra rebels. It thereby accused North and certain administration officials of illegally funding and supplying these militants without congressional authorization. Founded upon a year-long investigation incorporating interviews with fifty confidential sources, the Kerry report raised profound questions regarding U.S. compliance with statutory law in its management of Contra affairs over the preceding three-year period.

input: The first settlement is defined as Paleapolis (Παλεάπολις), the Ancient Greek world for "old city", in order to distinguish it from a second settlement built during the 5th century BC, called Neapolis (Νεάπολις), "new city". The neapolis was erected towards the east and along with it, monumental walls around the whole settlement were built to prevent attacks from foreign threats. Some part of this structure can still be seen in the Cassaro district. This district was named after the walls themselves; the word Cassaro deriving from the Arab al-qsr (castle, stronghold). Along the walls there were few doors to access and exit the city, suggesting that trade even toward the inner part of the island occurred frequently. Moreover, according to some studies, it may be possible that there were some walls that divided the old city from the new one too. The colony developed around a central street (decumanus), cut perpendicularly by minor streets. This street today has become the Corso Vittorio Emanuele.
rewrite: The initial settlement is designated as Paleapolis (Παλεάπολις), a term derived from Ancient Greek meaning "old city," to differentiate it from a subsequent foundation established in the 5th century BC, known as Neapolis (Νεάπολις) or "new city." This Neapolis was constructed eastward, accompanied by the erection of substantial fortification walls encircling the entire settlement as a defensive measure against external threats. Segments of this structure remain visible within the Cassaro district, an area named for these very fortifications; the term "Cassaro" originates from the Arabic *al-qsr* (denoting a castle or stronghold). The limited number of gates integrated into the walls indicates that commercial exchange, including with the island's interior, was a regular occurrence. Furthermore, scholarly analysis suggests the possible existence of additional walls demarcating the old city from the new. The colony itself was organized around a central thoroughfare, or *decumanus*, intersected perpendicularly by smaller streets. This primary artery corresponds to the modern Corso Vittorio Emanuele.

input: During the 16th and 17th centuries slave traders began to raid the region as part of the expansion of the Saharan and Nile River slave routes. Their captives were slaved and shipped to the Mediterranean coast, Europe, Arabia, the Western Hemisphere, or to the slave ports and factories along the West and North Africa or South the Ubanqui and Congo rivers. In the mid 19th century, the Bobangi people became major slave traders and sold their captives to the Americas using the Ubangi river to reach the coast. During the 18th century Bandia-Nzakara peoples established the Bangassou Kingdom along the Ubangi River.
rewrite: In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the expansion of Saharan and Nile River slave-trading networks initiated raids within the region. Captives were enslaved and transported to destinations including the Mediterranean coast, Europe, Arabia, the Western Hemisphere, and various slave ports and factories along the coasts of West and North Africa, as well as south of the Ubangi and Congo rivers. Subsequently, during the eighteenth century, Bandia-Nzakara peoples founded the Bangassou Kingdom along the Ubangi River. By the mid-nineteenth century, the Bobangi emerged as prominent slave traders, utilizing the Ubangi River to convey captives to the Americas.

input: Early Islamic philosophy and Islamic metaphysics, imbued as it is with Islamic theology, distinguishes more clearly than Aristotelianism between essence and existence. Whereas existence is the domain of the contingent and the accidental, essence endures within a being beyond the accidental. The philosophy of Ibn Sīnā, particularly that part relating to metaphysics, owes much to al-Farabi. The search for a definitive Islamic philosophy separate from Occasionalism can be seen in what is left of his work.
rewrite: Early Islamic philosophy and metaphysics, deeply informed by Islamic theology, delineate essence and existence more distinctly than Aristotelianism. Existence pertains to the contingent and accidental, while essence persists as a being's enduring core. The metaphysical dimensions of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy are significantly indebted to al-Farabi. The remnants of his work reflect a pursuit to establish a definitive Islamic philosophy distinct from Occasionalism.

input: The majority of British Jews live in London, with significant Jewish communities in Stamford Hill, Stanmore, Golders Green, Finchley, Hampstead, Hendon and Edgware in North London. Bevis Marks Synagogue in the City of London is affiliated to London's historic Sephardic Jewish community. It is the only synagogue in Europe which has held regular services continuously for over 300 years. Stanmore and Canons Park Synagogue has the largest membership of any single Orthodox synagogue in the whole of Europe, overtaking Ilford synagogue (also in London) in 1998. The community set up the London Jewish Forum in 2006 in response to the growing significance of devolved London Government.
rewrite: The British Jewish population is predominantly concentrated in London, with substantial communities located in several North London areas, including Stamford Hill, Stanmore, Golders Green, Finchley, Hampstead, Hendon, and Edgware. Bevis Marks Synagogue, affiliated with the historic Sephardic community, holds the distinction of being the only synagogue in Europe to have conducted regular services uninterrupted for over three centuries. Furthermore, the Stanmore and Canons Park Synagogue possesses the largest membership of any Orthodox synagogue in Europe, having surpassed Ilford Synagogue in 1998. Reflecting the increased importance of devolved governance, the community established the London Jewish Forum in 2006.

input: So that the maximum number of colors can be accurately reproduced on your computer screen, each color has been given a code number, or sRGB, which tells your computer the intensity of the red, green and blue components of that color. The intensity of each component is measured on a scale of zero to 255, which means the complete list includes 16,777,216 distinct colors and shades. The sRGB number of pure red, for example, is 255, 00, 00, which means the red component is at its maximum intensity, and there is no green or blue. The sRGB number for crimson is 220, 20, 60, which means that the red is slightly less intense and therefore darker, there is some green, which leans it toward orange; and there is a larger amount of blue,which makes it slightly blue-violet.
rewrite: To ensure the accurate reproduction of the maximum range of colors on a computer display, each color is assigned a standardized numerical code within the sRGB color space. This code specifies the precise intensity of its red, green, and blue constituent components. Each component is quantified on an integer scale from 0 to 255, yielding a total palette of 16,777,216 distinct colors and shades. For instance, pure red is encoded as (255, 0, 0), indicating maximum red intensity with an absence of green and blue. In contrast, the color crimson is defined by the sRGB value (220, 20, 60). Here, the reduced red intensity results in a darker hue, the minor green component introduces an orange tendency, and the more substantial blue presence shifts the color toward a blue-violet tone.

input: New Haven was the location of one of Jim Morrison's infamous arrests while he fronted the rock group The Doors. The near-riotous concert and arrest in 1967 at the New Haven Arena was commemorated by Morrison in the lyrics to "Peace Frog" which include the line "...blood in the streets in the town of New Haven..." This was the first time a rock star had ever been arrested in concert.[citation needed] This event is portrayed in the movie The Doors (1991), starring Val Kilmer as Morrison, with a concert hall in Los Angeles used to depict the New Haven Arena.
rewrite: One of Jim Morrison’s notable arrests occurred in New Haven while he was the lead vocalist for The Doors. This 1967 incident, which took place at the New Haven Arena and nearly incited a riot, is memorialized in the song "Peace Frog" through the lyric "...blood in the streets in the town of New Haven..." Cited as the first arrest of a rock star during a concert, the event is dramatized in Oliver Stone’s 1991 film *The Doors*, featuring Val Kilmer as Morrison, with a Los Angeles venue standing in for the arena.

input: When Zeus struck down Apollo's son Asclepius with a lightning bolt for resurrecting Hippolytus from the dead (transgressing Themis by stealing Hades's subjects), Apollo in revenge killed the Cyclopes, who had fashioned the bolt for Zeus. Apollo would have been banished to Tartarus forever for this, but was instead sentenced to one year of hard labor, due to the intercession of his mother, Leto. During this time he served as shepherd for King Admetus of Pherae in Thessaly. Admetus treated Apollo well, and, in return, the god conferred great benefits on Admetus.
rewrite: After Zeus slew Asclepius, Apollo’s son, with a lightning bolt for resurrecting Hippolytus—an act that violated divine order by usurping Hades—Apollo retaliated by killing the Cyclopes, the bolt’s forgers. This warranted eternal banishment to Tartarus, yet his mother Leto’s intercession commuted the sentence to a year of servitude. Apollo consequently labored as a shepherd for King Admetus of Pherae in Thessaly. In gratitude for Admetus’s just treatment, Apollo bestowed significant favors upon him.

input: Symptoms of mild zinc deficiency are diverse. Clinical outcomes include depressed growth, diarrhea, impotence and delayed sexual maturation, alopecia, eye and skin lesions, impaired appetite, altered cognition, impaired host defense properties, defects in carbohydrate utilization, and reproductive teratogenesis. Mild zinc deficiency depresses immunity, although excessive zinc does also. Animals with a diet deficient in zinc require twice as much food in order to attain the same weight gain as animals given sufficient zinc.
rewrite: Mild zinc deficiency presents with varied clinical manifestations, including growth retardation, diarrhea, sexual dysfunction, alopecia, dermatological and ocular lesions, anorexia, cognitive alterations, impaired immune function, defective carbohydrate metabolism, and teratogenic effects. Both deficiency and excess zinc can compromise immunity. Furthermore, zinc-deficient animals exhibit markedly reduced feed efficiency, requiring twice the intake for equivalent weight gain compared to sufficient controls.

input: Although not a centre for handicrafts itself, the patronage of the arts by the Mughals and Nizams attracted artisans from the region to Hyderabad. Such crafts include: Bidriware, a metalwork handicraft from neighbouring Karnataka, which was popularised during the 18th century and has since been granted a Geographical Indication (GI) tag under the auspices of the WTO act; and Zari and Zardozi, embroidery works on textile that involve making elaborate designs using gold, silver and other metal threads. Another example of a handicraft drawn to Hyderabad is Kalamkari, a hand-painted or block-printed cotton textile that comes from cities in Andhra Pradesh. This craft is distinguished in having both a Hindu style, known as Srikalahasti and entirely done by hand, and an Islamic style, known as Machilipatnam that uses both hand and block techniques. Examples of Hyderabad's arts and crafts are housed in various museums including the Salar Jung Museum (housing "one of the largest one-man-collections in the world"), the AP State Archaeology Museum, the Nizam Museum, the City Museum and the Birla Science Museum.
rewrite: While Hyderabad itself did not emerge as a primary centre for handicraft production, the sustained patronage offered by the Mughal and subsequent Nizam rulers attracted master artisans from across the region. This confluence fostered the establishment of several notable crafts within the city. Among these is Bidriware, a metalwork tradition originating in neighbouring Karnataka, which gained prominence in the 18th century and now holds a registered Geographical Indication. Also prevalent is Zari and Zardozi, an elaborate form of embroidery employing threads of gold and silver. Furthermore, the Kalamkari craft, involving hand-painted or block-printed cotton textiles from Andhra Pradesh, found a home in Hyderabad. It is notably represented by two distinct styles: the Hindu Srikalahasti tradition, executed entirely by hand, and the Islamic Machilipatnam style, which incorporates block-printing techniques. Exemplars of these and other arts are preserved in several city institutions, including the Salar Jung Museum, renowned for its extensive single-curator collection, the AP State Archaeology Museum, the Nizam Museum, the City Museum, and the Birla Science Museum.

input: Midway through the 19th century, the focus of geology shifted from description and classification to attempts to understand how the surface of the Earth had changed. The first comprehensive theories of mountain building were proposed during this period, as were the first modern theories of earthquakes and volcanoes. Louis Agassiz and others established the reality of continent-covering ice ages, and "fluvialists" like Andrew Crombie Ramsay argued that river valleys were formed, over millions of years by the rivers that flow through them. After the discovery of radioactivity, radiometric dating methods were developed, starting in the 20th century. Alfred Wegener's theory of "continental drift" was widely dismissed when he proposed it in the 1910s, but new data gathered in the 1950s and 1960s led to the theory of plate tectonics, which provided a plausible mechanism for it. Plate tectonics also provided a unified explanation for a wide range of seemingly unrelated geological phenomena. Since 1970 it has served as the unifying principle in geology.
rewrite: During the mid-nineteenth century, the geological discipline transitioned from a primarily descriptive and classificatory endeavor toward a focus on understanding the processes that have shaped the Earth's surface. This period witnessed the formulation of the first comprehensive theories of orogeny, alongside modern explanations for seismic and volcanic activity. Louis Agassiz and contemporaries substantiated the occurrence of continental-scale glaciations, while fluvialists, such as Andrew Crombie Ramsay, posited that river valleys were sculpted over immense temporal scales by the rivers occupying them. The twentieth century introduced radiometric dating techniques following the discovery of radioactivity. Although Alfred Wegener's early twentieth-century theory of continental drift was initially met with skepticism, subsequent data acquisition in the 1950s and 1960s culminated in the development of plate tectonic theory. This framework not only supplied a mechanistic explanation for continental drift but also offered a unified account for diverse geological phenomena. Since approximately 1970, plate tectonics has remained the central unifying paradigm within the field.

input: The patron saint of Galicia is Saint James the Greater, whose body was discovered – according to the Catholic tradition – in 814 near Compostela. After that date, the relics of Saint James became an extraordinary centre of pilgrimage and from the 9th century have been kept in the heart of the church – the modern-day cathedral – dedicated to him. There are many other Galician and associated saints; some of the best-known are: Saint Ansurius, Saint Rudesind, Saint Mariña of Augas Santas, Saint Senorina, Trahamunda and Froilan.
rewrite: According to Catholic tradition, the relics of Saint James the Greater, patron saint of Galicia, were discovered in 814 near Compostela. From the 9th century onward, these relics, housed within the cathedral dedicated to him, established a major pilgrimage center. Galicia venerates numerous other saints, including Saint Ansurius, Saint Rudesind, Saint Mariña of Augas Santas, Saint Senorina, Trahamunda, and Froilan.

input: After World War II Hudson's realized that the limited parking space at its downtown skyscraper would increasingly be a problem for its customers. The solution in 1954 was to open the Northland Center in nearby Southfield, just beyond the city limits. It was the largest suburban shopping center in the world, and quickly became the main shopping destination for northern and western Detroit, and for much of the suburbs. By 1961 the downtown skyscraper accounted for only half of Hudson's sales; it closed in 1986. The Northland Center Hudson's, rebranded Macy's in 2006 following acquisition by Federated Department Stores, was closed along with the remaining stores in the center in March 2015 due to the mall's high storefront vacancy, decaying infrastructure, and financial mismanagement.
rewrite: In the post-World War II era, Hudson's recognized that the constrained parking at its downtown Detroit skyscraper would pose a growing inconvenience for its clientele. Consequently, in 1954, the company inaugurated the Northland Center in the adjacent suburb of Southfield. As the world's largest suburban shopping complex at its opening, it rapidly evolved into the principal retail destination for northern and western Detroit, along with extensive suburban areas. By 1961, the flagship downtown store represented merely half of Hudson's sales; it ceased operations in 1986. Following its acquisition by Federated Department Stores, the Northland Center Hudson's was rebranded as Macy's in 2006. Both this store and the remaining mall tenants were shuttered in March 2015, attributable to high vacancy rates, deteriorating infrastructure, and financial mismanagement.

input: In the nearby parish of Stoke Damerel the first dockyard, HMNB Devonport, opened in 1690 on the eastern bank of the River Tamar. Further docks were built here in 1727, 1762 and 1793. The settlement that developed here was called "Dock" or "Plymouth Dock" at the time, and a new town, separate from Plymouth, grew up. In 1712 there were 318 men employed and by 1733 it had grown to a population of 3,000 people.
rewrite: The initial naval dockyard, HMNB Devonport, was established in 1690 on the eastern bank of the River Tamar within the adjacent parish of Stoke Damerel. Subsequent docks were added in 1727, 1762, and 1793. A distinct settlement, contemporaneously named "Dock" or "Plymouth Dock," emerged separately from Plymouth. Its workforce comprised 318 men in 1712, and by 1733, the population had expanded to 3,000 inhabitants.

input: Ibn Sina's first appointment was that of physician to the emir, Nuh II, who owed him his recovery from a dangerous illness (997). Ibn Sina's chief reward for this service was access to the royal library of the Samanids, well-known patrons of scholarship and scholars. When the library was destroyed by fire not long after, the enemies of Ibn Sina accused him of burning it, in order for ever to conceal the sources of his knowledge. Meanwhile, he assisted his father in his financial labors, but still found time to write some of his earliest works.
rewrite: Ibn Sina initially served as physician to Emir Nuh II, to whom he restored health from a perilous ailment in 997. His primary recompense was entry to the renowned royal library of the scholarly Samanid dynasty. Following the library's subsequent destruction by fire, his detractors alleged he ignited it to permanently obscure the origins of his erudition. Concurrently, while aiding his father in fiscal duties, he authored several of his first treatises.

input: With a population of 518,000, Hanover is a major centre of Northern Germany and the country's thirteenth largest city. Hanover also hosts annual commercial trade fairs such as the Hanover Fair and the CeBIT. Every year Hanover hosts the Schützenfest Hannover, the world's largest marksmen's festival, and the Oktoberfest Hannover, the second largest Oktoberfest in the world (beside Oktoberfest of Blumenau). In 2000, Hanover hosted the world fair Expo 2000. The Hanover fairground, due to numerous extensions, especially for the Expo 2000, is the largest in the world. Hanover is of national importance because of its universities and medical school, its international airport and its large zoo. The city is also a major crossing point of railway lines and highways (Autobahnen), connecting European main lines in both the east-west (Berlin–Ruhr area) and north-south (Hamburg–Munich, etc.) directions.
rewrite: With a population of 518,000, Hanover is a principal urban center in Northern Germany and the nation's thirteenth most populous city. It is distinguished by hosting major annual commercial trade fairs, including the Hanover Fair and the former CeBIT. The city further holds the Schützenfest Hannover, the world's largest marksmen's festival, and the Oktoberfest Hannover, the second largest such event globally. Hanover served as the host for the world exposition Expo 2000, and its fairground, expanded notably for that event, remains the world's largest. The city holds national significance due to its universities and medical school, its international airport, and its extensive zoo. Furthermore, Hanover constitutes a vital nexus for rail and motorway networks, connecting major European corridors along east-west and north-south axes.

input: Although the Reformation was a religious movement, it also had a strong impact on all other aspects of life: marriage and family, education, the humanities and sciences, the political and social order, the economy, and the arts. Protestant churches reject the idea of a celibate priesthood and thus allow their clergy to marry. Many of their families contributed to the development of intellectual elites in their countries. Since about 1950, women have entered the ministry, and some have assumed leading positions (e.g. bishops), in most Protestant churches.
rewrite: While fundamentally a religious movement, the Reformation profoundly influenced numerous societal domains, including marriage, family, education, the humanities, sciences, political and social structures, the economy, and the arts. By rejecting clerical celibacy, Protestantism permitted clergy to marry, with many such families fostering national intellectual elites. Furthermore, since approximately 1950, most Protestant denominations have ordained women, some of whom have attained high-ranking offices such as bishop.

input: At Princeton, the physicist Robert R. Wilson encouraged Feynman to participate in the Manhattan Project—the wartime U.S. Army project at Los Alamos developing the atomic bomb. Feynman said he was persuaded to join this effort to build it before Nazi Germany developed their own bomb. He was assigned to Hans Bethe's theoretical division and impressed Bethe enough to be made a group leader. He and Bethe developed the Bethe–Feynman formula for calculating the yield of a fission bomb, which built upon previous work by Robert Serber.
rewrite: At Princeton University, physicist Robert R. Wilson urged Richard Feynman to contribute to the Manhattan Project, the U.S. Army's wartime initiative in Los Alamos to develop an atomic bomb. Feynman recounted that his decision to join was motivated by the aim to complete the weapon before Nazi Germany could. Assigned to Hans Bethe's theoretical division, his performance led to a promotion to group leader. Collaborating with Bethe, he helped derive the Bethe–Feynman formula for fission bomb yield, extending prior research by Robert Serber.

input: London is the seat of the Government of the United Kingdom. Many government departments are based close to the Palace of Westminster, particularly along Whitehall, including the Prime Minister's residence at 10 Downing Street. The British Parliament is often referred to as the "Mother of Parliaments" (although this sobriquet was first applied to England itself by John Bright) because it has been the model for most other parliamentary systems. There are 73 Members of Parliament (MPs) from London, who correspond to local parliamentary constituencies in the national Parliament. As of May 2015, 45 are from the Labour Party, 27 are Conservatives, and one is a Liberal Democrat.
rewrite: London serves as the governmental centre of the United Kingdom. Numerous key departments are situated near the Palace of Westminster, notably on Whitehall, which also contains the Prime Minister’s official residence at 10 Downing Street. The British Parliament, frequently termed the "Mother of Parliaments"—an epithet originally applied to England by John Bright—has provided a foundational model for many global parliamentary systems. The city is represented by 73 Members of Parliament, each elected from distinct London constituencies. Following the May 2015 general election, this comprised 45 Labour, 27 Conservative, and one Liberal Democrat MP.

input: In 1681, in partial repayment of a debt, Charles II of England granted William Penn a charter for what would become the Pennsylvania colony. Despite the royal charter, Penn bought the land from the local Lenape to be on good terms with the Native Americans and ensure peace for his colony. Penn made a treaty of friendship with Lenape chief Tammany under an elm tree at Shackamaxon, in what is now the city's Fishtown section. Penn named the city Philadelphia, which is Greek for brotherly love (from philos, "love" or "friendship", and adelphos, "brother"). As a Quaker, Penn had experienced religious persecution and wanted his colony to be a place where anyone could worship freely. This tolerance, far more than afforded by most other colonies, led to better relations with the local Native tribes and fostered Philadelphia's rapid growth into America's most important city. Penn planned a city on the Delaware River to serve as a port and place for government. Hoping that Philadelphia would become more like an English rural town instead of a city, Penn laid out roads on a grid plan to keep houses and businesses spread far apart, with areas for gardens and orchards. The city's inhabitants did not follow Penn's plans, as they crowded by the Delaware River, the port, and subdivided and resold their lots. Before Penn left Philadelphia for the last time, he issued the Charter of 1701 establishing it as a city. It became an important trading center, poor at first, but with tolerable living conditions by the 1750s. Benjamin Franklin, a leading citizen, helped improve city services and founded new ones, such as fire protection, a library, and one of the American colonies' first hospitals.
rewrite:
In 1681, King Charles II of England granted a charter for the territory that would become the Pennsylvania colony to William Penn, partially in settlement of a debt owed to Penn’s father. Although this royal charter provided legal claim, Penn also negotiated a purchase of the land from the local Lenape people, seeking to establish amicable relations and ensure peace for the prospective settlement. This commitment was formalized in a treaty of friendship with Lenape chief Tammany, reputedly concluded beneath an elm tree at Shackamaxon, in the area now known as Fishtown. Penn named the principal city Philadelphia, derived from the Greek terms *philos* (love or friendship) and *adelphos* (brother), meaning "brotherly love." A Quaker who had endured religious persecution, Penn envisioned the colony as a haven for religious liberty. This policy of tolerance, which exceeded that of most contemporary colonies, contributed to more peaceful relations with Indigenous nations and facilitated Philadelphia’s rapid development into a major urban center.

Penn designed the city along the Delaware River to function as a port and administrative seat. Aspiring to create a verdant, spacious settlement reminiscent of an English country town rather than a dense city, he implemented a grid plan with widely spaced lots intended for houses, businesses, gardens, and orchards. However, inhabitants largely disregarded this plan, clustering near the riverfront port and subdividing plots for resale. Prior to his final departure, Penn issued the Charter of 1701, which formally incorporated Philadelphia as a city. It evolved into a vital commercial hub, initially characterized by poverty but achieving tolerable living standards by the mid-eighteenth century. Prominent citizens like Benjamin Franklin were instrumental in this progress, founding essential institutions and services including a fire company, a public library, and one of the first hospitals in colonial America.

input: On 20 April 1992, The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert was held at London's Wembley Stadium to a 72,000-strong crowd. Performers, including Def Leppard, Robert Plant, Guns N' Roses, Elton John, David Bowie, George Michael, Annie Lennox, Seal, Extreme, and Metallica performed various Queen songs along with the three remaining Queen members (and Spike Edney.) The concert is listed in the Guinness Book of Records as "The largest rock star benefit concert", as it was televised to over 1.2 billion viewers worldwide, and raised over £20,000,000 for AIDS charities.
rewrite: The Freddie Mercury Tribute Concert was held at London’s Wembley Stadium on 20 April 1992, attracting an audience of 72,000. It featured performances by numerous prominent artists, such as David Bowie, Elton John, and Metallica, who collaborated with Queen's surviving members. Notably, the event holds a Guinness World Record as the largest benefit concert by rock stars. It was broadcast globally to more than 1.2 billion viewers and generated over £20 million for AIDS charities.

input: Daylighting is the oldest method of interior lighting. Daylighting is simply designing a space to use as much natural light as possible. This decreases energy consumption and costs, and requires less heating and cooling from the building. Daylighting has also been proven to have positive effects on patients in hospitals as well as work and school performance. Due to a lack of information that indicate the likely energy savings, daylighting schemes are not yet popular among most buildings.
rewrite: Daylighting, the practice of designing spaces to maximize natural illumination, represents the most ancient form of interior lighting. It reduces energy consumption and associated costs by diminishing reliance on artificial lighting and mechanical heating and cooling. Furthermore, studies demonstrate its benefits for occupant well-being and productivity in healthcare, educational, and workplace settings. Despite these advantages, the adoption of daylighting strategies remains limited, largely due to insufficient data quantifying potential energy savings.

input: After 12 years as commissioner of the AFL, David Baker retired unexpectedly on July 25, 2008, just two days before ArenaBowl XXII; deputy commissioner Ed Policy was named interim commissioner until Baker's replacement was found. Baker explained, "When I took over as commissioner, I thought it would be for one year. It turned into 12. But now it's time."
rewrite: On July 25, 2008, AFL Commissioner David Baker announced his unexpected retirement, merely two days prior to ArenaBowl XXII. Deputy Commissioner Ed Policy was appointed as interim commissioner pending a permanent successor. Baker stated his initial one-year tenure had extended to twelve years and that his departure was now timely.

input: The uneasy alliance of Carranza, Obregón, Villa, and Zapata eventually led the rebels to victory. The fight against Huerta formally ended on August 15, 1914, when Álvaro Obregón signed a number of treaties in Teoloyucan in which the last of Huerta's forces surrendered to him and recognized the constitutional government. On August 20, 1914, Carranza made a triumphal entry into Mexico City. Carranza (supported by Obregón) was now the strongest candidate to fill the power vacuum and set himself up as head of the new government. This government successfully printed money, passed laws, etc.
rewrite: The provisional alliance among Carranza, Obregón, Villa, and Zapata ultimately secured the revolutionary triumph. Hostilities against Huerta concluded formally on August 15, 1914, with Álvaro Obregón's signing of the Teoloyucan treaties, wherein the remaining federal forces surrendered and acknowledged the constitutionalist authority. Following Carranza's triumphal entry into Mexico City on August 20, he, bolstered by Obregón's support, emerged as the preeminent figure to occupy the resulting power vacuum, establishing himself as the provisional government's head.
