This administration effectively exercised sovereign functions, including currency issuance and legislative enactment.

input: The low mechanical complexity of hydraulic elevators in comparison to traction elevators makes them ideal for low rise, low traffic installations. They are less energy efficient as the pump works against gravity to push the car and its passengers upwards; this energy is lost when the car descends on its own weight. The high current draw of the pump when starting up also places higher demands on a building’s electrical system. There are also environmental concerns should the lifting cylinder leak fluid into the ground.
rewrite: Hydraulic elevators offer reduced mechanical complexity relative to traction systems, suiting them for low-rise, low-traffic applications. However, their energy efficiency is inferior, as the pump expends energy to elevate the car against gravity, which is not recovered during the descent. The pump's high inrush current imposes greater electrical demands on a building. Furthermore, potential environmental risks exist due to the possibility of hydraulic fluid leakage from the lifting cylinder into the subsurface.

input: Muslim rule started in parts of north India in the 13th century when the Delhi Sultanate was founded in 1206 CE by the Central Asian Turks. The Delhi Sultanate ruled the major part of northern India in the early 14th century, but declined in the late 14th century when several powerful Hindu states such as the Vijayanagara Empire, Gajapati Kingdom, Ahom Kingdom, as well as Rajput dynasties and states, such as Mewar dynasty, emerged. The 15th century saw the emergence of Sikhism. In the 16th century, Mughals came from Central Asia and gradually covered most of India. The Mughal Empire suffered a gradual decline in the early 18th century, which provided opportunities for the Maratha Empire, Sikh Empire and Mysore Kingdom to exercise control over large areas of the subcontinent.
rewrite: The establishment of Muslim political authority in northern India commenced in the thirteenth century with the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 CE by Central Asian Turks. This sultanate achieved dominance over much of the north by the early fourteenth century, yet entered a period of decline in the late fourteenth century. This decline coincided with the rise of potent Hindu polities, including the Vijayanagara and Gajapati Kingdoms, the Ahom Kingdom, and various Rajput states such as Mewar. The fifteenth century witnessed the emergence of Sikhism. Subsequently, in the sixteenth century, the Mughals, also originating from Central Asia, expanded to control vast portions of the subcontinent. Following the Mughal Empire's gradual dissolution in the early eighteenth century, regional powers including the Maratha Empire, the Sikh Empire, and the Kingdom of Mysore ascended to exert control over extensive territories.

input: John, the youngest of five sons of King Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, was at first not expected to inherit significant lands. Following the failed rebellion of his elder brothers between 1173 and 1174, however, John became Henry's favourite child. He was appointed the Lord of Ireland in 1177 and given lands in England and on the continent. John's elder brothers William, Henry and Geoffrey died young; by the time Richard I became king in 1189, John was a potential heir to the throne. John unsuccessfully attempted a rebellion against Richard's royal administrators whilst his brother was participating in the Third Crusade. Despite this, after Richard died in 1199, John was proclaimed King of England, and came to an agreement with Philip II of France to recognise John's possession of the continental Angevin lands at the peace treaty of Le Goulet in 1200.
rewrite: Initially considered unlikely to inherit substantial territories, John, the youngest son of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, rose in prominence following the unsuccessful revolt of his elder brothers (1173-1174), becoming his father’s favoured heir. He was granted the Lordship of Ireland in 1177 and received further estates in England and on the continent. The premature deaths of his brothers William, Henry, and Geoffrey positioned John as a credible successor to the throne by Richard I’s accession in 1189. During Richard’s absence on the Third Crusade, John led an abortive rebellion against the king’s regents. Nevertheless, upon Richard’s death in 1199, John ascended to the English kingship. His reign commenced with the Treaty of Le Goulet (1200), wherein Philip II of France formally recognized John’s holdings within the Angevin domains.

input: With the fall of the Western Roman Empire, there arose a more diffuse arena for political studies. The rise of monotheism and, particularly for the Western tradition, Christianity, brought to light a new space for politics and political action[citation needed]. During the Middle Ages, the study of politics was widespread in the churches and courts. Works such as Augustine of Hippo's The City of God synthesized current philosophies and political traditions with those of Christianity, redefining the borders between what was religious and what was political. Most of the political questions surrounding the relationship between Church and State were clarified and contested in this period.
rewrite: The dissolution of the Western Roman Empire precipitated a decentralization of political inquiry. The ascendancy of monotheistic faiths, most notably Christianity within the Western tradition, introduced a novel conceptual sphere for political discourse and practice. Throughout the medieval era, political examination was principally conducted within ecclesiastical and royal courts. Seminal works, such as Augustine’s *The City of God*, synthesized classical philosophy and political thought with Christian doctrine, thereby renegotiating the boundaries between the sacred and the secular. This period was thus defined by the rigorous clarification and contestation of the fundamental relationship between ecclesiastical and temporal authority.

input: According to Thomas DeGregori, an economics professor at the University of Houston, in an article published by the Cato Institute, a libertarian think-tank operating in Washington D.C., "it is clear that technological and economic change are vital ingredients in getting children out of the workplace and into schools. Then they can grow to become productive adults and live longer, healthier lives. However, in poor countries like Bangladesh, working children are essential for survival in many families, as they were in our own heritage until the late 19th century. So, while the struggle to end child labour is necessary, getting there often requires taking different routes—and, sadly, there are many political obstacles.
rewrite: In an article for the Cato Institute, a libertarian think-tank based in Washington D.C., Professor Thomas DeGregori of the University of Houston asserts that technological and economic advancement are fundamental to transitioning children from workplaces into educational institutions, thereby enabling them to develop into productive adults with longer, healthier lives. He notes, however, that in impoverished nations such as Bangladesh, child labour remains an economic necessity for many families, a historical reality also prevalent in developed nations until the late nineteenth century. Consequently, while the abolition of child labour is imperative, achieving this goal necessitates varied approaches and must contend with significant political impediments.

input: Himachal was one of the few states that had remained largely untouched by external customs, largely due to its difficult terrain. With the technological advancements the state has changed very rapidly. It is a multireligional, multicultural as well as multilingual state like other Indian states. Some of the most commonly spoken languages includes Hindi, Pahari, Dogri, Mandeali Kangri, Mandyali, Gojri and Kinnauri. The caste communities residing in Himachal include the Khatri, Brahmins of the Hindu Faith and the Sikh Brahmin Caste Bhatra, Rajputs, Gujjars, Gaddis, Ghirth (choudhary), Kannets, Rathis and Kolis, Sood There are tribal populations in the state which mainly comprise Kinnars, Pangawals, Sulehria, and Lahaulis.The people Of Himachal Pradesh are very simple and live a traditional ´Pahari' lifestyle.
rewrite: Himachal Pradesh historically remained insulated from extensive external cultural influences, primarily due to its challenging topography. However, recent technological progress has accelerated its rate of change. The state is multireligious, multicultural, and multilingual, consistent with broader Indian demographics. Predominant languages encompass Hindi, Pahari, Dogri, Mandeali, Kangri, Mandyali, Gojri, and Kinnauri. Its caste composition includes communities such as Khatris, Brahmins, Rajputs, Gujjars, Gaddis, Ghirths, Kannets, Rathis, Kolis, and Soods. Additionally, tribal populations, mainly comprising Kinnars, Pangawals, Sulehrias, and Lahaulis, reside within the state. The populace is generally characterized by a simplicity of life, adhering to a traditional 'Pahari' lifestyle.

input: The term Muslim world, also known as Islamic world and the Ummah (Arabic: أمة‎, meaning "nation" or "community") has different meanings. In a religious sense, the Islamic Ummah refers to those who adhere to the teachings of Islam, referred to as Muslims. In a cultural sense, the Muslim Ummah refers to Islamic civilization, exclusive of non-Muslims living in that civilization. In a modern geopolitical sense, the term "Islamic Nation" usually refers collectively to Muslim-majority countries, states, districts, or towns.
rewrite: The term "Muslim world," synonymous with "Islamic world" and the Arabic "Ummah" (أمة‎, meaning "nation" or "community"), possesses multiple connotations. Religiously, it denotes the global community of Muslims adhering to Islamic teachings. Culturally, it references Islamic civilization, excluding non-Muslim populations within it. In a contemporary geopolitical context, the phrase typically refers to the collective of nation-states, regions, or municipalities with Muslim-majority populations.

input: The current iteration of the Canadian Armed Forces dates from 1 February 1968, when the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army, and Royal Canadian Air Force were merged into a unified structure and superseded by elemental commands. Its roots, however, lie in colonial militia groups that served alongside garrisons of the French and British armies and navies; a structure that remained in place until the early 20th century. Thereafter, a distinctly Canadian army and navy was established, followed by an air force, that, because of the constitutional arrangements at the time, remained effectively under the control of the British government until Canada gained legislative independence from the United Kingdom in 1931, in part due to the distinguished achievement and sacrifice of the Canadian Corps in the First World War.
rewrite: The contemporary Canadian Armed Forces originated on 1 February 1968 through the unification of the Royal Canadian Navy, Canadian Army, and Royal Canadian Air Force into a single structure governed by elemental commands. Its historical foundations, however, extend to colonial militia forces that operated alongside French and British imperial garrisons, an organizational model that persisted into the early twentieth century. Subsequently, a distinctly national army and navy were formed, followed by an air force. Owing to the constitutional framework of the period, these forces remained substantively under British authority until Canada attained legislative independence from the United Kingdom in 1931. This shift toward autonomy was precipitated in part by the exemplary service and sacrifice of the Canadian Corps during the First World War.

input: Rapid increases in a number of commodity prices followed the collapse in the housing bubble. The price of oil nearly tripled from $50 to $147 from early 2007 to 2008, before plunging as the financial crisis began to take hold in late 2008. Experts debate the causes, with some attributing it to speculative flow of money from housing and other investments into commodities, some to monetary policy, and some to the increasing feeling of raw materials scarcity in a fast-growing world, leading to long positions taken on those markets, such as Chinese increasing presence in Africa. An increase in oil prices tends to divert a larger share of consumer spending into gasoline, which creates downward pressure on economic growth in oil importing countries, as wealth flows to oil-producing states. A pattern of spiking instability in the price of oil over the decade leading up to the price high of 2008 has been recently identified. The destabilizing effects of this price variance has been proposed as a contributory factor in the financial crisis.
rewrite: The precipitous decline of the housing bubble was succeeded by a period of sharp escalation in numerous commodity prices. Notably, the price of crude oil surged from approximately $50 to $147 per barrel between early 2007 and mid-2008, before collapsing amidst the unfolding financial crisis in late 2008. Scholarly consensus on the primary drivers remains elusive. Proposed explanations include speculative capital flows from real estate and other assets into commodity futures; expansionary monetary policy; and perceptions of growing resource scarcity in a rapidly expanding global economy, which encouraged long positions—exemplified by China's heightened engagement in African resource extraction. Rising oil prices effectively transfer consumer expenditure to gasoline, diverting wealth to petroleum-exporting nations and thereby exerting a contractionary effect on economic growth in importing countries. Recent analysis identifies a pattern of increasing volatility in oil prices throughout the decade preceding the 2008 peak. This instability has been posited as a destabilizing force and a potential contributing element to the broader financial crisis.

input: Gaddafi was a very private individual, who described himself as a "simple revolutionary" and "pious Muslim" called upon by Allah to continue Nasser's work. Reporter Mirella Bianco found that his friends considered him particularly loyal and generous, and asserted that he adored children. She was told by Gaddafi's father that even as a child he had been "always serious, even taciturn", a trait he also exhibited in adulthood. His father said that he was courageous, intelligent, pious, and family oriented.
rewrite: Muammar Gaddafi presented himself as a private figure, a "simple revolutionary" and "pious Muslim" divinely tasked with continuing Gamal Abdel Nasser's mission. According to journalist Mirella Bianco, his associates viewed him as notably loyal and generous, with a particular affection for children. His father reported that from childhood, Gaddafi was "always serious, even taciturn," a disposition persisting into adulthood, and described him as courageous, intelligent, devout, and dedicated to family.

input: The idea of self-concept is known as the ability of a person to have opinions and beliefs that are defined confidently, consistent and stable. Early in adolescence, cognitive developments result in greater self-awareness, greater awareness of others and their thoughts and judgments, the ability to think about abstract, future possibilities, and the ability to consider multiple possibilities at once. As a result, adolescents experience a significant shift from the simple, concrete, and global self-descriptions typical of young children; as children, they defined themselves by physical traits whereas as adolescents, they define themselves based on their values, thoughts, and opinions.
rewrite: Self-concept refers to an individual's capacity to maintain defined, consistent, and stable beliefs and opinions. During early adolescence, cognitive development fosters increased self-awareness, heightened sensitivity to the perspectives of others, and the ability to engage in abstract and future-oriented thinking, including the consideration of multiple possibilities simultaneously. Consequently, adolescents transition from the simple, concrete, and global self-descriptions characteristic of childhood, which emphasize physical attributes, toward more complex definitions of the self grounded in personal values, thoughts, and opinions.

input: The University of Plymouth enrolls 25,895 total students as of 2014/15 (22nd largest in the UK out of 165). It also employs 3,000 staff with an annual income of around £160 million. It was founded in 1992 from Polytechnic South West (formerly Plymouth Polytechnic) following the Further and Higher Education Act 1992. It has courses in maritime business, marine engineering, marine biology and Earth, ocean and environmental sciences, surf science, shipping and logistics. The university formed a joint venture with the fellow Devonian University of Exeter in 2000, establishing the Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry. The college is ranked 8th out of 30 universities in the UK in 2011 for medicine. Its dental school was established in 2006, which also provides free dental care in an attempt to improve access to dental care in the South West.
rewrite: As of the 2014/15 academic year, the University of Plymouth had a total enrolment of 25,895 students, ranking it the 22nd largest institution among 165 in the United Kingdom. It employs approximately 3,000 staff and generates an annual income of around £160 million. Founded in 1992 under the Further and Higher Education Act, it originated from Polytechnic South West, formerly Plymouth Polytechnic. The university offers specialized programs in maritime business, marine engineering, marine biology, Earth, ocean and environmental sciences, surf science, and shipping and logistics. In 2000, it formed a joint venture with the University of Exeter, creating the Peninsula College of Medicine and Dentistry. This college was ranked 8th out of 30 UK medical schools in 2011. Its dental school, established in 2006, provides complimentary dental services to improve access to care in the South West region.

input: While H2 is not very reactive under standard conditions, it does form compounds with most elements. Hydrogen can form compounds with elements that are more electronegative, such as halogens (e.g., F, Cl, Br, I), or oxygen; in these compounds hydrogen takes on a partial positive charge. When bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, hydrogen can participate in a form of medium-strength noncovalent bonding with other similar molecules between their hydrogens called hydrogen bonding, which is critical to the stability of many biological molecules. Hydrogen also forms compounds with less electronegative elements, such as the metals and metalloids, in which it takes on a partial negative charge. These compounds are often known as hydrides.
rewrite: Under standard conditions, molecular hydrogen exhibits low reactivity, yet it forms compounds with a majority of the elements. With more electronegative elements, such as the halogens or oxygen, hydrogen assumes a partial positive charge. Notably, when bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen, it can engage in medium-strength, noncovalent hydrogen bonding with other molecules, a critical interaction for the stability of numerous biological structures. Conversely, in compounds with less electronegative elements, including metals and metalloids, hydrogen carries a partial negative charge; such substances are commonly classified as hydrides.

input: In 1877, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph. Unlike the phonautograph, it was capable of both recording and reproducing sound. Despite the similarity of name, there is no documentary evidence that Edison's phonograph was based on Scott's phonautograph. Edison first tried recording sound on a wax-impregnated paper tape, with the idea of creating a "telephone repeater" analogous to the telegraph repeater he had been working on. Although the visible results made him confident that sound could be physically recorded and reproduced, his notes do not indicate that he actually reproduced sound before his first experiment in which he used tinfoil as a recording medium several months later. The tinfoil was wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder and a sound-vibrated stylus indented the tinfoil while the cylinder was rotated. The recording could be played back immediately. The Scientific American article that introduced the tinfoil phonograph to the public mentioned Marey, Rosapelly and Barlow as well as Scott as creators of devices for recording but, importantly, not reproducing sound. Edison also invented variations of the phonograph that used tape and disc formats. Numerous applications for the phonograph were envisioned, but although it enjoyed a brief vogue as a startling novelty at public demonstrations, the tinfoil phonograph proved too crude to be put to any practical use. A decade later, Edison developed a greatly improved phonograph that used a hollow wax cylinder instead of a foil sheet. This proved to be both a better-sounding and far more useful and durable device. The wax phonograph cylinder created the recorded sound market at the end of the 1880s and dominated it through the early years of the 20th century.
rewrite: In 1877, Thomas Edison introduced the phonograph, a device distinguished by its capacity to both record and reproduce sound, unlike earlier instruments such as the phonautograph. While the names are similar, no documentary evidence suggests that Edison’s invention was directly derived from Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville’s phonautograph. Edison’s initial experiments involved recording sound onto wax-impregnated paper tape, conceived as a “telephone repeater” analogous to the telegraph repeaters he had previously developed. Although the visual traces from these tests convinced him that sound could be physically captured and replayed, his notes do not confirm that any audible reproduction was achieved prior to his subsequent experiment employing tinfoil as a medium several months later. In that pivotal demonstration, tinfoil was wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder; a stylus, vibrated by sound, indented the foil as the cylinder rotated, enabling immediate playback. An article in *Scientific American* that publicized the tinfoil phonograph acknowledged Scott, as well as Marey, Rosapelly, and Barlow, for having devised earlier sound-recording apparatuses, but emphasized that none had achieved sound reproduction. Edison also explored alternative phonograph designs using tape and disc formats. Although numerous applications were envisioned for the phonograph, and it initially attracted public fascination as a novel demonstration, the tinfoil model was too rudimentary for practical use. A decade later, Edison significantly refined the invention by replacing the foil with a hollow wax cylinder. This enhanced version offered superior audio fidelity, greater durability, and broader utility, ultimately establishing the recorded sound market in the late 1880s and maintaining dominance into the early twentieth century.

input: San Diego County has one of the highest counts of animal and plant species that appear on the endangered species list among counties in the United States. Because of its diversity of habitat and its position on the Pacific Flyway, San Diego County has recorded the presence of 492 bird species, more than any other region in the country. San Diego always scores very high in the number of bird species observed in the annual Christmas Bird Count, sponsored by the Audubon Society, and it is known as one of the "birdiest" areas in the United States.
rewrite: San Diego County contains one of the highest numbers of federally listed endangered plant and animal species of any county in the United States. Its diverse habitats and location along the Pacific Flyway contribute to a documented 492 bird species, the highest total for any region nationally. The county consistently achieves top rankings for species observed during the National Audubon Society’s annual Christmas Bird Count, solidifying its reputation as one of the nation’s premier areas for avian diversity.

input: At the same time, these movements were influenced by, and in some respects continued, philosophical thought within the Vedic tradition as reflected e.g. in the Upanishads. These movements included, besides Buddhism, various skeptics (such as Sanjaya Belatthiputta), atomists (such as Pakudha Kaccayana), materialists (such as Ajita Kesakambali), antinomians (such as Purana Kassapa); the most important ones in the 5th century BCE were the Ajivikas, who emphasized the rule of fate, the Lokayata (materialists), the Ajnanas (agnostics) and the Jains, who stressed that the soul must be freed from matter. Many of these new movements shared the same conceptual vocabulary—atman ("Self"), buddha ("awakened one"), dhamma ("rule" or "law"), karma ("action"), nirvana ("extinguishing"), samsara ("eternal recurrence") and yoga ("spiritual practice").[note 24] The shramanas rejected the Veda, and the authority of the brahmans, who claimed they possessed revealed truths not knowable by any ordinary human means. Moreover, they declared that the entire Brahmanical system was fraudulent: a conspiracy of the brahmans to enrich themselves by charging exorbitant fees to perform bogus rites and give useless advice.
rewrite: Concurrently, these movements were both shaped by and, in certain aspects, represented a continuation of philosophical currents within the Vedic tradition, as evidenced in texts such as the Upanishads. Beyond Buddhism, these included diverse schools of thought: skeptics like Sanjaya Belatthiputta, atomists like Pakudha Kaccayana, materialists like Ajita Kesakambali, and antinomians like Purana Kassapa. The most significant in the fifth century BCE were the Ajivikas, who stressed strict determinism; the Lokayata materialists; the Ajnana agnostics; and the Jains, who emphasized liberating the soul from material bondage. These groups largely employed a shared conceptual lexicon—including terms such as atman (self), buddha (awakened one), dhamma (law), karma (action), nirvana (extinction), samsara (cyclic existence), and yoga (discipline). The shramanas categorically rejected the authority of the Vedas and the Brahmanical priesthood, which claimed exclusive access to revealed truths. They further denounced the entire Brahmanical system as fraudulent, characterizing it as a brahman conspiracy to secure wealth through exorbitant fees for performing superfluous rituals and offering ineffective counsel.

input: In DC circuits and pulsed circuits, current and voltage reversal are affected by the damping of the system. Voltage reversal is encountered in RLC circuits that are under-damped. The current and voltage reverse direction, forming a harmonic oscillator between the inductance and capacitance. The current and voltage will tend to oscillate and may reverse direction several times, with each peak being lower than the previous, until the system reaches an equilibrium. This is often referred to as ringing. In comparison, critically damped or over-damped systems usually do not experience a voltage reversal. Reversal is also encountered in AC circuits, where the peak current will be equal in each direction.
rewrite: In direct current (DC) and pulsed electrical circuits, the phenomenon of current and voltage reversal is influenced by the damping characteristics of the system. Voltage reversal specifically occurs in under-damped RLC circuits, where the stored energy oscillates between the inductive and capacitive elements, forming a harmonic oscillator. The resulting oscillations cause successive reversals in direction, with each peak amplitude diminishing until equilibrium is attained—a process commonly termed "ringing." Conversely, critically damped or over-damped configurations typically preclude such reversal. In alternating current (AC) circuits, reversal is a fundamental periodic occurrence, with the peak current magnitude being equal in both directions.

input: In a June 2008 speech, President and CEO of the New York Federal Reserve Bank Timothy Geithner—who in 2009 became Secretary of the United States Treasury—placed significant blame for the freezing of credit markets on a "run" on the entities in the "parallel" banking system, also called the shadow banking system. These entities became critical to the credit markets underpinning the financial system, but were not subject to the same regulatory controls. Further, these entities were vulnerable because of maturity mismatch, meaning that they borrowed short-term in liquid markets to purchase long-term, illiquid and risky assets. This meant that disruptions in credit markets would make them subject to rapid deleveraging, selling their long-term assets at depressed prices. He described the significance of these entities:
rewrite: In a June 2008 address, Timothy Geithner, then President and CEO of the New York Federal Reserve Bank and later U.S. Treasury Secretary (2009), attributed substantial responsibility for the credit market seizure to a "run" on institutions within the "parallel" or shadow banking system. These entities had become integral to the credit markets supporting the broader financial system, yet operated outside equivalent regulatory oversight. Their structural vulnerability stemmed from a maturity mismatch, whereby they funded long-term, illiquid, and risky asset holdings with short-term borrowing in liquid markets. Consequently, any disruption in credit availability forced rapid deleveraging, compelling the fire-sale of long-term assets at severely diminished prices. Geithner emphasized the systemic importance of these institutions.

input: The AVL, created by the Valencian parliament, is in charge of dictating the official rules governing the use of Valencian, and its standard is based on the Norms of Castelló (Normes de Castelló). Currently, everyone who writes in Valencian uses this standard, except the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture (Acadèmia de Cultura Valenciana, RACV), which uses for Valencian an independent standard.
rewrite: The AVL, established by the Valencian parliament, is responsible for codifying the official norms of Valencian usage, adhering to the standard set by the Norms of Castelló. This standard is universally adopted by writers in Valencian, with the sole exception of the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture (RACV), which employs an independent normative system.

input: Many instruments originated during the Renaissance; others were variations of, or improvements upon, instruments that had existed previously. Some have survived to the present day; others have disappeared, only to be recreated in order to perform music of the period on authentic instruments. As in the modern day, instruments may be classified as brass, strings, percussion, and woodwind.
rewrite: Numerous instruments emerged during the Renaissance, while others were adaptations or enhancements of earlier models. Some persist today, whereas others, having fallen into disuse, have been reconstructed to perform period music authentically. Instruments from this era, much like contemporary ones, are categorized as brass, strings, percussion, and woodwind.

input: Various classes of Vajrayana literature developed as a result of royal courts sponsoring both Buddhism and Saivism. The Mañjusrimulakalpa, which later came to classified under Kriyatantra, states that mantras taught in the Saiva, Garuda and Vaisnava tantras will be effective if applied by Buddhists since they were all taught originally by Manjushri. The Guhyasiddhi of Padmavajra, a work associated with the Guhyasamaja tradition, prescribes acting as a Saiva guru and initiating members into Saiva Siddhanta scriptures and mandalas. The Samvara tantra texts adopted the pitha list from the Saiva text Tantrasadbhava, introducing a copying error where a deity was mistaken for a place.
rewrite: The development of diverse Vajrayana literary classes was facilitated by royal patronage extended to both Buddhist and Śaiva traditions. The *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*—later categorized as a Kriyātantra—asserts that mantras from Śaiva, Gāruḍa, and Vaiṣṇava tantras remain efficacious for Buddhists, as they were originally taught by Mañjuśrī. Within the Guhyasamāja tradition, Padmavajra’s *Guhyasiddhi* advises assuming the role of a Śaiva guru to initiate adherents into Śaiva Siddhānta scriptures and maṇḍalas. Furthermore, texts of the Samvara tradition incorporated a *pīṭha* list from the Śaiva *Tantrasadbhāva*, inadvertently perpetuating a scribal error that misidentified a deity as a sacred site.

input: The process was completed in 27 BC when the Roman Emperor Augustus annexed the rest of Greece and constituted it as the senatorial province of Achaea. Despite their military superiority, the Romans admired and became heavily influenced by the achievements of Greek culture, hence Horace's famous statement: Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit ("Greece, although captured, took its wild conqueror captive"). The epics of Homer inspired the Aeneid of Virgil, and authors such as Seneca the younger wrote using Greek styles. Roman heroes such as Scipio Africanus, tended to study philosophy and regarded Greek culture and science as an example to be followed. Similarly, most Roman emperors maintained an admiration for things Greek in nature. The Roman Emperor Nero visited Greece in AD 66, and performed at the Ancient Olympic Games, despite the rules against non-Greek participation. Hadrian was also particularly fond of the Greeks; before he became emperor he served as an eponymous archon of Athens.
rewrite: The annexation of the remaining Greek territories was finalized in 27 BC under Emperor Augustus, who organized them into the senatorial province of Achaea. Notwithstanding their military dominance, the Romans held profound admiration for Greek cultural achievements and were significantly shaped by them. This dynamic is encapsulated in Horace’s dictum, *Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit* (“Captive Greece captured her savage conqueror”). Greek influence permeated Roman literature, with Virgil’s *Aeneid* drawing upon Homeric epic and authors like Seneca the Younger adopting Hellenic styles. Roman elites, exemplified by Scipio Africanus, often studied Greek philosophy and esteemed its intellectual traditions. This reverence extended to the imperial level, with many emperors cultivating Hellenic tastes. Nero famously competed in the Olympic Games of AD 66, flouting prohibitions on non-Greek competitors. Similarly, Hadrian, who served as archon of Athens prior to his reign, demonstrated particular affinity for Greek culture.

input: The managing director of London Weekend Television (LWT), Greg Dyke, met with the representatives of the "big five" football clubs in England in 1990. The meeting was to pave the way for a break away from The Football League. Dyke believed that it would be more lucrative for LWT if only the larger clubs in the country were featured on national television and wanted to establish whether the clubs would be interested in a larger share of television rights money. The five clubs decided it was a good idea and decided to press ahead with it; however, the league would have no credibility without the backing of The Football Association and so David Dein of Arsenal held talks to see whether the FA were receptive to the idea. The FA did not enjoy an amicable relationship with the Football League at the time and considered it as a way to weaken the Football League's position.
rewrite: In 1990, Greg Dyke, the Managing Director of London Weekend Television (LWT), convened a meeting with representatives of England's five largest football clubs. The purpose was to explore the feasibility of forming a breakaway competition from the established Football League. Dyke's commercial rationale centered on the proposition that televising matches exclusively involving the nation's major clubs would prove more lucrative for LWT; he sought to ascertain the clubs' interest in securing a substantially larger portion of television rights revenue. The clubs responded favorably to the proposal and resolved to proceed. Recognizing that any new league would lack legitimacy without the sanction of The Football Association (FA), David Dein of Arsenal subsequently initiated discussions to gauge the FA's receptiveness. The FA, whose relationship with the Football League was strained at the time, perceived the initiative as a potential mechanism to diminish the League's authority.

input: In abstract algebra, more general structures are defined by relaxing some of the axioms defining a group. For example, if the requirement that every element has an inverse is eliminated, the resulting algebraic structure is called a monoid. The natural numbers N (including 0) under addition form a monoid, as do the nonzero integers under multiplication (Z ∖ {0}, ·), see above. There is a general method to formally add inverses to elements to any (abelian) monoid, much the same way as (Q ∖ {0}, ·) is derived from (Z ∖ {0}, ·), known as the Grothendieck group. Groupoids are similar to groups except that the composition a • b need not be defined for all a and b. They arise in the study of more complicated forms of symmetry, often in topological and analytical structures, such as the fundamental groupoid or stacks. Finally, it is possible to generalize any of these concepts by replacing the binary operation with an arbitrary n-ary one (i.e. an operation taking n arguments). With the proper generalization of the group axioms this gives rise to an n-ary group. The table gives a list of several structures generalizing groups.
rewrite: Within the domain of abstract algebra, more generalized algebraic structures are constructed by relaxing one or more of the axioms that define a group. For instance, removing the axiom requiring every element to possess an inverse yields a structure termed a monoid. The set of natural numbers ℕ (including zero) under addition constitutes a monoid, as does the set of nonzero integers under multiplication (ℤ ∖ {0}, ·). A formal procedure exists for adjoining inverses to the elements of any commutative monoid, analogous to the construction of the nonzero rationals (ℚ ∖ {0}, ·) from the nonzero integers; this yields a structure known as a Grothendieck group. Groupoids represent another generalization, relaxing the requirement that the binary operation be defined for every pair of elements. These structures are significant in the analysis of complex symmetries, frequently appearing within topological and analytical contexts, such as in the fundamental groupoid or in the theory of stacks. A further generalization involves replacing the binary operation with an n-ary operation (i.e., one taking n arguments). Appropriately adapting the group axioms for this context leads to the concept of an n-ary group. The accompanying table enumerates several of these group-like structures.

input: The most notable cricket club in Cork is Cork County Cricket Club, which was formed in 1874. Although located within the Munster jurisdiction, the club plays in the Leinster Senior League. The club plays at the Mardyke, a ground which has hosted three first-class matches in 1947, 1961 and 1973. All three involved Ireland playing Scotland. The Cork Cricket Academy operates within the city, with the stated aim of introducing the sport to schools in the city and county. Cork's other main cricket club, Harlequins Cricket Club, play close to Cork Airport.
rewrite: Cork County Cricket Club, established in 1874, is the city's preeminent cricket institution. Despite its location within the Munster region, it competes in the Leinster Senior League. Its home ground, the Mardyke, has hosted three first-class matches, all between Ireland and Scotland, in 1947, 1961, and 1973. The Cork Cricket Academy operates with the objective of promoting the sport in local schools. Another principal club, Harlequins Cricket Club, is situated near Cork Airport.

input: Throughout its prehistory and early history, the region and its vicinity in the Yangtze region was the cradle of unique local civilizations which can be dated back to at least the 15th century BC and coinciding with the later years of the Shang and Zhou dynasties in North China. Sichuan was referred to in ancient Chinese sources as Ba-Shu (巴蜀), an abbreviation of the kingdoms of Ba and Shu which existed within the Sichuan Basin. Ba included Chongqing and the land in eastern Sichuan along the Yangtze and some tributary streams, while Shu included today's Chengdu, its surrounding plain and adjacent territories in western Sichuan.
rewrite: The region encompassing the Sichuan Basin and adjacent areas of the Yangtze River valley served as a cradle for distinct local civilizations from prehistory through early history. These cultures, traceable to at least the 15th century BC, were contemporaneous with the later Shang and Zhou dynasties of North China. In ancient Chinese records, the area was denoted as Ba-Shu (巴蜀), a compound referencing the separate kingdoms of Ba and Shu. The kingdom of Ba occupied territory in eastern Sichuan, including present-day Chongqing and lands along the Yangtze and its tributaries, whereas Shu was centered on the Chengdu plain and western Sichuan.

input: In addressing the question of who invented the incandescent lamp, historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel list 22 inventors of incandescent lamps prior to Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. They conclude that Edison's version was able to outstrip the others because of a combination of three factors: an effective incandescent material, a higher vacuum than others were able to achieve (by use of the Sprengel pump) and a high resistance that made power distribution from a centralized source economically viable.
rewrite: Historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel identify twenty-two inventors of incandescent lamps preceding Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. Their analysis concludes that Edison's design surpassed its predecessors due to three critical factors: the development of an efficient incandescent material, the achievement of a superior vacuum via the Sprengel pump, and a high-resistance configuration that enabled economically viable centralized power distribution.

input: Literature consists of written productions, often restricted to those deemed to have artistic or intellectual value. Its Latin root literatura/litteratura (derived itself from littera, letter or handwriting) was used to refer to all written accounts, but intertwined with the roman concept of cultura: learning or cultivation. Literature often uses language differently than ordinary language (see literariness). Literature can be classified according to whether it is fiction or non-fiction and whether it is poetry or prose; it can be further distinguished according to major forms such as the novel, short story or drama; and works are often categorised according to historical periods or their adherence to certain aesthetic features or expectations (genre).
rewrite: Literature comprises written works, typically those ascribed artistic or intellectual merit. Etymologically, the term originates from the Latin *litteratura*, itself derived from *littera* (letter), which initially denoted all written records. This concept was closely allied with the Roman notion of *cultura*, meaning learning or cultivation. Literary language frequently employs distinctive stylistic devices, setting it apart from ordinary discourse—a quality termed literariness. Categorizations of literature include the divisions of fiction and non-fiction, poetry and prose. Further classification occurs through major forms like the novel, short story, and drama, as well as by historical period or adherence to specific aesthetic conventions and genres.

input: The court ruled in 2014, after lengthy testimony, that at least two districts had to be redrawn because of gerrymandering. After this was appealed, in July 2015 the Florida Supreme Court ruled that lawmakers had followed an illegal and unconstitutional process overly influenced by party operatives, and ruled that at least eight districts had to be redrawn. On December 2, 2015, a 5-2 majority of the Court accepted a new map of congressional districts, some of which was drawn by challengers. Their ruling affirmed the map previously approved by Leon County Judge Terry Lewis, who had overseen the original trial. It particularly makes changes in South Florida. There are likely to be additional challenges to the map and districts.
rewrite: In 2014, following extensive testimony, a court determined that a minimum of two districts required redrawing due to gerrymandering. Upon appeal, the Florida Supreme Court ruled in July 2015 that the legislature had employed an unconstitutional process unduly shaped by partisan operatives, ordering the revision of at least eight districts. Subsequently, on December 2, 2015, the Court, by a 5-2 majority, adopted a new congressional map—portions of which were submitted by the plaintiffs—thereby affirming a plan earlier ratified by Leon County Circuit Judge Terry Lewis, the presiding officer at the initial trial. The revisions notably affect South Florida, though the map remains subject to potential future legal challenges.

input: All signatories to the CPPCG are required to prevent and punish acts of genocide, both in peace and wartime, though some barriers make this enforcement difficult. In particular, some of the signatories—namely, Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and former Yugoslavia—signed with the proviso that no claim of genocide could be brought against them at the International Court of Justice without their consent. Despite official protests from other signatories (notably Cyprus and Norway) on the ethics and legal standing of these reservations, the immunity from prosecution they grant has been invoked from time to time, as when the United States refused to allow a charge of genocide brought against it by former Yugoslavia following the 1999 Kosovo War.
rewrite: All signatories to the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (CPPCG) are obligated to prevent and punish acts of genocide during both peacetime and war. However, the enforcement of this obligation faces significant challenges. A specific barrier arises from reservations lodged by several states—including Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and the former Yugoslavia. These reservations stipulate that no genocide claim may be brought against them at the International Court of Justice without their express consent. Despite formal objections from other parties, such as Cyprus and Norway, regarding the legality and propriety of these reservations, the conferred immunity has been utilized. This is exemplified by the United States’ rejection of a genocide charge filed by the former Yugoslavia related to the 1999 Kosovo War.

input: In the high villages people live in homes built according to medieval designs that withstand cold winters. The kitchen is separated from the living area (called the stube, the area of the home heated by a stove), and second-floor bedrooms benefit from rising heat. The typical Swiss chalet originated in the Bernese Oberland. Chalets often face south or downhill, and are built of solid wood, with a steeply gabled roof to allow accumulated snow to slide off easily. Stairs leading to upper levels are sometimes built on the outside, and balconies are sometimes enclosed.
rewrite: Inhabitants of elevated villages reside in dwellings constructed according to medieval designs, adapted to endure harsh winters. The kitchen is distinct from the primary living space, known as the *stube*, which is heated by a stove; second-floor bedrooms utilize this rising warmth. The archetypal Swiss chalet, originating in the Bernese Oberland, is typically oriented south or downhill. Built from solid timber with a steeply pitched roof to facilitate snow shedding, these structures may feature external staircases and enclosed balconies.

input: Like other governmental economic activities, also privatization, such as in the sale of government-owned property, is particularly at the risk of cronyism. Privatizations in Russia, Latin America, and East Germany were accompanied by large-scale corruption during the sale of the state owned companies. Those with political connections unfairly gained large wealth, which has discredited privatization in these regions. While media have reported widely the grand corruption that accompanied the sales, studies have argued that in addition to increased operating efficiency, daily petty corruption is, or would be, larger without privatization, and that corruption is more prevalent in non-privatized sectors. Furthermore, there is evidence to suggest that extralegal and unofficial activities are more prevalent in countries that privatized less.
rewrite: Similar to other state-led economic endeavors, privatization initiatives—including the divestment of public assets—are especially vulnerable to cronyism. The privatization processes in Russia, Latin America, and East Germany, for instance, were marred by extensive corruption during the transfer of state-owned enterprises, enabling politically connected individuals to amass substantial wealth and thereby discrediting such policies in these regions. Although media coverage has emphasized high-profile corruption associated with sales, research indicates that, alongside gains in operational efficiency, routine petty corruption is or would be greater in the absence of privatization, with corruption often more widespread in sectors that remain state-controlled. Additionally, evidence suggests that extralegal and informal economic activities tend to be more common in nations that have pursued less privatization.

input: Marvel held its own comic book convention, Marvelcon '75, in spring 1975, and promised a Marvelcon '76. At the 1975 event, Stan Lee used a Fantastic Four panel discussion to announce that Jack Kirby, the artist co-creator of most of Marvel's signature characters, was returning to Marvel after having left in 1970 to work for rival DC Comics. In October 1976, Marvel, which already licensed reprints in different countries, including the UK, created a superhero specifically for the British market. Captain Britain debuted exclusively in the UK, and later appeared in American comics.
rewrite: In the spring of 1975, Marvel hosted its proprietary convention, Marvelcon '75, and announced a subsequent event for 1976. During a Fantastic Four panel at the initial convention, Stan Lee declared the return of artist Jack Kirby to Marvel. Kirby, co-creator of many of Marvel's defining characters, had departed in 1970 for competitor DC Comics. Subsequently, in October 1976, Marvel—already engaged in international reprint licensing, such as in the United Kingdom—developed Captain Britain, a superhero tailored for the British market. The character debuted exclusively in the UK before later appearing in American publications.

input: Caesar became consul in 59 BC. His colleague, Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, was an extreme aristocrat. Caesar submitted the laws that he had promised Pompey to the assemblies. Bibulus attempted to obstruct the enactment of these laws, and so Caesar used violent means to ensure their passage. Caesar was then made governor of three provinces. He facilitated the election of the former patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher to the tribunate for 58 BC. Clodius set about depriving Caesar's senatorial enemies of two of their more obstinate leaders in Cato and Cicero. Clodius was a bitter opponent of Cicero because Cicero had testified against him in a sacrilege case. Clodius attempted to try Cicero for executing citizens without a trial during the Catiline conspiracy, resulting in Cicero going into self-imposed exile and his house in Rome being burnt down. Clodius also passed a bill that forced Cato to lead the invasion of Cyprus which would keep him away from Rome for some years. Clodius also passed a law to expand the previous partial grain subsidy to a fully free grain dole for citizens.
rewrite: In 59 BC, Gaius Julius Caesar assumed the consulship alongside his colleague, Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, a staunch optimate. Caesar presented to the popular assemblies the legislative measures he had pledged to Pompey. When Bibulus sought to obstruct their enactment, Caesar resorted to force to secure their passage. Following his consulship, Caesar obtained the governorship of three provinces. He subsequently engineered the election of the former patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher to the tribunate for 58 BC. Clodius proceeded to target two principal senatorial adversaries of Caesar: Marcus Porcius Cato and Marcus Tullius Cicero. Clodius harbored a personal enmity toward Cicero, who had testified against him in a prior sacrilege trial. Using his tribunician authority, Clodius prosecuted Cicero for executing Roman citizens without trial during the Catilinarian conspiracy, compelling Cicero into exile and leading to the destruction of his Roman residence. Furthermore, Clodius passed a bill appointing Cato to oversee the annexation of Cyprus, thereby removing him from Rome for an extended period. Additionally, Clodius enacted legislation transforming the existing partial grain subsidy into a fully free grain dole for the citizenry.

input: In the early 1970s (1973, to be particular) when the military junta took over power in Uruguay, art suffered in Montevideo. The art studios went into protest mode, with Rimer Cardillo, one of the country's leading artists, making the National Institute of Fine Arts, Montevideo a "hotbed of resistance". This resulted in the military junta coming down heavily on artists by closing the Fine Art Institute and carting away all the presses and other studio equipment. Consequently, the learning of fine arts was only in private studios run by people who had been let out of jail, in works of printing and on paper and also painting and sculpture. It resumed much later.
rewrite: Following the 1973 military coup in Uruguay, the artistic landscape in Montevideo was severely constrained. In protest, prominent artist Rimer Cardillo transformed the National Institute of Fine Arts into a center of dissent. The regime responded decisively, shuttering the Institute and confiscating its printing presses and studio equipment. Consequently, formal artistic instruction was displaced to private studios, often led by formerly imprisoned artists, where practices such as printmaking, works on paper, painting, and sculpture continued. This decentralized mode of education persisted until institutional training was restored much later.

input: Native American music in North America is almost entirely monophonic, but there are notable exceptions. Traditional Native American music often centers around drumming. Rattles, clappersticks, and rasps were also popular percussive instruments. Flutes were made of rivercane, cedar, and other woods. The tuning of these flutes is not precise and depends on the length of the wood used and the hand span of the intended player, but the finger holes are most often around a whole step apart and, at least in Northern California, a flute was not used if it turned out to have an interval close to a half step. The Apache fiddle is a single stringed instrument.
rewrite: The musical traditions of Native American cultures across North America are predominantly monophonic, with certain notable deviations. Central to these traditions is percussive instrumentation, primarily drumming, alongside rattles, clappersticks, and rasps. Melodic elements are often produced by flutes, constructed from materials such as rivercane and cedar. The tuning of these flutes is imprecise, contingent upon the length of the wood and the hand span of the player; finger holes are typically spaced approximately a whole step apart. Notably, in Northern California, flutes exhibiting intervals approaching a half step were traditionally avoided. Another distinct instrument is the single-string Apache fiddle.

input: A revolution in 1332 resulted in a broad-based city government with participation of the guilds, and Strasbourg declared itself a free republic. The deadly bubonic plague of 1348 was followed on 14 February 1349 by one of the first and worst pogroms in pre-modern history: over a thousand Jews were publicly burnt to death, with the remainder of the Jewish population being expelled from the city. Until the end of the 18th century, Jews were forbidden to remain in town after 10 pm. The time to leave the city was signalled by a municipal herald blowing the Grüselhorn (see below, Museums, Musée historique);. A special tax, the Pflastergeld (pavement money), was furthermore to be paid for any horse that a Jew would ride or bring into the city while allowed to.
rewrite: The revolution of 1332 established a broad-based municipal government incorporating guild participation, leading Strasbourg to declare itself a free republic. Subsequently, the devastating bubonic plague of 1348 was followed on 14 February 1349 by one of the earliest and most severe pogroms in pre-modern Europe, during which over a thousand Jews were publicly burned and the remainder expelled. Thereafter, until the late eighteenth century, Jewish individuals were prohibited from remaining within the city after 10 p.m., with a municipal herald sounding the *Grüselhorn* to signal the curfew. Additionally, a special levy known as the *Pflastergeld* (pavement money) was imposed on any horse ridden or brought into the city by a Jew during permitted hours.

input: Valleys and plains are found along the coastline and rivers. The north of the province lies just south of the Yangtze Delta, and consists of plains around the cities of Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou, where the Grand Canal of China enters from the northern border to end at Hangzhou. Another relatively flat area is found along the Qu River around the cities of Quzhou and Jinhua. Major rivers include the Qiangtang and Ou Rivers. Most rivers carve out valleys in the highlands, with plenty of rapids and other features associated with such topography. Well-known lakes include the West Lake of Hangzhou and the South Lake of Jiaxing.
rewrite: The province's topography features valleys and plains situated along the coastline and major rivers. Its northern region, positioned immediately south of the Yangtze Delta, comprises the plains surrounding Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou; here, the Grand Canal of China enters from the north and terminates at Hangzhou. A second area of relatively low relief is located along the Qu River near Quzhou and Jinhua. Principal rivers, such as the Qiangtang and Ou, predominantly flow through highland valleys characterized by rapids and associated topographic features. Notable lakes include Hangzhou's West Lake and Jiaxing's South Lake.

input: After almost a year in the area around Peenemünde, Soviet officials moved most of the captured German rocket specialists to Gorodomlya Island on Lake Seliger, about 240 kilometers (150 mi) northwest of Moscow. They were not allowed to participate in Soviet missile design, but were used as problem-solving consultants to the Soviet engineers. They helped in the following areas: the creation of a Soviet version of the A-4; work on "organizational schemes"; research in improving the A-4 main engine; development of a 100-ton engine; assistance in the "layout" of plant production rooms; and preparation of rocket assembly using German components. With their help, particularly Helmut Groettrup's group, Korolev reverse-engineered the A-4 and built his own version of the rocket, the R-1, in 1948. Later, he developed his own distinct designs, though many of these designs were influenced by the Groettrup Group's G4-R10 design from 1949. The Germans were eventually repatriated in 1951–53.
rewrite: Following approximately one year in the vicinity of Peenemünde, Soviet authorities relocated the majority of captured German rocket specialists to Gorodomlya Island on Lake Seliger, situated roughly 240 kilometers northwest of Moscow. Although prohibited from direct involvement in Soviet missile design, these specialists served as consulting problem-solvers for Soviet engineering teams. Their contributions encompassed several key areas: developing a Soviet variant of the A-4 rocket; advising on organizational methodologies; conducting research to enhance the A-4 main engine; participating in the development of a 100-ton engine; assisting in the spatial planning of production facilities; and preparing rocket assemblies utilizing German components. Notably, with assistance from Helmut Groettrup's team, Sergei Korolev successfully reverse-engineered the A-4, leading to the construction of the R-1 rocket in 1948. While Korolev's subsequent designs were original, they reflected the influence of the Groettrup Group's 1949 G4-R10 concept. The German specialists were ultimately repatriated between 1951 and 1953.

input: Various evolutionary ideas had already been proposed to explain new findings in biology. There was growing support for such ideas among dissident anatomists and the general public, but during the first half of the 19th century the English scientific establishment was closely tied to the Church of England, while science was part of natural theology. Ideas about the transmutation of species were controversial as they conflicted with the beliefs that species were unchanging parts of a designed hierarchy and that humans were unique, unrelated to other animals. The political and theological implications were intensely debated, but transmutation was not accepted by the scientific mainstream.
rewrite: Prior to the mid-nineteenth century, numerous evolutionary concepts had been advanced to account for emerging biological evidence. While such ideas garnered increasing support from dissenting anatomists and the public, the English scientific establishment of this period remained intimately connected to the Church of England, with science largely situated within natural theology. Theories of species transmutation proved particularly contentious, as they challenged the prevailing doctrines of fixed species within a designed hierarchy and human exceptionalism. Consequently, despite vigorous debate over their political and theological ramifications, transmutationist theories were not embraced by mainstream scientific thought.

input: In May 1967, the Eastern Region declared independence as a state called the Republic of Biafra, under the leadership of Lt. Colonel Emeka Ojukwu. The Nigerian Civil War began as the official Nigerian government side (predominated by soldiers from the North and West) attacked Biafra (Southeastern) on 6 July 1967 at Garkem. The 30 month war, with a long siege of Biafra and its isolation from trade and supplies, ended in January 1970. Estimates of the number of dead in the former Eastern Region are between 1 and 3 million people, from warfare, disease, and starvation, during the 30-month civil war.
rewrite: In May 1967, the Eastern Region of Nigeria seceded, proclaiming itself the Republic of Biafra under the leadership of Lieutenant Colonel Emeka Ojukwu. The ensuing Nigerian Civil War commenced on July 6, 1967, when federal forces, predominantly from the northern and western regions, launched an assault on Biafra at Garkem. A protracted thirty-month conflict followed, characterized by a prolonged siege of Biafra that severed its access to trade and supplies. The war concluded in January 1970. Estimates suggest that between one and three million people in the former Eastern Region perished as a consequence of warfare, disease, and starvation during the conflict.

input: Meleager and the infantry supported the candidacy of Alexander's half-brother, Philip Arrhidaeus, while Perdiccas, the leading cavalry commander, supported waiting until the birth of Alexander's unborn child by Roxana. After the infantry stormed the palace of Babylon, a compromise was arranged – Arrhidaeus (as Philip III) should become king, and should rule jointly with Roxana's child, assuming that it was a boy (as it was, becoming Alexander IV). Perdiccas himself would become regent (epimeletes) of the empire, and Meleager his lieutenant. Soon, however, Perdiccas had Meleager and the other infantry leaders murdered, and assumed full control. The generals who had supported Perdiccas were rewarded in the partition of Babylon by becoming satraps of the various parts of the empire, but Perdiccas' position was shaky, because, as Arrian writes, "everyone was suspicious of him, and he of them".
rewrite: Following the death of Alexander the Great, a succession dispute emerged between the infantry, led by Meleager, and the cavalry under Perdiccas. Meleager advocated for Alexander’s half-brother, Philip Arrhidaeus, while Perdiccas supported awaiting the birth of Alexander’s posthumous child by Roxana. After the infantry forced entry into the Babylonian palace, a compromise was established: Arrhidaeus would rule as Philip III, jointly with Roxana’s son if male (a condition fulfilled with the birth of Alexander IV). Perdiccas was appointed regent (epimeletes) with Meleager as his lieutenant. Perdiccas swiftly consolidated power, however, by orchestrating the murder of Meleager and other infantry commanders. He then rewarded his supporting generals with satrapies in the Partition of Babylon, yet his authority remained precarious. As noted by Arrian, mutual suspicion pervaded, leaving Perdiccas’s position inherently unstable.

input: In 1873, one of the first papers in modern medicine on the subject tried to explain the pathophysiology of the disease while one in 1872, concluded that asthma can be cured by rubbing the chest with chloroform liniment. Medical treatment in 1880, included the use of intravenous doses of a drug called pilocarpin. In 1886, F.H. Bosworth theorized a connection between asthma and hay fever. Epinephrine was first referred to in the treatment of asthma in 1905. Oral corticosteroids began to be used for this condition in the 1950s while inhaled corticosteroids and selective short acting beta agonist came into wide use in the 1960s.
rewrite: The evolution of asthma treatment reflects shifting medical paradigms. An 1873 publication offered an early pathophysiological explanation, contrasting with an 1872 conclusion advocating chest rubs with chloroform liniment. Therapeutic approaches in 1880 included intravenous pilocarpine. F.H. Bosworth postulated a link between asthma and hay fever in 1886. The therapeutic use of epinephrine was first documented in 1905. A significant transition occurred in the 1950s with the introduction of oral corticosteroids, followed in the 1960s by the widespread adoption of inhaled corticosteroids and selective short-acting beta-agonists.

input: In January 2008, Kaz Hirai, CEO of Sony Computer Entertainment, suggested that the console may start making a profit by early 2009, stating that, "the next fiscal year starts in April and if we can try to achieve that in the next fiscal year that would be a great thing" and that "[profitability] is not a definite commitment, but that is what I would like to try to shoot for". However, market analysts Nikko Citigroup have predicted that PlayStation 3 could be profitable by August 2008. In a July 2008 interview, Hirai stated that his objective is for PlayStation 3 to sell 150 million units by its ninth year, surpassing PlayStation 2's sales of 140 million in its nine years on the market. In January 2009 Sony announced that their gaming division was profitable in Q3 2008.
rewrite: In January 2008, Kaz Hirai, then Chief Executive Officer of Sony Computer Entertainment, indicated that the PlayStation 3 console might begin generating a profit by early 2009. He qualified this projection, stating that achieving profitability within the forthcoming fiscal year commencing in April would be a significant objective, while clarifying it was "not a definite commitment" but rather a target. Concurrently, analysts from Nikko Citigroup forecast potential profitability as early as August 2008. Furthermore, in a July 2008 interview, Hirai articulated a long-term goal for the platform to surpass 150 million units sold within nine years, exceeding the PlayStation 2's lifetime sales. This was subsequently followed by a January 2009 announcement from Sony confirming that its gaming division had returned to profitability during the third quarter of 2008.

input: Besides emptiness, Mahayana schools often place emphasis on the notions of perfected spiritual insight (prajñāpāramitā) and Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). There are conflicting interpretations of the tathāgatagarbha in Mahāyāna thought. The idea may be traced to Abhidharma, and ultimately to statements of the Buddha in the Nikāyas. In Tibetan Buddhism, according to the Sakya school, tathāgatagarbha is the inseparability of the clarity and emptiness of one's mind. In Nyingma, tathāgatagarbha also generally refers to inseparability of the clarity and emptiness of one's mind. According to the Gelug school, it is the potential for sentient beings to awaken since they are empty (i.e. dependently originated). According to the Jonang school, it refers to the innate qualities of the mind that expresses themselves as omniscience etc. when adventitious obscurations are removed. The "Tathāgatagarbha Sutras" are a collection of Mahayana sutras that present a unique model of Buddha-nature. Even though this collection was generally ignored in India, East Asian Buddhism provides some significance to these texts.
rewrite: In addition to the concept of emptiness, Mahayana Buddhist traditions frequently emphasize the principles of perfected wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). Within Mahāyāna thought, interpretations of tathāgatagarbha vary. The concept's origins can be traced to the Abhidharma and, ultimately, to discourses attributed to the Buddha in the Nikāyas. In Tibetan Buddhism, the Sakya and Nyingma schools generally define tathāgatagarbha as the inseparable unity of the mind's clarity and emptiness. The Gelug school interprets it as the inherent potential for awakening in all sentient beings, grounded in their empty, dependently originated nature. Conversely, the Jonang school regards it as the mind's innate qualities, such as future omniscience, which manifest when extrinsic obscurations are eliminated. These ideas are central to the "Tathāgatagarbha Sutras," a distinct set of Mahayana scriptures that advance a particular Buddha-nature doctrine. While this corpus received limited attention in India, it holds considerable doctrinal significance within East Asian Buddhist traditions.

input: In 1978, Josep Lluís Núñez became the first elected president of FC Barcelona, and, since then, the members of Barcelona have elected the club president. The process of electing a president of FC Barcelona was closely tied to Spain's transition to democracy in 1974 and the end of Franco's dictatorship. The new president's main objective was to develop Barcelona into a world-class club by giving it stability both on and off the pitch. His presidency was to last for 22 years, and it deeply affected the image of Barcelona, as Núñez held to a strict policy regarding wages and discipline, letting go of such players as Maradona, Romário and Ronaldo rather than meeting their demands.
rewrite: The 1978 election of Josep Lluís Núñez as the inaugural president of FC Barcelona marked a pivotal shift to a democratic governance model for the club, a transition paralleling Spain's broader democratization following the Franco regime. His central mandate was to establish institutional stability and elevate Barcelona to global prominence. Núñez's subsequent 22-year tenure profoundly shaped the club's identity through a stringent fiscal and disciplinary policy. This approach prioritized long-term institutional control over accommodating star players' demands, as evidenced by the departures of high-profile figures such as Diego Maradona, Romário, and Ronaldo.

input: The United Kingdom's constitution, being uncodified and largely unwritten, makes no mention of a prime minister. Though it had de facto existed for centuries, its first mention in official state documents did not occur until the first decade of the twentieth century. Accordingly, it is often said "not to exist", indeed there are several instances of parliament declaring this to be the case. The prime minister sits in the cabinet solely by virtue of occupying another office, either First Lord of the Treasury (office in commission), or more rarely Chancellor of the Exchequer (the last of whom was Balfour in 1905).
rewrite: The United Kingdom’s constitution, being uncodified and predominantly unwritten, contains no explicit reference to the office of prime minister. Although the role had existed de facto for centuries, it was not formally acknowledged in official state documents until the early twentieth century. Consequently, it is frequently described as “not existing,” a view parliament itself has affirmed on multiple occasions. The prime minister holds a place in the cabinet only by virtue of occupying another ministerial office, typically that of First Lord of the Treasury (an office in commission) or, more rarely, Chancellor of the Exchequer, last held concurrently by Arthur Balfour in 1905.

input: The earliest known avialan fossils come from the Tiaojishan Formation of China, which has been dated to the late Jurassic period (Oxfordian stage), about 160 million years ago. The avialan species from this time period include Anchiornis huxleyi, Xiaotingia zhengi, and Aurornis xui. The well-known early avialan, Archaeopteryx, dates from slightly later Jurassic rocks (about 155 million years old) from Germany. Many of these early avialans shared unusual anatomical features that may be ancestral to modern birds, but were later lost during bird evolution. These features include enlarged claws on the second toe which may have been held clear of the ground in life, and long feathers or "hind wings" covering the hind limbs and feet, which may have been used in aerial maneuvering.
rewrite: The earliest documented avialan fossils originate from the Tiaojishan Formation in China, dated to the Oxfordian stage of the late Jurassic period, approximately 160 million years ago. Representative species from this formation include *Anchiornis huxleyi*, *Xiaotingia zhengi*, and *Aurornis xui*. The renowned *Archaeopteryx*, a slightly later avialan, derives from German deposits dating to roughly 155 million years ago. These early avialans exhibit several distinctive anatomical traits, potentially ancestral to modern birds but subsequently lost in avian evolution. Notable among these are hypertrophied second-toe claws, likely held retracted from the substrate, and elongated pennaceous feathers on the hind limbs, forming "hind wings" that may have facilitated aerial maneuverability.

input: Also in 2005, Spielberg directed a modern adaptation of War of the Worlds (a co-production of Paramount and DreamWorks), based on the H. G. Wells book of the same name (Spielberg had been a huge fan of the book and the original 1953 film). It starred Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning, and, as with past Spielberg films, Industrial Light & Magic (ILM) provided the visual effects. Unlike E.T. and Close Encounters of the Third Kind, which depicted friendly alien visitors, War of the Worlds featured violent invaders. The film was another huge box office smash, grossing over $591 million worldwide.
rewrite: In 2005, Steven Spielberg directed a contemporary adaptation of H. G. Wells's *War of the Worlds*, a project co-produced by Paramount and DreamWorks. A longstanding admirer of both the original novel and its 1953 film adaptation, Spielberg cast Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning in leading roles. Industrial Light & Magic, a frequent collaborator, supplied the visual effects. Departing from the benevolent extraterrestrials of his earlier works *E.T.* and *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*, this film presented a narrative of hostile alien invasion. It achieved substantial commercial success, earning over $591 million in global box office revenue.

input: Alongside the capital, the most popular tourist destinations are Isfahan, Mashhad and Shiraz. In the early 2000s, the industry faced serious limitations in infrastructure, communications, industry standards and personnel training. The majority of the 300,000 tourist visas granted in 2003 were obtained by Asian Muslims, who presumably intended to visit important pilgrimage sites in Mashhad and Qom. Several organized tours from Germany, France and other European countries come to Iran annually to visit archaeological sites and monuments. In 2003, Iran ranked 68th in tourism revenues worldwide. Weak advertising, unstable regional conditions, a poor public image in some parts of the world, and absence of efficient planning schemes in the tourism sector have all hindered the growth of tourism.
