The Umayyads significantly expanded the Muslim realm through conquests, integrating regions including the Caucasus, Transoxiana, Sindh, the Maghreb, and the Iberian Peninsula (Al-Andalus). At its peak, the caliphate encompassed approximately 15 million square kilometers, constituting the most extensive empire by land area in history to that date and the fifth-largest such polity ever recorded.

input: The scope of the term "post-punk" has been subject to controversy. While some critics, such as AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine, have employed the term "post-punk" to denote "a more adventurous and arty form of punk", others have suggested it pertains to a set of artistic sensibilities and approaches rather than any unifying style. Music journalist and post-punk scholar Simon Reynolds has advocated that post-punk be conceived as "less a genre of music than a space of possibility", suggesting that "what unites all this activity is a set of open-ended imperatives: innovation; willful oddness; the willful jettisoning of all things precedented or 'rock'n'roll'". Nicholas Lezard, problematizing the categorization of post-punk as a genre, described the movement as "so multifarious that only the broadest use of the term is possible".
rewrite: The precise definition of "post-punk" remains contested. Some critics, including Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic, apply the term to describe a more experimental and art-oriented extension of punk rock. Conversely, others argue it signifies a particular collection of artistic philosophies and methodologies rather than a coherent musical style. Scholar Simon Reynolds posits that post-punk should be understood not as a genre but as "a space of possibility," united by open-ended principles such as innovation and a deliberate rejection of established rock conventions. Echoing this complexity, Nicholas Lezard contends the movement is "so multifarious that only the broadest use of the term is possible," thereby challenging its categorization as a conventional genre.

input: The centre of Paris contains the most visited monuments in the city, including the Notre Dame Cathedral and the Louvre as well as the Sainte-Chapelle; Les Invalides, where the tomb of Napoleon is located, and the Eiffel Tower are located on the Left Bank south-west of the centre. The banks of the Seine from the Pont de Sully to the Pont d'Iéna have been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. Other landmarks are laid out east to west along the historic axis of Paris, which runs from the Louvre through the Tuileries Garden, the Luxor Column in the Place de la Concorde, the Arc de Triomphe, to the Grande Arche of La Défense.
rewrite: The historic core of Paris encompasses many of the city's most frequented monuments, such as Notre Dame Cathedral, the Louvre Museum, and the Sainte-Chapelle. The Left Bank, situated southwest of this centre, hosts Les Invalides—the site of Napoleon's tomb—and the Eiffel Tower. Since 1991, the Seine riverbanks between the Pont de Sully and the Pont d'Iéna have been designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Additional major landmarks are aligned along the city's historic east-west axis, extending from the Louvre through the Tuileries Garden and the Place de la Concorde, past the Arc de Triomphe, and concluding at the Grande Arche in La Défense.

input: His family was long associated with the teaching of elocution: his grandfather, Alexander Bell, in London, his uncle in Dublin, and his father, in Edinburgh, were all elocutionists. His father published a variety of works on the subject, several of which are still well known, especially his The Standard Elocutionist (1860), which appeared in Edinburgh in 1868. The Standard Elocutionist appeared in 168 British editions and sold over a quarter of a million copies in the United States alone. In this treatise, his father explains his methods of how to instruct deaf-mutes (as they were then known) to articulate words and read other people's lip movements to decipher meaning. Bell's father taught him and his brothers not only to write Visible Speech but to identify any symbol and its accompanying sound. Bell became so proficient that he became a part of his father's public demonstrations and astounded audiences with his abilities. He could decipher Visible Speech representing virtually every language, including Latin, Scottish Gaelic, and even Sanskrit, accurately reciting written tracts without any prior knowledge of their pronunciation.
rewrite: The Bell family maintained a longstanding affiliation with the discipline of elocution instruction. His grandfather, Alexander Bell, practiced in London, an uncle in Dublin, and his father, Melville Bell, in Edinburgh, all pursued this profession. His father authored numerous works on the subject, several of which remain notable, particularly *The Standard Elocutionist* (first published in Edinburgh in 1868, though dated 1860). This treatise achieved considerable circulation, appearing in 168 British editions and selling in excess of 250,000 copies in the United States alone. Within it, his father delineates his pedagogical techniques for instructing deaf individuals—termed deaf-mutes at the time—in articulate speech and lip-reading. Bell’s father educated him and his brothers not only in writing Visible Speech, a phonetic notation system, but also in recognizing any of its symbols and corresponding sounds. Bell attained remarkable proficiency, participating in his father’s public demonstrations and astonishing audiences with his skill. He could interpret Visible Speech transcriptions of diverse languages, including Latin, Scottish Gaelic, and Sanskrit, accurately reciting written passages without prior familiarity with their pronunciation.

input: Melbourne has a temperate oceanic climate (Köppen climate classification Cfb) and is well known for its changeable weather conditions. This is mainly due to Melbourne's location situated on the boundary of the very hot inland areas and the cool southern ocean. This temperature differential is most pronounced in the spring and summer months and can cause very strong cold fronts to form. These cold fronts can be responsible for all sorts of severe weather from gales to severe thunderstorms and hail, large temperature drops, and heavy rain.
rewrite: Melbourne experiences a temperate oceanic climate (Köppen Cfb), characterized by notably variable weather. This variability primarily stems from the city's position between hot continental interiors and the cooler Southern Ocean. The resulting temperature gradient, most acute during spring and summer, frequently generates intense cold fronts. These systems can produce severe weather phenomena, including gales, significant thunderstorms, hail, abrupt temperature declines, and heavy precipitation.

input: John XXIII died of peritonitis caused by a perforated stomach at 19:49 local time on 3 June 1963 at the age of 81, ending a historic pontificate of four years and seven months. He died just as a Mass for him finished in Saint Peter's Square below, celebrated by Luigi Traglia. After he died, his brow was ritually tapped to see if he was dead, and those with him in the room said prayers. Then the room was illuminated, thus informing the people of what had happened. He was buried on 6 June in the Vatican grottos. Two wreaths, placed on the two sides of his tomb, were donated by the prisoners of the Regina Coeli prison and the Mantova jail in Verona. On 22 June 1963, one day after his friend and successor Pope Paul VI was elected, the latter prayed at his tomb.
rewrite: Pope John XXIII succumbed to peritonitis resulting from a gastric perforation at 19:49 local time on 3 June 1963, concluding his historic pontificate of four years and seven months at the age of eighty-one. His death coincided with the conclusion of a Mass celebrated for him in Saint Peter's Square by Cardinal Luigi Traglia. Following his passing, a ritual verification of death was performed by tapping his brow, accompanied by prayers from those present. The subsequent illumination of his room signaled the event to the public. His interment occurred on 6 June within the Vatican grottos. Two floral wreaths adorning his tomb were donated by inmates of Regina Coeli and Mantova prisons. On 22 June 1963, his successor, Pope Paul VI, offered prayers at the tomb one day after his election.

input: The capital city, Washington, District of Columbia, is a federal district located on land donated by the state of Maryland. (Virginia had also donated land, but it was returned in 1849.) The United States also has overseas territories with varying levels of independence and organization: in the Caribbean the territories of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and in the Pacific the inhabited territories of Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands, along with a number of uninhabited island territories.
rewrite: Washington, D.C., the national capital, is a federal district situated on land ceded by Maryland. (Virginia also contributed territory, which was retroceded in 1849.) Furthermore, the United States administers several overseas territories. In the Caribbean, these include Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In the Pacific, the inhabited territories are Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands, in addition to numerous uninhabited island possessions.

input: New York's non-white population was 36,620 in 1890. New York City was a prime destination in the early twentieth century for African Americans during the Great Migration from the American South, and by 1916, New York City was home to the largest urban African diaspora in North America. The Harlem Renaissance of literary and cultural life flourished during the era of Prohibition. The larger economic boom generated construction of skyscrapers competing in height and creating an identifiable skyline.
rewrite: In 1890, New York's non-white population numbered 36,620. The city became a principal destination for African Americans during the early twentieth-century Great Migration, hosting North America's largest urban African diaspora by 1916. During the Prohibition era, the Harlem Renaissance saw a flourishing of literary and cultural activity. Concurrently, a broader economic expansion spurred competitive skyscraper construction, forming the city's distinctive skyline.

input: In eastern Pennsylvania the Great Appalachian Valley, or Great Valley, was accessible by reason of a broad gateway between the end of South Mountain and the Highlands, and many Germans and Moravians settled here between the Susquehanna and Delaware Rivers forming the Pennsylvania Dutch community, some of whom even now speak a unique American dialect of German known as the "Pennsylvania German language" or "Pennsylvania Dutch." These latecomers to the New World were forced to the frontier to find cheap land. With their followers of both German, English and Scots-Irish origin, they worked their way southward and soon occupied all of the Shenandoah Valley, ceded by the Iroquois, and the upper reaches of the Great Valley tributaries of the Tennessee River, ceded by the Cherokee.
rewrite: The Great Appalachian Valley in eastern Pennsylvania was accessible via a broad passage between South Mountain and the Highlands. This area attracted substantial settlement by Germans and Moravians between the Susquehanna and Delaware Rivers, forming the Pennsylvania Dutch community. A distinctive American dialect of German, known as Pennsylvania German or Pennsylvania Dutch, persists among some descendants. As later arrivals seeking affordable land, these settlers were pushed toward the frontier. Accompanied by followers of German, English, and Scots-Irish origin, they migrated southward. They subsequently populated the entire Shenandoah Valley, lands ceded by the Iroquois, and the upper tributaries of the Tennessee River within the Great Valley, territories ceded by the Cherokee.

input: Temperatures below 0 °C (32 °F) or above 25 °C (77 °F) are rare. Cork Airport records an average of 1,227.9 millimetres (4.029 ft) of precipitation annually, most of which is rain. The airport records an average of 7 days of hail and 11 days of snow or sleet a year; though it only records lying snow for 2 days of the year. The low altitude of the city, and moderating influences of the harbour, mean that lying snow very rarely occurs in the city itself. There are on average 204 "rainy" days a year (over 0.2 millimetres (0.0079 in) of rainfall), of which there are 73 days with "heavy rain" (over 5 millimetres (0.20 in)). Cork is also a generally foggy city, with an average of 97 days of fog a year, most common during mornings and during winter. Despite this, however, Cork is also one of Ireland's sunniest cities, with an average of 3.9 hours of sunshine every day and only having 67 days where there is no "recordable sunshine", mostly during and around winter.
rewrite: Meteorological extremes, defined as temperatures below 0 °C (32 °F) or above 25 °C (77 °F), are infrequent. Annual precipitation at Cork Airport averages 1,227.9 millimetres (4.029 ft), predominantly in the form of rain. The site experiences an average of 7 days of hail and 11 days of snow or sleet annually; however, snow cover is typically recorded for only 2 days per year. Due to the city's low altitude and the moderating influence of its harbour, settled snow is exceptionally rare within the urban area. Annually, there are approximately 204 "rainy days" (with over 0.2 mm of rainfall), including 73 days of "heavy rain" (exceeding 5 mm). Cork also experiences considerable fog, averaging 97 days per year, most prevalent during morning hours in winter. Notwithstanding this, Cork ranks among Ireland's sunniest cities, receiving an average of 3.9 hours of sunshine daily. Only 67 days per year, primarily in winter, lack recordable sunshine.

input: After the scandal, actress Brigitte Nielsen came forward and stated that she too had an affair with Schwarzenegger while he was in a relationship with Shriver, saying, "Maybe I wouldn't have got into it if he said 'I'm going to marry Maria' and this is dead serious, but he didn't, and our affair carried on." input: A more sophisticated MP3 encoder can produce variable bitrate audio. MPEG audio may use bitrate switching on a per-frame basis, but only layer III decoders must support it. VBR is used when the goal is to achieve a fixed level of quality. The final file size of a VBR encoding is less predictable than with constant bitrate. Average bitrate is VBR implemented as a compromise between the two: the bitrate is allowed to vary for more consistent quality, but is controlled to remain near an average value chosen by the user, for predictable file sizes. Although an MP3 decoder must support VBR to be standards compliant, historically some decoders have bugs with VBR decoding, particularly before VBR encoders became widespread.
rewrite: A more advanced MP3 encoder is capable of generating variable bitrate (VBR) audio. While MPEG audio standards permit bitrate switching on a per-frame basis, such functionality is mandatory only for Layer III decoders. VBR encoding is employed to maintain a consistent perceptual quality, which results in a less predictable final file size compared to constant bitrate (CBR) methods. Average bitrate (ABR) presents a compromise, allowing bitrate fluctuation for improved quality while constraining it around a user-defined average to ensure more predictable file sizes. Although standards compliance requires MP3 decoders to support VBR, historically some decoders contained flaws in VBR processing, especially prior to the widespread adoption of VBR encoders.

input: During the early 20th century it became increasingly common to bury cremated remains rather than coffins in the abbey. In 1905 the actor Sir Henry Irving was cremated and his ashes buried in Westminster Abbey, thereby becoming the first person ever to be cremated prior to interment at the abbey. The majority of interments at the Abbey are of cremated remains, but some burials still take place - Frances Challen, wife of the Rev Sebastian Charles, Canon of Westminster, was buried alongside her husband in the south choir aisle in 2014. Members of the Percy Family have a family vault, The Northumberland Vault, in St Nicholas's chapel within the abbey.
rewrite: During the early twentieth century, interment of cremated remains, as opposed to coffins, became increasingly prevalent at Westminster Abbey. This practice was notably inaugurated in 1905 with the burial of the cremated remains of the actor Sir Henry Irving. While the majority of increments at the Abbey now involve cremated remains, traditional coffin burials occasionally occur, such as the 2014 interment of Frances Challen beside her husband in the south choir aisle. Furthermore, designated family vaults exist within the abbey, including the Northumberland Vault for the Percy family in St. Nicholas's Chapel.

input: Subsequently, it became one of Britain's most significant honours to be buried or commemorated in the abbey. The practice of burying national figures in the abbey began under Oliver Cromwell with the burial of Admiral Robert Blake in 1657. The practice spread to include generals, admirals, politicians, doctors and scientists such as Isaac Newton, buried on 4 April 1727, and Charles Darwin, buried 26 April 1882. Another was William Wilberforce who led the movement to abolish slavery in the United Kingdom and the Plantations, buried on 3 August 1833. Wilberforce was buried in the north transept, close to his friend, the former Prime Minister, William Pitt.[citation needed]
rewrite: The abbey subsequently evolved into one of Britain's most distinguished sites for interment or commemoration. This tradition of entombing national figures originated with Oliver Cromwell's regime, commencing with Admiral Robert Blake in 1657. It expanded to encompass generals, admirals, politicians, physicians, and eminent scientists, including Isaac Newton, interred on 4 April 1727, and Charles Darwin, on 26 April 1882. Also among them was William Wilberforce, leader of the movement to abolish slavery in the United Kingdom and its plantations, buried on 3 August 1833 in the north transept near his friend, former Prime Minister William Pitt.

input: The geographical regions in which Iranian languages were spoken were pushed back in several areas by newly neighbouring languages. Arabic spread into some parts of Western Iran (Khuzestan), and Turkic languages spread through much of Central Asia, displacing various Iranian languages such as Sogdian and Bactrian in parts of what is today Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. In Eastern Europe, mostly comprising the territory of modern-day Ukraine, southern European Russia, and parts of the Balkans, the core region of the native Scythians, Sarmatians, and Alans had been decisively been taken over as a result of absorption and assimilation (e.g. Slavicisation) by the various Proto-Slavic population of the region, by the 6th century AD. This resulted in the displacement and extinction of the once predominant Scythian languages of the region. Sogdian's close relative Yaghnobi barely survives in a small area of the Zarafshan valley east of Samarkand, and Saka as Ossetic in the Caucasus, which is the sole remnant of the once predominant Scythian languages in Eastern Europe proper and large parts of the North Caucasus. Various small Iranian languages in the Pamirs survive that are derived from Eastern Iranian.
rewrite: The territorial expanse of Iranian languages experienced significant contraction in several regions due to the encroachment of neighboring linguistic groups. Arabic advanced into portions of Western Iran, notably Khuzestan, while Turkic languages disseminated across Central Asia, supplanting Iranian varieties such as Sogdian and Bactrian in areas encompassing present-day Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. In Eastern Europe, encompassing much of modern Ukraine, southern European Russia, and sections of the Balkans—the historic core of Scythian, Sarmatian, and Alanic populations—the indigenous Iranian languages were decisively displaced by the sixth century AD. This occurred primarily through processes of absorption and assimilation (e.g., Slavicization) by Proto-Slavic populations, leading to the extinction of the once-dominant Scythian languages in the region. Only fragmentary remnants persist: Yaghnobi, a close relative of Sogdian, endures in a limited zone of the Zarafshan valley east of Samarkand, while Saka survives as Ossetic in the Caucasus, representing the sole vestige of the formerly widespread Scythian linguistic group in Eastern Europe and much of the North Caucasus. Additionally, several minor Eastern Iranian-derived languages persist in the Pamir region.

input: All iPods except for the iPod Touch can function in "disk mode" as mass storage devices to store data files but this may not be the default behavior, and in the case of the iPod Touch, requires special software.[citation needed] If an iPod is formatted on a Mac OS computer, it uses the HFS+ file system format, which allows it to serve as a boot disk for a Mac computer. If it is formatted on Windows, the FAT32 format is used. With the release of the Windows-compatible iPod, the default file system used on the iPod line switched from HFS+ to FAT32, although it can be reformatted to either file system (excluding the iPod Shuffle which is strictly FAT32). Generally, if a new iPod (excluding the iPod Shuffle) is initially plugged into a computer running Windows, it will be formatted with FAT32, and if initially plugged into a Mac running Mac OS it will be formatted with HFS+.
rewrite: With the exception of the iPod Touch, all iPod models are capable of operating in a "disk mode," enabling them to function as mass storage devices for general data files. However, this is not necessarily the default setting, and for the iPod Touch, it requires the use of specialized third-party software. The file system employed by an iPod is contingent upon the operating system used for its initial formatting. When formatted via a Mac OS computer, the device utilizes the HFS+ file system, which permits it to act as a bootable drive for a Mac. If formatted on a Windows system, it adopts the FAT32 format. Following the introduction of Windows-compatible iPods, the default file system across the product line shifted from HFS+ to FAT32, though most models (excluding the iPod Shuffle, which is restricted to FAT32) can be reformatted to either system. Typically, a new iPod (again excluding the Shuffle) connected first to a Windows computer will be formatted as FAT32, while one first connected to a Mac OS system will be formatted as HFS+.

input: Cardigan formed up his unit and charged the length of the Valley of the Balaclava, under fire from Russian batteries in the hills. The charge of the Light Brigade caused 278 casualties of the 700-man unit. The Light Brigade was memorialized in the famous poem by Alfred Lord Tennyson, "The Charge of the Light Brigade." Although traditionally the charge of the Light Brigade was looked upon as a glorious but wasted sacrifice of good men and horses, recent historians say that the charge of the Light Brigade did succeed in at least some of its objectives. The aim of any cavalry charge is to scatter the enemy lines and frighten the enemy off the battlefield. The charge of the Light Brigade had so unnerved the Russian cavalry, which had previously been routed by the Heavy Brigade, that the Russian Cavalry was set to full-scale flight by the subsequent charge of the Light Brigade.:252
rewrite: Under the command of Lord Cardigan, the Light Brigade advanced in formation along the length of the Balaclava Valley, enduring sustained artillery fire from Russian batteries positioned on the surrounding heights. This action resulted in 278 casualties from the approximately 700-strong unit. The event was later immortalized in Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s poem, "The Charge of the Light Brigade." While traditional historiography has often portrayed the charge as a tragically futile, if heroic, sacrifice, more recent scholarly assessments argue it achieved certain tactical objectives. The fundamental purpose of a cavalry charge is to disrupt enemy formations and induce a retreat. In this instance, the assault by the Light Brigade so thoroughly demoralized the Russian cavalry—which had already been disordered by the preceding attack of the Heavy Brigade—that it precipitated their full-scale withdrawal from the battlefield.

input: Larry Christenson, a Lutheran theologian based in San Pedro, California, did much in the 1960s and 1970s to interpret the charismatic movement for Lutherans. A very large annual conference regarding that matter was held in Minneapolis. Charismatic Lutheran congregations in Minnesota became especially large and influential; especially "Hosanna!" in Lakeville, and North Heights in St. Paul. The next generation of Lutheran charismatics cluster around the Alliance of Renewal Churches. There is considerable charismatic activity among young Lutheran leaders in California centered around an annual gathering at Robinwood Church in Huntington Beach. Richard A. Jensen's Touched by the Spirit published in 1974, played a major role of the Lutheran understanding to the charismatic movement.
rewrite: Lutheran theologian Larry Christenson, based in San Pedro, California, was instrumental during the 1960s and 1970s in interpreting the charismatic movement for Lutheran audiences. A major annual conference on this subject convened in Minneapolis. Charismatic Lutheran congregations in Minnesota, notably Hosanna! in Lakeville and North Heights in St. Paul, grew particularly large and influential.
