input: In 1355 in Buda King Casimir III the Great issued the first country-wide privilege for the nobility, in exchange for their agreement that in the lack of Casimir's male heirs, the throne would pass to his nephew, Louis I of Hungary. He decreed that the nobility would no longer be subject to 'extraordinary' taxes, or use their own funds for military expeditions abroad. He also promised that during travels of the royal court, the king and the court would pay for all expenses, instead of using facilities of local nobility.
rewrite: In 1355, King Casimir III of Poland issued a comprehensive privilege to the nobility in Buda. This was granted in return for their acceptance that, should he lack male heirs, the throne would pass to his nephew, Louis I of Hungary. The decree permanently exempted the nobility from extraordinary taxes and personal financial obligations for foreign military campaigns. Furthermore, it guaranteed that the royal court would bear all expenses during its travels, ceasing the practice of requisitioning resources from local nobles.

input: The trophy comes in three parts - the cup itself, plus a lid and a base. There have been two designs of trophy in use, but five physical trophies have been presented. The original trophy, known as the "little tin idol", was 18 inches high and made by Martin, Hall & Co. It was stolen in 1895 and never recovered, and so was replaced by an exact replica, used until 1910. The FA decided to change the design after the 1909 winners, Manchester United, made their own replica, leading the FA to realise they did not own the copyright. This new, larger design was by Messers Fattorini and Sons, and was used from 1911. In order to preserve this original, from 1992 it was replaced by an exact replica, although this had to be replaced after just over two decades, after showing wear and tear from being handled more than in previous eras. This third replica, first used in 2014, was built heavier to withstand the increased handling. Of the four surviving trophies, only the 1895 replica has entered private ownership.
rewrite: The trophy comprises three components: the cup, a lid, and a base. While only two distinct designs have been employed, five physical trophies have been awarded. The initial trophy, colloquially termed the "little tin idol," stood 18 inches high and was crafted by Martin, Hall & Co. Following its theft in 1895, which resulted in its permanent loss, an exact replica was commissioned and remained in use until 1910. The Football Association (FA) subsequently opted for a new design after the 1909 winners, Manchester United, produced their own copy, thereby revealing the FA's lack of copyright ownership. This larger replacement, designed by Messrs Fattorini and Sons, was introduced in 1911. To conserve this original artifact, an exact replica was substituted from 1992 onward. However, due to pronounced wear from increased handling compared to earlier periods, this replica required replacement after slightly more than twenty years. A third replica, first presented in 2014, was constructed with greater durability to endure contemporary handling. Among the four surviving trophies, only the 1895 replica has passed into private ownership.

input: Roman government was headed by two consuls, elected annually by the citizens and advised by a senate composed of appointed magistrates. As Roman society was very hierarchical by modern standards, the evolution of the Roman government was heavily influenced by the struggle between the patricians, Rome's land-holding aristocracy, who traced their ancestry to the founding of Rome, and the plebeians, the far more numerous citizen-commoners. Over time, the laws that gave patricians exclusive rights to Rome's highest offices were repealed or weakened, and leading plebeian families became full members of the aristocracy. The leaders of the Republic developed a strong tradition and morality requiring public service and patronage in peace and war, making military and political success inextricably linked. Many of Rome's legal and legislative structures (later codified into the Justinian Code, and again into the Napoleonic Code) can still be observed throughout Europe and much of the world in modern nation states and international organizations.
rewrite: The Roman government was led by two annually elected consuls, guided by a senate of appointed magistrates. Its political evolution was fundamentally shaped by the conflict between the patrician aristocracy, who claimed descent from Rome's founders and initially monopolized high office, and the far more numerous plebeian commoners. Gradually, legal barriers excluding plebeians were repealed, enabling leading plebeian families to integrate into the governing elite. Republican leadership cultivated a powerful ethos linking political and military achievement, emphasizing public service and patronage in both peace and war. Consequently, Rome’s legal and legislative frameworks, later systematized in codes such as those of Justinian and Napoleon, have exerted a lasting influence, with their principles remaining observable in modern nation-states and international institutions globally.

input: The assumption that black-body radiation is thermal leads to an accurate prediction: the total amount of emitted energy goes up with the temperature according to a definite rule, the Stefan–Boltzmann law (1879–84). But it was also known that the colour of the light given off by a hot object changes with the temperature, so that "white hot" is hotter than "red hot". Nevertheless, Wilhelm Wien discovered the mathematical relationship between the peaks of the curves at different temperatures, by using the principle of adiabatic invariance. At each different temperature, the curve is moved over by Wien's displacement law (1893). Wien also proposed an approximation for the spectrum of the object, which was correct at high frequencies (short wavelength) but not at low frequencies (long wavelength). It still was not clear why the spectrum of a hot object had the form that it has (see diagram).
rewrite: The premise that black-body radiation is thermal yields the precise prediction that total emitted energy increases with temperature, as described by the Stefan–Boltzmann law (1879–84). It was further recognized that the color of light emitted by a heated object shifts with temperature, such that "white hot" corresponds to a higher temperature than "red hot." Utilizing the principle of adiabatic invariance, Wilhelm Wien derived the mathematical relationship governing the peaks of these spectral curves at varying temperatures, formalized as Wien’s displacement law (1893). Wien also formulated an approximation for the spectral distribution, which proved accurate at high frequencies (short wavelengths) but failed at low frequencies (long wavelengths). Despite these advances, the underlying reason for the specific form of the thermal spectrum remained unresolved.

input: Until the 1950s guns firing ballistic munitions were the standard weapon; guided missiles then became dominant, except at the very shortest ranges. However, the type of shell or warhead and its fuzing and, with missiles the guidance arrangement, were and are varied. Targets are not always easy to destroy; nonetheless, damaged aircraft may be forced to abort their mission and, even if they manage to return and land in friendly territory, may be out of action for days or permanently. Ignoring small arms and smaller machine-guns, ground-based air defence guns have varied in calibre from 20 mm to at least 150 mm.
rewrite: Until the 1950s, ballistic artillery represented the standard armament for air defense, after which guided missiles achieved dominance in all but the shortest-range engagements. The specific characteristics of the projectile or warhead, its fuzing mechanism, and, in the case of missiles, the guidance system, have always been subject to considerable variation. While targets are not invariably destroyed, even damaged aircraft can be compelled to abort their missions. Those that return to friendly territory may still be rendered inoperative for extended periods or permanently. Excluding small arms, ground-based air defense guns have historically ranged in caliber from 20 mm to at least 150 mm.

input: The major soap operas on British television each feature a pub, and these pubs have become household names. The Rovers Return is the pub in Coronation Street, the British soap broadcast on ITV. The Queen Vic (short for the Queen Victoria) is the pub in EastEnders, the major soap on BBC One and the Woolpack in ITV's Emmerdale. The sets of each of the three major television soap operas have been visited by some of the members of the royal family, including Queen Elizabeth II. The centrepiece of each visit was a trip into the Rovers, the Queen Vic, or the Woolpack to be offered a drink. The Bull in the BBC Radio 4 soap opera The Archers is an important meeting point.
rewrite: Each of the principal soap operas on British television features a central public house, establishments that have themselves attained significant cultural recognition. In ITV's *Coronation Street*, this is The Rovers Return; in BBC One's *EastEnders*, The Queen Victoria (commonly The Queen Vic); and in ITV's *Emmerdale*, The Woolpack. The sets of these three flagship television programmes have been toured by members of the royal family, including Queen Elizabeth II, with a ceremonial visit to the respective pub and the offering of a drink constituting a focal point of each occasion. Furthermore, The Bull serves as a vital communal hub in the BBC Radio 4 serial drama *The Archers*.

input: Terry Eastland, the author who wrote From Ending Affirmative Action: The Case for Colorblind Justice states, "Most arguments for affirmative action fall into two categories: remedying past discrimination and promoting diversity". Eastland believes that the founders of affirmative action did not anticipate how the benefits of affirmative action would go to those who did not need it, mostly middle class minorities. Additionally, she argues that affirmative action carries with it a stigma that can create feelings of self-doubt and entitlement in minorities. Eastland believes that affirmative action is a great risk that only sometimes pays off, and that without it we would be able to compete more freely with one another. Libertarian economist Thomas Sowell identified what he says are negative results of affirmative action in his book, Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study. Sowell writes that affirmative action policies encourage non-preferred groups to designate themselves as members of preferred groups [i.e., primary beneficiaries of affirmative action] to take advantage of group preference policies; that they tend to benefit primarily the most fortunate among the preferred group (e.g., upper and middle class blacks), often to the detriment of the least fortunate among the non-preferred groups (e.g., poor white or Asian); that they reduce the incentives of both the preferred and non-preferred to perform at their best – the former because doing so is unnecessary and the latter because it can prove futile – thereby resulting in net losses for society as a whole; and that they engender animosity toward preferred groups as well.:115–147
rewrite:
Terry Eastland, author of *Ending Affirmative Action: The Case for Colorblind Justice*, observes that the primary justifications for affirmative action typically center on remedying historical discrimination and promoting diversity. Eastland contends, however, that the policy’s architects failed to foresee its benefits accruing disproportionately to more advantaged, often middle-class, minority individuals, rather than to those most in need. Furthermore, she argues that affirmative action imposes a stigmatizing effect, potentially fostering self-doubt among beneficiaries and perceptions of unwarranted entitlement. Eastland ultimately posits the policy as a high-risk endeavor with inconsistent returns, suggesting that its absence would foster a more genuinely meritocratic and freely competitive society.

This perspective finds empirical support in the work of libertarian economist Thomas Sowell. In his study, *Affirmative Action Around the World: An Empirical Study*, Sowell delineates several adverse consequences. He asserts that such policies incentivize individuals from non-preferred groups to reclassify themselves into preferred groups to gain preferential treatment. Additionally, the benefits flow primarily to the most advantaged members within the preferred group—such as upper- and middle-class Black individuals—often at the expense of the least fortunate in non-preferred groups, including poor white or Asian populations. Sowell also argues that affirmative action diminishes performance incentives: for preferred group members, because advancement may seem assured without maximal effort, and for non-preferred members, because effort can appear futile. This dynamic, he concludes, results in aggregate societal losses and fosters resentment toward the groups designated for preferential treatment (pp. 115–147).

input: James Liebman, a professor of law at Columbia Law School, stated in 1996 that his study found that when habeas corpus petitions in death penalty cases were traced from conviction to completion of the case that there was "a 40 percent success rate in all capital cases from 1978 to 1995." Similarly, a study by Ronald Tabak in a law review article puts the success rate in habeas corpus cases involving death row inmates even higher, finding that between "1976 and 1991, approximately 47 percent of the habeas petitions filed by death row inmates were granted." The different numbers are largely definitional, rather than substantive. Freedam's statistics looks at the percentage of all death penalty cases reversed, while the others look only at cases not reversed prior to habeas corpus review.
rewrite: In a 1996 statement, Columbia Law School professor James Liebman reported that his research, tracking habeas corpus petitions in capital cases from conviction to final disposition between 1978 and 1995, revealed a 40 percent success rate. Correspondingly, an analysis by Ronald Tabak published in a law review found an even higher rate, indicating that approximately 47 percent of such petitions from death row inmates were granted from 1976 to 1991. This discrepancy in figures is attributed primarily to definitional distinctions rather than substantive disagreement. Liebman's statistic reflects the proportion of all death penalty cases ultimately reversed, whereas the other study considers only those cases not overturned prior to habeas corpus review.

input: Modern Ottoman studies think that the change in relations between the Ottoman Turks and central Europe was caused by the opening of the new sea routes. It is possible to see the decline in the significance of the land routes to the East as Western Europe opened the ocean routes that bypassed the Middle East and Mediterranean as parallel to the decline of the Ottoman Empire itself. The Anglo-Ottoman Treaty, also known as the Treaty of Balta Liman that opened the Ottoman markets directly to English and French competitors, would be seen as one of the staging posts along this development.
rewrite: Contemporary Ottoman scholarship posits that the shift in relations between the Ottoman Empire and Central Europe was precipitated by the establishment of new maritime routes. The diminishing importance of overland passages to the East, as Western Europe inaugurated oceanic trade lanes circumventing the Middle East and Mediterranean, is viewed as concomitant with the Empire's own decline. Within this trajectory, the Anglo-Ottoman Treaty of Balta Liman, which exposed Ottoman markets directly to British and French commercial competition, is regarded as a pivotal juncture.

input: Traditionally, subspecies are seen as geographically isolated and genetically differentiated populations. That is, "the designation 'subspecies' is used to indicate an objective degree of microevolutionary divergence" One objection to this idea is that it does not specify what degree of differentiation is required. Therefore, any population that is somewhat biologically different could be considered a subspecies, even to the level of a local population. As a result, Templeton has argued that it is necessary to impose a threshold on the level of difference that is required for a population to be designated a subspecies.
rewrite: The traditional conception of subspecies characterizes them as geographically isolated and genetically distinct populations, representing an objective degree of microevolutionary divergence. A significant critique of this framework is its failure to specify the requisite threshold of differentiation. Consequently, any population exhibiting minor biological distinctions, potentially even at a local level, could qualify as a subspecies. In response to this ambiguity, Templeton contends that establishing a formal criterion for the necessary level of divergence is essential for the designation.

input: At the Salon d'Automne of the same year, in addition to the Indépendants group of Salle 41, were exhibited works by André Lhote, Marcel Duchamp, Jacques Villon, Roger de La Fresnaye, André Dunoyer de Segonzac and František Kupka. The exhibition was reviewed in the October 8, 1911 issue of The New York Times. This article was published a year after Gelett Burgess' The Wild Men of Paris, and two years prior to the Armory Show, which introduced astonished Americans, accustomed to realistic art, to the experimental styles of the European avant garde, including Fauvism, Cubism, and Futurism. The 1911 New York Times article portrayed works by Picasso, Matisse, Derain, Metzinger and others dated before 1909; not exhibited at the 1911 Salon. The article was titled The "Cubists" Dominate Paris' Fall Salon and subtitled Eccentric School of Painting Increases Its Vogue in the Current Art Exhibition - What Its Followers Attempt to Do.
rewrite: At the Salon d'Automne of 1911, works were exhibited not only by the Indépendants group of Salle 41, but also by artists including André Lhote, Marcel Duchamp, Jacques Villon, Roger de La Fresnaye, André Dunoyer de Segonzac, and František Kupka. This exhibition was reviewed in the October 8, 1911, issue of *The New York Times*. The article appeared one year after Gelett Burgess' "The Wild Men of Paris" and two years prior to the Armory Show, which would later expose American audiences—accustomed to realism—to European avant-garde movements such as Fauvism, Cubism, and Futurism. Notably, the *Times* article, entitled "The 'Cubists' Dominate Paris' Fall Salon" and subtitled "Eccentric School of Painting Increases Its Vogue in the Current Art Exhibition—What Its Followers Attempt to Do," described works by Picasso, Matisse, Derain, Metzinger, and others dated before 1909, which were not actually displayed at the 1911 Salon.

input: For example, 1920×1080p25 identifies progressive scanning format with 25 frames per second, each frame being 1,920 pixels wide and 1,080 pixels high. The 1080i25 or 1080i50 notation identifies interlaced scanning format with 25 frames (50 fields) per second, each frame being 1,920 pixels wide and 1,080 pixels high. The 1080i30 or 1080i60 notation identifies interlaced scanning format with 30 frames (60 fields) per second, each frame being 1,920 pixels wide and 1,080 pixels high. The 720p60 notation identifies progressive scanning format with 60 frames per second, each frame being 720 pixels high; 1,280 pixels horizontally are implied.
rewrite: For instance, the notation 1920×1080p25 specifies a progressive scanning format operating at 25 frames per second, with each frame comprising 1,920 horizontal and 1,080 vertical pixels. Similarly, 1080i25 (or 1080i50) denotes an interlaced format at 25 frames (50 fields) per second, while 1080i30 (or 1080i60) indicates 30 frames (60 fields) per second, both maintaining the same 1920×1080 pixel resolution. Conversely, 720p60 describes a progressive format at 60 frames per second, with a resolution of 1,280 horizontal and 720 vertical pixels.

input: No further attempts to establish English colonies in the Americas were made until well into the reign of Queen Elizabeth I, during the last decades of the 16th century. In the meantime the Protestant Reformation had turned England and Catholic Spain into implacable enemies . In 1562, the English Crown encouraged the privateers John Hawkins and Francis Drake to engage in slave-raiding attacks against Spanish and Portuguese ships off the coast of West Africa with the aim of breaking into the Atlantic trade system. This effort was rebuffed and later, as the Anglo-Spanish Wars intensified, Elizabeth I gave her blessing to further privateering raids against Spanish ports in the Americas and shipping that was returning across the Atlantic, laden with treasure from the New World. At the same time, influential writers such as Richard Hakluyt and John Dee (who was the first to use the term "British Empire") were beginning to press for the establishment of England's own empire. By this time, Spain had become the dominant power in the Americas and was exploring the Pacific ocean, Portugal had established trading posts and forts from the coasts of Africa and Brazil to China, and France had begun to settle the Saint Lawrence River area, later to become New France.
rewrite: Subsequent endeavors to found English colonies in the Americas did not resume until the latter part of the sixteenth century, during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I. This interim period witnessed the Protestant Reformation transforming England and Catholic Spain into intractable adversaries. In 1562, the English Crown sanctioned privateers John Hawkins and Francis Drake to conduct slaving raids against Iberian vessels off West Africa, aiming to infiltrate the Atlantic commercial system. Repelled in this initial objective, and as the Anglo-Spanish Wars escalated, Elizabeth subsequently authorized further privateering campaigns against Spanish American ports and Atlantic treasure fleets returning from the New World. Concurrently, influential figures including Richard Hakluyt and John Dee—who first coined the term "British Empire"—began advocating for the creation of an English imperial domain. By this era, Spanish hegemony was established in the Americas with Pacific exploration underway, Portugal had developed a network of fortified trading posts from Africa and Brazil to China, and France had initiated settlement in the Saint Lawrence River region, the future New France.

input: In a movie theater, steps in the aisles are usually marked with a row of small lights for convenience and safety, when the film has started and the other lights are off. Traditionally made up of small low wattage, low voltage lamps in a track or translucent tube, these are rapidly being replaced with LED based versions.
rewrite: Aisles in cinemas are typically illuminated by a series of low-intensity lights to ensure safety and convenience after the main lighting is dimmed. While traditionally composed of low-wattage lamps within a track or tube, these systems are now being swiftly supplanted by LED alternatives.

input: Chopin's polonaises show a marked advance on those of his Polish predecessors in the form (who included his teachers Zywny and Elsner). As with the traditional polonaise, Chopin's works are in triple time and typically display a martial rhythm in their melodies, accompaniments and cadences. Unlike most of their precursors, they also require a formidable playing technique.
rewrite: Chopin's polonaises demonstrate significant development beyond those of his Polish predecessors, including his teachers Zywny and Elsner. While retaining the traditional triple meter and martial rhythmic character, they distinguish themselves through a formidable technical demand absent in most earlier works.

input: Erich Koch headed the East Prussian Nazi party from 1928. He led the district from 1932. This period was characterized by efforts to collectivize the local agriculture and ruthlessness in dealing with his critics inside and outside the Party. He also had long-term plans for mass-scale industrialization of the largely agricultural province. These actions made him unpopular among the local peasants. In 1932 the local paramilitary SA had already started to terrorise their political opponents. On the night of 31 July 1932 there was a bomb attack on the headquarters of the Social Democrats in Königsberg, the Otto-Braun-House. The Communist politician Gustav Sauf was killed; the executive editor of the Social Democrat "Königsberger Volkszeitung", Otto Wyrgatsch, and the German People's Party politician Max von Bahrfeldt were severely injured. Members of the Reichsbanner were attacked and the local Reichsbanner Chairman of Lötzen, Kurt Kotzan, was murdered on 6 August 1932.
rewrite: Erich Koch assumed leadership of the Nazi Party in East Prussia in 1928 and became Gauleiter of the district in 1932. His tenure was marked by policies aimed at agricultural collectivization and the severe suppression of dissent, both within and outside the Party. Furthermore, he pursued long-term ambitions for the large-scale industrialization of the predominantly agrarian province, generating significant discontent among the local peasantry. Concurrently, the regional paramilitary SA intensified its campaign of political terror. This culminated in a bomb attack on the Social Democratic headquarters, the Otto-Braun-House in Königsberg, on the night of 31 July 1932. The assault killed Communist politician Gustav Sauf and severely injured Otto Wyrgatsch, editor of the "Königsberger Volkszeitung," and German People's Party politician Max von Bahrfeldt. Subsequent violence included attacks on Reichsbanner members and the murder of its Lötzen chairman, Kurt Kotzan, on 6 August 1932.

input:
Spanish Supreme Court is the highest court for all cases in Spain (both private and public). Only those cases related to human rights can be appealed at the Constitutional Court (which also decides about acts accordance with Spanish Constitution).
In Spain, high courts cannot create binding precedents; however, lower rank courts usually observe Supreme Court interpretations. In most private law cases, two Supreme Court judgements supporting a claim are needed to appeal at the Supreme Court.
Five sections form the Spanish Supreme court:
rewrite: The Spanish Supreme Court serves as the highest judicial body for all domestic cases, encompassing both private and public law matters. Appeals to the Constitutional Court are restricted to issues concerning fundamental rights and constitutional review. While judicial precedent is not formally binding, lower courts typically adhere to Supreme Court jurisprudence. In private law, appealing to the Supreme Court generally requires two prior consistent rulings on the claim. The Court itself is organized into five specialized chambers.

input: The High Middle Ages was a period of tremendous expansion of population. The estimated population of Europe grew from 35 to 80 million between 1000 and 1347, although the exact causes remain unclear: improved agricultural techniques, the decline of slaveholding, a more clement climate and the lack of invasion have all been suggested. As much as 90 per cent of the European population remained rural peasants. Many were no longer settled in isolated farms but had gathered into small communities, usually known as manors or villages. These peasants were often subject to noble overlords and owed them rents and other services, in a system known as manorialism. There remained a few free peasants throughout this period and beyond, with more of them in the regions of Southern Europe than in the north. The practice of assarting, or bringing new lands into production by offering incentives to the peasants who settled them, also contributed to the expansion of population.
rewrite: The High Middle Ages witnessed a significant demographic expansion across Europe. The continent's estimated population rose from approximately 35 million to 80 million between the years 1000 and 1347. While the precise causal mechanisms are not definitively established, scholars have posited several contributing factors, including advancements in agricultural technology, the decline of slavery, a period of more favorable climatic conditions, and the absence of major invasions. Approximately ninety percent of this population consisted of rural peasants. A considerable proportion now resided not in isolated homesteads but within small, organized communities, typically referred to as manors or villages. Within the manorial system, these peasants were generally subject to noble lords, to whom they owed rents and various labor services. Despite this predominant structure, a limited number of free peasants persisted, with a higher concentration in Southern Europe compared to the north. Furthermore, the practice of assarting—clearing and settling new arable lands, often by offering incentives to peasant settlers—constituted another factor in this demographic growth.

input: Small-scale artisanal mining of gold is another source of dangerous child labour in poor rural areas in certain parts of the world. This form of mining uses labour-intensive and low-tech methods. It is informal sector of the economy. Human Rights Watch group estimates that about 12 percent of global gold production comes from artisanal mines. In west Africa, in countries such as Mali - the third largest exporter of gold in Africa - between 20,000 and 40,000 children work in artisanal mining. Locally known as orpaillage, children as young as 6 years old work with their families. These children and families suffer chronic exposure to toxic chemicals including mercury, and do hazardous work such as digging shafts and working underground, pulling up, carrying and crushing the ore. The poor work practices harm the long term health of children, as well as release hundreds of tons of mercury every year into local rivers, ground water and lakes. Gold is important to the economy of Mali and Ghana. For Mali, it is the second largest earner of its export revenue. For many poor families with children, it is the primary and sometimes the only source of income.
rewrite: Artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) constitutes a significant source of hazardous child labor within impoverished rural regions of several countries. Operating within the informal economic sector, this form of mining employs labor-intensive, low-technology methods. According to estimates by Human Rights Watch, approximately twelve percent of global gold output originates from such artisanal operations. In West Africa, notably in nations like Mali—the continent’s third-largest gold exporter—an estimated 20,000 to 40,000 children are engaged in ASGM. Referred to locally as *orpaillage*, this practice involves children as young as six working alongside their families. These laborers face chronic exposure to toxic substances, particularly mercury, and perform perilous tasks including shaft excavation, underground work, and the hauling, transport, and crushing of ore. Such dangerous working conditions severely compromise children’s long-term health, while poor mining practices also result in the annual release of hundreds of tons of mercury into local rivers, groundwater, and lakes. Although gold is economically vital—for Mali, it represents the second-largest export revenue source—for many impoverished families with children, it remains a primary, and often sole, means of subsistence.

input: In past times, mending was an art. A meticulous tailor or seamstress could mend rips with thread raveled from hems and seam edges so skillfully that the tear was practically invisible. When the raw material – cloth – was worth more than labor, it made sense to expend labor in saving it. Today clothing is considered a consumable item. Mass-manufactured clothing is less expensive than the labor required to repair it. Many people buy a new piece of clothing rather than spend time mending. The thrifty still replace zippers and buttons and sew up ripped hems.
rewrite: Historically, textile repair was a skilled craft. A proficient tailor or seamstress could meticulously mend tears using thread unraveled from garment hems and seams, rendering the damage nearly undetectable. This practice was economically rational when fabric held greater value than labor. In contemporary society, however, clothing is largely viewed as a disposable commodity. Mass-produced garments are often less costly than the labor required for their repair, prompting many consumers to replace items rather than mend them. Nonetheless, frugal individuals continue to perform basic repairs, such as replacing fasteners and stitching seams.

input: In early 1757, Frederick II again took the initiative by marching into the Kingdom of Bohemia, hoping to inflict a decisive defeat on Austrian forces. After winning the bloody Battle of Prague on 6 May 1757, in which both forces suffered major casualties, the Prussians forced the Austrians back into the fortifications of Prague. The Prussian army then laid siege to the city. Following the battle at Prague, Frederick took 5,000 troops from the siege at Prague and sent them to reinforce the 19,000-man army under the Duke of Brunswick-Bevern at Kolin in Bohemia. Austrian Marshal Daun arrived too late to participate in the battle of Prague, but picked up 16,000 men who had escaped from the battle. With this army he slowly moved to relieve Prague. The Prussian army was too weak to simultaneously besiege Prague and keep Daun away, and Frederick was forced to attack prepared positions. The resulting Battle of Kolin was a sharp defeat for Frederick, his first military defeat. His losses further forced him to lift the siege and withdraw from Bohemia altogether.
rewrite: In early 1757, King Frederick II of Prussia resumed the offensive by invading the Kingdom of Bohemia, aiming to deliver a decisive blow to Austrian forces. This campaign culminated in the sanguinary Battle of Prague on 6 May 1757, where both armies sustained significant casualties. Following this engagement, Prussian forces compelled the Austrians to retreat into Prague’s fortifications and subsequently initiated a siege of the city. Thereafter, Frederick detached 5,000 troops from the siege to reinforce the 19,000-man Prussian army commanded by the Duke of Brunswick-Bevern at Kolin. Meanwhile, Austrian Marshal Daun, arriving too late for the Battle of Prague, consolidated approximately 16,000 survivors from that defeat. With this force, Daun advanced methodically to relieve the besieged city. Confronted with an army insufficient both to maintain the siege and to counter Daun’s advance, Frederick was compelled to assault fortified Austrian positions. The ensuing Battle of Kolin concluded in a clear Prussian defeat, marking Frederick’s first major military reversal. These losses necessitated the abandonment of the siege and a full Prussian withdrawal from Bohemia.

input: A new generation of clubs such as Liverpool's Cream and the Ministry of Sound were opened to provide a venue for more commercial sounds. Major record companies began to open "superclubs" promoting their own acts. These superclubs entered into sponsorship deals initially with fast food, soft drinks, and clothing companies. Flyers in clubs in Ibiza often sported many corporate logos. A new subgenre, Chicago hard house, was developed by DJs such as Bad Boy Bill, DJ Lynnwood, DJ Irene, Richard "Humpty" Vission and DJ Enrie, mixing elements of Chicago house, funky house and hard house together. Additionally, Producers such as George Centeno, Darren Ramirez, and Martin O. Cairo would develop the Los Angeles Hard House sound. Similar to gabber or hardcore techno from the Netherlands, this sound was often associated with the "rebel" culture of the time. These 3 producers are often considered "ahead of their time" since many of the sounds they engineered during the late 20th century became more prominent during the 21st century.
rewrite: The late twentieth century witnessed the emergence of a new generation of nightclubs, exemplified by institutions such as Liverpool's Cream and the Ministry of Sound, which were established to showcase more commercially oriented musical styles. Concurrently, major record labels initiated the development of "superclubs" to promote their own artists. These venues secured early sponsorship agreements with corporations in the fast food, soft drink, and apparel industries, a commercial synergy evidenced by the proliferation of corporate logos on promotional flyers in locales like Ibiza. Within this context, distinct regional subgenres evolved. In Chicago, DJs including Bad Boy Bill, DJ Lynnwood, DJ Irene, Richard "Humpty" Vission, and DJ Enrie synthesized elements of Chicago house, funky house, and hard house to create Chicago hard house. Parallelly, producers George Centeno, Darren Ramirez, and Martin O. Cairo developed the Los Angeles hard house sound. This aggressive style, bearing similarities to Dutch gabber or hardcore techno, was frequently linked to contemporary "rebel" culture. These three producers are often regarded as avant-garde, as many of the sonic elements they engineered in the late 1900s gained significantly greater prominence in the twenty-first century.

input: In August 1836, two real estate entrepreneurs—Augustus Chapman Allen and John Kirby Allen—from New York, purchased 6,642 acres (26.88 km2) of land along Buffalo Bayou with the intent of founding a city. The Allen brothers decided to name the city after Sam Houston, the popular general at the Battle of San Jacinto, who was elected President of Texas in September 1836. The great majority of slaves in Texas came with their owners from the older slave states. Sizable numbers, however, came through the domestic slave trade. New Orleans was the center of this trade in the Deep South, but there were slave dealers in Houston. Thousands of enslaved African-Americans lived near the city before the Civil War. Many of them near the city worked on sugar and cotton plantations, while most of those in the city limits had domestic and artisan jobs. In 1860 forty-nine percent of the city's population was enslaved. A few slaves, perhaps as many as 2,000 between 1835 and 1865, came through the illegal African trade. Post-war Texas grew rapidly as migrants poured into the cotton lands of the state. They also brought or purchased enslaved African Americans, whose numbers nearly tripled in the state from 1850 to 1860, from 58,000 to 182,566.
rewrite: In August 1836, the New York-based real estate entrepreneurs Augustus Chapman Allen and John Kirby Allen acquired 6,642 acres (26.88 km²) of land along Buffalo Bayou with the explicit purpose of establishing an urban settlement. The brothers designated the nascent city "Houston" in honor of Sam Houston, the prominent general victorious at the Battle of San Jacinto, who was elected President of the Republic of Texas that September. The enslaved population in Texas primarily originated from migration with their owners from older slaveholding states, though a substantial number were introduced via the domestic slave trade. While New Orleans functioned as the central hub for this trade in the Deep South, slave dealers also operated in Houston. Prior to the Civil War, thousands of enslaved African Americans resided in the vicinity. Many labored on surrounding sugar and cotton plantations, whereas most within the municipal boundaries performed domestic and artisanal roles. By 1860, enslaved persons constituted forty-nine percent of the city's population. A limited number, estimated as high as 2,000 between 1835 and 1865, were illicitly imported through the ongoing African slave trade. In the antebellum period, Texas experienced rapid growth as migrants entered its cotton lands, often bringing or acquiring enslaved African Americans. Consequently, the state's enslaved population expanded from approximately 58,000 in 1850 to 182,566 by 1860.

input: Early Muslim armies stayed in encampments away from cities because Umar feared that they might get attracted to wealth and luxury. In the process, they might turn away from the worship of God and start accumulating wealth and establishing dynasties. When Uthman ibn al-Affan became very old, Marwan I, a relative of Muawiyah I, slipped into the vacuum, became his secretary, slowly assumed more control and relaxed some of these restrictions. Marwan I had previously been excluded from positions of responsibility. In 656, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, the son of Abu Bakr, the adopted son of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and the great grandfather of Ja'far al-Sadiq, showed some Egyptians the house of Uthman ibn al-Affan. Later the Egyptians ended up killing Uthman ibn al-Affan.
rewrite: Early Muslim military forces were initially quartered in segregated encampments distant from urban centers. This policy, instituted under Caliph Umar, aimed to prevent the soldiers from being seduced by material wealth and luxury, which he feared would lead them to neglect religious devotion and instead pursue personal fortune and dynastic rule. Following Umar, as Caliph Uthman ibn al-Affan aged, his relative Marwan I—previously barred from authority—inserted himself as the caliph’s secretary, gradually assumed greater power, and relaxed these original prohibitions. Subsequently, in 656 CE, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, a figure linked through lineage to Abu Bakr and Ali ibn Abi Talib, guided a group of Egyptians to Uthman’s residence, an event that culminated in the caliph’s assassination by those same Egyptians.

input: In the lead up to the Iraq War, Kerry said on October 9, 2002; "I will be voting to give the President of the United States the authority to use force, if necessary, to disarm Saddam Hussein because I believe that a deadly arsenal of weapons of mass destruction in his hands is a real and grave threat to our security." Bush relied on that resolution in ordering the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Kerry also gave a January 23, 2003 speech to Georgetown University saying "Without question, we need to disarm Saddam Hussein. He is a brutal, murderous dictator; leading an oppressive regime he presents a particularly grievous threat because he is so consistently prone to miscalculation. So the threat of Saddam Hussein with weapons of mass destruction is real." Kerry did, however, warn that the administration should exhaust its diplomatic avenues before launching war: "Mr. President, do not rush to war, take the time to build the coalition, because it's not winning the war that's hard, it's winning the peace that's hard."
rewrite: In the period preceding the military intervention in Iraq, Senator John Kerry articulated a position of conditional support for authorizing the use of force. On October 9, 2002, he stated his intention to vote in favor of granting the President authority to disarm Saddam Hussein, asserting that "a deadly arsenal of weapons of mass destruction in his hands is a real and grave threat to our security." This congressional resolution subsequently formed a legal basis for the 2003 invasion. In a subsequent address at Georgetown University on January 23, 2003, Kerry reaffirmed the imperative to disarm Hussein, characterizing him as a brutal dictator whose propensity for miscalculation rendered him a grievous threat. He maintained that the danger of weapons of mass destruction was genuine. Concurrently, however, Kerry issued a cautionary admonition, urging the administration to exhaust all diplomatic channels prior to any conflict, noting the greater difficulty resided in securing a stable peace rather than achieving military victory.

input: The same considerations about barriers and detours that apply to long-distance land-bird migration apply to water birds, but in reverse: a large area of land without bodies of water that offer feeding sites may also be a barrier to a bird that feeds in coastal waters. Detours avoiding such barriers are observed: for example, brent geese Branta bernicla migrating from the Taymyr Peninsula to the Wadden Sea travel via the White Sea coast and the Baltic Sea rather than directly across the Arctic Ocean and northern Scandinavia.
rewrite: The principles of barriers and detours in long-distance migration apply analogously to waterbirds, albeit inversely. For species dependent on aquatic feeding, extensive terrestrial expanses lacking suitable water bodies can function as barriers. Consequently, migratory detours are documented. For instance, brent geese (*Branta bernicla*) traveling from the Taymyr Peninsula to the Wadden Sea follow a coastal route via the White and Baltic Seas, avoiding a direct trans-Arctic passage over northern Scandinavia.

input: Domestication of sheep and goats reached Egypt from the Near East possibly as early as 6,000 BC. Graeme Barker states "The first indisputable evidence for domestic plants and animals in the Nile valley is not until the early fifth millennium bc in northern Egypt and a thousand years later further south, in both cases as part of strategies that still relied heavily on fishing, hunting, and the gathering of wild plants" and suggests that these subsistence changes were not due to farmers migrating from the Near East but was an indigenous development, with cereals either indigenous or obtained through exchange. Other scholars argue that the primary stimulus for agriculture and domesticated animals (as well as mud-brick architecture and other Neolithic cultural features) in Egypt was from the Middle East.
rewrite: The introduction of domesticated sheep and goats to Egypt from the Near East may have occurred as early as 6000 BC. However, as noted by Graeme Barker, definitive evidence for domesticates within the Nile valley emerges only in the early fifth millennium BC in the north and a millennium later in the south. These early agricultural practices were integrated into broader subsistence strategies still dependent on fishing, hunting, and foraging. Barker posits this transition was not the result of migrating Near Eastern farmers but rather an indigenous development, with cereals either cultivated locally or acquired via exchange. Conversely, other scholars contend that the primary impetus for agriculture, animal domestication, and associated Neolithic traits in Egypt derived from the Middle East.

input: The story sees Bond pitted against the global criminal organisation Spectre, marking the group's first appearance in an Eon Productions film since 1971's Diamonds Are Forever,[N 2] and tying Craig's series of films together with an overarching storyline. Several recurring James Bond characters, including M, Q and Eve Moneypenny return, with the new additions of Léa Seydoux as Dr. Madeleine Swann, Dave Bautista as Mr. Hinx, Andrew Scott as Max Denbigh and Monica Bellucci as Lucia Sciarra.
rewrite: The narrative positions Bond in opposition to the global criminal syndicate Spectre, marking the organization's inaugural appearance in an Eon Productions film since *Diamonds Are Forever* (1971) and unifying Craig's film series through an overarching plot. Recurring characters M, Q, and Eve Moneypenny return, joined by new portrayals from Léa Seydoux as Dr. Madeleine Swann, Dave Bautista as Mr. Hinx, Andrew Scott as Max Denbigh, and Monica Bellucci as Lucia Sciarra.

input: Trading companies became active in Tuvalu in the mid-19th century; the trading companies engaged palagi traders who lived on the islands. John (also known as Jack) O'Brien was the first European to settle in Tuvalu, he became a trader on Funafuti in the 1850s. He married Salai, the daughter of the paramount chief of Funafuti. Louis Becke, who later found success as a writer, was a trader on Nanumanga from April 1880 until the trading-station was destroyed later that year in a cyclone. He then became a trader on Nukufetau.
rewrite: Trading companies commenced operations in Tuvalu during the mid-nineteenth century, employing resident *palagi* traders on the islands. The first European settler was John (or Jack) O'Brien, who established himself as a trader on Funafuti in the 1850s and married Salai, daughter of the Funafuti paramount chief. Later, the author Louis Becke worked as a trader on Nanumanga from April 1880 until a cyclone destroyed the station; he subsequently relocated his operations to Nukufetau.

input: Following their wedding, the couple leased Windlesham Moor, near Windsor Castle, until 4 July 1949, when they took up residence at Clarence House in London. At various times between 1949 and 1951, the Duke of Edinburgh was stationed in the British Crown Colony of Malta as a serving Royal Navy officer. He and Elizabeth lived intermittently, for several months at a time, in the hamlet of Gwardamanġa, at Villa Guardamangia, the rented home of Philip's uncle, Lord Mountbatten. The children remained in Britain.
rewrite: Following their marriage, the couple resided at the leased Windlesham Moor, near Windsor Castle, until 4 July 1949, when they moved to Clarence House in London. From 1949 to 1951, the Duke of Edinburgh was periodically stationed in Malta, then a British Crown Colony, for Royal Navy service. During these periods, he and Princess Elizabeth lived intermittently at Villa Guardamangia in Gwardamanġa, the rented residence of his uncle, Lord Mountbatten, while their children remained in Britain.

input: Ann Arbor is part of Michigan's 12th congressional district, represented in Congress by Representative Debbie Dingell, a Democrat. On the state level, the city is part of the 18th district in the Michigan Senate, represented by Democrat Rebekah Warren. In the Michigan House of Representatives, representation is split between the 55th district (northern Ann Arbor, part of Ann Arbor Township, and other surrounding areas, represented by Democrat Adam Zemke), the 53rd district (most of downtown and the southern half of the city, represented by Democrat Jeff Irwin) and the 52nd district (southwestern areas outside Ann Arbor proper and western Washtenaw County, represented by Democrat Gretchen Driskell).
rewrite: Ann Arbor is situated within Michigan’s 12th congressional district, represented in the United States Congress by Democratic Representative Debbie Dingell. At the state level, the city falls within the 18th district of the Michigan Senate, represented by Democrat Rebekah Warren. In the Michigan House of Representatives, its representation is divided among three districts: the 55th (encompassing northern Ann Arbor, a portion of Ann Arbor Township, and adjacent areas, represented by Democrat Adam Zemke); the 53rd (covering much of downtown and the city’s southern half, represented by Democrat Jeff Irwin); and the 52nd (including southwestern areas beyond the city limits and western Washtenaw County, represented by Democrat Gretchen Driskell).

input: On 5 July 2004, the BBC celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of its television news bulletins (although it had produced the Television Newsreel for several years before 1954). This event was marked by the release of a DVD, which showed highlights of the BBC's television coverage of significant events over the half-century, as well as changes in the format of the BBC television news; from the newsreel format of the first BBC Television News bulletins, to the 24-hour, worldwide news coverage available in 2004. A special edition of Radio Times was also produced, as well as a special section of the BBC News Online website. In 2005 the pioneering BBC television series Little Angels won a BAFTA award. Little Angels was the first reality parenting show and its most famous episode saw Welsh actress Jynine James try to cope with the tantrums of her six-year-old son.
rewrite: On 5 July 2004, the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) commemorated the fiftieth anniversary of its dedicated television news bulletins, having previously produced the *Television Newsreel* in the years preceding 1954. This milestone was observed through the issuance of a DVD featuring highlights of the BBC's televised reporting of major events across the preceding half-century. The compilation also documented the evolution of the news format, tracing its development from the initial newsreel style to the continuous, global coverage available by 2004. Supplementary commemorative materials included a special edition of *Radio Times* magazine and a dedicated segment on the BBC News Online website. The following year, in 2005, the pioneering BBC television programme *Little Angels* received a British Academy of Film and Television Arts (BAFTA) award. As the first reality parenting series, a notable episode featured Welsh actress Jynine James managing the behavioural challenges of her six-year-old son.

input: Though the true dimensions of species diversity remain uncertain, estimates range from 2.6–7.8 million species with a mean of 5.5 million. This probably represents less than 20% of all species on Earth[citation needed], and with only about 20,000 new species of all organisms being described each year, most species likely will remain undescribed for many years unless species descriptions increase in rate. About 850,000–1,000,000 of all described species are insects. Of the 24 orders of insects, four dominate in terms of numbers of described species, with at least 3 million species included in Coleoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera and Lepidoptera. A recent study estimated the number of beetles at 0.9–2.1 million with a mean of 1.5 million.
rewrite: While the precise magnitude of global species diversity is unresolved, current approximations span from 2.6 to 7.8 million species, with a mean estimate of 5.5 million. This likely constitutes less than twenty percent of the planet's total species. Given that only approximately 20,000 new species across all organisms are described annually, the majority will likely remain undescribed for the foreseeable future absent a substantial acceleration in taxonomic description rates. Insects comprise roughly 850,000 to 1,000,000 of all documented species. Among the twenty-four insect orders, four—Coleoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera, and Lepidoptera—are predominant, collectively encompassing at least three million described species. Recent analyses specifically estimate beetle diversity at 0.9–2.1 million species, with a mean of 1.5 million.

input: Since before 2000 BC, humans have utilized pesticides to protect their crops. The first known pesticide was elemental sulfur dusting used in ancient Sumer about 4,500 years ago in ancient Mesopotamia. The Rig Veda, which is about 4,000 years old, mentions the use of poisonous plants for pest control. By the 15th century, toxic chemicals such as arsenic, mercury, and lead were being applied to crops to kill pests. In the 17th century, nicotine sulfate was extracted from tobacco leaves for use as an insecticide. The 19th century saw the introduction of two more natural pesticides, pyrethrum, which is derived from chrysanthemums, and rotenone, which is derived from the roots of tropical vegetables. Until the 1950s, arsenic-based pesticides were dominant. Paul Müller discovered that DDT was a very effective insecticide. Organochlorines such as DDT were dominant, but they were replaced in the U.S. by organophosphates and carbamates by 1975. Since then, pyrethrin compounds have become the dominant insecticide. Herbicides became common in the 1960s, led by "triazine and other nitrogen-based compounds, carboxylic acids such as 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, and glyphosate".
rewrite: The application of pesticides for agricultural protection has been documented since antiquity, with the earliest known use occurring in ancient Sumer circa 2000 BC through the dusting of crops with elemental sulfur. Approximately 4,000 years ago, the Rig Veda referenced the utilization of poisonous plants for controlling pests. By the 15th century, highly toxic inorganic compounds, including arsenic, mercury, and lead, were employed for this purpose. The 17th century witnessed the extraction of nicotine sulfate from tobacco for insecticidal use. During the 19th century, further natural agents were introduced, namely pyrethrum, derived from chrysanthemums, and rotenone, obtained from the roots of certain tropical legumes. Arsenical pesticides remained prevalent until the mid-20th century, when the discovery of DDT's efficacy by Paul Müller led to the dominance of organochlorines. These were largely superseded in the United States by organophosphates and carbamates around 1975, after which pyrethrin compounds emerged as the predominant insecticides. Concurrently, herbicides gained widespread adoption from the 1960s onward, notably triazine and other nitrogen-based compounds, carboxylic acids like 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, and glyphosate.

input: Precipitation is moderate and somewhat evenly distributed throughout the year, although the warmer months such as May and June average more, averaging 33.5 inches (850 mm) annually, but historically ranging from 20.49 in (520 mm) in 1963 to 47.70 in (1,212 mm) in 2011. Snowfall, which typically falls in measurable amounts between November 15 through April 4 (occasionally in October and very rarely in May), averages 42.5 inches (108 cm) per season, although historically ranging from 11.5 in (29 cm) in 1881−82 to 94.9 in (241 cm) in 2013−14. A thick snowpack is not often seen, with an average of only 27.5 days with 3 in (7.6 cm) or more of snow cover. Thunderstorms are frequent in the Detroit area. These usually occur during spring and summer.
rewrite: Annual precipitation is moderately distributed throughout the year, averaging 33.5 inches (850 mm). However, monthly totals are typically higher during warmer periods, such as May and June. Historical annual extremes range from 20.49 inches (520 mm) in 1963 to 47.70 inches (1,212 mm) in 2011. The seasonal snowfall average is 42.5 inches (108 cm), occurring primarily from November 15 to April 4, with occasional instances in October and rare events in May. Historical seasonal extremes span from 11.5 inches (29 cm) in 1881–82 to 94.9 inches (241 cm) in 2013–14. A persistent snowpack is uncommon, with an average of only 27.5 days per season maintaining at least 3 inches (7.6 cm) of cover. Thunderstorms are frequent in the Detroit area, predominantly during spring and summer months.

input: Ben Goldacre has argued that regulators – such as the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in the UK, or the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the United States – advance the interests of the drug companies rather than the interests of the public due to revolving door exchange of employees between the regulator and the companies and friendships develop between regulator and company employees. He argues that regulators do not require that new drugs offer an improvement over what is already available, or even that they be particularly effective.
rewrite: Ben Goldacre contends that regulatory bodies, including the United Kingdom's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA), prioritize pharmaceutical industry interests over public welfare. This alignment is attributed to a "revolving door" of personnel and the cultivation of personal relationships between regulators and company employees. Consequently, he asserts, these agencies frequently approve new medications without mandating demonstrated superiority over existing treatments or even robust evidence of efficacy.

input: New Haven has a variety of museums, many of them associated with Yale. The Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library features an original copy of the Gutenberg Bible. There is also the Connecticut Children's Museum; the Knights of Columbus museum near that organization's world headquarters; the Peabody Museum of Natural History; the Yale University Collection of Musical Instruments; the Eli Whitney Museum (across the town line in Hamden, Connecticut, on Whitney Avenue); the Yale Center for British Art, which houses the largest collection of British art outside the U.K., and the Yale University Art Gallery, the nation's oldest college art museum.[citation needed] New Haven is also home to the New Haven Museum and Historical Society on Whitney Avenue, which has a library of many primary source treasures dating from Colonial times to the present.
rewrite: The city of New Haven hosts a diverse array of museums, several of which are affiliated with Yale University. These include the Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, housing an original Gutenberg Bible, and the Yale Center for British Art, which possesses the most extensive collection of British art outside the United Kingdom. Other notable institutions are the Peabody Museum of Natural History, the Yale University Art Gallery (the oldest college art museum in the United States), and the Yale Collection of Musical Instruments. Further cultural resources encompass the Connecticut Children’s Museum, the Knights of Columbus museum, and the Eli Whitney Museum, located in nearby Hamden. Additionally, the New Haven Museum and Historical Society maintains a library of primary source materials spanning from the Colonial era to the contemporary period.

input: From around 750, during the Abbasid Caliphate, women “became renowned for their brains as well as their beauty”. In particular, many well known women of the time were trained from childhood in music, dancing and poetry. Mahbuba was one of these. Another feminine figure to be remembered for her achievements was Tawaddud, "a slave girl who was said to have been bought at great cost by Hārūn al-Rashīd because she had passed her examinations by the most eminent scholars in astronomy, medicine, law, philosophy, music, history, Arabic grammar, literature, theology and chess". Moreover, among the most prominent feminine figures was Shuhda who was known as "the Scholar" or "the Pride of Women" during the 12th century in Baghdad. Despite the recognition of women's aptitudes during the Abbasid dynasty, all these came to an end in Iraq with the sack of Baghdad in 1258.
rewrite: Beginning around 750 CE under the Abbasid Caliphate, women gained renown for intellectual accomplishments alongside aesthetic qualities. Notably, numerous prominent women received rigorous childhood instruction in music, dance, and poetic composition. Figures such as Mahbuba exemplified this tradition. Particularly remarkable was Tawaddud, an enslaved woman reportedly purchased at considerable expense by Caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd after demonstrating exceptional scholarly proficiency. She was examined and validated by leading authorities in fields including astronomy, medicine, jurisprudence, philosophy, music, history, Arabic grammar, literature, theology, and chess. Another eminent figure, the twelfth-century Baghdadi scholar Shuhda, was honorifically titled "the Scholar" and "the Pride of Women." This era of recognized female erudition, however, largely concluded in Iraq following the Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258.

input: The classification of speech varieties as dialects or languages and their relationship to other varieties of speech can be controversial and the verdicts inconsistent. English and Serbo-Croatian illustrate the point. English and Serbo-Croatian each have two major variants (British and American English, and Serbian and Croatian, respectively), along with numerous other varieties. For political reasons, analyzing these varieties as "languages" or "dialects" yields inconsistent results: British and American English, spoken by close political and military allies, are almost universally regarded as dialects of a single language, whereas the standard languages of Serbia and Croatia, which differ from each other to a similar extent as the dialects of English, are being treated by some linguists from the region as distinct languages, largely because the two countries oscillate from being brotherly to being bitter enemies. (The Serbo-Croatian language article deals with this topic much more fully.)
rewrite: The classification of linguistic varieties as distinct languages or as dialects of a single language is often a subject of controversy, yielding inconsistent scholarly determinations. This inconsistency is exemplified by the cases of English and Serbo-Croatian. Each possesses two principal standardized forms—British and American English, and Serbian and Croatian, respectively—in addition to numerous other varieties. Political considerations, however, lead to divergent analyses. British and American English, spoken by nations with longstanding political and military alliances, are nearly universally classified as dialects of one language. In contrast, the standard varieties of Serbia and Croatia, which exhibit a comparable degree of mutual differentiation, are increasingly posited by some regional linguists as separate languages. This shift largely correlates with the volatile political relationship between the two nations, which alternates between fraternity and enmity.

input: Although the numbered streets begin just north of East Houston Street in the East Village, they generally do not extend west into Greenwich Village, which already had streets when the grid plan was laid out by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. Streets that do continue farther west change direction before reaching the Hudson River. The grid covers the length of the island from 14th Street north.
rewrite: The numbered street grid, established by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811, commences north of East Houston Street in the East Village. It does not generally extend westward into Greenwich Village, whose pre-existing street layout predated the plan. While some streets continue further west, they alter alignment before reaching the Hudson River. This orthogonal grid system encompasses Manhattan from 14th Street northward.

input: Another occasionally used criterion for discriminating dialects from languages is that of linguistic authority, a more sociolinguistic notion. According to this definition, two varieties are considered dialects of the same language if (under at least some circumstances) they would defer to the same authority regarding some questions about their language. For instance, to learn the name of a new invention, or an obscure foreign species of plant, speakers of Bavarian German and East Franconian German might each consult a German dictionary or ask a German-speaking expert in the subject. By way of contrast, although Yiddish is classified by linguists as a language in the "Middle High German" group of languages, a Yiddish speaker would not consult a German dictionary to determine the word to use in such a case.
rewrite: An additional criterion sometimes employed to distinguish dialects from languages involves the concept of linguistic authority, a fundamentally sociolinguistic construct. This perspective posits that two linguistic varieties constitute dialects of a single language if, under certain conditions, they acknowledge a common authoritative source for resolving linguistic queries. Such inquiries might include determining the appropriate term for a novel invention or an unfamiliar foreign species. For example, speakers of Bavarian German and East Franconian German would likely refer to a standard German dictionary or consult a German-language specialist. In contrast, Yiddish, while linguistically categorized within the Middle High German group, operates as a separate language by this criterion; its speakers would not defer to standard German authorities for such lexical decisions.

input: The northern side of the borough includes the largest park in New York City—Pelham Bay Park, which includes Orchard Beach—and the fourth largest, Van Cortlandt Park, which is west of Woodlawn Cemetery and borders Yonkers. Also in the northern Bronx, Wave Hill, the former estate of George W. Perkins—known for a historic house, gardens, changing site-specific art installations and concerts—overlooks the New Jersey Palisades from a promontory on the Hudson in Riverdale. Nearer the borough's center, and along the Bronx River, is Bronx Park; its northern end houses the New York Botanical Gardens, which preserve the last patch of the original hemlock forest that once covered the entire county, and its southern end the Bronx Zoo, the largest urban zoological gardens in the United States. Just south of Van Cortlandt Park is the Jerome Park Reservoir, surrounded by 2 miles (3 km) of stone walls and bordering several small parks in the Bedford Park neighborhood; the reservoir was built in the 1890s on the site of the former Jerome Park Racetrack. Further south is Crotona Park, home to a 3.3-acre (1.3 ha) lake, 28 species of trees, and a large swimming pool. The land for these parks, and many others, was bought by New York City in 1888, while land was still open and inexpensive, in anticipation of future needs and future pressures for development.

The northern sector of the borough encompasses Pelham Bay Park, the largest park in New York City—containing Orchard Beach—as well as the city's fourth largest, Van Cortlandt Park, situated west of Woodlawn Cemetery and adjacent to Yonkers. input: The public water supply network was completed in 1850, and in 1858 the architects Sebastián Monleón Estellés, Antonino Sancho, and Timoteo Calvo drafted a general expansion project for the city that included demolishing its ancient walls (a second version was printed in 1868). Neither proposed project received final approval, but they did serve as a guide, though not closely followed, for future growth. By 1860 the municipality had 140,416 inhabitants, and beginning in 1866 the ancient city walls were almost entirely demolished to facilitate urban expansion. Electricity was introduced to Valencia in 1882.

input: Fossilized spores suggest that higher plants (embryophytes) have lived on land for at least 475 million years. Early land plants reproduced sexually with flagellated, swimming sperm, like the green algae from which they evolved. An adaptation to terrestrialization was the development of upright meiosporangia for dispersal by spores to new habitats. This feature is lacking in the descendants of their nearest algal relatives, the Charophycean green algae. A later terrestrial adaptation took place with retention of the delicate, avascular sexual stage, the gametophyte, within the tissues of the vascular sporophyte. This occurred by spore germination within sporangia rather than spore release, as in non-seed plants. A current example of how this might have happened can be seen in the precocious spore germination in Selaginella, the spike-moss. The result for the ancestors of angiosperms was enclosing them in a case, the seed. The first seed bearing plants, like the ginkgo, and conifers (such as pines and firs), did not produce flowers. The pollen grains (males) of Ginkgo and cycads produce a pair of flagellated, mobile sperm cells that "swim" down the developing pollen tube to the female and her eggs.
rewrite: Fossilized spore evidence indicates that embryophytes have inhabited terrestrial environments for a minimum of 475 million years. Early land plants, evolving from green algae, maintained a sexual reproductive strategy involving flagellated, motile sperm. A key adaptation to terrestrial life was the development of erect meiosporangia for spore dispersal, a morphological innovation absent in their closest algal relatives, the Charophycean green algae. A subsequent major adaptation involved the retention of the vulnerable, avascular gametophyte generation within the tissues of the vascular sporophyte. This evolutionary shift was achieved through spore germination occurring internally within the sporangium, rather than via spore release as observed in non-seed plants. A contemporary analogue for this process may be observed in the precocious spore germination of *Selaginella* (spike-moss). For the ancestors of angiosperms, this retention ultimately led to the enclosure of the embryo within a protective structure, forming the seed. The earliest seed-bearing plants, such as *Ginkgo* and conifers (e.g., pines and firs), were non-flowering. Notably, the pollen grains of *Ginkgo* and cycads produce pairs of flagellated sperm cells that remain motile, navigating the pollen tube to reach the female gametes.

input: In July 2012, Ancestry.com reported on historic and DNA research by its staff that discovered that Obama is likely a descendant through his mother of John Punch, considered by some historians to be the first African slave in the Virginia colony. An indentured servant, he was "bound for life" in 1640 after trying to escape. The story of him and his descendants is that of multi-racial America since it appeared he and his sons married or had unions with white women, likely indentured servants and working-class like them. Their multi-racial children were free because they were born to free English women. Over time, Obama's line of the Bunch family (as they became known) were property owners and continued to "marry white"; they became part of white society, likely by the early to mid-18th century.
rewrite: In July 2012, Ancestry.com published findings from historical and genetic research indicating that President Barack Obama is a probable descendant, through his maternal line, of John Punch. Historians regard Punch, an indentured servant sentenced to lifelong bondage in 1640 following an attempted escape, as potentially the first African enslaved for life in the Virginia colony. His lineage exemplifies the multi-racial fabric of America, as he and his sons are recorded as having unions with white women, presumably indentured servants of similar social standing. Their children, born to free English women, were thus born free. This branch of the family, later known as Bunch, acquired property and continued intermarrying with white individuals, integrating into white society likely by the early to mid-eighteenth century.

input: Most French rulers since the Middle Ages made a point of leaving their mark on a city that, contrary to many other of the world's capitals, has never been destroyed by catastrophe or war. In modernising its infrastructure through the centuries, Paris has preserved even its earliest history in its street map.[citation needed] At its origin, before the Middle Ages, the city was composed around several islands and sandbanks in a bend of the Seine; of those, two remain today: the île Saint-Louis, the île de la Cité; a third one is the 1827 artificially created île aux Cygnes. Modern Paris owes much to its late 19th century Second Empire remodelling by the Baron Haussmann: many of modern Paris' busiest streets, avenues and boulevards today are a result of that city renovation. Paris also owes its style to its aligned street-fronts, distinctive cream-grey "Paris stone" building ornamentation, aligned top-floor balconies, and tree-lined boulevards. The high residential population of its city centre makes it much different from most other western global cities.
rewrite: Throughout the medieval and modern periods, successive French monarchs and governments have deliberately imprinted their legacy upon Paris, a capital distinguished from many others by its avoidance of catastrophic destruction by war or disaster. Consequently, centuries of infrastructural modernization have preserved even the earliest layers of the city's history within its urban plan. Originating as a settlement on several islands and sandbanks within a Seine river bend, Paris retains two of these natural cores—the Île de la Cité and Île Saint-Louis—alongside the artificial Île aux Cygnes, created in 1827. The city's contemporary form is largely indebted to the comprehensive Second Empire renovation directed by Baron Haussmann in the late nineteenth century, which produced many of its major thoroughfares. This cohesive urban aesthetic is further defined by uniform street-front alignments, distinctive cream-grey limestone facades, consistent top-floor balconies, and tree-lined boulevards. Additionally, Paris remains atypical among major Western global cities due to its densely populated central arrondissements.

input: A local industry manufacturing fibre from New Zealand flax was successfully reestablished in 1907 and generated considerable income during the First World War. Ascension Island was made a dependency of Saint Helena in 1922, and Tristan da Cunha followed in 1938. During the Second World War, the United States built Wideawake airport on Ascension in 1942, but no military use was made of Saint Helena.

Ascension Island became a dependency of Saint Helena in 1922, with Tristan da Cunha following in 1938. During the Second World War, the United States constructed Wideawake airfield on Ascension in 1942, though Saint Helena saw no military utilisation.

input: Scientists are still debating when people started wearing clothes. Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser and Mark Stoneking, anthropologists at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, have conducted a genetic analysis of human body lice that suggests clothing originated quite recently, around 170,000 years ago. Body lice is an indicator of clothes-wearing, since most humans have sparse body hair, and lice thus require human clothing to survive. Their research suggests the invention of clothing may have coincided with the northward migration of modern Homo sapiens away from the warm climate of Africa, thought to have begun between 50,000 and 100,000 years ago. However, a second group of researchers using similar genetic methods estimate that clothing originated around 540,000 years ago (Reed et al. 2004. PLoS Biology 2(11): e340). For now, the date of the origin of clothing remains unresolved.[citation needed]
rewrite: The chronological emergence of clothing remains a subject of scholarly debate. Research by anthropologists Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser, and Mark Stoneking at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology employed genetic analysis of human body lice, which are dependent on garments due to sparse human body hair. Their findings suggest a relatively recent origin approximately 170,000 years ago. This timing potentially aligns with the migration of *Homo sapiens* out of Africa into cooler climates, an event generally dated between 50,000 and 100,000 years ago. In contrast, a separate study utilizing analogous genetic methodologies proposed a substantially earlier origin around 540,000 years ago (Reed et al. 2004). Consequently, the precise dating of this cultural innovation is presently unresolved.

input: As soon as Schwarzenegger was elected governor, Willie Brown said he would start a drive to recall the governor.
