input: Besides their traditional areas of inhabitation in Greater Somalia, a Somali community mainly consisting of entrepreneurs, academics, and students also exists in Egypt. In addition, there is an historical Somali community in the general Sudan area. Primarily concentrated in the north and Khartoum, the expatriate community mainly consists of students as well as some businesspeople. More recently, Somali entrepreneurs have established themselves in Kenya, investing over $1.5 billion in the Somali enclave of Eastleigh alone. In South Africa, Somali businesspeople also provide most of the retail trade in informal settlements around the Western Cape province.
rewrite: Beyond their historic territories in Greater Somalia, Somali diaspora communities are present in Egypt, comprised largely of entrepreneurs, academics, and students. A longstanding community also resides in Sudan, primarily concentrated in the north and Khartoum, where its members are mainly students and businesspeople. More recently, significant Somali entrepreneurial investment, exceeding $1.5 billion in Nairobi's Eastleigh enclave, has been documented in Kenya. Furthermore, in South Africa's Western Cape province, Somali businesspeople dominate the retail trade within informal settlements.

input: Gaddafi organized demonstrations and distributed posters criticizing the monarchy. In October 1961, he led a demonstration protesting Syria's secession from the United Arab Republic. During this they broke windows of a local hotel accused of serving alcohol. Catching the authorities' attention, they expelled his family from Sabha. Gaddafi moved to Misrata, there attending Misrata Secondary School. Maintaining his interest in Arab nationalist activism, he refused to join any of the banned political parties active in the city – including the Arab Nationalist Movement, the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party, and the Muslim Brotherhood – claiming he rejected factionalism. He read voraciously on the subjects of Nasser and the French Revolution of 1789, as well as the works of Syrian political theorist Michel Aflaq and biographies of Abraham Lincoln, Sun Yat-sen, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

input: Although provision is made in Title 10 of the United States Code for the Secretary of the Air Force to appoint warrant officers, the Air Force does not currently use warrant officer grades, and is the only one of the U.S. Armed Services not to do so. The Air Force inherited warrant officer ranks from the Army at its inception in 1947, but their place in the Air Force structure was never made clear.[citation needed] When the Congress authorized the creation of two new senior enlisted ranks in 1958, Air Force officials privately concluded that these two new "super grades" could fill all Air Force needs then performed at the warrant officer level, although this was not publicly acknowledged until years later.[citation needed] The Air Force stopped appointing warrant officers in 1959, the same year the first promotions were made to the new top enlisted grade, Chief Master Sergeant. Most of the existing Air Force warrant officers entered the commissioned officer ranks during the 1960s, but small numbers continued to exist in the warrant officer grades for the next 21 years.
rewrite: While Title 10 of the United States Code authorizes the Secretary of the Air Force to appoint warrant officers, the Air Force presently maintains no personnel in such grades, distinguishing itself as the sole branch of the U.S. Armed Services in this regard. The service inherited the warrant officer rank structure from the Army upon its establishment in 1947, yet the functional role of these positions within the Air Force organizational hierarchy remained ambiguously defined. Following congressional authorization in 1958 for two new senior enlisted ranks, Air Force leadership determined internally that these "super grades" could fulfill all roles previously associated with warrant officers, a rationale not publicly disclosed until subsequent years. The cessation of warrant officer appointments commenced in 1959, coinciding with the inaugural promotions to the new senior enlisted rank of Chief Master Sergeant. Throughout the 1960s, the majority of remaining warrant officers transitioned to commissioned officer status, though a limited number continued to serve in warrant officer capacities for an additional two decades.

input: As a schoolboy, Gaddafi adopted the ideologies of Arab nationalism and Arab socialism, influenced in particular by Nasserism, the thought of Egyptian revolutionary and president Gamal Abdel Nasser, whom Gaddafi adopted as his hero. During the early 1970s, Gaddafi formulated his own particular approach to Arab nationalism and socialism, known as Third International Theory, which has been described as a combination of "utopian socialism, Arab nationalism, and the Third World revolutionary theory that was in vogue at the time". He laid out the principles of this Theory in the three volumes of The Green Book, in which he sought to "explain the structure of the ideal society." His Arab nationalist views led him to believe that there needed to be unity across the Arab world, combining the Arab nation under a single nation-state. He described his approach to economics as "Islamic socialism", although biographers Blundy and Lycett noted that Gaddafi's socialism had a "curiously Marxist undertone", with political scientist Sami Hajjar arguing that Gaddafi's model of socialism offered a simplification of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' theories. Gaddafi saw his socialist Jamahiriyah as a model for the Arab, Islamic, and non-aligned worlds to follow.
rewrite: During his formative years as a student, Muammar Gaddafi embraced the principles of Arab nationalism and Arab socialism, profoundly shaped by Nasserism—the ideological framework of Egyptian revolutionary and president Gamal Abdel Nasser, whom Gaddafi esteemed as a personal hero. By the early 1970s, he had developed a distinct doctrine termed the Third International Theory, characterized by scholars as a synthesis of utopian socialism, Arab nationalism, and contemporaneous Third World revolutionary thought. Gaddafi systematically elaborated this theory in his three-volume work, *The Green Book*, intending to articulate the framework for an ideal society. His commitment to Arab nationalism culminated in the conviction that the Arab world required unification into a singular nation-state. Economically, he advocated for a system he designated "Islamic socialism." However, biographers such as Blundy and Lycett observed a notably Marxist inflection within his socialist vision, while political scientist Sami Hajjar contended that Gaddafi’s model presented a simplified interpretation of theories advanced by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. Ultimately, Gaddafi regarded his socialist Jamahiriyah as a paradigmatic system for emulation across the Arab, Islamic, and non-aligned worlds.

input: Bird eggs are usually laid in a nest. Most species create somewhat elaborate nests, which can be cups, domes, plates, beds scrapes, mounds, or burrows. Some bird nests, however, are extremely primitive; albatross nests are no more than a scrape on the ground. Most birds build nests in sheltered, hidden areas to avoid predation, but large or colonial birds—which are more capable of defence—may build more open nests. During nest construction, some species seek out plant matter from plants with parasite-reducing toxins to improve chick survival, and feathers are often used for nest insulation. Some bird species have no nests; the cliff-nesting common guillemot lays its eggs on bare rock, and male emperor penguins keep eggs between their body and feet. The absence of nests is especially prevalent in ground-nesting species where the newly hatched young are precocial.
rewrite: Bird eggs are typically deposited within a nest structure. The majority of avian species construct relatively elaborate nests, which may take forms such as cups, domes, plates, scrapes, mounds, or burrows. Certain nests, however, are exceedingly rudimentary; for instance, albatross nests constitute mere scrapes on the ground. Most birds position nests in concealed, sheltered locations to minimize predation risk, whereas larger or colonial birds—possessing greater defensive capabilities—often build more exposed nests. During construction, some species selectively incorporate plant material containing parasite-reducing toxins to enhance offspring survival, and feathers are frequently utilized for insulation. Notably, some birds forgo nests entirely: the common guillemot, which nests on cliffs, lays eggs directly on bare rock, and male emperor penguins incubate eggs between their bodies and feet. This absence of nest-building is particularly common among ground-nesting species with precocial young.

input: The game features nine dungeons—large, contained areas where Link battles enemies, collects items, and solves puzzles. The dungeons are connected by a large overworld, across which Link can travel on foot; on his horse, Epona; or by teleporting.

Completing a dungeon by defeating its concluding boss yields critical items or narrative progression. input: Cork was originally a monastic settlement, reputedly founded by Saint Finbarr in the 6th century. Cork achieved an urban character at some point between 915 and 922 when Norseman (Viking) settlers founded a trading port. It has been proposed that, like Dublin, Cork was an important trading centre in the global Scandinavian trade network. The ecclesiastical settlement continued alongside the Viking longphort, with the two developing a type of symbiotic relationship; the Norsemen providing otherwise unobtainable trade goods for the monastery, and perhaps also military aid.
rewrite: Cork originated as a sixth-century monastic settlement, traditionally attributed to Saint Finbarr. It assumed an urban character following the establishment of a Viking trading port between 915 and 922. Scholarly analysis suggests Cork, akin to Dublin, functioned as a significant node within the wider Scandinavian trade network. The monastic and Viking settlements coexisted, developing a symbiotic relationship wherein the Norsemen supplied trade goods and possibly military support to the ecclesiastical community.

input: The abbey became the coronation site of Norman kings. None were buried there until Henry III, intensely devoted to the cult of the Confessor, rebuilt the abbey in Anglo-French Gothic style as a shrine to venerate King Edward the Confessor and as a suitably regal setting for Henry's own tomb, under the highest Gothic nave in England. The Confessor's shrine subsequently played a great part in his canonisation. The work continued between 1245 and 1517 and was largely finished by the architect Henry Yevele in the reign of Richard II. Henry III also commissioned unique Cosmati pavement in front of the High Altar (the pavement has recently undergone a major cleaning and conservation programme and was re-dedicated by the Dean at a service on 21 May 2010).
rewrite: The abbey served as the coronation venue for Norman monarchs, yet no interments occurred there until Henry III. Profoundly devoted to the cult of the Confessor, he reconstructed the abbey in the Anglo-French Gothic style to create both a shrine venerating King Edward the Confessor and a suitably regal setting for his own tomb, situated beneath England's highest Gothic nave. This shrine later significantly contributed to Edward's canonisation. Construction persisted from 1245 to 1517, with the architect Henry Yevele largely completing the work under Richard II. Henry III also commissioned the unique Cosmati pavement before the High Altar, which has recently undergone extensive cleaning and conservation and was re-dedicated by the Dean in a service on 21 May 2010.

input: The use of traditional Chinese characters versus simplified Chinese characters varies greatly, and can depend on both the local customs and the medium. Before the official reform, character simplifications were not officially sanctioned and generally adopted vulgar variants and idiosyncratic substitutions. Orthodox variants were mandatory in printed works, while the (unofficial) simplified characters would be used in everyday writing or quick notes. Since the 1950s, and especially with the publication of the 1964 list, the People's Republic of China has officially adopted simplified Chinese characters for use in mainland China, while Hong Kong, Macau, and the Republic of China (Taiwan) were not affected by the reform. There is no absolute rule for using either system, and often it is determined by what the target audience understands, as well as the upbringing of the writer.
rewrite: The employment of traditional versus simplified Chinese orthographies exhibits significant variation, often contingent upon regional conventions and communicative context. Prior to formal script reform, character simplifications lacked official sanction, typically deriving from colloquial variants and idiosyncratic substitutions. Orthodox forms were obligatory in published materials, whereas simplified characters remained confined to informal manuscripts and personal notes. Following the 1950s, and particularly after the promulgation of the official 1964 list, the People's Republic of China institutionalized simplified characters for use on the mainland. This reform did not extend to Hong Kong, Macau, or the Republic of China (Taiwan), where traditional characters persist. No definitive rule governs the selection of either system; usage is frequently determined by the anticipated readership's comprehension and the writer's own linguistic background.

input: In May 1778, Burke supported a parliamentary motion revising restrictions on Irish trade. His constituents, citizens of the great trading city of Bristol, however urged Burke to oppose free trade with Ireland. Burke resisted their protestations and said: "If, from this conduct, I shall forfeit their suffrages at an ensuing election, it will stand on record an example to future representatives of the Commons of England, that one man at least had dared to resist the desires of his constituents when his judgment assured him they were wrong".
rewrite: In May 1778, Edmund Burke supported a parliamentary motion to ease commercial restrictions on Ireland. This position directly conflicted with the demands of his constituents in Bristol, a major trading city, who urged him to oppose such liberalization. Burke defied their protests, asserting that should this cost him their electoral support, it would establish a precedent demonstrating that a representative must occasionally defy constituent demands when convinced of their error.

input: Her mature artistic statement was visible in True Blue (1986) and Like a Prayer (1989). In True Blue, she incorporated classical music in order to engage an older audience who had been skeptical of her music. Like a Prayer introduced live recorded songs and incorporated different genres of music, including dance, funk, R&B and gospel music. Her versatility was further shown on I'm Breathless, which consists predominantly of the 1940s Broadway showtune-flavoured jazz, swing and big band tracks. Madonna continued to compose ballads and uptempo dance songs for Erotica (1992) and Bedtime Stories (1994). Both albums explored element of new jack swing, with Jim Farber from Entertainment Weekly saying that "she could actually be viewed as new jack swing's godmother." She tried to remain contemporary by incorporating samples, drum loops and hip hop into her music. With Ray of Light, Madonna brought electronic music from its underground status into massive popularity in mainstream music scene.
rewrite: Madonna’s mature artistic statement emerged distinctly in *True Blue* (1986) and *Like a Prayer* (1989). The former strategically incorporated classical elements to engage an older, previously skeptical audience, while the latter utilized live recorded vocals and synthesized diverse genres—including dance, funk, R&B, and gospel—demonstrating her musical breadth. This versatility continued with *I’m Breathless*, which featured 1940s-inspired jazz, swing, and big band arrangements. Subsequent albums, *Erotica* (1992) and *Bedtime Stories* (1994), maintained a balance of ballads and uptempo dance tracks while integrating new jack swing; critic Jim Farber of *Entertainment Weekly* noted she could be considered “new jack swing’s godmother.” To remain contemporary, she employed samples, drum loops, and hip-hop influences. Ultimately, with *Ray of Light*, Madonna elevated electronic music from underground circles to widespread mainstream popularity.

input: Perhaps the most prominent, controversial and far-reaching theory in all of science has been the theory of evolution by natural selection put forward by the British naturalist Charles Darwin in his book On the Origin of Species in 1859. Darwin proposed that the features of all living things, including humans, were shaped by natural processes over long periods of time. The theory of evolution in its current form affects almost all areas of biology. Implications of evolution on fields outside of pure science have led to both opposition and support from different parts of society, and profoundly influenced the popular understanding of "man's place in the universe". In the early 20th century, the study of heredity became a major investigation after the rediscovery in 1900 of the laws of inheritance developed by the Moravian monk Gregor Mendel in 1866. Mendel's laws provided the beginnings of the study of genetics, which became a major field of research for both scientific and industrial research. By 1953, James D. Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins clarified the basic structure of DNA, the genetic material for expressing life in all its forms. In the late 20th century, the possibilities of genetic engineering became practical for the first time, and a massive international effort began in 1990 to map out an entire human genome (the Human Genome Project).
rewrite: Among the most significant, contentious, and expansive theories within the scientific canon is the theory of evolution by natural selection, advanced by the British naturalist Charles Darwin in his 1859 work, *On the Origin of Species*. Darwin posited that the characteristics of all organisms, including humans, were molded through natural processes across vast temporal scales. The modern evolutionary synthesis now underpins virtually all biological disciplines. Its implications beyond pure science have elicited both societal opposition and endorsement, while fundamentally reshaping conceptions of humanity’s position in the natural order. Concurrently, the early twentieth century witnessed the rise of heredity as a principal scientific pursuit, following the 1900 rediscovery of inheritance laws formulated by the Moravian monk Gregor Mendel in 1866. Mendel’s principles established the foundation for genetics, which subsequently emerged as a major domain of both academic and industrial investigation. By 1953, James D. Watson, Francis Crick, and Maurice Wilkins elucidated the fundamental structure of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), the molecular basis of heredity. In the late twentieth century, the feasibility of genetic engineering was realized, catalyzing a large-scale international initiative launched in 1990 to sequence the complete human genome—the Human Genome Project.

input: It has been pointed out that Khmer and Indonesian classical arts were concerned with depicting the life of the gods, but to the Southeast Asian mind the life of the gods was the life of the peoples themselves—joyous, earthy, yet divine. The Tai, coming late into Southeast Asia, brought with them some Chinese artistic traditions, but they soon shed them in favour of the Khmer and Mon traditions, and the only indications of their earlier contact with Chinese arts were in the style of their temples, especially the tapering roof, and in their lacquerware.
rewrite: Scholars have observed that classical Khmer and Indonesian arts focused on portraying divine life, which within the Southeast Asian worldview was synonymous with human existence—characterized by joy, earthiness, and sanctity. The Tai peoples, arriving later in the region, introduced certain Chinese artistic conventions. However, they rapidly assimilated the prevailing Khmer and Mon traditions. Residual Chinese influence persisted primarily in architectural features, notably the tapering temple roof, and in the craft of lacquerware.

input: Popular opinion remained firmly behind the celebration of Mary's conception. In 1439, the Council of Basel, which is not reckoned an ecumenical council, stated that belief in the immaculate conception of Mary is in accord with the Catholic faith. By the end of the 15th century the belief was widely professed and taught in many theological faculties, but such was the influence of the Dominicans, and the weight of the arguments of Thomas Aquinas (who had been canonised in 1323 and declared "Doctor Angelicus" of the Church in 1567) that the Council of Trent (1545–63)—which might have been expected to affirm the doctrine—instead declined to take a position.
rewrite: Popular sentiment continued to strongly favor the observance of Mary’s conception. In 1439, the Council of Basel—though not considered ecumenical—declared the belief in the Immaculate Conception to be consistent with Catholic faith. By the late fifteenth century, the doctrine was commonly professed and instructed within numerous theological faculties. However, due to the considerable influence of the Dominican Order and the enduring authority of Thomas Aquinas—canonized in 1323 and proclaimed the "Angelic Doctor" in 1567—the Council of Trent (1545–63) refrained from affirming the doctrine, despite expectations that it would do so.

input: In May 2014, the Government of China banned the internal purchase of Windows 8-based products under government contracts requiring "energy-efficient" devices. The Xinhua News Agency claimed that Windows 8 was being banned in protest of Microsoft's support lifecycle policy and the end of support for Windows XP (which, as of January 2014, had a market share of 49% in China), as the government "obviously cannot ignore the risks of running OS [sic] without guaranteed technical support." However, Ni Guangnan of the Chinese Academy of Sciences had also previously warned that Windows 8 could allegedly expose users to surveillance by the United States government due to its heavy use of internet-based services.
rewrite: In May 2014, the Chinese government prohibited the procurement of Windows 8 products for official use under contracts mandating energy-efficient devices. According to the state-run Xinhua News Agency, this measure was a response to Microsoft's product lifecycle policies, particularly the cessation of support for Windows XP. With XP holding a 49% market share in China as of January 2014, authorities stated they could not disregard the security risks of operating an unsupported operating system. Concurrently, academic commentary, notably from Ni Guangnan of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, cautioned that the operating system's reliance on internet services potentially facilitated surveillance by the United States government.

input: Filming temporarily returned to England to shoot scenes at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, which stood in for a location in Rome, before moving on to the city itself for a five-week shoot across the city, with locations including the Ponte Sisto bridge and the Roman Forum. The production faced opposition from a variety of special interest groups and city authorities, who were concerned about the potential for damage to historical sites around the city, and problems with graffiti and rubbish appearing in the film. A car chase scene set along the banks of the Tiber River and through the streets of Rome featured an Aston Martin DB10 and a Jaguar C-X75. The C-X75 was originally developed as a hybrid electric vehicle with four independent electric engines powered by two jet turbines, before the project was cancelled. The version used for filming was converted to use a conventional internal combustion engine, to minimise the potential for disruption from mechanical problems with the complex hybrid system. The C-X75s used for filming were developed by the engineering division of Formula One racing team Williams, who built the original C-X75 prototype for Jaguar.
rewrite:
Following a brief return to England, where Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire served as a stand-in for a Roman setting, the production relocated to Rome for a five-week schedule. Filming occurred at various locations across the city, including the Ponte Sisto bridge and the Roman Forum. This phase encountered objections from several special interest groups and municipal authorities, who expressed concerns regarding potential damage to historic sites and the undesirable inclusion of contemporary graffiti and litter within the film’s frame.

A principal automotive sequence, featuring an Aston Martin DB10 and a Jaguar C-X75, was shot along the Tiber River banks and through Roman streets. The Jaguar C-X75 presented unique logistical considerations. Originally conceived as a prototype hybrid electric vehicle utilizing four electric motors powered by twin jet turbines—a project later cancelled—the filming units were modified. To mitigate the risk of mechanical failure inherent in the complex hybrid system, the cars were converted to operate with conventional internal combustion engines. These specific vehicles were developed for production by the engineering division of the Williams Formula One team, which had also constructed Jaguar’s original C-X75 prototype.

input: The Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776) responded to Berkeley's criticisms of Locke, as well as other differences between early modern philosophers, and moved empiricism to a new level of skepticism. Hume argued in keeping with the empiricist view that all knowledge derives from sense experience, but he accepted that this has implications not normally acceptable to philosophers. He wrote for example, "Locke divides all arguments into demonstrative and probable. On this view, we must say that it is only probable that all men must die or that the sun will rise to-morrow, because neither of these can be demonstrated. But to conform our language more to common use, we ought to divide arguments into demonstrations, proofs, and probabilities—by ‘proofs’ meaning arguments from experience that leave no room for doubt or opposition." And,
rewrite: The Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776) advanced empiricism toward a more radical skepticism, engaging critically with George Berkeley’s objections to John Locke and other early modern philosophical disputes. While maintaining the empiricist principle that all knowledge originates in sensory experience, Hume acknowledged its deeply challenging implications. He illustrated this by refining Locke’s taxonomy of arguments. Hume noted that Locke classified arguments solely as either demonstrative or probable, thereby rendering even everyday expectations—such as human mortality or sunrise—merely probable, since they cannot be strictly demonstrated. To better align philosophical terminology with common usage, Hume proposed a threefold division: demonstrations, proofs, and probabilities. Here, “proofs” denote arguments derived from experience that are so compelling as to exclude doubt or contradiction.

input: Modern Nationalism, as developed especially since the French Revolution, has made the distinction between "language" and "dialect" an issue of great political importance. A group speaking a separate "language" is often seen as having a greater claim to being a separate "people", and thus to be more deserving of its own independent state, while a group speaking a "dialect" tends to be seen not as "a people" in its own right, but as a sub-group, part of a bigger people, which must content itself with regional autonomy.[citation needed] The distinction between language and dialect is thus inevitably made at least as much on a political basis as on a linguistic one, and can lead to great political controversy, or even armed conflict.
rewrite: The distinction between "language" and "dialect," particularly as framed within the context of Modern Nationalism emerging from the French Revolution, has acquired significant political import. A community identified with a distinct "language" is frequently accorded a stronger claim to constituting a separate "people," thereby legitimizing aspirations for sovereign statehood. Conversely, a group deemed to speak a "dialect" is often perceived not as an independent nation but as a subsidiary component of a larger people, its political ambitions typically limited to regional autonomy. Consequently, this critical classification is determined at least as much by political considerations as by linguistic criteria, a process that can generate substantial political contention and, in extreme cases, armed conflict.

input: In 2014 the Notre Dame student body consisted of 12,179 students, with 8,448 undergraduates, 2,138 graduate and professional and 1,593 professional (Law, M.Div., Business, M.Ed.) students. Around 21–24% of students are children of alumni, and although 37% of students come from the Midwestern United States, the student body represents all 50 states and 100 countries. As of March 2007[update] The Princeton Review ranked the school as the fifth highest 'dream school' for parents to send their children. As of March 2015[update] The Princeton Review ranked Notre Dame as the ninth highest. The school has been previously criticized for its lack of diversity, and The Princeton Review ranks the university highly among schools at which "Alternative Lifestyles [are] Not an Alternative." It has also been commended by some diversity oriented publications; Hispanic Magazine in 2004 ranked the university ninth on its list of the top–25 colleges for Latinos, and The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education recognized the university in 2006 for raising enrollment of African-American students. With 6,000 participants, the university's intramural sports program was named in 2004 by Sports Illustrated as the best program in the country, while in 2007 The Princeton Review named it as the top school where "Everyone Plays Intramural Sports." The annual Bookstore Basketball tournament is the largest outdoor five-on-five tournament in the world with over 700 teams participating each year, while the Notre Dame Men's Boxing Club hosts the annual Bengal Bouts tournament that raises money for the Holy Cross Missions in Bangladesh.
rewrite:
In 2014, the University of Notre Dame enrolled a total student population of 12,179, comprising 8,448 undergraduates, 2,138 graduate and professional students, and an additional 1,593 students in professional programs such as Law, Divinity, Business, and Education. Approximately 21 to 24 percent of students are children of alumni. While 37 percent originate from the Midwestern United States, the student body represents all fifty states and over one hundred nations. According to a March 2007 Princeton Review update, the institution was ranked as the fifth highest "dream school" among parents; by March 2015, it held the ninth position in that category. The university has faced historical criticism regarding limited demographic diversity, and The Princeton Review has consistently ranked it highly among institutions where "Alternative Lifestyles [are] Not an Alternative." Conversely, it has received recognition from some diversity-focused publications: Hispanic Magazine ranked Notre Dame ninth on its 2004 list of top twenty-five colleges for Latinos, and The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education acknowledged the university in 2006 for increasing African-American student enrollment.

Notre Dame’s extensive intramural sports program, involving roughly 6,000 participants, was acclaimed by Sports Illustrated in 2004 as the nation’s best. In 2007, The Princeton Review also designated it the top school where "Everyone Plays Intramural Sports." Notable athletic traditions include the annual Bookstore Basketball tournament, recognized as the world’s largest outdoor five-on-five tournament, with over 700 teams participating each year. Additionally, the Notre Dame Men’s Boxing Club organizes the Bengal Bouts tournament, an annual fundraising event supporting the Holy Cross Missions in Bangladesh.

input: The Constitution does not explicitly indicate the pre-eminence of any particular branch of government. However, James Madison wrote in Federalist 51, regarding the ability of each branch to defend itself from actions by the others, that "it is not possible to give to each department an equal power of self-defense. In republican government, the legislative authority necessarily predominates."
rewrite: The Constitution does not expressly designate any single governmental branch as supreme. James Madison, however, observed in Federalist 51 that while each branch must retain defensive capacities, absolute parity is unattainable. He concluded that within a republican system, "the legislative authority necessarily predominates."

input: To put it another way, a thing or person is often seen as having a "defining essence" or a "core identity" that is unchanging, and describes what the thing or person really is. In this way of thinking, things and people are seen as fundamentally the same through time, with any changes being qualitative and secondary to their core identity (e.g. "Mark's hair has turned gray as he has gotten older, but he is still the same person"). But in Whitehead's cosmology, the only fundamentally existent things are discrete "occasions of experience" that overlap one another in time and space, and jointly make up the enduring person or thing. On the other hand, what ordinary thinking often regards as "the essence of a thing" or "the identity/core of a person" is an abstract generalization of what is regarded as that person or thing's most important or salient features across time. Identities do not define people, people define identities. Everything changes from moment to moment, and to think of anything as having an "enduring essence" misses the fact that "all things flow", though it is often a useful way of speaking.
rewrite: In contrast to the conventional notion of a fixed, defining essence or core identity that persists unchanged through time—wherein entities are considered fundamentally self-identical, with alterations viewed as qualitative and peripheral (e.g., an individual aging yet remaining "the same person")—Alfred North Whitehead’s cosmology proposes a radically different ontology. Within this framework, the only fundamentally existent entities are discrete "occasions of experience." These occasions temporally and spatially overlap, collectively constituting what is perceived as an enduring object or person. What common parlance terms the "essence" of a thing or the "core identity" of a person is, in Whiteheadian terms, an abstract generalization derived from the most salient or significant features attributed to that entity across successive occasions. Consequently, identities do not ontologically precede or define persons; rather, persons (as nexūs of occasions) define identities. Reality is characterized by perpetual flux: every entity changes from moment to moment. To attribute an "enduring essence" to anything is to overlook the Heraclitean principle that "all things flow," even if such attribution remains a pragmatically useful mode of discourse.

input: According to statistics published by the American Pet Products Manufacturers Association in the National Pet Owner Survey in 2009–2010, it is estimated there are 77.5 million people with pet dogs in the United States. The same survey shows nearly 40% of American households own at least one dog, of which 67% own just one dog, 25% two dogs and nearly 9% more than two dogs. There does not seem to be any gender preference among dogs as pets, as the statistical data reveal an equal number of female and male dog pets. Yet, although several programs are undergoing to promote pet adoption, less than a fifth of the owned dogs come from a shelter.
rewrite: According to the 2009–2010 National Pet Owner Survey published by the American Pet Products Manufacturers Association, an estimated 77.5 million individuals in the United States own a dog. The data indicate that approximately 40% of American households possess at least one dog. Among these households, 67% own a single dog, 25% own two dogs, and nearly 9% own more than two. Statistics reveal no gender preference in dog ownership, with equal numbers of female and male pets. Despite ongoing programs to encourage adoption, fewer than one-fifth of owned dogs are acquired from shelters.

input: The second main principle, sola fide (by faith alone), states that faith in Christ is sufficient alone for eternal salvation. Though argued from scripture, and hence logically consequent to sola scriptura, this is the guiding principle of the work of Luther and the later reformers. Because sola scriptura placed the Bible as the only source of teaching, sola fide epitomises the main thrust of the teaching the reformers wanted to get back to, namely the direct, close, personal connection between Christ and the believer, hence the reformers' contention that their work was Christocentric.
rewrite: The second primary principle, *sola fide* (by faith alone), asserts that faith in Christ is solely sufficient for justification and eternal salvation. While derived scripturally from *sola scriptura*, it became the central doctrinal guide for Luther and subsequent reformers. By establishing scripture as the exclusive doctrinal authority, *sola fide* embodies the reformers' core objective: restoring a direct and personal soteriological connection between Christ and the believer, thereby rendering their theology fundamentally Christocentric.

input: A common misperception is that the Supreme Court is the only court that may determine constitutionality; the power is exercised even by the inferior courts. But only Supreme Court decisions are binding across the nation. Decisions of a Court of Appeals, for instance, are binding only in the circuit over which the court has jurisdiction.
rewrite: A prevalent misconception holds that only the Supreme Court can assess constitutionality; however, inferior courts also exercise this power. Yet, solely Supreme Court rulings are nationally binding. For example, a Court of Appeals decision is binding only within its specific judicial circuit.

input: Unicode has become the dominant scheme for internal processing and storage of text. Although a great deal of text is still stored in legacy encodings, Unicode is used almost exclusively for building new information processing systems. Early adopters tended to use UCS-2 (the fixed-width two-byte precursor to UTF-16) and later moved to UTF-16 (the variable-width current standard), as this was the least disruptive way to add support for non-BMP characters. The best known such system is Windows NT (and its descendants, Windows 2000, Windows XP, Windows Vista and Windows 7), which uses UTF-16 as the sole internal character encoding. The Java and .NET bytecode environments, Mac OS X, and KDE also use it for internal representation. Unicode is available on Windows 95 through Microsoft Layer for Unicode, as well as on its descendants, Windows 98 and Windows ME.
rewrite: Unicode has emerged as the predominant framework for the internal processing and storage of textual data. While substantial volumes of text persist in legacy encodings, Unicode is now almost universally employed in the development of new information processing systems. Early adopters frequently utilized UCS-2, the fixed-width, two-byte precursor to UTF-16, subsequently transitioning to the variable-width UTF-16 standard. This shift provided the least disruptive pathway for incorporating support for characters beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). A prominent example is the Windows NT lineage, including Windows 2000, XP, Vista, and 7, which adopts UTF-16 as its exclusive internal character encoding. This encoding is also utilized for internal representation within the Java and .NET bytecode environments, Mac OS X, and the KDE platform. Furthermore, Unicode support was extended to Windows 95, 98, and ME via the Microsoft Layer for Unicode.

input: In 1238, King James I of Aragon, with an army composed of Aragonese, Catalans, Navarrese and crusaders from the Order of Calatrava, laid siege to Valencia and on 28 September obtained a surrender. Fifty thousand Moors were forced to leave. Poets such as Ibn al-Abbar and Ibn Amira mourned this exile from their beloved Valencia. After the Christian victory and the expulsion of the Muslim population the city was divided between those who had participated in the conquest, according to the testimony in the Llibre del Repartiment (Book of Distribution). James I granted the city new charters of law, the Furs of Valencia, which later were extended to the whole kingdom of Valencia. Thenceforth the city entered a new historical stage in which a new society and a new language developed, forming the basis of the character of the Valencian people as they are known today.
rewrite: In 1238, King James I of Aragon, commanding a force of Aragonese, Catalans, Navarrese, and crusaders from the Order of Calatrava, successfully besieged Valencia, securing its surrender on 28 September. This conquest resulted in the expulsion of approximately fifty thousand Muslim inhabitants. Contemporary poets, including Ibn al-Abbar and Ibn Amira, subsequently lamented this exile from their homeland. Following the Christian victory and the removal of the Muslim populace, urban territories were allocated among the conquerors, as documented in the *Llibre del Repartiment* (Book of Distribution). King James I instituted new legal charters for the city, known as the Furs of Valencia, which were later expanded throughout the Kingdom of Valencia. Consequently, the city commenced a distinct historical phase characterized by the development of a novel social order and linguistic tradition, foundational elements in the formation of the Valencian identity recognized today.

input: The executive branch consists of the Governor, their staff, and other elected officials. The principal head of government, the Governor is the chief executive of the Oklahoma executive branch, serving as the ex officio Commander-in-Chief of the Oklahoma National Guard when not called into Federal use and reserving the power to veto bills passed through the Legislature. The responsibilities of the Executive branch include submitting the budget, ensuring that state laws are enforced, and ensuring peace within the state is preserved.
rewrite: The executive branch comprises the Governor, their staff, and other elected officials. As the chief executive and principal head of government, the Governor leads this branch. This role includes serving as the ex officio Commander-in-Chief of the Oklahoma National Guard when not federalized and retaining veto power over legislative bills. The branch's duties encompass budget submission, enforcement of state laws, and the preservation of public peace.

input: Some of the best-known traditions, including carnal parades and masquerade balls, were first recorded in medieval Italy. The carnival of Venice was, for a long time, the most famous carnival (although Napoleon abolished it in 1797 and only in 1979 was the tradition restored). From Italy, Carnival traditions spread to Spain, Portugal and France and from France to New France in North America. From Spain and Portugal it spread with colonization to the Caribbean and Latin America. In the early 19th century in the German Rhineland and Southern Netherlands, the weakened medieval tradition also revive. Continuously in the 18th and 19th centuries CE, as part of the annual Saturnalia abuse of the carnival in Rome, rabbis of the ghetto were forced to march through the city streets wearing foolish guise, jeered upon and pelted by a variety of missiles from the crowd. A petition of the Jewish community of Rome sent in 1836 to Pope Gregory XVI to stop the annual anti-semitic Saturnalia abuse got a negation: “It is not opportune to make any innovation.”
rewrite: Several of the most prominent Carnival traditions, such as elaborate parades and masquerade balls, trace their earliest documented origins to medieval Italy. The Carnival of Venice long stood as the preeminent celebration, though it was suppressed by Napoleon in 1797 and not formally reinstated until 1979. From its Italian origins, the custom proliferated to the Iberian Peninsula and France; French influence subsequently transported it to New France in North America. Concurrently, Spanish and Portuguese colonization facilitated its diffusion throughout the Caribbean and Latin America. A parallel revival of the attenuated medieval tradition occurred in the early nineteenth century within the German Rhineland and Southern Netherlands. Throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, a particularly virulent annual practice was observed in Rome during the Saturnalia, wherein ghetto rabbis were compelled to march in demeaning costumes, subjected to public derision and physical assault with thrown objects. A formal petition from Rome's Jewish community in 1836, entreating Pope Gregory XVI to halt this antisemitic abuse, was denied with the rationale that innovation was inopportune.

input: The first issue was ammunition. Before the war it was recognised that ammunition needed to explode in the air. Both high explosive (HE) and shrapnel were used, mostly the former. Airburst fuses were either igniferious (based on a burning fuse) or mechanical (clockwork). Igniferious fuses were not well suited for anti-aircraft use. The fuse length was determined by time of flight, but the burning rate of the gunpowder was affected by altitude. The British pom-poms had only contact-fused ammunition. Zeppelins, being hydrogen filled balloons, were targets for incendiary shells and the British introduced these with airburst fuses, both shrapnel type-forward projection of incendiary 'pot' and base ejection of an incendiary stream. The British also fitted tracers to their shells for use at night. Smoke shells were also available for some AA guns, these bursts were used as targets during training.
rewrite: The primary challenge pertained to ammunition, as pre-war analysis had determined the necessity for projectiles capable of detonating in mid-air. Both high explosive and shrapnel rounds were employed, with the former predominating. Fuses enabling airbursts were categorized as either igniferous, relying on a burning time train, or mechanical, utilizing clockwork mechanisms. Igniferous types proved inadequate for anti-aircraft purposes because, although the fuse length was set for a specific time of flight, the combustion rate of the gunpowder was adversely influenced by altitude. British pom-pom guns were initially limited to contact-fused ammunition. Against hydrogen-filled Zeppelins, incendiary shells became critical; the British developed airburst-fused variants, including types that projected incendiary material forward or ejected an incendiary stream from the base. Tracers were added for nocturnal engagements, while smoke shells, utilized as visual markers during training exercises, were also available for certain artillery pieces.

input: Eventually, the Licchavi ruler Gunakamadeva merged Koligram and Dakshin Koligram, founding the city of Kathmandu. The city was designed in the shape of Chandrahrasa, the sword of Manjushri. The city was surrounded by eight barracks guarded by Ajimas. One of these barracks is still in use at Bhadrakali (in front of Singha Durbar). The city served as an important transit point in the trade between India and Tibet, leading to tremendous growth in architecture. Descriptions of buildings such as Managriha, Kailaskut Bhawan, and Bhadradiwas Bhawan have been found in the surviving journals of travelers and monks who lived during this era. For example, the famous 7th-century Chinese traveller Xuanzang described Kailaskut Bhawan, the palace of the Licchavi king Amshuverma. The trade route also led to cultural exchange as well. The artistry of the Newar people—the indigenous inhabitants of the Kathmandu Valley—became highly sought after during this era, both within the Valley and throughout the greater Himalayas. Newar artists travelled extensively throughout Asia, creating religious art for their neighbors. For example, Araniko led a group of his compatriot artists through Tibet and China. Bhrikuti, the princess of Nepal who married Tibetan monarch Songtsän Gampo, was instrumental in introducing Buddhism to Tibet.
rewrite: The Licchavi ruler Gunakamadeva ultimately consolidated the settlements of Koligram and Dakshin Koligram to establish the city of Kathmandu. Its urban plan was deliberately fashioned in the form of Chandrahrasa, the sword of the bodhisattva Manjushri. The perimeter was fortified with eight military barracks, each protected by Ajima deities, one of which remains operational at the Bhadrakali site adjacent to Singha Durbar. Kathmandu’s strategic position along the vital trade corridor linking India and Tibet catalyzed significant architectural development. Contemporary structures such as Managriha, Kailaskut Bhawan, and Bhadradiwas Bhawan are documented in the extant records of travelers and monastic chroniclers from the period. Notably, the seventh-century Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang provided a description of Kailaskut Bhawan, the palace of Licchavi king Amshuverma. This commercial network further facilitated substantial cultural exchange. The artistic output of the Newars, the indigenous population of the Kathmandu Valley, gained considerable prestige across the Valley and the broader Himalayan region. Newar artisans traveled widely throughout Asia, producing religious artworks for neighboring societies. A prominent example is the master artist Araniko, who led a delegation of his peers across Tibet and into China. Additionally, the Nepali princess Bhrikuti, upon her marriage to the Tibetan ruler Songtsän Gampo, played a pivotal role in the transmission of Buddhism into Tibet.

input: In addition to concerns over subsidies, the cotton industries of some countries are criticized for employing child labor and damaging workers' health by exposure to pesticides used in production. The Environmental Justice Foundation has campaigned against the prevalent use of forced child and adult labor in cotton production in Uzbekistan, the world's third largest cotton exporter. The international production and trade situation has led to "fair trade" cotton clothing and footwear, joining a rapidly growing market for organic clothing, fair fashion or "ethical fashion". The fair trade system was initiated in 2005 with producers from Cameroon, Mali and Senegal.
rewrite: Beyond subsidy concerns, the global cotton industry faces criticism for utilizing child labor and endangering worker health through pesticide exposure. Notably, the Environmental Justice Foundation has highlighted the widespread use of forced labor, including children, in Uzbekistan, a leading cotton exporter. In response, "fair trade" cotton products have emerged within international markets, aligning with the expanding sector for organic and ethical fashion. This fair trade framework, established in 2005, initially involved producers from Cameroon, Mali, and Senegal.

input: The capital is Nashville, though Knoxville, Kingston, and Murfreesboro have all served as state capitals in the past. Memphis has the largest population of any city in the state. Nashville's 13-county metropolitan area has been the state's largest since c. 1990. Chattanooga and Knoxville, both in the eastern part of the state near the Great Smoky Mountains, each has approximately one-third of the population of Memphis or Nashville. The city of Clarksville is a fifth significant population center, some 45 miles (72 km) northwest of Nashville. Murfreesboro is the sixth-largest city in Tennessee, consisting of some 108,755 residents.
rewrite: Nashville presently serves as the state capital, succeeding prior capitals including Knoxville, Kingston, and Murfreesboro. Memphis is the most populous city, while the Nashville metropolitan area has been the largest since approximately 1990. Chattanooga and Knoxville, located in eastern Tennessee near the Great Smoky Mountains, each possess roughly one-third the population of Memphis or Nashville. Clarksville, situated about 72 kilometers northwest of Nashville, constitutes a fifth major population center. Murfreesboro, with approximately 108,755 residents, ranks as the state's sixth-largest city.

input: The first half of the 14th century saw much important scientific work being done, largely within the framework of scholastic commentaries on Aristotle's scientific writings. William of Ockham introduced the principle of parsimony: natural philosophers should not postulate unnecessary entities, so that motion is not a distinct thing but is only the moving object and an intermediary "sensible species" is not needed to transmit an image of an object to the eye. Scholars such as Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme started to reinterpret elements of Aristotle's mechanics. In particular, Buridan developed the theory that impetus was the cause of the motion of projectiles, which was a first step towards the modern concept of inertia. The Oxford Calculators began to mathematically analyze the kinematics of motion, making this analysis without considering the causes of motion.
rewrite: The early fourteenth century was a period of significant scientific advancement, primarily conducted through scholastic commentaries on Aristotle’s works. William of Ockham formulated the principle of parsimony, arguing that natural philosophers ought not to multiply entities beyond necessity. Consequently, motion should not be considered a distinct entity separate from the moving body, nor are intermediary "sensible species" required to explain visual perception. Concurrently, scholars including Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme commenced critical reinterpretations of Aristotelian mechanics. Buridan, notably, advanced the theory of impetus as the cause of projectile motion, representing an initial movement toward the modern concept of inertia. Furthermore, the Oxford Calculators initiated the mathematical analysis of kinematics, deliberately abstracting their study from the causal forces underlying motion.

input: The modern Conservative Party was created out of the 'Pittite' Tories of the early 19th century. In the late 1820s disputes over political reform broke up this grouping. A government led by the Duke of Wellington collapsed amidst dire election results. Following this disaster Robert Peel set about assembling a new coalition of forces. Peel issued the Tamworth Manifesto in 1834 which set out the basic principles of Conservatism; – the necessity in specific cases of reform in order to survive, but an opposition to unnecessary change, that could lead to "a perpetual vortex of agitation". Meanwhile, the Whigs, along with free trade Tory followers of Robert Peel, and independent Radicals, formed the Liberal Party under Lord Palmerston in 1859, and transformed into a party of the growing urban middle-class, under the long leadership of William Ewart Gladstone.
rewrite: The modern Conservative Party emerged from the Pittite Tory faction of the early nineteenth century. This grouping fragmented in the late 1820s over disputes concerning political reform, leading to the collapse of the Duke of Wellington's government after poor electoral performance. In the aftermath, Sir Robert Peel constructed a new political coalition. His 1834 Tamworth Manifesto established core Conservative principles, advocating measured reform when essential for preservation while rejecting needless change that might provoke a "perpetual vortex of agitation." Concurrently, the Whigs, Peelite Tories supportive of free trade, and independent Radicals coalesced into the Liberal Party in 1859 under Lord Palmerston. It subsequently evolved, particularly under William Ewart Gladstone's protracted leadership, into a party representing the expanding urban middle class.

input: Several versions of a semi-official, structured pantheon were developed during the political, social and religious instability of the Late Republican era. Jupiter, the most powerful of all gods and "the fount of the auspices upon which the relationship of the city with the gods rested", consistently personified the divine authority of Rome's highest offices, internal organization and external relations. During the archaic and early Republican eras, he shared his temple, some aspects of cult and several divine characteristics with Mars and Quirinus, who were later replaced by Juno and Minerva. A conceptual tendency toward triads may be indicated by the later agricultural or plebeian triad of Ceres, Liber and Libera, and by some of the complementary threefold deity-groupings of Imperial cult. Other major and minor deities could be single, coupled, or linked retrospectively through myths of divine marriage and sexual adventure. These later Roman pantheistic hierarchies are part literary and mythographic, part philosophical creations, and often Greek in origin. The Hellenization of Latin literature and culture supplied literary and artistic models for reinterpreting Roman deities in light of the Greek Olympians, and promoted a sense that the two cultures had a shared heritage.
rewrite: During the political, social, and religious upheavals of the Late Republican period, multiple iterations of a semi-official, structured pantheon emerged. Jupiter, as the supreme deity and "the fount of the auspices upon which the relationship of the city with the gods rested," consistently embodied the divine authority underpinning Rome's highest magistracies, its internal civic order, and its foreign affairs. In earlier archaic and early Republican times, he shared a temple, certain cultic features, and divine attributes with Mars and Quirinus, deities later supplanted by Juno and Minerva. A conceptual inclination toward triadic structures is further suggested by the subsequent plebeian triad of Ceres, Liber, and Libera, as well as by various threefold groupings within the Imperial cult. Additional major and minor deities could be venerated singly, in pairs, or connected retrospectively through mythological narratives of divine marriage and liaisons. These later hierarchical systematizations of Roman deities are partially literary and mythographic constructions, partially philosophical elaborations, frequently derived from Greek sources. The Hellenization of Roman literature and culture provided artistic and literary models for reinterpreting Roman gods in terms of the Greek Olympians, thereby fostering a perception of a shared mythological heritage between the two civilizations.

input: From the second half of the 20th century on parties which continued to rely on donations or membership subscriptions ran into mounting problems. Along with the increased scrutiny of donations there has been a long-term decline in party memberships in most western democracies which itself places more strains on funding. For example, in the United Kingdom and Australia membership of the two main parties in 2006 is less than an 1/8 of what it was in 1950, despite significant increases in population over that period.
rewrite: From the latter half of the twentieth century, political parties dependent on traditional funding sources such as donations and membership subscriptions encountered escalating difficulties. Heightened scrutiny of contributions coincided with a protracted decline in party membership across most Western democracies, intensifying financial pressures. For instance, in the United Kingdom and Australia, combined membership for the two major parties in 2006 was less than one-eighth of its 1950 level, notwithstanding substantial population growth during the intervening period.

input: A route through Beringia is seen as more likely than the Solutrean hypothesis. Kashani et al. 2012 state that "The similarities in ages and geographical distributions for C4c and the previously analyzed X2a lineage provide support to the scenario of a dual origin for Paleo-Indians. Taking into account that C4c is deeply rooted in the Asian portion of the mtDNA phylogeny and is indubitably of Asian origin, the finding that C4c and X2a are characterized by parallel genetic histories definitively dismisses the controversial hypothesis of an Atlantic glacial entry route into North America."
rewrite: A Beringian migration route is considered more probable than the Solutrean hypothesis. Kashani et al. (2012) argue that the parallel genetic histories of mitochondrial lineages C4c and X2a, sharing similar ages and distributions, support a dual origin for Paleo-Indians. Given that C4c is unequivocally of Asian origin and deeply rooted in Asian mitochondrial phylogeny, this correspondence definitively refutes the contested proposal of an Atlantic glacial entry into North America.

input: Fetuvalu offers the Cambridge syllabus. Motufoua offers the Fiji Junior Certificate (FJC) at year 10, Tuvaluan Certificate at Year 11 and the Pacific Senior Secondary Certificate (PSSC) at Year 12, set by the Fiji-based exam board SPBEA. Sixth form students who pass their PSSC go on to the Augmented Foundation Programme, funded by the government of Tuvalu. This program is required for tertiary education programmes outside of Tuvalu and is available at the University of the South Pacific (USP) Extension Centre in Funafuti.
rewrite: Fetuvalu School follows the Cambridge curriculum. In contrast, Motufoua Secondary School administers the Fiji Junior Certificate in Year 10, the Tuvaluan Certificate in Year 11, and the Pacific Senior Secondary Certificate (PSSC) in Year 12, as set by the Fiji-based SPBEA. Students who successfully complete the PSSC may enroll in the government-funded Augmented Foundation Programme. This prerequisite for tertiary study abroad is delivered at the University of the South Pacific Extension Centre in Funafuti.

input: The largest ethnic groups are Newar (29.6%), Matwali (25.1% Sunuwar, Gurung, Magars, Tamang etc.), Khas Brahmins (20.51%) and Chettris (18.5%) . Tamangs originating from surrounding hill districts can be seen in Kathmandu. More recently, other hill ethnic groups and Caste groups from Terai have come to represent a substantial proportion of the city's population. The major languages are Nepali and Nepal Bhasa, while English is understood by many, particularly in the service industry. The major religions are Hinduism and Buddhism.
rewrite: The predominant ethnic composition comprises Newars (29.6%), Matwali groups such as Sunuwar, Gurung, Magar, and Tamang (25.1%), Khas Brahmins (20.51%), and Chettris (18.5%). Tamang populations, originating from adjacent hill districts, are present in Kathmandu. More recently, additional hill ethnicities and Terai caste groups constitute a significant proportion. Primary languages are Nepali and Nepal Bhasa, with English widely understood, especially within services. Hinduism and Buddhism are the major religions.

input: Galileo Galilei was brought before the Inquisition for heresy, but abjured his views and was sentenced to house arrest, under which he spent the rest of his life. Galileo was found "vehemently suspect of heresy", namely of having held the opinions that the Sun lies motionless at the centre of the universe, that the Earth is not at its centre and moves, and that one may hold and defend an opinion as probable after it has been declared contrary to Holy Scripture. He was required to "abjure, curse and detest" those opinions.
rewrite: Galileo Galilei was tried by the Roman Inquisition and convicted of being "vehemently suspect of heresy." This charge stemmed from his adherence to the Copernican model, which posited a stationary Sun at the universe's center and a moving Earth, and from his defense of holding such theories as probable even after their condemnation as contrary to Scripture. Forced to formally abjure these views, he was subsequently sentenced to lifelong house arrest, where he remained until his death.

input: According to reciprocity, the efficiency of an antenna used as a receiving antenna is identical to the efficiency as defined above. The power that an antenna will deliver to a receiver (with a proper impedance match) is reduced by the same amount. In some receiving applications, the very inefficient antennas may have little impact on performance. At low frequencies, for example, atmospheric or man-made noise can mask antenna inefficiency. For example, CCIR Rep. 258-3 indicates man-made noise in a residential setting at 40 MHz is about 28 dB above the thermal noise floor. Consequently, an antenna with a 20 dB loss (due to inefficiency) would have little impact on system noise performance. The loss within the antenna will affect the intended signal and the noise/interference identically, leading to no reduction in signal to noise ratio (SNR).
rewrite: The principle of reciprocity dictates that the efficiency of an antenna in receiving mode is equivalent to its standard radiating efficiency. Consequently, the power delivered to a receiver under impedance-matched conditions is reduced proportionally by this efficiency factor. However, in certain reception scenarios, significant antenna inefficiency may not substantially degrade system performance. At lower frequencies, for instance, prevailing noise from atmospheric or anthropogenic sources can dominate, rendering antenna losses less critical. As an illustration, CCIR Report 258-3 specifies that man-made noise in a residential area at 40 MHz is approximately 28 dB above the thermal noise floor. Therefore, an antenna exhibiting a 20 dB loss due to inefficiency would have minimal effect on the overall noise performance. This is because the antenna's loss attenuates both the desired signal and the noise or interference equally, resulting in no degradation of the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).

input: In 2011, Bandai posted a countdown on a teaser site. Once the countdown was finished, it revealed a reboot of the Digimon World series titled Digimon World Re:Digitize. An enhanced version of the game released on Nintendo 3DS as Digimon World Re:Digitize Decode in 2013. Another role-playing game by the name Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth is set for release in 2015 for PlayStation Vita. It is part of the Digimon Story sub-series, originally on Nintendo DS and has also been released with English subtitles in North America.
rewrite: In 2011, Bandai initiated a promotional campaign via a teaser website featuring a countdown. Upon its conclusion, the campaign unveiled *Digimon World Re:Digitize*, a reboot of the *Digimon World* series. An enhanced edition, *Digimon World Re:Digitize Decode*, was subsequently released for the Nintendo 3DS in 2013. Furthermore, the role-playing game *Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth*, a title within the *Digimon Story* sub-series originally developed for the Nintendo DS, is scheduled for a 2015 release on the PlayStation Vita, including an English-subtitled North American version.

input: On 25 February 1991, the Warsaw Pact was declared disbanded at a meeting of defense and foreign ministers from remaining Pact countries meeting in Hungary. On 1 July 1991, in Prague, the Czechoslovak President Václav Havel formally ended the 1955 Warsaw Treaty Organization of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance and so disestablished the Warsaw Treaty after 36 years of military alliance with the USSR. In fact, the treaty was de facto disbanded in December 1989 during the violent revolution in Romania, which toppled the communist government, without military intervention form other member states. The USSR disestablished itself in December 1991.
rewrite: The Warsaw Pact was formally declared disbanded on 25 February 1991 at a meeting of defense and foreign ministers in Hungary. Subsequently, on 1 July 1991 in Prague, Czechoslovak President Václav Havel officially terminated the 1955 Warsaw Treaty, thereby dissolving the military alliance after thirty-six years. In practice, however, the Pact had ceased to function de facto in December 1989 following the Romanian Revolution, which overthrew its communist government without intervention from fellow members. The dissolution of the Soviet Union itself followed in December 1991.

input: Public funding and private investment have also been made with promises to rehabilitate neighborhoods. In April 2008, the city announced a $300-million stimulus plan to create jobs and revitalize neighborhoods, financed by city bonds and paid for by earmarking about 15% of the wagering tax. The city's working plans for neighborhood revitalizations include 7-Mile/Livernois, Brightmoor, East English Village, Grand River/Greenfield, North End, and Osborn. Private organizations have pledged substantial funding to the efforts. Additionally, the city has cleared a 1,200-acre (490 ha) section of land for large-scale neighborhood construction, which the city is calling the Far Eastside Plan. In 2011, Mayor Bing announced a plan to categorize neighborhoods by their needs and prioritize the most needed services for those neighborhoods.
rewrite: Public and private capital have been committed under initiatives pledging neighborhood rehabilitation. In April 2008, municipal authorities unveiled a $300-million stimulus strategy, funded through city bonds and supported by allocating approximately 15 percent of wagering tax revenue, aimed at job creation and community revitalization. Official revitalization frameworks designate several target areas, including 7-Mile/Livernois, Brightmoor, East English Village, Grand River/Greenfield, North End, and Osborn. Private entities have also pledged significant financial support to these endeavors. Furthermore, the city has prepared a 1,200-acre (490-hectare) parcel for extensive residential development under the Far Eastside Plan. In 2011, Mayor Bing introduced a systematic approach to classify neighborhoods according to specific needs, thereby prioritizing the allocation of essential services.

input: In Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968), the Supreme Court considered an Arkansas law that made it a crime "to teach the theory or doctrine that mankind ascended or descended from a lower order of animals," or "to adopt or use in any such institution a textbook that teaches" this theory in any school or university that received public funds. The court's opinion, written by Justice Abe Fortas, ruled that the Arkansas law violated "the constitutional prohibition of state laws respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. The overriding fact is that Arkansas' law selects from the body of knowledge a particular segment which it proscribes for the sole reason that it is deemed to conflict with a particular religious doctrine; that is, with a particular interpretation of the Book of Genesis by a particular religious group." The court held that the Establishment Clause prohibits the state from advancing any religion, and that "[T]he state has no legitimate interest in protecting any or all religions from views distasteful to them."
rewrite: In the case of *Epperson v. Arkansas*, 393 U.S. 97 (1968), the United States Supreme Court adjudicated the constitutionality of an Arkansas statute. This legislation criminalized the instruction of "the theory or doctrine that mankind ascended or descended from a lower order of animals," as well as the adoption of textbooks promoting this theory within any publicly funded educational institution. Delivering the opinion of the Court, Justice Abe Fortas determined the statute to be in violation of the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The Court found that the law singled out a specific scientific concept for prohibition solely on the grounds of its perceived conflict with a particular religious doctrine—namely, a specific interpretation of the Book of Genesis adhered to by certain religious groups. The ruling affirmed that the Establishment Clause forbids the state from promoting any religious viewpoint. Furthermore, it declared that the state possesses no legitimate secular interest in shielding religions from ideas they may find disagreeable, thereby invalidating the statute as an impermissible establishment of religion.

input: Although unpleasantness is an essential part of the IASP definition of pain, it is possible to induce a state described as intense pain devoid of unpleasantness in some patients, with morphine injection or psychosurgery. Such patients report that they have pain but are not bothered by it; they recognize the sensation of pain but suffer little, or not at all. Indifference to pain can also rarely be present from birth; these people have normal nerves on medical investigations, and find pain unpleasant, but do not avoid repetition of the pain stimulus.
rewrite: While unpleasantness is a core component of the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) definition, certain interventions, such as morphine administration or psychosurgery, can produce a state of intense pain sensation devoid of affective unpleasantness. Patients in this state acknowledge the sensory experience but report minimal or no associated suffering. Furthermore, a rare congenital condition manifests as pain indifference; despite possessing intact nociceptive pathways and finding pain unpleasant, affected individuals do not engage in typical pain-avoidance behaviors.

input: The Qur'an relates detailed narrative accounts of Maryam (Mary) in two places, Qur'an 3:35–47 and 19:16–34. These state beliefs in both the Immaculate Conception of Mary and the Virgin birth of Jesus. The account given in Sura 19 is nearly identical with that in the Gospel according to Luke, and both of these (Luke, Sura 19) begin with an account of the visitation of an angel upon Zakariya (Zecharias) and Good News of the birth of Yahya (John), followed by the account of the annunciation. It mentions how Mary was informed by an angel that she would become the mother of Jesus through the actions of God alone.
rewrite: The Qur’an presents detailed narratives concerning Maryam (Mary) in two passages: 3:35–47 and 19:16–34. These passages affirm the Islamic doctrines of Mary’s Immaculate Conception and the Virgin Birth of Jesus (‘Isa). The account in Surah 19 closely parallels the narrative in the Gospel of Luke. Both texts commence with the angelic visitation to Zakariya (Zechariah), announcing the birth of Yahya (John), followed by the annunciation to Mary. In this event, an angel informs Mary that she will conceive Jesus solely by divine decree.

input: As a relatively small and isolated oceanic island, Norfolk has few land birds but a high degree of endemicity among them. Many of the endemic species and subspecies have become extinct as a result of massive clearance of the island's native vegetation of subtropical rainforest for agriculture, hunting and persecution as agricultural pests. The birds have also suffered from the introduction of mammals such as rats, cats, pigs and goats, as well as from introduced competitors such as common blackbirds and crimson rosellas.
rewrite: Norfolk Island, being a small and isolated oceanic landmass, supports a limited number of land bird species, yet exhibits a high proportion of endemism within this avifauna. Numerous endemic species and subspecies have been driven to extinction, primarily due to extensive clearance of the native subtropical rainforest for agricultural purposes, coupled with hunting and persecution. Further declines have resulted from introduced mammalian predators, including rats, cats, pigs, and goats, as well as competitive pressure from non-native bird species.

input: Physical pain is an important political topic in relation to various issues, including pain management policy, drug control, animal rights or animal welfare, torture, and pain compliance. In various contexts, the deliberate infliction of pain in the form of corporal punishment is used as retribution for an offence, or for the purpose of disciplining or reforming a wrongdoer, or to deter attitudes or behaviour deemed unacceptable. In some cultures, extreme practices such as mortification of the flesh or painful rites of passage are highly regarded.
rewrite: Physical pain constitutes a significant political subject, intersecting with domains such as pain management policy, drug regulation, animal rights, torture, and pain compliance. Deliberately inflicted pain, often through corporal punishment, is employed across contexts as retribution, a disciplinary or reformative measure, or a deterrent against undesirable conduct. Furthermore, certain cultural frameworks valorize extreme practices involving physical suffering, including mortification of the flesh and painful rites of passage.

input: This trend for the king to rely on his own men at the expense of the barons was exacerbated by the tradition of Angevin royal ira et malevolentia – "anger and ill-will" – and John's own personality. From Henry II onwards, ira et malevolentia had come to describe the right of the king to express his anger and displeasure at particular barons or clergy, building on the Norman concept of malevoncia – royal ill-will. In the Norman period, suffering the king's ill-will meant difficulties in obtaining grants, honours or petitions; Henry II had infamously expressed his fury and ill-will towards Thomas Becket; this ultimately resulted in Becket's death. John now had the additional ability to "cripple his vassals" on a significant scale using his new economic and judicial measures, which made the threat of royal anger all the more serious.
rewrite: The tendency of the monarch to depend upon his personal adherents, thereby marginalizing the baronage, was intensified by the Angevin tradition of royal *ira et malevolentia*—"anger and ill-will"—coupled with King John's personal disposition. Evolving from the Norman concept of *malevolentia*, this principle, established from Henry II's reign, formally encapsulated the king's prerogative to manifest displeasure toward specific barons or clergy. Under Norman rule, incurring such ill-will hindered the acquisition of grants, titles, or favorable petitions; Henry II notoriously directed his fury and malevolence against Thomas Becket, leading to Becket's death. John augmented this existing threat by deploying novel fiscal and legal instruments to systematically impoverish his vassals, thereby rendering the prospect of royal wrath substantially more severe.

input: During the 1960s and 1970s, the city gained a reputation as an important center for liberal politics. Ann Arbor also became a locus for left-wing activism and served as a hub for the civil-rights movement and anti-Vietnam War movement, as well as the student movement. The first major meetings of the national left-wing campus group Students for a Democratic Society took place in Ann Arbor in 1960; in 1965, the city was home to the first U.S. teach-in against the Vietnam War.
