During the ensuing 15 years, many countercultural and New Left enterprises sprang up and developed large constituencies within the city. These influences washed into municipal politics during the early and mid-1970s when three members of the Human Rights Party (HRP) won city council seats on the strength of the student vote. During their time on the council, HRP representatives fought for measures including pioneering antidiscrimination ordinances, measures decriminalizing marijuana possession, and a rent-control ordinance; many of these remain in effect in modified form. Alongside these liberal and left-wing efforts, a small group of conservative institutions were born in Ann Arbor. These include Word of God (established in 1967), a charismatic inter-denominational movement; and the Thomas More Law Center (established in 1999), a religious-conservative advocacy group.
rewrite: During the 1960s and 1970s, Ann Arbor emerged as a significant nexus for liberal politics and left-wing activism, functioning as a central hub for the civil rights, anti-Vietnam War, and student movements. This period witnessed foundational events, including the inaugural major meetings of the national campus organization Students for a Democratic Society in 1960 and the first American teach-in against the Vietnam War, held in the city in 1965. Over the subsequent fifteen years, numerous countercultural and New Left enterprises arose, cultivating substantial local constituencies. Their influence permeated municipal governance in the early to mid-1970s, when three candidates from the Human Rights Party (HRP) were elected to the city council, propelled largely by student electoral support. While serving, HRP council members advocated for pioneering policies such as early antidiscrimination ordinances, measures to decriminalize marijuana possession, and rent-control legislation, many of which persist in adapted forms. Concurrently with these liberal and left-wing developments, a distinct cluster of conservative institutions also originated in Ann Arbor. Notable among these are the Word of God, a charismatic inter-denominational movement founded in 1967, and the Thomas More Law Center, a religious-conservative legal advocacy group established in 1999.

input: The USA PATRIOT Act of October 2001 dramatically reduces restrictions on law enforcement agencies' ability to search telephone, e-mail communications, medical, financial, and other records; eases restrictions on foreign intelligence gathering within the United States; expands the Secretary of the Treasury's authority to regulate financial transactions, particularly those involving foreign individuals and entities; and broadens the discretion of law enforcement and immigration authorities in detaining and deporting immigrants suspected of terrorism-related acts. The act also expanded the definition of terrorism to include domestic terrorism, thus enlarging the number of activities to which the USA PATRIOT Act's expanded law enforcement powers could be applied. A new Terrorist Finance Tracking Program monitored the movements of terrorists' financial resources (discontinued after being revealed by The New York Times). Global telecommunication usage, including those with no links to terrorism, is being collected and monitored through the NSA electronic surveillance program. The Patriot Act is still in effect.
rewrite: Enacted in October 2001, the USA PATRIOT Act significantly diminished constraints on law enforcement agencies regarding the surveillance of telephone and electronic communications, alongside access to medical, financial, and other personal records. It relaxed limitations on domestic foreign intelligence collection and augmented the Secretary of the Treasury’s regulatory control over financial transactions, especially those involving foreign parties. Furthermore, the act increased the discretionary authority of law enforcement and immigration officials to detain and deport immigrants suspected of terrorism-related activities. Its definition of terrorism was broadened to encompass domestic terrorism, thereby extending the scope of its enhanced investigative powers. Additional measures included the now-discontinued Terrorist Finance Tracking Program and bulk collection of global telecommunications data under NSA surveillance programs. The legislation remains in force.

input: On February 8, 1847, Doniphan continued his march with 924 men mostly from Missouri; he accompanied a train of 315 wagons of a large commercial caravan heading to the state capital. Meanwhile, the Mexican forces in the state had time to prepare a defense against the Americans. About 20 miles (32 km) north of the capital where two mountain ranges join from east to west is the only pass into the capital; known as Sacramento Pass, this point is now part of present-day Chihuahua City. The Battle of Sacramento was the most important battle fought in the state of Chihuahua because it was the sole defense for the state capital. The battle ended quickly because of some devastating defensive errors from the Mexican forces and the ingenious strategic moves by the American forces. After their loss at the Battle of Sacramento, the remaining Mexican soldiers retreated south, leaving the city to American occupation. Almost 300 Mexicans were killed in the battle, as well as almost 300 wounded. The Americans also confiscated large amounts of Mexican supplies and took 400 Mexican soldiers prisoners of war. American forces maintained an occupation of the state capital for the rest of the Mexican–American War.
rewrite: On February 8, 1847, Colonel Alexander Doniphan advanced with a force of 924 men, predominantly from Missouri, accompanying a commercial caravan of 315 wagons en route to the state capital of Chihuahua. During this period, Mexican forces within the state mobilized to organize a defensive position against the American advance. Approximately twenty miles (thirty-two kilometers) north of the capital, where two mountain ranges converge from east to west, lies the sole accessible pass into the city. This strategic location, known as the Sacramento Pass, is situated within what is now Chihuahua City. The Battle of Sacramento represented the most significant military engagement in Chihuahua, as it constituted the singular defensive effort for the state capital. The conflict concluded rapidly due to critical defensive errors by Mexican forces and effective tactical maneuvers by the Americans. Following their defeat, the remaining Mexican troops retreated southward, resulting in the American occupation of the city. Mexican casualties included nearly 300 fatalities and a comparable number of wounded. American forces also captured substantial Mexican supplies and took 400 soldiers as prisoners of war. The occupation of the Chihuahua capital was subsequently maintained by American forces for the remainder of the Mexican-American War.

input: Lester Brown has argued that "a world facing the prospect of economically disruptive climate change can no longer justify subsidies to expand the burning of coal and oil. Shifting these subsidies to the development of climate-benign energy sources such as wind, solar, biomass, and geothermal power is the key to stabilizing the earth's climate." The International Solar Energy Society advocates "leveling the playing field" by redressing the continuing inequities in public subsidies of energy technologies and R&D, in which the fossil fuel and nuclear power receive the largest share of financial support.
rewrite: Lester Brown contends that in a world confronting economically disruptive climate change, subsidizing the expansion of coal and oil combustion is no longer justifiable. Redirecting these subsidies toward climate-benign energy sources—such as wind, solar, biomass, and geothermal power—is essential for climate stabilization. Similarly, the International Solar Energy Society advocates for "leveling the playing field" by correcting persistent inequities in public subsidies and research funding, which disproportionately favor fossil fuel and nuclear technologies.

input: Several hundred pro-Tibet protesters gathered at the Trocadéro with banners and Tibetan flags, and remained there for a peaceful protest, never approaching the torch relay itself. Among them was Jane Birkin, who spoke to the media about the "lack of freedom of speech" in China. Also present was Thupten Gyatso, President of the French Tibetan community, who called upon pro-Tibet demonstrators to "remain calm, non-violent, peaceful".
rewrite: Several hundred pro-Tibet demonstrators assembled at the Trocadéro, displaying banners and Tibetan flags for a peaceful gathering that did not approach the torch relay. Attendee Jane Birkin addressed the media regarding perceived restrictions on freedom of expression in China. Thupten Gyatso, President of the French Tibetan community, urged protesters to maintain a calm, non-violent, and peaceful demeanor.

input: The Dutch written grammar has simplified over the past 100 years: cases are now mainly used for the pronouns, such as ik (I), mij, me (me), mijn (my), wie (who), wiens (whose: masculine or neuter singular), wier (whose: feminine singular; masculine, feminine or neuter plural). Nouns and adjectives are not case inflected (except for the genitive of proper nouns (names): -s, -'s or -'). In the spoken language cases and case inflections had already gradually disappeared from a much earlier date on (probably the 15th century) as in many continental West Germanic dialects.
rewrite: Over the past century, Dutch written grammar has undergone significant simplification. Case distinctions are now largely confined to pronouns, such as *ik* (I), *mij/me* (me), and *mijn* (my), as well as the interrogative *wie* (who) with its possessive forms *wiens* and *wier*. Nouns and adjectives no longer exhibit case inflection, with the exception of the genitive marker (-s, -'s, or -') for proper nouns. In spoken Dutch, however, the erosion of case systems began considerably earlier, likely around the 15th century, aligning with developments in other continental West Germanic dialects.

input: The World Health Organization and the UN Environment Programme estimate that each year, 3 million workers in agriculture in the developing world experience severe poisoning from pesticides, about 18,000 of whom die. Owing to inadequate regulation and safety precautions, 99% of pesticide related deaths occur in developing countries that account for only 25% of pesticide usage. According to one study, as many as 25 million workers in developing countries may suffer mild pesticide poisoning yearly. There are several careers aside from agriculture that may also put individuals at risk of health effects from pesticide exposure including pet groomers, groundskeepers, and fumigators.
rewrite: According to estimates from the World Health Organization and the UN Environment Programme, approximately 3 million agricultural workers in the developing world suffer acute pesticide poisoning annually, resulting in roughly 18,000 fatalities. Inadequate regulatory frameworks and safety measures contribute to a stark disparity, with 99% of pesticide-related deaths occurring in developing nations, which account for only a quarter of global pesticide use. One study suggests up to 25 million workers in these regions may experience mild pesticide poisoning each year. Beyond agriculture, occupations such as pet grooming, groundskeeping, and fumigation also pose significant risks of exposure-related health effects.

input: Peel, widely regarded as the father of modern policing, was heavily influenced by the social and legal philosophy of Jeremy Bentham, who called for a strong and centralized, but politically neutral, police force for the maintenance of social order, for the protection of people from crime and to act as a visible deterrent to urban crime and disorder. Peel decided to standardise the police force as an official paid profession, to organise it in a civilian fashion, and to make it answerable to the public.
rewrite: Sir Robert Peel, recognized as the founder of modern policing, was profoundly shaped by the utilitarian philosophy of Jeremy Bentham. Bentham advocated for a centralized, apolitical police institution to ensure social order, protect citizens, and serve as a visible deterrent against urban crime and disorder. Consequently, Peel systematically professionalized the force by establishing it as a standardized, salaried, and civilian-organized body, directly accountable to the public it served.

input: The western section of the state is part of the Appalachian Mountain range. Among the subranges of the Appalachians located in the state are the Great Smoky Mountains, Blue Ridge Mountains, Great Balsam Mountains, and Black Mountains. The Black Mountains are the highest in the eastern United States, and culminate in Mount Mitchell at 6,684 feet (2,037 m) the highest point east of the Mississippi River. Although agriculture still remains important, tourism has become a dominant industry in the mountains. Growing Christmas trees has recently become an important industry as well. Because of the higher altitude, the climate in the mountains often differs markedly from that of the rest of the state. Winter in western North Carolina typically features high snowfall and subfreezing temperatures more akin to those of a midwestern state than of a southern state.
rewrite: The western region of the state lies within the Appalachian Mountain system. This area encompasses several subranges, including the Great Smoky Mountains, the Blue Ridge Mountains, the Great Balsam Mountains, and the Black Mountains. The Black Mountains constitute the highest range in the eastern United States, with their summit, Mount Mitchell, reaching an elevation of 6,684 feet (2,037 m), which is the highest point east of the Mississippi River. While agriculture retains significance, tourism has emerged as the predominant economic sector in this region, supplemented by a growing industry in Christmas tree cultivation. The mountainous climate, characterized by higher altitudes, frequently contrasts sharply with conditions elsewhere in the state. Winters in western North Carolina typically involve substantial snowfall and subfreezing temperatures, more closely resembling the climate of a midwestern state than that of a southern one.

input: Within six years of the official criminalization of heresy by the Emperor, the first Christian heretic to be executed, Priscillian, was condemned in 386 by Roman secular officials for sorcery, and put to death with four or five followers. However, his accusers were excommunicated both by Ambrose of Milan and Pope Siricius, who opposed Priscillian's heresy, but "believed capital punishment to be inappropriate at best and usually unequivocally evil". For some years after the Reformation, Protestant churches were also known to execute those they considered heretics, including Catholics. The last known heretic executed by sentence of the Roman Catholic Church was Spanish schoolmaster Cayetano Ripoll in 1826. The number of people executed as heretics under the authority of the various "ecclesiastical authorities"[note 1] is not known.[note 2] One of the first examples of the word as translated from the Nag Hammadi's Apocalypse of Peter was" they will cleave to the name of a dead man thinking that they will become pure. But they will become greatly defiled and they will fall into the name of error and into the hands of an evil cunning man and a manifold dogma, and they will be ruled heretically".
rewrite: Within six years of heresy being formally criminalized under imperial authority, the first execution of a Christian heretic occurred in 386 with the condemnation of Priscillian. Roman secular officials charged him with sorcery, leading to his execution alongside four or five followers. Notably, his accusers were subsequently excommunicated by both Ambrose of Milan and Pope Siricius. While opposed to Priscillian’s doctrines, these church authorities deemed capital punishment for heresy inappropriate at best and fundamentally immoral. Following the Reformation, Protestant churches likewise employed execution against those they deemed heretical, including Catholics. The final known execution ordered by the Roman Catholic Church was that of the Spanish schoolmaster Cayetano Ripoll in 1826. The total number of individuals executed as heretics under various ecclesiastical authorities remains undetermined. An early conceptualization of heresy appears in a translation from the Nag Hammadi library’s Apocalypse of Peter, which describes individuals who “will cleave to the name of a dead man thinking that they will become pure. But they will become greatly defiled and they will fall into the name of error and into the hands of an evil cunning man and a manifold dogma, and they will be ruled heretically.”

input: Greece is today relatively homogeneous in linguistic terms, with a large majority of the native population using Greek as their first or only language. Among the Greek-speaking population, speakers of the distinctive Pontic dialect came to Greece from Asia Minor after the Greek genocide and constitute a sizable group. The Cappadocian dialect came to Greece due to the genocide as well, but is endangered and is barely spoken now. Indigenous Greek dialects include the archaic Greek spoken by the Sarakatsani, traditionally transhument mountain shepherds of Greek Macedonia and other parts of Northern Greece. The Tsakonian language, a distinct Greek language deriving from Doric Greek instead of Ionic Greek, is still spoken in some villages in the southeastern Peloponnese.
rewrite: Contemporary Greece exhibits considerable linguistic homogeneity, with the vast majority of the native population employing Greek as a primary or sole language. Within this Greek-speaking majority, several distinct groups exist. Speakers of the Pontic dialect, originating from Asia Minor, arrived following the early 20th-century Greek genocide and form a significant community. The Cappadocian dialect, also a product of that displacement, is now critically endangered. Among indigenous varieties, the archaic Greek of the Sarakatsani—traditionally transhumant shepherds in Greek Macedonia and northern regions—persists. Furthermore, the Tsakonian language, a separate Hellenic language descended from Doric rather than Ionic Greek, continues in limited use in certain southeastern Peloponnesian villages.

input: Lewis Latimer, employed at the time by Edison, developed an improved method of heat-treating carbon filaments which reduced breakage and allowed them to be molded into novel shapes, such as the characteristic "M" shape of Maxim filaments. On 17 January 1882, Latimer received a patent for the "Process of Manufacturing Carbons", an improved method for the production of light bulb filaments, which was purchased by the United States Electric Light Company. Latimer patented other improvements such as a better way of attaching filaments to their wire supports.
rewrite: Employed by Thomas Edison, Lewis Latimer devised a superior heat-treatment process for carbon filaments. This technique minimized breakage and enabled molding into innovative forms, including the distinctive "M" shape of Maxim filaments. On 17 January 1882, Latimer secured a patent for his "Process of Manufacturing Carbons," an enhanced method for producing light bulb filaments, subsequently acquired by the United States Electric Light Company. He also patented further refinements, such as an improved means of affixing filaments to their supporting wires.

input: On April 22, 1971, Kerry appeared before a U.S. Senate committee hearing on proposals relating to ending the war. The day after this testimony, Kerry participated in a demonstration with thousands of other veterans in which he and other Vietnam War veterans threw their medals and service ribbons over a fence erected at the front steps of the United States Capitol building to dramatize their opposition to the war. Jack Smith, a Marine, read a statement explaining why the veterans were returning their military awards to the government. For more than two hours, almost 1000 angry veterans tossed their medals, ribbons, hats, jackets, and military papers over the fence. Each veteran gave his or her name, hometown, branch of service and a statement. Kerry threw some of his own decorations and awards as well as some given to him by other veterans to throw. As Kerry threw his decorations over the fence, his statement was: "I'm not doing this for any violent reasons, but for peace and justice, and to try and make this country wake up once and for all."
rewrite: On April 22, 1971, John Kerry testified before a United States Senate committee regarding proposals to conclude the Vietnam War. The following day, he joined a demonstration of several thousand veterans in a symbolic protest against the conflict. To dramatize their opposition, Kerry and fellow veterans discarded their military medals and service ribbons over a fence erected before the steps of the United States Capitol. Marine veteran Jack Smith delivered a formal statement articulating the rationale for returning these awards to the government. Over a period exceeding two hours, nearly one thousand veterans participated, casting not only medals and ribbons but also hats, jackets, and military documents over the barrier. Each participant declared their name, hometown, branch of service, and a personal statement. Kerry discarded several of his own decorations, in addition to awards entrusted to him by other veterans for that purpose. During this act, he stated, “I am not doing this for any violent reasons, but for peace and justice, and to try and make this country wake up once and for all.”

input: Vinson Massif, the highest peak in Antarctica at 4,892 m (16,050 ft), is located in the Ellsworth Mountains. Antarctica contains many other mountains, on both the main continent and the surrounding islands. Mount Erebus on Ross Island is the world's southernmost active volcano. Another well-known volcano is found on Deception Island, which is famous for a giant eruption in 1970. Minor eruptions are frequent and lava flow has been observed in recent years. Other dormant volcanoes may potentially be active. In 2004, a potentially active underwater volcano was found in the Antarctic Peninsula by American and Canadian researchers.
rewrite: Vinson Massif, at 4,892 meters, is the highest peak in Antarctica and is situated within the Ellsworth Mountains. The continent and its surrounding islands feature numerous other significant mountains. Notably, Mount Erebus on Ross Island is the southernmost active volcano globally. Deception Island, renowned for a major 1970 eruption, hosts another prominent volcano, with frequent minor eruptions and observed lava flows in recent years. While other volcanoes remain dormant, they possess potential activity. In 2004, American and Canadian researchers identified a potentially active submarine volcano near the Antarctic Peninsula.

input: All birds lay amniotic eggs with hard shells made mostly of calcium carbonate. Hole and burrow nesting species tend to lay white or pale eggs, while open nesters lay camouflaged eggs. There are many exceptions to this pattern, however; the ground-nesting nightjars have pale eggs, and camouflage is instead provided by their plumage. Species that are victims of brood parasites have varying egg colours to improve the chances of spotting a parasite's egg, which forces female parasites to match their eggs to those of their hosts.
rewrite: Avian species universally produce amniotic eggs characterized by calcareous shells composed primarily of calcium carbonate. A general ecological correlation exists wherein cavity-nesting birds typically lay white or pale eggs, whereas species utilizing open nests deposit pigmented, camouflaged eggs. Notable exceptions occur, such as in ground-nesting nightjars, which possess pale eggs but rely on cryptic plumage for concealment. In host species targeted by brood parasites, egg coloration varies to facilitate parasite egg detection, exerting selective pressure for parasitic females to evolve eggshell mimicry of their specific hosts.

input: While successful predation results in a gain of energy, hunting invariably involves energetic costs as well. When hunger is not an issue, in general most predators will not seek to attack prey since the costs outweigh the benefits. For instance, a large predatory fish like a shark that is well fed in an aquarium will typically ignore the smaller fish swimming around it (while the prey fish take advantage of the fact that the apex predator is apparently uninterested). Surplus killing represents a deviation from this type of behaviour. The treatment of consumption in terms of cost-benefit analysis is known as optimal foraging theory, and has been quite successful in the study of animal behavior. In general, costs and benefits are considered in energy gain per unit time, though other factors are also important, such as essential nutrients that have no caloric value but are necessary for survival and health.
rewrite: While successful predation yields an energetic gain, the act of hunting inherently entails significant energetic expenditures. Consequently, when not driven by hunger, most predators generally avoid initiating attacks, as the associated costs typically exceed the benefits. This principle is illustrated by the behavior of a sated predatory fish, such as a shark in an aquarium, which will commonly ignore potential prey swimming nearby—a situation the prey fish may exploit. Surplus killing, however, constitutes a notable exception to this behavioral pattern. The analytical framework examining such consumption decisions through a cost-benefit lens is termed optimal foraging theory, a highly productive approach in behavioral ecology. This theory primarily evaluates trade-offs in terms of net energy acquisition per unit time, yet it also incorporates other critical factors, including the procurement of essential non-caloric nutrients vital for survival and physiological maintenance.

input: Initial reactions to the novel were varied. The New Yorker declared it "skilled, unpretentious, and totally ingenious", and The Atlantic Monthly's reviewer rated it as "pleasant, undemanding reading", but found the narrative voice—"a six-year-old girl with the prose style of a well-educated adult"—to be implausible. Time magazine's 1960 review of the book states that it "teaches the reader an astonishing number of useful truths about little girls and about Southern life" and calls Scout Finch "the most appealing child since Carson McCullers' Frankie got left behind at the wedding". The Chicago Sunday Tribune noted the even-handed approach to the narration of the novel's events, writing: "This is in no way a sociological novel. It underlines no cause ... To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel of strong contemporary national significance."
rewrite: Critical reception of Harper Lee’s novel was notably mixed upon its publication. *The New Yorker* praised the work as “skilled, unpretentious, and totally ingenious,” while *The Atlantic Monthly* characterized it as “pleasant, undemanding reading,” though its critic questioned the plausibility of the narrative voice—that of a six-year-old girl employing the prose style of a well-educated adult. In a 1960 assessment, *Time* magazine asserted that the novel “teaches the reader an astonishing number of useful truths about little girls and about Southern life,” describing protagonist Scout Finch as “the most appealing child since Carson McCullers’ Frankie got left behind at the wedding.” Conversely, *The Chicago Sunday Tribune* emphasized the novel’s balanced narration, observing, “This is in no way a sociological novel. It underlines no cause…” and concluding it was instead “a novel of strong contemporary national significance.”

input: In its Basic Laws, Israel defines itself as a Jewish and democratic state. Israel is a representative democracy with a parliamentary system, proportional representation and universal suffrage. The prime minister serves as head of government and the Knesset serves as the legislature. Israel is a developed country and an OECD member, with the 35th-largest economy in the world by nominal gross domestic product as of 2015[update]. The country benefits from a highly skilled workforce and is among the most educated countries in the world with the one of the highest percentage of its citizens holding a tertiary education degree. The country has the highest standard of living in the Middle East and the fourth highest in Asia, and has one of the highest life expectancies in the world.
rewrite: Israel is formally defined as both a Jewish and democratic state within its Basic Laws. It functions as a representative democracy, employing a parliamentary system characterized by proportional representation and universal suffrage. Executive authority rests with the prime minister as head of government, while legislative power is vested in the Knesset. As a developed nation and member of the OECD, Israel possessed the world's 35th-largest nominal GDP as of 2015. The country maintains a highly skilled and educated populace, with one of the highest global rates of tertiary education attainment. Consequently, Israel exhibits the highest standard of living in the Middle East, the fourth highest in Asia, and ranks among the world leaders in life expectancy.

input: Horizontal gene transfer is invoked to explain how there is often extreme similarity between small portions of the genomes of two organisms that are otherwise very distantly related. Horizontal gene transfer seems to be common among many microbes. Also, eukaryotic cells seem to have experienced a transfer of some genetic material from their chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes to their nuclear chromosomes.
rewrite: Horizontal gene transfer accounts for instances of pronounced genomic similarity in specific regions between otherwise distantly related organisms. This phenomenon is prevalent among numerous microbes. Additionally, eukaryotic cells appear to have undergone transfer of certain genetic material from their chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes to their nuclear chromosomes.

input: For example, in order to meet the expectations for good color rendering in retail applications, research suggests using the well-established CRI along with another metric called gamut area index (GAI). GAI represents the relative separation of object colors illuminated by a light source; the greater the GAI, the greater the apparent saturation or vividness of the object colors. As a result, light sources which balance both CRI and GAI are generally preferred over ones that have only high CRI or only high GAI.
rewrite: To achieve optimal color rendering in retail settings, research recommends supplementing the established Color Rendering Index (CRI) with the Gamut Area Index (GAI). GAI quantifies the relative separation of illuminated object colors, where a higher value corresponds to increased apparent saturation or vividness. Consequently, light sources that effectively balance both CRI and GAI are generally favored over those excelling in only one metric.

input: Alexander faced pressure from his brother, Duke Constantine, to make peace with Napoleon. Given the victory he had just achieved, the French emperor offered the Russians relatively lenient terms–demanding that Russia join the Continental System, withdraw its forces from Wallachia and Moldavia, and hand over the Ionian Islands to France. By contrast, Napoleon dictated very harsh peace terms for Prussia, despite the ceaseless exhortations of Queen Louise. Wiping out half of Prussian territories from the map, Napoleon created a new kingdom of 1,100 square miles called Westphalia. He then appointed his young brother Jérôme as the new monarch of this kingdom. Prussia's humiliating treatment at Tilsit caused a deep and bitter antagonism which festered as the Napoleonic era progressed. Moreover, Alexander's pretensions at friendship with Napoleon led the latter to seriously misjudge the true intentions of his Russian counterpart, who would violate numerous provisions of the treaty in the next few years. Despite these problems, the Treaties of Tilsit at last gave Napoleon a respite from war and allowed him to return to France, which he had not seen in over 300 days.
rewrite: Alexander I was compelled by his brother, Grand Duke Constantine, to negotiate peace with Napoleon. Following his recent military successes, the French emperor presented Russia with comparatively moderate conditions, requiring its adherence to the Continental System, the withdrawal of Russian troops from Wallachia and Moldavia, and the cession of the Ionian Islands to France. In stark contrast, Napoleon imposed severely punitive terms upon Prussia, disregarding the persistent appeals of Queen Louise. He eradicated half of Prussian territory, from which he carved a new kingdom of approximately 1,100 square miles named Westphalia, installing his younger brother Jérôme as its sovereign. The profound humiliation inflicted upon Prussia at Tilsit generated a lasting and resentful hostility that intensified throughout the subsequent Napoleonic period. Furthermore, Alexander’s overtures of amity toward Napoleon resulted in a significant miscalculation by the latter regarding the Tsar’s genuine intentions, leading Russia to contravene multiple treaty stipulations in the ensuing years. Notwithstanding these tensions, the Treaties of Tilsit ultimately provided Napoleon with a temporary cessation of hostilities and enabled his return to France after an absence of more than three hundred days.

input: Its written transmission, along with the veneration bestowed on certain classical works, has led to the expectation that performers will play a work in a way that realizes in detail the original intentions of the composer. During the 19th century the details that composers put in their scores generally increased. Yet the opposite trend—admiration of performers for new "interpretations" of the composer's work—can be seen, and it is not unknown for a composer to praise a performer for achieving a better realization of the original intent than the composer was able to imagine. Thus, classical performers often achieve high reputations for their musicianship, even if they do not compose themselves. Generally however, it is the composers who are remembered more than the performers.
rewrite: The written transmission of musical works, combined with the veneration accorded to canonical compositions, has fostered an expectation that performers will execute a piece in a manner that meticulously realizes the composer's original intentions. Throughout the nineteenth century, the level of detail specified in composers' scores generally expanded. Concurrently, however, an opposing trend emerged, characterized by an appreciation for novel interpretive approaches by performers. Notably, composers have occasionally praised performers for achieving a conception surpassing the composer's own initial imagination. Consequently, performers within the classical tradition frequently attain significant esteem for their musicianship, independent of compositional activity. Nonetheless, historical remembrance typically privileges composers over performers.

input: In the following months, NATO took a wide range of measures to respond to the threat of terrorism. On 22 November 2002, the member states of the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC) decided on a Partnership Action Plan against Terrorism, which explicitly states, "EAPC States are committed to the protection and promotion of fundamental freedoms and human rights, as well as the rule of law, in combating terrorism." NATO started naval operations in the Mediterranean Sea designed to prevent the movement of terrorists or weapons of mass destruction as well as to enhance the security of shipping in general called Operation Active Endeavour.
rewrite: In the subsequent months, NATO implemented a comprehensive array of measures to address the threat of terrorism. On 22 November 2002, the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC) member states adopted a Partnership Action Plan against Terrorism. This plan explicitly affirms the commitment of EAPC states to upholding fundamental freedoms, human rights, and the rule of law while countering terrorism. Concurrently, NATO initiated naval operations in the Mediterranean Sea, designated Operation Active Endeavour. This mission aimed to deter the movement of terrorists or weapons of mass destruction and to improve overall maritime security.

input: Tourism is also an important industry in Miami. Along with finance and business, the beaches, conventions, festivals and events draw over 38 million visitors annually into the city, from across the country and around the world, spending $17.1 billion. The Art Deco District in South Beach, is reputed as one of the most glamorous in the world for its nightclubs, beaches, historical buildings, and shopping. Annual events such as the Sony Ericsson Open, Art Basel, Winter Music Conference, South Beach Wine & Food Festival, and Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Miami attract millions to the metropolis every year.
rewrite: Tourism constitutes a significant sector within Miami's economy. Alongside finance and commerce, the city's beaches, conventions, festivals, and events attract in excess of 38 million domestic and international visitors annually. These visitors contribute approximately $17.1 billion in expenditures. South Beach's Art Deco District is globally renowned for its nightlife, beaches, historic architecture, and retail. Major annual events, including Art Basel, the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, and Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Miami, draw millions to the metropolitan area each year.

input: Some NPOs which are particularly well known, often for the charitable or social nature of their activities performed during a long period of time, include Amnesty International, Oxfam, Rotary International, Kiwanis International, Carnegie Corporation of New York, Nourishing USA, DEMIRA Deutsche Minenräumer (German Mine Clearers), FIDH International Federation for Human Rights, Goodwill Industries, United Way, ACORN (now defunct), Habitat for Humanity, Teach For America, the Red Cross and Red Crescent organizations, UNESCO, IEEE, INCOSE, World Wide Fund for Nature, Heifer International, Translators Without Borders and SOS Children's Villages.
rewrite: Several prominent non-profit organizations, distinguished by their longstanding charitable or social missions, include Amnesty International, Oxfam, Rotary International, Kiwanis International, Carnegie Corporation of New York, Nourishing USA, DEMIRA, FIDH, Goodwill Industries, United Way, ACORN (defunct), Habitat for Humanity, Teach For America, the Red Cross/Red Crescent, UNESCO, IEEE, INCOSE, World Wide Fund for Nature, Heifer International, Translators Without Borders, and SOS Children's Villages.

input: The United Nations designates Tuvalu as a least developed country (LDC) because of its limited potential for economic development, absence of exploitable resources and its small size and vulnerability to external economic and environmental shocks. Tuvalu participates in the Enhanced Integrated Framework for Trade-Related Technical Assistance to Least Developed Countries (EIF), which was established in October 1997 under the auspices of the World Trade Organisation. In 2013 Tuvalu deferred its graduation from least developed country (LDC) status to a developing country to 2015. Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga said that this deferral was necessary to maintain access by Tuvalu to the funds provided by the United Nations's National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA), as "Once Tuvalu graduates to a developed country, it will not be considered for funding assistance for climate change adaptation programmes like NAPA, which only goes to LDCs". Tuvalu had met targets so that Tuvalu was to graduate from LDC status. Prime minister, Enele Sopoaga wants the United Nations to reconsider its criteria for graduation from LDC status as not enough weight is given to the environmental plight of small island states like Tuvalu in the application of the Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI).
rewrite: The United Nations classifies Tuvalu as a Least Developed Country (LDC), a designation based on its constrained economic potential, lack of exploitable natural resources, and pronounced vulnerability due to its small size and exposure to external economic and environmental shocks. Tuvalu is a participant in the Enhanced Integrated Framework for Trade-Related Technical Assistance to Least Developed Countries (EIF), an initiative established under World Trade Organisation auspices in October 1997. In 2013, the nation deferred its scheduled graduation from LDC status to 2015. Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga justified this postponement as essential for preserving Tuvalu's access to financial support through the UN's National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA), noting that graduation would disqualify the country from such climate change adaptation funding, which is reserved for LDCs. Although Tuvalu had met the technical benchmarks for graduation, Prime Minister Sopoaga has called for the United Nations to reassess its graduation criteria. He argues that the Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI), as applied, inadequately accounts for the severe environmental challenges facing small island states, thereby failing to grant sufficient weight to their unique plight in the development status evaluation.

input: The same divine agencies who caused disease or harm also had the power to avert it, and so might be placated in advance. Divine consideration might be sought to avoid the inconvenient delays of a journey, or encounters with banditry, piracy and shipwreck, with due gratitude to be rendered on safe arrival or return. In times of great crisis, the Senate could decree collective public rites, in which Rome's citizens, including women and children, moved in procession from one temple to the next, supplicating the gods.
rewrite: The same deities believed to inflict illness or misfortune also possessed the capacity to prevent it, rendering them amenable to preemptive appeasement. Divine favor could be solicited to forestall travel delays or perilous encounters with bandits, pirates, or shipwrecks, with vows of gratitude upon safe passage. During grave emergencies, the Senate could mandate public supplications, wherein the citizenry—including women and children—processed between temples to entreat the gods collectively.

input: Yerevan Vernissage (arts and crafts market), close to Republic Square, bustles with hundreds of vendors selling a variety of crafts on weekends and Wednesdays (though the selection is much reduced mid-week). The market offers woodcarving, antiques, fine lace, and the hand-knotted wool carpets and kilims that are a Caucasus specialty. Obsidian, which is found locally, is crafted into assortment of jewellery and ornamental objects. Armenian gold smithery enjoys a long tradition, populating one corner of the market with a selection of gold items. Soviet relics and souvenirs of recent Russian manufacture – nesting dolls, watches, enamel boxes and so on – are also available at the Vernisage.
rewrite: The Yerevan Vernissage, an open-air arts and crafts market proximate to Republic Square, operates with particular vibrancy on weekends and Wednesdays, hosting numerous vendors; mid-week offerings are considerably diminished. Merchandise includes traditional woodcarvings, antiques, lace, and hand-knotted wool carpets and kilims, representative of Caucasian craftsmanship. Locally sourced obsidian is fashioned into jewellery and ornamental items. One section is devoted to Armenian goldsmithing, a practice with deep historical roots, displaying various gold objects. Additionally, the market vends Soviet-era relics and contemporary Russian souvenirs, such as matryoshka dolls, watches, and enamel boxes.

input: Botany was greatly stimulated by the appearance of the first "modern" text book, Matthias Schleiden's Grundzüge der Wissenschaftlichen Botanik, published in English in 1849 as Principles of Scientific Botany. Schleiden was a microscopist and an early plant anatomist who co-founded the cell theory with Theodor Schwann and Rudolf Virchow and was among the first to grasp the significance of the cell nucleus that had been described by Robert Brown in 1831. In 1855, Adolf Fick formulated Fick's laws that enabled the calculation of the rates of molecular diffusion in biological systems.
rewrite: The field of botany was significantly advanced by the 1849 English publication of Matthias Schleiden's *Principles of Scientific Botany*, a foundational modern textbook. Schleiden, a microscopist and early plant anatomist, co-founded cell theory and recognized the importance of the cell nucleus, first described by Robert Brown in 1831. Subsequently, in 1855, Adolf Fick established Fick's laws, providing a quantitative framework for calculating molecular diffusion rates in biological systems.

input: The Dean of the College of Cardinals, or Cardinal-dean, is the primus inter pares of the College of Cardinals, elected by the cardinal bishops holding suburbicarian sees from among their own number, an election, however, that must be approved by the Pope. Formerly the position of dean belonged by right to the longest-serving of the cardinal bishops.
rewrite: The Dean of the College of Cardinals serves as its primus inter pares. Elected by the cardinal bishops from the suburbicarian sees, the appointment requires papal approval. Historically, the deanship belonged by right to the cardinal bishop with the longest tenure.

input: One of the most important victories of the magnates was the late 16th century right to create ordynacja's (similar to majorats), which ensured that a family which gained wealth and power could more easily preserve this. Ordynacje's of families of Radziwiłł, Zamoyski, Potocki or Lubomirski often rivalled the estates of the king and were important power bases for the magnates.
rewrite: A pivotal achievement for the magnates was the late sixteenth-century right to establish *ordynacje* (entailed estates akin to majorats). This legal instrument enabled newly ascendant families to consolidate and perpetuate their wealth and power. The *ordynacje* of lineages such as the Radziwiłłs, Zamoyskis, Potockis, and Lubomirskis often rivaled royal domains, serving as crucial bases of magnate influence.

input: Adolescence is frequently characterized by a transformation of an adolescent's understanding of the world, the rational direction towards a life course, and the active seeking of new ideas rather than the unquestioning acceptance of adult authority. An adolescent begins to develop a unique belief system through his or her interaction with social, familial, and cultural environments. While organized religion is not necessarily a part of every adolescent's life experience, youth are still held responsible for forming a set of beliefs about themselves, the world around them, and whatever higher powers they may or may not believe in. This process is often accompanied or aided by cultural traditions that intend to provide a meaningful transition to adulthood through a ceremony, ritual, confirmation, or rite of passage.
rewrite: Adolescence is commonly marked by a shift in worldview, wherein youth increasingly pursue novel ideas and deliberate life trajectories rather than uncritically adhering to adult authority. Through engagement with social, familial, and cultural contexts, adolescents cultivate distinct personal belief systems. Although organized religion may not feature in every adolescent’s experience, young people nonetheless undertake the task of forming convictions regarding themselves, their surroundings, and any potential higher powers. This developmental process is frequently supported by cultural traditions, which aim to imbue the transition to adulthood with meaning through ceremonies, rituals, confirmations, or rites of passage.

input: Special procedures apply to legislation passed by Tynwald, the legislature of the Isle of Man. Before the lordship of the Island was purchased by the British Crown in 1765 (the Revestment), the assent of the Lord of Mann to a bill was signified by letter to the governor. After 1765, royal assent was at first signified by letter from the Secretary of State to the governor; but, during the British Regency, the practice began of granting royal assent by Order in Council, which continues to this day, though limited to exceptional cases since 1981.
rewrite: Special legislative procedures pertain to acts passed by Tynwald, the Isle of Man's legislature. Prior to the British Crown's purchase of the lordship in 1765 (the Revestment), the Lord of Mann signified assent to a bill via letter to the governor. Following this, royal assent was initially conveyed by letter from the Secretary of State. However, during the British Regency, the practice emerged of granting assent by Order in Council. This method persists, though its use has been restricted to exceptional circumstances since 1981.

input: The franchise was first created in 1997 as a series of virtual pets, akin to—and influenced in style by—the contemporary Tamagotchi or nano Giga Pet toys. The creatures were first designed to look cute and iconic even on the devices' small screens; later developments had them created with a harder-edged style influenced by American comics. The franchise gained momentum with its first anime incarnation, Digimon Adventure, and an early video game, Digimon World, both released in 1999. Several seasons of the anime and films based on them have aired, and the video game series has expanded into genres such as role-playing, racing, fighting, and MMORPGs. Other media forms have also been released.
rewrite: The franchise originated in 1997 as a series of virtual pets, stylistically analogous to and influenced by contemporary devices such as Tamagotchi and nano Giga Pets. Initial creature designs prioritized a cute, iconic appearance suitable for small screens, while subsequent iterations adopted a harder-edged aesthetic drawn from American comics. The property achieved significant traction with the 1999 releases of its first anime series, *Digimon Adventure*, and an early video game, *Digimon World*. The franchise has since expanded to include multiple anime seasons, film adaptations, and a diversified video game series encompassing role-playing, racing, fighting, and MMORPG genres, alongside other media forms.

input: Around 1300, centuries of prosperity and growth in Europe came to a halt. A series of famines and plagues, including the Great Famine of 1315–1317 and the Black Death, reduced the population to around half of what it was before the calamities. Along with depopulation came social unrest and endemic warfare. France and England experienced serious peasant uprisings, such as the Jacquerie and the Peasants' Revolt, as well as over a century of intermittent conflict in the Hundred Years' War. To add to the many problems of the period, the unity of the Catholic Church was shattered by the Western Schism. Collectively these events are sometimes called the Crisis of the Late Middle Ages.
rewrite: Commencing around 1300, Europe’s prolonged era of demographic and economic expansion concluded abruptly. A succession of catastrophes, most notably the Great Famine (1315–1317) and the Black Death, precipitated a demographic collapse, reducing the population by approximately half. This depopulation triggered profound social instability and pervasive warfare. In France and England, major peasant revolts—the Jacquerie and the Peasants’ Revolt—erupted alongside the protracted Hundred Years’ War. Concurrently, the authority of the Catholic Church was fractured by the Western Schism. This confluence of crises defines the period historians often term the Crisis of the Late Middle Ages.

input: La Cueva De Las Ventanas (The Cave of Windows), a series of cliff dwellings along an important trade route, and Las Jarillas Cave scrambled along the canyons of the Sierra Madre in Northwestern Chihuahua date between AD 1205 and 1260 and belong to the Paquimé culture. Cuarenta Casas is thought to have been a branch settlement from Paquime to protect the trade route from attack. Archaeologists believe the civilization began to decline during the 13th century and by the 15th century the inhabitants of Paquime sought refuge in the Sierra Madre Occidental while others are thought to have emigrated north and joined the Ancestral Pueblo peoples. According to anthropologist current natives tribes (Yaqui, Mayo, Opata, and Tarahumara) are descendants of the Casas Grandes culture.
rewrite: The cliff-dwelling complex known as La Cueva De Las Ventanas and the site of Las Jarillas Cave, situated within the canyons of the Sierra Madre in northwestern Chihuahua, are dated to between AD 1205 and 1260. These sites are associated with the Paquimé culture. The outpost of Cuarenta Casas is interpreted as a subsidiary settlement established to secure a major trade route. Scholarly consensus holds that the Paquimé civilization entered a period of decline during the thirteenth century. By the fifteenth century, its population is believed to have dispersed, with some groups seeking refuge in the Sierra Madre Occidental and others migrating north to integrate with Ancestral Pueblo communities. Anthropological research indicates that contemporary Indigenous groups, including the Yaqui, Mayo, Opata, and Tarahumara, are cultural descendants of the Casas Grandes tradition.

input: Three other efforts to improve regulation of international pesticide trade are the United Nations London Guidelines for the Exchange of Information on Chemicals in International Trade and the United Nations Codex Alimentarius Commission.[citation needed] The former seeks to implement procedures for ensuring that prior informed consent exists between countries buying and selling pesticides, while the latter seeks to create uniform standards for maximum levels of pesticide residues among participating countries. Both initiatives operate on a voluntary basis.
rewrite: Three additional initiatives aimed at enhancing the regulation of international pesticide trade are the United Nations London Guidelines for the Exchange of Information on Chemicals in International Trade and the United Nations Codex Alimentarius Commission. The London Guidelines establish procedures for prior informed consent between trading nations, whereas the Codex develops harmonized standards for maximum pesticide residue limits. Both frameworks function on a voluntary basis.

input: Christianity (59%), particularly Catholicism (33%), was the most prevalently practiced religion in New York as of 2014, followed by Judaism, with approximately 1.1 million Jews in New York City, over half living in Brooklyn. Islam ranks third in New York City, with official estimates ranging between 600,000 and 1,000,000 observers and including 10% of the city's public schoolchildren, followed by Hinduism, Buddhism, and a variety of other religions, as well as atheism. In 2014, 24% self-identified with no organized religious affiliation.
rewrite: As of 2014, Christianity was the predominant religion in New York, comprising 59% of adherents, with Catholicism alone accounting for 33%. Judaism followed, notably concentrated in New York City, which housed approximately 1.1 million Jewish residents, over half residing in Brooklyn. Islam constituted the third largest faith in the city, with estimates of 600,000 to 1,000,000 observers, including 10% of public school students. Hinduism, Buddhism, other religions, and atheism were also present. Notably, 24% of the population reported no formal religious affiliation.

input: Other awards and recognition for Popper included the City of Vienna Prize for the Humanities (1965), Karl Renner Prize (1978), Austrian Decoration for Science and Art (1980), Dr. Leopold Lucas Prize (1981), Ring of Honour of the City of Vienna (1983) and the Premio Internazionale of the Italian Federico Nietzsche Society (1988). In 1992, he was awarded the Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy for "symbolising the open spirit of the 20th century" and for his "enormous influence on the formation of the modern intellectual climate".
rewrite: Karl Popper received numerous additional honors, including the City of Vienna Prize for the Humanities (1965), the Karl Renner Prize (1978), the Austrian Decoration for Science and Art (1980), the Dr. Leopold Lucas Prize (1981), the Ring of Honour of the City of Vienna (1983), and the Premio Internazionale of the Italian Federico Nietzsche Society (1988). In 1992, he was granted the Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy for symbolizing the open spirit of the twentieth century and for his profound influence on the modern intellectual climate.

input: The traditional parish system persisted until the Reconstruction Era, when counties were imposed.[citation needed] Nevertheless, traditional parishes still exist in various capacities, mainly as public service districts. When the city of Charleston was formed, it was defined by the limits of the Parish of St. Philip and St. Michael, now also includes parts of St. James' Parish, St. George's Parish, St. Andrew's Parish, and St. John's Parish, although the last two are mostly still incorporated rural parishes.
rewrite: The traditional parish system endured until the Reconstruction Era, at which point counties were instituted. Parishes persist, however, primarily functioning as public service districts. The municipality of Charleston originated within the bounds of the Parish of St. Philip and St. Michael. Its contemporary jurisdiction has expanded to incorporate sections of St. James', St. George's, St. Andrew's, and St. John's Parishes, the latter two remaining largely rural, incorporated entities.

input: The last glacial period of the current ice age ended about 10,000 years ago. Ice melt caused world sea levels to rise about 35 metres (115 ft) in the early part of the Holocene. In addition, many areas above about 40 degrees north latitude had been depressed by the weight of the Pleistocene glaciers and rose as much as 180 metres (591 ft) over the late Pleistocene and Holocene, and are still rising today. The sea level rise and temporary land depression allowed temporary marine incursions into areas that are now far from the sea. Holocene marine fossils are known from Vermont, Quebec, Ontario and Michigan. Other than higher latitude temporary marine incursions associated with glacial depression, Holocene fossils are found primarily in lakebed, floodplain and cave deposits. Holocene marine deposits along low-latitude coastlines are rare because the rise in sea levels during the period exceeds any likely upthrusting of non-glacial origin. Post-glacial rebound in Scandinavia resulted in the emergence of coastal areas around the Baltic Sea, including much of Finland. The region continues to rise, still causing weak earthquakes across Northern Europe. The equivalent event in North America was the rebound of Hudson Bay, as it shrank from its larger, immediate post-glacial Tyrrell Sea phase, to near its present boundaries.
rewrite: The terminal phase of the most recent glacial period concluded approximately 10,000 years before present. Eustatic sea-level rise, driven by meltwater influx, elevated global ocean levels by roughly 35 meters during the early Holocene epoch. Concurrently, extensive regions situated above 40 degrees north latitude, which had experienced isostatic depression under the mass of Pleistocene ice sheets, underwent post-glacial rebound of up to 180 meters throughout the late Pleistocene and Holocene, a process that persists in some areas. This combination of marine transgression and transient terrestrial subsidence facilitated ephemeral inland incursions of seawater. Consequently, Holocene marine fossils are documented in locations now distant from modern coastlines, such as Vermont, Quebec, Ontario, and Michigan. With the exception of these high-latitude marine incursions linked to glacio-isostatic adjustment, Holocene fossils are predominantly recovered from lacustrine, fluvial, and speleological contexts. Marine deposits from this epoch along low-latitude coastlines are scarce, as the rate of eustatic sea-level rise generally outpaced any potential tectonic uplift of non-glacial origin. In Scandinavia, isostatic rebound precipitated the emergence of coastal terrain around the Baltic Sea, encompassing much of Finland; ongoing uplift in this region generates low-intensity seismicity across northern Europe. The analogous process in North America involved the rebound of the Hudson Bay region, which contracted from its larger, immediate post-glacial manifestation (the Tyrrell Sea) to approximately its current boundaries.

input: The Federal Council constitutes the federal government, directs the federal administration and serves as collective Head of State. It is a collegial body of seven members, elected for a four-year mandate by the Federal Assembly which also exercises oversight over the Council. The President of the Confederation is elected by the Assembly from among the seven members, traditionally in rotation and for a one-year term; the President chairs the government and assumes representative functions. However, the president is a primus inter pares with no additional powers, and remains the head of a department within the administration.
rewrite: The Federal Council functions as Switzerland's federal government, leading the federal administration and acting collectively as the Head of State. This collegial executive comprises seven members, each elected to a four-year term by the Federal Assembly, which also supervises the Council. Annually, the Assembly elects a President of the Confederation from among its members, typically following a rotational system. While the President chairs the government and fulfills ceremonial duties, the role is that of a *primus inter pares* without augmented authority, and the incumbent continues to lead a governmental department.

input: Washington University has a large number of student-run musical groups on campus, including 12 official a cappella groups. The Pikers, an all-male group, is the oldest such group on campus. The Greenleafs, an all-female group is the oldest (and only) female group on campus. The Mosaic Whispers, founded in 1991, is the oldest co-ed group on campus. They have produced 9 albums and have appeared on a number of compilation albums, including Ben Folds' Ben Folds Presents: University A Cappella! The Amateurs, who also appeared on this album, is another co-ed a cappella group on campus, founded in 1991. They have recorded seven albums and toured extensively. After Dark is a co-ed a cappella group founded in 2001. It has released three albums and has won several Contemporary A Capella Recording (CARA) awards. In 2008 the group performed on MSNBC during coverage of the vice presidential debate with specially written songs about Joe Biden and Sarah Palin. The Ghost Lights, founded in 2010, is the campus's newest and only Broadway, Movies, and Television soundtrack group. They have performed multiple philanthropic concerts in the greater St. Louis area and were honored in November 2010 with the opportunity to perform for Nobel Laureate Douglass North at his birthday celebration.
rewrite: Washington University hosts a substantial array of student-managed musical ensembles, among which are twelve officially recognized a cappella groups. The Pikers, an all-male ensemble, constitutes the oldest such group at the university. Conversely, The Greenleafs represent the oldest and sole all-female a cappella group on campus. Founded in 1991, The Mosaic Whispers is the institution's inaugural co-ed a cappella group; it has produced nine albums and been featured on several compilations, including *Ben Folds Presents: University A Cappella!* Another co-ed group founded that same year, The Amateurs, also appeared on that compilation, has recorded seven albums, and has undertaken extensive touring. Established in 2001, After Dark is a co-ed ensemble that has released three albums and garnered multiple Contemporary A Cappella Recording Awards (CARA). In 2008, this group performed on MSNBC during vice-presidential debate coverage, singing original compositions about candidates Joe Biden and Sarah Palin. The campus's most recent addition is The Ghost Lights, founded in 2010 as the only group dedicated to Broadway, film, and television soundtracks. They have performed numerous philanthropic concerts in the St. Louis region and, in November 2010, were selected to perform for Nobel Laureate Douglass North at his birthday celebration.

input: Not all introduced species are invasive, nor all invasive species deliberately introduced. In cases such as the zebra mussel, invasion of US waterways was unintentional. In other cases, such as mongooses in Hawaii, the introduction is deliberate but ineffective (nocturnal rats were not vulnerable to the diurnal mongoose). In other cases, such as oil palms in Indonesia and Malaysia, the introduction produces substantial economic benefits, but the benefits are accompanied by costly unintended consequences.
rewrite: Not all introduced species become invasive, nor are all invasive species introduced intentionally. For example, the zebra mussel invaded U.S. waterways accidentally. Conversely, species like the mongoose in Hawaii were introduced deliberately but proved ineffective, as nocturnal rats were not susceptible to this diurnal predator. Elsewhere, as with oil palms in Indonesia and Malaysia, introductions yield significant economic gains, yet these are often offset by substantial unintended costs.

input: The shift in the Cubs' fortunes was characterized June 23 on the "NBC Saturday Game of the Week" contest against the St. Louis Cardinals. it has since been dubbed simply "The Sandberg Game." With the nation watching and Wrigley Field packed, Sandberg emerged as a superstar with not one, but two game-tying home runs against Cardinals closer Bruce Sutter. With his shots in the 9th and 10th innings Wrigley Field erupted and Sandberg set the stage for a comeback win that cemented the Cubs as the team to beat in the East. No one would catch them, except the Padres in the playoffs.
rewrite: The pivotal shift in the Chicago Cubs' trajectory was epitomized during the nationally televised "NBC Saturday Game of the Week" on June 23 against the St. Louis Cardinals, an event subsequently memorialized as "The Sandberg Game." Before a capacity crowd at Wrigley Field, Ryne Sandberg ascended to superstar status by delivering two game-tying home runs in the ninth and tenth innings against premier closer Bruce Sutter. These pivotal hits catalyzed a comeback victory, decisively establishing the Cubs as the dominant force in the National League East, a status ultimately challenged only by the San Diego Padres in the postseason.

input: There is no single definition of an "aircraft carrier", and modern navies use several variants of the type. These variants are sometimes categorized as sub-types of aircraft carriers, and sometimes as distinct types of naval aviation-capable ships. Aircraft carriers may be classified according to the type of aircraft they carry and their operational assignments. Admiral Sir Mark Stanhope, former head of the Royal Navy, has said that "To put it simply, countries that aspire to strategic international influence have aircraft carriers".
rewrite: No universally accepted definition of the term "aircraft carrier" exists, with modern navies operating multiple variants. These designs are classified either as sub-types of carriers or as separate categories of aviation-capable warships. Classification often depends on embarked aircraft types and operational roles. As former Royal Navy First Sea Lord Admiral Sir Mark Stanhope noted, the possession of aircraft carriers is fundamentally linked to a nation's pursuit of strategic international influence.

input: Between 1872 and 1905, a series of protests took place in response to the sale of concessions to foreigners by Nasser od Din and Mozaffar od Din shahs of Qajar, and led to the Iranian Constitutional Revolution. The first Iranian Constitution and the first national parliament of Iran were founded in 1906, through the ongoing revolution. The Constitution included the official recognition of Iran's three religious minorities, namely Christians, Zoroastrians, and Jews, which has remained a basis in the legislation of Iran since then.
rewrite: Between 1872 and 1905, a succession of protests emerged in opposition to the Qajar rulers, Nasser od-Din Shah and Mozaffar od-Din Shah, for granting concessions to foreign interests. This unrest culminated in the Iranian Constitutional Revolution. The revolution achieved its foundational outcome in 1906 with the ratification of Iran's first constitution and the establishment of its inaugural national parliament. This document formally recognized the rights of three religious minorities—Christians, Zoroastrians, and Jews—a principle that has endured within Iranian law.

input: Saint FM provided a local radio service for the island which was also available on internet radio and relayed in Ascension Island. The station was not government funded. It was launched in January 2005 and closed on 21 December 2012. It broadcast news, features and music in collaboration with its sister newspaper, the St Helena Independent (which continues).
rewrite: Saint FM delivered a local radio service for Saint Helena, accessible via internet radio and relayed to Ascension Island. Operating independently of government funding from its launch in January 2005 until its closure on 21 December 2012, it broadcast news, features, and music in conjunction with its ongoing sister publication, the St Helena Independent.

input: The Red Rose of Lancaster is the county flower found on the county's heraldic badge and flag. The rose was a symbol of the House of Lancaster, immortalised in the verse "In the battle for England's head/York was white, Lancaster red" (referring to the 15th-century Wars of the Roses). The traditional Lancashire flag, a red rose on a white field, was not officially registered. When an attempt was made to register it with the Flag Institute it was found that it was officially registered by Montrose in Scotland, several hundred years earlier with the Lyon Office. Lancashire's official flag is registered as a red rose on a gold field.
rewrite: The Red Rose of Lancaster serves as the county flower, featured on Lancashire's heraldic badge and flag. Historically emblematic of the House of Lancaster, it is famously referenced in the couplet, "In the battle for England's head/York was white, Lancaster red," alluding to the fifteenth-century Wars of the Roses. The traditional design of a red rose on a white field was never officially registered; an attempt to do so with the Flag Institute revealed its prior registration by Montrose in Scotland centuries earlier with the Lyon Office. Consequently, Lancashire's officially registered flag displays a red rose upon a gold field.

input: The activities that constitute illegal corruption differ depending on the country or jurisdiction. For instance, some political funding practices that are legal in one place may be illegal in another. In some cases, government officials have broad or ill-defined powers, which make it difficult to distinguish between legal and illegal actions. Worldwide, bribery alone is estimated to involve over 1 trillion US dollars annually. A state of unrestrained political corruption is known as a kleptocracy, literally meaning "rule by thieves".
rewrite: The legal definition of corrupt activities varies significantly across national jurisdictions. Certain political financing practices permissible in one region may be prohibited in another. Ambiguous or broadly defined official powers can further obscure the line between legal and illicit conduct. Globally, annual monetary flows associated with bribery are estimated to exceed one trillion US dollars. A condition of systemic and unrestrained political corruption is termed a kleptocracy, which translates literally as "rule by thieves."

input: On February 14, 2009, The Walt Disney Company debuted "The American Idol Experience" at its Disney's Hollywood Studios theme park at the Walt Disney World Resort in Florida. In this live production, co-produced by 19 Entertainment, park guests chose from a list of songs and auditioned privately for Disney cast members. Those selected then performed on a stage in a 1000-seat theater replicating the Idol set. Three judges, whose mannerisms and style mimicked those of the real Idol judges, critiqued the performances. Audience members then voted for their favorite performer. There were several preliminary-round shows during the day that culminated in a "finals" show in the evening where one of the winners of the previous rounds that day was selected as the overall winner. The winner of the finals show received a "Dream Ticket" that granted them front-of-the-line privileges at any future American Idol audition. The attraction closed on August 30, 2014.
rewrite: On February 14, 2009, The Walt Disney Company launched "The American Idol Experience," a live theatrical attraction at Disney's Hollywood Studios within the Walt Disney World Resort in Florida. Co-produced with 19 Entertainment, the interactive production enabled park guests to audition privately for Disney cast members by selecting from a prescribed repertoire of songs. Successful candidates performed on a replicated *Idol* stage within a 1,000-seat theater. A panel of three judges, emulating the style and mannerisms of the television program's judges, provided critiques. Following each performance, the audience voted to determine a winner. Multiple preliminary shows were held throughout the day, culminating in an evening finals show. The daily victor, chosen from the earlier round winners, received a "Dream Ticket," which provided front-of-the-line privileges at any subsequent *American Idol* audition. The attraction ceased operations on August 30, 2014.

input: Leading up to the American Civil War, Baptists became embroiled in the controversy over slavery in the United States. Whereas in the First Great Awakening, Methodist and Baptist preachers had opposed slavery and urged manumission, over the decades they made more of an accommodation with the institution. They worked with slaveholders in the South to urge a paternalistic institution. Both denominations made direct appeals to slaves and free blacks for conversion. The Baptists particularly allowed them active roles in congregations. By the mid-19th century, northern Baptists tended to oppose slavery. As tensions increased, in 1844 the Home Mission Society refused to appoint a slaveholder as a missionary who had been proposed by Georgia. It noted that missionaries could not take servants with them, and also that the Board did not want to appear to condone slavery.
rewrite: In the antebellum period leading to the American Civil War, Baptists in the United States became deeply involved in the national controversy surrounding slavery. During the First Great Awakening, evangelical preachers from the Baptist and Methodist traditions had generally opposed the institution and advocated for manumission. However, across subsequent decades, these groups increasingly accommodated slavery, particularly in the South, where they cooperated with slaveholders to promote a paternalistic interpretation of the institution. Both denominations actively sought converts among enslaved and free Black populations, with Baptists notably permitting them active participatory roles within congregations. By the mid-nineteenth century, northern Baptists grew more opposed to slavery. Escalating sectional tensions culminated in 1844 when the Home Mission Society declined to appoint a slaveholder nominated by Georgia as a missionary. The Society asserted that missionaries could not be accompanied by servants and that the Board wished to avoid any appearance of condoning slavery.

input: With the occupation by Napoleon, Portugal began a slow but inexorable decline that lasted until the 20th century. This decline was hastened by the independence in 1822 of the country's largest colonial possession, Brazil. In 1807, as Napoleon's army closed in on Lisbon, the Prince Regent João VI of Portugal transferred his court to Brazil and established Rio de Janeiro as the capital of the Portuguese Empire. In 1815, Brazil was declared a Kingdom and the Kingdom of Portugal was united with it, forming a pluricontinental State, the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.
rewrite: The Napoleonic occupation initiated a protracted and irreversible decline in Portugal, extending into the twentieth century. This process was accelerated by the independence of Brazil, its principal colony, in 1822. In 1807, facing the advance of French forces, the Prince Regent João VI relocated the Portuguese court to Brazil, establishing Rio de Janeiro as the imperial capital. Subsequently, in 1815, Brazil was elevated to a kingdom, uniting with Portugal to form the pluricontinental United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.

input: The titles of state supreme court vary, which can cause confusion between jurisdictions because one state may use a name for its highest court that another uses for a lower court. In New York, Maryland, and the District of Columbia the highest court is called the Court of Appeals, a name used by many states for their intermediate appellate courts. Further, trial courts of general jurisdiction in New York are called the Supreme Court, and the intermediate appellate court is called the Supreme Court, Appellate Division. In West Virginia, the highest court of the state is the Supreme Court of Appeals. In Maine and Massachusetts the highest court is styled the "Supreme Judicial Court"; the last is the oldest appellate court of continuous operation in the Western Hemisphere.
rewrite: The nomenclature of state supreme courts exhibits significant variation across jurisdictions, potentially creating confusion as identical titles may designate the highest court in one state but an intermediate or trial court in another. For instance, the highest tribunals in New York, Maryland, and the District of Columbia are titled the Court of Appeals, a designation commonly used for intermediate appellate courts elsewhere. Conversely, New York labels its trial courts of general jurisdiction as the Supreme Court, with its intermediate appellate body termed the Supreme Court, Appellate Division. West Virginia employs the title Supreme Court of Appeals. In Maine and Massachusetts, the highest court is formally named the Supreme Judicial Court, with the latter being the Western Hemisphere's oldest continuously operating appellate court.
