input: A fundamental problem with software testing is that testing under all combinations of inputs and preconditions (initial state) is not feasible, even with a simple product.:17-18 This means that the number of defects in a software product can be very large and defects that occur infrequently are difficult to find in testing. More significantly, non-functional dimensions of quality (how it is supposed to be versus what it is supposed to do)—usability, scalability, performance, compatibility, reliability—can be highly subjective; something that constitutes sufficient value to one person may be intolerable to another.
rewrite: A core challenge in software testing is the infeasibility of exhaustive verification across all possible input combinations and initial states, even for simple products. Consequently, a product may contain numerous defects, with infrequent ones being particularly difficult to detect. Furthermore, non-functional quality attributes—such as usability, scalability, performance, compatibility, and reliability—are often highly subjective. Assessments of these dimensions can vary significantly, as a level deemed acceptable by one individual may be considered inadequate by another.

input: Austrian-born Adolf Hitler had a lifelong romantic fascination with the Alps and by the 1930s established a home in the Obersalzberg region outside of Berchtesgaden. His first visit to the area was in 1923 and he maintained a strong tie there until the end of his life. At the end of World War II the US Army occupied Obersalzberg, to prevent Hitler from retreating with the Wehrmacht into the mountains.
rewrite: Adolf Hitler, an Austrian native, maintained a lifelong romantic attachment to the Alps, establishing a residence in the Obersalzberg near Berchtesgaden by the 1930s. He first visited the area in 1923 and retained a strong connection to it. Following World War II, the US Army occupied Obersalzberg to preclude any potential retreat by Hitler with the Wehrmacht into the mountainous terrain.

input: Stone and brick became the city's building materials of choice after the construction of wood-frame houses was limited in the aftermath of the Great Fire of 1835. A distinctive feature of many of the city's buildings is the wooden roof-mounted water towers. In the 1800s, the city required their installation on buildings higher than six stories to prevent the need for excessively high water pressures at lower elevations, which could break municipal water pipes. Garden apartments became popular during the 1920s in outlying areas, such as Jackson Heights.
rewrite: Following the Great Fire of 1835, which prompted restrictions on wood-frame construction, stone and brick emerged as the predominant urban building materials. A notable architectural feature is the prevalence of wooden roof-mounted water towers. Mandated in the 19th century for structures exceeding six stories, these towers mitigated excessive street-level water pressure that risked rupturing municipal pipes. Meanwhile, the 1920s witnessed the popularity of garden apartments in peripheral districts like Jackson Heights.

input: The United States Mint produces Proof Sets specifically for collectors and speculators. Silver Proofs tend to be the standard designs but with the dime, quarter, and half dollar containing 90% silver. Starting in 1983 and ending in 1997, the Mint also produced proof sets containing the year's commemorative coins alongside the regular coins. Another type of proof set is the Presidential Dollar Proof Set where four special $1 coins are minted each year featuring a president. Because of budget constraints and increasing stockpiles of these relatively unpopular coins, the production of new Presidential dollar coins for circulation was suspended on December 13, 2011, by U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner. Future minting of such coins will be made solely for collectors.
rewrite: The United States Mint issues Proof Sets designed for collectors and investors. Among these, Silver Proof sets typically feature standard coin designs, with the dime, quarter, and half dollar composed of 90% silver. From 1983 through 1997, the Mint also produced annual proof sets that included both regular and commemorative coinage. A distinct variant is the Presidential Dollar Proof Set, comprising four yearly one-dollar coins bearing presidential portraits. Due to budgetary limitations and accumulating inventories of these less-circulated coins, the production of new presidential dollars for general circulation was halted on December 13, 2011, by Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner. Subsequent minting of these coins is to be conducted exclusively for the collector market.

input: Sicily fell under the control of the Holy Roman Empire in 1194. Palermo was the preferred city of the Emperor Frederick II. Muslims of Palermo emigrated or were expelled during Holy Roman rule. After an interval of Angevin rule (1266–1282), Sicily came under control of the Aragon and Barcelona dynasties. By 1330, Palermo's population had declined to 51,000. From 1479 until 1713 Palermo was ruled by the Kingdom of Spain, and again between 1717 and 1718. Palermo was also under Savoy control between 1713 and 1717 and 1718–1720 as a result of the Treaty of Utrecht. It was also ruled by Austria between 1720 and 1734.
rewrite: Sicily was incorporated into the Holy Roman Empire in 1194, with Palermo serving as the favored residence of Emperor Frederick II. During this period, the Muslim population of Palermo either emigrated or was expelled. Following a brief period of Angevin rule (1266–1282), sovereignty transferred to the dynasties of Aragon and Barcelona. By 1330, Palermo’s population had diminished to approximately 51,000. From 1479 to 1713, the city was governed by the Kingdom of Spain, a status briefly reinstated from 1717 to 1718. Interim control was held by Savoy (1713–1717; 1718–1720) under the Treaty of Utrecht, and by Austria from 1720 to 1734.

input: During the 1890s, the Armenian Revolutionary Federation, commonly known as Dashnaktsutyun, became active within the Ottoman Empire with the aim of unifying the various small groups in the empire that were advocating for reform and defending Armenian villages from massacres that were widespread in some of the Armenian-populated areas of the empire. Dashnaktsutyun members also formed fedayi groups that defended Armenian civilians through armed resistance. The Dashnaks also worked for the wider goal of creating a "free, independent and unified" Armenia, although they sometimes set aside this goal in favor of a more realistic approach, such as advocating autonomy.
rewrite: During the 1890s, the Armenian Revolutionary Federation (Dashnaktsutyun) emerged as an active political force within the Ottoman Empire. Its objectives were to consolidate disparate reformist factions and to organize the defense of Armenian villages against widespread massacres in certain regions. The party established armed *fedayi* units to protect civilians via militant resistance. While its ultimate aim was the establishment of a "free, independent and unified" Armenia, the organization periodically adopted a pragmatic stance, prioritizing more immediate goals such as regional autonomy.

input: There are many non-incandescent light sources, such as the fluorescent lamp, high-intensity discharge lamps and LED lamps, which have higher luminous efficiency, and some have been designed to be retrofitted in fixtures for incandescent lights. These devices produce light by luminescence. These lamps produce discrete spectral lines and do not have the broad "tail" of invisible infrared emissions. By careful selection of which electron energy level transitions are used, and fluorescent coatings which modify the spectral distribution, the spectrum emitted can be tuned to mimic the appearance of incandescent sources, or other different color temperatures of white light. Due to the discrete spectral lines rather than a continuous spectrum, the light is not ideal for applications such as photography and cinematography.
rewrite: Numerous non-incandescent light sources, including fluorescent, high-intensity discharge, and LED lamps, offer superior luminous efficacy. Many are engineered for direct retrofitting into fixtures designed for incandescent bulbs. These devices generate illumination through luminescence, producing discrete spectral lines rather than the broad continuum of infrared emissions characteristic of thermal radiators. Through precise selection of electron energy level transitions and the application of fluorescent coatings to modify spectral output, the emitted light can be tailored to approximate the chromatic qualities of incandescent sources or to achieve various white light color temperatures. However, the discontinuous nature of their spectra renders them suboptimal for applications demanding high color fidelity, such as photography and cinematography.

input: In the audition rounds, 121 contestants were selected from around 10,000 who attended the auditions. These were cut to 30 for the semifinal, with ten going on to the finals. One semifinalist, Delano Cagnolatti, was disqualified for lying to evade the show's age limit. One of the early favorites, Tamyra Gray, was eliminated at the top four, the first of several such shock eliminations that were to be repeated in later seasons. Christina Christian was hospitalized before the top six result show due to chest pains and palpitations, and she was eliminated while she was in the hospital. Jim Verraros was the first openly gay contestant on the show; his sexual orientation was revealed in his online journal, however it was removed during the competition after a request from the show producers over concerns that it might be unfairly influencing votes.
rewrite: From an initial audition pool of approximately 10,000 participants, 121 contestants were advanced. This group was subsequently reduced to 30 semifinalists, with ten ultimately progressing to the final round. Notably, semifinalist Delano Cagnolatti was disqualified for providing false information to circumvent the program's age restriction. Tamyra Gray, an early frontrunner, was unexpectedly eliminated at the final four stage, establishing a precedent for surprising outcomes in subsequent seasons. Prior to the top six results announcement, Christina Christian was hospitalized due to chest pains and palpitations and was eliminated during her hospitalization. Additionally, Jim Verraros is recognized as the first openly gay contestant; his sexual orientation, initially disclosed in a personal online journal, was removed during the competition at the producers' request, stemming from concerns regarding potential influence on voting.

input: The English Province was a component of the international order from which it obtained its laws, direction, and instructions. It was also, however, a group of Englishmen. Its direct supervisors were from England, and the members of the English Province dwelt and labored in English cities, towns, villages, and roadways. English and European ingredients constantly came in contact. The international side of the province's existence influenced the national, and the national responded to, adapted, and sometimes constrained the international.
rewrite: The English Province functioned as a constituent unit of a broader international order, deriving its statutes, governance, and directives therefrom. Simultaneously, it remained an assembly of English nationals, under English superiors and operating within English urban and rural settings. Within this context, persistent interaction occurred between English and European elements. The province's international dimension continually shaped its national character, which in turn responded to, adapted, and occasionally circumscribed those international influences.

input: Plymouth has about 150 churches and its Roman Catholic cathedral (1858) is in Stonehouse. The city's oldest church is St Andrew's (Anglican) located at the top of Royal Parade—it is the largest parish church in Devon and has been a site of gathering since AD 800. The city also includes five Baptist churches, over twenty Methodist chapels, and thirteen Roman Catholic churches. In 1831 the first Brethren assembly in England, a movement of conservative non-denominational Evangelical Christians, was established in the city, so that Brethren are often called Plymouth Brethren, although the movement did not begin locally.
rewrite: Plymouth contains approximately 150 churches. Its Roman Catholic cathedral, constructed in 1858, is situated in Stonehouse. The city's oldest ecclesiastical structure is the Anglican St Andrew's Church, positioned atop Royal Parade. As Devon's largest parish church, it has served as a gathering site since 800 AD. The inventory includes five Baptist churches, over twenty Methodist chapels, and thirteen Roman Catholic churches. Notably, the first assembly in England of the Brethren—a conservative, non-denominational Evangelical movement—was established here in 1831, leading to the common designation "Plymouth Brethren," despite the movement's origins lying elsewhere.

input: The appearance of more systematic, abstract thinking is another notable aspect of cognitive development during adolescence. For example, adolescents find it easier than children to comprehend the sorts of higher-order abstract logic inherent in puns, proverbs, metaphors, and analogies. Their increased facility permits them to appreciate the ways in which language can be used to convey multiple messages, such as satire, metaphor, and sarcasm. (Children younger than age nine often cannot comprehend sarcasm at all.) This also permits the application of advanced reasoning and logical processes to social and ideological matters such as interpersonal relationships, politics, philosophy, religion, morality, friendship, faith, democracy, fairness, and honesty.
rewrite: A further significant dimension of adolescent cognitive development is the emergence of more systematic and abstract thought. Adolescents demonstrate a greater capacity than children for understanding the higher-order logic embedded in puns, proverbs, metaphors, and analogies. This enhanced ability allows them to grasp nuanced uses of language, including satire and sarcasm, which are often inaccessible to children under age nine. Consequently, they can apply advanced reasoning to abstract social and ideological domains, such as interpersonal relationships, morality, politics, and philosophy.

input: The earliest recorded history of the region dates back to about 500 BCE when much, if not all, of modern Tajikistan was part of the Achaemenid Empire. Some authors have also suggested that in the 7th and 6th century BCE parts of modern Tajikistan, including territories in the Zeravshan valley, formed part of Kambojas before it became part of the Achaemenid Empire. After the region's conquest by Alexander the Great it became part of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, a successor state of Alexander's empire. Northern Tajikistan (the cities of Khujand and Panjakent) was part of Sogdia, a collection of city-states which was overrun by Scythians and Yuezhi nomadic tribes around 150 BCE. The Silk Road passed through the region and following the expedition of Chinese explorer Zhang Qian during the reign of Wudi (141–87 BCE) commercial relations between Han China and Sogdiana flourished. Sogdians played a major role in facilitating trade and also worked in other capacities, as farmers, carpetweavers, glassmakers, and woodcarvers.
rewrite: The earliest documented history of the region commences circa 500 BCE, when the territory comprising modern Tajikistan was largely incorporated within the Achaemenid Empire. Certain scholars posit that, during the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, areas including parts of the Zeravshan valley constituted a segment of Kambojas prior to Achaemenid annexation. Following its conquest by Alexander the Great, the region was integrated into the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, a Hellenistic successor state. Northern Tajikistan, encompassing Khujand and Panjakent, formed a component of Sogdia, a polity of city-states subsequently overrun by Scythian and Yuezhi nomadic groups around 150 BCE. Traversed by the Silk Road, the region saw commercial relations between Han China and Sogdiana expand significantly after the expedition of Zhang Qian under Emperor Wudi (141–87 BCE). The Sogdians were instrumental in mediating this trade and were also engaged in various agrarian and artisanal pursuits, such as carpet weaving, glassmaking, and woodcarving.

input: In the north Eristov pushed southwest, fought two battles, forced the Turks back to Batum, retired behind the Cholok River and suspended action for the rest of the year (June). In the far south Wrangel pushed west, fought a battle and occupied Bayazit. In the center the main forces stood at Kars and Gyumri. Both slowly approached along the Kars-Gyumri road and faced each other, neither side choosing to fight (June–July). On 4 August Russian scouts saw a movement which they thought was the start of a withdrawal, the Russians advanced and the Turks attacked first. They were defeated, losing 8000 men to the Russian 3000. 10000 irregulars deserted to their villages. Both sides withdrew to their former positions. About this time the Persians made a semi-secret agreement to remain neutral in exchange for the cancellation of the indemnity from the previous war.
rewrite: In the northern sector, General Eristov advanced southwest, engaged in two battles, and compelled Ottoman forces to retreat toward Batum. Subsequently, he withdrew behind the Cholok River and halted operations for the remainder of the year, beginning in June. To the far south, General Wrangel moved westward, fought an engagement, and occupied Bayazit. Centrally, the primary armies were positioned at Kars and Gyumri. Throughout June and July, both sides gradually advanced along the connecting road, maintaining a standoff without initiating combat. On August 4, Russian scouts interpreted Ottoman movements as the start of a withdrawal; as the Russians advanced, the Turks launched an attack. They were repelled, sustaining approximately 8,000 casualties against Russian losses of 3,000. An additional 10,000 irregular troops deserted to their villages. Following the battle, both armies returned to their previous positions. Concurrently, Persia entered a semi-secret agreement to maintain neutrality in exchange for the cancellation of indemnities from the prior conflict.

input: The disadvantage of the ski-jump is the penalty it exacts on aircraft size, payload, and fuel load (and thus range); heavily laden aircraft can not launch using a ski-jump because their high loaded weight requires either a longer takeoff roll than is possible on a carrier deck, or assistance from a catapult or JATO rocket. For example, the Russian Su-33 is only able to launch from the carrier Admiral Kuznetsov with a minimal armament and fuel load. Another disadvantage is on mixed flight deck operations where helicopters are also present such as a US Landing Helicopter Dock or Landing Helicopter Assault amphibious assault ship a ski jump is not included as this would eliminate one or more helicopter landing areas, this flat deck limits the loading of Harriers but is somewhat mitigated by the longer rolling start provided by a long flight deck compared to many STOVL carriers.
rewrite: The ski-jump ramp imposes significant limitations on aircraft operational capacity, primarily by restricting size, payload, and fuel volume, thereby reducing effective range. Aircraft with high gross weights cannot achieve launch from a ski-jump, as their required takeoff roll exceeds available deck length, necessitating alternative assistive mechanisms such as catapults or jet-assisted takeoff (JATO) systems. This constraint is illustrated by the Russian Su-33, which can only operate from the *Admiral Kuznetsov* with minimal armament and fuel. A further disadvantage arises in mixed-deck operations involving helicopters, as on U.S. Landing Helicopter Dock (LHD) or Landing Helicopter Assault (LHA) amphibious assault ships. Incorporating a ski-jump would eliminate crucial helicopter landing spots. Consequently, the flat deck limits Harrier aircraft loading, though this is partially offset by the extended rolling takeoff distance afforded by these vessels' longer decks relative to many dedicated short takeoff and vertical landing (STOVL) carriers.

input: The University of Swaziland, Southern African Nazarene University, Swaziland Christian University are the institutions that offer university education in the country. A campus of Limkokwing University of Creative Technology can be found at Sidvwashini, a suburb of the capital Mbabane. There are some teaching and nursing assistant colleges around the country. Ngwane Teacher's College and William Pitcher College are the country's teaching colleges. The Good Shepherd Hospital in Siteki is home to the College for Nursing Assistants.
rewrite: The nation's tertiary education system comprises the University of Eswatini, Southern African Nazarene University, and the University of Eswatini Christian Medical School. Additionally, a campus of Limkokwing University of Creative Technology is situated in Sidvwashini, a suburb of Mbabane. Teacher training is provided by Ngwane Teacher's College and William Pitcher College, while nursing assistant education is offered at the College for Nursing Assistants, located within Siteki's Good Shepherd Hospital.

input: Sho-1 called for V. Adm. Jisaburo Ozawa's force to use an apparently vulnerable carrier force to lure the U.S. 3rd Fleet away from Leyte and remove air cover from the Allied landing forces, which would then be attacked from the west by three Japanese forces: V. Adm. Takeo Kurita's force would enter Leyte Gulf and attack the landing forces; R. Adm. Shoji Nishimura's force and V. Adm. Kiyohide Shima's force would act as mobile strike forces. The plan was likely to result in the destruction of one or more of the Japanese forces, but Toyoda justified it by saying that there would be no sense in saving the fleet and losing the Philippines.
rewrite: Operation Sho-1 entailed employing Vice Admiral Jisaburo Ozawa’s ostensibly vulnerable carrier group as a decoy to draw the U.S. Third Fleet northward, thereby stripping air cover from the Allied invasion forces at Leyte. These exposed forces would subsequently be assaulted from the west by three Japanese naval elements: Vice Admiral Takeo Kurita’s center force would penetrate Leyte Gulf directly, while the separate forces of Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima and Rear Admiral Shoji Nishimura would operate as mobile striking units. Although the operation risked the probable destruction of one or more Japanese formations, Admiral Toyoda Soemu rationalized the strategy by contending that preserving the fleet while forfeiting the Philippines would be strategically futile.

input: A computer's memory can be viewed as a list of cells into which numbers can be placed or read. Each cell has a numbered "address" and can store a single number. The computer can be instructed to "put the number 123 into the cell numbered 1357" or to "add the number that is in cell 1357 to the number that is in cell 2468 and put the answer into cell 1595." The information stored in memory may represent practically anything. Letters, numbers, even computer instructions can be placed into memory with equal ease. Since the CPU does not differentiate between different types of information, it is the software's responsibility to give significance to what the memory sees as nothing but a series of numbers.
rewrite: Computer memory can be conceptually modeled as a sequential array of storage cells, each capable of holding a single numerical value and identified by a unique numerical address. The processor executes operations such as storing a specific value at a designated address or performing arithmetic—for instance, summing the contents of two addresses and storing the result in a third. The data residing in these cells is inherently versatile, representing letters, numeric data, or executable instructions with equal facility. The central processing unit interprets all such information uniformly as numerical values; consequently, any semantic distinction or meaningful interpretation of this data falls exclusively to the software layer, which assigns significance to what the memory system processes merely as sequences of numbers.

input: In September 2006, German officials seized MP3 players from SanDisk's booth at the IFA show in Berlin after an Italian patents firm won an injunction on behalf of Sisvel against SanDisk in a dispute over licensing rights. The injunction was later reversed by a Berlin judge, but that reversal was in turn blocked the same day by another judge from the same court, "bringing the Patent Wild West to Germany" in the words of one commentator.
rewrite: In September 2006, German authorities confiscated MP3 players from SanDisk's exhibition stand at the Berlin IFA trade show. This action followed an injunction, secured by an Italian patent firm for Sisvel, regarding a licensing dispute with SanDisk. Although a Berlin judge subsequently overturned this injunction, a different judge from the same court reinstated it that same day. One observer noted this rapid succession of rulings effectively imported a "Patent Wild West" scenario into Germany.

input: From 1898, it was commonly accepted that the name was of Celtic origin and meant place belonging to a man called *Londinos; this explanation has since been rejected. Richard Coates put forward an explanation in 1998 that it is derived from the pre-Celtic Old European *(p)lowonida, meaning 'river too wide to ford', and suggested that this was a name given to the part of the River Thames which flows through London; from this, the settlement gained the Celtic form of its name, *Lowonidonjon; this requires quite a serious amendment however. The ultimate difficulty lies in reconciling the Latin form Londinium with the modern Welsh Llundain, which should demand a form *(h)lōndinion (as opposed to *londīnion), from earlier *loundiniom. The possibility cannot be ruled out that the Welsh name was borrowed back in from English at a later date, and thus cannot be used as a basis from which to reconstruct the original name.
rewrite: Since 1898, the prevailing scholarly consensus held that the name London was of Celtic derivation, signifying a place belonging to an individual named *Londinos; this etymology has subsequently been dismissed. In 1998, Richard Coates proposed an alternative hypothesis, tracing the name to a pre-Celtic Old European root, *(p)lowonida, meaning 'a river too wide to ford'. He posited that this term described the section of the River Thames flowing through the area, from which the settlement later acquired a Celtic form, *Lowonidonjon—a theory that necessitates significant revision. A principal complication involves reconciling the Latin Londinium with the modern Welsh Llundain, which would imply an earlier form *(h)lōndinion, rather than *londīnion, from a precursor *loundiniom. The possibility remains that the Welsh form was a later borrowing from English, thereby precluding its use in reconstructing the original toponym.

input: The title of "world's oldest airport" is disputed, but College Park Airport in Maryland, US, established in 1909 by Wilbur Wright, is generally agreed to be the world's oldest continually operating airfield, although it serves only general aviation traffic. Bisbee-Douglas International Airport in Arizona was declared "the first international airport of the Americas" by US president Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1943. Pearson Field Airport in Vancouver, Washington had a dirigible land in 1905 and planes in 1911 and is still in use. Bremen Airport opened in 1913 and remains in use, although it served as an American military field between 1945 and 1949. Amsterdam Airport Schiphol opened on September 16, 1916 as a military airfield, but only accepted civil aircraft from December 17, 1920, allowing Sydney Airport in Sydney, Australia—which started operations in January 1920—to claim to be one of the world's oldest continually operating commercial airports. Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport in Minneapolis-Saint Paul, Minnesota, opened in 1920 and has been in continuous commercial service since. It serves about 35,000,000 passengers each year and continues to expand, recently opening a new 11,000 foot (3,355 meter) runway. Of the airports constructed during this early period in aviation, it is one of the largest and busiest that is still currently operating. Rome Ciampino Airport, opened 1916, is also a contender, as well as the Don Mueang International Airport near Bangkok,Thailand, which opened in 1914. Increased aircraft traffic during World War I led to the construction of landing fields. Aircraft had to approach these from certain directions and this led to the development of aids for directing the approach and landing slope.
rewrite: The designation of the "world's oldest airport" remains a subject of debate; however, College Park Airport in Maryland, United States, founded by Wilbur Wright in 1909, is widely recognized as the world's oldest airfield in continuous operation, albeit one that exclusively serves general aviation. Other historic airfields also make significant claims. For instance, Bisbee-Douglas International Airport in Arizona was proclaimed "the first international airport of the Americas" by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1943. Pearson Field in Vancouver, Washington, recorded a dirigible landing in 1905 and aircraft operations by 1911, maintaining activity to the present. Bremen Airport, inaugurated in 1913, continues in operation despite functioning as an American military installation from 1945 to 1949. Amsterdam Airport Schiphol, opened as a military base on September 16, 1916, commenced civilian service only on December 17, 1920. This later civilian inception permits Sydney Airport in Australia, which began operations in January 1920, to assert itself as one of the world's oldest continually operating commercial airports. Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport, launched in 1920, has provided uninterrupted commercial service since its opening. Currently accommodating approximately thirty-five million annual passengers, it continues to expand, most notably with a new 11,000-foot (3,355-meter) runway. Among airports constructed in this formative aviation period, it stands as one of the largest and busiest still in operation. Additional contenders include Rome Ciampino Airport (opened 1916) and Don Mueang International Airport near Bangkok, Thailand (opened 1914). The surge in aircraft traffic during World War I necessitated the construction of dedicated landing fields. The requirement for aircraft to approach from specific directions subsequently spurred the development of early navigational aids to guide approach paths and landing slopes.

input: Around 66 BC, a movement to use constitutional, or at least peaceful, means to address the plight of various classes began. After several failures, the movement's leaders decided to use any means that were necessary to accomplish their goals. The movement coalesced under an aristocrat named Lucius Sergius Catilina. The movement was based in the town of Faesulae, which was a natural hotbed of agrarian agitation. The rural malcontents were to advance on Rome, and be aided by an uprising within the city. After assassinating the consuls and most of the senators, Catiline would be free to enact his reforms. The conspiracy was set in motion in 63 BC. The consul for the year, Marcus Tullius Cicero, intercepted messages that Catiline had sent in an attempt to recruit more members. As a result, the top conspirators in Rome (including at least one former consul) were executed by authorisation (of dubious constitutionality) of the senate, and the planned uprising was disrupted. Cicero then sent an army, which cut Catiline's forces to pieces.
rewrite: In approximately 66 BC, an initiative emerged seeking to redress the grievances of various social orders through constitutional, or at minimum non-violent, methods. Following a series of unsuccessful attempts, the leadership resolved to employ all necessary measures to achieve its objectives. This movement consolidated under the aristocratic figure Lucius Sergius Catilina, operating from Faesulae, a town noted as a natural center for agrarian discontent. The strategy involved a coordinated advance of rural dissidents upon Rome, supported by an internal insurrection. Following the assassination of the consuls and a majority of senators, Catiline would then implement his proposed reforms. The conspiracy was activated in 63 BC. The consul for that year, Marcus Tullius Cicero, intercepted correspondence from Catiline soliciting further adherents. Consequently, the principal conspirators within Rome, including a former consul, were executed under a senatorial decree of questionable legality, thereby thwarting the intended revolt. Cicero subsequently dispatched military forces, which decisively defeated and dispersed Catiline’s army.

input: On September 9, 2007, West suggested that his race had something to do with his being overlooked for opening the 2007 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) in favor of Britney Spears; he claimed, "Maybe my skin’s not right." West was performing at the event; that night, he lost all five awards that he was nominated for, including Best Male Artist and Video of the Year. After the show, he was visibly upset that he had lost at the VMAs two years in a row, stating that he would not come back to MTV ever again. He also appeared on several radio stations saying that when he made the song "Stronger" that it was his dream to open the VMAs with it. He has also stated that Spears has not had a hit in a long period of time and that MTV exploited her for ratings.
rewrite: On September 9, 2007, Kanye West posited that racial bias may have been a factor in the decision to select Britney Spears, rather than himself, to open the 2007 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs), remarking, "Maybe my skin’s not right." West, who performed at the ceremony, lost all five of his nominations, including Best Male Artist and Video of the Year. Following the event, he expressed visible frustration at having lost at the VMAs for a second consecutive year, declaring he would not return to MTV. In subsequent radio interviews, West revealed it had been his aspiration to open the VMAs with his song "Stronger." He further contended that Spears had not achieved a notable hit in an extended period and that MTV had leveraged her involvement for ratings.

input: Every federal unit had a town or city with historic significance from the World War II period renamed to have Tito's name included. The largest of these was Titograd, now Podgorica, the capital city of Montenegro. With the exception of Titograd, the cities were renamed simply by the addition of the adjective "Tito's" ("Titov"). The cities were:
rewrite: Each federal unit designated a historically significant World War II-era town or city to be renamed in honor of Josip Broz Tito. The most prominent was Titograd, present-day Podgorica, Montenegro's capital. Apart from Titograd, renaming typically involved prefixing the existing name with the adjective "Titov" (Tito's).

input: Switzerland's most important economic sector is manufacturing. Manufacturing consists largely of the production of specialist chemicals, health and pharmaceutical goods, scientific and precision measuring instruments and musical instruments. The largest exported goods are chemicals (34% of exported goods), machines/electronics (20.9%), and precision instruments/watches (16.9%). Exported services amount to a third of exports. The service sector – especially banking and insurance, tourism, and international organisations – is another important industry for Switzerland.
rewrite: Switzerland's predominant economic sector is manufacturing, which primarily involves specialized chemicals, pharmaceuticals, scientific and precision instruments, and musical instruments. Key exports include chemicals (34% of export value), machinery and electronics (20.9%), and precision instruments and watches (16.9%). Exported services constitute one-third of total exports. Additionally, the service sector—notably banking, insurance, tourism, and international organizations—represents another vital industry for the Swiss economy.

input: Economic and political migrations made an impact across the empire. For example, the Russian and Austria-Habsburg annexation of the Crimean and Balkan regions respectively saw large influxes of Muslim refugees – 200,000 Crimean Tartars fleeing to Dobruja. Between 1783 and 1913, approximately 5–7 million refugees flooded into the Ottoman Empire, at least 3.8 million of whom were from Russia. Some migrations left indelible marks such as political tension between parts of the empire (e.g. Turkey and Bulgaria) whereas centrifugal effects were noticed in other territories, simpler demographics emerging from diverse populations. Economies were also impacted with the loss of artisans, merchants, manufacturers and agriculturists. Since the 19th century, a large proportion of Muslim peoples from the Balkans emigrated to present-day Turkey. These people are called Muhacir. By the time the Ottoman Empire came to an end in 1922, half of the urban population of Turkey was descended from Muslim refugees from Russia.
rewrite: Economic and political migrations exerted significant influence throughout the Ottoman Empire. For instance, the annexation of Crimea by Russia and Balkan territories by the Habsburg Empire precipitated substantial influxes of Muslim refugees, including approximately 200,000 Crimean Tatars relocating to Dobruja. Cumulatively, an estimated five to seven million refugees entered the empire between 1783 and 1913, with no fewer than 3.8 million originating from Russian territories. These population movements produced enduring consequences, including heightened political tensions between regions such as Turkey and Bulgaria, while simultaneously fostering centrifugal forces and demographic homogenization in other areas. Economically, the departure of skilled artisans, merchants, industrialists, and agricultural workers incurred considerable losses. From the nineteenth century onward, a substantial proportion of Balkan Muslims, termed *Muhacir*, emigrated to present-day Turkey. By the empire’s dissolution in 1922, half of Turkey’s urban population traced its descent to these Muslim refugees from Russian lands.

input: Architecture (Latin architectura, from the Greek ἀρχιτέκτων arkhitekton "architect", from ἀρχι- "chief" and τέκτων "builder") is both the process and the product of planning, designing, and constructing buildings and other physical structures. Architectural works, in the material form of buildings, are often perceived as cultural symbols and as works of art. Historical civilizations are often identified with their surviving architectural achievements.
rewrite: Architecture, derived from the Greek for "chief builder," encompasses the process and product of planning, designing, and erecting buildings and structures. Architectural works, materially realized as buildings, are frequently regarded as cultural symbols and artistic creations. Surviving architectural achievements are often emblematic of historical civilizations.

input: During a period of tough competition between mortgage lenders for revenue and market share, and when the supply of creditworthy borrowers was limited, mortgage lenders relaxed underwriting standards and originated riskier mortgages to less creditworthy borrowers. In the view of some analysts, the relatively conservative government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) policed mortgage originators and maintained relatively high underwriting standards prior to 2003. However, as market power shifted from securitizers to originators and as intense competition from private securitizers undermined GSE power, mortgage standards declined and risky loans proliferated. The worst loans were originated in 2004–2007, the years of the most intense competition between securitizers and the lowest market share for the GSEs.
rewrite: Amidst intense competition for revenue and market share among mortgage lenders, coupled with a constrained supply of creditworthy borrowers, underwriting standards were relaxed, leading to the origination of riskier mortgages to less qualified applicants. Some analysts contend that, prior to 2003, the more conservative government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) effectively policed originators and upheld relatively stringent standards. However, as market power shifted from securitizers to originators and fierce competition from private securitizers eroded GSE influence, underwriting quality deteriorated and high-risk lending proliferated. The most deficient loans emerged between 2004 and 2007, a period marked by peak competition among securitizers and the GSEs' lowest market share.

input: Think-tanks such as the World Pensions Council have also argued that European legislators have pushed somewhat dogmatically for the adoption of the Basel II recommendations, adopted in 2005, transposed in European Union law through the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD), effective since 2008. In essence, they forced European banks, and, more importantly, the European Central Bank itself e.g. when gauging the solvency of financial institutions, to rely more than ever on standardised assessments of credit risk marketed by two non-European private agencies: Moody's and S&P.
rewrite: Think-tanks, including the World Pensions Council, have contended that European legislators dogmatically promoted the implementation of the Basel II framework. This was incorporated into EU law via the 2008 Capital Requirements Directive. Consequently, European banks and, critically, the European Central Bank—particularly when evaluating institutional solvency—became increasingly dependent on standardized credit risk assessments provided by the U.S.-based private agencies Moody's and S&P.

input: In July 2015, Eton accidentally sent emails to 400 prospective students, offering them conditional entrance to the school in September 2017. The email was intended for nine students, but an IT glitch caused the email to be sent to 400 additional families, who didn't necessarily have a place. In response, the school issued the following statement: "This error was discovered within minutes and each family was immediately contacted to notify them that it should be disregarded and to apologise. We take this type of incident very seriously indeed and so a thorough investigation, overseen by the headmaster Tony Little and led by the tutor for admissions, is being carried out to find out exactly what went wrong and ensure it cannot happen again. Eton College offers its sincere apologies to those boys concerned and their families. We deeply regret the confusion and upset this must have caused."
rewrite: In July 2015, Eton College erroneously dispatched emails to 400 prospective students, extending conditional offers for entry in September 2017. This communication was intended for only nine recipients; however, a technical malfunction resulted in its transmission to the substantially larger group, none of whom were assured a place. Upon identifying the error, the institution promptly issued a formal statement. It indicated that the mistake was detected within minutes, with each family contacted immediately to retract the offer and extend an apology. The statement further affirmed that the matter was being treated with utmost seriousness, initiating a thorough investigation overseen by the Headmaster, Tony Little, and led by the Tutor for Admissions. The purpose of this inquiry was to ascertain the precise cause of the error and to implement preventative measures. Eton College offered its sincere apologies to the affected students and their families, expressing profound regret for the resultant confusion and distress.

input: MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 Audio Layer III, more commonly referred to as MP3, is an audio coding format for digital audio which uses a form of lossy data compression. It is a common audio format for consumer audio streaming or storage, as well as a de facto standard of digital audio compression for the transfer and playback of music on most digital audio players.
rewrite: MPEG-1 or MPEG-2 Audio Layer III, commonly known as MP3, is a lossy audio coding format for digital audio. It serves as a prevalent format for consumer audio streaming and storage, functioning as the de facto standard for compressed digital music transfer and playback on most digital audio players.

input: Guinea fowl originated in southern Africa, and the species most often kept as poultry is the helmeted guineafowl (Numida meleagris). It is a medium-sized grey or speckled bird with a small naked head with colourful wattles and a knob on top, and was domesticated by the time of the ancient Greeks and Romans. Guinea fowl are hardy, sociable birds that subsist mainly on insects, but also consume grasses and seeds. They will keep a vegetable garden clear of pests and will eat the ticks that carry Lyme disease. They happily roost in trees and give a loud vocal warning of the approach of predators. Their flesh and eggs can be eaten in the same way as chickens, young birds being ready for the table at the age of about four months.
rewrite: The helmeted guineafowl (Numida meleagris), the primary species domesticated for poultry, is indigenous to southern Africa. This medium-sized bird, characterized by grey or speckled plumage, possesses a small, unfeathered head adorned with colourful wattles and a distinctive cranial knob. Its domestication dates to the classical eras of ancient Greece and Rome. As hardy, gregarious omnivores, guineafowl predominantly consume insects while also foraging on grasses and seeds. They provide effective pest control in cultivated areas, including the consumption of ticks that vector Lyme disease. The birds naturally roost arboreally and emit loud alarm calls at the approach of predators. Both their flesh and eggs are palatable, analogous to domestic fowl, with young birds reaching suitable market weight at approximately four months of age.

input: Interracial relationships, common-law marriages, and marriages occurred since the earliest colonial years, especially before slavery hardened as a racial caste associated with people of African descent in the British colonies. Virginia and other English colonies passed laws in the 17th century that gave children the social status of their mother, according to the principle of partus sequitur ventrem, regardless of the father's race or citizenship. This overturned the principle in English common law by which a man gave his status to his children – this had enabled communities to demand that fathers support their children, whether legitimate or not. The change increased white men's ability to use slave women sexually, as they had no responsibility for the children. As master as well as father of mixed-race children born into slavery, the men could use these people as servants or laborers or sell them as slaves. In some cases, white fathers provided for their multiracial children, paying or arranging for education or apprenticeships and freeing them, particularly during the two decades following the American Revolution. (The practice of providing for the children was more common in French and Spanish colonies, where a class of free people of color developed who became educated and property owners.) Many other white fathers abandoned the mixed-race children and their mothers to slavery.
rewrite: From the earliest colonial period, prior to the rigid codification of slavery as a racial caste linked to individuals of African descent, unions—including interracial relationships, common-law marriages, and formal marriages—occurred within the British colonies. During the seventeenth century, Virginia and other English colonies enacted legislation that assigned children the social condition of their mother, adhering to the doctrine of *partus sequitur ventrem*, irrespective of the father’s race or legal standing. This statute effectively overturned the English common law principle wherein a father transmitted his status to his offspring, a convention that had empowered communities to compel paternal support for both legitimate and illegitimate children. The legal shift augmented the capacity of white men to engage in sexual exploitation of enslaved women without assuming responsibility for resulting offspring. As both masters and biological fathers of mixed-race children born into bondage, these men could exploit such individuals as domestic or agricultural laborers, or sell them as chattel. In certain instances, particularly during the two decades following the American Revolution, white fathers made provisions for their multiracial children, arranging for their education, apprenticeships, or manumission. This practice of paternal provision was more prevalent in French and Spanish colonies, fostering the emergence of a propertied and educated free population of color. Conversely, numerous white fathers consigned both their mixed-race children and the children’s mothers to perpetual enslavement.

input: Japan and Germany are great powers too, though due to their large advanced economies (having the third and fourth largest economies respectively) rather than their strategic and hard power capabilities (i.e., the lack of permanent seats and veto power on the UN Security Council or strategic military reach). Germany has been a member together with the five permanent Security Council members in the P5+1 grouping of world powers. Like China, France, Russia and the United Kingdom; Germany and Japan have also been referred to as middle powers.
rewrite: Japan and Germany are also considered major powers, primarily due to their substantial and advanced economies, which rank third and fourth globally, respectively. Their status, however, derives less from traditional strategic and hard power capabilities—such as permanent UN Security Council membership with veto authority or extended military reach. Notably, Germany has participated alongside the five permanent members in the P5+1 diplomatic group. Alongside China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, and one another, both Germany and Japan have alternatively been classified as middle powers.

input: The relative reactivity of zinc and its ability to attract oxidation to itself makes it an efficient sacrificial anode in cathodic protection (CP). For example, cathodic protection of a buried pipeline can be achieved by connecting anodes made from zinc to the pipe. Zinc acts as the anode (negative terminus) by slowly corroding away as it passes electric current to the steel pipeline.[note 2] Zinc is also used to cathodically protect metals that are exposed to sea water from corrosion. A zinc disc attached to a ship's iron rudder will slowly corrode, whereas the rudder stays unattacked. Other similar uses include a plug of zinc attached to a propeller or the metal protective guard for the keel of the ship.
rewrite: Zinc serves as an effective sacrificial anode in cathodic protection (CP) systems due to its relative reactivity and propensity for oxidation. In such applications, zinc is electrically connected to a more noble metal, such as steel, thereby functioning as the anode. It corrodes preferentially, supplying protective current to the cathode. A common implementation involves attaching zinc anodes to buried pipelines to mitigate corrosion. Similarly, in marine environments, zinc discs or plugs are affixed to components like ship rudders, propellers, and keel guards. The zinc sacrificially corrodes, thereby preventing the corrosion of the critical ferrous metals exposed to seawater.

input: The first British Mont Blanc ascent was in 1788; the first female ascent in 1819. By the mid-1850s Swiss mountaineers had ascended most of the peaks and were eagerly sought as mountain guides. Edward Whymper reached the top of the Matterhorn in 1865 (after seven attempts), and in 1938 the last of the six great north faces of the Alps was climbed with the first ascent of the Eiger Nordwand (north face of the Eiger).
rewrite: The inaugural British ascent of Mont Blanc occurred in 1788, followed by the first female ascent in 1819. By the mid-1850s, Swiss climbers, having ascended most major Alpine peaks, were highly sought as guides. Edward Whymper summited the Matterhorn in 1865 after seven attempts. Subsequently, the 1938 first ascent of the Eiger Nordwand marked the conquest of the last great north face in the Alps.

input: From the 2011 Census, the Office for National Statistics published that Plymouth's unitary authority area population was 256,384; 15,664 more people than that of the last census from 2001, which indicated that Plymouth had a population of 240,720. The Plymouth urban area had a population of 260,203 in 2011 (the urban sprawl which extends outside the authority's boundaries). The city's average household size was 2.3 persons. At the time of the 2011 UK census, the ethnic composition of Plymouth's population was 96.2% White (of 92.9% was White British), with the largest minority ethnic group being Chinese at 0.5%. The white Irish ethnic group saw the largest decline in its share of the population since the 2001 Census (-24%), while the Other Asian and Black African had the largest increases (360% and 351% respectively). This excludes the two new ethnic groups added to the 2011 census of Gypsy or Irish Traveller and Arab. The population rose rapidly during the second half of the 19th century, but declined by over 1.6% from 1931 to 1951.
rewrite: According to data published by the Office for National Statistics from the 2011 Census, the population within the Plymouth unitary authority area was recorded at 256,384. This figure represents an increase of 15,664 persons from the 2001 Census, which enumerated a population of 240,720. The broader Plymouth urban area, extending beyond the administrative boundaries, contained 260,203 residents in 2011. The average household size within the city was 2.3 persons. Ethnically, the 2011 population was 96.2% White, with White British comprising 92.9% of this total. The largest minority ethnic group was Chinese, at 0.5%. Comparative analysis with the 2001 Census reveals a significant decline in the White Irish share of the population (-24%), while the categories of Other Asian and Black African saw the most substantial proportional increases (360% and 351%, respectively). These calculations exclude the two new ethnic groups introduced in 2011: Gypsy or Irish Traveller and Arab. Historically, Plymouth's population expanded rapidly in the late 19th century but experienced a decline exceeding 1.6% between 1931 and 1951.

input: In nature, uranium is found as uranium-238 (99.2742%) and uranium-235 (0.7204%). Isotope separation concentrates (enriches) the fissionable uranium-235 for nuclear weapons and most nuclear power plants, except for gas cooled reactors and pressurised heavy water reactors. Most neutrons released by a fissioning atom of uranium-235 must impact other uranium-235 atoms to sustain the nuclear chain reaction. The concentration and amount of uranium-235 needed to achieve this is called a 'critical mass'.
rewrite: Naturally occurring uranium consists primarily of uranium-238 (99.2742%) and uranium-235 (0.7204%). For use in nuclear weapons and most reactor designs—excluding gas-cooled and pressurized heavy water reactors—the fissile isotope uranium-235 must be concentrated through isotopic enrichment. A sustained nuclear chain reaction requires that neutrons released from fissioning uranium-235 nuclei predominantly strike other uranium-235 nuclei. The requisite quantity and concentration for this self-sustaining reaction is termed the 'critical mass'.

input: Major outputs for the state include textiles, cotton, cattle, and electrical power. Tennessee has over 82,000 farms, roughly 59 percent of which accommodate beef cattle. Although cotton was an early crop in Tennessee, large-scale cultivation of the fiber did not begin until the 1820s with the opening of the land between the Tennessee and Mississippi Rivers. The upper wedge of the Mississippi Delta extends into southwestern Tennessee, and it was in this fertile section that cotton took hold. Soybeans are also heavily planted in West Tennessee, focusing on the northwest corner of the state.
rewrite: The state's principal economic outputs comprise textiles, cotton, livestock, and electrical power. Tennessee contains over 82,000 farms, with approximately 59 percent supporting beef cattle operations. While cotton was historically cultivated, its extensive production commenced only in the 1820s following the settlement of the region between the Tennessee and Mississippi Rivers. The fertile upper wedge of the Mississippi Delta, extending into southwestern Tennessee, became central to cotton cultivation. Additionally, soybean planting is concentrated heavily in West Tennessee, particularly in its northwestern corner.

input: Some of the cleaner energy facilities in Boston include the Allston green district, with three ecologically compatible housing facilities. Boston is also breaking ground on multiple green affordable housing facilities to help reduce the carbon footprint of the city while simultaneously making these initiatives financially available to a greater population. Boston's climate plan is updated every three years and was most recently modified in 2013. This legislature includes the Building Energy Reporting and Disclosure Ordinance, which requires the city's larger buildings to disclose their yearly energy and water use statistics and partake in an energy assessment every five years. These statistics are made public by the city, thereby increasing incentives for buildings to be more environmentally conscious.
rewrite: Boston's commitment to sustainable development is exemplified by initiatives such as the Allston green district, which features three ecologically integrated housing structures. The city is further advancing this agenda through the construction of multiple green affordable housing projects, aiming to reduce its carbon footprint while enhancing economic accessibility. Guiding these efforts is a municipal climate plan, updated triennially and last revised in 2013. A key component is the Building Energy Reporting and Disclosure Ordinance, mandating that larger buildings annually report their energy and water consumption and undergo quinquennial energy assessments. By making this data publicly available, the ordinance creates additional incentives for improved environmental performance.

input: Cognitive neuroscientists consider memory as the retention, reactivation, and reconstruction of the experience-independent internal representation. The term of internal representation implies that such definition of memory contains two components: the expression of memory at the behavioral or conscious level, and the underpinning physical neural changes (Dudai 2007). The latter component is also called engram or memory traces (Semon 1904). Some neuroscientists and psychologists mistakenly equate the concept of engram and memory, broadly conceiving all persisting after-effects of experiences as memory; others argue against this notion that memory does not exist until it is revealed in behavior or thought (Moscovitch 2007).
rewrite: Cognitive neuroscience defines memory as the retention, reactivation, and reconstruction of experience-independent internal representations. This definition inherently comprises two elements: the behavioral or conscious expression of memory and the underlying physical neural alterations, termed the engram or memory trace. A conceptual divergence exists wherein some scholars conflate the engram with memory itself, broadly classifying all persistent experiential after-effects as memory. Others contend that memory only manifests when expressed through behavior or cognition, challenging a purely physicalist account.

input: In the 2005–06 season, Barcelona repeated their league and Supercup successes. The pinnacle of the league season arrived at the Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in a 3–0 win over Real Madrid. It was Frank Rijkaard's second victory at the Bernabéu, making him the first Barcelona manager to win there twice. Ronaldinho's performance was so impressive that after his second goal, which was Barcelona's third, some Real Madrid fans gave him a standing ovation. In the Champions League, Barcelona beat the English club Arsenal in the final. Trailing 1–0 to a 10-man Arsenal and with less than 15 minutes remaining, they came back to win 2–1, with substitute Henrik Larsson, in his final appearance for the club, setting up goals for Samuel Eto'o and fellow substitute Juliano Belletti, for the club's first European Cup victory in 14 years.
rewrite: During the 2005–06 season, Barcelona secured both the domestic league title and the Supercup once again. A defining moment of the league campaign was a decisive 3–0 victory over Real Madrid at the Santiago Bernabéu Stadium. This result marked manager Frank Rijkaard's second win at that venue, establishing him as the first Barcelona coach to achieve two victories there. Ronaldinho delivered an exceptional performance, receiving a standing ovation from a segment of Real Madrid supporters following his second goal. In the UEFA Champions League final, Barcelona faced Arsenal. Despite conceding an early goal to a side reduced to ten men and trailing with under fifteen minutes remaining, Barcelona rallied to a 2–1 victory. Substitute Henrik Larsson, in his final match for the club, provided crucial assists for goals by Samuel Eto'o and fellow substitute Juliano Belletti, securing the club's first European Cup in fourteen years.

input: The game pad controllers were more-or-less copied directly from the Game & Watch machines, although the Famicom design team originally wanted to use arcade-style joysticks, even taking apart ones from American game consoles to see how they worked. However, it was eventually decided that children might step on joysticks left on the floor and their durability was also questioned. Katsuyah Nakawaka attached a Game & Watch D-pad to the Famicom prototype and found that it was easy to use and had no discomfort. Ultimately though, they did install a 15-pin expansion port on the front of the console so that an arcade-style joystick could be used optionally. The controllers were hard-wired to the console with no connectors for cost reasons.
rewrite: The design of the game pad controllers was largely derived directly from the Game & Watch devices. Initially, the Famicom development team considered employing arcade-style joysticks, even disassembling examples from American consoles to study their mechanisms. Concerns were subsequently raised regarding potential durability issues and the risk of children stepping on joysticks left on the floor. Engineer Katsuyah Nakawaka tested a Game & Watch directional pad on a prototype, determining it offered both ease of use and comfort. Consequently, the integrated controllers adopted this design and were permanently attached to the console to reduce costs. However, a 15-pin expansion port was incorporated on the front fascia to permit the optional use of an external arcade-style joystick.

input: A scientific study in the journal, Biological Conservation, states that trophy hunting is of "major importance to conservation in Africa by creating economic incentives for conservation over vast areas, including areas which may be unsuitable for alternative wildlife-based land uses such as photographic ecotourism." However, another study states that less than 3% of a trophy hunters' expenditures reach the local level, meaning that the economic incentive and benefit is "minimal, particularly when we consider the vast areas of land that hunting concessions occupy."
rewrite: A study in *Biological Conservation* asserts that trophy hunting is of major conservation importance in Africa, generating economic incentives across extensive areas unsuitable for alternative wildlife-based land uses like photographic ecotourism. Conversely, other research indicates less than 3% of trophy hunters' expenditures reach local communities, suggesting the economic benefit is minimal relative to the vast land area occupied by hunting concessions.

input: Nigeria is a Federal Republic modelled after the United States, with executive power exercised by the president. It is influenced by the Westminster System model[citation needed] in the composition and management of the upper and lower houses of the bicameral legislature. The president presides as both Head of State and head of the national executive; the leader is elected by popular vote to a maximum of two 4-year terms. In the March 28, 2015 presidential election, General Muhammadu Buhari emerged victorious to become the Federal President of Nigeria, defeating then incumbent Goodluck Jonathan.
rewrite: The Federal Republic of Nigeria employs a presidential system of governance, structurally analogous to that of the United States, wherein executive authority is vested in a directly elected president. Its bicameral legislature, however, reflects compositional and procedural influences from the Westminster parliamentary model. The president serves as both Head of State and head of government, eligible for a maximum of two four-year terms. In the presidential election of March 28, 2015, General Muhammadu Buhari was elected, defeating the incumbent, President Goodluck Jonathan.

input: There are typically 40 million bacterial cells in a gram of soil and a million bacterial cells in a millilitre of fresh water. There are approximately 5×1030 bacteria on Earth, forming a biomass which exceeds that of all plants and animals. Bacteria are vital in recycling nutrients, with many of the stages in nutrient cycles dependent on these organisms, such as the fixation of nitrogen from the atmosphere and putrefaction. In the biological communities surrounding hydrothermal vents and cold seeps, bacteria provide the nutrients needed to sustain life by converting dissolved compounds, such as hydrogen sulphide and methane, to energy. On 17 March 2013, researchers reported data that suggested bacterial life forms thrive in the Mariana Trench, which with a depth of up to 11 kilometres is the deepest part of the Earth's oceans. Other researchers reported related studies that microbes thrive inside rocks up to 580 metres below the sea floor under 2.6 kilometres of ocean off the coast of the northwestern United States. According to one of the researchers, "You can find microbes everywhere — they're extremely adaptable to conditions, and survive wherever they are."
rewrite: Bacterial populations are ubiquitous and abundant, with typical concentrations of approximately 40 million cells per gram of soil and one million cells per millilitre of fresh water. The global bacterial population is estimated at 5×10³⁰, constituting a collective biomass that surpasses that of all plant and animal life. Bacteria perform essential roles in nutrient cycling, including critical processes such as atmospheric nitrogen fixation and putrefaction. In extreme environments like hydrothermal vent and cold seep communities, they sustain life by chemosynthesis, converting dissolved compounds such as hydrogen sulphide and methane into energy. Evidence of their adaptability continues to expand; on 17 March 2013, researchers documented thriving bacterial life in the Mariana Trench, at depths reaching 11 kilometres. Concurrent studies reported microbial life within rocks 580 metres beneath the sea floor under 2.6 kilometres of ocean off the northwestern United States coast. As one researcher concluded, microbes are omnipresent, exhibiting extreme adaptability to diverse conditions and persisting in virtually every environment.

input: In 2013 a lot of media coverage was given to unclassified NSA's study in Cryptologic Spectrum that concluded that Tito did not speak the language as a native, and had features of other Slavic languages (Russian and Polish). The hypothesis that "a non-Yugoslav, perhaps a Russian or a Pole" assumed Tito's identity was included. The report also notes Draža Mihailović's impressions of Tito's Russian origins.
rewrite: A 2013 unclassified NSA study published in *Cryptologic Spectrum* received significant media attention for its linguistic analysis of Josip Broz Tito. It concluded his speech lacked native proficiency in the local language, instead exhibiting features of Russian and Polish. The report presented the hypothesis that an imposter of Russian or Polish origin assumed Tito's identity, a view corroborated by Draža Mihailović's own impressions of Tito's Russian background.

input: Under the doctrine of Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins (1938), there is no general federal common law. Although federal courts can create federal common law in the form of case law, such law must be linked one way or another to the interpretation of a particular federal constitutional provision, statute, or regulation (which in turn was enacted as part of the Constitution or after). Federal courts lack the plenary power possessed by state courts to simply make up law, which the latter are able to do in the absence of constitutional or statutory provisions replacing the common law. Only in a few narrow limited areas, like maritime law, has the Constitution expressly authorized the continuation of English common law at the federal level (meaning that in those areas federal courts can continue to make law as they see fit, subject to the limitations of stare decisis).
rewrite: Under the doctrine established in *Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins* (1938), a general federal common law does not exist. While federal courts may develop federal common law through judicial decisions, any such law must be derived from the interpretation of a specific federal constitutional provision, statute, or regulation—each itself enacted pursuant to constitutional authority. Federal courts do not possess the plenary authority held by state courts to formulate law absent governing constitutional or statutory directives, a power state courts retain where no such provisions supplant the common law. Only within select, narrowly defined domains, such as admiralty law, has the Constitution expressly permitted the continuation of English common law at the federal level. Consequently, in these limited areas, federal courts may continue to develop law subject to the constraints of stare decisis.

input: The BRA subsequently reevaluated its approach to urban renewal in its future projects, including the construction of Government Center. In 1965, the first Community Health Center in the United States opened, the Columbia Point Health Center, in the Dorchester neighborhood. It mostly served the massive Columbia Point public housing complex adjoining it, which was built in 1953. The health center is still in operation and was rededicated in 1990 as the Geiger-Gibson Community Health Center. The Columbia Point complex itself was redeveloped and revitalized into a mixed-income community called Harbor Point Apartments from 1984 to 1990. By the 1970s, the city's economy boomed after 30 years of economic downturn. A large number of high rises were constructed in the Financial District and in Boston's Back Bay during this time period. This boom continued into the mid-1980s and later began again. Hospitals such as Massachusetts General Hospital, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and Brigham and Women's Hospital lead the nation in medical innovation and patient care. Schools such as Boston College, Boston University, the Harvard Medical School, Northeastern University, Wentworth Institute of Technology, Berklee College of Music and Boston Conservatory attract students to the area. Nevertheless, the city experienced conflict starting in 1974 over desegregation busing, which resulted in unrest and violence around public schools throughout the mid-1970s.
rewrite: The Boston Redevelopment Authority subsequently revised its urban renewal methodologies in forthcoming initiatives, including the Government Center project. In 1965, the inaugural Community Health Center in the United States commenced operations as the Columbia Point Health Center in Dorchester. Primarily serving the adjacent Columbia Point public housing complex—constructed in 1953—this facility remains operational and was renamed the Geiger-Gibson Community Health Center upon its rededication in 1990. The Columbia Point complex itself underwent redevelopment from 1984 to 1990, transforming into the mixed-income Harbor Point Apartments. Following three decades of economic decline, the city's economy expanded markedly during the 1970s, prompting the construction of numerous high-rise buildings in the Financial District and Back Bay. This growth persisted into the mid-1980s and later resumed. Institutions such as Massachusetts General Hospital, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and Brigham and Women's Hospital are national leaders in medical innovation and patient care. Higher education establishments, including Boston College, Boston University, Harvard Medical School, Northeastern University, Wentworth Institute of Technology, Berklee College of Music, and the Boston Conservatory, draw substantial student populations to the region. Concurrently, the city encountered significant strife beginning in 1974 due to court-ordered desegregation busing, which incited unrest and violence in and around public schools throughout the mid-1970s.

input: The Thuringian population has a significant sex ratio gap, caused by the emigration of young women, especially in rural areas. Overall, there are 115 to 120 men per 100 women in the 25–40 age group ("family founders") which has negative consequences for the birth ratio. Furthermore, the population is getting older and older with some rural municipalities recording more than 30% of over-65s (pensioners). This is a problem for the regional labour market, as there are twice as many people leaving as entering the job market annually.
rewrite: The Thuringian population exhibits a pronounced sex ratio imbalance, driven by the outmigration of young women, particularly from rural regions. Among those aged 25–40, a critical demographic for family formation, there are 115 to 120 men for every 100 women, adversely impacting fertility rates. Concurrently, population aging is advancing, with some rural municipalities comprising over 30% pensioners aged 65 and above. This demographic shift strains the regional labour market, where annual exits now double the number of new entrants.

input: During World War II, Hitler's Generalplan Ost (general plan for the East) entailed killing, deporting, or enslaving the Slavic and Jewish population of occupied Eastern Europe to create Lebensraum (living space) for German settlers. The Nazi Hunger Plan and Generalplan Ost would have led to the starvation of 80 million people in the Soviet Union. These partially fulfilled plans resulted in the deaths of an estimated 19.3 million civilians and prisoners of war.
rewrite: Generalplan Ost, a Nazi strategy during World War II, envisioned the systematic extermination, expulsion, and enslavement of Slavic and Jewish populations in Eastern Europe to establish Lebensraum for German colonists. Combined with the Hunger Plan, it projected causing approximately 80 million Soviet deaths by starvation. While only partially implemented, these policies resulted in an estimated 19.3 million civilian and prisoner of war fatalities.

input: Gorbachev's inability to alleviate any of Armenia's problems created disillusionment among the Armenians and fed a growing hunger for independence. In May 1990, the New Armenian Army (NAA) was established, serving as a defence force separate from the Soviet Red Army. Clashes soon broke out between the NAA and Soviet Internal Security Forces (MVD) troops based in Yerevan when Armenians decided to commemorate the establishment of the 1918 First Republic of Armenia. The violence resulted in the deaths of five Armenians killed in a shootout with the MVD at the railway station. Witnesses there claimed that the MVD used excessive force and that they had instigated the fighting.
rewrite: Gorbachev's failure to address Armenia's mounting issues fostered widespread disillusionment and strengthened separatist aspirations. This culminated in the formation of the New Armenian Army (NAA) in May 1990 as an autonomous defense force distinct from the Soviet Red Army. Tensions escalated when the NAA clashed with Soviet Internal Security Forces (MVD) stationed in Yerevan during commemorations of the 1918 First Republic of Armenia. A confrontation at the railway station led to the deaths of five Armenians. Witness accounts asserted that the MVD employed disproportionate force and initiated the violence.

input: The city is home to the longest surviving stretch of medieval walls in England, as well as a number of museums such as Tudor House Museum, reopened on 30 July 2011 after undergoing extensive restoration and improvement; Southampton Maritime Museum; God's House Tower, an archaeology museum about the city's heritage and located in one of the tower walls; the Medieval Merchant's House; and Solent Sky, which focuses on aviation. The SeaCity Museum is located in the west wing of the civic centre, formerly occupied by Hampshire Constabulary and the Magistrates' Court, and focuses on Southampton's trading history and on the RMS Titanic. The museum received half a million pounds from the National Lottery in addition to interest from numerous private investors and is budgeted at £28 million.
rewrite: The city contains the longest surviving stretch of medieval walls in England, alongside several notable museums. These include the Tudor House Museum, which reopened on 30 July 2011 following a major restoration; the Southampton Maritime Museum; and God's House Tower, an archaeology museum housed within the tower walls and dedicated to local heritage. Other institutions are the Medieval Merchant's House and Solent Sky, with its focus on aviation. The SeaCity Museum, situated in the civic centre's west wing—a space previously used by Hampshire Constabulary and the Magistrates' Court—examines Southampton's maritime trade and its connection to the RMS Titanic. Funding for this museum included £500,000 from the National Lottery, contributions from private investors, and an overall budget of £28 million.

input: Beyoncé participated in George Clooney and Wyclef Jean's Hope for Haiti Now: A Global Benefit for Earthquake Relief telethon and was named the official face of the limited edition CFDA "Fashion For Haiti" T-shirt, made by Theory which raised a total of $1 million. On March 5, 2010, Beyoncé and her mother Tina opened the Beyoncé Cosmetology Center at the Brooklyn Phoenix House, offering a seven-month cosmetology training course for men and women.
