In April 2011, Beyoncé joined forces with US First Lady Michelle Obama and the National Association of Broadcasters Education Foundation, to help boost the latter's campaign against child obesity by reworking her single "Get Me Bodied". Following the death of Osama bin Laden, Beyoncé released her cover of the Lee Greenwood song "God Bless the USA", as a charity single to help raise funds for the New York Police and Fire Widows' and Children's Benefit Fund.
rewrite: Beyoncé contributed to earthquake relief efforts in Haiti through two distinct initiatives. First, she performed in the Hope for Haiti Now telethon, co-organized by George Clooney and Wyclef Jean. Subsequently, she served as the official ambassador for a limited-edition "Fashion For Haiti" T-shirt produced by Theory for the CFDA, a venture that generated one million dollars. On March 5, 2010, Beyoncé and her mother, Tina Knowles, inaugurated the Beyoncé Cosmetology Center at the Brooklyn Phoenix House, which provides a seven-month vocational training program in cosmetology. In April 2011, she collaborated with First Lady Michelle Obama and the National Association of Broadcasters Education Foundation, adapting her song "Get Me Bodied" to support a national campaign addressing childhood obesity. Following the demise of Osama bin Laden, Beyoncé released a charitable cover of Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the USA" to benefit the New York Police and Fire Widows' and Children's Benefit Fund.

input: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a soil rhizosphere bacterium, can attach to plant cells and infect them with a callus-inducing Ti plasmid by horizontal gene transfer, causing a callus infection called crown gall disease. Schell and Van Montagu (1977) hypothesised that the Ti plasmid could be a natural vector for introducing the Nif gene responsible for nitrogen fixation in the root nodules of legumes and other plant species. Today, genetic modification of the Ti plasmid is one of the main techniques for introduction of transgenes to plants and the creation of genetically modified crops.
rewrite: Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a soil-dwelling rhizobacterium, infects plant cells via horizontal gene transfer of its tumor-inducing (Ti) plasmid, resulting in crown gall disease. Schell and Van Montagu (1977) proposed that this plasmid could serve as a natural vector to introduce nitrogen-fixing (Nif) genes into legumes and other plants. Presently, engineered Ti plasmids are a principal method for plant transgene delivery and the development of genetically modified crops.

input: Depending on a number of considerations, a company may apply for and be granted a patent for the drug, or the process of producing the drug, granting exclusivity rights typically for about 20 years. However, only after rigorous study and testing, which takes 10 to 15 years on average, will governmental authorities grant permission for the company to market and sell the drug. Patent protection enables the owner of the patent to recover the costs of research and development through high profit margins for the branded drug. When the patent protection for the drug expires, a generic drug is usually developed and sold by a competing company. The development and approval of generics is less expensive, allowing them to be sold at a lower price. Often the owner of the branded drug will introduce a generic version before the patent expires in order to get a head start in the generic market. Restructuring has therefore become routine, driven by the patent expiration of products launched during the industry's "golden era" in the 1990s and companies' failure to develop sufficient new blockbuster products to replace lost revenues.
rewrite: The granting of a patent for a pharmaceutical compound or its manufacturing process, contingent upon various criteria, confers approximately two decades of market exclusivity to the originating firm. This protection is only secured following an extensive period of rigorous clinical study and regulatory testing, a process averaging between ten and fifteen years, after which marketing authorization is granted. The patent system functions to allow the patent holder to recoup substantial research and development investments through the premium pricing of the branded product. Upon patent expiry, competing firms typically introduce generic versions, the development and regulatory approval of which incur significantly lower costs, enabling reduced consumer prices. Strategically, the originator company may itself launch an authorized generic prior to patent expiration to establish early market presence. Consequently, widespread corporate restructuring has become commonplace within the industry. This trend is propelled by the sequential expiration of patents for major products launched during the sector's prolific 1990s, coupled with an insufficient pipeline of novel blockbuster therapies to offset the resultant revenue declines.

input: Pubertal development also affects circulatory and respiratory systems as an adolescents' heart and lungs increase in both size and capacity. These changes lead to increased strength and tolerance for exercise. Sex differences are apparent as males tend to develop "larger hearts and lungs, higher systolic blood pressure, a lower resting heart rate, a greater capacity for carrying oxygen to the blood, a greater power for neutralizing the chemical products of muscular exercise, higher blood hemoglobin and more red blood cells".
rewrite: Pubertal development further influences the circulatory and respiratory systems as the heart and lungs undergo significant growth in size and capacity. These physiological adaptations enhance muscular strength and exercise tolerance. Notable sexual dimorphism emerges, with males typically developing larger hearts and lungs, elevated systolic blood pressure, a lower resting heart rate, increased oxygen-carrying capacity, greater buffering of metabolic byproducts, and higher concentrations of hemoglobin and red blood cells.

input: Victoria wrote to her uncle Leopold, whom Victoria considered her "best and kindest adviser", to thank him "for the prospect of great happiness you have contributed to give me, in the person of dear Albert ... He possesses every quality that could be desired to render me perfectly happy. He is so sensible, so kind, and so good, and so amiable too. He has besides the most pleasing and delightful exterior and appearance you can possibly see." However at 17, Victoria, though interested in Albert, was not yet ready to marry. The parties did not undertake a formal engagement, but assumed that the match would take place in due time.
rewrite: In a letter to her uncle Leopold, whom she regarded as her "best and kindest adviser," Queen Victoria expressed gratitude for the "prospect of great happiness" afforded by the introduction of Prince Albert. She praised his character as sensible, kind, good, and amiable, further noting his "most pleasing and delightful exterior and appearance." Despite this favorable impression, the seventeen-year-old monarch was not prepared to enter matrimony at that time. Consequently, while no formal engagement was established, both parties anticipated the union would proceed at a future, appropriate date.

input: Photometric studies (also sometimes referred to as "layouts" or "point by points") are often used to simulate lighting designs for projects before they are built or renovated. This enables architects, lighting designers, and engineers to determine whether a proposed lighting setup will deliver the amount of light intended. They will also be able to determine the contrast ratio between light and dark areas. In many cases these studies are referenced against IESNA or CIBSE recommended lighting practices for the type of application. Depending on the type of area, different design aspects may be emphasized for safety or practicality (i.e. such as maintaining uniform light levels, avoiding glare or highlighting certain areas). Specialized software is often used to create these, which typically combine the use of two-dimensional digital CAD drawings and lighting calculation software (i.e. AGi32or Dialux).
rewrite: Photometric analyses, commonly termed "layouts" or "point-by-point" studies, are employed to simulate proposed illumination schemes prior to construction or renovation. These simulations allow architects, lighting designers, and engineers to evaluate whether a design will achieve target illuminance levels and to assess luminance contrasts within a space. The findings are frequently benchmarked against the recommended practices of organizations such as the IESNA or CIBSE, which provide application-specific guidelines. Design priorities, including uniformity, glare control, or focal accentuation, are emphasized according to the area's functional requirements for safety and practicality. These studies are typically generated using specialized software that integrates two-dimensional computer-aided design drawings with dedicated lighting calculation engines, for instance AGi32 or Dialux.

input: Frederick Lynch, the author of Invisible Victims: White Males and the Crisis of Affirmative Action, did a study on white males that said they were victims of reverse discrimination. Lynch explains that these white men felt frustrated and unfairly victimized by affirmative action. Shelby Steele, another author against affirmative action, wanted to see affirmative action go back to its original meaning of enforcing equal opportunity. He argued that blacks had to take full responsibility in their education and in maintaining a job. Steele believes that there is still a long way to go in America to reach our goals of eradicating discrimination.
rewrite: Frederick Lynch, in his work *Invisible Victims: White Males and the Crisis of Affirmative Action*, presents a study contending that white males perceive themselves as victims of reverse discrimination, experiencing frustration and a sense of unfair victimization. Similarly, critic Shelby Steele advocates for a return to affirmative action's original intent of ensuring equal opportunity. He asserts that African Americans must assume full responsibility for their educational and occupational advancement, while maintaining that significant progress remains necessary to eradicate discrimination in America.

input: The first video game based on the AFL was Arena Football for the C-64 released in 1988. On May 18, 2000, Kurt Warner's Arena Football Unleashed was released by Midway Games for the PlayStation game console. On February 7, 2006 EA Sports released Arena Football for the PlayStation 2 and Xbox. EA Sports released another AFL video game, titled Arena Football: Road to Glory, on February 21, 2007, for the PlayStation 2.
rewrite: The inaugural AFL-based video game, "Arena Football," debuted for the C-64 in 1988. Subsequently, "Kurt Warner's Arena Football Unleashed" was launched by Midway Games for the PlayStation on May 18, 2000. EA Sports released "Arena Football" for PlayStation 2 and Xbox on February 7, 2006, followed by "Arena Football: Road to Glory" for PlayStation 2 on February 21, 2007.

input: In 1422 King Władysław II Jagiełło by the Privilege of Czerwińsk (Polish: "przywilej czerwiński") established the inviolability of nobles' property (their estates could not be confiscated except upon a court verdict) and ceded some jurisdiction over fiscal policy to the Royal Council (later, the Senat of Poland), including the right to mint coinage.
rewrite: Through the 1422 Privilege of Czerwińsk, King Władysław II Jagiełło guaranteed the inviolability of noble estates, prohibiting confiscation without a court verdict. He also transferred certain fiscal authorities, such as coinage rights, to the Royal Council, later the Senat of Poland.

input: During the 12th century, the institutions of central government, which had hitherto accompanied the royal English court as it moved around the country, grew in size and sophistication and became increasingly fixed in one place. In most cases this was Westminster, although the royal treasury, having been moved from Winchester, came to rest in the Tower. While the City of Westminster developed into a true capital in governmental terms, its distinct neighbour, the City of London, remained England's largest city and principal commercial centre, and it flourished under its own unique administration, the Corporation of London. In 1100, its population was around 18,000; by 1300 it had grown to nearly 100,000.
rewrite: During the twelfth century, the central governmental institutions of England, which had previously travelled with the peripatetic royal court, expanded in both scale and complexity, becoming increasingly sedentary. This administrative fixation occurred predominantly at Westminster. An exception was the royal treasury, which, relocated from Winchester, was ultimately housed in the Tower of London. Consequently, Westminster evolved into the de facto political capital. Meanwhile, the adjacent yet distinct City of London persisted as the kingdom's primary commercial and most populous urban centre. Governed autonomously by its Corporation, the city prospered, its population surging from approximately 18,000 in 1100 to nearly 100,000 by 1300.

input: The Second Great Awakening began around 1790. It gained momentum by 1800. After 1820, membership rose rapidly among Baptist and Methodist congregations, whose preachers led the movement. It was past its peak by the late 1840s. It has been described as a reaction against skepticism, deism, and rationalism, although why those forces became pressing enough at the time to spark revivals is not fully understood. It enrolled millions of new members in existing evangelical denominations and led to the formation of new denominations.
rewrite: The Second Great Awakening commenced circa 1790, accelerating after 1800. Post-1820, Baptist and Methodist congregations, whose clergy spearheaded the movement, experienced rapid membership growth, peaking before the late 1840s. Interpreted as a reaction against skepticism, deism, and rationalism, the precise reasons these intellectual currents provoked such widespread revival remain unclear. The movement enrolled millions into existing evangelical denominations and stimulated the formation of new ones.

input: By 500 BCE, Greeks arrived in the desert. Greek traders spread along the eastern coast of the desert, establishing trading colonies along the Red Sea. The Carthaginians explored the Atlantic coast of the desert, but the turbulence of the waters and the lack of markets caused a lack of presence further south than modern Morocco. Centralized states thus surrounded the desert on the north and east; it remained outside the control of these states. Raids from the nomadic Berber people of the desert were a constant concern of those living on the edge of the desert.
rewrite: By approximately 500 BCE, Greek presence was established in the desert region. Greek merchants extended their activities along the eastern desert coast, founding trading colonies on the Red Sea. Concurrently, Carthaginians explored the Atlantic coastline; however, turbulent seas and insufficient commercial prospects prevented significant expansion south of present-day Morocco. Consequently, while centralized states bordered the desert to the north and east, the interior remained beyond their direct control. The sedentary populations along the desert periphery faced persistent threats from raids conducted by nomadic Berber groups inhabiting the desert.

input: In addition to the use of sound for communication, a wide range of insects have evolved chemical means for communication. These chemicals, termed semiochemicals, are often derived from plant metabolites include those meant to attract, repel and provide other kinds of information. Pheromones, a type of semiochemical, are used for attracting mates of the opposite sex, for aggregating conspecific individuals of both sexes, for deterring other individuals from approaching, to mark a trail, and to trigger aggression in nearby individuals. Allomonea benefit their producer by the effect they have upon the receiver. Kairomones benefit their receiver instead of their producer. Synomones benefit the producer and the receiver. While some chemicals are targeted at individuals of the same species, others are used for communication across species. The use of scents is especially well known to have developed in social insects.:96–105
rewrite: Beyond auditory signals, many insects have evolved sophisticated chemical communication systems. These chemical messengers, known as semiochemicals, are frequently derived from plant metabolites and serve to convey information such as attraction or repulsion. A key class, pheromones, facilitates intraspecific interactions including mate attraction, aggregation, trail marking, and the elicitation of aggression or deterrence. Interspecific communication is also mediated by semiochemicals, categorized by their adaptive benefits: allomones advantage the emitter, kairomones advantage the receiver, and synomones advantage both parties. The deployment of such olfactory cues is particularly advanced and well-documented in eusocial insect colonies, where they coordinate complex group behaviors.

input: Known as the world's automotive center, "Detroit" is a metonym for that industry. Detroit's auto industry, some of which was converted to wartime defense production, was an important element of the American "Arsenal of Democracy" supporting the Allied powers during World War II. It is an important source of popular music legacies celebrated by the city's two familiar nicknames, the Motor City and Motown. Other nicknames arose in the 20th century, including City of Champions, beginning in the 1930s for its successes in individual and team sport; The D; Hockeytown (a trademark owned by the city's NHL club, the Red Wings); Rock City (after the Kiss song "Detroit Rock City"); and The 313 (its telephone area code).
rewrite: The city of Detroit is widely recognized as a global center of automotive manufacturing, with its name serving as a metonym for the industry. During World War II, its industrial capacity, partially converted to defense production, became a crucial component of the American "Arsenal of Democracy" in support of the Allied war effort. Detroit is also notable as a significant source of popular music heritage, reflected in its two most prominent nicknames: the Motor City and Motown. Additional 20th-century monikers include the City of Champions, referencing athletic successes from the 1930s; The D; Hockeytown (a trademark of the Detroit Red Wings); Rock City; and The 313, derived from its telephone area code.

input: Due to the top secret nature of the work, Los Alamos was isolated. In Feynman's own words, "There wasn't anything to do there." Bored, he indulged his curiosity by learning to pick the combination locks on cabinets and desks used to secure papers. Feynman played many jokes on colleagues. In one case he found the combination to a locked filing cabinet by trying the numbers he thought a physicist would use (it proved to be 27–18–28 after the base of natural logarithms, e = 2.71828...), and found that the three filing cabinets where a colleague kept a set of atomic bomb research notes all had the same combination. He left a series of notes in the cabinets as a prank, which initially spooked his colleague, Frederic de Hoffmann, into thinking a spy or saboteur had gained access to atomic bomb secrets. On several occasions, Feynman drove to Albuquerque to see his ailing wife in a car borrowed from Klaus Fuchs, who was later discovered to be a real spy for the Soviets, transporting nuclear secrets in his car to Santa Fe.
rewrite: The highly classified nature of the Los Alamos project necessitated its isolation, which Richard Feynman described as offering little diversion. In response to this boredom, he cultivated an interest in manipulating the combination locks securing cabinets and desks containing sensitive documents. Feynman frequently engaged in pranks against his colleagues. Notably, he deduced the combination to a locked filing cabinet by hypothesizing the numbers a physicist might employ; it was set to 27-18-28, derived from the base of the natural logarithm (e = 2.71828…). He subsequently discovered that three cabinets containing a colleague’s atomic bomb research notes shared this identical combination. As a jest, he placed a series of notes inside, which initially alarmed his colleague, Frederic de Hoffmann, who suspected a security breach by a spy or saboteur. Furthermore, Feynman periodically traveled to Albuquerque to visit his ill wife, using an automobile borrowed from Klaus Fuchs—who was later revealed to be an actual Soviet agent transporting nuclear secrets in that same vehicle to Santa Fe.

input: The resultant South Korean government promulgated a national political constitution on 17 July 1948, and elected Syngman Rhee as President on 20 July 1948. The Republic of Korea (South Korea) was established on 15 August 1948. In the Russian Korean Zone of Occupation, the Soviet Union established a Communist North Korean government led by Kim Il-sung. President Rhee's régime excluded communists and leftists from southern politics. Disenfranchised, they headed for the hills, to prepare for guerrilla war against the US-sponsored ROK Government.
rewrite: On 17 July 1948, the newly formed South Korean government enacted a national constitution, electing Syngman Rhee as president on 20 July. The Republic of Korea was formally established on 15 August 1948. Concurrently, the Soviet Union established a communist government under Kim Il-sung in its occupation zone. The Rhee administration's exclusion of communists and leftists from southern politics prompted many of the disenfranchised to retreat to mountainous areas to organize guerrilla resistance against the U.S.-supported South Korean state.

input: In addition, the city has about 160 museums—the world's greatest single metropolitan concentration —over 100 art galleries, and some 30 concert halls, all of which maintain a constant cultural activity during the whole year. It has either the third or fourth-highest number of theatres in the world after New York, London and perhaps Toronto. Many areas (e.g. Palacio Nacional and the National Institute of Cardiology) have murals painted by Diego Rivera. He and his wife Frida Kahlo lived in Coyoacán, where several of their homes, studios, and art collections are open to the public. The house where Leon Trotsky was initially granted asylum and finally murdered in 1940 is also in Coyoacán.
rewrite: Furthermore, the city possesses approximately 160 museums—representing the world's largest concentration within a single metropolis—alongside over 100 art galleries and roughly 30 concert halls, all sustaining continuous cultural programming throughout the year. It ranks third or fourth globally in number of theatres, following New York, London, and possibly Toronto. Numerous sites, including the Palacio Nacional and the National Institute of Cardiology, feature murals by Diego Rivera. Rivera and his wife, Frida Kahlo, resided in Coyoacán, where several of their former homes, studios, and art collections are now publicly accessible. The Coyoacán district also contains the house where Leon Trotsky was initially granted asylum and was later assassinated in 1940.

input: Stressful life experiences may be a cause of memory loss as a person ages. Glucocorticoids that are released during stress damage neurons that are located in the hippocampal region of the brain. Therefore, the more stressful situations that someone encounters, the more susceptible they are to memory loss later on. The CA1 neurons found in the hippocampus are destroyed due to glucocorticoids decreasing the release of glucose and the reuptake of glutamate. This high level of extracellular glutamate allow calcium to enter NMDA receptors which in return kills neurons. Stressful life experiences can also cause repression of memories where a person moves an unbearable memory to the unconscious mind. This directly relates to traumatic events in one's past such as kidnappings, being prisoners of war or sexual abuse as a child.
rewrite: Stressful life experiences are implicated in age-related memory decline. The release of glucocorticoids during stress induces neuronal damage within the hippocampus. Consequently, cumulative exposure to stress heightens vulnerability to subsequent memory impairment. Specifically, glucocorticoids compromise CA1 hippocampal neurons by reducing glucose availability and inhibiting glutamate reuptake. The resultant elevation in extracellular glutamate permits excessive calcium influx through NMDA receptors, leading to excitotoxic neuronal death. Furthermore, stress can precipitate memory repression, a psychological defense mechanism whereby traumatic memories are relegated to the unconscious. This process is frequently associated with severe past traumas, including kidnapping, imprisonment during war, or childhood sexual abuse.

input: The battle in the Marshall Islands caused irreparable damage, especially on Japanese bases. During the American bombing, the islands' population suffered from lack of food and various injuries. U.S. attacks started in mid-1943, and caused half the Japanese garrison of 5,100 people in the atoll Mili to die from hunger by August 1945.
rewrite: The conflict in the Marshall Islands inflicted severe destruction, particularly upon Japanese installations. Commencing in mid-1943, U.S. assaults led to widespread civilian deprivation and casualties. By August 1945, starvation alone had claimed half of the 5,100-strong Japanese garrison on Mili Atoll.

input: For at least a century before the establishment of the Augustan principate, Jews and Judaism were tolerated in Rome by diplomatic treaty with Judaea's Hellenised elite. Diaspora Jews had much in common with the overwhelmingly Hellenic or Hellenised communities that surrounded them. Early Italian synagogues have left few traces; but one was dedicated in Ostia around the mid-1st century BC and several more are attested during the Imperial period. Judaea's enrollment as a client kingdom in 63 BC increased the Jewish diaspora; in Rome, this led to closer official scrutiny of their religion. Their synagogues were recognised as legitimate collegia by Julius Caesar. By the Augustan era, the city of Rome was home to several thousand Jews. In some periods under Roman rule, Jews were legally exempt from official sacrifice, under certain conditions. Judaism was a superstitio to Cicero, but the Church Father Tertullian described it as religio licita (an officially permitted religion) in contrast to Christianity.
rewrite: For at least a century prior to the institution of the Augustan principate, Jewish communities and their religious practices were tolerated in Rome under diplomatic treaties established with the Hellenized elite of Judaea. The diaspora populations shared significant cultural commonalities with the predominantly Hellenic or Hellenized societies amidst which they resided. Archaeological evidence for early Italian synagogues is sparse; however, one such structure was consecrated in Ostia circa the mid-first century BCE, with several additional congregations attested during the subsequent Imperial era. The formal establishment of Judaea as a client kingdom in 63 BCE expanded the Jewish diaspora, which in Rome prompted heightened official scrutiny of their religious observances. Their synagogues received formal recognition as legitimate *collegia* under Julius Caesar. By the Augustan period, the city of Rome housed a community of several thousand Jews. During certain phases of Roman administration, Jews were granted specific legal exemptions from mandatory state sacrifices. While Cicero classified Judaism as a *superstitio*, the Church Father Tertullian later characterized it, in contrast to Christianity, as a *religio licita*—a legally permitted religion.

input: The existence of a "global carrying capacity", limiting the amount of life that can live at once, is debated, as is the question of whether such a limit would also cap the number of species. While records of life in the sea shows a logistic pattern of growth, life on land (insects, plants and tetrapods)shows an exponential rise in diversity. As one author states, "Tetrapods have not yet invaded 64 per cent of potentially habitable modes, and it could be that without human influence the ecological and taxonomic diversity of tetrapods would continue to increase in an exponential fashion until most or all of the available ecospace is filled."
rewrite: The concept of a "global carrying capacity," which would impose a limit on the total biomass and potentially the number of species, remains a subject of debate. Marine fossil records exhibit a logistic growth pattern, whereas terrestrial life—including insects, plants, and tetrapods—demonstrates an exponential increase in diversity. As noted by one authority, tetrapods currently occupy only 64 percent of viable ecological niches. Absent anthropogenic interference, their ecological and taxonomic diversity might therefore continue expanding exponentially until the majority of available ecospace is utilized.

input: In manufacturing the glass bulb, a type of "ribbon machine" is used. A continuous ribbon of glass is passed along a conveyor belt, heated in a furnace, and then blown by precisely aligned air nozzles through holes in the conveyor belt into molds. Thus the glass bulbs are created. After the bulbs are blown, and cooled, they are cut off the ribbon machine; a typical machine of this sort produces 50,000 bulbs per hour. The filament and its supports are assembled on a glass stem, which is fused to the bulb. The air is pumped out of the bulb, and the evacuation tube in the stem press is sealed by a flame. The bulb is then inserted into the lamp base, and the whole assembly tested.
rewrite: The fabrication of glass bulbs employs a specialized apparatus known as a "ribbon machine." Within this system, a continuous glass ribbon advances along a conveyor belt, enters a furnace for heating, and is subsequently forced by precisely calibrated air nozzles through apertures in the belt into awaiting molds, thereby forming the bulbs. Following a cooling period, the individual bulbs are severed from the ribbon; a standard machine operates at a rate of approximately 50,000 units per hour. Subsequently, the filament and its support structure are mounted onto a glass stem, which is then fused to the bulb. The internal atmosphere is evacuated, and the stem's exhaust tube is hermetically sealed using a flame. Finally, the bulb is affixed to the lamp base, and the complete assembly undergoes rigorous testing.

input: Jews originated as a national and religious group in the Middle East during the second millennium BCE, in the part of the Levant known as the Land of Israel. The Merneptah Stele appears to confirm the existence of a people of Israel, associated with the god El, somewhere in Canaan as far back as the 13th century BCE. The Israelites, as an outgrowth of the Canaanite population, consolidated their hold with the emergence of the Kingdom of Israel, and the Kingdom of Judah. Some consider that these Canaanite sedentary Israelites melded with incoming nomadic groups known as 'Hebrews'. Though few sources in the Bible mention the exilic periods in detail, the experience of diaspora life, from the Ancient Egyptian rule over the Levant, to Assyrian Captivity and Exile, to Babylonian Captivity and Exile, to Seleucid Imperial rule, to the Roman occupation, and the historical relations between Israelites and the homeland, became a major feature of Jewish history, identity and memory.
rewrite: The Jewish people trace their origins to the emergence of a distinct national and religious community in the Middle East during the second millennium BCE, specifically within the Levantine region known as the Land of Israel. Archaeological evidence, such as the Merneptah Stele, attests to the presence of an Israelite people in Canaan by the 13th century BCE, associated with the deity El. Evolving from the indigenous Canaanite population, these sedentary Israelites established the Kingdoms of Israel and Judah, potentially integrating with nomadic 'Hebrew' groups. Subsequent history was profoundly shaped by a series of dispersions and foreign dominations. These exilic periods—encompassing Egyptian, Assyrian, Babylonian, Seleucid, and Roman rule—though sparsely detailed in biblical sources, fundamentally forged the diaspora experience. This enduring relationship between the people and their ancestral homeland became a central pillar of Jewish historical consciousness, identity, and collective memory.

input: In 1948, Eisenhower became President of Columbia University, an Ivy League university in New York City. The assignment was described as not being a good fit in either direction. During that year Eisenhower's memoir, Crusade in Europe, was published. Critics regarded it as one of the finest U.S. military memoirs, and it was a major financial success as well. Eisenhower's profit on the book was substantially aided by an unprecedented ruling by the U.S. Department of the Treasury that Eisenhower was not a professional writer, but rather, marketing the lifetime asset of his experiences, and thus he only had to pay capital gains tax on his $635,000 advance instead of the much higher personal tax rate. This ruling saved Eisenhower about $400,000.
rewrite: In 1948, Dwight D. Eisenhower assumed the presidency of Columbia University, an Ivy League institution in New York City. Contemporary accounts characterized this appointment as an imperfect fit for both parties. That same year witnessed the publication of Eisenhower's memoir, *Crusade in Europe*. It was critically acclaimed as among the finest U.S. military memoirs and proved a considerable commercial success. His financial return was significantly augmented by an unprecedented ruling from the U.S. Department of the Treasury. The department determined that Eisenhower, not being a professional author, was effectively marketing the capital asset of his experiences. Consequently, his $635,000 advance was taxed at the lower capital gains rate rather than the higher personal income rate, yielding an estimated savings of $400,000.

input: After the defeat of the Confederacy, federal forces remained in Charleston during the city's reconstruction. The war had shattered the prosperity of the antebellum city. Freed slaves were faced with poverty and discrimination, but a large community of free people of color had been well-established in the city before the war and became the leaders of the postwar Republican Party and its legislators. Men who had been free people of color before the war comprised 26% of those elected to state and federal office in South Carolina from 1868 to 1876.
rewrite: Following the Confederacy's defeat, federal troops remained stationed in Charleston throughout the city's Reconstruction era. The conflict had devastated the antebellum city's prosperity. While newly emancipated individuals confronted profound poverty and systemic discrimination, a significant prewar community of free people of color provided critical leadership. This group formed the core of the postwar Republican Party in the state, with men from this background constituting 26% of South Carolina's elected officials to state and federal positions between 1868 and 1876.

input: In 1880, the newspapers News and Observer combined to form The News & Observer. It remains Raleigh's primary daily newspaper. The North Carolina College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts, now known as North Carolina State University, was founded as a land-grant college in 1887. The city's Rex Hospital opened in 1889 and included the state's first nursing school. The Baptist Women's College, now known as Meredith College, opened in 1891, and in 1898, The Academy of Music, a private music conservatory, was established.
rewrite: Founded in 1880 through the merger of the News and the Observer, The News & Observer persists as Raleigh's principal daily newspaper. Subsequently, North Carolina State University originated in 1887 as the North Carolina College of Agriculture and Mechanic Arts under the land-grant system. Rex Hospital, established in 1889, housed the state's inaugural nursing school. Meredith College, initially the Baptist Women's College, opened in 1891, followed by the private Academy of Music conservatory in 1898.

input: The free trade spirit of the time received a strong augmentation through the development of a modern, effective stock market in the Low Countries. The Netherlands has the oldest stock exchange in the world, founded in 1602 by the Dutch East India Company. While Rotterdam has the oldest bourse in the Netherlands, the world's first stock exchange – that of the Dutch East-India Company – went public in six different cities. Later, a court ruled that the company had to reside legally in a single city, so Amsterdam is recognized as the oldest such institution based on modern trading principles. While the banking system evolved in the Low Countries, it was quickly incorporated by the well-connected English, stimulating English economic output.
rewrite: The prevailing free trade ethos was significantly reinforced by the establishment of a sophisticated and efficient securities market in the Low Countries. The world's oldest stock exchange originated with the Dutch East India Company in 1602. Although Rotterdam hosts the Netherlands' oldest bourse, this pioneering exchange initially operated publicly across six cities. A subsequent legal mandate required the company to establish a singular legal domicile, leading to Amsterdam's recognition as the oldest institution functioning on modern trading principles. Concurrently, the evolving financial systems of the Low Countries were rapidly adopted by the well-connected English, thereby stimulating England's economic productivity.

input: In 2000, Apple released the Power Mac G4 Cube, their first desktop since the discontinued Power Macintosh G3, to slot between the iMac G3 and the Power Mac G4. Even with its innovative design, it was initially priced US$200 higher than the comparably-equipped and more-expandable base Power Mac G4, while also not including a monitor, making it too expensive and resulting in slow sales. Apple sold just 29,000 Cubes in Q4 of 2000 which was one third of expectations, compared to 308,000 Macs during that same quarter, and Cube sales dropped to 12,000 units in Q1 of 2001. A price drop and hardware upgrades could not offset the earlier perception of the Cube's reduced value compared to the iMac and Power Mac G4 lineup, and it was discontinued in July 2001.
rewrite: In the year 2000, Apple introduced the Power Mac G4 Cube, its first new desktop computer following the discontinuation of the Power Macintosh G3. Positioned to occupy a market segment between the iMac G3 and the Power Mac G4, the Cube featured a notably innovative design. However, its initial launch price was set approximately US$200 higher than the comparably equipped and more expandable base model Power Mac G4, and it did not include a monitor. This pricing strategy rendered the product prohibitively expensive, leading to poor sales performance. Only 29,000 units were sold in the fourth quarter of 2000, representing merely one-third of projected sales and a small fraction of the 308,000 total Macs sold that quarter. Sales further declined to 12,000 units in the first quarter of 2001. Subsequent price reductions and hardware revisions failed to counteract the established market perception of the Cube's poor value relative to the iMac and Power Mac G4. Consequently, the product line was discontinued in July 2001.

input: It is commonly believed that the earlier a defect is found, the cheaper it is to fix it. The following table shows the cost of fixing the defect depending on the stage it was found. For example, if a problem in the requirements is found only post-release, then it would cost 10–100 times more to fix than if it had already been found by the requirements review. With the advent of modern continuous deployment practices and cloud-based services, the cost of re-deployment and maintenance may lessen over time.
rewrite: It is widely accepted that identifying defects earlier in the development process reduces the cost of remediation. The accompanying table illustrates how these costs escalate based on the detection phase. For instance, a requirements defect discovered post-release can be 10 to 100 times more expensive to correct than if identified during the requirements review. However, contemporary practices like continuous deployment and cloud services may gradually reduce the expenses associated with re-deployment and ongoing maintenance.

input: The owner, tenant or manager (licensee) of a pub is properly known as the "pub landlord". The term publican (in historical Roman usage a public contractor or tax farmer) has come into use since Victorian times to designate the pub landlord. Known as "locals" to regulars, pubs are typically chosen for their proximity to home or work, the availability of a particular beer, as a place to smoke (or avoid it), hosting a darts team, having a pool or snooker table, or appealing to friends.
rewrite: The licensee of a public house, whether owner, tenant, or manager, is formally designated the "pub landlord." Since the Victorian era, the historical term "publican" has been adopted to denote this role. Patrons commonly refer to such establishments as "locals," selecting them based on proximity, specific beverage offerings, smoking policies, the presence of games like darts or pool, and social affiliations.

input: On 7 June 1981, the Israeli air force destroyed Iraq's sole nuclear reactor, in order to impede Iraq's nuclear weapons program. The reactor was under construction just outside Baghdad. Following a series of PLO attacks in 1982, Israel invaded Lebanon that year to destroy the bases from which the PLO launched attacks and missiles into northern Israel. In the first six days of fighting, the Israelis destroyed the military forces of the PLO in Lebanon and decisively defeated the Syrians. An Israeli government inquiry – the Kahan Commission – would later hold Begin, Sharon and several Israeli generals as indirectly responsible for the Sabra and Shatila massacre. In 1985, Israel responded to a Palestinian terrorist attack in Cyprus by bombing the PLO headquarters in Tunis. Israel withdrew from most of Lebanon in 1986, but maintained a borderland buffer zone in southern Lebanon until 2000, from where Israeli forces engaged in conflict with Hezbollah.
rewrite: On 7 June 1981, the Israeli Air Force executed a preemptive strike against Iraq's Osirak nuclear reactor, then under construction near Baghdad, with the stated objective of crippling Iraq's nascent nuclear weapons program. Subsequently, in 1982, Israel initiated a military incursion into Lebanon following a series of attacks by the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), aiming to dismantle PLO infrastructure used to launch assaults into northern Israel. Israeli forces rapidly neutralized PLO military capabilities in Lebanon and achieved a decisive victory over Syrian forces within the initial six days of combat. A subsequent Israeli judicial inquiry, the Kahan Commission, would later assign indirect responsibility for the Sabra and Shatila massacres to Prime Minister Menachem Begin, Defense Minister Ariel Sharon, and several military officials. In 1985, Israel conducted an aerial bombardment of the PLO headquarters in Tunis in retaliation for a Palestinian terrorist attack in Cyprus. While Israel withdrew the bulk of its forces from Lebanon by 1986, it maintained a security zone in southern Lebanon until the year 2000, during which period it engaged in recurrent hostilities with the Hezbollah militia.

input: Mīmāṃsā gave rise to the study of philology and the philosophy of language. While their deep analysis of language and linguistics influenced other schools, their views were not shared by others. Mīmāṃsākas considered the purpose and power of language was to clearly prescribe the proper, correct and right. In contrast, Vedantins extended the scope and value of language as a tool to also describe, develop and derive. Mīmāṃsākas considered orderly, law-driven, procedural life as central purpose and noblest necessity of dharma and society, and divine (theistic) sustenance means to that end. The Mimamsa school was influential and foundational to the Vedanta school, with the difference that Mīmāṃsā school developed and emphasized karmakāṇḍa (that part of the śruti which relates to ceremonial acts and sacrificial rites, the early parts of the Vedas), while the Vedanta school developed and emphasized jñānakāṇḍa (that portion of the Vedas which relates to knowledge of monism, the latter parts of the Vedas).
rewrite: The Mīmāṃsā school generated foundational contributions to philology and the philosophy of language. Although its profound linguistic analyses influenced other traditions, its specific doctrines were not universally adopted. Mīmāṃsākas posited that the essential purpose and potency of language resided in its prescriptive function, specifically to enjoin correct, proper, and righteous action. Conversely, Vedantins expanded language’s scope and value to include its capacity to describe reality, develop understanding, and derive metaphysical truths. For Mīmāṃsā, the central purpose of dharma and society was an orderly, rule-governed, and procedural existence, viewing theistic devotion primarily as a means to that end. While Mīmāṃsā served as an influential precursor to Vedanta, a key distinction lies in their respective emphases: Mīmāṃsā developed the *karmakāṇḍa* (the portions of śruti concerning ritual acts and sacrifices, found in the earlier Vedas), whereas Vedanta focused on the *jñānakāṇḍa* (the portions pertaining to the knowledge of monism, found in the later Vedas).

input: Nothing in the principle of any of the motors described above requires that the iron (steel) portions of the rotor actually rotate. If the soft magnetic material of the rotor is made in the form of a cylinder, then (except for the effect of hysteresis) torque is exerted only on the windings of the electromagnets. Taking advantage of this fact is the coreless or ironless DC motor, a specialized form of a PM DC motor. Optimized for rapid acceleration, these motors have a rotor that is constructed without any iron core. The rotor can take the form of a winding-filled cylinder, or a self-supporting structure comprising only the magnet wire and the bonding material. The rotor can fit inside the stator magnets; a magnetically soft stationary cylinder inside the rotor provides a return path for the stator magnetic flux. A second arrangement has the rotor winding basket surrounding the stator magnets. In that design, the rotor fits inside a magnetically soft cylinder that can serve as the housing for the motor, and likewise provides a return path for the flux.
rewrite: None of the motor principles previously discussed inherently depend upon the rotation of the ferrous (steel) components within the rotor. Should the rotor's soft magnetic material be configured as a cylinder, the resultant torque—excluding hysteresis effects—acts solely upon the electromagnetic windings. This principle is exploited in the coreless or ironless DC motor, a specialized variant of the permanent magnet DC motor. Designed for optimal acceleration, these motors feature a rotor devoid of an iron core. The rotor may consist of a cylinder containing the windings or a self-supporting structure composed exclusively of magnet wire and a bonding agent. In one configuration, the rotor is positioned within the stator magnets, with a stationary cylinder of magnetically soft material inside the rotor completing the magnetic circuit for the stator flux. An alternative arrangement positions the rotor winding basket around the stator magnets. Here, the rotor resides inside a magnetically soft cylinder that functions as both the motor housing and a return path for the magnetic flux.

input: Unlike in multicellular organisms, increases in cell size (cell growth) and reproduction by cell division are tightly linked in unicellular organisms. Bacteria grow to a fixed size and then reproduce through binary fission, a form of asexual reproduction. Under optimal conditions, bacteria can grow and divide extremely rapidly, and bacterial populations can double as quickly as every 9.8 minutes. In cell division, two identical clone daughter cells are produced. Some bacteria, while still reproducing asexually, form more complex reproductive structures that help disperse the newly formed daughter cells. Examples include fruiting body formation by Myxobacteria and aerial hyphae formation by Streptomyces, or budding. Budding involves a cell forming a protrusion that breaks away and produces a daughter cell.
rewrite: In multicellular organisms, cellular growth and division are distinct processes, whereas in unicellular organisms they are tightly coupled. Bacteria, for instance, grow to a predetermined size before undergoing binary fission, an asexual reproductive process yielding two genetically identical daughter cells. Under ideal conditions, this cycle occurs with remarkable speed, enabling population doubling in as little as 9.8 minutes. Although reproduction remains asexual, some bacteria employ more complex strategies to disseminate offspring. Notable examples include the formation of fruiting bodies by Myxobacteria, the production of aerial hyphae by Streptomyces, and the process of budding, wherein a new cell develops as a protrusion that detaches from the parent.

input: The elimination of wolves from Yellowstone National Park had profound impacts on the trophic pyramid. Without predation, herbivores began to over-graze many woody browse species, affecting the area's plant populations. In addition, wolves often kept animals from grazing in riparian areas, which protected beavers from having their food sources encroached upon. The removal of wolves had a direct effect on beaver populations, as their habitat became territory for grazing. Furthermore, predation keeps hydrological features such as creeks and streams in normal working order. Increased browsing on willows and conifers along Blacktail Creek due to a lack of predation caused channel incision because they helped slow the water down and hold the soil in place.
rewrite: The extirpation of wolves from Yellowstone National Park precipitated significant disruptions to the trophic cascade. Absent apex predation, herbivore populations increased, leading to the overbrowsing of woody vegetation and altering plant community dynamics. Wolves had previously limited grazing in riparian zones, thereby indirectly protecting beaver food sources. Their removal degraded this habitat through intensive herbivory, adversely impacting beaver populations. Furthermore, predation regulates hydrologic processes; for instance, excessive browsing of willows and conifers along Blacktail Creek, which stabilize banks and moderate flow, resulted in pronounced channel incision following the wolves' disappearance.

input: Symbiosis (from Greek σύν "together" and βίωσις "living") is close and often long-term interaction between two different biological species. In 1877 Albert Bernhard Frank used the word symbiosis (which previously had been used to depict people living together in community) to describe the mutualistic relationship in lichens. In 1879, the German mycologist Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it as "the living together of unlike organisms."
rewrite: Symbiosis, derived from Greek terms meaning "together" and "living," denotes a prolonged, intimate interaction between distinct biological species. Albert Bernhard Frank first applied the term in 1877 to describe lichen mutualism, adapting its prior social usage. Subsequently, in 1879, mycologist Heinrich Anton de Bary formally defined it as "the living together of unlike organisms."

input: Of the territories of Poland annexed by the Soviet Union between 1939 and 1940, the region around Białystok and a minor part of Galicia east of the San river around Przemyśl were returned to the Polish state at the end of World War II. Of all other territories annexed by the USSR in 1939–40, the ones detached from Finland (Karelia, Petsamo), Estonia (Ingrian area and Petseri County) and Latvia (Abrene) remained part of the Russian Federation, the successor state of the Soviet Union, after 1991. Northern Bukovina, Southern Bessarabia and Hertza remain part of Ukraine.
rewrite: Following the Soviet annexations of Polish territory between 1939 and 1940, only the Białystok region and a portion of Galicia east of the San River near Przemyśl were restored to Poland after the Second World War. All other territories annexed by the USSR during that period were retained by its successor, the Russian Federation, after 1991. These include regions taken from Finland (Karelia, Petsamo), Estonia (the Ingrian area and Petseri County), and Latvia (Abrene). Furthermore, Northern Bukovina, Southern Bessarabia, and Hertza remain incorporated within Ukraine.

input: The city is home to 261,546 (mid-2014 est.) people, making it the 30th most populous built-up area in the United Kingdom. It is governed locally by Plymouth City Council and is represented nationally by three MPs. Plymouth's economy remains strongly influenced by shipbuilding and seafaring including ferry links to Brittany (Roscoff and St Malo) and Spain (Santander), but has tended toward a service-based economy since the 1990s. It has the largest operational naval base in Western Europe – HMNB Devonport and is home to Plymouth University.
rewrite: With an estimated population of 261,546 (mid-2014), Plymouth ranks as the United Kingdom's 30th most populous built-up area. Local governance is administered by Plymouth City Council, with national representation through three Members of Parliament. Historically dominated by shipbuilding and maritime activities, including ferry services to Roscoff, St Malo, and Santander, the city's economy has shifted toward services since the 1990s. Key institutions include HMNB Devonport, Western Europe's largest operational naval base, and the University of Plymouth.

input: The northern section of the Divide, where the mountains give way rapidly to prairie, is part of the Rocky Mountain Front. The front is most pronounced in the Lewis Range, located primarily in Glacier National Park. Due to the configuration of mountain ranges in Glacier National Park, the Northern Divide (which begins in Alaska's Seward Peninsula) crosses this region and turns east in Montana at Triple Divide Peak. It causes the Waterton River, Belly, and Saint Mary rivers to flow north into Alberta, Canada. There they join the Saskatchewan River, which ultimately empties into Hudson Bay.
rewrite: The northern segment of the Continental Divide, where the Rocky Mountains transition abruptly to plains, constitutes the Rocky Mountain Front. This feature is most distinct within Glacier National Park's Lewis Range. Owing to the regional topography, the Northern Divide—originating on Alaska's Seward Peninsula—traverses this area and deflects eastward at Montana's Triple Divide Peak. This alignment directs the Waterton, Belly, and Saint Mary rivers northward into Alberta, Canada. These tributaries converge with the Saskatchewan River, which eventually discharges into Hudson Bay.

input: In The Open Society and Its Enemies and The Poverty of Historicism, Popper developed a critique of historicism and a defence of the "Open Society". Popper considered historicism to be the theory that history develops inexorably and necessarily according to knowable general laws towards a determinate end. He argued that this view is the principal theoretical presupposition underpinning most forms of authoritarianism and totalitarianism. He argued that historicism is founded upon mistaken assumptions regarding the nature of scientific law and prediction. Since the growth of human knowledge is a causal factor in the evolution of human history, and since "no society can predict, scientifically, its own future states of knowledge", it follows, he argued, that there can be no predictive science of human history. For Popper, metaphysical and historical indeterminism go hand in hand.
rewrite: In *The Open Society and Its Enemies* and *The Poverty of Historicism*, Karl Popper articulates a systematic critique of historicism while advocating for the "Open Society." He defines historicism as the doctrine that history progresses inexorably according to discernible general laws toward a predetermined end. Popper contends this perspective forms the core theoretical foundation of authoritarian and totalitarian systems. His critique asserts that historicism rests on flawed assumptions about scientific law and prediction. He reasons that because the growth of human knowledge itself causally influences historical development, and because no society can scientifically foretell its future states of knowledge, a predictive science of history is impossible. Consequently, Popper links metaphysical and historical indeterminism as fundamentally interconnected.

input: IBM's employee management practices can be traced back to its roots. In 1914, CEO Thomas J. Watson boosted company spirit by creating employee sports teams, hosting family outings, and furnishing a company band. IBM sports teams still continue in the present day; the IBM Big Blue continue to exist as semi-professional company rugby and American football teams. In 1924 the Quarter Century Club, which recognizes employees with 25 years of service, was organized and the first issue of Business Machines, IBM's internal publication, was published. In 1925, the first meeting of the Hundred Percent Club, composed of IBM salesmen who meet their quotas, convened in Atlantic City, New Jersey.
rewrite: IBM's foundational employee management practices originated in the early twentieth century. In 1914, Chief Executive Thomas J. Watson cultivated corporate morale by establishing employee sports teams, organizing family outings, and founding a company band. These athletic programs persist, exemplified by the semi-professional IBM Big Blue rugby and football teams. Subsequent institutional developments included the 1924 formation of the Quarter Century Club to honor twenty-five-year service anniversaries and the inaugural publication of the internal periodical *Business Machines*. Furthermore, the Hundred Percent Club, recognizing sales personnel who achieved their quotas, held its first convention in Atlantic City, New Jersey, in 1925.

input: Appointments to the Order of the British Empire were at first made on the nomination of the self-governing Dominions of the Empire, the Viceroy of India, and the colonial governors, as well as on nominations from within the United Kingdom. As the Empire evolved into the Commonwealth, nominations continued to come from the Commonwealth realms, in which the monarch remained head of state. These overseas nominations have been discontinued in realms that have established their own Orders—such as the Order of Australia, the Order of Canada, and the New Zealand Order of Merit—but members of the Order are still appointed in the British Overseas Territories.
rewrite: Initially, appointments to the Order of the British Empire were based upon nominations from the self-governing Dominions, the Viceroy of India, colonial governors, and domestic United Kingdom sources. Following the Empire's transition into the Commonwealth, nominations persisted from those Commonwealth realms retaining the monarch as head of state. Such overseas nominations have ceased in realms that have instituted their own national honors, like the Order of Australia, the Order of Canada, and the New Zealand Order of Merit. However, appointments to the Order continue within the British Overseas Territories.

input: After several failed attempts, in 1930 the first aeroplane reached Bermuda. A Stinson Detroiter seaplane flying from New York, it had to land twice in the ocean: once because of darkness and again to refuel. Navigation and weather forecasting improved in 1933 when the Royal Air Force (then responsible for providing equipment and personnel for the Royal Navy's Fleet Air Arm) established a station at the Royal Naval Dockyard to repair (and supply replacement) float planes for the fleet. In 1936 Luft Hansa began to experiment with seaplane flights from Berlin via the Azores with continuation to New York City.
rewrite: Following several unsuccessful endeavors, the inaugural aircraft arrival in Bermuda occurred in 1930. This Stinson Detroiter seaplane, departing from New York, was compelled to alight upon the ocean on two occasions: first due to darkness and subsequently for refueling. Advancements in navigation and meteorology were realized in 1933 upon the Royal Air Force establishing a station at the Royal Naval Dockyard. This facility maintained float planes for the Fleet Air Arm. Subsequently, in 1936, Luft Hansa commenced experimental seaplane services from Berlin, transiting the Azores en route to New York City.

input: There are four hundred securities listed on the stock exchange, of which almost three hundred are offshore funds and alternative investment structures attracted by Bermuda's regulatory environment. The Exchange specialises in listing and trading of capital market instruments such as equities, debt issues, funds (including hedge fund structures) and depository receipt programmes. The BSX is a full member of the World Federation of Exchanges and is located in an OECD member nation. It also has Approved Stock Exchange status under Australia's Foreign Investment Fund (FIF) taxation rules and Designated Investment Exchange status by the UK's Financial Services Authority.
rewrite: The Bermuda Stock Exchange (BSX) lists four hundred securities, with nearly three-quarters comprising offshore funds and alternative investment vehicles drawn to the jurisdiction's regulatory framework. It specialises in the listing and trading of capital market instruments, including equities, debt issues, various funds, and depository receipt programmes. As a full member of the World Federation of Exchanges and located within an OECD nation, the BSX holds Approved Stock Exchange status under Australian Foreign Investment Fund rules and Designated Investment Exchange recognition from the UK Financial Services Authority.

input: During the Protestant Reformation, the Church of England (Anglicans) separated from the Roman Catholic Church. There were some Christians who were not content with the achievements of the mainstream Protestant Reformation. There also were Christians who were disappointed that the Church of England had not made corrections of what some considered to be errors and abuses. Of those most critical of the Church's direction, some chose to stay and try to make constructive changes from within the Anglican Church. They became known as "Puritans" and are described by Gourley as cousins of the English Separatists. Others decided they must leave the Church because of their dissatisfaction and became known as the Separatists.
rewrite: The Protestant Reformation precipitated the separation of the Church of England from Roman Catholicism. However, certain Christians remained dissatisfied with the outcomes of the mainstream Reformation and perceived persistent errors within the newly established Anglican Church. Among these critics, a faction, later termed Puritans, elected to remain within the Anglican communion to advocate for further reform, characterized by Gourley as cousins to the Separatists. Conversely, those whose discontent compelled a complete break from the established church became known as the Separatists.

input: Important Justinian era mosaics decorated the Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai in Egypt. Generally wall mosaics have not survived in the region because of the destruction of buildings but the St. Catherine's Monastery is exceptional. On the upper wall Moses is shown in two panels on a landscape background. In the apse we can see the Transfiguration of Jesus on a golden background. The apse is surrounded with bands containing medallions of apostles and prophets, and two contemporary figure, "Abbot Longinos" and "John the Deacon". The mosaic was probably created in 565/6.
rewrite: The significant Justinian-era mosaics at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai in Egypt represent a rare preservation of wall mosaics in the region, where such works have typically been lost to architectural destruction. The upper wall depicts Moses in two panels against a landscape, while the apse presents the Transfiguration on a gold ground. This central scene is framed by bands containing medallions of apostles and prophets, along with two contemporary figures, Abbot Longinos and John the Deacon. The mosaic's likely creation date is 565 or 566 CE.

input: The rivalry between Nintendo and Sega resulted in what has been described as one of the most notable console wars in video game history, in which Sega positioned the Genesis as the "cool" console, with more mature titles aimed at older gamers, and edgy advertisements that occasionally attacked the competition. Nintendo however, scored an early public relations advantage by securing the first console conversion of Capcom's arcade classic Street Fighter II for SNES, which took over a year to make the transition to Genesis. Despite the Genesis's head start, much larger library of games, and lower price point, the Genesis only represented an estimated 60% of the American 16-bit console market in June 1992, and neither console could maintain a definitive lead for several years. Donkey Kong Country is said to have helped establish the SNES's market prominence in the latter years of the 16-bit generation, and for a time, maintain against the PlayStation and Saturn. According to Nintendo, the company had sold more than 20 million SNES units in the U.S. According to a 2014 Wedbush Securities report based on NPD sales data, the SNES ultimately outsold the Genesis in the U.S. market.
rewrite: The competition between Nintendo and Sega constituted one of the most significant console rivalries in video game history. Sega strategically marketed its Genesis console as a more mature alternative, emphasizing edgier advertising campaigns and a library of titles targeted at an older demographic, often directly contrasting itself with Nintendo. Nintendo, however, gained a crucial public relations advantage by securing the first home console port of Capcom’s seminal arcade title, *Street Fighter II*, for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES), a conversion that required over a year to appear on the Genesis. Despite the Genesis's earlier launch, substantially larger game library, and lower price point, it commanded only an estimated 60% of the American 16-bit market by mid-1992, with neither platform achieving a sustained definitive lead for several years. The release of *Donkey Kong Country* is widely credited with solidifying the SNES's market prominence in the later 16-bit era and temporarily sustaining its competitiveness against the subsequent PlayStation and Saturn systems. While Nintendo reports over 20 million SNES units sold in the United States, a 2014 Wedbush Securities analysis of NPD data confirms the SNES ultimately outsold the Genesis in the U.S. market.

input: Economic sanctions against Iran, such as the embargo against Iranian crude oil, have affected the economy. Sanctions have led to a steep fall in the value of the rial, and as of April 2013 one US dollar is worth 36,000 rial, compared with 16,000 in early 2012. Following a successful implementation of the 2015 nuclear and sanctions relief deal, the resulting benefits might not be distributed evenly across the Iranian economy as political elites such as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have garnered more resources and economic interests.
rewrite: The imposition of economic sanctions, including the embargo on Iranian crude oil, has significantly impacted Iran's economy. These measures precipitated a sharp devaluation of the rial, with the exchange rate falling from approximately 16,000 to 36,000 rials per US dollar between early 2012 and April 2013. Furthermore, even following the implementation of the 2015 nuclear agreement and associated sanctions relief, the ensuing economic benefits may not be equitably distributed. Political elites, notably the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, have historically captured a disproportionate share of resources and economic interests.

input: Norfolk Island was originally a colony acquired by settlement but was never within the British Settlements Act. It was accepted as a territory of Australia, separate from any state, by the Norfolk Island Act 1913 (Cth), passed under the territories power (Constitution section 122) and made effective in 1914. In 1976 the High Court of Australia held unanimously that Norfolk Island is a part of the Commonwealth. Again, in 2007 the High Court of Australia affirmed the validity of legislation that made Australian citizenship a necessary qualification for voting for, and standing for election to, the Legislative Assembly of Norfolk Island.
rewrite: Norfolk Island was initially established as a settlement colony, remaining outside the scope of the British Settlements Act. Its status as a distinct Australian territory, separate from any state, was formalized by the Norfolk Island Act 1913 (Cth). This legislation, enacted pursuant to section 122 of the Constitution, took effect in 1914. The High Court of Australia unanimously confirmed in 1976 that the island constitutes part of the Commonwealth. Furthermore, in 2007, the Court upheld the validity of laws requiring Australian citizenship for both voting and candidacy in Norfolk Island’s Legislative Assembly elections.

input: In some cases and in some places the edicts were strictly enforced: some Christians resisted and were imprisoned or martyred. Others complied. Some local communities were not only pre-dominantly Christian, but powerful and influential; and some provincial authorities were lenient, notably the Caesar in Gaul, Constantius Chlorus, the father of Constantine I. Diocletian's successor Galerius maintained anti-Christian policy until his deathbed revocation in 311, when he asked Christians to pray for him. "This meant an ofﬁcial recognition of their importance in the religious world of the Roman empire, although one of the tetrarchs, Maximinus Daia, still oppressed Christians in his part of the empire up to 313."
rewrite: The enforcement of Diocletian's edicts varied regionally. While some Christians faced imprisonment or martyrdom for resistance, others complied. Certain local communities were both predominantly Christian and politically influential. Provincial authorities exhibited leniency, most notably Constantius Chlorus in Gaul. Following Diocletian, Galerius maintained the persecution until his deathbed edict of 311, which requested Christian prayers, thereby granting official recognition to their significance within the imperial religious landscape. However, persecution persisted under Maximinus Daia in the eastern provinces until approximately 313.

input: These areas contain some spectacular scenery as well, as evidenced by such national parks as Yosemite and Mount Rainier. West of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada is a series of valleys, such as the Central Valley in California and the Willamette Valley in Oregon. Along the coast is a series of low mountain ranges known as the Pacific Coast Ranges. Much of the Pacific Northwest coast is inhabited by some of the densest vegetation outside of the Tropics, and also the tallest trees in the world (the Redwoods).
rewrite: The region features notable scenic landscapes, exemplified by national parks including Yosemite and Mount Rainier. West of the Cascade and Sierra Nevada ranges lie fertile valleys, such as California’s Central Valley and Oregon’s Willamette Valley. Adjacent to the coast, the Pacific Coast Ranges comprise a series of low mountains. Much of the Pacific Northwest coastline supports exceptionally dense vegetation, rivaling tropical forests, and is home to the world’s tallest trees, the coastal redwoods.

input: In the field of music, Germany claims some of the most renowned classical composers of the world including Bach, Mozart and Beethoven, who marked the transition between the Classical and Romantic eras in Western classical music. Other composers of the Austro-German tradition who achieved international fame include Brahms, Wagner, Haydn, Schubert, Händel, Schumann, Liszt, Mendelssohn Bartholdy, Johann Strauss II, Bruckner, Mahler, Telemann, Richard Strauss, Schoenberg, Orff, and most recently, Henze, Lachenmann, and Stockhausen.
rewrite: Germany is distinguished within Western classical music for producing many of its most eminent composers. Figures such as Bach, Beethoven, and Mozart were pivotal in the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era. The broader Austro-German tradition further encompasses internationally celebrated composers from Brahms, Wagner, and Mahler to more contemporary figures like Stockhausen, Henze, and Lachenmann.

input: iPods have been criticized for alleged short life-span and fragile hard drives. A 2005 survey conducted on the MacInTouch website found that the iPod line had an average failure rate of 13.7% (although they note that comments from respondents indicate that "the true iPod failure rate may be lower than it appears"). It concluded that some models were more durable than others. In particular, failure rates for iPods employing hard drives was usually above 20% while those with flash memory had a failure rate below 10%. In late 2005, many users complained that the surface of the first generation iPod Nano can become scratched easily, rendering the screen unusable. A class action lawsuit was also filed. Apple initially considered the issue a minor defect, but later began shipping these iPods with protective sleeves.[citation needed]
rewrite: iPods have faced criticism regarding their purported limited durability and vulnerable hard drives. A 2005 survey published on the MacInTouch website reported an average failure rate of 13.7% across the iPod line, while noting that respondent comments suggested the actual rate might be lower. The survey indicated variability in reliability among models, with hard drive-based iPods exhibiting failure rates typically exceeding 20%, compared to below 10% for flash memory models. Later that year, numerous users reported that the first-generation iPod Nano’s surface was prone to scratching, often impairing screen functionality and prompting a class action lawsuit. Initially dismissing the problem as minor, Apple subsequently addressed it by including protective sleeves with new units.

input: Numerous recordings of Chopin's works are available. On the occasion of the composer's bicentenary, the critics of The New York Times recommended performances by the following contemporary pianists (among many others): Martha Argerich, Vladimir Ashkenazy, Emanuel Ax, Evgeny Kissin, Murray Perahia, Maurizio Pollini and Krystian Zimerman. The Warsaw Chopin Society organizes the Grand prix du disque de F. Chopin for notable Chopin recordings, held every five years.
rewrite: A substantial corpus of recordings of Chopin's compositions exists. Marking the composer's bicentenary, *The New York Times* critics highlighted exemplary interpretations by contemporary pianists including Martha Argerich, Vladimir Ashkenazy, Emanuel Ax, Evgeny Kissin, Murray Perahia, Maurizio Pollini, and Krystian Zimerman. Furthermore, the Warsaw Chopin Society bestows the Grand prix du disque de F. Chopin every five years to recognize distinguished recorded works.

input: In 1978, Jim Shooter became Marvel's editor-in-chief. Although a controversial personality, Shooter cured many of the procedural ills at Marvel, including repeatedly missed deadlines. During Shooter's nine-year tenure as editor-in-chief, Chris Claremont and John Byrne's run on the Uncanny X-Men and Frank Miller's run on Daredevil became critical and commercial successes. Shooter brought Marvel into the rapidly evolving direct market, institutionalized creator royalties, starting with the Epic Comics imprint for creator-owned material in 1982; introduced company-wide crossover story arcs with Contest of Champions and Secret Wars; and in 1986 launched the ultimately unsuccessful New Universe line to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Marvel Comics imprint. Star Comics, a children-oriented line differing from the regular Marvel titles, was briefly successful during this period.
rewrite: Appointed as Marvel Comics' editor-in-chief in 1978, Jim Shooter proved a pivotal, if contentious, figure. His nine-year tenure addressed significant operational deficiencies, most notably chronic deadline failures. This period witnessed major critical and commercial achievements, including the celebrated runs on *Uncanny X-Men* by Chris Claremont and John Byrne and on *Daredevil* by Frank Miller. Shooter strategically aligned Marvel with the growing direct market distribution system and formalized creator royalties, initiating the Epic Comics imprint for creator-owned work in 1982. He further instituted company-wide crossover events, beginning with *Contest of Champions* and *Secret Wars*. In 1986, he launched the ultimately unsuccessful New Universe line for Marvel's 25th anniversary. The children-oriented Star Comics imprint also saw transient success during this era.

input: While the cardinalate has long been expanded beyond the Roman pastoral clergy and Roman Curia, every cardinal priest has a titular church in Rome, though they may be bishops or archbishops elsewhere, just as cardinal bishops are given one of the suburbicarian dioceses around Rome. Pope Paul VI abolished all administrative rights cardinals had with regard to their titular churches, though the cardinal's name and coat of arms are still posted in the church, and they are expected to celebrate mass and preach there if convenient when they are in Rome.
rewrite: Although the College of Cardinals now extends well beyond the Roman pastoral clergy and Curia, each cardinal priest retains a titular church in Rome, analogous to the suburbicarian dioceses assigned to cardinal bishops. Pope Paul VI eliminated all administrative authority cardinals held over these titular churches. Nevertheless, a cardinal's name and coat of arms remain displayed within the church, and he is expected to celebrate Mass and preach there when present in Rome, circumstances permitting.

input: Retail versions of Windows 8 are only able to install these apps through Windows Store—a namesake distribution platform which offers both apps, and listings for desktop programs certified for comparability with Windows 8. A method to sideload apps from outside Windows Store is available to devices running Windows 8 Enterprise and joined to a domain; Windows 8 Pro and Windows RT devices that are not part of a domain can also sideload apps, but only after special product keys are obtained through volume licensing.
