rewrite: Retail editions of Windows 8 restrict application installation to the Windows Store, a dedicated platform distributing both apps and certified desktop program listings. Sideloading from external sources is permitted for domain-joined Windows 8 Enterprise devices. Non-domain Windows 8 Pro and Windows RT systems may also sideload applications, but this requires acquiring specific product keys via volume licensing agreements.

input: Raleigh is home to numerous cultural, educational, and historic sites. The Duke Energy Center for the Performing Arts in Downtown Raleigh features three theater venues and serves as the home for the North Carolina Symphony and the Carolina Ballet. Walnut Creek Amphitheatre is a large music amphitheater located in Southeast Raleigh. Museums in Raleigh include the North Carolina Museum of Art in West Raleigh, as well as the North Carolina Museum of History and North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences located next to each other near the State Capitol in Downtown Raleigh. Several major universities and colleges call Raleigh home, including North Carolina State University, the largest public university in the state, and Shaw University, the first historically black university in the American South and site of the foundation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, an important civil rights organization of the 1960s. One U.S. president, Andrew Johnson, was born in Raleigh.
rewrite: The city of Raleigh hosts a significant array of cultural, educational, and historical institutions. Its performing arts hub is the Duke Energy Center for the Performing Arts in downtown, comprising three theaters and serving as the principal venue for the North Carolina Symphony and Carolina Ballet. For large-scale concerts, the Walnut Creek Amphitheatre is situated in southeast Raleigh. Notable museums include the North Carolina Museum of Art in west Raleigh, while the North Carolina Museum of History and the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences are co-located near the State Capitol. The city is also a major academic center, anchored by North Carolina State University, the state's largest public university, and Shaw University, the American South's first historically black university and the founding site of the seminal 1960s civil rights organization, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Furthermore, Raleigh is the birthplace of U.S. President Andrew Johnson.

input: Federal law and treaties, so long as they are in accordance with the Constitution, preempt conflicting state and territorial laws in the 50 U.S. states and in the territories. However, the scope of federal preemption is limited because the scope of federal power is not universal. In the dual-sovereign system of American federalism (actually tripartite because of the presence of Indian reservations), states are the plenary sovereigns, each with their own constitution, while the federal sovereign possesses only the limited supreme authority enumerated in the Constitution. Indeed, states may grant their citizens broader rights than the federal Constitution as long as they do not infringe on any federal constitutional rights. Thus, most U.S. law (especially the actual "living law" of contract, tort, property, criminal, and family law experienced by the majority of citizens on a day-to-day basis) consists primarily of state law, which can and does vary greatly from one state to the next.
rewrite: Within the United States, federal statutes and treaties, provided they are constitutional, supersede any contradictory state or territorial legislation. This principle of federal preemption is nevertheless constrained by the non-universal nature of federal authority. Under the nation's dual-sovereign federalist structure—more accurately tripartite when considering tribal jurisdictions—the states function as plenary sovereigns, each governed by its own constitution. In contrast, the federal government possesses only that supreme power explicitly enumerated in the U.S. Constitution. Consequently, states may confer upon their citizens rights more expansive than those in the federal charter, provided no federal constitutional right is violated. As a result, the predominant body of U.S. law, particularly the everyday "living law" of contracts, torts, property, crime, and family relations encountered by most citizens, is state law. This corpus of law exhibits significant variation across the several states.

input: In four months, Aonuma's team managed to present realistic horseback riding,[l] which Nintendo later revealed to the public with a trailer at Electronic Entertainment Expo 2004. The game was scheduled to be released the next year, and was no longer a follow-up to The Wind Waker; a true sequel to it was released for the Nintendo DS in 2007, in the form of Phantom Hourglass. Miyamoto explained in interviews that the graphical style was chosen to satisfy demand, and that it better fit the theme of an older incarnation of Link. The game runs on a modified The Wind Waker engine.
rewrite: Within a four-month period, Aonuma's development team successfully implemented a realistic horseback riding system. This achievement was subsequently showcased by Nintendo in a trailer at the 2004 Electronic Entertainment Expo. Originally slated for release the following year, the project ultimately diverged from being a direct sequel to *The Wind Waker*; that role was later fulfilled by *Phantom Hourglass* for the Nintendo DS in 2007. In interviews, Miyamoto clarified that the selected graphical style responded to player feedback and more appropriately suited the theme of an older Link. The game operates on a modified version of *The Wind Waker* engine.

input: Freedom of the press is ostensibly officially guaranteed by the government, but independent press outlets remain restricted, as does a substantial amount of web content. According to the Institute for War & Peace Reporting, access is blocked to local and foreign websites including avesta.tj, Tjknews.com, ferghana.ru, centrasia.ru and journalists are often obstructed from reporting on controversial events. In practice, no public criticism of the regime is tolerated and all direct protest is severely suppressed and does not receive coverage in the local media.
rewrite: Although the government formally guarantees press freedom, independent media outlets face significant restrictions, as does considerable online content. The Institute for War & Peace Reporting notes that access to various local and foreign websites is blocked and journalists are frequently hindered from covering sensitive topics. In practice, public criticism of the regime is not tolerated, direct protest is harshly suppressed, and such events are excluded from coverage in domestic media.

input: The most commonly used forms of medium distance transport in Hyderabad include government owned services such as light railways and buses, as well as privately operated taxis and auto rickshaws. Bus services operate from the Mahatma Gandhi Bus Station in the city centre and carry over 130 million passengers daily across the entire network.:76 Hyderabad's light rail transportation system, the Multi-Modal Transport System (MMTS), is a three line suburban rail service used by over 160,000 passengers daily. Complementing these government services are minibus routes operated by Setwin (Society for Employment Promotion & Training in Twin Cities). Intercity rail services also operate from Hyderabad; the main, and largest, station is Secunderabad Railway Station, which serves as Indian Railways' South Central Railway zone headquarters and a hub for both buses and MMTS light rail services connecting Secunderabad and Hyderabad. Other major railway stations in Hyderabad are Hyderabad Deccan Station, Kachiguda Railway Station, Begumpet Railway Station, Malkajgiri Railway Station and Lingampally Railway Station. The Hyderabad Metro, a new rapid transit system, is to be added to the existing public transport infrastructure and is scheduled to operate three lines by 2015.
rewrite: Hyderabad's medium-distance public transportation network comprises both publicly administered and privately operated services. Government-run options include an extensive bus system, originating primarily from the central Mahatma Gandhi Bus Station, which facilitates over 130 million passenger journeys daily across its network. The suburban rail service, known as the Multi-Modal Transport System (MMTS), operates three lines with a daily ridership exceeding 160,000. This public framework is supplemented by minibus services managed by the Society for Employment Promotion & Training in Twin Cities (Setwin) and by private taxis and auto-rickshaws. For intercity rail travel, Secunderabad Railway Station functions as the principal terminus and headquarters for Indian Railways' South Central zone, integrating bus and MMTS connectivity between Secunderabad and Hyderabad. Other significant stations include Hyderabad Deccan, Kachiguda, Begumpet, Malkajgiri, and Lingampally. Furthermore, the forthcoming Hyderabad Metro rapid transit system, planned to inaugurate three lines by 2015, is anticipated to augment the existing transit infrastructure.

input: Philadelphia is home to many national historical sites that relate to the founding of the United States. Independence National Historical Park is the center of these historical landmarks being one of the country's 22 UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Independence Hall, where the Declaration of Independence was signed, and the Liberty Bell are the city's most famous attractions. Other historic sites include homes for Edgar Allan Poe, Betsy Ross, and Thaddeus Kosciuszko, early government buildings like the First and Second Banks of the United States, Fort Mifflin, and the Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church. Philadelphia alone has 67 National Historic Landmarks, the third most of any city in the country.
rewrite: Philadelphia contains numerous national historical sites integral to the founding of the United States. The centerpiece is Independence National Historical Park, one of the nation's 22 UNESCO World Heritage Sites. This area encompasses the city's most iconic attractions: Independence Hall, where the Declaration of Independence was signed, and the Liberty Bell. Additional significant sites include residences of figures such as Edgar Allan Poe, Betsy Ross, and Thaddeus Kosciuszko; early government buildings like the First and Second Banks of the United States; Fort Mifflin; and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church. With 67 National Historic Landmarks, Philadelphia holds the third-highest concentration of any U.S. city.

input: New York is a prominent location for the American entertainment industry, with many films, television series, books, and other media being set there. As of 2012, New York City was the second largest center for filmmaking and television production in the United States, producing about 200 feature films annually, employing 130,000 individuals, and generating an estimated $7.1 billion in direct expenditures, and by volume, New York is the world leader in independent film production; one-third of all American independent films are produced in New York City. The Association of Independent Commercial Producers is also based in New York. In the first five months of 2014 alone, location filming for television pilots in New York City exceeded the record production levels for all of 2013, with New York surpassing Los Angeles as the top North American city for the same distinction during the 2013/2014 cycle.
rewrite: New York City serves as a preeminent hub for the American entertainment sector, with a vast array of films, television series, books, and other media utilizing it as a setting. As of 2012, it ranked as the nation's second-largest center for film and television production, generating approximately 200 feature films per year. This industry employed 130,000 people and accounted for an estimated $7.1 billion in direct expenditures. By volume, New York is the global leader in independent film production, responsible for one-third of all American independent films. The Association of Independent Commercial Producers is also headquartered there. Notably, during the first five months of 2014, location filming for television pilots in New York City surpassed the total record for all of 2013, and it exceeded Los Angeles as the top North American city for such production in the 2013/2014 cycle.

input: Control of labour and inter-group conflict is characteristic of corporate-level or 'tribal' groups, headed by a charismatic individual; whether a 'big man' or a proto-chief, functioning as a lineage-group head. Whether a non-hierarchical system of organization existed is debatable, and there is no evidence that explicitly suggests that Neolithic societies functioned under any dominating class or individual, as was the case in the chiefdoms of the European Early Bronze Age. Theories to explain the apparent implied egalitarianism of Neolithic (and Paleolithic) societies have arisen, notably the Marxist concept of primitive communism.
rewrite: The regulation of labor and management of inter-group disputes are defining features of corporate or 'tribal' units, typically led by a charismatic figure such as a 'big man' or proto-chief acting as a lineage head. The existence of entirely non-hierarchical social organization remains uncertain, with no explicit evidence indicating Neolithic societies were governed by a dominant class or individual, unlike subsequent Early Bronze Age chiefdoms. Interpretations of this implied egalitarianism, particularly in Neolithic and Paleolithic contexts, include theories like the Marxist framework of primitive communism.

input: Following the success of season one, the second season was moved up to air in January 2003. The number of episodes increased, as did the show's budget and the charge for commercial spots. Dunkleman left the show, leaving Seacrest as the lone host. Kristin Adams was a correspondent for this season.
rewrite: Due to the success of its first season, the second season premiered early in January 2003. It featured an increased episode count, budget, and advertising rates. Dunkleman departed, leaving Seacrest as sole host, while Kristin Adams served as a correspondent.

input: The Times Literary Supplement (TLS) first appeared in 1902 as a supplement to The Times, becoming a separately paid-for weekly literature and society magazine in 1914. The Times and the TLS have continued to be co-owned, and as of 2012 the TLS is also published by News International and cooperates closely with The Times, with its online version hosted on The Times website, and its editorial offices based in Times House, Pennington Street, London.
rewrite: First published in 1902 as a supplement to *The Times*, *The Times Literary Supplement* (TLS) became an independent paid weekly periodical covering literature and society in 1914. It has remained under the same ownership as *The Times*. Since 2012, News International has published the TLS, which maintains close operational ties to *The Times*, sharing its website for digital content and being headquartered at Times House on Pennington Street in London.

input: Congo is located in the central-western part of sub-Saharan Africa, along the Equator, lying between latitudes 4°N and 5°S, and longitudes 11° and 19°E. To the south and east of it is the Democratic Republic of Congo. It is also bounded by Gabon to the west, Cameroon and the Central African Republic to the north, and Cabinda (Angola) to the southwest. It has a short coast on the Atlantic Ocean.
rewrite: The Republic of the Congo is situated in central-western sub-Saharan Africa, astride the Equator within approximately 4°N to 5°S latitude and 11° to 19°E longitude. It shares borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the south and east, Gabon to the west, Cameroon and the Central African Republic to the north, and the Angolan exclave of Cabinda to the southwest. The nation possesses a limited Atlantic coastline.

input: In 1219 Pope Honorius III invited Saint Dominic and his companions to take up residence at the ancient Roman basilica of Santa Sabina, which they did by early 1220. Before that time the friars had only a temporary residence in Rome at the convent of San Sisto Vecchio which Honorius III had given to Dominic circa 1218 intending it to become a convent for a reformation of nuns at Rome under Dominic's guidance. In May 1220 at Bologna the order's first General Chapter mandated that each new priory of the order maintain its own studium conventuale thus laying the foundation of the Dominican tradition of sponsoring widespread institutions of learning. The official foundation of the Dominican convent at Santa Sabina with its studium conventuale occurred with the legal transfer of property from Honorius III to the Order of Preachers on June 5, 1222. This studium was transformed into the order's first studium provinciale by Saint Thomas Aquinas in 1265. Part of the curriculum of this studium was relocated in 1288 at the studium of Santa Maria sopra Minerva which in the 16th century world be transformed into the College of Saint Thomas (Latin: Collegium Divi Thomæ). In the 20th century the college would be relocated to the convent of Saints Dominic and Sixtus and would be transformed into the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas, Angelicum.
rewrite: In 1219, Pope Honorius III extended an invitation to Saint Dominic and his companions to establish a residence at the ancient Roman basilica of Santa Sabina, a move completed by early 1220. Previously, the friars had occupied only a temporary dwelling at the convent of San Sisto Vecchio in Rome, granted to Dominic around 1218 by Honorius III with the intention of forming a reformed convent of nuns under Dominic’s direction. A significant development occurred in May 1220 at Bologna during the order’s first General Chapter, which decreed that each new priory must maintain its own *studium conventuale*, thereby instituting the Dominican commitment to broad educational sponsorship. The formal establishment of the Dominican convent at Santa Sabina, inclusive of its *studium conventuale*, was effected through the legal transfer of property from Honorius III to the Order of Preachers on June 5, 1222. This *studium* was elevated to the order’s first *studium provinciale* by Saint Thomas Aquinas in 1265. In 1288, portions of its curriculum were transferred to the *studium* of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, which in the sixteenth century would become the College of Saint Thomas (Collegium Divi Thomæ). During the twentieth century, this institution was relocated to the convent of Saints Dominic and Sixtus and ultimately transformed into the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas, known as the Angelicum.

input: Because of Oklahoma's position between zones of differing prevailing temperature and winds, weather patterns within the state can vary widely over relatively short distances and can change drastically in a short time. As an example, on November 11, 1911, the temperature at Oklahoma City reached 83 °F (28 °C) in the afternoon (the record high for that date), then an Arctic cold front of unprecedented intensity slammed across the state, causing the temperature to crash 66 degrees, down to 17 °F (−8 °C) at midnight (the record low for that date); thus, both the record high and record low for November 11 were set on the same date. This type of phenomenon is also responsible for many of the tornadoes in the area, such as the 1912 Oklahoma tornado outbreak, when a warm front traveled along a stalled cold front, resulting in an average of about one tornado per hour over the course of a day.
rewrite: Owing to its geographic location at the confluence of distinct climatic zones characterized by divergent prevailing temperatures and wind patterns, Oklahoma experiences considerable meteorological variability across relatively short distances, with conditions subject to abrupt and dramatic shifts. A notable illustration occurred on November 11, 1911, when Oklahoma City recorded an afternoon high of 83°F (28°C), the historic maximum for that calendar date. Subsequently, an Arctic cold front of exceptional intensity traversed the state, precipitating a temperature decline of 66 degrees to a midnight low of 17°F (-8°C), which concurrently established the historic minimum for November 11. Thus, both the daily record high and low were established within a single date. This propensity for violent atmospheric contrasts also drives frequent tornadic activity, exemplified by the 1912 Oklahoma tornado outbreak. During that event, the interaction of a warm front with a stalled cold front generated tornadoes at an approximate rate of one per hour over a twenty-four-hour period.

input: On September 21, 1529, Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón commanded the Spanish ship Florida, on his second attempt to recross the Pacific from the Maluku Islands. He stood off a group of islands from which local inhabitants hurled stones at his ship. These islands, which he named "Los Pintados", may have been Ujelang. On October 1, he found another group of islands where he went ashore for eight days, exchanged gifts with the local inhabitants and took on water. These islands, which he named "Los Jardines", may have been Enewetak or Bikini Atoll.
rewrite: On September 21, 1529, during his second Pacific crossing attempt from the Maluku Islands, Spanish commander Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón, aboard the *Florida*, encountered an island group. Inhabitants there threw stones at his vessel; he named these islands "Los Pintados," possibly Ujelang. Subsequently, on October 1, he located another archipelago, likely Enewetak or Bikini Atoll. He disembarked for eight days, engaged in gift exchanges with the local population, and replenished his water supplies, bestowing the name "Los Jardines" upon these islands.

input: Modern navies that operate such aircraft carriers treat them as the capital ship of the fleet, a role previously held by the battleship. This change took place during World War II in response to air power becoming a significant factor in warfare, driven by the superior range, flexibility and effectiveness of carrier-launched aircraft. Following the war, carrier operations continued to increase in size and importance. Supercarriers, displacing 75,000 tonnes or greater, have become the pinnacle of carrier development. Some are powered by nuclear reactors and form the core of a fleet designed to operate far from home. Amphibious assault ships, such as USS Tarawa and HMS Ocean, serve the purpose of carrying and landing Marines, and operate a large contingent of helicopters for that purpose. Also known as "commando carriers" or "helicopter carriers", many have the capability to operate VSTOL aircraft.
rewrite: In contemporary naval forces, the aircraft carrier has supplanted the battleship as the fleet's capital ship. This doctrinal shift, consolidated during the Second World War, resulted from the ascendancy of air power, enabled by the superior range, flexibility, and combat effectiveness of carrier-based aviation. Post-war development has seen carriers grow in both scale and strategic significance. The supercarrier, defined by a displacement exceeding 75,000 tonnes, represents the apex of this evolution; nuclear-powered variants form the core of expeditionary fleets capable of prolonged, distant operations. Concurrently, amphibious assault ships, such as the USS *Tarawa* and HMS *Ocean*, function as dedicated platforms for marine deployment, embarking large contingents of helicopters and, in many cases, possessing flight decks configured for V/STOL aircraft, earning them the designations "commando carrier" or "helicopter carrier."

input: The earliest known human activity on the island dates to around the 10th millennium BC. Archaeological remains from this period include the well-preserved Neolithic village of Khirokitia, and Cyprus is home to some of the oldest water wells in the world. Cyprus was settled by Mycenaean Greeks in two waves in the 2nd millennium BC. As a strategic location in the Middle East, it was subsequently occupied by several major powers, including the empires of the Assyrians, Egyptians and Persians, from whom the island was seized in 333 BC by Alexander the Great. Subsequent rule by Ptolemaic Egypt, the Classical and Eastern Roman Empire, Arab caliphates for a short period, the French Lusignan dynasty and the Venetians, was followed by over three centuries of Ottoman rule between 1571 and 1878 (de jure until 1914).
rewrite: The earliest documented human presence on Cyprus originates circa the 10th millennium BC. Archaeological evidence from this era encompasses the exceptionally preserved Neolithic settlement of Khirokitia, alongside some of the world's most ancient water wells. The island was subsequently colonized by Mycenaean Greeks during two distinct waves in the 2nd millennium BC. Owing to its strategic position in the Eastern Mediterranean, Cyprus later fell under the control of successive imperial powers, including the Assyrian, Egyptian, and Persian empires. Alexander the Great annexed the island in 333 BC. A succession of rulers followed, comprising Ptolemaic Egypt, the Roman and Byzantine Empires, brief Arab caliphate administration, the Frankish Lusignan dynasty, and the Venetian Republic. This was superseded by over three centuries of Ottoman governance from 1571 to 1878, *de jure* persisting until 1914.

input: Several Americans, especially Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson, played a major role in bringing Enlightenment ideas to the New World and in influencing British and French thinkers. Franklin was influential for his political activism and for his advances in physics. The cultural exchange during the Age of Enlightenment ran in both directions across the Atlantic. Thinkers such as Paine, Locke, and Rousseau all take Native American cultural practices as examples of natural freedom. The Americans closely followed English and Scottish political ideas, as well as some French thinkers such as Montesquieu. As deists, they were influenced by ideas of John Toland (1670–1722) and Matthew Tindal (1656–1733). During the Enlightenment there was a great emphasis upon liberty, democracy, republicanism and religious tolerance. Attempts to reconcile science and religion resulted in a widespread rejection of prophecy, miracle and revealed religion in preference for Deism – especially by Thomas Paine in The Age of Reason and by Thomas Jefferson in his short Jefferson Bible – from which all supernatural aspects were removed.
rewrite: The transatlantic exchange of Enlightenment thought significantly involved American intellectuals, notably Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson, who both imported European ideas and influenced thinkers in Britain and France. Franklin contributed through political activism and scientific work in physics. This intellectual commerce was reciprocal; figures like Paine, Locke, and Rousseau referenced Native American societies as models of natural liberty. American thought primarily engaged with English and Scottish political philosophy, alongside French influences such as Montesquieu. In theology, deistic principles from John Toland (1670–1722) and Matthew Tindal (1656–1733) were formative. Core Enlightenment values—liberty, democracy, republicanism, and religious tolerance—were paramount. The effort to harmonize reason and faith led many to reject prophecy, miracles, and revealed religion in favor of Deism. This is exemplified in Thomas Paine’s *The Age of Reason* and Thomas Jefferson’s edited scripture, the "Jefferson Bible," which systematically excised supernatural elements.

input: In 2013, China led the world in renewable energy production, with a total capacity of 378 GW, mainly from hydroelectric and wind power. As of 2014, China leads the world in the production and use of wind power, solar photovoltaic power and smart grid technologies, generating almost as much water, wind and solar energy as all of France and Germany's power plants combined. China's renewable energy sector is growing faster than its fossil fuels and nuclear power capacity. Since 2005, production of solar cells in China has expanded 100-fold. As Chinese renewable manufacturing has grown, the costs of renewable energy technologies have dropped. Innovation has helped, but the main driver of reduced costs has been market expansion.
rewrite: By 2013, China possessed the world’s largest renewable energy capacity, totaling 378 gigawatts, predominantly from hydroelectric and wind sources. As of 2014, it maintained global leadership in wind power, solar photovoltaic capacity, and smart grid deployment, with combined hydro, wind, and solar output nearly equaling the total generation of France and Germany. The renewable sector in China has expanded more rapidly than its fossil fuel and nuclear capacities. Since 2005, domestic solar cell production has increased one hundredfold. This manufacturing scale has driven substantial reductions in the cost of renewable technologies, where market expansion, more than innovation alone, has been the primary catalyst for declining prices.

input: Rapid decompression can be much more dangerous than vacuum exposure itself. Even if the victim does not hold his or her breath, venting through the windpipe may be too slow to prevent the fatal rupture of the delicate alveoli of the lungs. Eardrums and sinuses may be ruptured by rapid decompression, soft tissues may bruise and seep blood, and the stress of shock will accelerate oxygen consumption leading to hypoxia. Injuries caused by rapid decompression are called barotrauma. A pressure drop of 13 kPa (100 Torr), which produces no symptoms if it is gradual, may be fatal if it occurs suddenly.
rewrite: Rapid decompression presents a greater hazard than the vacuum exposure per se. Even without breath-holding, decompression through the trachea may be insufficiently rapid to prevent fatal rupture of the delicate pulmonary alveoli. Additional effects can include ruptured eardrums and sinuses, bruising and hemorrhage in soft tissues, and shock-induced acceleration of oxygen consumption culminating in hypoxia. Such injuries are classified as barotrauma. Crucially, a pressure drop of 13 kPa (100 Torr), which is asymptomatic if gradual, can prove fatal if it occurs suddenly.

input: After World War I, when Britain and France divided up the Middle East's countries, apart from Turkey, between them, pursuant to the Sykes-Picot agreement—in violation of solemn wartime promises of postwar Arab autonomy—there came an immediate reaction: the Muslim Brotherhood emerged in Egypt, the House of Saud took over the Hijaz, and regimes led by army officers came to power in Iran and Turkey. "[B]oth illiberal currents of the modern Middle East," writes de Bellaigne, "Islamism and militarism, received a major impetus from Western empire-builders." As often happens in countries undergoing social crisis, the aspirations of the Muslim world's translators and modernizers, such as Muhammad Abduh, largely had to yield to retrograde currents.
rewrite: In the aftermath of World War I, the British and French division of the Middle East—excluding Turkey—under the Sykes-Picot Agreement contravened explicit wartime pledges of Arab self-determination. This precipitated an immediate political realignment, marked by the emergence of the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt, the Saudi conquest of the Hijaz, and the rise of military-led regimes in Iran and Turkey. Historian Christopher de Bellaigne observes that these events provided a major impetus to the region’s two dominant illiberal currents: Islamism and militarism. Consequently, during this period of profound social crisis, the progressive aspirations of modernist reformers like Muhammad Abduh were largely superseded by more reactionary forces.

input: In 2002, Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" was voted "the UK's favourite hit of all time" in a poll conducted by the Guinness World Records British Hit Singles Book. In 2004 the song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Many scholars consider the "Bohemian Rhapsody" music video ground-breaking, and credit it with popularising the medium. Rock historian Paul Fowles states the song is "widely credited as the first global hit single for which an accompanying video was central to the marketing strategy". It has been hailed as launching the MTV age. Acclaimed for their stadium rock, in 2005 an industry poll ranked Queen's performance at Live Aid in 1985 as the best live act in history. In 2007, they were also voted the greatest British band in history by BBC Radio 2 listeners.
rewrite: In 2002, Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" was designated "the UK's favourite hit of all time" in a poll by the *Guinness World Records British Hit Singles Book*. The recording was subsequently inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2004. Academic analysis frequently identifies its accompanying video as a ground-breaking work that significantly advanced the medium's popularity. Rock historian Paul Fowles notes the single is "widely credited as the first global hit for which an accompanying video was central to the marketing strategy," a factor often cited as heralding the MTV era. Renowned for their stadium rock prowess, Queen's 1985 Live Aid performance was ranked the greatest live act in history in a 2005 industry poll. Furthermore, BBC Radio 2 listeners voted them the greatest British band in history in 2007.

input: By the early years of the 21st century, western clothing styles had, to some extent, become international styles. This process began hundreds of years earlier, during the periods of European colonialism. The process of cultural dissemination has perpetuated over the centuries as Western media corporations have penetrated markets throughout the world, spreading Western culture and styles. Fast fashion clothing has also become a global phenomenon. These garments are less expensive, mass-produced Western clothing. Donated used clothing from Western countries are also delivered to people in poor countries by charity organizations.
rewrite: By the early twenty-first century, Western apparel had largely evolved into a global sartorial standard. This phenomenon originated centuries prior during eras of European colonial expansion. The dissemination of these cultural norms has been sustained over time, particularly through the worldwide market penetration of Western media conglomerates, which propagate associated cultural and stylistic values. Concurrently, the rise of inexpensive, mass-produced fast fashion has become a worldwide occurrence. Furthermore, charitable organizations distribute donated used garments from Western nations to populations in less affluent countries.

input: As the century wore on, the factions slowly began to adopt more coherent political tendencies as the interests of their power bases began to diverge. The Whig party's initial base of support from the great aristocratic families, widened to include the emerging industrial interests and wealthy merchants. As well as championing constitutional monarchy with strict limits on the monarch's power, the Whigs adamantly opposed a Catholic king as a threat to liberty, and believed in extending toleration to nonconformist Protestants, or dissenters. A major influence on the Whigs were the liberal political ideas of John Locke, and the concepts of universal rights employed by Locke and Algernon Sidney.
rewrite: Over the course of the century, the factions gradually coalesced around more distinct political ideologies, driven by the diverging interests of their core constituencies. The Whig Party, originally supported by the great aristocratic families, expanded its base to incorporate emerging industrial and commercial wealth. Its platform advocated for a constitutional monarchy with firmly limited royal prerogatives, opposed a Catholic monarch as a threat to liberty, and supported toleration for Protestant dissenters. Whig thought was significantly shaped by the liberal philosophies of John Locke and Algernon Sidney, particularly their concepts of universal rights.

input: Although the new licensing laws prevented new beer houses from being created, those already in existence were allowed to continue and many did not close until nearly the end of the 19th century. A very small number remained into the 21st century. The vast majority of the beer houses applied for the new licences and became full pubs. These usually small establishments can still be identified in many towns, seemingly oddly located in the middle of otherwise terraced housing part way up a street, unlike purpose-built pubs that are usually found on corners or road junctions. Many of today's respected real ale micro-brewers in the UK started as home based Beer House brewers under the 1830 Act.
rewrite: While the revised licensing legislation prohibited the establishment of new beer houses, extant premises were permitted to continue operating, with many persisting until the late nineteenth century; a minimal number survived into the twenty-first. The majority of these establishments successfully transitioned by obtaining full public house licenses. These typically modest venues remain identifiable in numerous urban settings, often situated peculiarly within terraced housing mid-street, in contrast to purpose-built public houses typically located at corners or intersections. Furthermore, many contemporary and esteemed real ale micro-breweries in the United Kingdom originated as domestic-scale Beer House brewers operating under the 1830 Act.

input: On January 8, 2006, while Schwarzenegger was riding his Harley Davidson motorcycle in Los Angeles, with his son Patrick in the sidecar, another driver backed into the street he was riding on, causing him and his son to collide with the car at a low speed. While his son and the other driver were unharmed, the governor sustained a minor injury to his lip, requiring 15 stitches. "No citations were issued", said Officer Jason Lee, a Los Angeles Police Department spokesman. Schwarzenegger did not obtain his motorcycle license until July 3, 2006.
rewrite: On January 8, 2006, Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger was involved in a low-speed collision in Los Angeles while operating a Harley Davidson motorcycle, with his son Patrick as a passenger in a sidecar. The incident occurred when another motorist reversed into their path. Although his son and the other driver emerged unharmed, Schwarzenegger sustained a minor lip laceration necessitating fifteen stitches. According to Los Angeles Police Department spokesman Officer Jason Lee, no traffic citations were issued. Notably, Schwarzenegger did not acquire his formal motorcycle license until July 3, 2006.

input: Seattle in this period attracted widespread attention as home to these many companies, but also by hosting the 1990 Goodwill Games and the APEC leaders conference in 1993, as well as through the worldwide popularity of grunge, a sound that had developed in Seattle's independent music scene. Another bid for worldwide attention—hosting the World Trade Organization Ministerial Conference of 1999—garnered visibility, but not in the way its sponsors desired, as related protest activity and police reactions to those protests overshadowed the conference itself. The city was further shaken by the Mardi Gras Riots in 2001, and then literally shaken the following day by the Nisqually earthquake.
rewrite: During this era, Seattle garnered significant international recognition, not only as the headquarters of numerous prominent corporations but also through hosting the 1990 Goodwill Games and the 1993 APEC leaders' conference. The global ascendancy of grunge music, which originated in the city's independent music scene, further amplified its profile. An additional bid for attention, the 1999 World Trade Organization Ministerial Conference, achieved visibility in an unintended manner, as extensive protest activity and the ensuing police response eclipsed the event itself. Subsequently, the city was disrupted by the 2001 Mardi Gras riots and, the following day, by the Nisqually earthquake.

input: On November 18, 1990, the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church enthroned Mstyslav as Patriarch of Kiev and all Ukraine during ceremonies at Saint Sophia's Cathedral. Also on November 18, Canada announced that its consul-general to Kiev would be Ukrainian-Canadian Nestor Gayowsky. On November 19, the United States announced that its consul to Kiev would be Ukrainian-American John Stepanchuk. On November 19, the chairmen of the Ukrainian and Russian parliaments, respectively, Kravchuk and Yeltsin, signed a 10-year bilateral pact. In early December 1990 the Party of Democratic Rebirth of Ukraine was founded; on December 15, the Democratic Party of Ukraine was founded.
rewrite: On November 18, 1990, the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church elevated Mstyslav to the patriarchal throne of Kiev and All Ukraine in a ceremony at Saint Sophia's Cathedral. That same day, Canada appointed Ukrainian-Canadian Nestor Gayowsky as its consul-general to Kiev. The following day, the United States designated Ukrainian-American John Stepanchuk as its consul to Kiev. Also on November 19, the chairmen of the Ukrainian and Russian parliaments, Leonid Kravchuk and Boris Yeltsin, signed a ten-year bilateral treaty. In early December 1990, the Party of Democratic Rebirth of Ukraine was established, followed by the founding of the Democratic Party of Ukraine on December 15.

input: The library is based at two public sites: the Reading Room at the RIBA's headquarters, 66 Portland Place, London; and the RIBA Architecture Study Rooms in the Henry Cole Wing of the V&A. The Reading Room, designed by the building's architect George Grey Wornum and his wife Miriam, retains its original 1934 Art Deco interior with open bookshelves, original furniture and double-height central space. The study rooms, opened in 2004, were designed by Wright & Wright. The library is funded entirely by the RIBA but it is open to the public without charge. It operates a free education programme aimed at students, education groups and families, and an information service for RIBA members and the public through the RIBA Information Centre.
rewrite: The library operates across two publicly accessible locations: the Reading Room at the RIBA's headquarters, 66 Portland Place, London, and the RIBA Architecture Study Rooms within the Henry Cole Wing of the Victoria and Albert Museum. The Reading Room, conceived by the building's architect George Grey Wornum and his wife Miriam, preserves its original 1934 Art Deco interior, featuring open shelving, period furniture, and a double-height central volume. The Study Rooms, inaugurated in 2004, were designed by Wright & Wright. Funded solely by the RIBA, the library offers complimentary public access. It maintains a free educational programme for students, educational groups, and families, alongside an information service for both RIBA members and the general public via the RIBA Information Centre.

input: Historical records show evidence of Jewish communities north of the Alps and Pyrenees as early as the 8th and 9th century. By the 11th century Jewish settlers, moving from southern European and Middle Eastern centers, appear to have begun to settle in the north, especially along the Rhine, often in response to new economic opportunities and at the invitation of local Christian rulers. Thus Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, invited Jacob ben Yekutiel and his fellow Jews to settle in his lands; and soon after the Norman Conquest of England, William the Conqueror likewise extended a welcome to continental Jews to take up residence there. Bishop Rüdiger Huzmann called on the Jews of Mainz to relocate to Speyer. In all of these decisions, the idea that Jews had the know-how and capacity to jump-start the economy, improve revenues, and enlarge trade seems to have played a prominent role. Typically Jews relocated close to the markets and churches in town centres, where, though they came under the authority of both royal and ecclesiastical powers, they were accorded administrative autonomy.
rewrite: Historical evidence attests to the presence of Jewish communities north of the Alpine and Pyrenean ranges as early as the eighth and ninth centuries. By the eleventh century, a more deliberate northward migration from southern European and Middle Eastern centres is discernible, particularly along the Rhine River. This movement was frequently instigated by emerging economic prospects and the explicit invitations of Christian secular authorities. For instance, Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, solicited Jacob ben Yekutiel and other Jews to settle in his territories, while William the Conqueror issued a similar invitation to continental Jews following the Norman Conquest of England. Likewise, Bishop Rüdiger Huzmann encouraged the Jews of Mainz to resettle in Speyer. A common motivating factor in these solicitations appears to have been the perception that Jewish communities possessed the specialised expertise and capacity to stimulate economic activity, enhance fiscal revenues, and expand commercial networks. These settlers typically established themselves in urban centres near markets and churches. Although subject to royal and ecclesiastical jurisdiction, they were generally granted a significant degree of administrative autonomy within their own affairs.

input: The exact nature of relations between Tibet and the Ming dynasty of China (1368–1644) is unclear. Analysis of the relationship is further complicated by modern political conflicts and the application of Westphalian sovereignty to a time when the concept did not exist. Some Mainland Chinese scholars, such as Wang Jiawei and Nyima Gyaincain, assert that the Ming dynasty had unquestioned sovereignty over Tibet, pointing to the Ming court's issuing of various titles to Tibetan leaders, Tibetans' full acceptance of these titles, and a renewal process for successors of these titles that involved traveling to the Ming capital. Scholars within China also argue that Tibet has been an integral part of China since the 13th century and that it was thus a part of the Ming Empire. But most scholars outside China, such as Turrell V. Wylie, Melvin C. Goldstein, and Helmut Hoffman, say that the relationship was one of suzerainty, that Ming titles were only nominal, that Tibet remained an independent region outside Ming control, and that it simply paid tribute until the Jiajing Emperor (1521–1566), who ceased relations with Tibet.
rewrite: The precise character of the relationship between Tibet and the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) remains ambiguous. Scholarly interpretation is complicated by contemporary political disputes and the anachronistic imposition of modern Westphalian sovereignty concepts onto the pre-modern period. Within Mainland China, scholars such as Wang Jiawei and Nyima Gyaincain maintain that the Ming dynasty exercised unequivocal sovereignty over Tibet. Their argument rests upon the Ming court’s bestowal of official titles upon Tibetan leaders, the apparent acceptance of these titles by Tibetan recipients, and the requirement for successors to travel to the Ming capital for renewal. These scholars often posit that Tibet has constituted an integral part of China since the 13th century, thereby being encompassed within the Ming Empire. Conversely, many scholars outside China, including Turrell V. Wylie, Melvin C. Goldstein, and Helmut Hoffman, characterize the relationship as one of suzerainty. They contend that Ming titles were largely nominal, that Tibet retained its independence from direct Ming administrative control, and that its engagement was primarily tributary until the Jiajing Emperor (1521–1566) severed formal relations.

input: Many beers are sold in cans, though there is considerable variation in the proportion between different countries. In Sweden in 2001, 63.9% of beer was sold in cans. People either drink from the can or pour the beer into a glass. A technology developed by Crown Holdings for the 2010 FIFA World Cup is the 'full aperture' can, so named because the entire lid is removed during the opening process, turning the can into a drinking cup. Cans protect the beer from light (thereby preventing "skunked" beer) and have a seal less prone to leaking over time than bottles. Cans were initially viewed as a technological breakthrough for maintaining the quality of a beer, then became commonly associated with less expensive, mass-produced beers, even though the quality of storage in cans is much like bottles. Plastic (PET) bottles are used by some breweries.
rewrite: Beer is frequently packaged in cans, with notable international variation in market share. For instance, in Sweden during 2001, cans accounted for 63.9% of beer sales. Consumption occurs either directly from the can or following transfer to a glass. A significant packaging innovation, introduced by Crown Holdings for the 2010 FIFA World Cup, is the 'full aperture' can. This design involves removing the entire lid, effectively converting the container into a drinking vessel. Cans offer superior protection against light exposure, which prevents the development of undesirable flavors ("skunking"), and provide a seal generally more resistant to leakage compared to traditional bottles. Historically, cans were celebrated as a technological advancement for preserving beer quality, yet later became predominantly linked with inexpensive, mass-produced varieties, despite offering comparable protective qualities to glass bottles. Some breweries also utilize plastic (PET) bottles for packaging.

input: Older letters of the Russian alphabet include ⟨ѣ⟩, which merged to ⟨е⟩ (/je/ or /ʲe/); ⟨і⟩ and ⟨ѵ⟩, which both merged to ⟨и⟩ (/i/); ⟨ѳ⟩, which merged to ⟨ф⟩ (/f/); ⟨ѫ⟩, which merged to ⟨у⟩ (/u/); ⟨ѭ⟩, which merged to ⟨ю⟩ (/ju/ or /ʲu/); and ⟨ѧ/⟨ѩ⟩⟩, which later were graphically reshaped into ⟨я⟩ and merged phonetically to /ja/ or /ʲa/. While these older letters have been abandoned at one time or another, they may be used in this and related articles. The yers ⟨ъ⟩ and ⟨ь⟩ originally indicated the pronunciation of ultra-short or reduced /ŭ/, /ĭ/.
rewrite: Several archaic characters of the Russian alphabet, now obsolete, underwent historical mergers: ⟨ѣ⟩ merged with ⟨е⟩ (/je/ or /ʲe/); ⟨і⟩ and ⟨ѵ⟩ with ⟨и⟩ (/i/); ⟨ѳ⟩ with ⟨ф⟩ (/f/); ⟨ѫ⟩ with ⟨у⟩ (/u/); ⟨ѭ⟩ with ⟨ю⟩ (/ju/ or /ʲu/); and ⟨ѧ/ѩ⟩, graphically reshaped into ⟨я⟩, merging phonetically as /ja/ or /ʲa/. The yers ⟨ъ⟩ and ⟨ь⟩ originally denoted reduced vowels /ŭ/ and /ĭ/. Though abandoned, these letters may appear in scholarly contexts.

input: Colin Humphreys and W. G. Waddington of Oxford University considered the possibility that a lunar, rather than solar, eclipse might have taken place. They concluded that such an eclipse would have been visible, for thirty minutes, from Jerusalem and suggested the gospel reference to a solar eclipse was the result of a scribe wrongly amending a text. Historian David Henige dismisses this explanation as 'indefensible' and astronomer Bradley Schaefer points out that the lunar eclipse would not have been visible during daylight hours.
rewrite: Colin Humphreys and W. G. Waddington of Oxford University proposed that the biblical darkness could refer to a lunar eclipse, visible from Jerusalem for thirty minutes. They attributed the gospel's solar eclipse description to a potential scribal error. However, historian David Henige deems this theory 'indefensible,' and astronomer Bradley Schaefer notes a lunar eclipse would not have been observable in daylight, challenging the hypothesis.

input: Today, Greeks are the majority ethnic group in the Hellenic Republic, where they constitute 93% of the country's population, and the Republic of Cyprus where they make up 78% of the island's population (excluding Turkish settlers in the occupied part of the country). Greek populations have not traditionally exhibited high rates of growth; nonetheless, the population of Greece has shown regular increase since the country's first census in 1828. A large percentage of the population growth since the state's foundation has resulted from annexation of new territories and the influx of 1.5 million Greek refugees after the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey. About 80% of the population of Greece is urban, with 28% concentrated in the city of Athens
rewrite: The Hellenic Republic is predominantly composed of ethnic Greeks, who constitute 93% of its population, as well as 78% of the population in the Republic of Cyprus (excluding Turkish settlers in the occupied northern region). Historically, Greek demographic growth has been modest; however, the population of Greece has experienced a consistent increase since its inaugural census in 1828. A significant portion of this growth since the state's establishment is attributable to territorial expansions and the influx of approximately 1.5 million Greek refugees following the 1923 population exchange with Turkey. Approximately 80% of Greece's population is urbanized, with 28% residing in the metropolitan area of Athens.

input: The word "dollar" is one of the words in the first paragraph of Section 9 of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution. In that context, "dollars" is a reference to the Spanish milled dollar, a coin that had a monetary value of 8 Spanish units of currency, or reales. In 1792 the U.S. Congress adopted legislation titled An act establishing a mint, and regulating the Coins of the United States. Section 9 of that act authorized the production of various coins, including "DOLLARS OR UNITS—each to be of the value of a Spanish milled dollar as the same is now current, and to contain three hundred and seventy-one grains and four sixteenth parts of a grain of pure, or four hundred and sixteen grains of standard silver". Section 20 of the act provided, "That the money of account of the United States shall be expressed in dollars, or units... and that all accounts in the public offices and all proceedings in the courts of the United States shall be kept and had in conformity to this regulation". In other words, this act designated the United States dollar as the unit of currency of the United States.
rewrite: The term "dollar" appears within the initial paragraph of Article I, Section 9 of the United States Constitution. In this constitutional context, "dollars" denotes the Spanish milled dollar, a coin valued at eight Spanish reales. Subsequently, the Coinage Act of 1792, formally titled "An act establishing a mint, and regulating the Coins of the United States," provided the legislative foundation for a national currency. Its Section 9 authorized the minting of several coins, specifying that the "DOLLARS OR UNITS" must correspond in value to a current Spanish milled dollar and contain precisely 371.25 grains of pure silver, or 416 grains of standard silver. Furthermore, Section 20 of the act stipulated that the monetary unit of account for the United States was to be expressed in dollars, mandating that all public accounts and federal judicial proceedings adhere to this standard. Thus, this seminal legislation formally established the United States dollar as the nation's standard unit of currency.

input: The Bronx's highest elevation at 280 feet (85 m) is in the northwest corner, west of Van Cortlandt Park and in the Chapel Farm area near the Riverdale Country School. The opposite (southeastern) side of the Bronx has four large low peninsulas or "necks" of low-lying land that jut into the waters of the East River and were once salt marsh: Hunt's Point, Clason's Point, Screvin's Neck and Throg's Neck. Further up the coastline, Rodman's Neck lies between Pelham Bay Park in the northeast and City Island. The Bronx's irregular shoreline extends for 75 square miles (194 km2).
rewrite: The Bronx attains its maximum elevation of 280 feet (85 m) in its northwestern quadrant, specifically west of Van Cortlandt Park within the Chapel Farm vicinity adjacent to the Riverdale Country School. Conversely, the southeastern region features four expansive, low-lying peninsulas—historically saline marshland—projecting into the East River: Hunt's Point, Clason's Point, Screvin's Neck, and Throg's Neck. Northward along the coast, Rodman's Neck is situated between Pelham Bay Park and City Island. The borough's highly irregular coastline spans 75 square miles (194 km²).

input: Three weeks later, on May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space, launched in a ballistic trajectory on Mercury-Redstone 3, in a spacecraft he named Freedom 7. Though he did not achieve orbit like Gagarin, he was the first person to exercise manual control over his spacecraft's attitude and retro-rocket firing. After his successful return, Shepard was celebrated as a national hero, honored with parades in Washington, New York and Los Angeles, and received the NASA Distinguished Service Medal from President John F. Kennedy.
rewrite: On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Mercury-Redstone 3 mission. His spacecraft, Freedom 7, followed a ballistic trajectory. Unlike Gagarin’s orbital flight, Shepard’s suborbital journey featured the first manual control of a spacecraft’s attitude and retro-rocket firing. Following his successful recovery, Shepard was hailed as a national hero, celebrated with parades in Washington, New York, and Los Angeles, and awarded the NASA Distinguished Service Medal by President John F. Kennedy.

input: The 1961 eruption of Queen Mary's Peak forced the evacuation of the entire population via Cape Town to England. The following year a Royal Society expedition went to the islands to assess the damage, and reported that the settlement of Edinburgh of the Seven Seas had been only marginally affected. Most families returned in 1963.

A subsequent Royal Society expedition in 1962 determined the settlement of Edinburgh of the Seven Seas sustained only marginal damage, enabling most families to return in 1963.

input: During the First World War, Plymouth was the port of entry for many troops from around the Empire and also developed as a facility for the manufacture of munitions. Although major units of the Royal Navy moved to the safety of Scapa Flow, Devonport was an important base for escort vessels and repairs. Flying boats operated from Mount Batten.
rewrite: During the First World War, Plymouth served as a key port for imperial troop arrivals and expanded its munitions production. While major Royal Navy units relocated to Scapa Flow, Devonport remained a vital base for escort vessels and repairs. Additionally, flying boat operations were conducted from Mount Batten.

input: Charleston is the primary medical center for the eastern portion of the state. The city has several major hospitals located in the downtown area: Medical University of South Carolina Medical Center (MUSC), Ralph H. Johnson VA Medical Center, and Roper Hospital. MUSC is the state's first school of medicine, the largest medical university in the state, and the sixth-oldest continually operating school of medicine in the United States. The downtown medical district is experiencing rapid growth of biotechnology and medical research industries coupled with substantial expansions of all the major hospitals. Additionally, more expansions are planned or underway at another major hospital located in the West Ashley portion of the city: Bon Secours-St Francis Xavier Hospital. The Trident Regional Medical Center located in the City of North Charleston and East Cooper Regional Medical Center located in Mount Pleasant also serve the needs of residents of the city of Charleston.
rewrite: Charleston serves as the principal medical hub for the eastern region of the state. Its downtown area hosts several major hospitals, including the Medical University of South Carolina Medical Center (MUSC), the Ralph H. Johnson VA Medical Center, and Roper Hospital. MUSC constitutes the state's inaugural medical school, its largest medical university, and the nation's sixth-oldest continuously operating medical school. Additionally, the Trident Regional Medical Center in North Charleston and the East Cooper Regional Medical Center in Mount Pleasant provide essential healthcare services to Charleston residents.

input: Goetz set out an ambitious schedule. Universal-International became responsible for the American distribution of Rank's British productions, including such classics as David Lean's Great Expectations (1946) and Laurence Olivier's Hamlet (1948). Broadening its scope further, Universal-International branched out into the lucrative non-theatrical field, buying a majority stake in home-movie dealer Castle Films in 1947, and taking the company over entirely in 1951. For three decades, Castle would offer "highlights" reels from the Universal film library to home-movie enthusiasts and collectors. Goetz licensed Universal's pre–Universal-International film library to Jack Broeder's Realart Pictures for cinema re-release but Realart was not allowed to show the films on television.

input: An Ancient Chinese document from the 9th century referred to the northern Somali coast — which was then called "Berbera" by Arab geographers in reference to the region's "Berber" (Cushitic) inhabitants — as Po-pa-li. The first clear written reference of the sobriquet Somali, however, dates back to the 15th century. During the wars between the Sultanate of Ifat based at Zeila and the Solomonic Dynasty, the Abyssinian Emperor had one of his court officials compose a hymn celebrating a military victory over the Sultan of Ifat's eponymous troops.
rewrite: A ninth-century Chinese document identifies the northern Somali coast, termed "Berbera" by contemporary Arab geographers in acknowledgment of its Cushitic inhabitants, as Po-pa-li. The earliest definitive written usage of the demonym "Somali" emerges later, in a fifteenth-century context. Following a military triumph by the Abyssinian Emperor over the Ifat Sultanate based at Zeila, a court official was commissioned to compose a victory hymn referencing the defeated eponymous troops.

input: Germany's high-altitude needs were originally going to be filled by a 75 mm gun from Krupp, designed in collaboration with their Swedish counterpart Bofors, but the specifications were later amended to require much higher performance. In response Krupp's engineers presented a new 88 mm design, the FlaK 36. First used in Spain during the Spanish Civil War, the gun proved to be one of the best anti-aircraft guns in the world, as well as particularly deadly against light, medium, and even early heavy tanks.
rewrite: Germany’s requirement for a high-altitude anti-aircraft weapon was initially to be met by a 75 mm Krupp design, developed in cooperation with the Swedish firm Bofors. After specifications demanded significantly greater performance, Krupp engineers produced a new 88 mm model, the FlaK 36. First deployed in the Spanish Civil War, it proved to be among the world’s most effective anti-aircraft guns and demonstrated exceptional lethality against light, medium, and even early heavy tanks.

input: Women could not be professed to the Dominican religious life before the age of thirteen. The formula for profession contained in the Constitutions of Montargis Priory (1250) demands that nuns pledge obedience to God, the Blessed Virgin, their prioress and her successors according to the Rule of St. Augustine and the institute of the order, until death. The clothing of the sisters consisted of a white tunic and scapular, a leather belt, a black mantle, and a black veil. Candidates to profession were tested to reveal whether they were actually married women who had merely separated from their husbands. Their intellectual abilities were also tested. Nuns were to be silent in places of prayer, the cloister, the dormitory, and refectory. Silence was maintained unless the prioress granted an exception for a specific cause. Speaking was allowed in the common parlor, but it was subordinate to strict rules, and the prioress, subprioress or other senior nun had to be present.
rewrite: Admission to the Dominican religious life required women to be at least thirteen years of age. As stipulated in the 1250 Constitutions of Montargis Priory, the profession ceremony involved a vow of obedience until death to God, the Blessed Virgin, the prioress, and her successors, in accordance with the Rule of Saint Augustine and the order's institute. The prescribed habit comprised a white tunic and scapular, a leather belt, and a black mantle and veil. Prior to profession, candidates underwent examination to ascertain they were not merely separated from husbands and to assess their intellectual capacities. Strict silence was enjoined in the oratory, cloister, dormitory, and refectory, with exceptions permitted only by the prioress for a legitimate cause. While conversation was allowed in the common parlor, it remained subject to rigorous regulation and required the presence of the prioress, subprioress, or another senior nun.

input: Bipolar transistors are so named because they conduct by using both majority and minority carriers. The bipolar junction transistor, the first type of transistor to be mass-produced, is a combination of two junction diodes, and is formed of either a thin layer of p-type semiconductor sandwiched between two n-type semiconductors (an n–p–n transistor), or a thin layer of n-type semiconductor sandwiched between two p-type semiconductors (a p–n–p transistor). This construction produces two p–n junctions: a base–emitter junction and a base–collector junction, separated by a thin region of semiconductor known as the base region (two junction diodes wired together without sharing an intervening semiconducting region will not make a transistor).
rewrite: Bipolar transistors derive their name from their conduction mechanism, which involves both majority and minority charge carriers. The bipolar junction transistor, the earliest transistor type to achieve mass production, structurally comprises two junction diodes. It is fabricated either as a thin p-type semiconductor layer between two n-type semiconductors, forming an n–p–n transistor, or as a thin n-type layer between two p-type semiconductors, constituting a p–n–p transistor. This configuration creates two distinct p–n junctions: the base–emitter junction and the base–collector junction. These junctions are separated by a narrow semiconductor zone, the base region, which is essential for transistor action; merely connecting two diodes without this shared semiconducting region does not yield a transistor.

input: This steady economic progress has earned Armenia increasing support from international institutions. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), and other international financial institutions (IFIs) and foreign countries are extending considerable grants and loans. Loans to Armenia since 1993 exceed $1.1 billion. These loans are targeted at reducing the budget deficit and stabilizing the currency; developing private businesses; energy; agriculture; food processing; transportation; the health and education sectors; and ongoing rehabilitation in the earthquake zone. The government joined the World Trade Organization on 5 February 2003. But one of the main sources of foreign direct investments remains the Armenian diaspora, which finances major parts of the reconstruction of infrastructure and other public projects. Being a growing democratic state, Armenia also hopes to get more financial aid from the Western World.
rewrite: Armenia's sustained economic advancement has garnered growing support from international institutions. Significant grants and loans are being extended by entities including the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and other international financial institutions and foreign states. Since 1993, such loans have surpassed $1.1 billion. These funds are allocated to objectives including budget deficit reduction and currency stabilization; private sector development; the energy, agricultural, food processing, transportation, health, and education sectors; and ongoing rehabilitation in the earthquake zone. Following its accession to the World Trade Organization on 5 February 2003, Armenia anticipates further integration. Nonetheless, a primary source of foreign direct investment remains the Armenian diaspora, which finances substantial infrastructure reconstruction and public projects. As a developing democracy, Armenia also anticipates increased financial assistance from Western nations.

input: Typical American families did not fare as well, nor did those "wealthy-but-not wealthiest" families just beneath the pyramid's top. On the other hand, half of the poorest families did not have wealth declines at all during the crisis. The Federal Reserve surveyed 4,000 households between 2007 and 2009, and found that the total wealth of 63 percent of all Americans declined in that period. 77 percent of the richest families had a decrease in total wealth, while only 50 percent of those on the bottom of the pyramid suffered a decrease.
rewrite: The financial crisis differentially impacted American households by wealth stratum. While median and upper-middle class families experienced significant declines, approximately half of the poorest households saw no reduction in net worth. Federal Reserve data from 4,000 households surveyed between 2007 and 2009 indicate that 63% of all Americans suffered a wealth decrease. This burden was most pronounced among the affluent, with 77% of the wealthiest families affected, compared to 50% of those in the lowest wealth quintile.

input: The Earth contains about 434 billion cubic meters of growing stock forest, 47% of which is commercial. As an abundant, carbon-neutral renewable resource, woody materials have been of intense interest as a source of renewable energy. In 1991, approximately 3.5 cubic kilometers of wood were harvested. Dominant uses were for furniture and building construction.
rewrite: The global forest growing stock comprises approximately 434 billion cubic meters, with 47% classified as commercial. As a plentiful, carbon-neutral renewable resource, wood attracts significant interest for energy production. In 1991, harvest volumes reached roughly 3.5 cubic kilometers, primarily utilized for construction and furniture manufacturing.

input: The novel is renowned for its warmth and humor, despite dealing with the serious issues of rape and racial inequality. The narrator's father, Atticus Finch, has served as a moral hero for many readers and as a model of integrity for lawyers. One critic explains the novel's impact by writing, "In the twentieth century, To Kill a Mockingbird is probably the most widely read book dealing with race in America, and its protagonist, Atticus Finch, the most enduring fictional image of racial heroism."
rewrite: The novel is distinguished by its warmth and humor, notwithstanding its engagement with grave themes of racial injustice and sexual assault. Atticus Finch, the narrator's father, endures as a moral exemplar for readers and a professional ideal for attorneys. As one critic observes, the work is likely the most widely read twentieth-century American narrative confronting race, with Finch persisting as fiction's most enduring image of racial heroism.

input: Much of Tucson's economic development has been centered on the development of the University of Arizona, which is currently the second largest employer in the city. Davis-Monthan Air Force Base, located on the southeastern edge of the city, also provides many jobs for Tucson residents. Its presence, as well as the presence of the US Army Intelligence Center (Fort Huachuca, the largest employer in the region in nearby Sierra Vista), has led to the development of a significant number of high-tech industries, including government contractors, in the area. The city of Tucson is also a major hub for the Union Pacific Railroad's Sunset Route that links the Los Angeles ports with the South/Southeast regions of the country.
rewrite: Tucson's economic growth has been substantially shaped by the University of Arizona, the city's second-largest employer. Additionally, Davis-Monthan Air Force Base on the city's southeastern periphery provides significant employment. The presence of this base, along with the U.S. Army Intelligence Center at Fort Huachuca—the largest regional employer in nearby Sierra Vista—has catalyzed the emergence of a considerable high-tech sector, including numerous government contractors, within the area. Furthermore, Tucson serves as a primary nexus for the Union Pacific Railroad's Sunset Route, a critical freight corridor connecting the ports of Los Angeles with the South and Southeastern United States.

input: Under New York State's gradual abolition act of 1799, children of slave mothers were born to be eventually liberated but were held in indentured servitude until their mid-to-late twenties. Together with slaves freed by their masters after the Revolutionary War and escaped slaves, a significant free-black population gradually developed in Manhattan. Under such influential United States founders as Alexander Hamilton and John Jay, the New York Manumission Society worked for abolition and established the African Free School to educate black children. It was not until 1827 that slavery was completely abolished in the state, and free blacks struggled afterward with discrimination. New York interracial abolitionist activism continued; among its leaders were graduates of the African Free School. The city's black population reached more than 16,000 in 1840.
rewrite: Under New York State's 1799 Act for the Gradual Abolition of Slavery, children born to enslaved mothers were legally destined for eventual freedom but were bound by extended terms of indentured servitude, often until their mid-to-late twenties. This group, alongside individuals manumitted by their owners following the Revolutionary War and those who had escaped bondage, contributed to the emergence of a substantial free Black community in Manhattan. Influential figures such as Alexander Hamilton and John Jay supported the New York Manumission Society, which advocated for abolition and founded the African Free School to provide education for Black youth. Although slavery was fully abolished in the state in 1827, free Black citizens continued to confront significant discrimination. Interracial abolitionist efforts persisted in New York, led in part by alumni of the African Free School, as the city's Black population grew to over 16,000 by 1840.

There were 20 physicians per 100,000 persons in the early 2000s (decade).

input: Developed at roughly the same time as the USB 3.1 specification, but distinct from it, the USB Type-C Specification 1.0 was finalized in August 2014 and defines a new small reversible-plug connector for USB devices. The Type-C plug connects to both hosts and devices, replacing various Type-A and Type-B connectors and cables with a standard meant to be future-proof, similar to Apple Lightning and Thunderbolt. The 24-pin double-sided connector provides four power/ground pairs, two differential pairs for USB 2.0 data bus (though only one pair is implemented in a Type-C cable), four pairs for high-speed data bus, two "sideband use" pins, and two configuration pins for cable orientation detection, dedicated biphase mark code (BMC) configuration data channel, and VCONN +5 V power for active cables. Type-A and Type-B adaptors and cables are required for older devices to plug into Type-C hosts. Adapters and cables with a Type-C receptacle are not allowed.[citation needed]
rewrite: The USB Type-C Specification 1.0, finalized in August 2014, was developed concurrently with yet remains distinct from the USB 3.1 specification. It establishes a novel, compact, and reversible plug connector for universal serial bus devices. This plug interfaces with both hosts and devices, intending to supersede various Type-A and Type-B connectors with a singular, forward-compatible standard, analogous to proprietary interfaces like Apple's Lightning and Thunderbolt. The connector's 24-pin, double-sided design incorporates four power/ground pairs, two differential pairs for the USB 2.0 data bus (with only one pair typically utilized in a cable), four pairs for high-speed data buses, two pins reserved for sideband use, and two configuration pins. These configuration pins manage cable orientation detection, a dedicated biphase mark code (BMC) configuration data channel, and VCONN power for active cables. To ensure backward compatibility, Type-A and Type-B adapters are necessary for connecting legacy devices to Type-C hosts, whereas adapters featuring a Type-C receptacle are prohibited.

input: For over 40 years, the FBI crime lab in Quantico believed lead in bullets had unique chemical signatures. It analyzed the bullets with the goal of matching them chemically, not only to a single batch of ammunition coming out of a factory, but also to a single box of bullets. The National Academy of Sciences conducted an 18-month independent review of comparative bullet-lead analysis. In 2003, its National Research Council published a report whose conclusions called into question 30 years of FBI testimony. It found the analytic model used by the FBI for interpreting results was deeply flawed, and the conclusion, that bullet fragments could be matched to a box of ammunition, was so overstated that it was misleading under the rules of evidence. One year later, the FBI decided to stop doing bullet lead analysis.
rewrite: For more than four decades, the FBI crime laboratory in Quantico operated under the premise that lead composition within bullets possessed unique chemical signatures. The laboratory’s analytical objective was to chemically match bullet fragments not merely to a specific production batch of ammunition, but to an individual box. An independent 18-month review of comparative bullet-lead analysis was subsequently undertaken by the National Academy of Sciences. In 2003, its National Research Council issued a report that critically challenged three decades of FBI expert testimony. The report determined the FBI’s statistical model for interpreting analytical results was fundamentally flawed and concluded that asserting a definitive match between a fragment and a particular box of ammunition constituted a significant overstatement, rendering such testimony misleading under evidentiary standards. Consequently, the FBI discontinued this analytical method in 2004.

input: Some 97 percent of male BYU graduates and 32 percent of female graduates took a hiatus from their undergraduate studies at one point to serve as LDS missionaries. In October 2012, the LDS Church announced at its general conference that young men could serve a mission after they turn 18 and have graduated from high school, rather than after age 19 under the old policy. Many young men would often attend a semester or two of higher education prior to beginning missionary service. This policy change will likely impact what has been the traditional incoming freshman class at BYU. Female students may now begin their missionary service anytime after turning 19, rather than age 21 under the previous policy.
