A hardwood fingerboard sits on top of or is flush with the sound table. Very old instruments may use wooden tuning pegs, while newer instruments tend to use geared metal tuners. The bridge is a movable length of hardwood. A pickguard is glued below the sound hole under the strings. European roundbacks commonly use a 13-inch scale instead of the 13.876 common on archtop Mandolins.
rewrite: The Neapolitan mandolin features an almond-shaped, bowl-like body formed from curved wooden ribs. Its soundboard is intentionally bent and angled in two planes to withstand the tension of eight metal strings arranged in four paired courses. A hardwood fingerboard is positioned atop or flush with the soundboard. Historically, instruments employed wooden friction pegs, though modern versions typically utilize geared metal tuners. The bridge consists of a movable hardwood component, and a pickguard is affixed beneath the soundhole. Notably, European roundback mandolins commonly employ a 13-inch scale length, contrasting with the 13.876-inch scale frequently found on archtop models.

input: Midtown Raleigh is a residential and commercial area just North of the I-440 Beltline and is part of North Raleigh. It is roughly framed by Glenwood/Creedmoor Road to the West, Wake Forest Road to the East, and Millbrook Road to the North. It includes shopping centers such as North Hills and Crabtree Valley Mall. It also includes North Hills Park and part of the Raleigh Greenway System. The term was coined by the Greater Raleigh Chamber of Commerce, developer John Kane and planning director Mitchell Silver. The News & Observer newspaper started using the term for marketing purposes only. The Midtown Raleigh Alliance was founded on July 25, 2011 as a way for community leaders to promote the area.
rewrite: Midtown Raleigh, a residential and commercial district situated north of the I-440 Beltline within North Raleigh, is bounded approximately by Glenwood/Creedmoor Road to the west, Wake Forest Road to the east, and Millbrook Road to the north. The area encompasses major commercial centers, including North Hills and Crabtree Valley Mall, as well as North Hills Park and a segment of the Raleigh Greenway System. The designation "Midtown Raleigh" originated from a collaboration between the Greater Raleigh Chamber of Commerce, developer John Kane, and planning director Mitchell Silver. Subsequently adopted for marketing by *The News & Observer*, the area's promotion was further institutionalized with the establishment of the Midtown Raleigh Alliance on July 25, 2011.

input: During the fighting, the Communards killed c. 500 people, including the Archbishop of Paris, and burned down many government buildings, including the Tuileries Palace and the Hotel de Ville. Communards captured with weapons were routinely shot by the army and Government troops killed from 7,000–30,000 Communards in the fighting and in massacres of men, women, and children during and after the Commune. More recent histories, based on studies of the number buried in Paris cemeteries and in mass graves after the fall of the Commune, put the number killed at between 6,000 and 10,000. Twenty-six courts were established to try more than 40,000 people who had been arrested, which took until 1875 and imposed 95 death sentences, of which 23 were inflicted. Forced labour for life was imposed on 251 people, 1,160 people were transported to "a fortified place" and 3,417 people were transported. About 20,000 Communards were held in prison hulks until released in 1872 and a great many Communards fled abroad to England, Switzerland, Belgium or the United States. The survivors were amnestied by a bill introduced by Gambetta in 1880 and allowed to return.
rewrite: The conflict witnessed the execution of approximately 500 individuals by the Communards, among them the Archbishop of Paris, alongside the deliberate destruction of key governmental structures such as the Tuileries Palace and the Hôtel de Ville. In response, governmental forces summarily executed captured armed Communards, with estimates of those killed during the combat and subsequent massacres—encompassing men, women, and children—ranging from 7,000 to 30,000. Contemporary historical scholarship, drawing upon analyses of interments in Parisian cemeteries and mass graves following the Commune’s suppression, revises this figure to between 6,000 and 10,000 fatalities. Judicial proceedings, extending until 1875, adjudicated over 40,000 detainees through twenty-six tribunals, resulting in 95 death sentences (23 carried out), 251 life sentences of forced labor, and the deportation of 1,160 individuals to fortified locations alongside 3,417 others transported. Approximately 20,000 Communards were detained aboard prison hulks until 1872, while many others sought exile in England, Switzerland, Belgium, or the United States. Ultimately, the surviving Communards received amnesty through legislation introduced by Gambetta in 1880, permitting their repatriation.

input: In the Roman Catholic Church, obstinate and willful manifest heresy is considered to spiritually cut one off from the Church, even before excommunication is incurred. The Codex Justinianus (1:5:12) defines "everyone who is not devoted to the Catholic Church and to our Orthodox holy Faith" a heretic. The Church had always dealt harshly with strands of Christianity that it considered heretical, but before the 11th century these tended to centre around individual preachers or small localised sects, like Arianism, Pelagianism, Donatism, Marcionism and Montanism. The diffusion of the almost Manichaean sect of Paulicians westwards gave birth to the famous 11th and 12th century heresies of Western Europe. The first one was that of Bogomils in modern day Bosnia, a sort of sanctuary between Eastern and Western Christianity. By the 11th century, more organised groups such as the Patarini, the Dulcinians, the Waldensians and the Cathars were beginning to appear in the towns and cities of northern Italy, southern France and Flanders.
rewrite: Within the Roman Catholic Church, obstinate and willfully manifest heresy is understood to effect a spiritual separation from the Church antecedent to any formal sentence of excommunication. This principle finds legal expression in the *Codex Justinianus* (1:5:12), which designates as heretical "everyone who is not devoted to the Catholic Church and to our Orthodox holy Faith." Historically, the Church responded with severity to Christian movements deemed heterodox. Prior to the eleventh century, however, such deviations typically coalesced around individual theologians or localized sects, including Arianism, Pelagianism, Donatism, Marcionism, and Montanism. The westward diffusion of the Paulicians, a sect with quasi-Manichaean doctrines, precipitated the more substantial heresies of the eleventh and twelfth centuries in Western Europe. Initially, this included the Bogomils in the region of modern Bosnia, which served as an interstitial zone between Eastern and Western Christendom. By the eleventh century, more organized groups, such as the Patarini, Dulcinians, Waldensians, and Cathars, emerged within the urban centers of northern Italy, southern France, and Flanders.

input: Relying exclusively on unedited machine translation, however, ignores the fact that communication in human language is context-embedded and that it takes a person to comprehend the context of the original text with a reasonable degree of probability. It is certainly true that even purely human-generated translations are prone to error; therefore, to ensure that a machine-generated translation will be useful to a human being and that publishable-quality translation is achieved, such translations must be reviewed and edited by a human.
rewrite: Sole reliance on unedited machine translation overlooks the inherently contextual nature of human language, which requires human comprehension to interpret the source text with reasonable accuracy. While even human translations are fallible, to ensure a machine-generated translation achieves publishable quality and utility for a human reader, it necessitates mandatory review and editing by a person.

input: During the same court battle, Viacom won a court ruling requiring YouTube to hand over 12 terabytes of data detailing the viewing habits of every user who has watched videos on the site. The decision was criticized by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the court ruling "a setback to privacy rights". In June 2010, Viacom's lawsuit against Google was rejected in a summary judgment, with U.S. federal Judge Louis L. Stanton stating that Google was protected by provisions of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Viacom announced its intention to appeal the ruling.
rewrite: In the course of concurrent litigation, Viacom secured a judicial order compelling YouTube to provide 12 terabytes of data documenting the viewing histories of all its users. This order was denounced by the Electronic Frontier Foundation as a significant erosion of privacy rights. Subsequently, in June 2010, Viacom's suit against Google was dismissed via summary judgment. U.S. District Judge Louis L. Stanton held that Google qualified for safe harbor protections under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Viacom promptly declared its plan to appeal the decision.

input: The largest and bloodiest American battle came at Okinawa, as the U.S. sought airbases for 3,000 B-29 bombers and 240 squadrons of B-17 bombers for the intense bombardment of Japan's home islands in preparation for a full-scale invasion in late 1945. The Japanese, with 115,000 troops augmented by thousands of civilians on the heavily populated island, did not resist on the beaches—their strategy was to maximize the number of soldier and Marine casualties, and naval losses from Kamikaze attacks. After an intense bombardment the Americans landed on 1 April 1945 and declared victory on 21 June. The supporting naval forces were the targets for 4,000 sorties, many by Kamikaze suicide planes. U.S. losses totaled 38 ships of all types sunk and 368 damaged with 4,900 sailors killed. The Americans suffered 75,000 casualties on the ground; 94% of the Japanese soldiers died along with many civilians.
rewrite: The Battle of Okinawa stands as the largest and most costly engagement for American forces in the Pacific Theater. The United States sought to secure airfields to support an extensive strategic bombing campaign against the Japanese home islands, utilizing thousands of B-29 and B-24 bombers in preparation for a planned invasion. Japanese forces, numbering approximately 115,000 soldiers and supplemented by a large civilian population, eschewed beachhead defenses. Their strategy aimed instead to inflict maximum casualties on American infantry and naval assets, the latter through concentrated Kamikaze attacks. Following a preliminary bombardment, U.S. forces commenced amphibious landings on April 1, 1945, securing the island by June 21. The campaign resulted in severe losses: American ground forces sustained roughly 75,000 casualties, while the supporting fleet endured 4,900 sailors killed and extensive ship damage from over 4,000 Kamikaze sorties. Japanese military fatalities exceeded 94%, with significant civilian deaths.

input: Plymouth is home to the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom (MBA) which conducts research in all areas of the marine sciences. The Plymouth Marine Laboratory is an offshoot of the MBA. Together with the National Marine Aquarium, the Sir Alister Hardy Foundation for Ocean Sciences, Plymouth University's Marine Institute and the Diving Diseases Research Centre, these marine-related organisations form the Plymouth Marine Sciences Partnership. The Plymouth Marine Laboratory, which focuses on global issues of climate change and sustainability. It monitors the effects of ocean acidity on corals and shellfish and reports the results to the UK government. It also cultivates algae that could be used to make biofuels or in the treatment of waste water by using technology such as photo-bioreactors. It works alongside the Boots Group to investigate the use of algae in skin care protects, taking advantage of the chemicals they contain that adapt to protect themselves from the sun.
rewrite: The city of Plymouth hosts the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom (MBA), an institution dedicated to comprehensive research across the marine sciences. An affiliated entity, the Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML), operates alongside other key organisations including the National Marine Aquarium, the Sir Alister Hardy Foundation for Ocean Science, the University of Plymouth’s Marine Institute, and the Diving Diseases Research Centre. Collectively, these bodies constitute the Plymouth Marine Sciences Partnership. The PML specifically addresses global challenges of climate change and sustainability. Its research activities include monitoring the impacts of ocean acidification on coral and shellfish populations, with findings reported to the UK government. Furthermore, the laboratory cultivates algae via technologies such as photo-bioreactors for potential applications in biofuel production and wastewater treatment. In collaboration with the Boots Group, it also investigates the utilisation of photoprotective compounds derived from algae for skincare products.

input: Hellenistic poets now sought patronage from kings, and wrote works in their honor. The scholars at the libraries in Alexandria and Pergamon focused on the collection, cataloging, and literary criticism of classical Athenian works and ancient Greek myths. The poet-critic Callimachus, a staunch elitist, wrote hymns equating Ptolemy II to Zeus and Apollo. He promoted short poetic forms such as the epigram, epyllion and the iambic and attacked epic as base and common ("big book, big evil" was his doctrine). He also wrote a massive catalog of the holdings of the library of Alexandria, the famous Pinakes. Callimachus was extremely influential in his time and also for the development of Augustan poetry. Another poet, Apollonius of Rhodes, attempted to revive the epic for the Hellenistic world with his Argonautica. He had been a student of Callimachus and later became chief librarian (prostates) of the library of Alexandria, Apollonius and Callimachus spent much of their careers feuding with each other. Pastoral poetry also thrived during the Hellenistic era, Theocritus was a major poet who popularized the genre.
rewrite: During the Hellenistic period, poets increasingly turned to royal courts for patronage, composing encomiastic works dedicated to their sovereign benefactors. Concurrently, scholars at institutions such as the libraries of Alexandria and Pergamon dedicated themselves to the systematic collection, cataloging, and critical analysis of classical Athenian texts and ancient Greek mythology. A central figure was the poet-critic Callimachus, a pronounced elitist who composed hymns identifying Ptolemy II with deities such as Zeus and Apollo. He championed refined, concise poetic forms—including the epigram, epyllion, and iambic—while denigrating epic poetry as aesthetically vulgar, famously declaring "a big book is a big evil." His scholarly output included the *Pinakes*, a comprehensive catalog of the Alexandrian library's holdings. Callimachus exerted profound contemporary influence and significantly shaped subsequent Augustan poetry. His pupil, Apollonius of Rhodes, countered this stance by seeking to revive the epic tradition through his *Argonautica*; he later served as chief librarian (*prostates*) of Alexandria, and their professional rivalry was protracted and well-documented. Additionally, the Hellenistic era witnessed the flourishing of pastoral poetry, largely due to the innovations and popularity of Theocritus, the genre's foremost exponent.

input: Chopin was educated in the tradition of Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart and Clementi; he used Clementi's piano method with his own students. He was also influenced by Hummel's development of virtuoso, yet Mozartian, piano technique. He cited Bach and Mozart as the two most important composers in shaping his musical outlook. Chopin's early works are in the style of the "brilliant" keyboard pieces of his era as exemplified by the works of Ignaz Moscheles, Friedrich Kalkbrenner, and others. Less direct in the earlier period are the influences of Polish folk music and of Italian opera. Much of what became his typical style of ornamentation (for example, his fioriture) is taken from singing. His melodic lines were increasingly reminiscent of the modes and features of the music of his native country, such as drones.
rewrite: Chopin’s education was grounded in the classical tradition of Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, and Clementi, whose piano method he employed in his own teaching. He further absorbed Hummel’s synthesis of virtuosic and Mozartian piano technique. Chopin identified Bach and Mozart as the foremost influences on his musical philosophy. His initial compositions align with the contemporary “brilliant” style for the keyboard, as seen in the works of figures like Ignaz Moscheles and Friedrich Kalkbrenner. During this early period, the impact of Polish folk music and Italian opera was less direct but discernible. A hallmark of his mature style is ornamental figuration, particularly fioriture, derived from vocal practice. His melodies increasingly incorporated modal traits and devices, such as drones, evocative of the music of Poland.

input: Work is undertaken from an early age by vast numbers of children in the world and may have a natural place in growing up. Work can contribute to the well-being of children in a variety of ways; children often choose to work to improve their lives, both in the short- and long-term. At the material level, children’s work often contributes to producing food or earning income that benefits themselves and their families; and such income is especially important when the families are poor. Work can provide an escape from debilitating poverty, sometimes by allowing a young person to move away from an impoverished environment. Young people often enjoy their work, especially paid work, or when work involves the company of peers. Even when work is intensive and enforced, children often find ways to combine their work with play.
rewrite: A significant proportion of children worldwide engage in labor from an early age, a practice which may constitute a normative element of development. Such employment can enhance child well-being through multiple pathways, as children frequently elect to work for immediate and future life improvement. Materially, their labor often aids in food production or income generation, thereby supporting both the children and their households; this economic contribution proves particularly critical under conditions of familial poverty. Work may further offer a means to overcome severe deprivation, potentially enabling youth to transition from impoverished circumstances. Many adolescents derive satisfaction from their labor, particularly when it is remunerated or occurs alongside peers. Even in instances of demanding or compulsory work, children commonly integrate elements of play into their activities.

input: The 18th century saw a huge growth in the number of drinking establishments, primarily due to the introduction of gin. Gin was brought to England by the Dutch after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and became very popular after the government created a market for "cuckoo grain" or "cuckoo malt" that was unfit to be used in brewing and distilling by allowing unlicensed gin and beer production, while imposing a heavy duty on all imported spirits. As thousands of gin-shops sprang up all over England, brewers fought back by increasing the number of alehouses. By 1740 the production of gin had increased to six times that of beer and because of its cheapness it became popular with the poor, leading to the so-called Gin Craze. Over half of the 15,000 drinking establishments in London were gin shops.
rewrite: The eighteenth century witnessed a significant proliferation of drinking establishments, largely attributable to the rise of gin consumption. Introduced to England from the Dutch following the Glorious Revolution of 1688, gin's popularity surged after governmental policies created a market for substandard "cuckoo malt" by permitting unlicensed domestic production while heavily taxing imported spirits. In response to the thousands of ensuing gin-shops, brewers expanded the number of alehouses. By 1740, gin output was sixfold that of beer. Its low cost drove widespread consumption among the impoverished, creating the period known as the Gin Craze. In London, gin shops constituted over half of the city's 15,000 drinking venues.

input: The east coast Appalachian system, originally forest covered, is relatively low and narrow and is bordered on the southeast and south by an important coastal plain. The Cordilleran system on the western side of the continent is lofty, broad and complicated having two branches, the Rocky Mountain System and the Pacific Mountain System. In between these mountain systems lie the Intermontaine Plateaus. Both the Columbia River and Colorado River rise far inland near the easternmost members of the Cordilleran system, and flow through plateaus and intermontaine basins to the ocean. Heavy forests cover the northwest coast, but elsewhere trees are found only on the higher ranges below the Alpine region. The intermontane valleys, plateaus and basins range from treeless to desert with the most arid region being in the southwest.
rewrite: The Appalachian system along the eastern coast, originally forested, is comparatively low and narrow, bounded to the southeast and south by a significant coastal plain. In contrast, the western Cordilleran system is elevated, broad, and structurally complex, comprising two primary branches: the Rocky Mountain System and the Pacific Mountain System. Situated between these major systems are the Intermontane Plateaus. Both the Columbia and Colorado Rivers originate far inland near the easternmost components of the Cordilleras, traversing plateaus and intermontane basins en route to the ocean. Dense forests characterize the northwestern coast, while elsewhere trees are largely confined to higher elevations below the alpine zone. The intermontane valleys, plateaus, and basins vary from treeless to desert conditions, with the most arid region located in the southwest.

input: Philip V, who came to power when Doson died in 221 BC, was the last Macedonian ruler with both the talent and the opportunity to unite Greece and preserve its independence against the "cloud rising in the west": the ever-increasing power of Rome. He was known as "the darling of Hellas". Under his auspices the Peace of Naupactus (217 BC) brought the latest war between Macedon and the Greek leagues (the social war 220-217) to an end, and at this time he controlled all of Greece except Athens, Rhodes and Pergamum.
rewrite: Ascending to the throne following the death of Antigonus III Doson in 221 BC, Philip V was the final Macedonian monarch possessing the requisite capability and circumstance to unify Greece and safeguard its autonomy against the expanding Roman threat. Hailed as "the darling of Hellas," he brokered the Peace of Naupactus in 217 BC, concluding the Social War. At this juncture, his hegemony extended over most of Greece, with the notable exceptions of Athens, Rhodes, and Pergamum.

input: Many were surprised by these changes to the CBC schedule, which were apparently intended to attract a younger audience to the network; some suggested they might alienate the core CBC viewership. Another note of criticism was made when the network decided to move The National in some time zones to simulcast the American version of The One over the summer. This later became a moot point, as The One was taken off the air after two weeks after extremely low American and Canadian ratings, and the newscast resumed its regular schedule.
rewrite: The alterations to the CBC schedule, ostensibly designed to attract a younger demographic, elicited surprise and criticism for potentially alienating the network's core viewership. Further critique arose when *The National* was displaced in certain time zones to simulcast the American program *The One* during the summer. This decision became inconsequential, however, as *The One* was cancelled after two weeks due to exceedingly poor ratings in both nations, allowing the newscast to resume its customary broadcast schedule.

input: Natural theology was not a unified doctrine, and while some such as Louis Agassiz were strongly opposed to the ideas in the book, others sought a reconciliation in which evolution was seen as purposeful. In the Church of England, some liberal clergymen interpreted natural selection as an instrument of God's design, with the cleric Charles Kingsley seeing it as "just as noble a conception of Deity". In the second edition of January 1860, Darwin quoted Kingsley as "a celebrated cleric", and added the phrase "by the Creator" to the closing sentence, which from then on read "life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one". While some commentators have taken this as a concession to religion that Darwin later regretted, Darwin's view at the time was of God creating life through the laws of nature, and even in the first edition there are several references to "creation".
rewrite: Natural theology did not constitute a unified doctrine, and reactions to Darwin’s work varied significantly. While figures like Louis Agassiz vehemently opposed its ideas, others sought a reconciliation, viewing evolution as a purposeful process. Within the Church of England, certain liberal clergymen interpreted natural selection as an instrument of divine design. The cleric Charles Kingsley, for instance, regarded it as “just as noble a conception of Deity.” Darwin incorporated this perspective into the second edition (January 1860), quoting Kingsley as “a celebrated cleric” and inserting the phrase “by the Creator” into the closing sentence. The revised passage described life as “having been originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one.” Although some commentators interpret this as a religious concession Darwin later regretted, his contemporary view held that God created life through natural laws. References to “creation” were, in fact, present even in the first edition.

input: The concept of a group arose from the study of polynomial equations, starting with Évariste Galois in the 1830s. After contributions from other fields such as number theory and geometry, the group notion was generalized and firmly established around 1870. Modern group theory—an active mathematical discipline—studies groups in their own right.a[›] To explore groups, mathematicians have devised various notions to break groups into smaller, better-understandable pieces, such as subgroups, quotient groups and simple groups. In addition to their abstract properties, group theorists also study the different ways in which a group can be expressed concretely (its group representations), both from a theoretical and a computational point of view. A theory has been developed for finite groups, which culminated with the classification of finite simple groups announced in 1983.aa[›] Since the mid-1980s, geometric group theory, which studies finitely generated groups as geometric objects, has become a particularly active area in group theory.
rewrite: The concept of a group originated in the study of polynomial equations, notably through the work of Évariste Galois in the 1830s. Following subsequent contributions from fields such as number theory and geometry, the notion was generalized and firmly established as an abstract algebraic structure around 1870. Modern group theory, now a major mathematical discipline, investigates groups as entities in their own right. To analyze their structure, mathematicians employ concepts like subgroups, quotient groups, and simple groups to decompose groups into more comprehensible components. Research encompasses both the abstract properties of groups and their concrete realizations, known as group representations, examined from theoretical and computational perspectives. A significant achievement is the classification of finite simple groups, largely completed by 1983. Since the mid-1980s, geometric group theory, which interprets finitely generated groups as geometric objects, has emerged as a particularly dynamic subfield.

input: Many visitors to BYU, and Utah Valley as a whole, report being surprised by the culturally conservative environment. Brigham Young University's Honor Code, which all BYU students agree to follow as a condition of studying at BYU, prohibits the consumption of alcoholic beverages, tobacco, etc. As mentioned earlier, The Princeton Review has rated BYU the "#1 stone cold sober school" in the nation for several years running, an honor which the late LDS Church president Gordon B. Hinckley had commented on with pride. BYU's 2014 "#1 stone cold" sober rating marked the 17th year in a row that the school had earned that rating. BYU has used this and other honors awarded to the school to advertise itself to prospective students, showing that BYU is proud of the rating. According to the Uniform Crime Reports, incidents of crime in Provo are lower than the national average. Murder is rare, and robberies are about 1/10 the national average. Business Insider rated BYU as the #1 safest college campus in the nation.
rewrite: Visitors to Brigham Young University and the broader Utah Valley frequently express surprise at the region's pronounced cultural conservatism. This environment is formally codified at BYU through its Honor Code, a set of behavioral standards to which all students must adhere as a condition of enrollment. The code explicitly prohibits the consumption of alcohol and tobacco, among other substances. This policy contributes directly to the university’s consistent recognition by The Princeton Review as the nation’s "#1 stone cold sober school," a distinction it held for seventeen consecutive years, including 2014. The late LDS Church President Gordon B. Hinckley notably expressed pride in this accolade, and the university actively promotes it in recruitment materials. This climate of strict behavioral standards correlates with a notably low crime environment. According to Uniform Crime Reports, Provo experiences crime rates below the national average, with murder being rare and robberies occurring at approximately one-tenth the national rate. Consequently, Business Insider has ranked BYU as the safest college campus in the United States.

input: Grazing organisms may also kill their prey species, but this is seldom the case. While some herbivores like zooplankton live on unicellular phytoplankton and therefore, by the individualized nature of the organism, kill their prey, many only eat a small part of the plant. Grazing livestock may pull some grass out at the roots, but most is simply grazed upon, allowing the plant to regrow once again. Kelp is frequently grazed in subtidal kelp forests, but regrows at the base of the blade continuously to cope with browsing pressure. Animals may also be 'grazed' upon; female mosquitos land on hosts briefly to gain sufficient proteins for the development of their offspring. Starfish may be grazed on, being capable of regenerating lost arms.
rewrite: Grazing organisms occasionally cause mortality in their prey species, though this outcome is infrequent. Certain herbivores, such as zooplankton feeding on unicellular phytoplankton, inherently kill their individualized prey. However, many grazers consume only a portion of the plant, permitting regrowth. For instance, livestock might uproot some grasses, yet most plants are merely cropped and subsequently recover. In subtidal kelp forests, kelp withstands browsing through continuous basal regrowth of its blades. The concept of grazing extends to animals as well. Female mosquitoes engage in brief feeding on hosts to procure proteins for offspring development, while starfish can regenerate limbs lost to grazing pressures.

input: On April 26, 1496 King John I Albert granted the Privilege of Piotrków (Polish: "Przywilej piotrkowski", "konstytucja piotrkowska" or "statuty piotrkowskie"), increasing the nobility's feudal power over serfs. It bound the peasant to the land, as only one son (not the eldest) was permitted to leave the village; townsfolk (Polish: "mieszczaństwo") were prohibited from owning land; and positions in the Church hierarchy could be given only to nobles.
rewrite: Granted by King John I Albert on April 26, 1496, the Privilege of Piotrków substantially augmented the nobility's feudal authority. It legally bound peasants to the land, permitting only one non‑eldest son to depart his village. Furthermore, it prohibited townspeople from owning land and reserved positions within the Church hierarchy exclusively for the nobility.

input: Christoph Waltz was cast in the role of Franz Oberhauser, though he refused to comment on the nature of the part. It was later revealed with the film's release that he is Ernst Stavro Blofeld. Dave Bautista was cast as Mr. Hinx after producers sought an actor with a background in contact sports. After casting Bérénice Lim Marlohe, a relative newcomer, as Sévérine in Skyfall, Mendes consciously sought out a more experienced actor for the role of Madeleine Swann, ultimately casting Léa Seydoux in the role. Monica Bellucci joined the cast as Lucia Sciarra, becoming, at the age of fifty, the oldest actress to be cast as a Bond girl. In a separate interview with Danish website Euroman, Jesper Christensen revealed he would be reprising his role as Mr. White from Casino Royale and Quantum of Solace. Christensen's character was reportedly killed off in a scene intended to be used as an epilogue to Quantum of Solace, before it was removed from the final cut of the film, enabling his return in Spectre.
rewrite: The casting of Christoph Waltz as Franz Oberhauser was initially conducted without public commentary on the character's specifics; his eventual portrayal as Ernst Stavro Blofeld was only confirmed upon the film's release. For the role of Mr. Hinx, producers specifically sought an actor with a background in contact sports, leading to the selection of Dave Bautista. Following the casting of relative newcomer Bérénice Lim Marlohe in the previous film, director Sam Mendes deliberately pursued a more seasoned performer for Madeleine Swann, ultimately appointing Léa Seydoux. Monica Bellucci joined the production as Lucia Sciarra, thereby becoming, at age fifty, the eldest actress cast as a Bond girl. In a separate development, Jesper Christensen confirmed in an interview with the Danish publication *Euroman* that he would reprise his role as Mr. White. His character's return was facilitated by the deletion of a scene intended as an epilogue to *Quantum of Solace*, which had depicted his apparent death.

input: Although John was the Count of Poitou and therefore the rightful feudal lord over the Lusignans, they could legitimately appeal John's actions in France to his own feudal lord, Philip. Hugh did exactly this in 1201 and Philip summoned John to attend court in Paris in 1202, citing the Le Goulet treaty to strengthen his case. John was unwilling to weaken his authority in western France in this way. He argued that he need not attend Philip's court because of his special status as the Duke of Normandy, who was exempt by feudal tradition from being called to the French court. Philip argued that he was summoning John not as the Duke of Normandy, but as the Count of Poitou, which carried no such special status. When John still refused to come, Philip declared John in breach of his feudal responsibilities, reassigned all of John's lands that fell under the French crown to Arthur – with the exception of Normandy, which he took back for himself – and began a fresh war against John.
rewrite: Despite his position as Count of Poitou, which established him as the legitimate feudal lord over the Lusignans, John’s governance in France remained subject to appeal to his own superior, King Philip II. Hugh IX de Lusignan exercised this right in 1201, prompting Philip to summon John to the royal court in Paris in 1202, invoking the Treaty of Le Goulet to substantiate the demand. John, unwilling to compromise his authority in western France, refused. He contended that his role as Duke of Normandy traditionally exempted him from such summonses to the French crown. Philip countered that the citation pertained specifically to John’s status as Count of Poitou, which carried no equivalent privilege. Following John’s persistent refusal, Philip declared him in breach of his feudal obligations. Consequently, Philip reassigned all John’s French lands—save Normandy, which he reclaimed directly—to Arthur of Brittany, thereby initiating renewed hostilities.

input: The Jordan River runs along the Jordan Rift Valley, from Mount Hermon through the Hulah Valley and the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, the lowest point on the surface of the Earth. Further south is the Arabah, ending with the Gulf of Eilat, part of the Red Sea. Unique to Israel and the Sinai Peninsula are makhteshim, or erosion cirques. The largest makhtesh in the world is Ramon Crater in the Negev, which measures 40 by 8 kilometers (25 by 5 mi). A report on the environmental status of the Mediterranean basin states that Israel has the largest number of plant species per square meter of all the countries in the basin.
rewrite: The Jordan River flows southward through the Jordan Rift Valley, originating at Mount Hermon and traversing the Hulah Valley and the Sea of Galilee before terminating at the Dead Sea, the Earth's lowest terrestrial point. The valley continues south as the Arabah, concluding at the Gulf of Eilat on the Red Sea. Geologically distinctive to this region are makhteshim, or erosion cirques, with the Negev's Ramon Crater being the world's largest at 40 by 8 kilometers. Furthermore, Israel exhibits the highest density of plant species per unit area within the Mediterranean basin.

input: Manhattan Island is linked to New York City's outer boroughs and New Jersey by several tunnels as well. The Lincoln Tunnel, which carries 120,000 vehicles a day under the Hudson River between New Jersey and Midtown Manhattan, is the busiest vehicular tunnel in the world. The tunnel was built instead of a bridge to allow unfettered passage of large passenger and cargo ships that sailed through New York Harbor and up the Hudson River to Manhattan's piers. The Holland Tunnel, connecting Lower Manhattan to Jersey City, New Jersey, was the world's first mechanically ventilated vehicular tunnel when it opened in 1927. The Queens-Midtown Tunnel, built to relieve congestion on the bridges connecting Manhattan with Queens and Brooklyn, was the largest non-federal project in its time when it was completed in 1940. President Franklin D. Roosevelt was the first person to drive through it. The Hugh L. Carey Tunnel runs underneath Battery Park and connects the Financial District at the southern tip of Manhattan to Red Hook in Brooklyn.
rewrite: Manhattan Island is connected to the outer boroughs of New York City and to New Jersey via a series of significant vehicular tunnels. The Lincoln Tunnel, accommodating approximately 120,000 vehicles daily beneath the Hudson River between New Jersey and Midtown Manhattan, is the world's busiest vehicular tunnel. Its subterranean design was selected over a bridge to preserve unimpeded access for large passenger and cargo vessels navigating New York Harbor and the Hudson River to Manhattan's piers. The Holland Tunnel, linking Lower Manhattan to Jersey City, New Jersey, pioneered mechanical ventilation for vehicular tunnels upon its 1927 opening. To alleviate bridge congestion between Manhattan, Queens, and Brooklyn, the Queens-Midtown Tunnel was constructed; it was the largest non-federal project of its era upon completion in 1940, with President Franklin D. Roosevelt as its first motorist. Finally, the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel passes under Battery Park, connecting Manhattan's Financial District to Red Hook in Brooklyn.

input: However, civil war flared again when the Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Lepidus and Mark Antony failed. The ambitious Octavian built a power base of patronage and then launched a campaign against Mark Antony. At the naval Battle of Actium off the coast of Greece, Octavian decisively defeated Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian was granted a series of special powers including sole "imperium" within the city of Rome, permanent consular powers and credit for every Roman military victory, since all future generals were assumed to be acting under his command. In 27 BC Octavian was granted the use of the names "Augustus" and "Princeps", indicating his primary status above all other Romans, and he adopted the title "Imperator Caesar" making him the first Roman Emperor.
rewrite: The resumption of civil conflict followed the dissolution of the Second Triumvirate, comprising Octavian, Lepidus, and Mark Antony. Octavian, having consolidated authority through extensive patronage, initiated hostilities against Antony. Their decisive confrontation occurred at the naval Battle of Actium near Greece, where Octavian vanquished the combined forces of Antony and Cleopatra. Subsequently, the Senate conferred extraordinary authorities upon Octavian, including exclusive *imperium* within Rome, permanent consular powers, and formal credit for all military victories, as commanders were thereafter deemed his subordinates. In 27 BC, he accepted the honorific titles "Augustus" and "Princeps," denoting supreme preeminence, and adopted the designation "Imperator Caesar," thereby establishing the principate and his position as the first Roman emperor.

input: On June 14, 1987, about 5,000 people gathered again at Freedom Monument in Riga, and laid flowers to commemorate the anniversary of Stalin's mass deportation of Latvians in 1941. This was the first large demonstration in the Baltic republics to commemorate the anniversary of an event contrary to official Soviet history. The authorities did not crack down on demonstrators, which encouraged more and larger demonstrations throughout the Baltic States. The next major anniversary after the August 23 Molotov Pact demonstration was on November 18, the date of Latvia’s independence in 1918. On November 18, 1987, hundreds of police and civilian militiamen cordoned off the central square to prevent any demonstration at Freedom Monument, but thousands lined the streets of Riga in silent protest regardless.
rewrite: On June 14, 1987, approximately 5,000 individuals assembled at the Freedom Monument in Riga to commemorate the anniversary of the 1941 mass deportations of Latvians under Stalin. This gathering constituted the first large-scale public demonstration within the Baltic republics to formally mark a historical event contravening official Soviet narratives. The state’s decision not to suppress this assembly encouraged subsequent and larger demonstrations across the region. Following a major demonstration on August 23 marking the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the next significant anniversary was November 18, Latvia’s Independence Day. On that date in 1987, authorities deployed hundreds of police and militia to cordon off the central square, intending to prevent a demonstration at the monument. Despite this, thousands of citizens lined the streets of Riga in a silent protest.

input: In 1989, Gaddafi was overjoyed by the foundation of the Arab Maghreb Union, uniting Libya in an economic pact with Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria, viewing it as beginnings of a new Pan-Arab union. Meanwhile, Libya stepped up its support for anti-western militants such as the Provisional IRA, and in 1988, Pan Am Flight 103 was blown up over Lockerbie in Scotland, killing 243 passengers and 16 crew members, plus 11 people on the ground. British police investigations identified two Libyans – Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah – as the chief suspects, and in November 1991 issued a declaration demanding that Libya hand them over. When Gaddafi refused, citing the Montreal Convention, the United Nations (UN) imposed Resolution 748 in March 1992, initiating economic sanctions against Libya which had deep repercussions for the country's economy. The country suffered an estimated $900 million financial loss as a result. Further problems arose with the west when in January 1989, two Libyan warplanes were shot down by the U.S. off the Libyan coast. Many African states opposed the UN sanctions, with Mandela criticising them on a visit to Gaddafi in October 1997, when he praised Libya for its work in fighting apartheid and awarded Gaddafi the Order of Good Hope. They would only be suspended in 1998 when Libya agreed to allow the extradition of the suspects to the Scottish Court in the Netherlands, in a process overseen by Mandela.
rewrite: The establishment of the Arab Maghreb Union in 1989, which created an economic bloc comprising Libya, Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, and Algeria, was met with considerable enthusiasm by Muammar Gaddafi. He interpreted this development as a potential precursor to a broader Pan-Arab entity. Concurrently, Libya intensified its backing of various anti-Western militant groups, including the Provisional Irish Republican Army. This period was further marred by the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, in December 1988, which resulted in 270 fatalities. Subsequent investigations by British authorities identified two Libyan nationals, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah, as the primary suspects. Following a formal request for their extradition in November 1991, which Gaddafi refused on legal grounds citing the Montreal Convention, the United Nations Security Council enacted Resolution 748 in March 1992. This resolution imposed comprehensive economic sanctions on Libya, leading to severe economic repercussions, including estimated financial losses of $900 million. Tensions with Western powers were further exacerbated by a January 1989 incident in which United States forces shot down two Libyan military aircraft over international waters near the Libyan coast. While the sanctions regime garnered significant opposition from many African states, a pivotal critique came from South African President Nelson Mandela during an October 1997 visit to Libya. Mandela commended Libya's historical opposition to apartheid and conferred upon Gaddafi the Order of Good Hope. The sanctions were ultimately suspended in 1998 following an agreement, facilitated by Mandela, to transfer the two suspects for trial before a Scottish court convened in the Netherlands.

input: Each code point has a single General Category property. The major categories are: Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator and Other. Within these categories, there are subdivisions. The General Category is not useful for every use, since legacy encodings have used multiple characteristics per single code point. E.g., U+000A <control-000A> Line feed (LF) in ASCII is both a control and a formatting separator; in Unicode the General Category is "Other, Control". Often, other properties must be used to specify the characteristics and behaviour of a code point. The possible General Categories are:
rewrite: Every code point is assigned a singular General Category property, comprising major classifications such as Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator, and Other, each containing further subdivisions. However, this categorization is not universally applicable, as legacy encodings frequently assigned multiple characteristics to individual code points. For instance, U+000A (Line Feed) in ASCII functions as both a control character and a formatting separator, whereas Unicode classifies it under "Other, Control." Consequently, additional properties are often necessary to fully define a code point's attributes and behavior.

input: French political scientist Maurice Duverger drew a distinction between cadre parties and mass parties. Cadre parties were political elites that were concerned with contesting elections and restricted the influence of outsiders, who were only required to assist in election campaigns. Mass parties tried to recruit new members who were a source of party income and were often expected to spread party ideology as well as assist in elections.Socialist parties are examples of mass parties, while the British Conservative Party and the German Christian Democratic Union are examples of hybrid parties. In the United States, where both major parties were cadre parties, the introduction of primaries and other reforms has transformed them so that power is held by activists who compete over influence and nomination of candidates.
rewrite: Maurice Duverger, a French political scientist, distinguished between cadre parties and mass parties. Cadre parties, composed of political elites, focused on electoral contestation and limited external influence, mobilizing outsiders primarily for campaign assistance. In contrast, mass parties actively recruited members, who served as a financial base and were typically tasked with disseminating party ideology in addition to electoral support. Socialist parties exemplify the mass party model, whereas entities like the British Conservative Party and the German Christian Democratic Union represent hybrid forms. In the United States, both major parties historically functioned as cadre organizations; however, the adoption of primaries and related reforms has shifted power toward activists, who now contend over internal influence and candidate nominations.

input: The NTFS file system used by recent versions of Windows stores the file with a UTC time stamp, but displays it corrected to local—or seasonal—time. However, the FAT filesystem commonly used on removable devices stores only the local time. Consequently, when a file is copied from the hard disk onto separate media, its time will be set to the current local time. If the time adjustment is changed, the timestamps of the original file and the copy will be different. The same effect can be observed when compressing and uncompressing files with some file archivers. It is the NTFS file that changes seen time. This effect should be kept in mind when trying to determine if a file is a duplicate of another, although there are other methods of comparing files for equality (such as using a checksum algorithm).
rewrite: The NTFS file system, employed in modern Windows operating systems, records file timestamps in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) but presents them adjusted to the local or seasonal time zone. In contrast, the FAT file system, frequently utilized on removable storage media, stores timestamps solely in local time. As a result, transferring a file from an NTFS-formatted hard disk to FAT-formatted external media resets its timestamp to the current local time. Subsequent alterations to time zone or daylight saving settings can thereby create discrepancies between the original and copied file timestamps. A similar phenomenon may occur during file compression and extraction with certain archiving utilities, wherein the NTFS file's displayed time is altered. This potential for timestamp variance must be considered during duplicate file analysis, notwithstanding the availability of more deterministic comparison methods, such as cryptographic checksum verification.

input: The tourism industry began in the early 19th century when foreigners visited the Alps, traveled to the bases of the mountains to enjoy the scenery, and stayed at the spa-resorts. Large hotels were built during the Belle Époque; cog-railways, built early in the 20th century, brought tourists to ever higher elevations, with the Jungfraubahn terminating at the Jungfraujoch, well above the eternal snow-line, after going through a tunnel in Eiger. During this period winter sports were slowly introduced: in 1882 the first figure skating championship was held in St. Moritz, and downhill skiing became a popular sport with English visitors early in the 20th century, as the first ski-lift was installed in 1908 above Grindelwald.
rewrite: The origins of modern tourism can be traced to the early nineteenth century, when foreign visitors journeyed to the Alpine region to appreciate the landscape, often residing in spa resorts. The subsequent Belle Époque era witnessed the construction of grand hotels. Technological advancements, such as early twentieth-century cog-railways, facilitated access to higher altitudes; notably, the Jungfraubahn, traversing a tunnel through the Eiger, culminates at the Jungfraujoch above the permanent snow line. Concurrently, winter sports gradually emerged, exemplified by the inaugural figure skating championship in St. Moritz in 1882. Downhill skiing gained popularity among English tourists in the early 1900s, a development accelerated by the installation of the first ski-lift above Grindelwald in 1908.

input: The last king of the Roman Kingdom, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown in 509 BC by a group of noblemen led by Lucius Junius Brutus. Tarquin made a number of attempts to retake the throne, including the Tarquinian conspiracy, the war with Veii and Tarquinii and finally the war between Rome and Clusium, all of which failed to achieve Tarquin's objectives. The most important constitutional change during the transition from kingdom to republic concerned the chief magistrate. Before the revolution, a king would be elected by the senators for a life term. Now, two consuls were elected by the citizens for an annual term. Each consul would check his colleague, and their limited term in office would open them up to prosecution if they abused the powers of their office. Consular political powers, when exercised conjointly with a consular colleague, were no different from those of the old king.
rewrite: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the final monarch of the Roman Kingdom, was deposed in 509 BC in a revolt led by the nobleman Lucius Junius Brutus. Following his exile, Tarquin initiated several unsuccessful campaigns to reclaim power, notably the Tarquinian conspiracy, conflicts with the cities of Veii and Tarquinii, and ultimately a war between Rome and Clusium. The pivotal constitutional reform in the shift from monarchy to republic pertained to the executive authority. Previously, a king was elected for life by the senate. This was replaced by a system of two consuls, elected annually by the citizenry. Their concurrent powers mirrored those of the former king, but the abbreviated term and the principle of collegiality, wherein each consul could check the other, served as crucial constraints. Furthermore, this limited tenure made consuls subject to prosecution for any abuses of power after leaving office.

input: Antibiotics are screened for any negative effects on humans or other mammals before approval for clinical use, and are usually considered safe and most are well tolerated. However, some antibiotics have been associated with a range of adverse side effects. Side-effects range from mild to very serious depending on the antibiotics used, the microbial organisms targeted, and the individual patient. Side effects may reflect the pharmacological or toxicological properties of the antibiotic or may involve hypersensitivity reactions or anaphylaxis. Safety profiles of newer drugs are often not as well established as for those that have a long history of use. Adverse effects range from fever and nausea to major allergic reactions, including photodermatitis and anaphylaxis. Common side-effects include diarrhea, resulting from disruption of the species composition in the intestinal flora, resulting, for example, in overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria, such as Clostridium difficile. Antibacterials can also affect the vaginal flora, and may lead to overgrowth of yeast species of the genus Candida in the vulvo-vaginal area. Additional side-effects can result from interaction with other drugs, such as elevated risk of tendon damage from administration of a quinolone antibiotic with a systemic corticosteroid. Some scientists have hypothesized that the indiscriminate use of antibiotics alter the host microbiota and this has been associated with chronic disease.
rewrite: Prior to clinical approval, antibiotics undergo rigorous screening to assess potential adverse effects on humans and other mammals, and are generally regarded as safe with a high degree of tolerability. Nevertheless, certain antibiotics have been linked to a spectrum of undesirable reactions. The severity of these effects varies from mild to severe, contingent upon the specific antibiotic, the targeted microbial organisms, and individual patient factors. Adverse manifestations may arise from the inherent pharmacological or toxicological properties of the agent, or may involve immunological mechanisms such as hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis. While established antibiotics possess well-characterized safety profiles, those of newer agents are often less comprehensively documented. Clinical presentations range from minor symptoms like fever and nausea to significant allergic reactions, including photodermatitis and anaphylaxis. A frequent complication is diarrhea, often attributable to disruption of the intestinal microbiota, which can permit pathogenic overgrowth of organisms such as *Clostridium difficile*. Antibacterial agents may similarly disturb vaginal flora, potentially leading to overgrowth of *Candida* species. Drug interactions present additional risks, exemplified by the heightened potential for tendon damage when quinolones are co-administered with systemic corticosteroids. Furthermore, some researchers posit that indiscriminate antibiotic use may induce persistent alterations to the host microbiota, an outcome hypothesized to contribute to the development of chronic diseases.

input: Beginning in August, the competition proceeds as a knockout tournament throughout, consisting of twelve rounds, a semi-final and then a final, in May. A system of byes ensures clubs above Level 9 and 10 enter the competition at later stages. There is no seeding, the fixtures in each round being determined by a random draw. Prior to the semi-finals, fixtures ending in a tie are replayed once only. The first six rounds are qualifiers, with the draws organised on a regional basis. The next six rounds are the "proper" rounds where all clubs are in one draw.
rewrite: Commencing in August, the competition adopts a knockout format comprising twelve rounds, followed by semi-finals and a final in May. Clubs above Levels 9 and 10 enter at later stages via a bye system. There is no seeding; fixtures in each round are determined by random draw. Ties before the semi-finals are replayed once only. The initial six rounds function as regional qualifiers. The subsequent six rounds constitute the "proper" competition, wherein all remaining clubs are included within a single national draw.

input: Gaddafi's earliest education was of a religious nature, imparted by a local Islamic teacher. Subsequently moving to nearby Sirte to attend elementary school, he progressed through six grades in four years. Education in Libya was not free, but his father thought it would greatly benefit his son despite the financial strain. During the week Gaddafi slept in a mosque, and at weekends walked 20 miles to visit his parents. Bullied for being a Bedouin, he was proud of his identity and encouraged pride in other Bedouin children. From Sirte, he and his family moved to the market town of Sabha in Fezzan, south-central Libya, where his father worked as a caretaker for a tribal leader while Muammar attended secondary school, something neither parent had done. Gaddafi was popular at school; some friends made there received significant jobs in his later administration, most notably his best friend Abdul Salam Jalloud.
rewrite: Muammar Gaddafi's initial education was religious, provided by a local Islamic instructor. He later relocated to the nearby town of Sirte to complete his elementary schooling, advancing through six grades within a four-year period. Although education in Libya was not free, his father, despite financial hardship, deemed it a crucial investment. During the school week, Gaddafi resided in a mosque, walking approximately twenty miles to visit his family on weekends. Subject to bullying for his Bedouin heritage, he maintained a strong pride in this identity and fostered similar sentiments among other Bedouin children. Subsequently, his family moved to Sabha, a market town in the Fezzan region of south-central Libya. There, his father worked as a caretaker for a tribal leader while Gaddafi attended secondary school, an educational level his parents had not attained. He was a popular student, and several friendships formed during this period, most notably with Abdul Salam Jalloud, later translated into significant appointments within his future administration.

input: At the end of the Rigvedic period, the Aryan society began to expand from the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, into the western Ganges plain. It became increasingly agricultural and was socially organised around the hierarchy of the four varnas, or social classes. This social structure was characterized both by syncretising with the native cultures of northern India, but also eventually by the excluding of indigenous peoples by labelling their occupations impure. During this period, many of the previous small tribal units and chiefdoms began to coalesce into monarchical, state-level polities.
rewrite: Toward the conclusion of the Rigvedic era, Aryan society extended its presence from the northwestern Indian subcontinent into the western Gangetic plain. This expansion coincided with a shift toward a more agrarian economy and the crystallization of a social hierarchy structured around the four varnas. This system integrated aspects of indigenous northern Indian cultures while simultaneously marginalizing local populations by deeming their occupations ritually impure. Concurrently, smaller tribal entities and chiefdoms consolidated into more complex, monarchical states.

input: After being rendered obsolete by the redesign, the 1895 replica was presented in 1910 to the FA's long-serving president Lord Kinnaird. Kinnaird died in 1923, and his family kept it in their possession, out of view, until putting it up for auction in 2005. It was duly sold at Christie's auction house on 19 May 2005 for £420,000 (£478,400 including auction fees and taxes). The sale price set a new world record for a piece of football memorabilia, surpassing the £254,000 paid for the Jules Rimet World Cup Trophy in 1997. The successful bidder was David Gold, the then joint chairman of Birmingham City; claiming the FA and government were doing nothing proactive to ensure the trophy remained in the country, Gold stated his purchase was motivated by wanting to save it for the nation. Accordingly, Gold presented the trophy to the National Football Museum in Preston on 20 April 2006, where it went on immediate public display. It later moved with the museum to its new location in Manchester. In November 2012, it was ceremonially presented to Royal Engineers, after they beat Wanderers 7–1 in a charity replay of the first FA Cup final.
rewrite: Following its obsolescence due to a redesign, the 1895 replica trophy was bestowed in 1910 upon Lord Kinnaird, the Football Association's long-tenured president. Upon his death in 1923, the artifact remained in his family's private possession until its consignment to auction in 2005. The sale was conducted at Christie's on 19 May 2005, achieving a final price of £420,000 (£478,400 inclusive of fees and taxes). This figure established a new global record for football memorabilia, exceeding the £254,000 paid for the Jules Rimet Trophy in 1997. The successful bidder was David Gold, then joint chairman of Birmingham City Football Club. Gold asserted that his acquisition was driven by a desire to preserve the trophy for the nation, citing a lack of proactive measures by the FA and government to retain it domestically. In accordance with this stated intent, he formally presented the trophy to the National Football Museum in Preston on 20 April 2006, where it entered public exhibition. It subsequently relocated with the museum to Manchester. In a ceremonial gesture in November 2012, the trophy was presented to the Royal Engineers following their 7–1 victory over Wanderers in a charitable re-enactment of the inaugural FA Cup final.

input: In 1971, Akira Endo, a Japanese biochemist working for the pharmaceutical company Sankyo, identified mevastatin (ML-236B), a molecule produced by the fungus Penicillium citrinum, as an inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, a critical enzyme used by the body to produce cholesterol. Animal trials showed very good inhibitory effect as in clinical trials, however a long term study in dogs found toxic effects at higher doses and as a result mevastatin was believed to be too toxic for human use. Mevastatin was never marketed, because of its adverse effects of tumors, muscle deterioration, and sometimes death in laboratory dogs.
rewrite: In 1971, Japanese biochemist Akira Endo, employed by Sankyo, identified mevastatin (ML-236B), a compound derived from the fungus *Penicillium citrinum*, as an inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, a key enzyme in cholesterol biosynthesis. Initial animal and clinical trials demonstrated potent inhibitory effects. However, subsequent long-term canine studies revealed significant toxicity at elevated doses, including tumors, muscle deterioration, and occasional fatalities. Consequently, mevastatin was deemed unsuitable for human therapeutic use due to these adverse effects and was never commercially marketed.

input: In his Science of Logic (1812–1814) Hegel argues that finite qualities are not fully "real" because they depend on other finite qualities to determine them. Qualitative infinity, on the other hand, would be more self-determining and hence more fully real. Similarly finite natural things are less "real"—because they are less self-determining—than spiritual things like morally responsible people, ethical communities and God. So any doctrine, such as materialism, that asserts that finite qualities or natural objects are fully real is mistaken.
rewrite: In his *Science of Logic* (1812–1814), Hegel contends that finite qualities lack complete reality, as their determination relies upon other finite qualities. In contrast, qualitative infinity, being more self-determining, attains a fuller reality. By this logic, finite natural entities are less real due to their diminished self-determination compared to spiritual realities—such as moral agents, ethical communities, and God. Consequently, doctrines like materialism, which posit finite qualities or natural objects as fully real, are erroneous.

input: Technology magazine T3 gave the Super Slim model a positive review, stating the console is almost "nostalgic" in the design similarities to the original "fat" model, "While we don’t know whether it will play PS3 games or Blu-ray discs any differently yet, the look and feel of the new PS3 Slim is an obvious homage to the original PS3, minus the considerable excess weight. Immediately we would be concerned about the durability of the top loading tray that feels like it could be yanked straight out off the console, but ultimately it all feels like Sony's nostalgic way of signing off the current generation console in anticipation for the PS4."
rewrite: In a favorable assessment, T3 magazine commended the Super Slim model, noting its design evokes a sense of nostalgia through its resemblance to the original "fat" PlayStation 3. The publication observed that, while performance regarding PS3 games and Blu-ray discs remains unconfirmed, the new Slim variant constitutes a clear aesthetic homage to its predecessor, albeit without the original's substantial bulk. A concern was raised regarding the potential fragility of the top-loading disc tray, which appears susceptible to detachment. Overall, the review interprets the design as Sony's nostalgic farewell to the current console generation ahead of the PlayStation 4's anticipated release.

input: The British, for their part, lacked both a unified command and a clear strategy for winning. With the use of the Royal Navy, the British were able to capture coastal cities, but control of the countryside eluded them. A British sortie from Canada in 1777 ended with the disastrous surrender of a British army at Saratoga. With the coming in 1777 of General von Steuben, the training and discipline along Prussian lines began, and the Continental Army began to evolve into a modern force. France and Spain then entered the war against Great Britain as Allies of the US, ending its naval advantage and escalating the conflict into a world war. The Netherlands later joined France, and the British were outnumbered on land and sea in a world war, as they had no major allies apart from Indian tribes.
rewrite: The British war effort was hindered by a lack of unified command and a coherent strategic plan for achieving victory. While the Royal Navy enabled the capture of key coastal cities, establishing control over the interior proved impossible. This was exemplified by the failed 1777 campaign from Canada, which concluded with a British army’s surrender at Saratoga. Concurrently, the Continental Army underwent significant professionalization under General von Steuben, who instituted rigorous Prussian-style training and discipline. The American cause was further strengthened in 1777 by the entry of France and Spain as allies, which negated British naval supremacy and transformed the conflict into a global war. Subsequent Dutch involvement compounded British isolation, leaving them without major European allies and outnumbered on multiple fronts.

input: The word genocide was later included as a descriptive term to the process of indictment, but not yet as a formal legal term According to Lemming, genocide was defined as "a coordinated strategy to destroy a group of people, a process that could be accomplished through total annihilation as well as strategies that eliminate key elements of the group's basic existence, including language, culture, and economic infrastructure.” He created a concept of mobilizing much of the international relations and community, to working together and preventing the occurrence of such events happening within history and the international society. Australian anthropologist Peg LeVine coined the term "ritualcide" to describe the destruction of a group's cultural identity without necessarily destroying its members.
rewrite: The term genocide was subsequently incorporated as a descriptive element within indictments, though not yet as a formal legal charge. According to Lemkin, genocide constituted "a coordinated plan of action aimed at the destruction of the essential foundations of the life of national groups." This encompassed not only physical annihilation but also the eradication of fundamental elements such as language, cultural institutions, and economic structures. His conceptualization sought to mobilize international relations and the global community toward collective action to prevent such atrocities. In a related conceptual development, Australian anthropologist Peg LeVine introduced the term "ritualcide" to denote the systematic destruction of a group's cultural identity, distinct from the physical destruction of its members.

input: Production capacity in Britain and the United States was improved by the invention of the cotton gin by the American Eli Whitney in 1793. Before the development of cotton gins, the cotton fibers had to be pulled from the seeds tediously by hand. By the late 1700s a number of crude ginning machines had been developed. However, to produce a bale of cotton required over 600 hours of human labor, making large-scale production uneconomical in the United States, even with the use of humans as slave labor. The gin that Whitney manufactured (the Holmes design) reduced the hours down to just a dozen or so per bale. Although Whitney patented his own design for a cotton gin, he manufactured a prior design from Henry Odgen Holmes, for which Holmes filed a patent in 1796. Improving technology and increasing control of world markets allowed British traders to develop a commercial chain in which raw cotton fibers were (at first) purchased from colonial plantations, processed into cotton cloth in the mills of Lancashire, and then exported on British ships to captive colonial markets in West Africa, India, and China (via Shanghai and Hong Kong).
rewrite: The invention of the cotton gin by American Eli Whitney in 1793 significantly enhanced production capacity in both Britain and the United States. Prior to this development, the extraction of cotton fibers from seeds was a laborious manual process. Although rudimentary ginning machines existed by the late eighteenth century, producing a single bale of cotton still demanded over six hundred hours of human labor. This rendered large-scale production economically unviable in the United States, even with the reliance on enslaved labor. Whitney’s manufactured gin, based on the Holmes design, drastically reduced this requirement to approximately twelve hours per bale. Notably, while Whitney patented his own gin design, the device he produced utilized an earlier mechanism by Henry Odgen Holmes, who secured a patent in 1796. Concurrently, advancing technology and British dominance in global markets facilitated the establishment of an integrated commercial system. This chain involved sourcing raw cotton from colonial plantations, manufacturing cotton cloth in Lancashire mills, and exporting the finished goods via British ships to colonial markets in West Africa, India, and China, particularly through Shanghai and Hong Kong.

input: The inclusiveness of Weinreich's definition (above) directs attention to the totality of one's identity at a given phase in time, and assists in elucidating component aspects of one's total identity, such as one's gender identity, ethnic identity, occupational identity and so on. The definition readily applies to the young child, to the adolescent, to the young adult, and to the older adult in various phases of the life cycle. Depending on whether one is a young child or an adult at the height of one's powers, how one construes oneself as one was in the past will refer to very different salient experiential markers. Likewise, how one construes oneself as one aspires to be in the future will differ considerably according to one's age and accumulated experiences. (Weinreich & Saunderson, (eds) 2003, pp 26–34).
rewrite: The comprehensiveness of Weinreich's definition emphasizes the complete configuration of an individual's identity at a specific temporal juncture, thereby facilitating the examination of its constituent dimensions, including gender, ethnicity, and occupation. This conceptual framework remains applicable across the lifespan, encompassing early childhood, adolescence, young adulthood, and later adulthood. The process of construing one's past self invokes distinct and salient experiential markers, which vary significantly depending on developmental stage, such as whether one is a young child or an adult at the peak of one's capacities. Similarly, the construction of one's aspirational future self is substantially influenced by age and the totality of accumulated experience (Weinreich & Saunderson, eds., 2003, pp. 26–34).

input: The Crimean War marked the ascendancy of France to the position of pre-eminent power on the Continent,:411 the continued decline of the Ottoman Empire, and the beginning of a decline for Tsarist Russia. As Fuller notes, "Russia had been beaten on the Crimean peninsula, and the military feared that it would inevitably be beaten again unless steps were taken to surmount its military weakness." The Crimean War marks the demise of the Concert of Europe, the balance of power that had dominated Europe since the Congress of Vienna in 1815, and which had included France, Russia, Austria and the United Kingdom.
rewrite: The Crimean War signified the rise of France as the preeminent continental power, alongside the ongoing deterioration of the Ottoman Empire and the onset of decline for Tsarist Russia. As Fuller observes, Russia's defeat prompted military fears of future losses without substantive reforms to address its weaknesses. Furthermore, the conflict precipitated the collapse of the Concert of Europe. This system, established by the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and maintained by major powers including France, Russia, Austria, and Britain, had preserved a continental balance of power until the war.

input: On the field at the beginning of a play are two teams of 12 (unlike 11 in American football). The team in possession of the ball is the offence and the team defending is referred to as the defence. Play begins with a backwards pass through the legs (the snap) by a member of the offensive team, to another member of the offensive team. This is usually the quarterback or punter, but a "direct snap" to a running back is also not uncommon. If the quarterback or punter receives the ball, he may then do any of the following:
rewrite: At the commencement of a play, two teams of twelve players each are positioned on the field, contrasting with the eleven players per side in American football. The team controlling the ball is designated the offense, while the opposing team constitutes the defense. The play initiates with a backward pass, known as the snap, delivered between the legs of an offensive player to a teammate. This recipient is typically the quarterback or punter, though a direct snap to a running back also occurs with regularity. Upon receiving the snap, the quarterback or punter may then execute a range of subsequent actions.

input: New York City's commuter rail network is the largest in North America. The rail network, connecting New York City to its suburbs, consists of the Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and New Jersey Transit. The combined systems converge at Grand Central Terminal and Pennsylvania Station and contain more than 250 stations and 20 rail lines. In Queens, the elevated AirTrain people mover system connects JFK International Airport to the New York City Subway and the Long Island Rail Road; a separate AirTrain system is planned alongside the Grand Central Parkway to connect LaGuardia Airport to these transit systems. For intercity rail, New York City is served by Amtrak, whose busiest station by a significant margin is Pennsylvania Station on the West Side of Manhattan, from which Amtrak provides connections to Boston, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. along the Northeast Corridor, as well as long-distance train service to other North American cities.
rewrite: New York City possesses the most extensive commuter rail network in North America. This system, which links the city to its suburban regions, comprises the Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and New Jersey Transit.
