input: Canada's Armed forces operate out of 27 Canadian Forces bases (CFB) across the country, including NDHQ. This number has been gradually reduced since the 1970s with bases either being closed or merged. Both officers and non-commissioned members receive their basic training at the Canadian Forces Leadership and Recruit School in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu. Officers will generally either directly enter the Canadian Armed Forces with a degree from a civilian university, or receive their commission upon graduation from the Royal Military College of Canada. Specific element and trade training is conducted at a variety of institutions throughout Canada, and to a lesser extent, the world.
rewrite: The Canadian Armed Forces are headquartered across 27 Canadian Forces Bases (CFBs), a total that has been progressively reduced since the 1970s through closures and consolidations. All personnel undergo basic training at the Canadian Forces Leadership and Recruit School in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu. Officers typically enter via direct entry with a civilian university degree or receive a commission upon graduating from the Royal Military College of Canada. Subsequent specialized training for specific elements and trades is delivered at various institutions primarily within Canada, and to a lesser degree, internationally.

input: The Taragaon Museum presents the modern history of the Kathmandu Valley. It seeks to document 50 years of research and cultural heritage conservation of the Kathmandu Valley, documenting what artists photographers architects anthropologists from abroad had contributed in the second half of the 20th century. The actual structure of the Museum showcases restoration and rehabilitation efforts to preserve the built heritage of Kathmandu. It was designed by Carl Pruscha (master-planner of the Kathmandy Valley ) in 1970 and constructed in 1971. Restoration works began in 2010 to rehabilitate the Taragaon hostel into the Taragaon Museum. The design uses local brick along with modern architectural design elements, as well as the use of circle, triangles and squares. The Museum is within a short walk from the Boudhnath stupa, which itself can be seen from the Museum tower.
rewrite: The Taragaon Museum chronicles the modern history of the Kathmandu Valley. Its purpose is to archive five decades of research and cultural heritage conservation within the valley, specifically documenting contributions made by foreign artists, photographers, architects, and anthropologists during the latter half of the twentieth century. The museum building itself exemplifies restoration and rehabilitation efforts to preserve Kathmandu's built heritage. Originally designed in 1970 by Carl Pruscha, the valley's master-planner, and constructed in 1971, the structure was rehabilitated from the Taragaon Hostel beginning in 2010. Its architectural design integrates local brick with modernist elements, employing geometric forms such as circles, triangles, and squares. The museum is situated within walking distance of the Boudhanath Stupa, which is visible from the museum tower.

input: If any boy produces an outstanding piece of work, it may be "Sent Up For Good", storing the effort in the College Archives for posterity. This award has been around since the 18th century. As Sending Up For Good is fairly infrequent, the process is rather mysterious to many of Eton's boys. First, the master wishing to Send Up For Good must gain the permission of the relevant Head of Department. Upon receiving his or her approval, the piece of work will be marked with Sent Up For Good and the student will receive a card to be signed by House Master, tutor and division master.
rewrite: The distinction of being "Sent Up For Good" is conferred upon a pupil who produces work of exceptional merit, resulting in its preservation within the College Archives. This practice, dating to the 18th century, remains relatively uncommon and thus somewhat enigmatic to many students. The procedure requires the initiating master to first secure approval from the pertinent Head of Department. Following this endorsement, the work is formally marked with the accolade, and the pupil receives a commemorative card to be signed by their House Master, tutor, and division master.

input: Shorter, black-and-white daily strips began to appear early in the 20th century, and became established in newspapers after the success in 1907 of Bud Fisher's Mutt and Jeff. Humour strips predominated at first, and in the 1920s and 1930s strips with continuing stories in genres such as adventure and drama also became popular. Thin periodicals called comic books appeared in the 1930s, at first reprinting newspaper comic strips; by the end of the decade, original content began to dominate. The success in 1938 of Action Comics and its lead hero Superman marked the beginning of the Golden Age of Comic Books, in which the superhero genre was prominent.
rewrite: The emergence of shorter, black-and-white daily comic strips occurred in the early twentieth century, solidifying in newspapers following the 1907 success of Bud Fisher's *Mutt and Jeff*. Initially dominated by humour, the medium expanded in the 1920s and 1930s to include popular serialized narratives in adventure and drama genres. The 1930s also saw the advent of comic books—thin periodicals that first reprinted newspaper strips before shifting to primarily original content by the decade's end. The 1938 debut of *Action Comics* and its protagonist Superman inaugurated the superhero-centric Golden Age of Comic Books.

input: Umar is honored for his attempt to resolve the fiscal problems attendant upon conversion to Islam. During the Umayyad period, the majority of people living within the caliphate were not Muslim, but Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, or members of other small groups. These religious communities were not forced to convert to Islam, but were subject to a tax (jizyah) which was not imposed upon Muslims. This situation may actually have made widespread conversion to Islam undesirable from the point of view of state revenue, and there are reports that provincial governors actively discouraged such conversions. It is not clear how Umar attempted to resolve this situation, but the sources portray him as having insisted on like treatment of Arab and non-Arab (mawali) Muslims, and on the removal of obstacles to the conversion of non-Arabs to Islam.
rewrite: Umar is recognized for his efforts to address the fiscal challenges arising from conversion to Islam. Under the Umayyad Caliphate, most inhabitants were not Muslim but belonged to Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, or other minority faiths. These communities were permitted to retain their religions but were required to pay a poll tax (jizyah), from which Muslims were exempt. Consequently, widespread conversion potentially threatened state revenues, leading some provincial governors to actively discourage it. Although the precise mechanisms of Umar’s response remain unclear, historical accounts indicate that he advocated for equal treatment of Arab and non-Arab Muslims (mawali) and sought to eliminate barriers to the conversion of non-Arabs.

input: In the following decades there was a constant battle between the company lobby and the Parliament. The company sought a permanent establishment, while the Parliament would not willingly allow it greater autonomy and so relinquish the opportunity to exploit the company's profits. In 1712, another act renewed the status of the company, though the debts were repaid. By 1720, 15% of British imports were from India, almost all passing through the company, which reasserted the influence of the company lobby. The licence was prolonged until 1766 by yet another act in 1730.
rewrite: Over the ensuing decades, a persistent conflict existed between the company's lobby and Parliament. The company pursued a permanent charter, whereas Parliament resisted granting greater autonomy to avoid relinquishing control over its profitable operations. An act in 1712 renewed the company's status despite its repaid debts. By 1720, approximately 15% of British imports originated in India, predominantly channeled through the company, thereby reinforcing its lobby's influence. A further act in 1730 subsequently extended its operating licence until 1766.

input: In 1899, the university opened a national design contest for the new campus. The renowned Philadelphia firm Cope & Stewardson won unanimously with its plan for a row of Collegiate Gothic quadrangles inspired by Oxford and Cambridge Universities. The cornerstone of the first building, Busch Hall, was laid on October 20, 1900. The construction of Brookings Hall, Ridgley, and Cupples began shortly thereafter. The school delayed occupying these buildings until 1905 to accommodate the 1904 World's Fair and Olympics. The delay allowed the university to construct ten buildings instead of the seven originally planned. This original cluster of buildings set a precedent for the development of the Danforth Campus; Cope & Stewardson’s original plan and its choice of building materials have, with few exceptions, guided the construction and expansion of the Danforth Campus to the present day.
rewrite: In 1899, the university initiated a national competition to select a design for its new campus. The Philadelphia architectural firm Cope & Stewardson achieved unanimous selection with a proposal featuring a series of Collegiate Gothic quadrangles, drawing inspiration from Oxford and Cambridge. The cornerstone for the inaugural structure, Busch Hall, was placed on October 20, 1900. Construction promptly commenced on Brookings Hall, Ridgley, and Cupples. Occupancy was deferred until 1905 to accommodate the 1904 World’s Fair and Olympic Games. This postponement enabled the erection of ten buildings rather than the initially planned seven. This original architectural ensemble established a enduring precedent for the Danforth Campus; Cope & Stewardson’s master plan and specified materials have, with limited deviation, continued to guide all subsequent construction and expansion.

input: Each team consists of a maximum of eleven players (excluding substitutes), one of whom must be the goalkeeper. Competition rules may state a minimum number of players required to constitute a team, which is usually seven. Goalkeepers are the only players allowed to play the ball with their hands or arms, provided they do so within the penalty area in front of their own goal. Though there are a variety of positions in which the outfield (non-goalkeeper) players are strategically placed by a coach, these positions are not defined or required by the Laws.
rewrite: A team may comprise up to eleven players, including a designated goalkeeper, with substitutes additional. Competitive regulations typically establish a minimum team size, often seven players. Only the goalkeeper is permitted to handle the ball, and solely within the confines of the penalty area. While coaches strategically deploy outfield players in various positions, such tactical arrangements are not mandated by the formal Laws of the Game.

input: The clergy was divided into two types: the secular clergy, who lived out in the world, and the regular clergy, who lived under a religious rule and were usually monks. Throughout the period monks remained a very small proportion of the population, usually less than one per cent. Most of the regular clergy were drawn from the nobility, the same social class that served as the recruiting ground for the upper levels of the secular clergy. The local parish priests were often drawn from the peasant class. Townsmen were in a somewhat unusual position, as they did not fit into the traditional three-fold division of society into nobles, clergy, and peasants. During the 12th and 13th centuries, the ranks of the townsmen expanded greatly as existing towns grew and new population centres were founded. But throughout the Middle Ages the population of the towns probably never exceeded 10 per cent of the total population.
rewrite: The clergy was bifurcated into two categories: the secular clergy, who operated within the broader society, and the regular clergy, who adhered to a monastic rule, typically within religious orders. Monastic populations consistently constituted a minor fraction of the total populace, generally remaining below one percent. Recruitment for the regular clergy, as well as for the upper echelons of the secular clergy, was predominantly from the nobility. In contrast, local parish priests were frequently drawn from the peasantry. Urban dwellers occupied an anomalous social position, as they did not align with the traditional tripartite model of nobles, clergy, and peasants. During the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the urban population expanded significantly through the growth of established towns and the foundation of new settlements. Nevertheless, throughout the medieval period, the proportion of the population residing in towns likely never surpassed ten percent.

input: It is in this time that the notation of music on a staff and other elements of musical notation began to take shape. This invention made possible the separation of the composition of a piece of music from its transmission; without written music, transmission was oral, and subject to change every time it was transmitted. With a musical score, a work of music could be performed without the composer's presence. The invention of the movable-type printing press in the 15th century had far-reaching consequences on the preservation and transmission of music.
rewrite: During this period, the development of staff notation and related notational systems emerged. This innovation enabled the separation of musical composition from its transmission, which had previously relied on oral tradition and was inherently mutable with each performance. The musical score thereby allowed for accurate reproduction of a work without the composer's direct involvement. Subsequently, the advent of movable-type printing in the fifteenth century profoundly expanded the capacity for preserving and disseminating musical works.

input: Formal schooling did not start in Hungary until the age of ten. Instead, governesses taught von Neumann, his brothers and his cousins. Max believed that knowledge of languages other than Hungarian was essential, so the children were tutored in English, French, German and Italian. By the age of 8, von Neumann was familiar with differential and integral calculus, but he was particularly interested in history, reading his way through Wilhelm Oncken's Allgemeine Geschichte in Einzeldarstellungen. A copy was contained in a private library Max purchased. One of the rooms in the apartment was converted into a library and reading room, with bookshelves from ceiling to floor.
rewrite: Formal education in Hungary commenced only at age ten. Prior to this, von Neumann and his siblings received instruction from governesses. Their father, Max, deemed foreign languages indispensable, ensuring tutoring in English, French, German, and Italian. By eight, von Neumann had acquired knowledge of differential and integral calculus. His principal fascination, however, was history, evidenced by his reading of Wilhelm Oncken’s *Allgemeine Geschichte in Einzeldarstellungen*. This volume was part of a private library Max acquired, for which a dedicated room with floor-to-ceiling bookshelves was established as a library and reading room.

input: Despite competition from other materials, copper remains the preferred electrical conductor in nearly all categories of electrical wiring with the major exception being overhead electric power transmission where aluminium is often preferred. Copper wire is used in power generation, power transmission, power distribution, telecommunications, electronics circuitry, and countless types of electrical equipment. Electrical wiring is the most important market for the copper industry. This includes building wire, communications cable, power distribution cable, appliance wire, automotive wire and cable, and magnet wire. Roughly half of all copper mined is used to manufacture electrical wire and cable conductors. Many electrical devices rely on copper wiring because of its multitude of inherent beneficial properties, such as its high electrical conductivity, tensile strength, ductility, creep (deformation) resistance, corrosion resistance, low thermal expansion, high thermal conductivity, solderability, and ease of installation.
rewrite: Copper persists as the predominant electrical conductor across nearly all wiring applications, with aluminum being the principal alternative primarily in overhead power transmission. It is integral to power generation, transmission, and distribution, as well as to telecommunications, electronic circuitry, and diverse electrical equipment. Consequently, electrical wiring—encompassing building wire, communications and power cable, appliance and automotive wire, and magnet wire—constitutes the copper industry's most significant market. Approximately half of all mined copper is dedicated to producing these wire and cable conductors. This preference is attributable to copper's optimal combination of properties, including high electrical and thermal conductivity, tensile strength, ductility, corrosion and creep resistance, low thermal expansion, solderability, and ease of installation.

input: Canada allows nonprofits to be incorporated or unincorporated. Nonprofits may incorporate either federally, under Part II of the Canada Business Corporations Act or under provincial legislation. Many of the governing Acts for Canadian nonprofits date to the early 1900s, meaning that nonprofit legislation has not kept pace with legislation that governs for-profit corporations; particularly with regards to corporate governance. Federal, and in some provinces (such as Ontario), incorporation is by way of Letters Patent, and any change to the Letters Patent (even a simple name change) requires formal approval by the appropriate government, as do by-law changes. Other provinces (such as Alberta) permit incorporation as of right, by the filing of Articles of Incorporation or Articles of Association.
rewrite: In Canada, nonprofit organizations may exist in either incorporated or unincorporated forms. Incorporation can occur at the federal level, pursuant to Part II of the Canada Business Corporations Act, or under various provincial statutes. Much of the governing legislation for Canadian nonprofits originates from the early twentieth century, resulting in a regulatory framework that has not evolved in parallel with that governing for-profit corporations, especially concerning corporate governance standards. At the federal level and in certain provinces, including Ontario, incorporation is effected through Letters Patent; any amendments to these documents or to organizational bylaws require formal governmental sanction. Conversely, jurisdictions such as Alberta permit incorporation as a matter of right via the filing of Articles of Incorporation or Association.

input: In addition to the above, Greece is also to start oil and gas exploration in other locations in the Ionian Sea, as well as the Libyan Sea, within the Greek exclusive economic zone, south of Crete. The Ministry of the Environment, Energy and Climate Change announced that there was interest from various countries (including Norway and the United States) in exploration, and the first results regarding the amount of oil and gas in these locations were expected in the summer of 2012. In November 2012, a report published by Deutsche Bank estimated the value of natural gas reserves south of Crete at €427 billion.

The Ministry of the Environment, Energy and Climate Change reported international interest from nations including Norway and the United States, with preliminary resource estimates anticipated by summer 2012. Subsequently, a Deutsche Bank report from November 2012 appraised the natural gas reserves south of Crete at approximately €427 billion.

input: In Canada, there are Affiliate Schools, Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities that offer instruction in a variety of programs that can lead to: engineering and applied science degrees, apprenticeship and trade programs, certificates, and diplomas. Affiliate Schools are polytechnic divisions belonging to a national university and offer select technical and engineering programs. Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities tend to be independent institutions.
rewrite: The Canadian post-secondary education system comprises Affiliate Schools, Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities. These institutions deliver diverse programs, including engineering and applied science degrees, apprenticeships, trades, certificates, and diplomas. Affiliate Schools are polytechnic divisions of a national university, offering specific technical and engineering programs. In contrast, Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities are generally independent entities.

input: The Richmond metro area is served by many local television and radio stations. As of 2010[update], the Richmond-Petersburg designated market area (DMA) is the 58th largest in the U.S. with 553,950 homes according to Nielsen Market Research. The major network television affiliates are WTVR-TV 6 (CBS), WRIC-TV 8 (ABC), WWBT 12 (NBC), WRLH-TV 35 (Fox), and WUPV 65 (CW). Public Broadcasting Service stations include WCVE-TV 23 and WCVW 57. There are also a wide variety of radio stations in the Richmond area, catering to many different interests, including news, talk radio, and sports, as well as an eclectic mix of musical interests.
rewrite: The Richmond metropolitan area is served by numerous local broadcast outlets. According to 2010 Nielsen Market Research data, the Richmond-Petersburg designated market area (DMA) ranks as the 58th largest in the United States, encompassing 553,950 television households. Primary network television affiliates consist of WTVR-TV 6 (CBS), WRIC-TV 8 (ABC), WWBT 12 (NBC), WRLH-TV 35 (Fox), and WUPV 65 (CW). Public Broadcasting Service stations are WCVE-TV 23 and WCVW 57. input: Another Alaskan transportation method is the dogsled. In modern times (that is, any time after the mid-late 1920s), dog mushing is more of a sport than a true means of transportation. Various races are held around the state, but the best known is the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, a 1,150-mile (1,850 km) trail from Anchorage to Nome (although the distance varies from year to year, the official distance is set at 1,049 miles or 1,688 km). The race commemorates the famous 1925 serum run to Nome in which mushers and dogs like Togo and Balto took much-needed medicine to the diphtheria-stricken community of Nome when all other means of transportation had failed. Mushers from all over the world come to Anchorage each March to compete for cash, prizes, and prestige. The "Serum Run" is another sled dog race that more accurately follows the route of the famous 1925 relay, leaving from the community of Nenana (southwest of Fairbanks) to Nome.
rewrite: An additional mode of transportation in Alaska is the dogsled. In contemporary contexts, particularly following the late 1920s, dog mushing has transitioned from a practical conveyance to primarily a sporting pursuit. Numerous competitions occur statewide, with the most prominent being the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race. This event covers approximately 1,150 miles (1,850 km) from Anchorage to Nome, though its official distance is standardized at 1,049 miles (1,688 km). The race serves as a memorial to the historic 1925 serum run to Nome, during which mushers and sled dogs, including Togo and Balto, successfully delivered diphtheria antitoxin after conventional transport methods proved inadequate. Each March, international mushers gather in Anchorage to compete for monetary rewards, prizes, and distinction. Alternatively, the "Serum Run" race more precisely retraces the 1925 relay route, commencing in Nenana and concluding in Nome.

input: Digimon was first conceived as a virtual pet toy in the vein of Tamagotchis and, as such, took influence from Tamagotchis' cute and round designs. The small areas of the screens (16 by 16 pixels) meant that character designers had to create monsters whose forms would be easily recognizable. As such, many of the early Digimon—including Tyrannomon, the first one ever created—were based on dinosaurs. Many further designs were created by Kenji Watanabe, who was brought in to help with the "X-Antibody" creatures and art for the Digimon collectible card game. Watanabe was one influenced by American comics, which were beginning to gain popularity in Japan, and as such began to make his characters look stronger and "cool." The character creation process, however, has for most of the franchise's history been collaborative and reliant on conversation and brainstorming.
rewrite: The digital monster franchise, Digimon, originated as a virtual pet toy, drawing direct aesthetic inspiration from the cute, rounded forms of predecessors like Tamagotchi. Due to the severe graphical limitations of early devices, which featured screens of only 16 by 16 pixels, initial creature designs required highly recognizable silhouettes. This led to the creation of numerous early Digimon based on dinosaurs, such as Tyrannomon, the inaugural monster. Subsequent design evolution was significantly shaped by artist Kenji Watanabe, who contributed to projects including the "X-Antibody" creatures and the collectible card game. Influenced by the growing popularity of American comics in Japan, Watanabe introduced a more robust and stylized aesthetic. Throughout the franchise's history, however, the character creation process has remained fundamentally collaborative, relying on concerted discussion and brainstorming.

input: China's network security and information technology leadership team was established February 27, 2014. The leadership team is tasked with national security and long-term development and co-ordination of major issues related to network security and information technology. Economic, political, cultural, social and military fields as related to network security and information technology strategy, planning and major macroeconomic policy are being researched. The promotion of national network security and information technology law are constantly under study for enhanced national security capabilities.
rewrite: The Central Leading Group for Cyberspace Affairs was established in China on February 27, 2014. Its mandate encompasses national security and long-term development, requiring the coordination of major issues in cybersecurity and information technology. The group researches strategic planning and core policies for these domains as they intersect with economic, political, cultural, social, and military affairs. It also continually examines the advancement of relevant legal frameworks to strengthen national security capabilities.

input: In 1996, Marvel had some of its titles participate in "Heroes Reborn", a crossover that allowed Marvel to relaunch some of its flagship characters such as the Avengers and the Fantastic Four, and outsource them to the studios of two of the former Marvel artists turned Image Comics founders, Jim Lee and Rob Liefeld. The relaunched titles, which saw the characters transported to a parallel universe with a history distinct from the mainstream Marvel Universe, were a solid success amidst a generally struggling industry, but Marvel discontinued the experiment after a one-year run and returned the characters to the Marvel Universe proper. In 1998, the company launched the imprint Marvel Knights, taking place within Marvel continuity; helmed by soon-to-become editor-in-chief Joe Quesada, it featured tough, gritty stories showcasing such characters as the Inhumans, Black Panther and Daredevil.
rewrite: In 1996, Marvel Comics initiated the "Heroes Reborn" crossover event, a strategic relaunch of flagship titles including the Avengers and the Fantastic Four. This venture involved outsourcing production to studios led by former Marvel artists and Image Comics founders Jim Lee and Rob Liefeld. The narratives relocated these characters to a distinct parallel universe, diverging from mainstream Marvel continuity. Despite a generally depressed comic book market, the initiative achieved notable commercial success. Nevertheless, Marvel concluded the experiment after one year, reintegrating the characters into their primary universe. Subsequently, in 1998, the company introduced the Marvel Knights imprint under the editorial direction of Joe Quesada. Operating within established continuity, this imprint presented darker, more mature narratives featuring characters such as Daredevil, Black Panther, and the Inhumans.

input: In Han government, the emperor was the supreme judge and lawgiver, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and sole designator of official nominees appointed to the top posts in central and local administrations; those who earned a 600-dan salary-rank or higher. Theoretically, there were no limits to his power. However, state organs with competing interests and institutions such as the court conference (tingyi 廷議)—where ministers were convened to reach majority consensus on an issue—pressured the emperor to accept the advice of his ministers on policy decisions. If the emperor rejected a court conference decision, he risked alienating his high ministers. Nevertheless, emperors sometimes did reject the majority opinion reached at court conferences.
rewrite: Within the Han governmental structure, the emperor held ultimate authority as the supreme judicial and legislative figure, commander of the military, and the exclusive appointing power for all high-ranking central and local officials—specifically those at a salary-rank of 600 *dan* or above. Theoretically, his power was boundless. In practice, however, institutional mechanisms like the court conference (*tingyi*), which convened ministers to deliberate and reach a majority consensus, functioned to constrain imperial autonomy by pressuring the emperor to adopt ministerial counsel. Defying such a consensus risked alienating the senior bureaucracy, though emperors occasionally did reject majority opinions.

input: Bush focused his campaign on national security, presenting himself as a decisive leader and contrasted Kerry as a "flip-flopper." This strategy was designed to convey to American voters the idea that Bush could be trusted to be tough on terrorism while Kerry would be "uncertain in the face of danger." Bush (just as his father did with Dukakis in the 1988 election) also sought to portray Kerry as a "Massachusetts liberal" who was out of touch with mainstream Americans. One of Kerry's slogans was "Stronger at home, respected in the world." This advanced the suggestion that Kerry would pay more attention to domestic concerns; it also encapsulated Kerry's contention that Bush had alienated American allies by his foreign policy.
rewrite: During his campaign, President Bush emphasized national security, framing himself as a resolute leader while characterizing Senator Kerry as indecisive. This approach aimed to persuade voters that Bush offered steadfast commitment against terrorism, whereas Kerry might exhibit uncertainty in critical moments. Mirroring a tactic from the 1988 election, Bush further depicted Kerry as a “Massachusetts liberal,” suggesting a disconnect from mainstream American values. In contrast, Kerry’s slogan, “Stronger at home, respected in the world,” highlighted his focus on domestic priorities and implied that Bush’s foreign policy had weakened international alliances.

input: Unlike many religions, Buddhism has no single central text that is universally referred to by all traditions. However, some scholars have referred to the Vinaya Pitaka and the first four Nikayas of the Sutta Pitaka as the common core of all Buddhist traditions.[page needed] This could be considered misleading, as Mahāyāna considers these merely a preliminary, and not a core, teaching. The Tibetan Buddhists have not even translated most of the āgamas (though theoretically they recognize them) and they play no part in the religious life of either clergy or laity in China and Japan. Other scholars say there is no universally accepted common core. The size and complexity of the Buddhist canons have been seen by some (including Buddhist social reformer Babasaheb Ambedkar) as presenting barriers to the wider understanding of Buddhist philosophy.
rewrite: Buddhism lacks a singular central text universally acknowledged across all traditions. While some scholars identify the Vinaya Pitaka and the first four Nikayas of the Sutta Pitaka as a common core, this characterization is problematic. Mahāyāna traditions regard these texts as preliminary rather than foundational. Furthermore, in Tibetan Buddhism, most āgamas remain untranslated and are doctrinally recognized yet practically irrelevant; they similarly hold no place in the religious practices of East Asian clergy or laity. Consequently, other academics contend no universally accepted common core exists. The considerable size and complexity of the Buddhist canons have also been noted, including by figures like social reformer B. R. Ambedkar, as potential obstacles to broader comprehension of Buddhist philosophy.

input: All of the executions which have taken place since the 1936 hanging of Bethea in Owensboro have been conducted within a wall or enclosure. For example, Fred Adams was legally hanged in Kennett, Missouri, on April 2, 1937, within a 10-foot (3 m) wooden stockade. Roscoe "Red" Jackson was hanged within a stockade in Galena, Missouri, on May 26, 1937. Two Kentucky hangings were conducted after Galena in which numerous persons were present within a wooden stockade, that of John "Peter" Montjoy in Covington, Kentucky on December 17, 1937, and that of Harold Van Venison in Covington on June 3, 1938. An estimated 400 witnesses were present for the hanging of Lee Simpson in Ryegate, Montana, on December 30, 1939. The execution of Timothy McVeigh on June 11, 2001 was witnessed by some 300 people, some by closed-circuit television.
rewrite: All executions conducted since the 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Owensboro have occurred within a walled or enclosed space. For instance, Fred Adams was lawfully hanged within a ten-foot wooden stockade in Kennett, Missouri, on April 2, 1937. Similarly, Roscoe "Red" Jackson was executed inside a stockade in Galena, Missouri, on May 26, 1937. Subsequent Kentucky hangings also utilized wooden stockades accommodating numerous witnesses: John "Peter" Montjoy was hanged in Covington on December 17, 1937, followed by Harold Van Venison at the same location on June 3, 1938. An estimated 400 spectators attended the hanging of Lee Simpson in Ryegate, Montana, on December 30, 1939. More recently, the execution of Timothy McVeigh on June 11, 2001, was witnessed by approximately 300 individuals, both in person and via closed-circuit television.

input: Of the remaining land area, the state of Alaska owns 101 million acres (41 million hectares), its entitlement under the Alaska Statehood Act. A portion of that acreage is occasionally ceded to organized boroughs, under the statutory provisions pertaining to newly formed boroughs. Smaller portions are set aside for rural subdivisions and other homesteading-related opportunities. These are not very popular due to the often remote and roadless locations. The University of Alaska, as a land grant university, also owns substantial acreage which it manages independently.

input: By 1640, the town's theocratic government and nine-square grid plan were in place, and the town was renamed Newhaven from Quinnipiac. However, the area north of New Haven remained Quinnipiac until 1678, when it was renamed Hamden. The settlement became the headquarters of the New Haven Colony. At the time, the New Haven Colony was separate from the Connecticut Colony, which had been established to the north centering on Hartford. One of the principal differences between the two colonies was that the New Haven colony was an intolerant theocracy that did not permit other churches to be established, while the Connecticut colony permitted the establishment of other churches.

The territory north of New Haven retained the name Quinnipiac until 1678, when it was redesignated as Hamden. This settlement served as the capital of the New Haven Colony. This colony existed separately from the Connecticut Colony, which was founded earlier and centered on Hartford. input: The institutions and practices of canon law paralleled the legal development of much of Europe, and consequently both modern civil law and common law (legal system) bear the influences of canon law. Edson Luiz Sampel, a Brazilian expert in canon law, says that canon law is contained in the genesis of various institutes of civil law, such as the law in continental Europe and Latin American countries. Sampel explains that canon law has significant influence in contemporary society.

According to Brazilian canon law scholar Edson Luiz Sampel, canon law is foundational to numerous civil law institutions, particularly within continental Europe and Latin America. Sampel further asserts that canon law maintains a significant role in shaping contemporary legal and social frameworks.

input: Broadly speaking, Enlightenment science greatly valued empiricism and rational thought, and was embedded with the Enlightenment ideal of advancement and progress. The study of science, under the heading of natural philosophy, was divided into physics and a conglomerate grouping of chemistry and natural history, which included anatomy, biology, geology, mineralogy, and zoology. As with most Enlightenment views, the benefits of science were not seen universally; Rousseau criticized the sciences for distancing man from nature and not operating to make people happier. Science during the Enlightenment was dominated by scientific societies and academies, which had largely replaced universities as centres of scientific research and development. Societies and academies were also the backbone of the maturation of the scientific profession. Another important development was the popularization of science among an increasingly literate population. Philosophes introduced the public to many scientific theories, most notably through the Encyclopédie and the popularization of Newtonianism by Voltaire and Émilie du Châtelet. Some historians have marked the 18th century as a drab period in the history of science; however, the century saw significant advancements in the practice of medicine, mathematics, and physics; the development of biological taxonomy; a new understanding of magnetism and electricity; and the maturation of chemistry as a discipline, which established the foundations of modern chemistry.
rewrite: Enlightenment science was fundamentally characterized by an emphasis on empiricism and rational inquiry, reflecting the era's broader ideals of progress and advancement. The domain of scientific study, then termed natural philosophy, was principally organized into physics and a composite field encompassing chemistry and natural history; the latter included anatomy, biology, geology, mineralogy, and zoology. However, the perceived benefits of science were not universally accepted, as exemplified by Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s critique that it alienated humanity from nature and failed to enhance happiness. Institutionally, scientific societies and academies became the dominant centers of research and development, largely supplanting universities and serving as the cornerstone for the professionalization of science. Concurrently, the popularization of science emerged as a significant trend, with philosophes disseminating theories to an increasingly literate public. This was achieved notably through works such as the Encyclopédie and the promotion of Newtonian physics by figures like Voltaire and Émilie du Châtelet. While some historians have characterized the eighteenth century as unremarkable in scientific history, it in fact witnessed substantial progress. Key developments included advances in medicine, mathematics, and physics; the establishment of biological taxonomy; novel insights into magnetism and electricity; and the maturation of chemistry as a discipline, which laid the groundwork for its modern form.

input: Hospitals in Liberia include the John F. Kennedy Medical Center in Monrovia and several others. Life expectancy in Liberia is estimated to be 57.4 years in 2012. With a fertility rate of 5.9 births per woman, the maternal mortality rate stood at 990 per 100,000 births in 2010. A number of highly communicable diseases are widespread, including tuberculosis, diarrheal diseases and malaria. In 2007, the HIV infection rates stood at 2% of the population aged 15–49  whereas the incidence of tuberculosis was 420 per 100,000 people in 2008. Approximately 58.2% – 66% of women are estimated to have undergone female genital mutilation.

input: On July 8, 2007 The Washington Post published excerpts from UCLA Professor Amy Zegart's book Spying Blind: The CIA, the FBI, and the Origins of 9/11. The Post reported from Zegart's book that government documents show the CIA and FBI missed 23 potential chances to disrupt the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. The primary reasons for the failures included: agency cultures resistant to change and new ideas; inappropriate incentives for promotion; and a lack of cooperation between the FBI, CIA and the rest of the United States Intelligence Community. The book blamed the FBI's decentralized structure, which prevented effective communication and cooperation among different FBI offices. The book suggested that the FBI has not evolved into an effective counter-terrorism or counter-intelligence agency, due in large part to deeply ingrained agency cultural resistance to change. For example, FBI personnel practices continue to treat all staff other than special agents as support staff, classifying intelligence analysts alongside the FBI's auto mechanics and janitors.
rewrite: On July 8, 2007, *The Washington Post* published excerpts from Professor Amy Zegart’s monograph, *Spying Blind: The CIA, the FBI, and the Origins of 9/11*. Drawing upon government documents, the excerpts detailed that the CIA and FBI collectively missed twenty-three potential opportunities to disrupt the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Zegart’s analysis identifies several systemic causes for these failures: institutional cultures resistant to innovation and adaptation, promotion incentives misaligned with counterterrorism objectives, and insufficient interagency cooperation within the broader U.S. Intelligence Community. The work particularly critiques the FBI’s decentralized organizational architecture, which impeded internal communication and coordination. It argues that the Bureau has failed to transform into an effective counterterrorism and counterintelligence entity, largely due to entrenched cultural opposition to reform. This is exemplified by personnel policies that categorize intelligence analysts as mere support staff, a classification grouping them with automotive mechanics and custodial personnel.

input: Zhu Yousong, however, fared a lot worse than his ancestor Zhu Yuanzhang three centuries earlier. Beset by factional conflicts, his regime could not offer effective resistance to Qing forces, when the Qing army, led by the Manchu prince Dodo approached Jiangnan the next spring. Days after Yangzhou fell to the Manchus in late May 1645, the Hongguang Emperor fled Nanjing, and the imperial Ming Palace was looted by local residents. On June 6, Dodo's troops approached Nanjing, and the commander of the city's garrison, Zhao the Earl of Xincheng, promptly surrendered the city to them. The Manchus soon ordered all male residents of the city to shave their heads in the Manchu queue way. They requisitioned a large section of the city for the bannermen's cantonment, and destroyed the former imperial Ming Palace, but otherwise the city was spared the mass murders and destruction that befell Yangzhou.
rewrite: Zhu Yousong’s fate proved markedly less favorable than that of his ancestor Zhu Yuanzhang three centuries prior. Plagued by internal factionalism, his regime proved incapable of mounting an effective defense against the advancing Qing forces. In the spring following his accession, the Qing army, commanded by the Manchu Prince Dodo, moved into Jiangnan. Shortly after the fall of Yangzhou to the Manchus in late May 1645, the Hongguang Emperor fled Nanjing, and the imperial Ming Palace was looted by the local populace. On June 6, Dodo’s forces reached Nanjing, where Zhao, the Earl of Xincheng and commander of the city’s garrison, promptly surrendered. The Manchus subsequently mandated that all male residents adopt the Manchu queue hairstyle. They appropriated a substantial portion of the city for a bannermen’s cantonment and razed the former imperial palace. However, Nanjing was otherwise spared the widespread slaughter and devastation inflicted upon Yangzhou.

input: The Princess Margaret Hospital on Funafuti is the only hospital in Tuvalu. The Tuvaluan medical staff at PMH in 2011 comprised the Director of Health & Surgeon, the Chief Medical Officer Public Health, an anaesthetist, a paediatric medical officer and an obstetrics and gynaecology medical officer. Allied health staff include two radiographers, two pharmacists, three laboratory technicians, two dieticians and 13 nurses with specialised training in fields including surgical nursing, anaesthesia nursing/ICU, paediatric nursing and midwifery. PMH also employs a dentist. The Department of Health also employs nine or ten nurses on the outer islands to provide general nursing and midwifery services.

input: By the late 2000s, Dell's "configure to order" approach of manufacturing—delivering individual PCs configured to customer specifications from its US facilities was no longer as efficient or competitive with high-volume Asian contract manufacturers as PCs became powerful low-cost commodities. Dell closed plants that produced desktop computers for the North American market, including the Mort Topfer Manufacturing Center in Austin, Texas (original location) and Lebanon, Tennessee (opened in 1999) in 2008 and early 2009, respectively. The desktop production plant in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, received US$280 million in incentives from the state and opened in 2005, but ceased operations in November 2010. Dell's contract with the state required them to repay the incentives for failing to meet the conditions, and they sold the North Carolina plant to Herbalife. Most of the work that used to take place in Dell's U.S. plants was transferred to contract manufacturers in Asia and Mexico, or some of Dell's own factories overseas. The Miami, Florida, facility of its Alienware subsidiary remains in operation, while Dell continues to produce its servers (its most profitable products) in Austin, Texas. On January 8, 2009, Dell announced the closure of its manufacturing plant in Limerick, Ireland, with the loss of 1,900 jobs and the transfer of production to its plant in Łodź in Poland.
rewrite: By the late 2000s, Dell's "configure-to-order" manufacturing model—which involved assembling individual personal computers to customer specifications at its United States facilities—had become less efficient and competitive. This shift occurred as PCs evolved into high-volume, low-cost commodity goods, a market increasingly dominated by large-scale contract manufacturers based in Asia. Consequently, Dell initiated a series of domestic plant closures. The Mort Topfer Manufacturing Center in Austin, Texas (its original site) and a facility in Lebanon, Tennessee (opened in 1999) were shuttered in 2008 and early 2009, respectively, ending their production of desktop units for the North American market. A desktop manufacturing plant in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, which opened in 2005 after receiving $280 million in state incentives, ceased operations in November 2010. For failing to meet the associated conditions, Dell was required to repay these incentives and subsequently sold the facility to Herbalife. Production from these and other U.S. sites was largely relocated to contract manufacturers in Asia and Mexico, as well as to Dell's own overseas factories. Notably, Dell's Alienware subsidiary facility in Miami, Florida, remained operational, and the company continued manufacturing its highly profitable servers in Austin, Texas. In a parallel international consolidation, Dell announced on January 8, 2009, the closure of its Limerick, Ireland, plant, resulting in 1,900 job losses and the transfer of that production to its facility in Łódź, Poland.

input: President Franklin D. Roosevelt promoted a "good neighbor" policy that sought better relations with Mexico. In 1935 a federal judge ruled that three Mexican immigrants were ineligible for citizenship because they were not white, as required by federal law. Mexico protested, and Roosevelt decided to circumvent the decision and make sure the federal government treated Hispanics as white. The State Department, the Census Bureau, the Labor Department, and other government agencies therefore made sure to uniformly classify people of Mexican descent as white. This policy encouraged the League of United Latin American Citizens in its quest to minimize discrimination by asserting their whiteness.
rewrite: In pursuit of improved relations with Mexico under the "Good Neighbor" policy, President Franklin D. Roosevelt confronted a 1935 federal court ruling which denied citizenship to three Mexican immigrants on the grounds that they were not white. In response to Mexican diplomatic protests, Roosevelt's administration systematically directed federal agencies, including the State Department, the Census Bureau, and the Labor Department, to uniformly classify individuals of Mexican descent as white. This institutional alignment subsequently bolstered the efforts of groups like the League of United Latin American Citizens, which sought to mitigate discrimination by formally asserting a white racial identity.

input: During the Cold War, the Asian power of Japan and the European powers of the United Kingdom, France, and West Germany rebuilt their economies. France and the United Kingdom maintained technologically advanced armed forces with power projection capabilities and maintain large defence budgets to this day. Yet, as the Cold War continued, authorities began to question if France and the United Kingdom could retain their long-held statuses as great powers. China, with the world's largest population, has slowly risen to great power status, with large growth in economic and military power in the post-war period. After 1949, the Republic of China began to lose its recognition as the sole legitimate government of China by the other great powers, in favour of the People's Republic of China. Subsequently, in 1971, it lost its permanent seat at the UN Security Council to the People's Republic of China.
rewrite: Throughout the Cold War, Japan in Asia alongside the European states of the United Kingdom, France, and West Germany underwent significant economic reconstruction. France and the United Kingdom sustained technologically sophisticated militaries with global power projection, a commitment reflected in their substantial, enduring defense expenditures. However, as the Cold War progressed, analysts questioned the ability of these two nations to preserve their traditional status as great powers. Concurrently, the People's Republic of China, possessing the world's largest population, ascended to great power standing through considerable post-war economic and military expansion. Following its establishment in 1949, the People's Republic gradually supplanted the Republic of China in international recognition as the legitimate government. This diplomatic shift culminated in 1971 with the transfer of the Chinese permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council to the People's Republic.

input: Hayek was concerned about the general view in Britain's academia that fascism was a capitalist reaction to socialism and The Road to Serfdom arose from those concerns. It was written between 1940 and 1943. The title was inspired by the French classical liberal thinker Alexis de Tocqueville's writings on the "road to servitude." It was first published in Britain by Routledge in March 1944 and was quite popular, leading Hayek to call it "that unobtainable book," also due in part to wartime paper rationing. When it was published in the United States by the University of Chicago in September of that year, it achieved greater popularity than in Britain. At the arrangement of editor Max Eastman, the American magazine Reader's Digest also published an abridged version in April 1945, enabling The Road to Serfdom to reach a far wider audience than academics. The book is widely popular among those advocating individualism and classical liberalism.
rewrite: Friedrich Hayek authored *The Road to Serfdom* between 1940 and 1943, motivated by his opposition to the prevailing intellectual sentiment within British academia that viewed fascism as a capitalist response to socialism. The treatise’s title derives from Alexis de Tocqueville’s reflections on the “road to servitude.” Initially published in Britain by Routledge in March 1944, the work quickly gained significant popularity. Wartime paper rationing contributed to its scarcity, prompting Hayek to refer to it as “that unobtainable book.” Its American release by the University of Chicago Press in September 1944 surpassed its British success in readership. An abridged version, arranged by editor Max Eastman, appeared in *Reader’s Digest* in April 1945, substantially expanding its audience beyond academic circles. The book remains a seminal text, widely esteemed by proponents of individualism and classical liberalism.

input: Physically, clothing serves many purposes: it can serve as protection from the elements, and can enhance safety during hazardous activities such as hiking and cooking. It protects the wearer from rough surfaces, rash-causing plants, insect bites, splinters, thorns and prickles by providing a barrier between the skin and the environment. Clothes can insulate against cold or hot conditions. Further, they can provide a hygienic barrier, keeping infectious and toxic materials away from the body. Clothing also provides protection from harmful UV radiation.
rewrite: Clothing fulfills several essential physical functions. Primarily, it offers protection from environmental elements, including insulation against thermal extremes and a barrier against ultraviolet radiation. It enhances safety by shielding the body from abrasive surfaces, irritant plants, insects, and sharp objects during activities like hiking. Furthermore, garments act as a hygienic shield, preventing contact with infectious agents and toxic substances, thereby safeguarding the wearer's health.

input: Whereas most Christians believe the gibbet on which Jesus was executed was the traditional two-beamed cross, the Jehovah's Witnesses hold the view that a single upright stake was used. The Greek and Latin words used in the earliest Christian writings are ambiguous. The Koine Greek terms used in the New Testament are stauros (σταυρός) and xylon (ξύλον). The latter means wood (a live tree, timber or an object constructed of wood); in earlier forms of Greek, the former term meant an upright stake or pole, but in Koine Greek it was used also to mean a cross. The Latin word crux was also applied to objects other than a cross.
rewrite: While mainstream Christian doctrine typically asserts that Jesus was executed on a two-beamed cross, Jehovah's Witnesses maintain he died on a single upright stake. The key terminology in the earliest sources is linguistically ambiguous. The New Testament's Koine Greek employs *stauros*, which originally denoted a stake but in that period could signify a cross, and *xylon*, meaning simply "wood." Similarly, the Latin *crux* was applied to various structures beyond the traditional cross. This lexical range permits differing interpretations of the execution instrument's precise form.

input: Required attendance at school is 10 years for males and 11 years for females (2001). The adult literacy rate is 99.0% (2002). Nauti School on Funafuti is the largest primary in Tuvalu with more than 900 students (45 percent of the total primary school enrolment). The pupil-teacher ratio for Tuvalu is low compared to the Pacific region (ratio of 1:29).

input: The physical relief of the island is dominated by two mountain ranges, the Troodos Mountains and the smaller Kyrenia Range, and the central plain they encompass, the Mesaoria. The Mesaoria plain is drained by the Pedieos River, the longest on the island. The Troodos Mountains cover most of the southern and western portions of the island and account for roughly half its area. The highest point on Cyprus is Mount Olympus at 1,952 m (6,404 ft), located in the centre of the Troodos range. The narrow Kyrenia Range, extending along the northern coastline, occupies substantially less area, and elevations are lower, reaching a maximum of 1,024 m (3,360 ft). The island lies within the Anatolian Plate.

This plain is principally drained by the Pedieos River, the island's longest watercourse. Encompassing much of the south and west, the Troodos range constitutes approximately half of the island's area and features its highest peak, Mount Olympus, at 1,952 meters. In contrast, the narrow Kyrenia Range, aligned with the northern coast, covers a significantly smaller area with a maximum elevation of 1,024 meters. Geologically, Cyprus is situated upon the Anatolian Plate.

input: Many pesticides can be grouped into chemical families. Prominent insecticide families include organochlorines, organophosphates, and carbamates. Organochlorine hydrocarbons (e.g., DDT) could be separated into dichlorodiphenylethanes, cyclodiene compounds, and other related compounds. They operate by disrupting the sodium/potassium balance of the nerve fiber, forcing the nerve to transmit continuously. Their toxicities vary greatly, but they have been phased out because of their persistence and potential to bioaccumulate.:239–240 Organophosphate and carbamates largely replaced organochlorines. Both operate through inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, allowing acetylcholine to transfer nerve impulses indefinitely and causing a variety of symptoms such as weakness or paralysis. Organophosphates are quite toxic to vertebrates, and have in some cases been replaced by less toxic carbamates.:136–137 Thiocarbamate and dithiocarbamates are subclasses of carbamates. Prominent families of herbicides include phenoxy and benzoic acid herbicides (e.g. 2,4-D), triazines (e.g., atrazine), ureas (e.g., diuron), and Chloroacetanilides (e.g., alachlor). Phenoxy compounds tend to selectively kill broad-leaf weeds rather than grasses. The phenoxy and benzoic acid herbicides function similar to plant growth hormones, and grow cells without normal cell division, crushing the plant's nutrient transport system.:300 Triazines interfere with photosynthesis.:335 Many commonly used pesticides are not included in these families, including glyphosate.
rewrite: Pesticides are frequently classified into distinct chemical families based on their structural characteristics. Among insecticides, the principal families are organochlorines, organophosphates, and carbamates. Organochlorine hydrocarbons, such as DDT, are further categorized into dichlorodiphenylethanes, cyclodiene compounds, and other derivatives. Their mechanism of action involves disrupting sodium and potassium ion channels in nerve fibers, leading to uncontrolled, continuous nerve transmission. Although their specific toxicities differ, organochlorines have been largely discontinued due to their environmental persistence and capacity for bioaccumulation. Organophosphates and carbamates subsequently became their predominant replacements. Both families function by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, resulting in the accumulation of acetylcholine and the indefinite propagation of nerve impulses, which manifests in symptoms including muscular weakness and paralysis. Organophosphates exhibit high toxicity to vertebrates, prompting a partial substitution with generally less toxic carbamates in certain applications. Thiocarbamates and dithiocarbamates represent subclasses within the carbamate family. Major herbicide families encompass phenoxy and benzoic acid compounds (e.g., 2,4-D), triazines (e.g., atrazine), ureas (e.g., diuron), and chloroacetanilides (e.g., alachlor). Phenoxy herbicides, for instance, selectively target broad-leaf weeds over grasses by mimicking plant growth hormones; this induces abnormal cellular growth without division, ultimately disrupting the vascular system. Triazines primarily act by inhibiting photosynthesis. It is noteworthy that many widely utilized pesticides, such as glyphosate, fall outside these established chemical families.

input: The state united behind the Plan of Ayutla and ratified the new constitution in 1855. The state was able to survive through the Reform War with minimal damage due to the large number of liberal political figures. The 1858 conservative movement did not succeed in the state even after the successful military campaign of the conservative Zuloaga with 1,000 men occupied the cities of Chihuahua and Parral. In August 1859, Zuloaga and his forces were defeated by the liberal Orozco and his forces; Orozco soon after deposed the state governor, but had to flee to Durango two months later. In the late 1860s the conservative General Cajen briefly entered the state after his campaign through the state of Jalisco and helped establish conservative politicians and ran out the liberal leaders Jesús González Ortega and José María Patoni. Cajen took possession of the state capital and established himself as governor; he brooked no delay in uniting a large force to combat the liberal forces which he defeated in La Batalla del Gallo. Cajen attained several advantages over the liberals within the state, but soon lost his standing due to a strong resurgence of the liberal forces within the state. The successful liberal leaders José María Patoni of Durango and J.E. Muñoz of Chihuahua quickly strengthened their standing by limiting the political rights of the clergy implementing the presidential decree. The state elected General Luis Terrazas, a liberal leader, as governor; he would continue to fight small battles within the state to suppress conservative uprisings during 1861.
