rewrite: Believing that wasta—the assistance of an influential intermediary—was essential to elevate his application above others, Nasser arranged a meeting with Under-Secretary of War Ibrahim Khairy Pasha, who chaired the military academy’s selection board, to solicit his support. Khairy Pasha consented and sponsored Nasser’s second application, leading to its acceptance in late 1937. Thereafter, Nasser dedicated himself to his military career, maintaining minimal contact with his family. At the academy, he formed associations with Abdel Hakim Amer and Anwar Sadat, both of whom later served as key aides during his presidency. Following his graduation in July 1938, he was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the infantry and stationed at Mankabad. There, Nasser and his closest comrades, including Sadat and Amer, first articulated their shared discontent with pervasive national corruption and their aspiration to overthrow the monarchy. Sadat subsequently recorded that Nasser’s “energy, clear-thinking, and balanced judgement” established him as the group’s unquestioned leader.

input: Once inside the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom, there are no lines to see the individual documents and visitors are allowed to walk from document to document as they wish. For over 30 years the National Archives have forbidden flash photography but the advent of cameras with automatic flashes have made the rules increasingly difficult to enforce. As a result, all filming, photographing, and videotaping by the public in the exhibition areas has been prohibited since February 25, 2010.
rewrite: Within the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom, visitors may proceed without queuing to view each foundational document at their own pace. Although flash photography has been prohibited by the National Archives for more than three decades, the proliferation of cameras with automatic flashes has complicated enforcement. Consequently, a comprehensive ban on all public photography, videography, and filming within the exhibition areas was instituted on February 25, 2010.

input: The FAA has been cited as an example of regulatory capture, "in which the airline industry openly dictates to its regulators its governing rules, arranging for not only beneficial regulation, but placing key people to head these regulators." Retired NASA Office of Inspector General Senior Special Agent Joseph Gutheinz, who used to be a Special Agent with the Office of Inspector General for the Department of Transportation and with FAA Security, is one of the most outspoken critics of FAA. Rather than commend the agency for proposing a $10.2 million fine against Southwest Airlines for its failure to conduct mandatory inspections in 2008, he was quoted as saying the following in an Associated Press story: "Penalties against airlines that violate FAA directives should be stiffer. At $25,000 per violation, Gutheinz said, airlines can justify rolling the dice and taking the chance on getting caught. He also said the FAA is often too quick to bend to pressure from airlines and pilots." Other experts have been critical of the constraints and expectations under which the FAA is expected to operate. The dual role of encouraging aerospace travel and regulating aerospace travel are contradictory. For example, to levy a heavy penalty upon an airline for violating an FAA regulation which would impact their ability to continue operating would not be considered encouraging aerospace travel.
rewrite:
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is frequently presented as a case study in regulatory capture, a phenomenon wherein a regulated industry is perceived to exert excessive influence over its governing body. Critics contend the airline industry effectively dictates regulatory policies, securing favorable rules and the appointment of key personnel to leadership positions within the agency. This perspective is notably advanced by Joseph Gutheinz, a retired NASA Office of Inspector General Senior Special Agent and former Special Agent with the Department of Transportation’s and FAA’s own investigative offices. In a 2008 Associated Press report concerning a proposed $10.2 million fine against Southwest Airlines for inspection failures, Gutheinz argued that such penalties remain insufficient. He asserted that at a rate of $25,000 per violation, airlines possess a financial incentive to non-comply, calculating potential fines as a tolerable cost of business. Furthermore, he criticized the FAA for being overly susceptible to pressure from airline operators and pilot associations.

This criticism extends to a fundamental structural conflict within the FAA’s mandate. The agency operates under the contradictory dual mission of both promoting and regulating aerospace travel. These roles are inherently oppositional; for instance, imposing a severe penalty that could jeopardize an airline’s operational viability directly conflicts with the objective of fostering industry growth. Consequently, experts argue that the regulatory framework and expectations imposed upon the FAA are intrinsically compromised, limiting its enforcement efficacy.

input: Plymouth has the first known reference to Jews in the South West from Sir Francis Drake's voyages in 1577 to 1580, as his log mentioned "Moses the Jew" – a man from Plymouth. The Plymouth Synagogue is a Listed Grade II* building, built in 1762 and is the oldest Ashkenazi Synagogue in the English speaking world. There are also places of worship for Islam, Bahá'í, Buddhism, Unitarianism, Chinese beliefs and Humanism.
rewrite: The earliest documented reference to Jewish presence in South West England originates from Plymouth, noted in Sir Francis Drake’s logs from 1577–1580, which mention "Moses the Jew," a local resident. Plymouth’s synagogue, constructed in 1762 and designated a Grade II* listed building, is the oldest Ashkenazi synagogue in the English-speaking world. The city also hosts diverse religious communities, including Islamic, Bahá'í, Buddhist, Unitarian, Chinese traditional, and Humanist groups.

input: In several countries, like Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Turkey, institutes of technology and polytechnics are institutions of higher education, and have been accredited to award academic degrees and doctorates. Famous examples are the Istanbul Technical University, ETH Zurich, İYTE, Delft University of Technology and RWTH Aachen, all considered universities.[citation needed]
rewrite: In nations such as Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Turkey, institutes of technology and polytechnics constitute accredited higher education institutions, possessing the authority to confer academic degrees and doctorates. Prominent examples, regarded as universities, include Istanbul Technical University, ETH Zurich, İYTE, Delft University of Technology, and RWTH Aachen.

input: The Licchavi era was followed by the Malla era. Rulers from Tirhut, upon being attacked by Muslims, fled north to the Kathmandu valley. They intermarried with Nepali royalty, and this led to the Malla era. The early years of the Malla era were turbulent, with raids and attacks from Khas and Turk Muslims. There was also a devastating earthquake which claimed the lives of a third of Kathmandu's population, including the king Abhaya Malla. These disasters led to the destruction of most of the architecture of the Licchavi era (such as Mangriha and Kailashkut Bhawan), and the loss of literature collected in various monasteries within the city. Despite the initial hardships, Kathmandu rose to prominence again and, during most of the Malla era, dominated the trade between India and Tibet. Nepali currency became the standard currency in trans-Himalayan trade.
rewrite: The Licchavi period was succeeded by the Malla era. This transition occurred when rulers from the Tirhut region, facing incursions by Muslim forces, migrated northward to the Kathmandu Valley. Through intermarriage with local nobility, they established the Malla dynasty. The dynasty's inception was marked by instability, including raids by Khas and Turkic Muslim groups. A catastrophic earthquake further compounded these troubles, devastating the population and claiming the life of King Abhaya Malla. These calamities resulted in the widespread destruction of Licchavi-era monuments, such as Mangriha and Kailashkut Bhawan, and the loss of literary collections housed in urban monasteries. Notwithstanding this turbulent commencement, Kathmandu subsequently regained its stature. For much of the Malla period, it served as the preeminent hub for Indo-Tibetan trade, with Nepali currency becoming the standard medium of exchange throughout the trans-Himalayan region.

input: In February 2010 Shell and Cosan formed a 50:50 joint-venture, Raízen, comprising all of Cosan's Brazilian ethanol, energy generation, fuel distribution and sugar activities, and all of Shell's Brazilian retail fuel and aviation distribution businesses. In March 2010, Shell announced the sale of some of its assets, including its liquid petroleum gas (LPG) business, to meet the cost of a planned $28bn capital spending programme. Shell invited buyers to submit indicative bids, due by 22 March, with a plan to raise $2–3bn from the sale. In June 2010, Royal Dutch Shell agreed to acquire all the business of East Resources for a cash consideration of $4.7 billion. The transaction included East Resources' tight gas fields.
rewrite: In February 2010, Shell and Cosan established Raízen, a 50:50 joint venture. This entity consolidated all of Cosan's Brazilian operations in ethanol, energy generation, fuel distribution, and sugar with Shell's entire Brazilian retail fuel and aviation distribution businesses. Subsequently, in March 2010, Shell announced a divestment of certain assets, including its liquid petroleum gas (LPG) business, to fund a planned $28 billion capital expenditure program. The company solicited indicative bids by March 22, aiming to generate $2–3 billion. Furthermore, in June 2010, Royal Dutch Shell agreed to acquire East Resources in its entirety for $4.7 billion in cash, including its tight gas fields.

input: Near the end of the NES's lifespan, upon the release of the AV Famicom and the top-loading NES 2, the design of the game controllers was modified slightly. Though the original button layout was retained, the redesigned device abandoned the brick shell in favor of a dog bone shape. In addition, the AV Famicom joined its international counterpart and dropped the hardwired controllers in favor of detachable controller ports. However, the controllers included with the Famicom AV had cables which were 90 cm (3 feet) long, as opposed to the standard 180 cm(6 feet) of NES controllers.
rewrite: Toward the conclusion of the Nintendo Entertainment System's commercial lifecycle, coinciding with the introductions of the AV Famicom and the top-loading NES 2, the associated game controllers underwent a modest redesign. While preserving the original button configuration, the revised model exchanged the prior rectangular shell for an ergonomic "dog bone" form factor. Furthermore, the AV Famicom adopted the detachable controller ports found on its international counterpart, abandoning hardwired controllers. Notably, the cables for the AV Famicom controllers measured 90 cm (3 feet), half the length of the standard 180 cm (6 feet) cables supplied with NES controllers.

input: Centered on Post Oak Boulevard and Westheimer Road, the Uptown District boomed during the 1970s and early 1980s when a collection of mid-rise office buildings, hotels, and retail developments appeared along Interstate 610 west. Uptown became one of the most prominent instances of an edge city. The tallest building in Uptown is the 64-floor, 901-foot (275 m)-tall, Philip Johnson and John Burgee designed landmark Williams Tower (known as the Transco Tower until 1999). At the time of construction, it was believed to be the world's tallest skyscraper outside of a central business district. The new 20-story Skanska building and BBVA Compass Plaza are the newest office buildings built in Uptown after 30 years. The Uptown District is also home to buildings designed by noted architects I. M. Pei, César Pelli, and Philip Johnson. In the late 1990s and early 2000s decade, there was a mini-boom of mid-rise and high-rise residential tower construction, with several over 30 stories tall. Since 2000 more than 30 high-rise buildings have gone up in Houston; all told, 72 high-rises tower over the city, which adds up to about 8,300 units. In 2002, Uptown had more than 23 million square feet (2,100,000 m²) of office space with 16 million square feet (1,500,000 m²) of Class A office space.
rewrite: The Uptown District, geographically centered on the intersection of Post Oak Boulevard and Westheimer Road, experienced its primary period of growth during the 1970s and early 1980s. This era witnessed the construction of a concentration of mid-rise office structures, hotels, and retail developments along the Interstate 610 corridor to the west, establishing Uptown as a quintessential example of an edge city. Its architectural landscape is distinguished by the 64-story, 901-foot (275-meter) Williams Tower, a landmark designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee (originally named the Transco Tower until 1999). Upon completion, it was considered the world’s tallest skyscraper situated outside a traditional central business district. The district features works by notable architects including I. M. Pei, César Pelli, and Philip Johnson. Following a thirty-year hiatus in major commercial development, recent additions include the 20-story Skanska building and BBVA Compass Plaza. A secondary surge of construction occurred in the late 1990s and early 2000s, marked by numerous mid-rise and high-rise residential towers, several exceeding thirty stories. Since the year 2000, over thirty high-rise buildings have been erected in Houston, contributing to a citywide total of 72 such structures containing approximately 8,300 residential units. As of 2002, the Uptown District contained more than 23 million square feet (2.1 million m²) of office space, of which 16 million square feet (1.5 million m²) was classified as Class A.

input: The Communist Party of China, founded in 1920, adopted the red flag and hammer and sickle emblem of the Soviet Union, which became the national symbols when the Party took power in China in 1949. Under Party leader Mao Zedong, the Party anthem became "The East Is Red", and Mao Zedong himself was sometimes referred to as a "red sun". During the Cultural Revolution in China, Party ideology was enforced by the Red Guards, and the sayings of Mao Zedong were published as a small red book in hundreds of millions of copies. Today the Communist Party of China claims to be the largest political party in the world, with eighty million members.
rewrite: Founded in 1920, the Communist Party of China adopted the red flag and hammer and sickle emblem from the Soviet Union; these were subsequently established as national symbols following the Party's assumption of power in 1949. Under the leadership of Mao Zedong, the anthem "The East Is Red" was adopted, and Mao was occasionally symbolized as a "red sun." During the Cultural Revolution, ideological conformity was enforced by the Red Guards, while Mao's quotations were disseminated globally via hundreds of millions of copies of the "Little Red Book." Presently, the Communist Party of China asserts its status as the world's largest political party, comprising approximately eighty million members.

input: Manifold vacuum can be used to drive accessories on automobiles. The best-known application is the vacuum servo, used to provide power assistance for the brakes. Obsolete applications include vacuum-driven windscreen wipers and Autovac fuel pumps. Some aircraft instruments (Attitude Indicator (AI) and the Heading Indicator (HI)) are typically vacuum-powered, as protection against loss of all (electrically powered) instruments, since early aircraft often did not have electrical systems, and since there are two readily available sources of vacuum on a moving aircraft—the engine and an external venturi. Vacuum induction melting uses electromagnetic induction within a vacuum.
rewrite: Manifold vacuum serves as a power source for various automotive accessories, most notably in vacuum servo units for brake assistance. Historically, it also operated windscreen wipers and Autovac fuel pumps. In aviation, vacuum power is traditionally used for instruments such as the Attitude and Heading Indicators. This provides redundancy against electrical failure, as early aircraft often lacked electrical systems, and vacuum is readily available from engine intake or venturi sources. Separately, vacuum induction melting employs electromagnetic induction within a vacuum environment.

input: Sanskrit, as defined by Pāṇini, evolved out of the earlier Vedic form. The present form of Vedic Sanskrit can be traced back to as early as the second millennium BCE (for Rig-vedic). Scholars often distinguish Vedic Sanskrit and Classical or "Pāṇinian" Sanskrit as separate dialects. Though they are quite similar, they differ in a number of essential points of phonology, vocabulary, grammar and syntax. Vedic Sanskrit is the language of the Vedas, a large collection of hymns, incantations (Samhitas) and theological and religio-philosophical discussions in the Brahmanas and Upanishads. Modern linguists consider the metrical hymns of the Rigveda Samhita to be the earliest, composed by many authors over several centuries of oral tradition. The end of the Vedic period is marked by the composition of the Upanishads, which form the concluding part of the traditional Vedic corpus; however, the early Sutras are Vedic, too, both in language and content.
rewrite: Sanskrit, as systematized by Pāṇini, developed from an earlier Vedic form. The attested form of Vedic Sanskrit dates to at least the second millennium BCE, as evidenced by the Rigveda. Scholars frequently classify Vedic Sanskrit and Classical, or "Pāṇinian," Sanskrit as distinct dialects. While closely related, they exhibit significant differences in phonology, lexicon, grammar, and syntax. Vedic Sanskrit comprises the language of the Vedas, an extensive corpus of hymns, ritual incantations (Saṃhitās), and theological discourses within the Brāhmaṇas and Upaniṣads. Modern linguistic analysis regards the metrical hymns of the Rigveda Saṃhitā as the earliest stratum, composed by multiple authors across centuries of oral transmission. The conclusion of the Vedic period is generally identified with the composition of the Upaniṣads, which constitute the final portion of the traditional Vedic canon; nevertheless, the early Sūtra texts also remain Vedic in both linguistic form and thematic content.

input: Another 44 million acres (18 million hectares) are owned by 12 regional, and scores of local, Native corporations created under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) of 1971. Regional Native corporation Doyon, Limited often promotes itself as the largest private landowner in Alaska in advertisements and other communications. Provisions of ANCSA allowing the corporations' land holdings to be sold on the open market starting in 1991 were repealed before they could take effect. Effectively, the corporations hold title (including subsurface title in many cases, a privilege denied to individual Alaskans) but cannot sell the land. Individual Native allotments can be and are sold on the open market, however.
rewrite: An additional 44 million acres (18 million hectares) are held by twelve regional and numerous local Native corporations, established pursuant to the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) of 1971. For instance, the regional corporation Doyon, Limited frequently asserts in its promotional materials that it is Alaska's largest private landowner. Although initial ANCSA provisions would have permitted these corporations to sell their lands on the open market beginning in 1991, those provisions were repealed prior to taking effect. Consequently, while corporations retain title—often including subsurface rights, a privilege not afforded to individual Alaskans—they cannot alienate the land. In contrast, individual Native allotments may be and are sold publicly.

input: Following the defeat in World War I, influence of German-speaking elites over Central and Eastern Europe was greatly limited. At the treaty of Versailles Germany was substantially reduced in size. Austria-Hungary was split up. Rump-Austria, which to a certain extent corresponded to the German-speaking areas of Austria-Hungary (a complete split into language groups was impossible due to multi-lingual areas and language-exclaves) adopted the name "German-Austria" (German: Deutschösterreich). The name German-Austria was forbidden by the victorious powers of World War I. Volga Germans living in the Soviet Union were interned in gulags or forcibly relocated during the Second World War.
rewrite: The aftermath of World War I significantly curtailed the political influence of German-speaking elites across Central and Eastern Europe. The Treaty of Versailles drastically reduced German territory, while the Austro-Hungarian Empire was dissolved. Its core German-speaking regions, though inseparable from multilingual areas, formed a rump state initially designated "German-Austria" (Deutschösterreich). This name was subsequently prohibited by the Allied powers. Furthermore, during World War II, the Soviet Union interned or forcibly relocated ethnic Germans from the Volga region.

input: By the verse Quran, 2:124, Shias believe that Imamah is a divine position always Imamah is accompanied by the word guidance, of course a guidance by God's Command.A kind of guidance which brings humanity to the goal. Regarding 17:71, no age can be without an Imam. So, according to the upper verse 1.Imamah is a position which is appointed by God and must be specified by Him 2.Imam is protected by a divine protection and no one exceles him in nobility 3. No age can be without an Imam and finally Imam knows everything which is needed for human being to get to the truth and goal.
rewrite: According to Quranic verse 2:124, Shia theology posits that Imamah constitutes a divinely ordained station, intrinsically linked to divinely commanded guidance. This form of guidance directs humanity toward its ultimate purpose. Verse 17:71 further establishes that no era may be devoid of an Imam. Consequently, based on these scriptures, the doctrine asserts that: firstly, Imamah is a position appointed and explicitly designated by God; secondly, the Imam is endowed with divine protection and unsurpassed nobility; and thirdly, the Imam possesses comprehensive knowledge requisite for leading humanity to truth and salvation.

input: Ibn Sīnā wrote extensively on early Islamic philosophy, especially the subjects logic, ethics, and metaphysics, including treatises named Logic and Metaphysics. Most of his works were written in Arabic – then the language of science in the Middle East – and some in Persian. Of linguistic significance even to this day are a few books that he wrote in nearly pure Persian language (particularly the Danishnamah-yi 'Ala', Philosophy for Ala' ad-Dawla'). Ibn Sīnā's commentaries on Aristotle often criticized the philosopher,[citation needed] encouraging a lively debate in the spirit of ijtihad.
rewrite: Ibn Sīnā authored numerous works central to early Islamic philosophy, particularly concerning logic, ethics, and metaphysics, with dedicated treatises on these subjects. His corpus was primarily composed in Arabic, the lingua franca of scientific discourse in the medieval Islamic world, though several works appear in Persian. Among these, texts like the *Danishnamah-yi 'Ala'* are linguistically significant for their use of nearly pure Persian. His commentaries on Aristotle frequently involved critique, fostering a tradition of scholarly debate and intellectual exertion (*ijtihad*).

input: From the German point of view, March 1941 saw an improvement. The Luftwaffe flew 4,000 sorties that month, including 12 major and three heavy attacks. The electronic war intensified but the Luftwaffe flew major inland missions only on moonlit nights. Ports were easier to find and made better targets. To confuse the British, radio silence was observed until the bombs fell. X- and Y-Gerät beams were placed over false targets and switched only at the last minute. Rapid frequency changes were introduced for X-Gerät, whose wider band of frequencies and greater tactical flexibility ensured it remained effective at a time when British selective jamming was degrading the effectiveness of Y-Gerät.
rewrite: From the German perspective, March 1941 marked a period of operational improvement. The Luftwaffe executed 4,000 sorties that month, comprising twelve major and three heavy attacks. While the electronic warfare intensified, major inland missions were confined to moonlit nights. Ports, being more readily identifiable, presented superior targets. To deceive British defenses, radio silence was maintained until bomb release. X- and Y-Gerät beams were initially directed over false objectives, shifting to true targets only at the last moment. Rapid frequency changes were implemented for X-Gerät; its broader frequency band and greater tactical flexibility maintained its efficacy, whereas British selective jamming increasingly degraded the Y-Gerät system.

input: President Benito Juárez was re-elected in the general election of 1867 in which he received strong liberal support, especially in Chihuahua. Luis Terrazas was confirmed by the people of Chihuahua to be governor of the state. But soon after the election, President Juárez had another crisis on his hands; the Juárez administration was suspected to be involved in the assassination of the military chief José María Patoni executed by General Canto in August 1868. General Canto turned himself over to Donato Guerra. Canto was sentenced to death, but later his sentence changed to 10 years imprisonment. The sense of injustice gave rise to a new rebellion in 1869 that threatened the federal government. In response, the Juárez administration took drastic measures by temporarily suspending constitutional rights, but the governor of Chihuahua did not support this action. Hostilities continued to increase especially after the election of 1871 which was perceived to be fraudulent. A new popular leader arose among the rebels, Porfirio Díaz. The federal government was successful in quelling rebellions in Durango an Chihuahua. On July 18, 1872, President Juárez died from a heart attack; soon after, many of his supporters ceased the fighting. Peace returned to Chihuahua and the new government was led by Governor Antonio Ochoa (formerly a co-owner of the Batopilas silver mines) in 1873 after Luis Terrazas finished his term in 1872.
rewrite:
Following his re-election in the general election of 1867, President Benito Juárez, who garnered substantial liberal support particularly in Chihuahua, confronted a significant political crisis. This emerged from allegations that his administration was complicit in the August 1868 assassination of military chief José María Patoni, carried out by General Canto. After surrendering to Donato Guerra, General Canto received a death sentence, later commuted to ten years' imprisonment. This outcome fostered a widespread perception of injustice, precipitating a new rebellion in 1869 that directly challenged federal authority. In reaction, the Juárez government enacted drastic measures, including the temporary suspension of constitutional guarantees, a move opposed by Chihuahua’s governor, Luis Terrazas, who had been confirmed in his office by popular vote.

Tensions escalated further following the contentious and widely perceived fraudulent presidential election of 1871, during which the rebel leader Porfirio Díaz gained prominence. Although federal forces succeeded in suppressing insurrections in Durango and Chihuahua, the political landscape shifted abruptly upon President Juárez’s death from a heart attack on July 18, 1872, leading many of his adherents to abandon hostilities. Consequently, peace was restored in Chihuahua. After Governor Terrazas concluded his term in 1872, the state government was subsequently led by Governor Antonio Ochoa, a former co-owner of the Batopilas silver mines, in 1873.

input: After the war, Nasser returned to his role as an instructor at the Royal Military Academy. He sent emissaries to forge an alliance with the Muslim Brotherhood in October 1948, but soon concluded that the religious agenda of the Brotherhood was not compatible with his nationalism. From then on, Nasser prevented the Brotherhood's influence over his cadres' activities without severing ties with the organization. Nasser was sent as a member of the Egyptian delegation to Rhodes in February 1949 to negotiate a formal armistice with Israel, and reportedly considered the terms to be humiliating, particularly because the Israelis were able to easily occupy the Eilat region while negotiating with the Arabs in March.
rewrite: Following the war, Gamal Abdel Nasser resumed his position as an instructor at the Royal Military Academy. In October 1948, he dispatched emissaries to establish an alliance with the Muslim Brotherhood. However, he promptly determined that the Brotherhood's religious objectives were incompatible with his nationalist vision. Consequently, Nasser acted to insulate his cadres from the organization's influence while maintaining a nominal relationship. In February 1949, he served as a member of the Egyptian delegation to Rhodes to negotiate a formal armistice with Israel. He reportedly viewed the resulting terms as humiliating, especially due to Israel's unopposed occupation of the Eilat region during the negotiations in March.

input: Monopole antennas consist of a single radiating element such as a metal rod, often mounted over a conducting surface, a ground plane. One side of the feedline from the receiver or transmitter is connected to the rod, and the other side to the ground plane, which may be the Earth. The most common form is the quarter-wave monopole which is one-quarter of a wavelength long and has a gain of 5.12 dBi when mounted over a ground plane. Monopoles have an omnidirectional radiation pattern, so they are used for broad coverage of an area, and have vertical polarization. The ground waves used for broadcasting at low frequencies must be vertically polarized, so large vertical monopole antennas are used for broadcasting in the MF, LF, and VLF bands. Small monopoles are used as nondirectional antennas on portable radios in the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
rewrite: A monopole antenna comprises a singular radiating element, typically a metallic rod, positioned above a conductive ground plane. The feedline from the associated transmitter or receiver connects one terminal to this element and the other to the ground plane, which may be the Earth itself. The predominant configuration is the quarter-wave monopole, with a length equaling one-quarter of the operational wavelength; when situated over an ideal ground plane, it exhibits a gain of approximately 5.12 dBi. This antenna type produces an omnidirectional radiation pattern with vertical polarization, enabling broad spatial coverage. Consequently, large vertical monopoles are employed for broadcasting within the MF, LF, and VLF bands, where vertically polarized ground wave propagation is essential. Smaller monopoles function as nondirectional antennas for portable radio equipment operating at HF, VHF, and UHF frequencies.

input: The official English name of the system is BeiDou Navigation Satellite System. It is named after the Big Dipper constellation, which is known in Chinese as Běidǒu. The name literally means "Northern Dipper", the name given by ancient Chinese astronomers to the seven brightest stars of the Ursa Major constellation. Historically, this set of stars was used in navigation to locate the North Star Polaris. As such, the name BeiDou also serves as a metaphor for the purpose of the satellite navigation system.
rewrite: The BeiDou Navigation Satellite System derives its official English designation from the Big Dipper constellation, termed Běidǒu in Chinese. Translated as "Northern Dipper," this name historically refers to the seven primary stars of Ursa Major, which ancient Chinese astronomers employed for celestial navigation by identifying Polaris. Consequently, the name BeiDou metaphorically reflects the system's fundamental purpose of providing navigational guidance.

input: Luís Cabral, brother of Amílcar and co-founder of PAIGC, was appointed the first President of Guinea-Bissau. Following independence, the PAIGC killed thousands of local Guinean soldiers who had fought along with the Portuguese Army against guerrillas. Some escaped to settle in Portugal or other African nations. One of the massacres occurred in the town of Bissorã. In 1980 the PAIGC acknowledged in its newspaper Nó Pintcha (dated 29 November 1980) that many Gueinean soldiers had been executed and buried in unmarked collective graves in the woods of Cumerá, Portogole, and Mansabá.
rewrite: Luís Cabral, brother of Amílcar Cabral and co-founder of the PAIGC, became the inaugural President of Guinea-Bissau. Post-independence, the PAIGC executed thousands of indigenous Guinean soldiers who had served alongside the Portuguese Army during the conflict. While some soldiers fled to Portugal or other African states, a notable massacre occurred in Bissorã. In 1980, the PAIGC’s official newspaper, *Nó Pintcha* (29 November), acknowledged these executions, confirming victims were interred in unmarked mass graves within the forests of Cumerá, Portogole, and Mansabá.

input: In the Battle of Cowan's Ford, Cornwallis met resistance along the banks of the Catawba River at Cowan's Ford on February 1, 1781, in an attempt to engage General Morgan's forces during a tactical withdrawal. Morgan had moved to the northern part of the state to combine with General Greene's newly recruited forces. Generals Greene and Cornwallis finally met at the Battle of Guilford Courthouse in present-day Greensboro on March 15, 1781. Although the British troops held the field at the end of the battle, their casualties at the hands of the numerically superior Continental Army were crippling. Following this "Pyrrhic victory", Cornwallis chose to move to the Virginia coastline to get reinforcements, and to allow the Royal Navy to protect his battered army. This decision would result in Cornwallis' eventual defeat at Yorktown, Virginia, later in 1781. The Patriots' victory there guaranteed American independence.
rewrite: On February 1, 1781, British forces under General Cornwallis encountered resistance at Cowan’s Ford on the Catawba River while attempting to intercept General Morgan’s tactically withdrawing troops. Morgan had proceeded northward to consolidate with the newly recruited army of General Greene. The two principal armies ultimately engaged at the Battle of Guilford Courthouse near present-day Greensboro on March 15, 1781. While British forces retained possession of the field, they sustained crippling casualties against the numerically superior Continental Army. In the wake of this Pyrrhic victory, Cornwallis elected to relocate to the Virginia coastline to procure reinforcements and secure protection from the Royal Navy for his depleted army. This strategic movement, however, culminated in his decisive defeat at Yorktown, Virginia, later that same year—a pivotal Patriot victory that ensured American independence.

input: Having been capital of a vast pre-Hispanic empire, and also the capital of richest viceroyalty within the Spanish Empire (ruling over a vast territory in the Americas and Spanish West Indies), and, finally, the capital of the United Mexican States, Mexico City has a rich history of artistic expression. Since the mesoamerican pre-Classical period the inhabitants of the settlements around Lake Texcoco produced many works of art and complex craftsmanship, some of which are today displayed at the world-renowned National Museum of Anthropology and the Templo Mayor museum. While many pieces of pottery and stone-engraving have survived, the great majority of the Amerindian iconography was destroyed during the Conquest of Mexico.
rewrite: Mexico City possesses a profound historical legacy as the capital of a major pre-Hispanic empire, the wealthiest viceroyalty of the Spanish Empire, and, ultimately, the modern United Mexican States. This enduring centrality has fostered a rich tradition of artistic expression. From the Mesoamerican Preclassic period, inhabitants of the Lake Texcoco settlements produced sophisticated artworks and craftsmanship, examples of which are housed in the National Museum of Anthropology and the Templo Mayor museum. Although significant ceramic and lithic works endure, the majority of Indigenous iconography was lost during the Spanish conquest.

input: In 1853, Victoria gave birth to her eighth child, Leopold, with the aid of the new anaesthetic, chloroform. Victoria was so impressed by the relief it gave from the pain of childbirth that she used it again in 1857 at the birth of her ninth and final child, Beatrice, despite opposition from members of the clergy, who considered it against biblical teaching, and members of the medical profession, who thought it dangerous. Victoria may have suffered from post-natal depression after many of her pregnancies. Letters from Albert to Victoria intermittently complain of her loss of self-control. For example, about a month after Leopold's birth Albert complained in a letter to Victoria about her "continuance of hysterics" over a "miserable trifle".
rewrite: In 1853, Queen Victoria delivered her eighth child, Prince Leopold, utilizing the novel anaesthetic chloroform. So appreciative was she of the pain relief it provided that she employed it again in 1857 during the birth of her ninth and final child, Princess Beatrice. This occurred notwithstanding opposition from certain clergy, who deemed it biblically proscribed, and from some medical practitioners, who considered it hazardous. Historical evidence suggests Victoria may have experienced post-natal depression following several pregnancies. Correspondence from Prince Albert to the Queen intermittently references a loss of emotional regulation on her part. For instance, approximately one month after Leopold's birth, Albert lamented in a letter what he described as her "continuance of hysterics" over a "miserable trifle."

input: In 1978, Hayek came into conflict with the Liberal Party leader, David Steel, who claimed that liberty was possible only with "social justice and an equitable distribution of wealth and power, which in turn require a degree of active government intervention" and that the Conservative Party were more concerned with the connection between liberty and private enterprise than between liberty and democracy. Hayek claimed that a limited democracy might be better than other forms of limited government at protecting liberty but that an unlimited democracy was worse than other forms of unlimited government because "its government loses the power even to do what it thinks right if any group on which its majority depends thinks otherwise".
rewrite: In 1978, Friedrich Hayek disputed assertions made by Liberal Party leader David Steel. Steel had argued that liberty necessitated social justice and an equitable distribution of wealth and power, objectives requiring active government intervention. He further contended that the Conservative Party prioritized the link between liberty and private enterprise over that between liberty and democracy. Hayek countered that while a constitutionally limited democracy could be superior to other constrained governments in safeguarding liberty, an unlimited democracy was more dangerous than other absolute regimes. He maintained that in such a system, a government forfeits the capacity to act on its principles if any faction within its majority coalition objects.

input: Since the early history of the United States, Amerindians, African–Americans, and European Americans have been classified as belonging to different races. Efforts to track mixing between groups led to a proliferation of categories, such as mulatto and octoroon. The criteria for membership in these races diverged in the late 19th century. During Reconstruction, increasing numbers of Americans began to consider anyone with "one drop" of known "Black blood" to be Black, regardless of appearance.3 By the early 20th century, this notion was made statutory in many states.4 Amerindians continue to be defined by a certain percentage of "Indian blood" (called blood quantum). To be White one had to have perceived "pure" White ancestry. The one-drop rule or hypodescent rule refers to the convention of defining a person as racially black if he or she has any known African ancestry. This rule meant that those that were mixed race but with some discernible African ancestry were defined as black. The one-drop rule is specific to not only those with African ancestry but to the United States, making it a particularly African-American experience.
rewrite: From the nation’s early history, American society has formally categorized Native Americans, African Americans, and European Americans as distinct racial groups. Attempts to monitor intergroup mixture subsequently multiplied racial classifications, introducing terms such as “mulatto” and “octoroon.” The criteria for assigning individuals to these races shifted significantly in the late nineteenth century. The Reconstruction era saw the rise of the “one-drop rule,” wherein any known African ancestry rendered a person socially and legally Black, irrespective of phenotypic appearance. By the early twentieth century, numerous states had codified this principle into law. In contrast, definitions for Native American identity often relied on specific “blood quantum” thresholds. Whiteness, meanwhile, was contingent upon the presumption of exclusively European ancestry. Formally termed the rule of hypodescent, the one-drop rule classified any individual with discernible African ancestry as Black, thereby subsuming mixed-race persons within that category. This social and legal convention is unique to the United States and is tied specifically to African ancestry, constituting a distinct element of the African American historical experience.

input: After the expulsion of the German population ethnic Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians were settled in the northern part. In the Soviet part of the region, a policy of eliminating all remnants of German history was pursued. All German place names were replaced by new Russian names. The exclave was a military zone, which was closed to foreigners; Soviet citizens could only enter with special permission. In 1967 the remnants of Königsberg Castle were demolished on the orders of Leonid Brezhnev to make way for a new "House of the Soviets".
rewrite: Following the expulsion of the German populace, ethnic Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians were resettled in the northern area. Within the Soviet portion, authorities enacted a policy to erase all vestiges of German heritage, systematically replacing German toponyms with new Russian designations. The exclave functioned as a restricted military zone, inaccessible to foreigners and requiring Soviet citizens to obtain special entry permits. In 1967, by order of Leonid Brezhnev, the remains of Königsberg Castle were demolished to clear the site for the construction of a new "House of the Soviets."

input: The College of Arts and Letters was established as the university's first college in 1842 with the first degrees given in 1849. The university's first academic curriculum was modeled after the Jesuit Ratio Studiorum from Saint Louis University. Today the college, housed in O'Shaughnessy Hall, includes 20 departments in the areas of fine arts, humanities, and social sciences, and awards Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degrees in 33 majors, making it the largest of the university's colleges. There are around 2,500 undergraduates and 750 graduates enrolled in the college.
rewrite: Founded in 1842 as the institution's inaugural college, the College of Arts and Letters conferred its first degrees in 1849. Its original curriculum was patterned after the Jesuit *Ratio Studiorum* from Saint Louis University. Currently located in O'Shaughnessy Hall, the college comprises 20 departments spanning the fine arts, humanities, and social sciences. It offers Bachelor of Arts degrees across 33 majors, constituting the university's largest college, with an enrollment of approximately 2,500 undergraduate and 750 graduate students.

input: Ann Arbor has a council-manager form of government. The City Council has 11 voting members: the mayor and 10 city council members. The mayor and city council members serve two-year terms: the mayor is elected every even-numbered year, while half of the city council members are up for election annually (five in even-numbered and five in odd-numbered years). Two council members are elected from each of the city's five wards. The mayor is elected citywide. The mayor is the presiding officer of the City Council and has the power to appoint all Council committee members as well as board and commission members, with the approval of the City Council. The current mayor of Ann Arbor is Christopher Taylor, a Democrat who was elected as mayor in 2014. Day-to-day city operations are managed by a city administrator chosen by the city council.
rewrite: The city of Ann Arbor operates under a council-manager system of governance. Legislative authority resides in an eleven-member City Council, comprising the mayor and ten council members, all serving two-year terms. The mayor is elected at-large in even-numbered years. Council members are elected from each of the city's five wards, with two representatives per ward. Staggered terms ensure continuity, as five seats are contested in even-numbered years and five in odd-numbered years. The mayor presides over the Council and holds appointment powers for Council committees and municipal boards and commissions, subject to Council confirmation. The current mayor, Christopher Taylor, a Democrat, was initially elected to the office in 2014. Daily administrative functions are executed by a professional city administrator appointed by the Council.

input: During the Hundred Years' War, the army of the Duke of Burgundy and a force of about two hundred English soldiers occupied Paris from May 1420 until 1436. They repelled an attempt by Joan of Arc to liberate the city in 1429. A century later, during the French Wars of Religion, Paris was a stronghold of the Catholic League. On 24 August 1572, Paris was the site of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre, when thousands of French Protestants were killed. The last of these wars, the eighth one, ended in 1594, after Henri IV had converted to Catholicism and was finally able to enter Paris as he supposedly declared Paris vaut bien une messe ("Paris is well worth a Mass"). The city had been neglected for decades; by the time of his assassination in 1610, Henry IV had rebuilt the Pont Neuf, the first Paris bridge with sidewalks and not lined with buildings, linked with a new wing the Louvre to the Tuileries Palace, and created the first Paris residential square, the Place Royale, now Place des Vosges.
rewrite: From May 1420 until 1436, during the Hundred Years' War, Paris was occupied by the Burgundian army alongside a contingent of approximately two hundred English soldiers. This occupation force successfully repelled an assault led by Joan of Arc aimed at liberating the city in 1429. A century later, during the French Wars of Religion, Paris served as a principal stronghold for the Catholic League. The city was the site of the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre on 24 August 1572, wherein thousands of French Protestants were killed. The conclusion of the eighth and final war in 1594 followed Henry IV’s conversion to Catholicism, which enabled his entry into Paris, famously accompanied by the declaration, "Paris vaut bien une messe" ("Paris is well worth a Mass"). Having suffered from prolonged neglect, the city underwent significant renovation under Henry IV before his assassination in 1610. These projects included the completion of the Pont Neuf, the first bridge in Paris featuring sidewalks and devoid of built structures, the connection of the Louvre to the Tuileries Palace via a new wing, and the establishment of the inaugural residential square, the Place Royale, now known as the Place des Vosges.

input: The name Montana comes from the Spanish word Montaña, meaning "mountain", or more broadly, "mountainous country". Montaña del Norte was the name given by early Spanish explorers to the entire mountainous region of the west. The name Montana was added to a bill by the United States House Committee on Territories, which was chaired at the time by Rep. James Ashley of Ohio, for the territory that would become Idaho Territory. The name was successfully changed by Representatives Henry Wilson (Massachusetts) and Benjamin F. Harding (Oregon), who complained that Montana had "no meaning". When Ashley presented a bill to establish a temporary government in 1864 for a new territory to be carved out of Idaho, he again chose Montana Territory. This time Rep. Samuel Cox, also of Ohio, objected to the name. Cox complained that the name was a misnomer given that most of the territory was not mountainous and that a Native American name would be more appropriate than a Spanish one. Other names such as Shoshone were suggested, but it was eventually decided that the Committee on Territories could name it whatever they wanted, so the original name of Montana was adopted.
rewrite: The appellation "Montana" is derived from the Spanish term *Montaña*, signifying "mountain" or, more expansively, "mountainous country." Early Spanish explorers designated the western mountainous region as *Montaña del Norte*. The name was initially introduced into legislation for the area that would become Idaho Territory by the United States House Committee on Territories, then chaired by Representative James Ashley of Ohio. However, Representatives Henry Wilson of Massachusetts and Benjamin F. Harding of Oregon successfully moved to strike it, arguing Montana possessed "no meaning." When Ashley later proposed a bill in 1864 to establish a temporary government for a new territory carved from Idaho, he again selected Montana Territory. Representative Samuel Cox, also of Ohio, objected, contending the name was a misnomer, as much of the territory was not mountainous, and a Native American name would be more appropriate. Alternative suggestions, including Shoshone, were offered. Ultimately, it was determined that the Committee on Territories held the prerogative of designation, and the original name Montana was retained.

input: The Old Swiss Confederacy had acquired a reputation of invincibility during these earlier wars, but expansion of the federation suffered a setback in 1515 with the Swiss defeat in the Battle of Marignano. This ended the so-called "heroic" epoch of Swiss history. The success of Zwingli's Reformation in some cantons led to inter-cantonal religious conflicts in 1529 and 1531 (Wars of Kappel). It was not until more than one hundred years after these internal wars that, in 1648, under the Peace of Westphalia, European countries recognized Switzerland's independence from the Holy Roman Empire and its neutrality.
rewrite: The Old Swiss Confederacy had established a reputation for military invincibility in prior conflicts, yet its territorial expansion encountered a significant reversal following the Swiss defeat at the Battle of Marignano in 1515. This concluded the so-called "heroic" era of Swiss history. Subsequently, the advancement of Zwingli's Reformation in certain cantons precipitated inter-cantonal religious warfare in 1529 and 1531, known as the Wars of Kappel. Only over a century later, with the 1648 Peace of Westphalia, did European powers formally recognize both Swiss independence from the Holy Roman Empire and its neutrality.

input: The period between the foundation of the Han dynasty and Wang Mang's reign is known as the Western Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 西汉; traditional Chinese: 西漢; pinyin: Xī Hàn) or Former Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 前汉; traditional Chinese: 前漢; pinyin: Qiánhàn) (206 BC – 9 AD). During this period the capital was at Chang'an (modern Xi'an). From the reign of Guangwu the capital was moved eastward to Luoyang. The era from his reign until the fall of Han is known as the Eastern Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 东汉; traditional Chinese: 東漢; pinyin: Dōng Hàn) or the Later Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 后汉; traditional Chinese: 後漢; pinyin: Hòu Hàn) (25–220 AD).
rewrite: The era from the establishment of the Han dynasty in 206 BCE to the interregnum of Wang Mang in 9 CE is designated the Western Han or Former Han dynasty, with its administrative center at Chang'an (contemporary Xi'an). Following the restoration under Emperor Guangwu, the capital was relocated eastward to Luoyang. The subsequent period from 25 CE until the dynasty's dissolution in 220 CE is consequently termed the Eastern Han or Later Han dynasty. This bifurcation into Western and Eastern periods is primarily defined by the geographical shift of the imperial capital.

input: The sociology of culture grew from the intersection between sociology (as shaped by early theorists like Marx, Durkheim, and Weber) with the growing discipline of anthropology, where in researchers pioneered ethnographic strategies for describing and analyzing a variety of cultures around the world. Part of the legacy of the early development of the field lingers in the methods (much of cultural sociological research is qualitative), in the theories (a variety of critical approaches to sociology are central to current research communities), and in the substantive focus of the field. For instance, relationships between popular culture, political control, and social class were early and lasting concerns in the field.
rewrite: The sociology of culture emerged from the convergence of classical sociological theory, as developed by foundational figures such as Marx, Durkheim, and Weber, with the methodological advances of anthropology, particularly its ethnographic approaches to studying diverse societies. Enduring legacies of this formative period remain evident in the field's predominant qualitative methodologies, its sustained engagement with critical theoretical frameworks, and its substantive foci. Among these lasting concerns is the examination of the relationships among popular culture, mechanisms of political control, and social stratification.

input: In October 2004, Sarah Forsyth claimed that she had been dismissed unfairly by Eton College and had been bullied by senior staff. She also claimed she was instructed to do some of Prince Harry's coursework to enable him to pass AS Art. As evidence, Forsyth provided secretly recorded conversations with both Prince Harry and her Head of Department, Ian Burke. An employment tribunal in July 2005 found that she had been unfairly dismissed and criticised Burke for bullying her and for repeatedly changing his story. It also criticised the school for failing to produce its capability procedures and criticised the Head Master for not reviewing the case independently.
rewrite: In October 2004, Sarah Forsyth alleged unfair dismissal from Eton College and bullying by senior staff. She further contended that she was directed to complete portions of Prince Harry’s coursework to facilitate his passing of AS Art. Forsyth submitted as evidence covertly recorded conversations with both the Prince and her Head of Department, Ian Burke. A July 2005 employment tribunal ruled her dismissal unfair. It censured Burke for bullying and for providing inconsistent testimony, criticised the school for failing to furnish its capability procedures, and faulted the Head Master for neglecting to conduct an independent review of the case.

input: Because of its limited land area, Bermuda has had difficulty with over-population. In the first two centuries of settlement, it relied on steady human emigration to keep the population manageable.[citation needed] Before the American Revolution more than ten thousand Bermudians (over half of the total population through the years) gradually emigrated, primarily to the Southern United States. As Great Britain displaced Spain as the dominant European imperial power, it opened up more land for colonial development. A steady trickle of outward migration continued. With seafaring the only real industry in the early decades, by the end of the 18th century, at least a third of the island's manpower was at sea at any one time.
rewrite: Bermuda’s limited land area has historically presented challenges of overpopulation. During its first two centuries of settlement, the colony relied on sustained emigration to maintain a manageable population. Prior to the American Revolution, over ten thousand Bermudians—more than half of the cumulative population—emigrated, chiefly to the Southern United States. As Great Britain supplanted Spain as the preeminent imperial power, additional colonial territories became available, facilitating further outward migration. With maritime activities constituting the primary industry in the early period, by the late eighteenth century at least one-third of the island’s male workforce was engaged in seafaring at any given time.

input: Although an alloy is technically an impure metal, when referring to alloys, the term "impurities" usually denotes those elements which are not desired. These impurities are often found in the base metals or the solutes, but they may also be introduced during the alloying process. For instance, sulfur is a common impurity in steel. Sulfur combines readily with iron to form iron sulfide, which is very brittle, creating weak spots in the steel. Lithium, sodium and calcium are common impurities in aluminium alloys, which can have adverse effects on the structural integrity of castings. Conversely, otherwise pure-metals that simply contain unwanted impurities are often called "impure metals" and are not usually referred to as alloys. Oxygen, present in the air, readily combines with most metals to form metal oxides; especially at higher temperatures encountered during alloying. Great care is often taken during the alloying process to remove excess impurities, using fluxes, chemical additives, or other methods of extractive metallurgy.
rewrite: While an alloy is, by definition, an impure metal, within metallurgical contexts the term "impurities" specifically denotes undesired elements. These may originate from the base metals or alloying solutes, or be introduced during processing. For example, sulfur is a frequent impurity in steel, readily combining with iron to form brittle iron sulfide that compromises mechanical strength. Similarly, lithium, sodium, and calcium are common deleterious impurities in aluminium alloys, adversely affecting casting integrity. In contrast, metals containing only such unwanted elements are typically termed "impure metals" rather than alloys. A significant concern is atmospheric oxygen, which readily oxidizes many metals, particularly at elevated alloying temperatures. Consequently, meticulous efforts are undertaken during manufacture to remove excess impurities through fluxes, chemical additives, or other extractive metallurgical techniques.

input: According to the 2002 Census, 4.6% of the Chilean population, including the Rapanui (a Polynesian people) of Easter Island, was indigenous, although most show varying degrees of mixed heritage. Many are descendants of the Mapuche, and live in Santiago, Araucanía and the lake district. The Mapuche successfully fought off defeat in the first 300–350 years of Spanish rule during the Arauco War. Relations with the new Chilean Republic were good until the Chilean state decided to occupy their lands. During the Occupation of Araucanía the Mapuche surrendered to the country's army in the 1880s. Their land was opened to settlement by Chileans and Europeans. Conflict over Mapuche land rights continues to the present.
rewrite: According to the 2002 Census, 4.6% of Chile's population was classified as indigenous, a figure which includes the Rapanui people of Easter Island, though most individuals possess varying degrees of mixed ancestry. A significant portion are Mapuche descendants, concentrated in Santiago, Araucanía, and the lake district. The Mapuche successfully resisted Spanish conquest for approximately three centuries during the Arauco War. Relations with the nascent Chilean Republic were initially stable but deteriorated when the state moved to annex their territories. Following their military defeat in the 1880s during the Occupation of Araucanía, Mapuche lands were expropriated for Chilean and European settlement. Disputes regarding these land rights persist.

input: Temperature extremes are moderated by the adjacent Puget Sound, greater Pacific Ocean, and Lake Washington. The region is largely shielded from Pacific storms by the Olympic Mountains and from Arctic air by the Cascade Range. Despite being on the margin of the rain shadow of the Olympic Mountains, the city has a reputation for frequent rain. This reputation stems from the frequency of light precipitation in the fall, winter, and spring. In an average year, at least 0.01 inches (0.25 mm) of precipitation falls on 150 days, more than nearly all U.S. cities east of the Rocky Mountains. It is cloudy 201 days out of the year and partly cloudy 93 days. Official weather and climatic data is collected at Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, located about 19 km (12 mi) south of downtown in the city of SeaTac, which is at a higher elevation, and records more cloudy days and fewer partly cloudy days per year.
rewrite: The moderating influence of the adjacent Puget Sound, the broader Pacific Ocean, and Lake Washington mitigates temperature extremes in the region. The Olympic Mountains provide a shield from Pacific storm systems, while the Cascade Range blocks Arctic air masses. Although situated on the periphery of the Olympic Mountains' rain shadow, the area is renowned for its frequent rainfall. This reputation arises from the high incidence of light precipitation during autumn, winter, and spring. Annually, measurable precipitation of at least 0.01 inches (0.25 mm) occurs on approximately 150 days, a frequency exceeding that of nearly all major U.S. cities east of the Rocky Mountains. Skies are fully overcast 201 days per year and partly cloudy 93 days. Official climatological data is recorded at Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, situated approximately 19 km (12 mi) south of downtown Seattle in the city of SeaTac. This elevated location experiences a greater number of overcast days and fewer partly cloudy days annually compared to the city center.

input: Norfolk Island is the only non-mainland Australian territory to have achieved self-governance. The Norfolk Island Act 1979, passed by the Parliament of Australia in 1979, is the Act under which the island was governed until the passing of the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015. The Australian government maintains authority on the island through an Administrator, currently Gary Hardgrave. From 1979 to 2015, a Legislative Assembly was elected by popular vote for terms of not more than three years, although legislation passed by the Australian Parliament could extend its laws to the territory at will, including the power to override any laws made by the assembly.
rewrite: Norfolk Island is distinguished as the sole non-mainland Australian territory to have attained self-government. This status was established under the Norfolk Island Act 1979, enacted by the Australian Parliament. The island was governed by this legislation until the passage of the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015. Australian authority is represented on the island by an Administrator, a position currently held by Gary Hardgrave. Between 1979 and 2015, a locally elected Legislative Assembly served terms of up to three years. However, the Australian Parliament retained the power to extend its own legislation to the territory and to override any laws enacted by the Assembly.

input: Richard Owen showed that fossils of extinct species Darwin found in South America were allied to living species on the same continent. In March 1837, ornithologist John Gould announced that Darwin's rhea was a separate species from the previously described rhea (though their territories overlapped), that mockingbirds collected on the Galápagos Islands represented three separate species each unique to a particular island, and that several distinct birds from those islands were all classified as finches. Darwin began speculating, in a series of notebooks, on the possibility that "one species does change into another" to explain these findings, and around July sketched a genealogical branching of a single evolutionary tree, discarding Lamarck's independent lineages progressing to higher forms. Unconventionally, Darwin asked questions of fancy pigeon and animal breeders as well as established scientists. At the zoo he had his first sight of an ape, and was profoundly impressed by how human the orangutan seemed.
rewrite: Richard Owen demonstrated that fossils of extinct species discovered by Darwin in South America were closely related to living species on that continent. In March 1837, ornithologist John Gould declared that Darwin's rhea constituted a distinct species from the previously documented rhea, despite overlapping ranges. Gould further indicated that mockingbirds collected in the Galápagos Islands comprised three separate species, each unique to an individual island, and that several birds from those islands were all classified as finches. Darwin subsequently began speculating in a series of notebooks that "one species does change into another" to explain these observations. By approximately July, he sketched a genealogical branching diagram of a single evolutionary tree, thereby rejecting Lamarckian concepts of independent lineages progressing toward higher forms. In an unconventional methodology, Darwin consulted both fancy pigeon and animal breeders alongside established scientists. During a visit to the zoo, his first encounter with an ape, specifically an orangutan, profoundly impressed him with its seemingly human qualities.

input: Near-infrared is the region closest in wavelength to the radiation detectable by the human eye, mid- and far-infrared are progressively further from the visible spectrum. Other definitions follow different physical mechanisms (emission peaks, vs. bands, water absorption) and the newest follow technical reasons (the common silicon detectors are sensitive to about 1,050 nm, while InGaAs's sensitivity starts around 950 nm and ends between 1,700 and 2,600 nm, depending on the specific configuration). Unfortunately, international standards for these specifications are not currently available.
rewrite: The near-infrared region is adjacent to the visible spectrum, while mid- and far-infrared are increasingly distant. Alternative definitions are based on distinct physical criteria, such as emission peaks or atmospheric absorption bands. More recent delineations cite technical considerations, including the sensitivity ranges of common silicon (up to ~1,050 nm) and indium gallium arsenide (~950 nm to 2,600 nm) detectors. Presently, a lack of international standardization governs these specifications.

input: The Allied disaster at Austerlitz significantly shook the faith of Emperor Francis in the British-led war effort. France and Austria agreed to an armistice immediately and the Treaty of Pressburg followed shortly after on 26 December. Pressburg took Austria out of both the war and the Coalition while reinforcing the earlier treaties of Campo Formio and of Lunéville between the two powers. The treaty confirmed the Austrian loss of lands to France in Italy and Bavaria, and lands in Germany to Napoleon's German allies. It also imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs on the defeated Habsburgs and allowed the fleeing Russian troops free passage through hostile territories and back to their home soil. Napoleon went on to say, "The battle of Austerlitz is the finest of all I have fought." Frank McLynn suggests that Napoleon was so successful at Austerlitz that he lost touch with reality, and what used to be French foreign policy became a "personal Napoleonic one". Vincent Cronin disagrees, stating that Napoleon was not overly ambitious for himself, "he embodied the ambitions of thirty million Frenchmen".
rewrite: The Allied defeat at Austerlitz critically undermined Emperor Francis’s confidence in the British-directed coalition. This resulted in an immediate Franco-Austrian armistice, culminating in the Treaty of Pressburg on 26 December. This agreement formally removed Austria from both the war and the Third Coalition, while reaffirming the prior terms established at Campo Formio and Lunéville. The treaty ratified Austrian territorial cessions to France in Italy and to French-aligned states in Bavaria and Germany, levied a substantial indemnity of forty million francs upon the Habsburg monarchy, and guaranteed safe passage for retreating Russian forces. Napoleon himself later declared Austerlitz his greatest military victory. Historian Frank McLynn argues that the scale of this triumph precipitated a detachment from strategic reality, transforming French state policy into a personal Napoleonic venture. Conversely, Vincent Cronin contests this view, proposing that Napoleon’s aims were not merely self-aggrandizing but rather representative of the collective aspirations of the French populace.

input: During the three years following its inception, the university bore three different names. The board first approved "Eliot Seminary," but William Eliot was uncomfortable with naming a university after himself and objected to the establishment of a seminary, which would implicitly be charged with teaching a religious faith. He favored a nonsectarian university. In 1854, the Board of Trustees changed the name to "Washington Institute" in honor of George Washington. Naming the University after the nation's first president, only seven years before the American Civil War and during a time of bitter national division, was no coincidence. During this time of conflict, Americans universally admired George Washington as the father of the United States and a symbol of national unity. The Board of Trustees believed that the university should be a force of unity in a strongly divided Missouri. In 1856, the University amended its name to "Washington University." The university amended its name once more in 1976, when the Board of Trustees voted to add the suffix "in St. Louis" to distinguish the university from the nearly two dozen other universities bearing Washington's name.
rewrite: In the initial triennium following its establishment, the institution operated under three distinct designations. The board initially ratified "Eliot Seminary," yet William Eliot expressed reservations both about the use of his name and the term "seminary," which connoted instruction in a specific religious doctrine, preferring instead a nonsectarian university. Consequently, in 1854, the Board of Trustees adopted "Washington Institute" in tribute to George Washington. This choice, occurring merely seven years prior to the American Civil War amid profound national discord, was deliberate. Washington was universally venerated as a unifying national symbol, and the Board envisioned the university as a consolidating force within a deeply divided Missouri. By 1856, the name was revised to "Washington University." A final modification occurred in 1976, when the Board appended "in St. Louis" to differentiate the institution from numerous other universities bearing Washington’s name.

input: According to the preamble in The Law of Treaties, treaties are a source of international law. If an act or lack thereof is condemned under international law, the act will not assume international legality even if approved by internal law. This means that in case of a conflict with domestic law, international law will always prevail.
rewrite: As articulated in the preamble to The Law of Treaties, treaties constitute a source of international law. Consequently, an act condemned under international law cannot attain international legality through domestic approval. In any conflict between domestic and international law, the latter invariably prevails.

input: The Farmington Canal Trail is a rail trail that will eventually run continuously from downtown New Haven to Northampton, Massachusetts. The scenic trail follows the path of the historic New Haven and Northampton Company and the Farmington Canal. Currently, there is a continuous 14-mile (23 km) stretch of the trail from downtown, through Hamden and into Cheshire, making bicycle commuting between New Haven and those suburbs possible. The trail is part of the East Coast Greenway, a proposed 3,000-mile (4,800 km) bike path that would link every major city on the East Coast from Florida to Maine.
rewrite: The Farmington Canal Trail is a rail trail projected to extend continuously from New Haven, Connecticut, to Northampton, Massachusetts. This scenic route traces the historic corridors of the New Haven and Northampton Company and the Farmington Canal. Presently, a contiguous 14-mile (23 km) segment extends from downtown New Haven through Hamden into Cheshire, enabling bicycle commuting to these suburbs. The trail constitutes a segment of the proposed East Coast Greenway, a 3,000-mile (4,800 km) bicycle pathway intended to connect major urban centers along the eastern seaboard from Florida to Maine.

input: According to the International Organization for Migration, Nigeria witnessed a dramatic increase in remittances sent home from overseas Nigerians, going from USD 2.3 billion in 2004 to 17.9 billion in 2007. The United States accounts for the largest portion of official remittances, followed by the United Kingdom, Italy, Canada, Spain and France. On the African continent, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Chad, Libya and South Africa are important source countries of remittance flows to Nigeria, while China is the biggest remittance-sending country in Asia.
rewrite: Data from the International Organization for Migration indicate a substantial rise in remittance inflows to Nigeria, escalating from USD 2.3 billion in 2004 to USD 17.9 billion in 2007. The United States constitutes the primary source of official remittances, with the United Kingdom, Italy, Canada, Spain, and France following. Within Africa, key originating nations include Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Chad, Libya, and South Africa, while China represents the predominant remittance source in Asia.

input: The islands are located about halfway between Hawaii and Australia, north of Nauru and Kiribati, east of the Federated States of Micronesia, and south of the U.S. territory of Wake Island, to which it lays claim. The atolls and islands form two groups: the Ratak (sunrise) and the Ralik (sunset). The two island chains lie approximately parallel to one another, running northwest to southeast, comprising about 750,000 square miles (1,900,000 km2) of ocean but only about 70 square miles (180 km2) of land mass. Each includes 15 to 18 islands and atolls. The country consists of a total of 29 atolls and five isolated islands.
rewrite: Situated approximately midway between Hawaii and Australia, the islands are positioned north of Nauru and Kiribati, east of the Federated States of Micronesia, and south of the U.S. territory of Wake Island, which they claim. The archipelago is organized into two primary groups: the Ratak (sunrise) and Ralik (sunset) chains. These chains run roughly parallel from northwest to southeast, encompassing an oceanic area of about 750,000 square miles (1,900,000 km²) yet containing only approximately 70 square miles (180 km²) of land. The nation comprises 29 atolls and five isolated islands, with each chain containing between 15 and 18 islands and atolls.

input: The Caribbean initially provided England's most important and lucrative colonies, but not before several attempts at colonisation failed. An attempt to establish a colony in Guiana in 1604 lasted only two years, and failed in its main objective to find gold deposits. Colonies in St Lucia (1605) and Grenada (1609) also rapidly folded, but settlements were successfully established in St. Kitts (1624), Barbados (1627) and Nevis (1628). The colonies soon adopted the system of sugar plantations successfully used by the Portuguese in Brazil, which depended on slave labour, and—at first—Dutch ships, to sell the slaves and buy the sugar. To ensure that the increasingly healthy profits of this trade remained in English hands, Parliament decreed in 1651 that only English ships would be able to ply their trade in English colonies. This led to hostilities with the United Dutch Provinces—a series of Anglo-Dutch Wars—which would eventually strengthen England's position in the Americas at the expense of the Dutch. In 1655, England annexed the island of Jamaica from the Spanish, and in 1666 succeeded in colonising the Bahamas.
rewrite: England’s earliest ventures in Caribbean colonisation encountered repeated failures before yielding its most valuable colonial possessions. Initial efforts, such as the 1604 settlement in Guiana—abandoned after two years without discovering gold—and short-lived colonies in St. Lucia (1605) and Grenada (1609), proved unsuccessful. However, enduring settlements were established in St. Kitts (1624), Barbados (1627), and Nevis (1628). These colonies rapidly adopted the Portuguese sugar plantation model from Brazil, a system reliant on enslaved labour and, initially, Dutch shipping for both the slave trade and sugar exports. To secure the growing profits for England, Parliament passed the 1651 Navigation Act, restricting colonial trade to English vessels. This provoked hostilities with the United Dutch Provinces in the Anglo-Dutch Wars, ultimately consolidating English dominance in the Americas at Dutch expense. Further expansion followed with the capture of Jamaica from Spain in 1655 and the successful colonisation of the Bahamas in 1666.

input: New York City has been a metropolitan municipality with a mayor-council form of government since its consolidation in 1898. The government of New York is more centralized than that of most other U.S. cities. In New York City, the city government is responsible for public education, correctional institutions, public safety, recreational facilities, sanitation, water supply, and welfare services.
rewrite: Since its 1898 consolidation, New York City has operated as a metropolitan municipality under a mayor-council system. Its governmental structure is notably more centralized than those of most other U.S. cities. This centralized authority oversees essential functions including public education, corrections, safety, recreation, sanitation, water supply, and welfare services.
