input: Apple debuted the iTunes Wi-Fi Music Store on September 5, 2007, in its Media Event entitled "The Beat Goes On...". This service allows users to access the Music Store from either an iPhone or an iPod Touch and download songs directly to the device that can be synced to the user's iTunes Library over a WiFi connection, or, in the case of an iPhone, the telephone network.
rewrite: On September 5, 2007, Apple introduced the iTunes Wi-Fi Music Store during its "The Beat Goes On..." Media Event. This service enabled users of the iPhone or iPod Touch to access the Music Store, download songs directly to the device, and subsequently synchronize them with their iTunes Library via a WiFi connection. iPhone users also had the alternative of utilizing the cellular network for this purpose.

input: Society throughout Europe was disturbed by the dislocations caused by the Black Death. Lands that had been marginally productive were abandoned, as the survivors were able to acquire more fertile areas. Although serfdom declined in Western Europe it became more common in Eastern Europe, as landlords imposed it on those of their tenants who had previously been free. Most peasants in Western Europe managed to change the work they had previously owed to their landlords into cash rents. The percentage of serfs amongst the peasantry declined from a high of 90 to closer to 50 per cent by the end of the period. Landlords also became more conscious of common interests with other landholders, and they joined together to extort privileges from their governments. Partly at the urging of landlords, governments attempted to legislate a return to the economic conditions that existed before the Black Death. Non-clergy became increasingly literate, and urban populations began to imitate the nobility's interest in chivalry.
rewrite: The societal fabric across Europe was profoundly disrupted by the dislocations resulting from the Black Death. Marginally productive lands were frequently abandoned, as diminished populations enabled survivors to consolidate holdings on more fertile terrain. While serfdom waned in Western Europe, it intensified in the East, where landlords increasingly imposed servile status upon previously free tenants. In the West, most peasants successfully commuted traditional labor obligations into monetary rents, reducing the proportion of serfs within the peasantry from approximately ninety percent to near fifty by the late medieval period. Landlords, growing more conscious of shared class interests, collectively petitioned governments for privileges. Partly in response to this pressure, authorities sought to legislate a return to pre-plague economic conditions. Concurrently, literacy expanded beyond the clergy, and urban populations began to emulate the nobility’s preoccupation with chivalric culture.

input: Muslim sects regarded as heretical, such as the Druze, Ismailis, Alevis, and Alawites, ranked below Jews and Christians. In 1514, Sultan Selim I, nicknamed "the Grim" because of his cruelty, ordered the massacre of 40,000 Anatolian Alevis (Qizilbash), whom he considered heretics, reportedly proclaiming that "the killing of one Alevi had as much otherworldly reward as killing 70 Christians."[page needed] Selim was also responsible for an unprecedented and rapid expansion of the Ottoman Empire into the Middle East, especially through his conquest of the entire Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, which included much of the region. With these conquests, Selim further solidified the Ottoman claim for being an Islamic caliphate, although Ottoman sultans had been claiming the title of caliph since the 14th century starting with Murad I (reigned 1362 to 1389). The caliphate would remain held by Ottoman sultans for the rest of the office's duration, which ended with its abolition on 3 March 1924 by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey and the exile of the last caliph, Abdülmecid II, to France.
rewrite: Within the Ottoman Empire's religious hierarchy, Muslim sects deemed heterodox, including the Druze, Ismailis, Alevis, and Alawites, occupied a status inferior even to that of Jews and Christians. This was starkly demonstrated in 1514 by Sultan Selim I, whose epithet "the Grim" reflected his severe policies. He ordered the massacre of approximately 40,000 Anatolian Alevis (Qizilbash), whom he considered heretics, and is reported to have declared that killing one Alevi brought greater spiritual merit than killing seventy Christians. Selim I also presided over a dramatic expansion of the empire into the Middle East, most notably through his conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate, which encompassed Egypt and much of the surrounding region. These victories significantly bolstered the Ottoman assertion of legitimacy as an Islamic caliphate, a title claimed by sultans since the 14th century. The Ottoman dynasty retained the caliphate until its official abolition by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey on 3 March 1924, an act followed by the exile of the final caliph, Abdülmecid II, to France.

input: The U.S. Census Bureau reported that in 2000, 24.0% of San Diego residents were under 18, and 10.5% were 65 and over. As of 2011[update] the median age was 35.6; more than a quarter of residents were under age 20 and 11% were over age 65. Millennials (ages 18 through 34) constitute 27.1% of San Diego's population, the second-highest percentage in a major U.S. city. The San Diego County regional planning agency, SANDAG, provides tables and graphs breaking down the city population into 5-year age groups.
rewrite: According to U.S. Census Bureau data from 2000, 24.0% of San Diego's population was under 18 years of age, while 10.5% was 65 or older. By 2011, the median age was 35.6, with over a quarter of residents under 20 and 11% over 65. Millennials (ages 18–34) comprise 27.1% of the population, representing the second-highest proportion among major U.S. cities. Detailed demographic tables and graphs, featuring five-year age cohorts, are published by the regional planning agency SANDAG.

input: By the Middle Ages, large numbers of Jews lived in the Holy Roman Empire and had assimilated into German culture, including many Jews who had previously assimilated into French culture and had spoken a mixed Judeo-French language. Upon assimilating into German culture, the Jewish German peoples incorporated major parts of the German language and elements of other European languages into a mixed language known as Yiddish. However tolerance and assimilation of Jews in German society suddenly ended during the Crusades with many Jews being forcefully expelled from Germany and Western Yiddish disappeared as a language in Germany over the centuries, with German Jewish people fully adopting the German language.
rewrite: During the medieval period, a significant Jewish population resided within the Holy Roman Empire, having assimilated into German society. This community included individuals who had previously integrated into French culture and utilized a Judeo-French vernacular. Through this process of German acculturation, they developed Yiddish, a language primarily derived from German while incorporating elements from other European tongues. However, this era of relative tolerance concluded abruptly with the Crusades, which precipitated the forceful expulsion of many Jews from German territories. Consequently, Western Yiddish gradually vanished as a distinct language in the region, as the remaining Jewish population fully adopted standard German.

input: Inner and outer vestibules lead to the octagonal chapter house, which is of exceptional architectural purity. It is built in a Geometrical Gothic style with an octagonal crypt below. A pier of eight shafts carries the vaulted ceiling. To the sides are blind arcading, remains of 14th-century paintings and numerous stone benches above which are innovatory large 4-light quatre-foiled windows. These are virtually contemporary with the Sainte-Chapelle, Paris.
rewrite: The inner and outer vestibules provide access to the octagonal chapter house, a structure of notable architectural purity executed in the Geometrical Gothic manner. Beneath it lies an octagonal crypt. An eight-shaft pier supports the vaulted ceiling, while the side walls feature blind arcading, remnants of fourteenth-century paintings, and numerous stone benches. Above these benches are innovative large quatre-foiled four-light windows, which are nearly contemporaneous with those of the Paris Sainte-Chapelle.

input: A new government was appointed on 31 March 2013, which consisted of members of Séléka and representatives of the opposition to Bozizé, one pro-Bozizé individual, and a number representatives of civil society. On 1 April, the former opposition parties declared that they would boycott the government. After African leaders in Chad refused to recognize Djotodia as President, proposing to form a transitional council and the holding of new elections, Djotodia signed a decree on 6 April for the formation of a council that would act as a transitional parliament. The council was tasked with electing a president to serve prior to elections in 18 months.
rewrite: On 31 March 2013, a new government was appointed, comprising members of the Séléka coalition, opposition representatives to former President Bozizé, a single pro-Bozizé figure, and several civil society delegates. The following day, former opposition parties announced a boycott of this administration. Subsequently, following the refusal of African leaders meeting in Chad to recognize Michel Djotodia’s presidency—instead proposing a transitional council and new elections—Djotodia issued a decree on 6 April to establish such a council, which would function as an interim parliament. This body was mandated to elect a president to serve until elections could be held within eighteen months.

input: The bipolar junction transistor (BJT) was the most commonly used transistor in the 1960s and 70s. Even after MOSFETs became widely available, the BJT remained the transistor of choice for many analog circuits such as amplifiers because of their greater linearity and ease of manufacture. In integrated circuits, the desirable properties of MOSFETs allowed them to capture nearly all market share for digital circuits. Discrete MOSFETs can be applied in transistor applications, including analog circuits, voltage regulators, amplifiers, power transmitters and motor drivers.
rewrite: The bipolar junction transistor (BJT) was the predominant transistor type during the 1960s and 1970s. Despite the subsequent broad availability of MOSFETs, BJTs remained preferred for many analog applications, notably amplifiers, due to superior linearity and simpler fabrication. In integrated circuits, MOSFET properties enabled them to dominate digital circuit markets. Discrete MOSFETs, however, are utilized in various applications, including analog circuits, voltage regulators, amplifiers, and power control systems such as transmitters and motor drivers.

input: The centuries-long geopolitical and ideological rivalry between Safavid Iran and the neighboring Ottoman Empire, led to numerous Ottoman–Persian Wars. The Safavid Era peaked in the reign of Abbas the Great, 1587–1629, surpassing their Ottoman arch rivals in strength, and making the empire a leading hub in Western Eurasia for the sciences and arts. The Safavid Era saw the start of mass integration from Caucasian populations into new layers of the society of Iran, as well as mass resettlement of them within the heartlands of Iran, playing a pivotal role in the history of Iran for centuries onwards. Following a gradual decline in the late 1600s and early 1700s, which was caused by the internal conflicts, the continuous wars with the Ottomans, and the foreign interference (most notably the Russian interference), the Safavid rule was ended by the Pashtun rebels who besieged Isfahan and defeated Soltan Hosein in 1722.
rewrite: The protracted geopolitical and ideological conflict between Safavid Iran and the adjacent Ottoman Empire precipitated a series of Ottoman–Persian Wars. The apogee of Safavid power was achieved during the reign of Abbas the Great (1587–1629), a period in which the empire eclipsed its Ottoman rival in strength and emerged as a preeminent Western Eurasian center for scientific and artistic endeavor. This era also initiated the extensive integration of Caucasian populations into new societal strata within Iran, alongside their substantial resettlement into its central territories, processes that proved pivotal for subsequent Iranian history. After a gradual decline in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, attributable to internal discord, persistent warfare with the Ottomans, and foreign interference—most notably from Russia—Safavid rule was terminated by Pashtun rebels, who captured Isfahan and deposed Sultan Husayn in 1722.

input: The president serves as a chief of state and commander in chief of the armed forces. A prime minister appointed by the president serves as head of government and in turn appoints the Council of Ministers. The unicameral National Assembly is Mali's sole legislative body, consisting of deputies elected to five-year terms. Following the 2007 elections, the Alliance for Democracy and Progress held 113 of 160 seats in the assembly. The assembly holds two regular sessions each year, during which it debates and votes on legislation that has been submitted by a member or by the government.
rewrite: The president functions as both head of state and commander-in-chief of the armed forces. A prime minister, appointed by the president, acts as head of government and subsequently appoints the Council of Ministers. Legislative authority resides solely in the unicameral National Assembly, whose deputies are elected for five-year terms. After the 2007 elections, the Alliance for Democracy and Progress controlled 113 of the assembly's 160 seats. This body convenes for two annual ordinary sessions to debate and vote on legislation proposed by either its members or the government.

input: Pope Paul VI knew the Roman Curia well, having worked there for a generation from 1922 to 1954. He implemented his reforms in stages, rather than in one fell swoop. On 1 March 1968, he issued a regulation, a process that had been initiated by Pius XII and continued by John XXIII. On 28 March, with Pontificalis Domus, and in several additional Apostolic Constitutions in the following years, he revamped the entire Curia, which included reduction of bureaucracy, streamlining of existing congregations and a broader representation of non-Italians in the curial positions.
rewrite: Pope Paul VI, having served within the Roman Curia from 1922 to 1954, possessed intimate institutional knowledge. He enacted his reforms incrementally. Following a regulatory issuance on 1 March 1968, which continued processes begun by his predecessors Pius XII and John XXIII, he promulgated *Pontificalis Domus* on 28 March. Through subsequent Apostolic Constitutions, he comprehensively reorganized the Curia. These changes reduced bureaucratic complexity, streamlined congregations, and expanded the representation of non-Italians within curial offices.

input: A new approach to avoiding overhead wires is taken by the "second generation" tram/streetcar system in Bordeaux, France (entry into service of the first line in December 2003; original system discontinued in 1958) with its APS (alimentation par sol – ground current feed). This involves a third rail which is flush with the surface like the tops of the running rails. The circuit is divided into segments with each segment energized in turn by sensors from the car as it passes over it, the remainder of the third rail remaining "dead". Since each energized segment is completely covered by the lengthy articulated cars, and goes dead before being "uncovered" by the passage of the vehicle, there is no danger to pedestrians. This system has also been adopted in some sections of the new tram systems in Reims, France (opened 2011) and Angers, France (also opened 2011). Proposals are in place for a number of other new services including Dubai, UAE; Barcelona, Spain; Florence, Italy; Marseille, France; Gold Coast, Australia; Washington, D.C., U.S.A.; Brasília, Brazil and Tours, France.
rewrite: The "second generation" tram system in Bordeaux, France, which commenced operation in December 2003, employs a novel method to eliminate overhead wires known as Alimentation par Sol (APS), or ground current feed. This system utilizes a third rail embedded flush with the road surface. The conductive rail is segmented, and each section is activated only when sensors detect a tram passing over it, ensuring all other segments remain inert. Because the lengthy articulated vehicles completely cover any live segment, and power is cut before the segment is exposed, the design poses no hazard to pedestrians. This technology has been implemented in sections of newer tram networks in Reims and Angers, both inaugurated in 2011. Furthermore, its adoption is proposed for several forthcoming systems in cities including Dubai, Barcelona, Florence, Marseille, Gold Coast, Washington, D.C., Brasília, and Tours.

input: Beginning in first decade of the 15th century, Jan Hus—a Roman Catholic priest, Czech reformist and professor—influenced by John Wycliffe's writings, founded the Hussite movement. He strongly advocated his reformist Bohemian religious denomination. He was excommunicated and burned at the stake in Constance, Bishopric of Constance in 1415 by secular authorities for unrepentant and persistent heresy. After his execution, a revolt erupted. Hussites defeated five continuous crusades proclaimed against them by the Pope.
rewrite: In the early fifteenth century, Jan Hus, a Czech priest and professor influenced by John Wycliffe, established the Hussite movement, advocating for Bohemian religious reform. Excommunicated and executed for heresy in Constance in 1415, his death sparked a revolt. The Hussites subsequently repelled five consecutive papal crusades directed against them.

input: Efforts have been made to protect Guam's coral reef habitats from pollution, eroded silt and overfishing, problems that have led to decreased fish populations. (Since Guam is a significant vacation spot for scuba divers, this is important.) In recent years, the Department of Agriculture, Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources has established several new marine preserves where fish populations are monitored by biologists. Before adopting U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards, portions of Tumon Bay were dredged by the hotel chains to provide a better experience for hotel guests. Tumon Bay has since been made into a preserve. A federal Guam National Wildlife Refuge in northern Guam protects the decimated sea turtle population in addition to a small colony of Mariana fruit bats.
rewrite: Efforts have been undertaken to safeguard the coral reef habitats of Guam from degradation caused by pollution, sedimentation, and overfishing, which have contributed to declines in fish populations. This is particularly significant given Guam's status as a major destination for scuba diving tourism. Recently, the Department of Agriculture's Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources has instituted multiple new marine preserves, within which biologists monitor aquatic life. Prior to the implementation of U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards, sections of Tumon Bay were dredged by hotel enterprises to enhance guest amenities; this area has subsequently been designated as a preserve. Additionally, a federal Guam National Wildlife Refuge in northern Guam protects the severely reduced sea turtle population alongside a small colony of Mariana fruit bats.

input: The Karabakh war ended after a Russian-brokered cease-fire was put in place in 1994. The war was a success for the Karabakh Armenian forces who managed to capture 16% of Azerbaijan's internationally recognised territory including Nagorno-Karabakh itself. Since then, Armenia and Azerbaijan have held peace talks, mediated by the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE). The status of Karabakh has yet to be determined. The economies of both countries have been hurt in the absence of a complete resolution and Armenia's borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan remain closed. By the time both Azerbaijan and Armenia had finally agreed to a ceasefire in 1994, an estimated 30,000 people had been killed and over a million had been displaced.
rewrite: The Nagorno-Karabakh conflict concluded with a Russian-mediated ceasefire in 1994. This outcome represented a military success for Karabakh Armenian forces, which secured control over approximately 16% of Azerbaijan's internationally recognized territory, encompassing the Nagorno-Karabakh region itself. Subsequent peace negotiations, facilitated by the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), have failed to produce a final settlement regarding the territory's status. The protracted dispute has inflicted economic damage on both nations and resulted in the continued closure of Armenia's borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. The conflict's human cost was severe, with an estimated 30,000 fatalities and over one million individuals displaced by the 1994 ceasefire.

input: On 27 August 2007, Royal Dutch Shell and Reitan Group, the owner of the 7-Eleven brand in Scandinavia, announced an agreement to re-brand some 269 service stations across Norway, Sweden, Finland and Denmark, subject to obtaining regulatory approvals under the different competition laws in each country. On April 2010 Shell announced that the corporation is in process of trying to find a potential buyer for all of its operations in Finland and is doing similar market research concerning Swedish operations. On October 2010 Shell's gas stations and the heavy vehicle fuel supply networks in Finland and Sweden, along with a refinery located in Gothenburg, Sweden were sold to St1, a Finnish energy company, more precisely to its major shareholding parent company Keele Oy. Shell branded gas stations will be rebranded within maximum of five years from the acquisition and the number of gas stations is likely to be reduced. Until then the stations will operate under Shell brand licence.
rewrite: On 27 August 2007, Royal Dutch Shell and the Reitan Group, holder of the 7-Eleven brand franchise in Scandinavia, announced an agreement to rebrand approximately 269 service stations across Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark. This agreement was contingent upon securing requisite regulatory approvals under the respective national competition laws of each country. In April 2010, Shell disclosed it was seeking a potential buyer for its entire Finnish operations and was conducting analogous market research regarding its Swedish assets. Subsequently, in October 2010, Shell's retail fuel stations and heavy vehicle fuel supply networks in Finland and Sweden, along with a refinery in Gothenburg, Sweden, were divested to the Finnish energy company St1, specifically to its major shareholder, Keele Oy. The acquired stations will be rebranded from the Shell identity within a maximum period of five years post-acquisition, during which they will operate under a Shell brand license, with a likely reduction in the total number of outlets.

input: There are many different patterns of gas exchange demonstrated by different groups of insects. Gas exchange patterns in insects can range from continuous and diffusive ventilation, to discontinuous gas exchange.:65–68 During continuous gas exchange, oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide is released in a continuous cycle. In discontinuous gas exchange, however, the insect takes in oxygen while it is active and small amounts of carbon dioxide are released when the insect is at rest. Diffusive ventilation is simply a form of continuous gas exchange that occurs by diffusion rather than physically taking in the oxygen. Some species of insect that are submerged also have adaptations to aid in respiration. As larvae, many insects have gills that can extract oxygen dissolved in water, while others need to rise to the water surface to replenish air supplies which may be held or trapped in special structures.
rewrite: Insects exhibit diverse patterns of gas exchange, which can be categorized primarily as continuous, discontinuous, or diffusive ventilation. In continuous gas exchange, oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide release occur in an unbroken cycle. Discontinuous gas exchange, by contrast, involves active oxygen intake punctuated by periods of rest, during which only minimal amounts of carbon dioxide are emitted. Diffusive ventilation constitutes a specific form of continuous exchange, relying on diffusion processes rather than active respiratory movements. Additionally, various aquatic or submerged insects possess specialized respiratory adaptations. Many larval forms utilize gills to extract dissolved oxygen from water, while others must return to the water surface to access atmospheric air, which is often stored within specialized anatomical structures.

input: About 30 people have been indicted for participating in genocide or complicity in genocide during the early 1990s in Bosnia. To date, after several plea bargains and some convictions that were successfully challenged on appeal two men, Vujadin Popović and Ljubiša Beara, have been found guilty of committing genocide, Zdravko Tolimir has been found guilty of committing genocide and conspiracy to commit genocide, and two others, Radislav Krstić and Drago Nikolić, have been found guilty of aiding and abetting genocide. Three others have been found guilty of participating in genocides in Bosnia by German courts, one of whom Nikola Jorgić lost an appeal against his conviction in the European Court of Human Rights. A further eight men, former members of the Bosnian Serb security forces were found guilty of genocide by the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina (See List of Bosnian genocide prosecutions).
rewrite: Approximately thirty individuals have been indicted for genocide or complicity in genocide during the Bosnian conflict of the early 1990s. Judicial outcomes to date include several plea agreements and appealed convictions. Specifically, Vujadin Popović and Ljubiša Beara have been conclusively convicted of genocide, while Zdravko Tolimir has been found guilty of both genocide and conspiracy to commit genocide. Radislav Krstić and Drago Nikolić have been convicted for aiding and abetting genocide. Separately, German courts have convicted three individuals for genocide in Bosnia, one of whom, Nikola Jorgić, had his appeal rejected by the European Court of Human Rights. Additionally, the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina has convicted eight former members of Bosnian Serb security forces for genocide (refer to List of Bosnian genocide prosecutions).

input: In 1713 Farrukhsiyar, the Mughal emperor, appointed Asif Jah I to be Viceroy of the Deccan, with the title Nizam-ul-Mulk (Administrator of the Realm). In 1724, Asif Jah I defeated Mubariz Khan to establish autonomy over the Deccan Suba, named the region Hyderabad Deccan, and started what came to be known as the Asif Jahi dynasty. Subsequent rulers retained the title Nizam ul-Mulk and were referred to as Asif Jahi Nizams, or Nizams of Hyderabad. The death of Asif Jah I in 1748 resulted in a period of political unrest as his sons, backed by opportunistic neighbouring states and colonial foreign forces, contended for the throne. The accession of Asif Jah II, who reigned from 1762 to 1803, ended the instability. In 1768 he signed the treaty of Masulipatnam, surrendering the coastal region to the East India Company in return for a fixed annual rent.
rewrite: In 1713, the Mughal emperor Farrukhsiyar appointed Asif Jah I as Viceroy of the Deccan, bestowing upon him the title Nizam-ul-Mulk, meaning Administrator of the Realm. By 1724, Asif Jah I had defeated Mubariz Khan, secured autonomy for the Deccan Suba, and designated the region Hyderabad Deccan, thereby founding the Asif Jahi dynasty. Successive rulers maintained the title Nizam ul-Mulk and were commonly known as the Asif Jahi Nizams or the Nizams of Hyderabad. Following Asif Jah I’s death in 1748, a succession conflict ensued among his sons, exacerbated by intervention from neighboring states and colonial powers, leading to political instability. This turmoil concluded with the accession of Asif Jah II, whose reign from 1762 to 1803 restored order. Notably, in 1768 he ratified the Treaty of Masulipatnam, ceding the coastal territories to the East India Company in exchange for a stipulated annual payment.

input: Insects are the only invertebrates to have developed active flight capability, and this has played an important role in their success.:186 Their muscles are able to contract multiple times for each single nerve impulse, allowing the wings to beat faster than would ordinarily be possible. Having their muscles attached to their exoskeletons is more efficient and allows more muscle connections; crustaceans also use the same method, though all spiders use hydraulic pressure to extend their legs, a system inherited from their pre-arthropod ancestors. Unlike insects, though, most aquatic crustaceans are biomineralized with calcium carbonate extracted from the water.
rewrite: Insects represent the sole invertebrate group to have evolved active flight, a key factor in their evolutionary success.:186 Their flight muscles contract multiple times per nerve impulse, enabling wingbeat frequencies exceeding typical neuromuscular limits. Attachment of these muscles to the exoskeleton improves mechanical efficiency and increases potential connection points—a trait shared with crustaceans. However, spiders utilize hydraulic pressure for leg extension, an ancestral pre-arthropod characteristic. Furthermore, most aquatic crustaceans are distinctively biomineralized with calcium carbonate obtained from their environment.

input: A liberal foreign investment law was approved in June 1994, and a law on privatisation was adopted in 1997, as well as a program of state property privatisation. Continued progress will depend on the ability of the government to strengthen its macroeconomic management, including increasing revenue collection, improving the investment climate, and making strides against corruption. However, unemployment, which currently stands at around 15%, still remains a major problem due to the influx of thousands of refugees from the Karabakh conflict.
rewrite: In June 1994, a liberal foreign investment law was enacted, followed by the adoption of a privatization law and a corresponding state property program in 1997. Sustained advancement will require enhanced governmental macroeconomic management, particularly through improved revenue collection, a more favorable investment climate, and reduced corruption. A significant ongoing challenge, however, is unemployment, which remains at approximately 15% largely due to the arrival of thousands of refugees from the Karabakh conflict.

input: Due to the often political and cultural contours of blackness in the United States, the notion of blackness can also be extended to non-black people. Toni Morrison once described Bill Clinton as the first black President of the United States, because, as she put it, he displayed "almost every trope of blackness". Christopher Hitchens was offended by the notion of Clinton as the first black president, noting, "Mr Clinton, according to Toni Morrison, the Nobel Prize-winning novelist, is our first black President, the first to come from the broken home, the alcoholic mother, the under-the-bridge shadows of our ranking systems. Thus, we may have lost the mystical power to divine diabolism, but we can still divine blackness by the following symptoms: broken homes, alcoholic mothers, under-the-bridge habits and (presumable from the rest of [Arthur] Miller's senescent musings) the tendency to sexual predation and to shameless perjury about same." Some black activists were also offended, claiming that Clinton used his knowledge of black culture to exploit black people for political gain as no other president had before, while not serving black interests. They cite the lack of action during the Rwandan Genocide and his welfare reform, which Larry Roberts said had led to the worst child poverty since the 1960s. Others cited that the number of black people in jail increased during his administration.
rewrite: The concept of blackness in the United States, frequently defined by political and cultural parameters, possesses a discursive elasticity that permits its metaphorical extension to individuals not racially classified as Black. Nobel laureate Toni Morrison notably characterized President Bill Clinton as the nation's "first black President," arguing he embodied "almost every trope of blackness." This assertion provoked critique. Author Christopher Hitchens objected, contending that Morrison's framework reductively diagnosed blackness through tropes of familial dysfunction, socioeconomic marginality, and, extrapolating from her reference to Arthur Miller, alleged moral failings. Concurrently, certain Black activists expressed offense, accusing Clinton of appropriating cultural familiarity to secure political support from Black constituencies without advancing their substantive interests. These critics pointed to policy outcomes as evidence, including his administration's non-intervention during the Rwandan Genocide and the 1996 welfare reform legislation. Scholars such as Larry Roberts have argued this reform exacerbated child poverty to levels unseen since the 1960s. Further criticism highlighted the significant expansion of the incarcerated Black population during his tenure, framing it as a failure of his domestic policy. Thus, the Morrison designation ignited debate concerning the boundaries of racial identity, political symbolism, and material policy consequences.

input: As of 2008[update], the population was 47.5% male and 52.5% female. The population was made up of 44,032 Swiss men (35.4% of the population) and 15,092 (12.1%) non-Swiss men. There were 51,531 Swiss women (41.4%) and 13,726 (11.0%) non-Swiss women. Of the population in the municipality, 39,008 or about 30.3% were born in Bern and lived there in 2000. There were 27,573 or 21.4% who were born in the same canton, while 25,818 or 20.1% were born somewhere else in Switzerland, and 27,812 or 21.6% were born outside of Switzerland.
rewrite: According to 2008 data, the population comprised 47.5% males and 52.5% females. This included 44,032 Swiss males (35.4%) and 15,092 non-Swiss males (12.1%), alongside 51,531 Swiss females (41.4%) and 13,726 non-Swiss females (11.0%). Regarding place of birth, 39,008 inhabitants (30.3%) were native to Bern as of 2000, while 27,573 (21.4%) originated from the same canton. A further 25,818 (20.1%) were born elsewhere in Switzerland, and 27,812 (21.6%) were born abroad.

input: Namibia is one of few countries in the world to specifically address conservation and protection of natural resources in its constitution. Article 95 states, "The State shall actively promote and maintain the welfare of the people by adopting international policies aimed at the following: maintenance of ecosystems, essential ecological processes, and biological diversity of Namibia, and utilisation of living natural resources on a sustainable basis for the benefit of all Namibians, both present and future."
rewrite: Namibia is among a limited number of nations that enshrine the conservation and protection of natural resources within its constitutional framework. Specifically, Article 95 mandates the state to promote public welfare through policies ensuring the maintenance of ecosystems, essential ecological processes, and biological diversity. It further stipulates that living natural resources must be utilized sustainably for the benefit of all Namibians, present and future.

input: After a series of test transmissions and special broadcasts that began in August, regular BBC television broadcasts officially resumed on 1 October 1936, from a converted wing of Alexandra Palace in London, which housed two studios, various scenery stores, make-up areas, dressing rooms, offices, and the transmitter itself, now broadcasting on the VHF band. BBC television initially used two systems, on alternate weeks: the 240-line Baird intermediate film system and the 405-line Marconi-EMI system, each making the BBC the world's first regular high-definition television service, broadcasting Monday to Saturday from 15:00 to 16:00 and 21:00 to 22:00.
rewrite: Following a period of experimental transmissions and special broadcasts commencing in August, the British Broadcasting Corporation formally reinstated its regular television service on 1 October 1936. Operations originated from a repurposed section of London's Alexandra Palace, containing two studios, scenery storage, make-up and dressing rooms, offices, and the VHF transmitter. The service, broadcasting Monday to Saturday from 15:00–16:00 and 21:00–22:00, initially alternated weekly between two systems: the 240-line Baird intermediate film process and the 405-line Marconi-EMI system. This dual-system operation established the BBC as the world's first regular high-definition television broadcaster.

input: Napoleon was born on 15 August 1769, to Carlo Maria di Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino, in his family's ancestral home Casa Buonaparte in Ajaccio, the capital of the island of Corsica. He was their fourth child and third son. This was a year after the island was transferred to France by the Republic of Genoa. He was christened Napoleone di Buonaparte, probably named after an uncle (an older brother who did not survive infancy was the first of the sons to be called Napoleone). In his 20s, he adopted the more French-sounding Napoléon Bonaparte.[note 2]
rewrite: Napoleon Bonaparte was born Napoleone di Buonaparte on 15 August 1769 in the Casa Buonaparte in Ajaccio, Corsica. He was the fourth child and third son of Carlo Maria di Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino. His birth occurred one year after Genoa ceded Corsica to France. The name likely honored a paternal uncle, as an earlier deceased brother had also been called Napoleone. As a young adult, he adopted the francized form of his name, Napoléon Bonaparte.

input: In the 9th century, the rise of the cult of the Apostle James in Santiago de Compostela gave Galicia a particular symbolic importance among Christians, an importance it would hold throughout the Reconquista. As the Middle Ages went on, Santiago became a major pilgrim destination and the Way of Saint James (Camiño de Santiago) a major pilgrim road, a route for the propagation of Romanesque art and the words and music of the troubadors. During the 10th and 11th centuries, a period during which Galician nobility become related to the royal family, Galicia was at times headed by its own native kings, while Vikings (locally known as Leodemanes or Lordomanes) occasionally raided the coasts. The Towers of Catoira (Pontevedra) were built as a system of fortifications to prevent and stop the Viking raids on Santiago de Compostela.
rewrite: During the ninth century, the emergence of the cult of the Apostle James in Santiago de Compostela endowed Galicia with a distinct symbolic significance for Christendom, a status maintained throughout the Reconquista. Throughout the medieval period, Santiago evolved into a principal pilgrimage destination, with the Way of Saint James serving as a crucial route. This pathway facilitated the dissemination of Romanesque art and the literary and musical traditions of the troubadours. In the tenth and eleventh centuries, a period marked by marital alliances between Galician nobility and the royal family, the region was intermittently governed by its own native monarchs. Concurrently, Viking forces, referred to locally as Leodemanes or Lordomanes, conducted periodic coastal raids. The Towers of Catoira in Pontevedra were constructed as a defensive fortification system to deter these Viking incursions aimed at Santiago de Compostela.

input: In Turkey and the Ottoman Empire, the oldest technical university is Istanbul Technical University. Its graduates contributed to a wide variety of activities in scientific research and development. In 1950s, 2 technical universities were opened in Ankara and Trabzon. In recent years, Yildiz University is reorganized as Yildiz Technical University and 2 institutes of technology were founded in Kocaeli and Izmir. In 2010, another technical university named Bursa Technical University was founded in Bursa. Moreover, a sixth technical university is about to be opened in Konya named Konya Technical University.
rewrite: Istanbul Technical University stands as the oldest institution of its kind in Turkey and the Ottoman Empire, with its graduates making significant contributions to scientific research and development. The 1950s saw the establishment of two further technical universities in Ankara and Trabzon. Subsequent expansions include the reorganization of Yildiz University into Yildiz Technical University and the founding of institutes of technology in Kocaeli and Izmir. More recently, Bursa Technical University was established in 2010, and a sixth, Konya Technical University, is planned for Konya.

input: Even at high latitudes, glacier formation is not inevitable. Areas of the Arctic, such as Banks Island, and the McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica are considered polar deserts where glaciers cannot form because they receive little snowfall despite the bitter cold. Cold air, unlike warm air, is unable to transport much water vapor. Even during glacial periods of the Quaternary, Manchuria, lowland Siberia, and central and northern Alaska, though extraordinarily cold, had such light snowfall that glaciers could not form.
rewrite: Glacier formation is not assured even at high latitudes. Certain Arctic and Antarctic regions, including Banks Island and the McMurdo Dry Valleys, are polar deserts where minimal precipitation precludes glaciation despite extreme cold. This is because cold air has a limited capacity to carry water vapor. Similarly, during Quaternary glacial periods, areas such as Manchuria, lowland Siberia, and parts of Alaska remained largely unglaciated due to insufficient snowfall.

input: The northern supercontinent of Laurasia began to break up, as Europe, Greenland and North America drifted apart. In western North America, mountain building started in the Eocene, and huge lakes formed in the high flat basins among uplifts. In Europe, the Tethys Sea finally vanished, while the uplift of the Alps isolated its final remnant, the Mediterranean, and created another shallow sea with island archipelagos to the north. Though the North Atlantic was opening, a land connection appears to have remained between North America and Europe since the faunas of the two regions are very similar. India continued its journey away from Africa and began its collision with Asia, creating the Himalayan orogeny.
rewrite: During the Eocene, the northern supercontinent Laurasia underwent fragmentation, resulting in the separation of Europe, Greenland, and North America. Concurrently, orogenic activity commenced in western North America, where extensive lakes developed within the elevated, intermontane basins. In Europe, the closure of the Tethys Sea was completed; the Alpine orogeny both isolated its final remnant, the Mediterranean Sea, and generated a northern shallow sea punctuated by archipelagos. Despite the ongoing opening of the North Atlantic, persistent faunal similarities suggest a land connection remained between North America and Europe. Simultaneously, India, having separated from Africa, initiated its collision with Asia, giving rise to the Himalayan orogeny.

input: 40°48′52″N 73°56′53″W﻿ / ﻿40.814583°N 73.947944°W﻿ / 40.814583; -73.947944 132nd Street runs east-west above Central Park and is located in Harlem just south of Hamilton Heights. The main portion of 132nd Street runs eastbound from Frederick Douglass Boulevard to northern end of Park Avenue where there is a southbound exit from/entrance to the Harlem River Drive. After an interruption from St. Nicholas Park and City College, there is another small stretch of West 132nd Street between Broadway and Twelfth Avenue
rewrite: The coordinates 40°48′52″N 73°56′53″W situate 132nd Street in Harlem, positioned south of Hamilton Heights and running east-west above Central Park. Its primary segment extends eastward from Frederick Douglass Boulevard to the northern terminus of Park Avenue, which features a dedicated southbound interchange with the Harlem River Drive. input: Stanley Crouch wrote in a New York Daily News piece "Obama's mother is of white U.S. stock. His father is a black Kenyan," in a column entitled "What Obama Isn't: Black Like Me." During the 2008 campaign, the African-American columnist David Ehrenstein of the LA Times accused white liberals of flocking to Obama because he was a "Magic Negro", a term that refers to a black person with no past who simply appears to assist the mainstream white (as cultural protagonists/drivers) agenda. Ehrenstein went on to say "He's there to assuage white 'guilt' they feel over the role of slavery and racial segregation in American history."
rewrite: In a New York Daily News column titled "What Obama Isn't: Black Like Me," Stanley Crouch observed that Barack Obama's mother was a white American and his father a black Kenyan. During the 2008 campaign, Los Angeles Times columnist David Ehrenstein, who is African American, argued that many white liberals supported Obama because he functioned as a "Magic Negro"—a term denoting a black figure devoid of historical context who emerges to advance a primarily white cultural agenda. Ehrenstein further contended that this figure served to alleviate white guilt stemming from America's history of slavery and segregation.

input: Industry is diversified, ranging from automotive (Volkswagen Autoeuropa and Peugeot Citroen), aerospace (Embraer and OGMA), electronics and textiles, to food, chemicals, cement and wood pulp. Volkswagen Group's AutoEuropa motor vehicle assembly plant in Palmela is among the largest foreign direct investment projects in Portugal. Modern non-traditional technology-based industries, such as aerospace, biotechnology and information technology, have been developed in several locations across the country. Alverca, Covilhã, Évora, and Ponte de Sor are the main centres of the Portuguese aerospace industry, which is led by Brazil-based company Embraer and the Portuguese company OGMA. Following the turn of the 21st century, many major biotechnology and information technology industries have been founded, and are concentrated in the metropolitan areas of Lisbon, Porto, Braga, Coimbra and Aveiro.[citation needed]
rewrite: Portugal's industrial sector is notably diversified, encompassing automotive manufacturing (including Volkswagen Autoeuropa and Peugeot Citroën), aerospace (Embraer and OGMA), electronics, textiles, food processing, chemicals, cement, and wood pulp. The Volkswagen Autoeuropa plant in Palmela represents one of the nation's most significant foreign direct investments. Concurrently, modern technology-based industries have expanded, with aerospace clusters located in Alverca, Covilhã, Évora, and Ponte de Sor. Since the early 21st century, substantial growth has also occurred in biotechnology and information technology, which are primarily concentrated within the major metropolitan areas of Lisbon, Porto, Braga, Coimbra, and Aveiro.

input: Naturally occurring crude asphalt/bitumen impregnated in sedimentary rock is the prime feed stock for petroleum production from "Oil sands", currently under development in Alberta, Canada. Canada has most of the world's supply of natural asphalt/bitumen, covering 140,000 square kilometres (an area larger than England), giving it the second-largest proven oil reserves in the world. The Athabasca oil sands is the largest asphalt/bitumen deposit in Canada and the only one accessible to surface mining, although recent technological breakthroughs have resulted in deeper deposits becoming producible by in situ methods. Because of oil price increases after 2003, producing bitumen became highly profitable, but as a result of the decline after 2014 it became uneconomic to build new plants again. By 2014, Canadian crude asphalt/bitumen production averaged about 2.3 million barrels (370,000 m3) per day and was projected to rise to 4.4 million barrels (700,000 m3) per day by 2020. The total amount of crude asphalt/bitumen in Alberta which could be extracted is estimated to be about 310 billion barrels (50×10^9 m3), which at a rate of 4,400,000 barrels per day (700,000 m3/d) would last about 200 years.
rewrite: Naturally occurring crude asphalt and bitumen, impregnated within sedimentary rock formations, constitute the primary feedstock for petroleum derived from oil sands. These deposits, notably under development in Alberta, Canada, represent the majority of the world's supply of natural asphalt and bitumen, encompassing approximately 140,000 square kilometres—an area exceeding that of England. This resource endowment affords Canada the world's second-largest proven oil reserves. The Athabasca oil sands constitute the nation's largest such deposit and the only one amenable to surface mining, though technological advances now enable *in situ* extraction of deeper resources. Following 2003, rising oil prices rendered bitumen production highly profitable; however, the post-2014 price decline rendered new capital investments uneconomic. By 2014, Canadian production averaged approximately 2.3 million barrels per day, with projections anticipating a rise to 4.4 million barrels daily by 2020. The total extractable crude asphalt and bitumen in Alberta is estimated at roughly 310 billion barrels. At a hypothetical sustained extraction rate of 4.4 million barrels per day, this resource would last approximately two centuries.

input: On ancient reliefs, especially from Mesopotamia, kings are often depicted as hunters of big game such as lions and are often portrayed hunting from a war chariot. The cultural and psychological importance of hunting in ancient societies is represented by deities such as the horned god Cernunnos and lunar goddesses of classical antiquity, the Greek Artemis or Roman Diana. Taboos are often related to hunting, and mythological association of prey species with a divinity could be reflected in hunting restrictions such as a reserve surrounding a temple. Euripides' tale of Artemis and Actaeon, for example, may be seen as a caution against disrespect of prey or impudent boasting.
rewrite: Ancient Mesopotamian reliefs frequently depict monarchs hunting formidable prey, such as lions, often from a war chariot. This underscores the profound cultural and psychological significance of the hunt, further exemplified by divine associations, as seen with the horned god Cernunnos or lunar deities like Artemis and Diana. Hunting taboos often emerged from such mythological connections, where a species' sacred status could lead to practical restrictions, like protected temple precincts. Narratives such as Euripides' tale of Artemis and Actaeon serve as didactic warnings against disrespecting prey or hubristic boasting by hunters.

input: Many Baptist churches choose to affiliate with organizational groups that provide fellowship without control. The largest such group is the Southern Baptist Convention. There also are a substantial number of smaller cooperative groups. Finally, there are Baptist churches that choose to remain autonomous and independent of any denomination, organization, or association. It has been suggested that a primary Baptist principle is that local Baptist Churches are independent and self-governing, and if so the term 'Baptist denomination' may be considered somewhat incongruous.
rewrite: Numerous Baptist churches elect to affiliate with cooperative bodies that offer fellowship without exerting control, the largest being the Southern Baptist Convention, alongside many smaller associations. Conversely, a significant number of churches remain fully autonomous, independent of any denomination or organization. Scholars note that a core Baptist principle emphasizes the independence and self-governance of local congregations. Consequently, the term "Baptist denomination" may be viewed as somewhat incongruous with this foundational tenet.

input: Sexual identity and sexual behavior are closely related to sexual orientation, but they are distinguished, with sexual identity referring to an individual's conception of themselves, behavior referring to actual sexual acts performed by the individual, and orientation referring to "fantasies, attachments and longings." Individuals may or may not express their sexual orientation in their behaviors. People who have a homosexual sexual orientation that does not align with their sexual identity are sometimes referred to as 'closeted'. The term may, however, reflect a certain cultural context and particular stage of transition in societies which are gradually dealing with integrating sexual minorities. In studies related to sexual orientation, when dealing with the degree to which a person's sexual attractions, behaviors and identity match, scientists usually use the terms concordance or discordance. Thus, a woman who is attracted to other women, but calls herself heterosexual and only has sexual relations with men, can be said to experience discordance between her sexual orientation (homosexual or lesbian) and her sexual identity and behaviors (heterosexual).
rewrite: Sexual orientation, sexual identity, and sexual behavior are interrelated yet distinct constructs. Sexual orientation encompasses enduring patterns of emotional, romantic, and/or sexual attractions, often described in terms of fantasies and longings. Sexual identity denotes an individual’s personal and social labeling of these feelings, while sexual behavior refers to enacted sexual practices. These components may not always align; individuals may not express their orientation through their behavior or chosen identity. A state of incongruence, often termed ‘discordance,’ exists when attractions, identity, and behaviors are mismatched. For instance, a woman attracted to other women may identify as heterosexual and engage exclusively in sexual relations with men. The concept of being ‘closeted’ describes individuals whose homosexual orientation is not reflected in their public identity, a term situated within specific cultural contexts and historical phases of societal integration for sexual minorities. In research, scientists analyze these alignments using the framework of concordance or discordance.

input: Kathmandu is located in the northwestern part of the Kathmandu Valley to the north of the Bagmati River and covers an area of 50.67 km2 (19.56 sq mi). The average elevation is 1,400 metres (4,600 ft) above sea level. The city is directly bounded by several other municipalities of the Kathmandu valley: south of the Bagmati by Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City (Patan) with which it today forms one urban area surrounded by a ring road, to the southwest by Kirtipur Municipality and to the east by Madyapur Thimi Municipality. To the north the urban area extends into several Village Development Committees. However, the urban agglomeration extends well beyond the neighboring municipalities, e. g. to Bhaktapur and just about covers the entire Kathmandu valley.
rewrite: Kathmandu is situated in the northwestern region of the Kathmandu Valley, north of the Bagmati River, encompassing an area of 50.67 square kilometers. Its average elevation is 1,400 meters above sea level. The city is directly adjacent to several other municipalities within the valley: to the south, beyond the Bagmati River, lies Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City (Patan), with which it now constitutes a contiguous urban area encircled by a ring road. It is bordered to the southwest by Kirtipur Municipality and to the east by Madyapur Thimi Municipality. The northern extent merges into several Village Development Committees. The broader urban agglomeration, however, significantly exceeds these immediate boundaries, extending to include areas such as Bhaktapur and effectively covering most of the Kathmandu Valley.

input: The first emperor of the Ming dynasty, Zhu Yuanzhang (the Hongwu Emperor), who overthrew the Yuan dynasty, renamed the city Yingtian, rebuilt it, and made it the dynastic capital in 1368. He constructed a 48 km (30 mi) long city wall around Yingtian, as well as a new Ming Palace complex, and government halls. It took 200,000 laborers 21 years to finish the project. The present-day City Wall of Nanjing was mainly built during that time and today it remains in good condition and has been well preserved. It is among the longest surviving city walls in China. The Jianwen Emperor ruled from 1398 to 1402.
rewrite: Upon ascending the throne in 1368 after overthrowing the Yuan dynasty, the Hongwu Emperor, Zhu Yuanzhang, established Yingtian as the Ming capital. He commissioned extensive construction, including a new palace complex, government halls, and a formidable city wall extending approximately 48 kilometers. This project, requiring 200,000 laborers over twenty-one years, produced the core of the extant Nanjing City Wall. Remarkably well-preserved, it remains one of China's longest surviving historic fortifications. Subsequently, the Jianwen Emperor reigned from 1398 until 1402.

input: Critical and commercial reception to PS3 improved over time, after a series of price revisions, Blu-ray's victory over HD DVD, and the release of several well received titles. Ars Technica's original launch review gave PS3 only a 6/10, but second review of the console in June 2008 rated it a 9/10. In September 2009, IGN named PlayStation 3 the 15th best gaming console of all time, behind both of its competitors: Wii (10th) and Xbox 360 (6th). However, PS3 has won IGN's "Console Showdown"—based on which console offers the best selection of games released during each year—in three of the four years since it began (2008, 2009 and 2011, with Xbox winning in 2010). IGN judged PlayStation 3 to have the best game line-up of 2008, based on their review scores in comparison to those of Wii and Xbox 360. In a comparison piece by PC mag's Will Greenwald in June 2012, PS3 was selected as an overall better console compared to Xbox 360. Pocket-lint said of the console "The PS3 has always been a brilliant games console," and that "For now, this is just about the best media device for the money."
rewrite: The critical and commercial reception of the PlayStation 3 (PS3) improved substantially following its initial launch, a shift attributable to successive price reductions, the market triumph of its integrated Blu-ray format over HD DVD, and the subsequent release of numerous acclaimed titles. This evolution in perception is evidenced by contemporaneous reviews; for instance, Ars Technica revised its initial launch rating of 6/10 to a 9/10 in a June 2008 reassessment. While IGN’s 2009 ranking of the greatest consoles placed the PS3 at 15th, behind both the Wii (10th) and Xbox 360 (6th), the platform demonstrated consistent strength in annual software comparisons. IGN’s "Console Showdown," which evaluates each year’s best game library, was won by the PS3 in 2008, 2009, and 2011, with the Xbox 360 winning only in 2010. IGN specifically judged the PS3 to have the superior 2008 lineup based on comparative review scores. Further endorsements emerged later in the console’s lifecycle, with PC Magazine’s June 2012 analysis concluding the PS3 was the overall superior platform compared to the Xbox 360. Similarly, Pocket-lint characterized the PS3 as “a brilliant games console” and, at the time, “just about the best media device for the money.”

input: The linguistic heritage of the British Isles is rich, with twelve languages from six groups across four branches of the Indo-European family. The Insular Celtic languages of the Goidelic sub-group (Irish, Manx and Scottish Gaelic) and the Brittonic sub-group (Cornish, Welsh and Breton, spoken in north-western France) are the only remaining Celtic languages—the last of their continental relations becoming extinct before the 7th century. The Norman languages of Guernésiais, Jèrriais and Sarkese spoken in the Channel Islands are similar to French. A cant, called Shelta, is spoken by Irish Travellers, often as a means to conceal meaning from those outside the group. However, English, sometimes in the form of Scots, is the dominant language, with few monoglots remaining in the other languages of the region. The Norn language of Orkney and Shetland became extinct around 1880.
rewrite: The British Isles possess a substantial linguistic heritage, comprising twelve languages distributed across four branches of the Indo-European family, within six distinct groups. The Insular Celtic languages, consisting of the Goidelic (Irish, Manx, Scottish Gaelic) and Brittonic (Cornish, Welsh, and Breton, the latter spoken in northwestern France) sub-groups, represent the sole surviving Celtic languages; their continental counterparts became extinct prior to the seventh century. In the Channel Islands, the Norman languages of Guernésiais, Jèrriais, and Sarkese exhibit similarities to French. Irish Travellers employ a cant known as Shelta, frequently to obscure meaning from outsiders. Despite this diversity, English—including its Scots variety—is overwhelmingly dominant, with few monolingual speakers persisting in the region's other languages. Notably, the Norn language of Orkney and Shetland became extinct circa 1880.

input: Local anesthetic injections into the nerves or sensitive areas of the stump may relieve pain for days, weeks, or sometimes permanently, despite the drug wearing off in a matter of hours; and small injections of hypertonic saline into the soft tissue between vertebrae produces local pain that radiates into the phantom limb for ten minutes or so and may be followed by hours, weeks or even longer of partial or total relief from phantom pain. Vigorous vibration or electrical stimulation of the stump, or current from electrodes surgically implanted onto the spinal cord, all produce relief in some patients.
rewrite: Injections of local anesthetic into stump nerves or sensitive regions can yield pain relief lasting days, weeks, or even permanently, despite the pharmacological effects dissipating within hours. Similarly, minor injections of hypertonic saline into the intervertebral soft tissue can induce localized pain radiating into the phantom limb for approximately ten minutes, often followed by partial or complete relief lasting hours to weeks or longer. Furthermore, vigorous stump vibration, electrical stimulation, or currents from surgically implanted spinal cord electrodes provide relief for certain patients.

input: Green is common in nature, as many plants are green because of a complex chemical known as chlorophyll, which is involved in photosynthesis. Chlorophyll absorbs the long wavelengths of light (red) and short wavelengths of light (blue) much more efficiently than the wavelengths that appear green to the human eye, so light reflected by plants is enriched in green. Chlorophyll absorbs green light poorly because it first arose in organisms living in oceans where purple halobacteria were already exploiting photosynthesis. Their purple color arose because they extracted energy in the green portion of the spectrum using bacteriorhodopsin. The new organisms that then later came to dominate the extraction of light were selected to exploit those portions of the spectrum not used by the halobacteria.
rewrite: The prevalence of green in nature is attributable to chlorophyll, the complex chemical central to photosynthesis. Chlorophyll exhibits high absorption efficiency for long (red) and short (blue) wavelengths of light, while reflecting the middle (green) wavelengths, thereby imparting a green appearance to vegetation. This spectral absorption profile is an evolutionary adaptation. Chlorophyll-based photosynthesis first emerged in oceanic organisms following the establishment of purple halobacteria, which utilized bacteriorhodopsin to harness energy primarily from green light. Consequently, selective pressure favored subsequent photosynthetic organisms that could exploit the unutilized red and blue portions of the spectrum, leading to the dominance of chlorophyll and the resultant green coloration of plants.

input: The craft has also been popular in early medieval Rus, inherited as part of the Byzantine tradition. Yaroslav, the Grand Prince of the Kievan Rus' built a large cathedral in his capital, Kiev. The model of the church was the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, and it was also called Saint Sophia Cathedral. It was built mainly by Byzantine master craftsmen, sent by Constantine Monomachos, between 1037 and 1046. Naturally the more important surfaces in the interior were decorated with golden mosaics. In the dome we can see the traditional stern Pantokrator supported by angels. Between the 12 windows of the drum were apostles and the four evangelists on the pendentives. The apse is dominated by an orant Theotokos with a Deesis in three medallions above. Below is a Communion of the Apostles.
rewrite: The craft also flourished in early medieval Rus, where it was adopted from Byzantine tradition. Grand Prince Yaroslav of Kievan Rus' commissioned a major cathedral in the capital, Kiev. Modeled after the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, it was similarly dedicated as Saint Sophia Cathedral. Constructed primarily by Byzantine artisans dispatched by Emperor Constantine Monomachos between 1037 and 1046, its interior featured golden mosaics on the most significant surfaces. The dome displays the conventional austere Pantokrator, flanked by angels. Apostles were positioned between the twelve windows of the drum, with the four evangelists on the pendentives. The apse is occupied by an orant Theotokos, surmounted by a Deesis in three medallions, and below this, a representation of the Communion of the Apostles.

input: In a simple model, often referred to as the transmission model or standard view of communication, information or content (e.g. a message in natural language) is sent in some form (as spoken language) from an emisor/ sender/ encoder to a destination/ receiver/ decoder. This common conception of communication simply views communication as a means of sending and receiving information. The strengths of this model are simplicity, generality, and quantifiability. Claude Shannon and Warren Weaver structured this model based on the following elements:
rewrite: The transmission model, also termed the standard view of communication, conceptualizes the process as a linear conveyance of information. In this framework, a sender encodes a message, typically in linguistic form, and transmits it to a receiver who decodes it. This paradigm reduces communication to a mechanistic transfer of data. Its primary advantages are its simplicity, broad applicability, and amenability to quantification. Claude Shannon and Warren Weaver formally established this model, defining its core components.

input: The language possesses five vowels (or six, under the St. Petersburg Phonological School), which are written with different letters depending on whether or not the preceding consonant is palatalized. The consonants typically come in plain vs. palatalized pairs, which are traditionally called hard and soft. (The hard consonants are often velarized, especially before front vowels, as in Irish). The standard language, based on the Moscow dialect, possesses heavy stress and moderate variation in pitch. Stressed vowels are somewhat lengthened, while unstressed vowels tend to be reduced to near-close vowels or an unclear schwa. (See also: vowel reduction in Russian.)
rewrite: The language features five vowel phonemes (or six within the St. Petersburg Phonological School), whose orthographic representation depends on the palatalization status of the preceding consonant. Consonants typically form plain versus palatalized pairs, conventionally termed hard and soft. Hard consonants are frequently velarized, particularly preceding front vowels. Based on the Moscow dialect, the standard language employs prominent stress and moderate pitch variation. Stressed vowels undergo lengthening, whereas unstressed vowels are subject to reduction to near-close positions or a central schwa.

input: Yale's central campus in downtown New Haven covers 260 acres (1.1 km2) and comprises its main, historic campus and a medical campus adjacent to the Yale-New Haven Hospital. In western New Haven, the university holds 500 acres (2.0 km2) of athletic facilities, including the Yale Golf Course. In 2008, Yale purchased the 136-acre (0.55 km2) former Bayer Pharmaceutical campus in West Haven, Connecticut, the buildings of which are now used as laboratory and research space. Yale also owns seven forests in Connecticut, Vermont, and New Hampshire—the largest of which is the 7,840-acre (31.7 km2) Yale-Myers Forest in Connecticut's Quiet Corner—and nature preserves including Horse Island.
rewrite: Yale University’s primary campus occupies 260 acres (1.1 km²) in downtown New Haven, encompassing its historic core and an adjacent medical campus near Yale-New Haven Hospital. Additionally, the university maintains a 500-acre (2.0 km²) athletic complex in western New Haven, which includes the Yale Golf Course. A former 136-acre (0.55 km²) Bayer Pharmaceutical site in West Haven, Connecticut, acquired in 2008, now provides laboratory and research facilities. Yale also possesses extensive natural holdings, comprising seven forests across Connecticut, Vermont, and New Hampshire—the largest being the 7,840-acre (31.7 km²) Yale-Myers Forest—as well as preserves such as Horse Island.

input: Melbourne's rich and diverse literary history was recognised in 2008 when it became the second UNESCO City of Literature. The State Library of Victoria is one of Australia's oldest cultural institutions and one of many public and university libraries across the city. Melbourne also has Australia's widest range of bookstores, as well the nation's largest publishing sector. The city is home to significant writers' festivals, most notably the Melbourne Writers Festival. Several major literary prizes are open to local writers including the Melbourne Prize for Literature and the Victorian Premier's Literary Awards. Significant novels set in Melbourne include Fergus Hume's The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, Helen Garner's Monkey Grip and Christos Tsiolkas' The Slap. Notable writers and poets from Melbourne include Thomas Browne, C. J. Dennis, Germaine Greer and Peter Carey.
rewrite: In 2008, Melbourne was designated a UNESCO City of Literature, acknowledging its substantial and varied literary heritage. The city hosts numerous public and university libraries, including the State Library of Victoria, among Australia's oldest cultural institutions. It contains the nation's most extensive collection of bookstores and its largest publishing industry. Major literary events, such as the Melbourne Writers Festival, are held there, and prominent prizes like the Melbourne Prize for Literature and the Victorian Premier's Literary Awards are accessible to its authors. The metropolitan setting has been featured in significant works, including *The Mystery of a Hansom Cab* by Fergus Hume, *Monkey Grip* by Helen Garner, and *The Slap* by Christos Tsiolkas. Distinguished literary figures from Melbourne encompass Thomas Browne, C. J. Dennis, Germaine Greer, and Peter Carey.

input: In the United States, two of the wealthiest nonprofit organizations are the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, which has an endowment of US$38 billion, and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute originally funded by Hughes Aircraft prior to divestiture, which has an endowment of approximately $14.8 billion. Outside the United States, another large NPO is the British Wellcome Trust, which is a "charity" by British usage. See: List of wealthiest foundations. Note that this assessment excludes universities, at least a few of which have assets in the tens of billions of dollars. For example; List of U.S. colleges and universities by endowment.
rewrite: Among the wealthiest nonprofit organizations in the United States are the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, with an endowment of US$38 billion, and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, originally funded by Hughes Aircraft prior to its divestiture, holding approximately $14.8 billion. Externally, a prominent example is the United Kingdom's Wellcome Trust, classified as a charity under British law. This evaluation, referencing lists of the wealthiest foundations, deliberately excludes universities, several of which possess endowments exceeding tens of billions of dollars, as documented in listings of U.S. college and university endowments.

input: The success of the show's alumni however has led to a more positive assessment of the show, and the show was described as having "proven it has a valid way to pick talent and a proven way to sell records". While the industry is divided on the show success, its impact is felt particularly strongly in the country music format. According to a CMT exec, reflecting on the success of Idol alumni in the country genre, "if you want to try and get famous fast by going to a cattle call audition on TV, Idol reasonably remains the first choice for anyone," and that country music and Idol "go together well".

Although industry opinion on its success remains divided, its influence is especially pronounced within country music. A CMT executive, noting the achievements of *Idol* alumni in that genre, stated that for those seeking rapid fame through open television auditions, "*Idol* reasonably remains the first choice," adding that country music and the program "go together well."

input: The structure of QD-LEDs used for the electrical-excitation scheme is similar to basic design of OLEDs. A layer of quantum dots is sandwiched between layers of electron-transporting and hole-transporting materials. An applied electric field causes electrons and holes to move into the quantum dot layer and recombine forming an exciton that excites a QD. This scheme is commonly studied for quantum dot display. The tunability of emission wavelengths and narrow bandwidth is also beneficial as excitation sources for fluorescence imaging. Fluorescence near-field scanning optical microscopy (NSOM) utilizing an integrated QD-LED has been demonstrated.
rewrite: The architecture of electrically-excited quantum dot light-emitting diodes (QD-LEDs) closely resembles that of organic LEDs. In this configuration, a quantum dot emissive layer is situated between electron- and hole-transport layers. Under an applied electric field, charge carriers inject into the quantum dot layer, where they recombine to form excitons that subsequently excite the quantum dots. This scheme is actively researched for display applications. Furthermore, the spectral tunability and narrow emission profiles of QDs make them advantageous as excitation sources in fluorescence imaging, as demonstrated in fluorescence near-field scanning optical microscopy using an integrated QD-LED.

input: Historically, the channel's programming consisted mainly of featured classic theatrically released feature films from the Turner Entertainment film library – which comprises films from Warner Bros. Pictures (covering films released before 1950) and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer (covering films released before May 1986). However, TCM now has licensing deals with other Hollywood film studios as well as its Time Warner sister company, Warner Bros. (which now controls the Turner Entertainment library and its own later films), and occasionally shows more recent films. Turner Classic Movies is a dedicated film channel and is available in United States, United Kingdom, France (TCM Cinéma), Spain (TCM España), Nordic countries, Middle East and Africa.
rewrite: Historically, the channel's programming was primarily devoted to featuring classic theatrically released films drawn from the Turner Entertainment library. This collection encompasses Warner Bros. Pictures films released prior to 1950 and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer films released before May 1986. Presently, Turner Classic Movies (TCM) also licenses content from other Hollywood studios and its corporate sibling, Warner Bros., occasionally broadcasting more contemporary films. As a dedicated film channel, TCM is available in numerous territories, including the United States, the United Kingdom, France (TCM Cinéma), Spain (TCM España), the Nordic region, the Middle East, and Africa.

input: Groups of humans have always identified themselves as distinct from neighboring groups, but such differences have not always been understood to be natural, immutable and global. These features are the distinguishing features of how the concept of race is used today. In this way the idea of race as we understand it today came about during the historical process of exploration and conquest which brought Europeans into contact with groups from different continents, and of the ideology of classification and typology found in the natural sciences.
rewrite: Human collectives have historically distinguished themselves from proximate groups, yet these distinctions were not consistently regarded as inherent, fixed, or universal. Such attributes characterize the modern conception of race. This contemporary understanding emerged through historical processes of exploration and conquest, which facilitated European encounters with populations across continents, alongside the development of classificatory and typological frameworks within the natural sciences.

input: Olin has a network of more than 16,000 alumni worldwide. Over the last several years, the school’s endowment has increased to $213 million (2004) and annual gifts average $12 million per year.[citation needed] Simon Hall was opened in 1986 after a donation from John E. Simon. On May 2, 2014, the $90 million conjoined Knight and Bauer Halls were dedicated, following a $15 million gift from Charles F. Knight and Joanne Knight and a $10 million gift from George and Carol Bauer through the Bauer Foundation.
rewrite: Olin maintains a global alumni network exceeding 16,000 individuals. Its endowment has grown, reaching $213 million in 2004, while annual philanthropic contributions average $12 million. Simon Hall was established in 1986 following a donation from John E. Simon. Subsequently, on May 2, 2014, the $90 million Knight and Bauer Halls complex was dedicated, funded by gifts of $15 million from Charles F. and Joanne Knight and $10 million from George and Carol Bauer via the Bauer Foundation.

input: The initial cost of an incandescent bulb is small compared to the cost of the energy it uses over its lifetime. Incandescent bulbs have a shorter life than most other lighting, an important factor if replacement is inconvenient or expensive. Some types of lamp, including incandescent and fluorescent, emit less light as they age; this may be an inconvenience, or may reduce effective lifetime due to lamp replacement before total failure.
