His Open Skies Policy attempted to legitimize illegal Lockheed U-2 flyovers and Project Genetrix while paving the way for spy satellite technology to orbit over sovereign territory, created NASA as a civilian space agency, signed a landmark science education law, and fostered improved relations with American scientists.
rewrite: President Eisenhower's endorsement of the nascent U.S. space program remained measured until the 1957 Soviet launch of Sputnik, which conferred significant international prestige upon its Cold War rival. In response, he initiated a comprehensive national effort that substantially increased funding for space exploration, scientific research, and higher education. His administration advanced the Open Skies Policy to justify aerial reconnaissance, facilitated the development of orbital surveillance technology, established NASA as a civilian agency, enacted pivotal science education legislation, and cultivated more productive relations with the American scientific community.

input: The Alps are split into five climatic zones, each with different vegetation. The climate, plant life and animal life vary among the different sections or zones of the mountains. The lowest zone is the colline zone, which exists between 500 and 1,000 m (1,640 and 3,281 ft), depending on the location. The montane zone extends from 800 to 1,700 m (2,625 to 5,577 ft), followed by the sub-Alpine zone from 1,600 to 2,400 m (5,249 to 7,874 ft). The Alpine zone, extending from tree line to snow line, is followed by the glacial zone, which covers the glaciated areas of the mountain. Climatic conditions show variances within the same zones; for example, weather conditions at the head of a mountain valley, extending directly from the peaks, are colder and more severe than those at the mouth of a valley which tend to be less severe and receive less snowfall.
rewrite: The Alps are characterized by five distinct climatic zones, each supporting unique vegetation and fauna. These zones are stratified by elevation, beginning with the colline zone at the lowest altitudes, ranging from 500 to 1,000 meters. Above this lies the montane zone, extending from approximately 800 to 1,700 meters, succeeded by the sub-Alpine zone from 1,600 to 2,400 meters. The Alpine zone spans from the tree line to the snow line, and is followed by the glacial zone, encompassing permanently ice-covered regions. Notably, microclimatic variations occur within individual zones; conditions at a valley head, directly adjacent to high peaks, are significantly colder and more severe than at the valley mouth, which experiences milder temperatures and reduced snowfall.

input: Han Chinese Banners were made up of Han Chinese who defected to the Qing up to 1644 and joined the Eight Banners, giving them social and legal privileges in addition to being acculturated to Manchu culture. So many Han defected to the Qing and swelled the ranks of the Eight Banners that ethnic Manchus became a minority, making up only 16% in 1648, with Han Bannermen dominating at 75% and Mongol Bannermen making up the rest. This multi-ethnic force in which Manchus were only a minority conquered China for the Qing.
rewrite: Han Chinese Banners comprised Han individuals who aligned with the Qing prior to 1644, integrating into the Eight Banners system. This affiliation granted them distinct social and legal privileges while facilitating their acculturation into Manchu norms. The scale of Han defections substantially expanded the Banners' composition, reducing ethnic Manchus to a minority of merely 16% by 1648. In contrast, Han Bannermen constituted 75%, with Mongol Bannermen comprising the remainder. This predominantly non-Manchu, multi-ethnic military force was instrumental in securing China for the Qing dynasty.

input: BBC Television is a service of the British Broadcasting Corporation. The corporation, which has operated in the United Kingdom under the terms of a Royal charter since 1927, has produced television programmes from its own since 1932, although the start of its regular service of television broadcasts is dated to 2 November 1936.
rewrite: BBC Television, a service of the British Broadcasting Corporation, has produced programming since 1932. Operating under a Royal Charter from 1927, its regular television broadcast service formally commenced on 2 November 1936.

input: The word madrasah derives from the triconsonantal Semitic root د-ر-س D-R-S 'to learn, study', through the wazn (form/stem) مفعل(ة)‎; mafʻal(ah), meaning "a place where something is done". Therefore, madrasah literally means "a place where learning and studying take place". The word is also present as a loanword with the same innocuous meaning in many Arabic-influenced languages, such as: Urdu, Bengali, Hindi, Persian, Turkish, Azeri, Kurdish, Indonesian, Malay and Bosnian / Croatian. In the Arabic language, the word مدرسة madrasah simply means the same as school does in the English language, whether that is private, public or parochial school, as well as for any primary or secondary school whether Muslim, non-Muslim, or secular. Unlike the use of the word school in British English, the word madrasah more closely resembles the term school in American English, in that it can refer to a university-level or post-graduate school as well as to a primary or secondary school. For example, in the Ottoman Empire during the Early Modern Period, madaris had lower schools and specialised schools where the students became known as danişmends. The usual Arabic word for a university, however, is جامعة (jāmiʻah). The Hebrew cognate midrasha also connotes the meaning of a place of learning; the related term midrash literally refers to study or learning, but has acquired mystical and religious connotations.
rewrite: The term *madrasah* originates from the triconsonantal Semitic root د-ر-س (D-R-S), signifying “to learn” or “to study.” It is formed through the morphological pattern *mafʻal(ah)*, which denotes a location where an action occurs. Consequently, *madrasah* literally translates to “a place where learning and studying are conducted.” This lexical item has been adopted as a loanword with the same neutral meaning in numerous languages influenced by Arabic, including Urdu, Bengali, Hindi, Persian, Turkish, Azeri, Kurdish, Indonesian, Malay, and Bosnian/Croatian. Within Arabic itself, *madrasah* functions as a direct equivalent to the English word “school,” encompassing private, public, or parochial institutions, as well as primary or secondary establishments, irrespective of their religious or secular character. In contrast to British English usage, the term aligns more closely with American English, where “school” may refer to university-level or postgraduate institutions in addition to elementary and secondary education. Historically, in the Ottoman Empire during the Early Modern Period, *madaris* (plural) included both foundational schools and specialized advanced institutions, the latter of whose students were termed *danişmends*. It should be noted that the standard Arabic word for a university is *jāmiʻah* (جامعة). The Hebrew cognate *midrasha* similarly denotes a place of learning, while the related term *midrash*—literally meaning study—has accrued specific mystical and religious connotations.

input: In 2010, a number of workers committed suicide at a Foxconn operations in China. Apple, HP, and others stated that they were investigating the situation. Foxconn guards have been videotaped beating employees. Another employee killed himself in 2009 when an Apple prototype went missing, and claimed in messages to friends, that he had been beaten and interrogated.
rewrite: In 2010, multiple suicides occurred at a Foxconn facility in China. Apple and Hewlett-Packard announced investigations into the conditions. Separately, security personnel were recorded assaulting employees. A prior incident in 2009 involved an employee's suicide following the loss of an Apple prototype; prior messages indicated he had been subjected to beating and interrogation.

input: Vietnam: The event was held in Ho Chi Minh City on April 29. Some 60 torchbearers carried the torch from the downtown Opera House to the Military Zone 7 Competition Hall stadium near Tan Son Nhat International Airport along an undisclosed route. Vietnam is involved in a territorial dispute with China (and other countries) for sovereignty of the Spratly and Paracel Islands; tensions have risen recently[when?] following reports that the Chinese government had established a county-level city named Sansha in the disputed territories, resulting in anti-Chinese demonstrations in December 2007 in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. However to sustain its relationship with China the Vietnamese government has actively sought to head off protests during the torch relay, with Prime Minister Nguyễn Tấn Dũng warning government agencies that "hostile forces" may try to disrupt the torch relay.
rewrite: On April 29, a torch relay event was conducted in Ho Chi Minh City. Approximately sixty torchbearers proceeded along a route that was not publicly disclosed, transporting the torch from the downtown Opera House to the Military Zone 7 Competition Hall stadium adjacent to Tan Son Nhat International Airport. This event occurred within a context of heightened bilateral tensions due to the ongoing territorial dispute between Vietnam and China over the Spratly and Paracel Islands. These tensions were exacerbated following China's establishment of the county-level city of Sansha in the contested region, which had previously prompted anti-Chinese demonstrations in Vietnamese cities in December 2007. To maintain diplomatic relations with China, the Vietnamese government proactively worked to prevent protests during the relay, with Prime Minister Nguyễn Tấn Dũng cautioning state agencies that "hostile forces" might attempt to disrupt the proceedings.

input: Han Chinese make up the vast majority of the population, and the largest Han subgroup are the speakers of Wu varieties of Chinese. There are also 400,000 members of ethnic minorities, including approximately 200,000 She people and approximately 20,000 Hui Chinese[citation needed]. Jingning She Autonomous County in Lishui is the only She autonomous county in China.
rewrite: The Han Chinese constitute the overwhelming demographic majority, with speakers of Wu Chinese varieties representing the largest subgroup. Ethnic minorities, totaling approximately 400,000 individuals, include around 200,000 She people and 20,000 Hui Chinese. China's sole She autonomous county is Jingning, located within Lishui.

input: The sensitivity of Earth-based infrared telescopes is significantly limited by water vapor in the atmosphere, which absorbs a portion of the infrared radiation arriving from space outside of selected atmospheric windows. This limitation can be partially alleviated by placing the telescope observatory at a high altitude, or by carrying the telescope aloft with a balloon or an aircraft. Space telescopes do not suffer from this handicap, and so outer space is considered the ideal location for infrared astronomy.
rewrite: The sensitivity of terrestrial infrared telescopes is substantially constrained by atmospheric water vapor, which absorbs much of the incoming infrared radiation except within specific transmission windows. This impediment can be partially mitigated by situating observatories at high-altitude sites or by deploying telescopes on high-altitude balloons or aircraft. Space-based telescopes, however, are entirely free from this atmospheric absorption, thereby establishing outer space as the optimal environment for conducting infrared astronomical observations.

input: Dogs bear their litters roughly 58 to 68 days after fertilization, with an average of 63 days, although the length of gestation can vary. An average litter consists of about six puppies, though this number may vary widely based on the breed of dog. In general, toy dogs produce from one to four puppies in each litter, while much larger breeds may average as many as twelve.
rewrite: The gestation period in dogs typically spans 58 to 68 days post-fertilization, averaging 63 days, with some variation. Litter size averages approximately six offspring but differs considerably by breed. Toy breeds generally produce litters of one to four puppies, whereas significantly larger breeds may average up to twelve.

input: A UCLA research study published in the June 2006 issue of the American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry found that people can improve cognitive function and brain efficiency through simple lifestyle changes such as incorporating memory exercises, healthy eating, physical fitness and stress reduction into their daily lives. This study examined 17 subjects, (average age 53) with normal memory performance. Eight subjects were asked to follow a "brain healthy" diet, relaxation, physical, and mental exercise (brain teasers and verbal memory training techniques). After 14 days, they showed greater word fluency (not memory) compared to their baseline performance. No long term follow up was conducted, it is therefore unclear if this intervention has lasting effects on memory.
rewrite: A study conducted by UCLA and published in the June 2006 *American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry* indicates that cognitive function and neural efficiency may be enhanced through basic lifestyle modifications. These modifications include integrating memory exercises, a nutritious diet, physical activity, and stress management into daily routines. The research involved 17 participants with average memory performance, whose mean age was 53. Over a 14-day period, eight subjects adhered to a regimen comprising a "brain healthy" diet, relaxation practices, physical exercise, and cognitive training. Results demonstrated a significant improvement in verbal fluency, though not in memory, relative to baseline measures. As no longitudinal assessment was performed, the durability of these effects on memory remains uncertain.

input: In a WRIM, the rotor winding is made of many turns of insulated wire and is connected to slip rings on the motor shaft. An external resistor or other control devices can be connected in the rotor circuit. Resistors allow control of the motor speed, although significant power is dissipated in the external resistance. A converter can be fed from the rotor circuit and return the slip-frequency power that would otherwise be wasted back into the power system through an inverter or separate motor-generator.
rewrite: In a wound rotor induction motor (WRIM), the rotor winding consists of multiple turns of insulated wire connected to slip rings on the shaft. External resistors or control devices may be integrated into the rotor circuit. While resistors enable speed regulation, they dissipate substantial power externally. Alternatively, a converter can extract slip-frequency power from the rotor circuit and redirect it back into the electrical system via an inverter or a dedicated motor-generator set, thereby recovering energy otherwise lost.

input: As civil wars engulfed several Central American countries in the 1980s, hundreds of thousands of Salvadorans fled their country and came to the United States. Between 1980 and 1990, the Salvadoran immigrant population in the United States increased nearly fivefold from 94,000 to 465,000. The number of Salvadoran immigrants in the United States continued to grow in the 1990s and 2000s as a result of family reunification and new arrivals fleeing a series of natural disasters that hit El Salvador, including earthquakes and hurricanes. By 2008, there were about 1.1 million Salvadoran immigrants in the United States.
rewrite: During the civil conflicts that afflicted multiple Central American nations in the 1980s, significant numbers of Salvadorans sought refuge in the United States. The Salvadoran immigrant population expanded from approximately 94,000 to 465,000 between 1980 and 1990. Growth persisted in subsequent decades, driven by family reunification and further displacement caused by a succession of natural disasters in El Salvador, such as earthquakes and hurricanes. Consequently, by 2008, the Salvadoran immigrant community in the United States had reached an estimated 1.1 million individuals.

input: Close to Richmond Park is Kew Gardens which has the world's largest collection of living plants. In 2003, the gardens were put on the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites. There are also numerous parks administered by London's borough Councils, including Victoria Park in the East End and Battersea Park in the centre. Some more informal, semi-natural open spaces also exist, including the 320-hectare (790-acre) Hampstead Heath of North London, and Epping Forest, which covers 2,476 hectares (6,118.32 acres) in the east. Both are controlled by the City of London Corporation. Hampstead Heath incorporates Kenwood House, the former stately home and a popular location in the summer months where classical musical concerts are held by the lake, attracting thousands of people every weekend to enjoy the music, scenery and fireworks. Epping Forest is a popular venue for various outdoor activities, including mountain biking, walking, horse riding, golf, angling, and orienteering.
rewrite: Situated near Richmond Park, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, which houses the world's most extensive collection of living plants, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. London's borough councils administer numerous parks, such as Victoria Park in the East End and Battersea Park in the central area. Additionally, there are significant informal, semi-natural spaces, including the 320-hectare Hampstead Heath in North London and the 2,476-hectare Epping Forest to the east, both managed by the City of London Corporation. Hampstead Heath incorporates Kenwood House, a former stately home. This site serves as a popular summer venue for lakeside classical concerts, drawing substantial weekend audiences for music, scenery, and fireworks. Epping Forest is a frequented location for outdoor pursuits, including mountain biking, walking, horse riding, golf, angling, and orienteering.

input: On 11 April 2006, Brian May and Roger Taylor appeared on the American singing contest television show American Idol. Each contestant was required to sing a Queen song during that week of the competition. Songs which appeared on the show included "Bohemian Rhapsody", "Fat Bottomed Girls", "The Show Must Go On", "Who Wants to Live Forever", and "Innuendo". Brian May later criticised the show for editing specific scenes, one of which made the group's time with contestant Ace Young look negative, despite it being the opposite. Taylor and May again appeared on the American Idol season 8 finale in May 2009, performing "We Are the Champions" with finalists Adam Lambert and Kris Allen. On 15 November 2009, Brian May and Roger Taylor appeared on the singing contest television show X Factor in the UK.
rewrite: On 11 April 2006, Queen members Brian May and Roger Taylor made a guest appearance on the American television competition *American Idol*. During that week's episode, contestants were each required to perform a song by Queen. The selections included "Bohemian Rhapsody," "Fat Bottomed Girls," "The Show Must Go On," "Who Wants to Live Forever," and "Innuendo." May subsequently criticized the program's editorial decisions, noting that one edited segment inaccurately portrayed their interaction with contestant Ace Young in a negative light. The duo returned for the season eight finale in May 2009, performing "We Are the Champions" with finalists Adam Lambert and Kris Allen. Later that year, on 15 November 2009, May and Taylor appeared on the British singing competition *The X Factor*.

input: Following a custom she maintained throughout her widowhood, Victoria spent the Christmas of 1900 at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight. Rheumatism in her legs had rendered her lame, and her eyesight was clouded by cataracts. Through early January, she felt "weak and unwell", and by mid-January she was "drowsy ... dazed, [and] confused". She died on Tuesday, 22 January 1901, at half past six in the evening, at the age of 81. Her son and successor King Edward VII, and her eldest grandson, Emperor Wilhelm II of Germany, were at her deathbed. Her favourite pet Pomeranian, Turri, was laid upon her deathbed as a last request.
rewrite: In accordance with a tradition upheld during her widowhood, Queen Victoria observed the Christmas of 1900 at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight. Afflicted by lameness due to rheumatism in her legs and diminished eyesight from cataracts, her health declined in early January. By mid-month, she was described as drowsy, dazed, and confused. She died at 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, 22 January 1901, at the age of eighty-one. Present at her deathbed were her son and successor, King Edward VII, and her eldest grandson, German Emperor Wilhelm II. As a final request, her favoured Pomeranian, Turri, was placed upon the bed.

input: Education is the process of facilitating learning, or the acquisition of knowledge, skills, values, beliefs, and habits. Educational methods include storytelling, discussion, teaching, training, and directed research. Education frequently takes place under the guidance of educators, but learners may also educate themselves. Education can take place in formal or informal settings and any experience that has a formative effect on the way one thinks, feels, or acts may be considered educational. The methodology of teaching is called pedagogy.
rewrite: Education constitutes the systematic facilitation of learning, encompassing the acquisition of knowledge, skills, values, beliefs, and habits. Instructional methods range from storytelling and discussion to teaching, training, and directed research. While often guided by educators, learning can also be self-directed. It occurs within both formal and informal contexts; any experience exerting a formative influence on cognition, affect, or behavior may be deemed educational. The study of teaching methodologies is termed pedagogy.

input: Hayek disapproved of the notion of 'social justice'. He compared the market to a game in which 'there is no point in calling the outcome just or unjust' and argued that 'social justice is an empty phrase with no determinable content'; likewise "the results of the individual's efforts are necessarily unpredictable, and the question as to whether the resulting distribution of incomes is just has no meaning". He generally regarded government redistribution of income or capital as an unacceptable intrusion upon individual freedom: "the principle of distributive justice, once introduced, would not be fulfilled until the whole of society was organized in accordance with it. This would produce a kind of society which in all essential respects would be the opposite of a free society."
rewrite: Friedrich Hayek rejected the concept of ‘social justice’ as intellectually vacuous. He analogized the market to a game, contending that its outcomes cannot be meaningfully characterized as just or unjust. In his view, the inherent unpredictability of individual efforts renders any assessment of the resulting income distribution as just or unjust nonsensical. Hayek further argued that state-led redistribution of income or capital constitutes a profound infringement upon individual liberty. He warned that the adoption of distributive justice as an organizing principle would necessitate the comprehensive reorganization of society, ultimately creating a system diametrically opposed to a free society.

input: While consulting for the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at the University of Pennsylvania on the EDVAC project, von Neumann wrote an incomplete First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. The paper, whose premature distribution nullified the patent claims of EDVAC designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, described a computer architecture in which the data and the program are both stored in the computer's memory in the same address space. This architecture is to this day the basis of modern computer design, unlike the earliest computers that were "programmed" using a separate memory device such as a paper tape or plugboard. Although the single-memory, stored program architecture is commonly called von Neumann architecture as a result of von Neumann's paper, the architecture's description was based on the work of J. Presper Eckert and John William Mauchly, inventors of the ENIAC computer at the University of Pennsylvania.
rewrite: During his consultancy for the University of Pennsylvania’s Moore School of Electrical Engineering on the EDVAC project, John von Neumann produced an unfinished *First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC*. This document, whose early circulation invalidated potential patent claims by EDVAC designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, outlined a computational architecture wherein both data and program instructions reside in a unified memory address space. This stored-program model remains foundational to contemporary computer design, contrasting with earlier machines that relied on external programming media like paper tape or plugboards. Although this single-memory architecture is widely termed the "von Neumann architecture" due to his report, its conceptual underpinnings derived principally from the prior work of Eckert and Mauchly, the inventors of the ENIAC computer at the same institution.

input: In a factor analysis of the latest wave of World Values Survey data, Arno Tausch (Corvinus University of Budapest) found that Protestantism emerges to be very close to combining religion and the traditions of liberalism. The Global Value Development Index, calculated by Tausch, relies on the World Values Survey dimensions such as trust in the state of law, no support for shadow economy, postmaterial activism, support for democracy, a non-acceptance of violence, xenophobia and racism, trust in transnational capital and Universities, confidence in the market economy, supporting gender justice, and engaging in environmental activism, etc.
rewrite: In a factor analysis of the most recent World Values Survey wave, Arno Tausch (Corvinus University of Budapest) identifies Protestantism as closely aligned with a synthesis of religious faith and liberal traditions. Tausch's Global Value Development Index, derived from the survey, incorporates dimensions including trust in the rule of law, rejection of the shadow economy, postmaterial activism, democratic endorsement, non-acceptance of violence, xenophobia and racism, trust in transnational capital and universities, confidence in the market economy, support for gender justice, and engagement in environmental activism.

input: Russian Imperialism led to the Russian Empire's conquest of Central Asia during the late 19th century's Imperial Era. Between 1864 and 1885 Russia gradually took control of the entire territory of Russian Turkestan, the Tajikistan portion of which had been controlled by the Emirate of Bukhara and Khanate of Kokand. Russia was interested in gaining access to a supply of cotton and in the 1870s attempted to switch cultivation in the region from grain to cotton (a strategy later copied and expanded by the Soviets).[citation needed] By 1885 Tajikistan's territory was either ruled by the Russian Empire or its vassal state, the Emirate of Bukhara, nevertheless Tajiks felt little Russian influence.[citation needed]
rewrite: The expansion of Russian imperialism during the late nineteenth century precipitated the Russian Empire’s conquest of Central Asia. Between 1864 and 1885, Russia systematically annexed the region designated as Russian Turkestan, including territories of contemporary Tajikistan previously governed by the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanate of Kokand. Imperial motivations included securing cotton supplies, prompting efforts in the 1870s to convert agricultural production from grain to cotton—a policy later intensified under Soviet rule. By 1885, all Tajik territory fell under either direct imperial control or the dominion of the Russian vassal state of Bukhara, yet direct Russian cultural and administrative influence remained limited.

input: In 2004, West had his first of a number of public incidents during his attendance at music award events. At the American Music Awards of 2004, West stormed out of the auditorium after losing Best New Artist to country singer Gretchen Wilson. He later commented, "I felt like I was definitely robbed [...] I was the best new artist this year." After the 2006 Grammy nominations were released, West said he would "really have a problem" if he did not win the Album of the Year, saying, "I don't care what I do, I don't care how much I stunt – you can never take away from the amount of work I put into it. I don't want to hear all of that politically correct stuff." On November 2, 2006, when his "Touch the Sky" failed to win Best Video at the MTV Europe Music Awards, West went onto the stage as the award was being presented to Justice and Simian for "We Are Your Friends" and argued that he should have won the award instead. Hundreds of news outlets worldwide criticized the outburst. On November 7, 2006, West apologized for this outburst publicly during his performance as support act for U2 for their Vertigo concert in Brisbane. He later spoofed the incident on the 33rd season premiere of Saturday Night Live in September 2007.
rewrite: The year 2004 marked the onset of a series of public incidents involving Kanye West at music industry ceremonies. His first notable outburst occurred at the 2004 American Music Awards, where he departed the auditorium abruptly following his loss for Best New Artist to country performer Gretchen Wilson. West subsequently asserted that he had been unjustly denied the award, stating, "I felt like I was definitely robbed [...] I was the best new artist this year." Following the announcement of the 2006 Grammy nominations, he preemptively declared he would "really have a problem" if not awarded Album of the Year, dismissing what he termed "politically correct" considerations and emphasizing his substantial creative labor. A further incident transpired on November 2, 2006, at the MTV Europe Music Awards. When his video for "Touch the Sky" lost Best Video to Justice and Simian's "We Are Your Friends," West mounted the stage during the acceptance ceremony to protest the outcome. This act drew widespread censure from international media. Five days later, on November 7, 2006, West issued a public apology for the disruption during his opening performance for U2’s Vertigo Tour in Brisbane. He later engaged in self-parody regarding the event during the September 2007 season premiere of *Saturday Night Live*.

input: In 1993, to complement its own direct sales channel, Dell planned to sell PCs at big-box retail outlets such as Wal-Mart, which would have brought in an additional $125 million in annual revenue. Bain consultant Kevin Rollins persuaded Michael Dell to pull out of these deals, believing they would be money losers in the long run. Margins at retail were thin at best and Dell left the reseller channel in 1994. Rollins would soon join Dell full-time and eventually become the company President and CEO.
rewrite: In 1993, Dell sought to augment its direct sales model by distributing personal computers through major retail chains, including Wal-Mart, a strategy projected to generate $125 million in annual revenue. However, consultant Kevin Rollins convinced CEO Michael Dell to terminate these agreements, arguing that the inherently low retail margins would prove unprofitable. Consequently, Dell exited the reseller channel in 1994. Rollins subsequently joined the company full-time and later ascended to the roles of President and Chief Executive Officer.

input: Avoidance of triggers is a key component of improving control and preventing attacks. The most common triggers include allergens, smoke (tobacco and other), air pollution, non selective beta-blockers, and sulfite-containing foods. Cigarette smoking and second-hand smoke (passive smoke) may reduce the effectiveness of medications such as corticosteroids. Laws that limit smoking decrease the number of people hospitalized for asthma. Dust mite control measures, including air filtration, chemicals to kill mites, vacuuming, mattress covers and others methods had no effect on asthma symptoms. Overall, exercise is beneficial in people with stable asthma. Yoga could provide small improvements in quality of life and symptoms in people with asthma.
rewrite: The avoidance of identified triggers is a fundamental strategy for enhancing disease control and preventing exacerbations. Common precipitants encompass allergens, smoke from tobacco and other sources, air pollution, non-selective beta-blockers, and sulfite-containing foods. Notably, both active and passive tobacco smoke may attenuate the efficacy of medications like corticosteroids, and legislative smoking restrictions are associated with reduced asthma-related hospitalizations. While comprehensive dust mite mitigation strategies demonstrate no significant impact on symptoms, regular exercise is beneficial for individuals with stable asthma. Practices such as yoga may yield modest improvements in symptom burden and quality of life.

input: The Romans held off Hannibal in three battles, but then Hannibal smashed a succession of Roman consular armies. By this time Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal Barca sought to cross the Alps into Italy and join his brother with a second army. Hasdrubal managed to break through into Italy only to be defeated decisively on the Metaurus River. Unable to defeat Hannibal on Italian soil, the Romans boldly sent an army to Africa under Scipio Africanus to threaten the Carthaginian capital. Hannibal was recalled to Africa, and defeated at the Battle of Zama.
rewrite: Following three initial defeats, Hannibal overcame successive Roman consular armies. Concurrently, his brother Hasdrubal Barca attempted to reinforce him by crossing the Alps with a second Carthaginian force. Although Hasdrubal penetrated Italy, he was decisively defeated at the Metaurus River. Unable to expel Hannibal from Italy, Rome strategically shifted the war to Africa by dispatching Scipio Africanus to threaten Carthage. This compelled Hannibal's recall, culminating in his final defeat at the Battle of Zama.

input: During regular, day-to-day activities, Somali women usually wear the guntiino, a long stretch of cloth tied over the shoulder and draped around the waist. It is usually made out of alandi, which is a textile common in the Horn region and some parts of North Africa. The garment can be worn in different styles. It can also be made with other fabrics, including white cloth with gold borders. For more formal settings, such as at weddings or religious celebrations like Eid, women wear the dirac. It is a long, light, diaphanous voile dress made of silk, chiffon, taffeta or saree fabric. The gown is worn over a full-length half-slip and a brassiere. Known as the gorgorad, the underskirt is made out of silk and serves as a key part of the overall outfit. The dirac is usually sparkly and very colorful, the most popular styles being those with gilded borders or threads. The fabric is typically acquired from Somali clothing stores in tandem with the gorgorad. In the past, dirac fabric was also frequently purchased from South Asian merchandisers.
rewrite: In the context of daily activities, Somali women traditionally don the *guntiino*, a length of cloth secured over the shoulder and wrapped around the waist. This garment is commonly constructed from *alandi*, a textile prevalent throughout the Horn of Africa and parts of North Africa, though other materials such as white cloth with gold borders are also employed. The *guntiino* permits various stylistic adaptations. For formal occasions, including weddings and religious observances such as Eid, women wear the *dirac*. This is a long, lightweight dress of diaphanous voile, typically fashioned from silk, chiffon, taffeta, or saree fabric. It is worn over a full underskirt, the *gorgorad*, which is itself silk-made and constitutes an essential component of the ensemble. The *dirac* is characteristically vibrant and embellished, with gilded borders or threads being particularly favored. These fabrics are generally procured from Somali clothing retailers alongside the *gorgorad*, whereas historically, *dirac* material was often sourced from South Asian merchants.

input: From 1889, when Guangxu began to rule in his own right, to 1898, the Empress Dowager lived in semi-retirement, spending the majority of the year at the Summer Palace. On November 1, 1897, two German Roman Catholic missionaries were murdered in the southern part of Shandong Province (the Juye Incident). In response, Germany used the murders as a pretext for a naval occupation of Jiaozhou Bay. The occupation prompted a "scramble for concessions" in 1898, which included the German lease of Jiazhou Bay, the Russian acquisition of Liaodong, and the British lease of the New Territories of Hong Kong.
rewrite: Following Emperor Guangxu's assumption of personal rule in 1889, the Empress Dowager Cixi entered a period of semi-retirement, predominantly residing at the Summer Palace. The assassination of two German missionaries in Shandong's Juye County on November 1, 1897, provided the pretext for Germany's naval seizure of Jiaozhou Bay. This act precipitated a broader imperialist scramble for territorial concessions throughout 1898, notably including the German lease of Jiaozhou, the Russian acquisition of Liaodong, and the British lease of the Hong Kong New Territories.

input: The emperor was at the pinnacle of Han society. He presided over the Han government but shared power with both the nobility and appointed ministers who came largely from the scholarly gentry class. The Han Empire was divided into areas directly controlled by the central government using an innovation inherited from the Qin known as commanderies, and a number of semi-autonomous kingdoms. These kingdoms gradually lost all vestiges of their independence, particularly following the Rebellion of the Seven States. From the reign of Emperor Wu onward, the Chinese court officially sponsored Confucianism in education and court politics, synthesized with the cosmology of later scholars such as Dong Zhongshu. This policy endured until the fall of the Qing dynasty in AD 1911.
rewrite: The emperor occupied the apex of Han dynasty society. While presiding over the imperial government, he shared administrative authority with the hereditary nobility and appointed ministers, the latter predominantly drawn from the scholarly gentry class. Territorially, the empire was organized into administrative units directly controlled by the central government, known as commanderies—a system inherited from the Qin—and several semi-autonomous kingdoms. These kingdoms progressively forfeited their independence, especially after the Rebellion of the Seven States. From the reign of Emperor Wu onward, the court formally endorsed Confucianism, integrated with the cosmological frameworks of later scholars like Dong Zhongshu, as the basis for state education and political doctrine. This ideological commitment persisted until the collapse of the Qing dynasty in 1911 AD.

input: North Carolina averages fewer than 20 tornadoes per year, many of them produced by hurricanes or tropical storms along the coastal plain. Tornadoes from thunderstorms are a risk, especially in the eastern part of the state. The western Piedmont is often protected by the mountains, which tend to break up storms as they try to cross over; the storms will often re-form farther east. Also a weather phenomenon known as "cold air damming" often occurs in the northwestern part of the state, which can also weaken storms but can also lead to major ice events in winter.
rewrite: North Carolina experiences an average of fewer than twenty tornadoes annually, with many generated by hurricanes or tropical storms along the coastal plain. Tornadic thunderstorms also pose a risk, particularly in the eastern region. The western Piedmont is frequently shielded by mountainous terrain, which disrupts storm systems; these storms commonly redevelop farther east. Furthermore, a meteorological process termed "cold air damming" frequently occurs in the northwest, which can attenuate storms but also contribute to significant winter ice events.

input: Bronx native Nancy Savoca's 1989 comedy, True Love, explores two Italian-American Bronx sweethearts in the days before their wedding. The film, which debuted Annabella Sciorra and Ron Eldard as the betrothed couple, won the Grand Jury Prize at that year's Sundance Film Festival. The CBS television sitcom Becker, 1998–2004, was more ambiguous. The show starred Ted Danson as Dr. John Becker, a doctor who operated a small practice and was constantly annoyed by his patients, co-workers, friends, and practically everything and everybody else in his world. It showed his everyday life as a doctor working in a small clinic in the Bronx.
rewrite: Nancy Savoca's 1989 comedy *True Love*, which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival where it won the Grand Jury Prize, examines the experiences of an Italian-American engaged couple in the Bronx in the days preceding their wedding. The film features the debut performances of Annabella Sciorra and Ron Eldard. In contrast, the CBS sitcom *Becker* (1998–2004) presents a more ambiguous portrayal of the borough. It chronicles the daily life of the misanthropic Dr. John Becker, portrayed by Ted Danson, as he manages a small clinic and contends with patients and colleagues.

input: In December 2011, the system went into operation on a trial basis. It has started providing navigation, positioning and timing data to China and the neighbouring area for free from 27 December. During this trial run, Compass will offer positioning accuracy to within 25 meters, but the precision will improve as more satellites are launched. Upon the system's official launch, it pledged to offer general users positioning information accurate to the nearest 10 m, measure speeds within 0.2 m per second, and provide signals for clock synchronisation accurate to 0.02 microseconds.
rewrite: The Compass navigation system commenced trial operations in December 2011, initiating the provision of complimentary navigation, positioning, and timing services to China and its surrounding regions from December 27th. Throughout this preliminary phase, the system delivers positioning accuracy within 25 meters, a capability projected to improve with subsequent satellite launches. Upon its official inauguration, the system is designed to provide public users with positioning data precise to 10 meters, velocity measurements within 0.2 meters per second, and clock synchronization signals accurate to 0.02 microseconds.

input: In soil, microorganisms that reside in the rhizosphere (a zone that includes the root surface and the soil that adheres to the root after gentle shaking) carry out nitrogen fixation, converting nitrogen gas to nitrogenous compounds. This serves to provide an easily absorbable form of nitrogen for many plants, which cannot fix nitrogen themselves. Many other bacteria are found as symbionts in humans and other organisms. For example, the presence of over 1,000 bacterial species in the normal human gut flora of the intestines can contribute to gut immunity, synthesise vitamins, such as folic acid, vitamin K and biotin, convert sugars to lactic acid (see Lactobacillus), as well as fermenting complex undigestible carbohydrates. The presence of this gut flora also inhibits the growth of potentially pathogenic bacteria (usually through competitive exclusion) and these beneficial bacteria are consequently sold as probiotic dietary supplements.
rewrite: Within the rhizosphere—a region encompassing the root surface and the soil closely associated with it following gentle agitation—specific microorganisms perform biological nitrogen fixation, transforming atmospheric nitrogen into bioavailable nitrogenous compounds. This process supplies an assimilable nitrogen source to numerous plants incapable of independent fixation. Separately, diverse bacterial communities exist as symbionts in hosts such as humans. The typical human intestinal microbiota, comprising over 1,000 bacterial species, contributes substantially to host physiology. Functions include supporting gut immunity, synthesizing essential vitamins (e.g., folic acid, vitamin K, and biotin), converting sugars to lactic acid, and fermenting complex indigestible polysaccharides. Furthermore, this resident flora competitively excludes potential pathogens, thereby providing a protective effect. Due to these beneficial roles, such bacteria are commercially formulated as probiotic supplements.

input: The possibility of unlikely victories in the earlier rounds of the competition, where lower ranked teams beat higher placed opposition, known as "giant killings", is much anticipated by the public, and is considered an integral part of the tradition and prestige of the competition, alongside that gained by teams winning the competition. Almost every club in the League Pyramid has a fondly remembered giant-killing act in its history. It is considered particularly newsworthy when a top Premier League team suffers an upset defeat, or where the giant-killer is a non-league club, i.e. from outside the professional levels of The Football League.
rewrite: The phenomenon of "giant killings," wherein lower-ranked teams defeat superior opponents in the early stages of the competition, is a widely anticipated element that significantly contributes to its tradition and prestige. This aspect is valued alongside the ultimate triumph of the tournament winner. Nearly every club within the football league pyramid cherishes a historic giant-killing achievement. Such upsets are deemed especially notable when a leading Premier League side falls to a defeat or when the victorious team is a non-league club, operating outside the professional Football League structure.

input: Although each institution is organized differently, nearly all universities have a board of trustees; a president, chancellor, or rector; at least one vice president, vice-chancellor, or vice-rector; and deans of various divisions. Universities are generally divided into a number of academic departments, schools or faculties. Public university systems are ruled over by government-run higher education boards. They review financial requests and budget proposals and then allocate funds for each university in the system. They also approve new programs of instruction and cancel or make changes in existing programs. In addition, they plan for the further coordinated growth and development of the various institutions of higher education in the state or country. However, many public universities in the world have a considerable degree of financial, research and pedagogical autonomy. Private universities are privately funded and generally have broader independence from state policies. However, they may have less independence from business corporations depending on the source of their finances.
rewrite: While institutional structures vary, most universities are governed by a board of trustees and led by a president, chancellor, or rector, supported by vice-presidents and deans. Organizationally, they are typically subdivided into academic departments, schools, or faculties. Public university systems are overseen by state or national higher education boards. These bodies evaluate financial requests, allocate budgets, and authorize or modify academic programs. Furthermore, they strategize for the coordinated expansion and development of higher education within their jurisdiction. Despite this oversight, many public universities globally retain significant autonomy in financial, research, and pedagogical matters. In contrast, private universities are funded through non-governmental sources and generally enjoy greater independence from state control, though their reliance on corporate funding may constrain their operational autonomy.

input: Various industrial businesses are located in Hannover. The Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles Transporter (VWN) factory at Hannover-Stöcken is the biggest employer in the region and operates a huge plant at the northern edge of town adjoining the Mittellandkanal and Motorway A2. Jointly with a factory of German tire and automobile parts manufacturer Continental AG, they have a coal-burning power plant. Continental AG, founded in Hanover in 1871, is one of the city's major companies, as is Sennheiser. Since 2008 a take-over is in progress: the Schaeffler Group from Herzogenaurach (Bavaria) holds the majority of the stock but were required due to the financial crisis to deposit the options as securities at banks. TUI AG has its HQ in Hanover. Hanover is home to many insurance companies, many of which operate only in Germany. One major global reinsurance company is Hannover Re, whose headquarters are east of the city centre.
rewrite: Hannover hosts a diverse range of industrial enterprises. The most significant employer in the region is the Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles (VWN) plant in Hannover-Stöcken, which operates an extensive facility at the city's northern periphery, adjacent to both the Mittellandkanal and the A2 motorway. This site shares a coal-fired power station with a factory belonging to Continental AG, a major tire and automotive parts manufacturer founded in Hanover in 1871. Continental, alongside Sennheiser, ranks among the city's principal corporations. Since 2008, a takeover has been underway, with the Schaeffler Group of Herzogenaurach acquiring a majority stake; however, due to the financial crisis, its options were required to be deposited as securities with banks. The global tourism group TUI AG is headquartered in Hanover, which is also a notable center for the insurance sector, hosting numerous domestic insurers. A leading global reinsurance firm, Hannover Re, is situated east of the city center.

input: In matches with multiple competitors, an elimination system may be used. Any wrestler who has a fall scored against them is forced out of the match, and the match continues until only one remains. However, it is much more common when more than two wrestlers are involved to simply go one fall, with the one scoring the fall, regardless of who they scored it against, being the winner. In championship matches, this means that, unlike one-on-one matches (where the champion can simply disqualify themselves or get themselves counted out to retain the title via the "champion's advantag"), the champion does not have to be pinned or involved in the decision to lose the championship. However, heel champions often find advantages, not in champion's advantage, but in the use of weapons and outside interference, as these poly-sided matches tend to involve no holds barred rules.
rewrite: In contests featuring multiple participants, an elimination format may be employed, whereby any wrestler who suffers a fall is removed, and the match proceeds until a single competitor remains. More frequently, however, multi-wrestler matches utilize a single-fall stipulation, awarding victory to whichever participant secures a fall, irrespective of the opponent pinned. This structure significantly alters championship dynamics. Unlike in standard one-on-one title matches, where a champion can exploit the "champion's advantage" to retain by disqualification or count-out, the champion in a multi-competitor match can lose the title without being directly pinned or submitting. Consequently, heel champions often forgo traditional advantage, instead leveraging no-disqualification rules common to such bouts to utilize weapons and external interference.

input: Immunology is strongly experimental in everyday practice but is also characterized by an ongoing theoretical attitude. Many theories have been suggested in immunology from the end of the nineteenth century up to the present time. The end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century saw a battle between "cellular" and "humoral" theories of immunity. According to the cellular theory of immunity, represented in particular by Elie Metchnikoff, it was cells – more precisely, phagocytes – that were responsible for immune responses. In contrast, the humoral theory of immunity, held by Robert Koch and Emil von Behring, among others, stated that the active immune agents were soluble components (molecules) found in the organism’s “humors” rather than its cells.
rewrite: Immunology, while fundamentally an experimental discipline in its daily application, is equally distinguished by a persistent theoretical orientation. Since the late nineteenth century, the field has generated numerous theoretical frameworks. A pivotal intellectual conflict emerged around the turn of the 20th century between the "cellular" and "humoral" theories of immunity. Proponents of the cellular theory, most notably Elie Metchnikoff, posited that specialized cells—specifically phagocytes—were the primary agents of immune defense. Conversely, advocates of the humoral theory, including Robert Koch and Emil von Behring, contended that soluble molecular components within the body's humors, rather than its cells, constituted the essential mediators of immunity.

input: Italy became a major industrialized country again, due to its post-war economic miracle. The European Union (EU) involved the division of powers, with taxation, health and education handled by the nation states, while the EU had charge of market rules, competition, legal standards and environmentalism. The Soviet economic and political system collapsed, leading to the end of communism in the satellite countries in 1989, and the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself in 1991. As a consequence, Europe's integration deepened, the continent became depolarised, and the European Union expanded to subsequently include many of the formerly communist European countries – Romania and Bulgaria (2007) and Croatia (2013).
rewrite: Italy re-emerged as a significant industrial power following its post-war economic miracle. The European Union (EU) operates on a principle of divided competencies, wherein member states retain authority over taxation, health, and education, while the EU governs market regulations, competition policy, legal standards, and environmental protection. The collapse of the Soviet political and economic system precipitated the fall of communism in its satellite states in 1989 and the USSR's dissolution in 1991. Consequently, European integration intensified, the continent's geopolitical divisions diminished, and the EU enlarged to incorporate several former communist states, including Romania and Bulgaria in 2007 and Croatia in 2013.

input: Major religious groups in the Republic of the Marshall Islands include the United Church of Christ (formerly Congregational), with 51.5% of the population; the Assemblies of God, 24.2%; the Roman Catholic Church, 8.4%; and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons), 8.3%; Also represented are Bukot Nan Jesus (also known as Assembly of God Part Two), 2.2%; Baptist, 1.0%; Seventh-day Adventists, 0.9%; Full Gospel, 0.7%; and the Baha'i Faith, 0.6%; Persons without any religious affiliation account for a very small percentage of the population. There is also a small community of Ahmadiyya Muslims based in Majuro, with the first mosque opening in the capital in September 2012.
rewrite: The Republic of the Marshall Islands is characterized by a predominantly Christian religious demographic. The United Church of Christ constitutes the majority at 51.5% of the population, followed by the Assemblies of God at 24.2%. Other significant affiliations include the Roman Catholic Church (8.4%) and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (8.3%). Smaller represented groups are Bukot Nan Jesus (2.2%), Baptist (1.0%), Seventh-day Adventists (0.9%), Full Gospel (0.7%), and the Baha'i Faith (0.6%). Non-affiliated persons form a minimal segment. Additionally, a small Ahmadiyya Muslim community is present in Majuro, where the nation's first mosque opened in September 2012.

input: The official policy became one of biological and cultural assimilation: "Eliminate the full-blood and permit the white admixture to half-castes and eventually the race will become white". This led to different treatment for "black" and "half-caste" individuals, with lighter-skinned individuals targeted for removal from their families to be raised as "white" people, restricted from speaking their native language and practising traditional customs, a process now known as the Stolen Generation.
rewrite: Official policy mandated biological and cultural assimilation, explicitly aiming to "eliminate the full-blood" and use "white admixture" to render the population "white." This instituted a racial hierarchy, whereby lighter-skinned "half-caste" individuals were forcibly removed from their families to be raised as "white," prohibited from using their native languages and practising customs. This systematic process is now identified as the Stolen Generation.

input: Some bird species undertake shorter migrations, travelling only as far as is required to avoid bad weather or obtain food. Irruptive species such as the boreal finches are one such group and can commonly be found at a location in one year and absent the next. This type of migration is normally associated with food availability. Species may also travel shorter distances over part of their range, with individuals from higher latitudes travelling into the existing range of conspecifics; others undertake partial migrations, where only a fraction of the population, usually females and subdominant males, migrates. Partial migration can form a large percentage of the migration behaviour of birds in some regions; in Australia, surveys found that 44% of non-passerine birds and 32% of passerines were partially migratory. Altitudinal migration is a form of short distance migration in which birds spend the breeding season at higher altitudes elevations and move to lower ones during suboptimal conditions. It is most often triggered by temperature changes and usually occurs when the normal territories also become inhospitable due to lack of food. Some species may also be nomadic, holding no fixed territory and moving according to weather and food availability. Parrots as a family are overwhelmingly neither migratory nor sedentary but considered to either be dispersive, irruptive, nomadic or undertake small and irregular migrations.
rewrite: Certain avian species engage in abbreviated migratory movements, traveling minimal distances necessary to evade inclement conditions or secure nutritional resources. Irruptive migrants, exemplified by boreal finches, typify this pattern, often appearing in a given locality one year and being absent the next—a behavior predominantly linked to fluctuations in food supply. Additionally, some species exhibit shorter migratory journeys across portions of their range, with individuals from higher latitudes moving into the established ranges of conspecifics. Others display partial migration, wherein only a segment of the population, frequently females and subordinate males, undertakes seasonal movement. This partial migration constitutes a substantial proportion of avian migratory behavior in certain regions; for instance, surveys in Australia indicate that 44% of non-passerine and 32% of passerine species are partially migratory. Altitudinal migration represents another form of short-distance movement, wherein birds breed at higher elevations and descend to lower altitudes under suboptimal conditions, typically prompted by temperature shifts and concurrent resource scarcity. Furthermore, some species adopt a nomadic existence, eschewing fixed territories and relocating in response to meteorological and trophic variations. Notably, parrots as a taxonomic family are predominantly neither fully migratory nor sedentary but are generally characterized as dispersive, irruptive, nomadic, or engaging in limited and irregular migrations.

input: While there is no convincing evidence for meditation in pre-Buddhist early Brahminic texts, Wynne argues that formless meditation originated in the Brahminic or Shramanic tradition, based on strong parallels between Upanishadic cosmological statements and the meditative goals of the two teachers of the Buddha as recorded in the early Buddhist texts. He mentions less likely possibilities as well. Having argued that the cosmological statements in the Upanishads also reflect a contemplative tradition, he argues that the Nasadiya Sukta contains evidence for a contemplative tradition, even as early as the late Rig Vedic period.
rewrite: While compelling evidence for meditation practices is absent from pre-Buddhist Brahminical texts, Wynne posits that formless meditation originated within either the Brahminical or Śramaṇic tradition. This conclusion is drawn from pronounced parallels between Upanishadic cosmological descriptions and the meditative aims of the Buddha’s teachers as documented in early Buddhist sources. Wynne further contends that Upanishadic cosmology itself reflects a contemplative tradition, evidence for which he traces to the late Rigvedic period, as exemplified in the Naṣadīya Sūkta.

input: USB mice and keyboards can usually be used with older computers that have PS/2 connectors with the aid of a small USB-to-PS/2 adapter. For mice and keyboards with dual-protocol support, an adaptor that contains no logic circuitry may be used: the hardware in the USB keyboard or mouse is designed to detect whether it is connected to a USB or PS/2 port, and communicate using the appropriate protocol. Converters also exist that connect PS/2 keyboards and mice (usually one of each) to a USB port. These devices present two HID endpoints to the system and use a microcontroller to perform bidirectional data translation between the two standards.
rewrite: USB mice and keyboards are generally compatible with older computers featuring PS/2 connectors through the use of a simple USB-to-PS/2 adapter. For peripherals with dual-protocol support, a passive adapter lacking internal logic may suffice, as the device itself detects the connection type and selects the appropriate communication protocol. Conversely, active converters enable PS/2 keyboards and mice—typically one of each—to interface with a USB port. These converters present two HID endpoints to the system and employ a microcontroller to perform bidirectional data translation between the two standards.

input: In some jurisdictions, copyright or the right to enforce it can be contractually assigned to a third party which did not have a role in producing the work. When this outsourced litigator appears to have no intention of taking any copyright infringement cases to trial, but rather only takes them just far enough through the legal system to identify and exact settlements from suspected infringers, critics commonly refer to the party as a "copyright troll." Such practices have had mixed results in the U.S.
rewrite: In certain legal systems, copyright or its enforcement rights may be contractually transferred to a third party uninvolved in the work’s creation. When such an external litigant appears to pursue infringement claims not for trial, but primarily to identify alleged infringers and extract settlements through preliminary legal actions, critics often label the entity a "copyright troll." These practices have yielded varied legal outcomes within the United States.

input: Australia had been shocked by the speedy collapse of British Malaya and Fall of Singapore in which around 15,000 Australian soldiers became prisoners of war. Curtin predicted that the "battle for Australia" would now follow. The Japanese established a major base in the Australian Territory of New Guinea in early 1942. On 19 February, Darwin suffered a devastating air raid, the first time the Australian mainland had been attacked. Over the following 19 months, Australia was attacked from the air almost 100 times.
rewrite: The rapid collapse of British Malaya and the subsequent Fall of Singapore, which resulted in the capture of approximately 15,000 Australian soldiers, profoundly shocked Australia. Prime Minister Curtin declared that the "battle for Australia" would ensue. Following Japan's establishment of a major base in Australian New Guinea in early 1942, the mainland was first attacked during a devastating air raid on Darwin, 19 February. Subsequently, Australia endured nearly 100 aerial assaults over the following nineteen months.

input: The team's commitment to contend was complete when Green made a midseason deal on June 15 to shore up the starting rotation due to injuries to Rick Reuschel (5–5) and Sanderson. The deal brought 1979 NL Rookie of the Year pitcher Rick Sutcliffe from the Cleveland Indians. Joe Carter (who was with the Triple-A Iowa Cubs at the time) and center fielder Mel Hall were sent to Cleveland for Sutcliffe and back-up catcher Ron Hassey (.333 with Cubs in 1984). Sutcliffe (5–5 with the Indians) immediately joined Sanderson (8–5 3.14), Eckersley (10–8 3.03), Steve Trout (13–7 3.41) and Dick Ruthven (6–10 5.04) in the starting rotation. Sutcliffe proceeded to go 16–1 for Cubs and capture the Cy Young Award.
rewrite: The organization's dedication to pursuing championship contention was decisively demonstrated on June 15, when General Manager Dallas Green executed a midseason trade to address injuries within the starting rotation, specifically to Rick Reuschel (5–5) and Scott Sanderson. This transaction acquired 1979 National League Rookie of the Year pitcher Rick Sutcliffe from the Cleveland Indians. In exchange, the Cubs sent prospects Joe Carter and center fielder Mel Hall to Cleveland, also receiving backup catcher Ron Hassey (.333 in 1984). Sutcliffe (5–5 with Cleveland) was integrated into a rotation featuring Sanderson (8–5, 3.14 ERA), Dennis Eckersley (10–8, 3.03), Steve Trout (13–7, 3.41), and Dick Ruthven (6–10, 5.04). He subsequently achieved a remarkable 16–1 record for Chicago, securing the Cy Young Award.

input: Regular flights to most villages and towns within the state that are commercially viable are challenging to provide, so they are heavily subsidized by the federal government through the Essential Air Service program. Alaska Airlines is the only major airline offering in-state travel with jet service (sometimes in combination cargo and passenger Boeing 737-400s) from Anchorage and Fairbanks to regional hubs like Bethel, Nome, Kotzebue, Dillingham, Kodiak, and other larger communities as well as to major Southeast and Alaska Peninsula communities.
rewrite: Providing regular, commercially viable flights to most state villages and towns is challenging, necessitating substantial federal subsidies via the Essential Air Service program. Alaska Airlines operates as the sole major carrier offering in-state jet service, utilizing Boeing 737-400 aircraft, sometimes configured for combined cargo and passenger transport. It connects Anchorage and Fairbanks to regional hubs such as Bethel, Nome, and Kotzebue, as well as to larger communities across Southeast Alaska and the Alaska Peninsula.

input: Depopulation, deurbanisation, invasion, and movement of peoples, which had begun in Late Antiquity, continued in the Early Middle Ages. The barbarian invaders, including various Germanic peoples, formed new kingdoms in what remained of the Western Roman Empire. In the 7th century, North Africa and the Middle East—once part of the Eastern Roman Empire—came under the rule of the Caliphate, an Islamic empire, after conquest by Muhammad's successors. Although there were substantial changes in society and political structures, the break with Antiquity was not complete. The still-sizeable Byzantine Empire survived in the east and remained a major power. The empire's law code, the Code of Justinian, was rediscovered in Northern Italy in 1070 and became widely admired later in the Middle Ages. In the West, most kingdoms incorporated the few extant Roman institutions. Monasteries were founded as campaigns to Christianise pagan Europe continued. The Franks, under the Carolingian dynasty, briefly established the Carolingian Empire during the later 8th and early 9th century. It covered much of Western Europe, but later succumbed to the pressures of internal civil wars combined with external invasions—Vikings from the north, Magyars from the east, and Saracens from the south.
rewrite: The processes of depopulation, deurbanisation, invasion, and migration, initiated in Late Antiquity, persisted into the Early Middle Ages. Germanic and other barbarian groups established new kingdoms within the former territories of the Western Roman Empire. During the seventh century, the eastern and southern provinces of the former Eastern Roman Empire, namely North Africa and the Middle East, were subsumed into the Islamic Caliphate following conquests by the successors of Muhammad. Despite these profound societal and political transformations, a complete rupture with the ancient world did not occur. The Byzantine Empire, a diminished but still significant power, endured in the east. Its legal heritage, particularly the Code of Justinian rediscovered in Northern Italy in 1070, gained considerable influence in later medieval jurisprudence. In Western Europe, most successor kingdoms integrated surviving Roman administrative frameworks. Concurrently, monastic foundations proliferated as part of ongoing efforts to Christianise pagan regions. The Carolingian dynasty of the Franks consolidated a brief hegemony over much of Western Europe in the late eighth and early ninth centuries. This Carolingian Empire ultimately fragmented due to internal dynastic conflicts compounded by external assaults from Viking, Magyar, and Saracen forces.

input: Melbourne has a highly diversified economy with particular strengths in finance, manufacturing, research, IT, education, logistics, transportation and tourism. Melbourne houses the headquarters for many of Australia's largest corporations, including five of the ten largest in the country (based on revenue), and four of the largest six in the country (based on market capitalisation) (ANZ, BHP Billiton (the world's largest mining company), the National Australia Bank and Telstra), as well as such representative bodies and think tanks as the Business Council of Australia and the Australian Council of Trade Unions. Melbourne's suburbs also have the Head Offices of Wesfarmers companies Coles (including Liquorland), Bunnings, Target, K-Mart & Officeworks. The city is home to Australia's largest and busiest seaport which handles more than $75 billion in trade every year and 39% of the nation's container trade. Melbourne Airport provides an entry point for national and international visitors, and is Australia's second busiest airport.[citation needed]
rewrite: The economy of Melbourne is characterized by a high degree of diversification, with prominent sectors including finance, manufacturing, research, information technology, education, logistics, transport, and tourism. The city serves as the corporate headquarters for numerous major Australian entities. This includes five of the nation's ten largest companies by revenue and four of the six largest by market capitalization, such as ANZ, BHP Billiton, the National Australia Bank, and Telstra. Furthermore, Melbourne hosts significant national institutions including the Business Council of Australia and the Australian Council of Trade Unions. The metropolitan area also contains the head offices of key Wesfarmers subsidiaries, including Coles, Bunnings, Target, K-Mart, and Officeworks. Critical infrastructure underpins this activity, featuring Australia's largest and busiest seaport, which manages over $75 billion in annual trade and 39% of national container traffic, alongside Melbourne Airport, the nation's second busiest aviation hub.

input: Although Turkey and Israel did not establish full diplomatic relations until 1991, Turkey has cooperated with the State since its recognition of Israel in 1949. Turkey's ties to the other Muslim-majority nations in the region have at times resulted in pressure from Arab and Muslim states to temper its relationship with Israel. Relations between Turkey and Israel took a downturn after the 2008–09 Gaza War and Israel's raid of the Gaza flotilla. IHH, which organized the flotilla, is a Turkish charity that has been challenged on ties to Hamas and Al-Qaeda. Relations between Israel and Greece have improved since 1995 due to the decline of Israeli-Turkish relations. The two countries have a defense cooperation agreement and in 2010, the Israeli Air Force hosted Greece’s Hellenic Air Force in a joint exercise at the Uvda base. Israel is the second largest importer of Greek products in the Middle East. The joint Cyprus-Israel oil and gas explorations centered on the Leviathan gas field are an important factor for Greece, given its strong links with Cyprus. Cooperation in the world's longest sub-sea electric power cable, the EuroAsia Interconnector, has strengthened relations between Cyprus and Israel.
rewrite: Diplomatic relations between Turkey and Israel were formally established in 1991, yet cooperative engagement existed following Turkey’s recognition of the State of Israel in 1949. Turkey’s concurrent affiliations with regional Muslim-majority nations have periodically subjected it to external pressures from Arab and Muslim states to moderate its ties with Israel. A significant deterioration in bilateral relations occurred following the 2008–09 Gaza War and the 2010 Israeli raid on the Gaza-bound flotilla. The flotilla’s organizer, the Turkish humanitarian foundation IHH, has faced international scrutiny over alleged connections to Hamas and Al-Qaeda. Concurrently, the decline in Israeli-Turkish relations has facilitated a rapprochement between Israel and Greece since 1995, marked by a defense cooperation agreement and joint military exercises, such as the 2010 Hellenic Air Force training at Israel’s Uvda base. Israel now ranks as the second-largest Middle Eastern importer of Greek goods. Furthermore, trilateral energy cooperation involving Cyprus, Israel, and Greece—centered on the Leviathan gas field—constitutes a strategic priority for Greece, given its close ties to Cyprus. This partnership is further reinforced by collaborative infrastructure projects like the EuroAsia Interconnector, a sub-sea power cable linking the three nations.

input: The discovery of infrared radiation is ascribed to William Herschel, the astronomer, in the early 19th century. Herschel published his results in 1800 before the Royal Society of London. Herschel used a prism to refract light from the sun and detected the infrared, beyond the red part of the spectrum, through an increase in the temperature recorded on a thermometer. He was surprised at the result and called them "Calorific Rays". The term 'Infrared' did not appear until late in the 19th century.
rewrite: The discovery of infrared radiation is attributed to the astronomer William Herschel in 1800. He presented his findings to the Royal Society of London, detailing an experiment in which sunlight was refracted through a prism. Herschel detected radiation beyond the red end of the visible spectrum by observing a temperature increase on a thermometer. He termed these "Calorific Rays," with the designation 'infrared' not emerging until the late nineteenth century.

input: Until this time the British, at RAF insistence, continued their World War I use of machine guns, and introduced twin MG mountings for AAAD. The army was forbidden from considering anything larger than .50-inch. However, in 1935 their trials showed that the minimum effective round was an impact fused 2 lb HE shell. The following year they decided to adopt the Bofors 40 mm and a twin barrel Vickers 2-pdr (40 mm) on a modified naval mount. The air-cooled Bofors was vastly superior for land use, being much lighter than the water-cooled pom-pom, and UK production of the Bofors 40 mm was licensed. The Predictor AA No 3, as the Kerrison Predictor was officially known, was introduced with it.
rewrite: Prior to this period, British anti-aircraft doctrine, influenced by the Royal Air Force, maintained the use of machine guns from World War I and developed twin machine gun mounts for anti-aircraft artillery defense. The army was restricted from considering armaments exceeding .50-inch caliber. However, 1935 trials concluded that a 2-pound high-explosive shell with an impact fuse represented the minimum effective ordnance. Consequently, the following year saw the decision to adopt the Bofors 40 mm gun and a twin-barrel Vickers 2-pounder (40 mm) on an adapted naval mounting. The air-cooled Bofors was deemed far superior for land deployment due to its significantly lighter weight compared to the water-cooled pom-pom, leading to licensed UK production. The Kerrison Predictor, formally designated the Predictor AA No. 3, was introduced concurrently.

input: The name of the winning team is engraved on the silver band around the base as soon as the final has finished, in order to be ready in time for the presentation ceremony. This means the engraver has just five minutes to perform a task which would take twenty under normal conditions, although time is saved by engraving the year on during the match, and sketching the presumed winner. During the final, the trophy wears is decorated with ribbons in the colours of both finalists, with the loser's ribbons being removed at the end of the game. Traditionally, at Wembley finals, the presentation is made at the Royal Box, with players, led by the captain, mounting a staircase to a gangway in front of the box and returning by a second staircase on the other side of the box. At Cardiff the presentation was made on a podium on the pitch.
rewrite: Immediately following the final match, the name of the victorious team is engraved onto the silver band encircling the trophy's base, ensuring its readiness for the subsequent presentation ceremony. This allows the engraver a mere five minutes to complete a task ordinarily requiring twenty, though time is conserved by pre-engraving the year during the match and sketching the presumed winner's name. Throughout the final, the trophy is adorned with ribbons representing both finalists' colours; those of the runner-up are removed post-match. Traditionally, at Wembley Stadium, the presentation occurs at the Royal Box, where players, led by their captain, ascend one staircase to a gangway before the box and descend via a second on its opposite side. In Cardiff, the ceremony was conducted from a podium situated on the pitch.

input: Football is the most popular national sport of Egypt. The Cairo Derby is one of the fiercest derbies in Africa, and the BBC picked it as one of the 7 toughest derbies in the world. Al Ahly is the most successful club of the 20th century in the African continent according to CAF, closely followed by their rivals Zamalek SC. Al Ahly was named in 2000 by the Confederation of African Football as the "African Club of the Century".
