Alexander Hamilton, writing in "Federalist No. 28," suggested that both levels of government would exercise authority to the citizens' benefit: "If their [the peoples'] rights are invaded by either, they can make use of the other as the instrument of redress." (1)
rewrite: Federalism in the United States constitutes the dynamic constitutional relationship between state and national authorities. The American system has transitioned from a model of dual federalism to one of associative federalism. James Madison, in "Federalist No. 46," described the state and federal governments as "different agents and trustees of the people, constituted with different powers." Similarly, Alexander Hamilton argued in "Federalist No. 28" that the two levels would check one another, noting that if the people's rights were "invaded by either, they can make use of the other as the instrument of redress" (1).

input: Of the approximately 850 municipalities of Thuringia, 126 are classed as towns (within a district) or cities (forming their own urban district). Most of the towns are small with a population of less than 10,000; only the ten biggest ones have a population greater than 30,000. The first towns emerged during the 12th century, whereas the latest ones received town status only in the 20th century. Today, all municipalities within districts are equal in law, whether they are towns or villages. Independent cities (i.e. urban districts) have greater powers (the same as any district) than towns within a district.
rewrite: Thuringia comprises approximately 850 municipalities, of which 126 hold the legal status of either towns (situated within a district) or independent cities (constituting urban districts). The majority of these towns are small, with populations under 10,000; only the ten largest exceed 30,000 inhabitants. The earliest towns originated in the 12th century, while the most recent acquired their status in the 20th. Currently, all municipalities within districts possess equal legal standing, irrespective of being towns or villages. Independent cities, however, exercise greater authority, equivalent to that of an entire district.

input: In 1976 Montini became the first pontiff in modern history to deny the accusation of homosexuality. Published by his order in January 1976 was a homily Persona Humana: Declaration on Certain Questions concerning Sexual Ethics, which outlawed pre or extra-marital sex, condemned homosexuality, and forbade masturbation. It provoked French author and former diplomat Roger Peyrefitte, in an interview published by the magazine Tempo, to accuse Montini of hypocrisy, and of having a longtime lover who was a movie actor. According to rumors prevalent both inside the Curia and in Italian society, this was Paolo Carlini, who had a bit part as a hairdresser in the Audrey Hepburn film Roman Holiday. Peyrefitte had previously published the accusation in two books, but the interview (previously published in a French gay magazine) brought the rumors to a wider public and caused an uproar. In a brief address to a crowd of approximately 20,000 in St. Peters Square on April 18, Montini called the charges "horrible and slanderous insinuations" and appealed for prayers on his behalf. Special prayers for Montini were said in all Italian Roman Catholic churches in "a day of consolation". In 1984 a New York Times correspondent repeated the allegations.
rewrite: In 1976, Pope Paul VI (born Giovanni Battista Montini) became the first modern pontiff to publicly refute allegations of homosexuality. This denial was issued in response to accusations proliferating following the January 1976 publication, under his authority, of the declaration *Persona Humana: Declaration on Certain Questions concerning Sexual Ethics*. This document proscribed all sexual activity outside of marriage, explicitly condemned homosexual acts, and forbade masturbation. The declaration provoked French author and former diplomat Roger Peyrefitte, who in an interview with *Tempo* magazine, accused Montini of hypocrisy and alleged a long-term relationship with a film actor. Peyrefitte identified this individual as Paolo Carlini, an actor with a minor role in *Roman Holiday*, a figure already subject to rumors within both the Curia and Italian society. While Peyrefitte had previously leveled these claims in two books, the magazine interview, having first appeared in a French gay publication, significantly amplified their reach and provoked public controversy. On April 18, addressing a crowd of roughly 20,000 in St. Peter’s Square, Montini denounced the allegations as "horrible and slanderous insinuations" and requested prayers. Subsequently, all Italian Roman Catholic churches observed "a day of consolation," offering special prayers for the pontiff. The allegations resurfaced in 1984, reiterated by a *New York Times* correspondent.

input: In November 2008, 720p HD support was added. At the time of the 720p launch, the YouTube player was changed from a 4:3 aspect ratio to a widescreen 16:9. With this new feature, YouTube began a switchover to H.264/MPEG-4 AVC as its default video compression format. In November 2009, 1080p HD support was added. In July 2010, YouTube announced that it had launched a range of videos in 4K format, which allows a resolution of up to 4096×3072 pixels. In June 2015, support for 8K resolution was added, with the videos playing at 7680×4320 pixels.
rewrite: In November 2008, YouTube introduced 720p high-definition (HD) support, concurrently updating its video player from a 4:3 to a 16:9 widescreen aspect ratio. This period also marked the platform's transition to the H.264/MPEG-4 AVC codec as its default compression standard. Support for 1080p HD followed in November 2009. Subsequently, in July 2010, YouTube announced the launch of 4K format videos, offering resolutions up to 4096×3072 pixels. Finally, 8K resolution support, featuring 7680×4320 pixels, was implemented in June 2015.

input: In the controversial elections in 2002, Sassou won with almost 90% of the vote cast. His two main rivals, Lissouba and Bernard Kolelas, were prevented from competing and the only remaining credible rival, Andre Milongo, advised his supporters to boycott the elections and then withdrew from the race. A new constitution, agreed upon by referendum in January 2002, granted the president new powers, extended his term to seven years, and introduced a new bicameral assembly. International observers took issue with the organization of the presidential election and the constitutional referendum, both of which were reminiscent in their organization of Congo's era of the one-party state. Following the presidential elections, fighting restarted in the Pool region between government forces and rebels led by Pastor Ntumi; a peace treaty to end the conflict was signed in April 2003.
rewrite: In the contentious 2002 elections, Denis Sassou Nguesso secured victory with nearly 90% of the vote. His principal opponents, Pascal Lissouba and Bernard Kolelas, were barred from participation, while the sole remaining credible candidate, André Milongo, urged a boycott before withdrawing. A new constitution, ratified by referendum in January 2002, augmented presidential powers, extended the term to seven years, and established a bicameral legislature. International observers criticized the administration of both the presidential election and the constitutional referendum, noting their resemblance to the procedures of Congo's former single-party era. Subsequent to the election, conflict resumed in the Pool region between governmental forces and rebels under Pastor Ntumi; a peace agreement concluding this conflict was signed in April 2003.

input: Track lighting, invented by Lightolier, was popular at one period of time because it was much easier to install than recessed lighting, and individual fixtures are decorative and can be easily aimed at a wall. It has regained some popularity recently in low-voltage tracks, which often look nothing like their predecessors because they do not have the safety issues that line-voltage systems have, and are therefore less bulky and more ornamental in themselves. A master transformer feeds all of the fixtures on the track or rod with 12 or 24 volts, instead of each light fixture having its own line-to-low voltage transformer. There are traditional spots and floods, as well as other small hanging fixtures. A modified version of this is cable lighting, where lights are hung from or clipped to bare metal cables under tension.
rewrite: Originally developed by Lightolier, track lighting gained initial popularity due to its simpler installation compared to recessed systems, along with the decorative and adjustable nature of its individual fixtures. It has recently experienced a resurgence, particularly in low-voltage configurations. These contemporary systems often bear little resemblance to earlier line-voltage models, as they eliminate associated safety concerns, resulting in less bulky and more inherently ornamental designs. A single master transformer supplies 12 or 24 volts to all fixtures on the track, replacing the need for individual transformers per light. Available fixtures include traditional spots and floods, alongside other suspended units. A related variant is cable lighting, wherein fixtures are suspended from or attached to taut, bare metal cables.

Typically, the lower limit of the saturation speed is determined by the sensor itself, but with the gain of the amplifier between the sensor and the analog-to-digital converter, the saturation speed can be increased. The factor 78 is chosen such that exposure settings based on a standard light meter and an 18-percent reflective surface will result in an image with a grey level of 18%/√2 = 12.7% of saturation. The factor √2 indicates that there is half a stop of headroom to deal with specular reflections that would appear brighter than a 100% reflecting white surface.
rewrite: The maximum permissible exposure is defined as the level at which camera output remains free from clipping or blooming artifacts. While the lower threshold of saturation speed is inherently constrained by the sensor, it can be elevated through amplification gain applied between the sensor and the analog-to-digital converter. The coefficient 78 is selected so that exposure settings derived from a standard light meter and an 18-percent reflective surface yield a grey level equivalent to 12.7% of saturation, calculated as 18%/√2. The inclusion of the √2 factor provides half a stop of headroom to accommodate specular reflections, which may exceed the luminance of a perfectly white, 100% reflective surface.

input: Gorbachev also radically expanded the scope of Glasnost, stating that no subject was off-limits for open discussion in the media. Even so, the cautious Soviet intelligentsia took almost a year to begin pushing the boundaries to see if he meant what he said. For the first time, the Communist Party leader had appealed over the heads of Central Committee members for the people's support in exchange for expansion of liberties. The tactic proved successful: Within two years political reform could no longer be sidetracked by Party "conservatives." An unintended consequence was that having saved reform, Gorbachev's move ultimately killed the very system it was designed to save.
rewrite: Gorbachev significantly extended the parameters of Glasnost, declaring that no topics were prohibited from public media discourse. Nevertheless, the Soviet intelligentsia, initially cautious, required nearly a year to test these proclaimed limits. This marked the first instance wherein a Communist Party leader directly solicited popular support, bypassing the Central Committee, by pledging expanded freedoms. This strategy succeeded; within two years, Party conservatives could no longer obstruct political reform. An unintended outcome, however, was that while salvaging reform, this maneuver ultimately precipitated the collapse of the system it aimed to preserve.

input: Tiberius Gracchus was elected tribune in 133 BC. He attempted to enact a law which would have limited the amount of land that any individual could own. The aristocrats, who stood to lose an enormous amount of money, were bitterly opposed to this proposal. Tiberius submitted this law to the Plebeian Council, but the law was vetoed by a tribune named Marcus Octavius. Tiberius then used the Plebeian Council to impeach Octavius. The theory, that a representative of the people ceases to be one when he acts against the wishes of the people, was counter to Roman constitutional theory. If carried to its logical end, this theory would remove all constitutional restraints on the popular will, and put the state under the absolute control of a temporary popular majority. His law was enacted, but Tiberius was murdered with 300 of his associates when he stood for reelection to the tribunate.
rewrite: In 133 BC, Tiberius Gracchus was elected tribune and proposed an agrarian law to restrict individual landholdings, provoking intense opposition from the senatorial aristocracy, whose substantial economic interests were threatened. When his bill was presented to the Plebeian Council, it was vetoed by the tribune Marcus Octavius. In response, Tiberius orchestrated Octavius’s removal from office through the same council, advancing a radical constitutional principle: that a representative forfeits his mandate by acting contrary to the popular will. This doctrine challenged traditional Roman constitutionalism, as its logical extension would eliminate all institutional checks on majority rule, potentially subjecting the state to the absolute discretion of a transient popular majority. Although his law was ultimately passed, Tiberius and approximately 300 of his followers were killed during his campaign for reelection to the tribunate.

input: The city is also home to two large colleges. The City College Plymouth provides courses from the most basic to Foundation degrees for approximately 26,000 students. Plymouth College of Art offers a selection of courses including media. It was started 153 years ago and is now one of only four independent colleges of art and design in the UK.
rewrite: The city hosts two significant higher education institutions. City College Plymouth delivers a comprehensive curriculum, ranging from foundational to degree-level courses, serving around 26,000 students. Plymouth College of Art, established 153 years ago, provides specialized programs in fields such as media and is one of only four independent art and design colleges in the United Kingdom.

input: Between 1853 and 1870, the Emperor Napoleon III and the city's first director of parks and gardens, Jean-Charles Alphand, created the Bois de Boulogne, the Bois de Vincennes, Parc Montsouris and the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, located at the four points of the compass around the city, as well as many smaller parks, squares and gardens in the Paris' quarters. Since 1977, the city has created 166 new parks, most notably the Parc de la Villette (1987), Parc André Citroën (1992), and Parc de Bercy (1997). One of the newest parks, the Promenade des Berges de la Seine (2013), built on a former highway on the Left Bank of the Seine between the Pont de l'Alma and the Musée d'Orsay, has floating gardens and gives a view of the city's landmarks.
rewrite: Between 1853 and 1870, under the direction of Emperor Napoleon III and the chief administrator of parks and gardens, Jean-Charles Alphand, a comprehensive system of green spaces was established in Paris. This included the major parks of the Bois de Boulogne, Bois de Vincennes, Parc Montsouris, and Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, situated at the cardinal points of the city, alongside numerous smaller parks and squares within its arrondissements. Subsequent municipal efforts since 1977 have added 166 new parks, including significant projects such as the Parc de la Villette (1987) and the Parc André Citroën (1992). A recent addition, the Promenade des Berges de la Seine (2013), created on a repurposed Left Bank expressway, features floating gardens and provides notable vistas of urban landmarks.

input: PlayStation Network is the unified online multiplayer gaming and digital media delivery service provided by Sony Computer Entertainment for PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable, announced during the 2006 PlayStation Business Briefing meeting in Tokyo. The service is always connected, free, and includes multiplayer support. The network enables online gaming, the PlayStation Store, PlayStation Home and other services. PlayStation Network uses real currency and PlayStation Network Cards as seen with the PlayStation Store and PlayStation Home.
rewrite: The PlayStation Network, introduced by Sony Computer Entertainment at the 2006 PlayStation Business Briefing in Tokyo, is a unified, always-connected online service for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable. This complimentary platform facilitates multiplayer gaming, digital media delivery, and integrated services such as the PlayStation Store and PlayStation Home. Transactions are conducted using real currency or dedicated PlayStation Network Cards.

input: The Community Tool Box is a public service of the University maintained by the Work Group for Community Health and Development. It is a free, online resource that contains more than 7,000 pages of practical information for promoting community health and development, and is a global resource for both professionals and grassroots groups engaged in the work of community health and development.
rewrite: The Community Tool Box, a public service of the University maintained by the Work Group for Community Health and Development, is a free online resource. Its over 7,000 pages provide practical information for promoting community health and development, serving as a global resource for professionals and grassroots groups alike.

input: According to the writer of Luke, Mary was a relative of Elizabeth, wife of the priest Zechariah of the priestly division of Abijah, who was herself part of the lineage of Aaron and so of the tribe of Levi.[Luke 1:5;1:36] Some of those who consider that the relationship with Elizabeth was on the maternal side, consider that Mary, like Joseph, to whom she was betrothed, was of the House of David and so of the Tribe of Judah, and that the genealogy of Jesus presented in Luke 3 from Nathan, third son of David and Bathsheba, is in fact the genealogy of Mary,[need quotation to verify] while the genealogy from Solomon given in Matthew 1 is that of Joseph. (Aaron's wife Elisheba was of the tribe of Judah, so all their descendants are from both Levi and Judah.)[Num.1:7 & Ex.6:23]
rewrite: The Gospel of Luke identifies Mary as a kinswoman of Elizabeth, who was married to Zechariah, a priest of the division of Abijah and a descendant of Aaron from the tribe of Levi (Luke 1:5, 1:36). Scholars who interpret this kinship as matrilineal propose that Mary, like her betrothed Joseph, belonged to the House of David and the tribe of Judah. Consequently, they argue that the Lukan genealogy tracing descent from Nathan, son of David and Bathsheba (Luke 3), may reflect Mary’s lineage, whereas the Matthean genealogy through Solomon (Matthew 1) pertains to Joseph’s. This view is sometimes supported by noting that Aaron’s wife Elisheba was of Judah, thereby uniting both tribal lines in their descendants (Numbers 1:7; Exodus 6:23).

input: Each year, nearly $200 million in hunters' federal excise taxes are distributed to state agencies to support wildlife management programs, the purchase of lands open to hunters, and hunter education and safety classes. Since 1934, the sale of Federal Duck Stamps, a required purchase for migratory waterfowl hunters over sixteen years old, has raised over $700 million to help purchase more than 5,200,000 acres (8,100 sq mi; 21,000 km2) of habitat for the National Wildlife Refuge System lands that support waterfowl and many other wildlife species and are often open to hunting. States also collect money from hunting licenses to assist with management of game animals, as designated by law. A key task of federal and state park rangers and game wardens is to enforce laws and regulations related to hunting, including species protection, hunting seasons, and hunting bans.
rewrite: Annually, approximately $200 million in federal excise taxes paid by hunters is allocated to state agencies. These funds finance wildlife management initiatives, the acquisition of public hunting lands, and educational programs focused on hunter safety. Concurrently, since 1934, revenue from Federal Duck Stamps—mandatory for migratory waterfowl hunters aged sixteen and above—has exceeded $700 million. This revenue has facilitated the acquisition of over 5.2 million acres of habitat for the National Wildlife Refuge System, which sustains waterfowl and numerous other species and frequently permits hunting. Further financial support is derived from state-collected hunting license fees, legally designated for game species management. Enforcement of hunting regulations, encompassing species protections, seasonal restrictions, and prohibited areas, constitutes a primary duty for federal and state park rangers and game wardens.

input: Morning (2008) looked at high school biology textbooks during the 1952-2002 period and initially found a similar pattern with only 35% directly discussing race in the 1983–92 period from initially 92% doing so. However, this has increased somewhat after this to 43%. More indirect and brief discussions of race in the context of medical disorders have increased from none to 93% of textbooks. In general, the material on race has moved from surface traits to genetics and evolutionary history. The study argues that the textbooks' fundamental message about the existence of races has changed little.
rewrite: Morning's (2008) analysis of high school biology textbooks from 1952 to 2002 reveals a shift in the presentation of race. While explicit discussion declined from 92% to 35% by 1983–1992, it later rose to 43%. Concurrently, indirect references to race within medical contexts surged from 0% to 93%. The content evolved from emphasizing superficial traits to incorporating genetics and evolutionary history. Nonetheless, the study concludes that the core textbook message affirming the biological existence of races remained largely unchanged.

input: FDR's New Deal programs often contained equal opportunity clauses stating "no discrimination shall be made on account of race, color or creed",:11 but the true forerunner to affirmative action was the Interior Secretary of the time, Harold L. Ickes. Ickes prohibited discrimination in hiring for Public Works Administration funded projects and oversaw not only the institution of a quota system, where contractors were required to employ a fixed percentage of Black workers, by Robert C. Weaver and Clark Foreman,:12 but also the equal pay of women proposed by Harry Hopkins.:14FDR's largest contribution to affirmative action, however, lay in his Executive Order 8802 which prohibited discrimination in the defense industry or government.:22 The executive order promoted the idea that if taxpayer funds were accepted through a government contract, then all taxpayers should have an equal opportunity to work through the contractor.:23–4 To enforce this idea, Roosevelt created the Fair Employment Practices Committee (FEPC) with the power to investigate hiring practices by government contractors.:22
rewrite: The New Deal initiatives of Franklin D. Roosevelt frequently incorporated clauses mandating equal opportunity, explicitly prohibiting discrimination based on race, color, or creed. However, the substantive precursor to modern affirmative action policy is more accurately identified as Interior Secretary Harold L. Ickes. Ickes enforced non-discrimination in hiring for Public Works Administration projects and supervised the implementation of a racial quota system, designed by Robert C. Weaver and Clark Foreman, which obligated contractors to hire a specified proportion of Black workers. He also oversaw policies ensuring equal pay for women, as advocated by Harry Hopkins. Roosevelt's most significant direct contribution was Executive Order 8802, which banned discrimination in the defense industry and federal employment. This order advanced the principle that entities accepting public funds through government contracts must provide equitable employment access to all taxpayers. To administer this policy, Roosevelt established the Fair Employment Practices Committee, vested with authority to investigate the hiring practices of government contractors.

input: In 1579 the northern seven provinces signed the Union of Utrecht, in which they decided to join forces against Spanish rule. The Union of Utrecht is seen as the beginning of the Dutch Republic. In 1580 the new and predominantly Protestant state abolished the bishoprics, including the archbishopric of Utrecht. The stadtholders disapproved of the independent course of the Utrecht bourgeoisie and brought the city under much more direct control of the republic; which shifted the power towards its dominant province Holland. This was the start of a long period of stagnation of trade and development in Utrecht. Utrecht remained an atypical city in the new republic with about 40% Catholic in the mid-17th century, and even more among the elite groups, who included many rural nobility and gentry with town houses there.
rewrite: The Union of Utrecht, signed in 1579 by the seven northern provinces, established a military alliance against Spanish Habsburg authority and is widely regarded as the foundational act of the Dutch Republic. The following year, this newly formed, predominantly Protestant state dissolved the existing bishoprics, including the Archbishopric of Utrecht. Subsequently, the republic's stadtholders, disapproving of the independent policies of Utrecht's burghers, imposed much more direct control from The Hague. This shift consolidated power within the dominant province of Holland and initiated a prolonged economic and developmental stagnation in Utrecht. Throughout the seventeenth century, Utrecht remained an anomaly within the republic, with a substantial Catholic minority—approximately forty percent of the population—and an elite class, including many rural nobles maintaining townhouses, that was even more predominantly Catholic.

input: Genetic engineering is the modification of an organism's genome through biotechnology. Since the 1970s, a variety of techniques have been developed to specifically add, remove and edit genes in an organism. Recently developed genome engineering techniques use engineered nuclease enzymes to create targeted DNA repair in a chromosome to either disrupt or edit a gene when the break is repaired. The related term synthetic biology is sometimes used to refer to extensive genetic engineering of an organism.
rewrite: Genetic engineering involves the deliberate modification of an organism's genome using biotechnological methods. Since the 1970s, numerous techniques have been developed to precisely insert, delete, or alter genetic material. Contemporary genome engineering often employs engineered nucleases to induce targeted DNA breaks, facilitating specific gene disruption or editing during cellular repair processes. The broader field of synthetic biology may encompass extensive organismal redesign through such genetic manipulation.

input: Orthodox Judaism considers views on the part of Jews who depart from traditional Jewish principles of faith heretical. In addition, the more right-wing groups within Orthodox Judaism hold that all Jews who reject the simple meaning of Maimonides's 13 principles of Jewish faith are heretics. As such, most of Orthodox Judaism considers Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism heretical movements, and regards most of Conservative Judaism as heretical. The liberal wing of Modern Orthodoxy is more tolerant of Conservative Judaism, particularly its right wing, as there is some theological and practical overlap between these groups.
rewrite: Orthodox Judaism deems theological positions diverging from traditional Jewish tenets heretical. Its more conservative factions specifically classify as heretics any Jews who reject the plain interpretation of Maimonides’s thirteen principles of faith. Consequently, most Orthodox authorities view Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism as heretical movements and regard much of Conservative Judaism similarly. However, the liberal wing of Modern Orthodoxy exhibits greater tolerance toward Conservative Judaism, especially its traditionalist sector, due to appreciable theological and practical commonalities.

input: However, the NSA's report was completely disproved by Croatian experts. The report failed to recognize that Tito was a native speaker of the very distinctive local Kajkavian dialect of Zagorje. The acute accent, present only in Croatian dialects, which Tito is perfectly pronouncing, is the strongest proof of Tito's belonging to Kajkavian dialect.
rewrite: Croatian experts have refuted the NSA's report, noting its failure to acknowledge that Tito was a native speaker of the distinct Kajkavian dialect of Zagorje. His precise pronunciation of the acute accent, unique to Croatian dialects, constitutes definitive proof of his linguistic origin.

input: One of the most significant impacts To Kill a Mockingbird has had is Atticus Finch's model of integrity for the legal profession. As scholar Alice Petry explains, "Atticus has become something of a folk hero in legal circles and is treated almost as if he were an actual person." Morris Dees of the Southern Poverty Law Center cites Atticus Finch as the reason he became a lawyer, and Richard Matsch, the federal judge who presided over the Timothy McVeigh trial, counts Atticus as a major judicial influence. One law professor at the University of Notre Dame stated that the most influential textbook he taught from was To Kill a Mockingbird, and an article in the Michigan Law Review claims, "No real-life lawyer has done more for the self-image or public perception of the legal profession," before questioning whether, "Atticus Finch is a paragon of honor or an especially slick hired gun".
rewrite: A principal legacy of Harper Lee’s *To Kill a Mockingbird* lies in its provision of a model of integrity for the legal profession through the character of Atticus Finch. As scholar Alice Petry observes, “Atticus has become something of a folk hero in legal circles and is treated almost as if he were an actual person.” This influence is evidenced in practice: Morris Dees, founder of the Southern Poverty Law Center, credits Finch as his inspiration to practice law, while federal judge Richard Matsch, who presided over the Timothy McVeigh trial, cites him as a major judicial influence. Notably, a University of Notre Dame law professor identified the novel as his most influential textbook. An article in the Michigan Law Review contends that “no real-life lawyer has done more for the self-image or public perception of the legal profession,” yet simultaneously probes whether Atticus Finch constitutes “a paragon of honor or an especially slick hired gun.”

input: Roughly one quarter of all zinc output in the United States (2009), is consumed in the form of zinc compounds; a variety of which are used industrially. Zinc oxide is widely used as a white pigment in paints, and as a catalyst in the manufacture of rubber. It is also used as a heat disperser for the rubber and acts to protect its polymers from ultraviolet radiation (the same UV protection is conferred to plastics containing zinc oxide). The semiconductor properties of zinc oxide make it useful in varistors and photocopying products. The zinc zinc-oxide cycle is a two step thermochemical process based on zinc and zinc oxide for hydrogen production.
rewrite: In 2009, approximately one quarter of total zinc production in the United States was utilized in the form of zinc compounds, which serve diverse industrial functions. Zinc oxide, for instance, is extensively employed as a white pigment in paints and as a catalyst in rubber manufacturing. It further acts as a heat dispersant in rubber and provides ultraviolet radiation protection for polymeric materials, a function it also performs in plastics. Due to its semiconductor properties, zinc oxide is valuable in varistors and photocopying products. Additionally, the zinc zinc-oxide cycle represents a two-step thermochemical process for generating hydrogen.

input: Between the 8th and 18th centuries, the use of glazed ceramics was prevalent in Islamic art, usually assuming the form of elaborate pottery. Tin-opacified glazing was one of the earliest new technologies developed by the Islamic potters. The first Islamic opaque glazes can be found as blue-painted ware in Basra, dating to around the 8th century. Another contribution was the development of stone-paste ceramics, originating from 9th century Iraq. Other centers for innovative ceramic pottery in the Old world included Fustat (from 975 to 1075), Damascus (from 1100 to around 1600) and Tabriz (from 1470 to 1550).
rewrite: From the eighth to the eighteenth century, glazed ceramics constituted a prominent medium within Islamic art, predominantly manifesting as intricately crafted pottery. Islamic artisans pioneered several technical innovations, including the early adoption of tin-opacified glazes. The earliest instances of these opaque glazes appear on eighth-century blue-painted ware from Basra. A further significant contribution was the invention of stone-paste ceramics, which emerged in ninth-century Iraq. Major centers of ceramic production and innovation included Fustat (c. 975–1075), Damascus (c. 1100–1600), and Tabriz (c. 1470–1550).

input: Paris today has more than 421 municipal parks and gardens, covering more than 3,000 hectares and containing more than 250,000 trees. Two of Paris' oldest and most famous gardens are the Tuileries Garden, created in 1564 for the Tuileries Palace, and redone by André Le Nôtre between 1664 and 1672, and the Luxembourg Garden, for the Luxembourg Palace, built for Marie de' Medici in 1612, which today houses the French Senate. The Jardin des Plantes was the first botanical garden in Paris, created in 1626 by Louis XIII's doctor Guy de La Brosse for the cultivation of medicinal plants.
rewrite: The contemporary city of Paris encompasses over 421 municipal parks and gardens, spanning more than 3,000 hectares and containing in excess of 250,000 trees. Among its most historic and notable green spaces are the Tuileries Garden, originally established in 1564 and later redesigned by André Le Nôtre from 1664 to 1672, and the Luxembourg Garden, created alongside its palace for Marie de' Medici in 1612, which now serves as the seat of the French Senate. The Jardin des Plantes, founded in 1626 by royal physician Guy de La Brosse for medicinal plant cultivation, constitutes Paris's inaugural botanical garden.

input: Saxophones appear in some scores from the late 19th century onwards. While appearing only as featured solo instruments in some works, for example Maurice Ravel's orchestration of Modest Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition and Sergei Rachmaninoff's Symphonic Dances, the saxophone is included in other works, such as Ravel's Boléro, Sergei Prokofiev's Romeo and Juliet Suites 1 and 2 and many other works as a member of the orchestral ensemble. The euphonium is featured in a few late Romantic and 20th-century works, usually playing parts marked "tenor tuba", including Gustav Holst's The Planets, and Richard Strauss's Ein Heldenleben.
rewrite: The saxophone has been incorporated into orchestral compositions since the late nineteenth century. It appears as a featured solo instrument in works such as Maurice Ravel’s orchestration of *Pictures at an Exhibition* and Sergei Rachmaninoff’s *Symphonic Dances*. In other compositions, including Ravel’s *Boléro* and Sergei Prokofiev’s *Romeo and Juliet* Suites, it functions as an integrated member of the ensemble. Similarly, the euphonium, often designated as "tenor tuba," is featured in select late-Romantic and twentieth-century works, including Gustav Holst’s *The Planets* and Richard Strauss’s *Ein Heldenleben*.

input: The record transfer fee for a Premier League player has risen steadily over the lifetime of the competition. Prior to the start of the first Premier League season Alan Shearer became the first British player to command a transfer fee of more than £3 million. The record rose steadily in the Premier League's first few seasons, until Alan Shearer made a record breaking £15 million move to Newcastle United in 1996. The three highest transfer in the sport's history had a Premier League club on the selling end, with Tottenham Hotspur selling Gareth Bale to Real Madrid for £85 million in 2013, Manchester United's sale of Cristiano Ronaldo to Real Madrid for £80 million in 2009, and Liverpool selling Luis Suárez to Barcelona for £75 million in 2014.
rewrite: The record transfer fee for a Premier League player has demonstrated a consistent upward trajectory throughout the competition's history. Prior to its inaugural season, Alan Shearer became the first British player to command a fee exceeding £3 million. This record increased incrementally in the league's early years, culminating in Shearer's own landmark £15 million transfer to Newcastle United in 1996. Notably, the three highest fees in football history all involved Premier League clubs as sellers: Tottenham Hotspur's £85 million sale of Gareth Bale to Real Madrid (2013), Manchester United's £80 million sale of Cristiano Ronaldo to Real Madrid (2009), and Liverpool's £75 million sale of Luis Suárez to Barcelona (2014).

input: On 15 December 1944 landings against minimal resistance were made on the southern beaches of the island of Mindoro, a key location in the planned Lingayen Gulf operations, in support of major landings scheduled on Luzon. On 9 January 1945, on the south shore of Lingayen Gulf on the western coast of Luzon, General Krueger's Sixth Army landed his first units. Almost 175,000 men followed across the twenty-mile (32 km) beachhead within a few days. With heavy air support, Army units pushed inland, taking Clark Field, 40 miles (64 km) northwest of Manila, in the last week of January.
rewrite: On 15 December 1944, amphibious forces conducted unopposed landings on the southern coast of Mindoro, securing a strategic position for the forthcoming Lingayen Gulf campaign in support of the main Luzon invasion. The Sixth Army, under General Krueger, initiated its assault on the south shore of Lingayen Gulf on 9 January 1945. Approximately 175,000 troops were deployed across the twenty-mile (32 km) beachhead within several days. Supported by substantial air power, these units advanced inland, capturing Clark Field—located 40 miles (64 km) northwest of Manila—by the final week of January.

input: In the later Imperial era, the burial and commemorative practises of Christian and non-Christians overlapped. Tombs were shared by Christian and non-Christian family members, and the traditional funeral rites and feast of novemdialis found a part-match in the Christian Constitutio Apostolica. The customary offers of wine and food to the dead continued; St Augustine (following St Ambrose) feared that this invited the "drunken" practices of Parentalia but commended funeral feasts as a Christian opportunity to give alms of food to the poor. Christians attended Parentalia and its accompanying Feralia and Caristia in sufficient numbers for the Council of Tours to forbid them in AD 567. Other funerary and commemorative practices were very different. Traditional Roman practice spurned the corpse as a ritual pollution; inscriptions noted the day of birth and duration of life. The Christian Church fostered the veneration of saintly relics, and inscriptions marked the day of death as a transition to "new life".
rewrite: During the later Imperial period, burial and commemorative practices exhibited significant overlap between Christian and non-Christian populations. Shared familial tombs containing both Christian and non-Christian members were common, and traditional Roman rites, such as the novemdialis feast, found parallels within Christian texts like the Constitutio Apostolica. Customary offerings of food and wine to the deceased persisted; although Saint Augustine, influenced by Saint Ambrose, warned that such practices risked echoing the "drunken" excesses of the Parentalia, he endorsed funeral feasts as a Christian act of providing alms to the poor. Christian participation in the traditional festivals of Parentalia, Feralia, and Caristia remained widespread, prompting their formal prohibition by the Council of Tours in AD 567. Nevertheless, key divergences persisted. Traditional Roman custom treated the corpse as a source of ritual pollution, with inscriptions typically recording the date of birth and length of life. In contrast, the Christian Church promoted the veneration of saintly relics, and epitaphs commemorated the date of death as a passage into eternal life.

input: When infection attacks the body, anti-infective drugs can suppress the infection. Several broad types of anti-infective drugs exist, depending on the type of organism targeted; they include antibacterial (antibiotic; including antitubercular), antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic (including antiprotozoal and antihelminthic) agents. Depending on the severity and the type of infection, the antibiotic may be given by mouth or by injection, or may be applied topically. Severe infections of the brain are usually treated with intravenous antibiotics. Sometimes, multiple antibiotics are used in case there is resistance to one antibiotic. Antibiotics only work for bacteria and do not affect viruses. Antibiotics work by slowing down the multiplication of bacteria or killing the bacteria. The most common classes of antibiotics used in medicine include penicillin, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, macrolides, quinolones and tetracyclines.[citation needed]
rewrite: Anti-infective agents are employed to suppress pathogenic invasions within the host organism. These therapeutics are categorized according to the target pathogen, encompassing antibacterial (including antitubercular), antiviral, antifungal, and antiparasitic (such as antiprotozoal and antihelminthic) classes. Administration routes—oral, injectable, or topical—are determined by infection severity and type, with severe cerebral infections typically necessitating intravenous delivery. To counter bacterial resistance, combination therapy utilizing multiple agents may be implemented. It is critical to note that antibiotics are exclusively effective against bacterial pathogens, exerting no influence on viral infections. Their mechanisms involve either inhibiting bacterial proliferation or causing bacterial cell death. Prominent antibiotic classes in clinical use comprise penicillins, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, macrolides, quinolones, and tetracyclines.

input: Tito's greatest strength, in the eyes of the western communists, had been in suppressing nationalist insurrections and maintaining unity throughout the country. It was Tito's call for unity, and related methods, that held together the people of Yugoslavia. This ability was put to a test several times during his reign, notably during the Croatian Spring (also referred as the Masovni pokret, maspok, meaning "Mass Movement") when the government suppressed both public demonstrations and dissenting opinions within the Communist Party. Despite this suppression, much of maspok's demands were later realized with the new constitution, heavily backed by Tito himself against opposition from the Serbian branch of the party.[citation needed] On 16 May 1974, the new Constitution was passed, and the aging Tito was named president for life, a status which he would enjoy for five years.
rewrite: From the perspective of Western communist observers, Tito's paramount strength lay in his capacity to quell nationalist insurrections and preserve the unity of the Yugoslav state. His consistent appeals for cohesion, and the attendant methods employed, were instrumental in binding the federation's diverse populations. This unifying capability faced significant challenges, most notably during the Croatian Spring of the early 1970s—a period also termed the *Masovni pokret* (maspok)—wherein authorities suppressed public demonstrations and intraparty dissent. Nevertheless, a substantial portion of the movement's demands were subsequently incorporated into the new constitution, which Tito personally championed against resistance from the Serbian party leadership. Ratified on 16 May 1974, this constitution conferred upon the aging leader the title of president for life, a position he held until his death.

input: The Great Plains is the broad expanse of flat land (a plain), much of it covered in prairie, steppe and grassland, that lies west of the Mississippi River tallgrass prairie states and east of the Rocky Mountains in the United States and Canada. This area covers parts, but not all, of the states of Colorado, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, and the Canadian provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The region is known for supporting extensive cattle ranching and dry farming.
rewrite: The Great Plains constitute a vast, predominantly level terrain characterized by prairie, steppe, and grassland. This region extends westward from the Mississippi River's tallgrass prairie and eastward from the Rocky Mountains, spanning portions of the central United States and Canada. It encompasses sections of ten U.S. states and three Canadian provinces. The Plains are notably defined by their agricultural economy, which is historically centered on extensive cattle ranching and dry farming practices.

input: Many of the crucial events of the American Revolution—the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, Paul Revere's midnight ride, the battles of Lexington and Concord and Bunker Hill, the Siege of Boston, and many others—occurred in or near Boston. After the Revolution, Boston's long seafaring tradition helped make it one of the world's wealthiest international ports, with rum, fish, salt, and tobacco being particularly important.
rewrite: Numerous pivotal events of the American Revolution transpired in the vicinity of Boston, including the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, Paul Revere's ride, and the early battles. Subsequently, the city's maritime heritage facilitated its rise as a preeminent global port, with significant trade in rum, fish, salt, and tobacco underpinning its considerable wealth.

input: "Baseball's Sad Lexicon," also known as "Tinker to Evers to Chance" after its refrain, is a 1910 baseball poem by Franklin Pierce Adams. The poem is presented as a single, rueful stanza from the point of view of a New York Giants fan seeing the talented Chicago Cubs infield of shortstop Joe Tinker, second baseman Johnny Evers, and first baseman Frank Chance complete a double play. The trio began playing together with the Cubs in 1902, and formed a double play combination that lasted through April 1912. The Cubs won the pennant four times between 1906 and 1910, often defeating the Giants en route to the World Series.
rewrite: Franklin Pierce Adams’ 1910 poem, "Baseball's Sad Lexicon," commonly referenced by its refrain "Tinker to Evers to Chance," presents a single lamenting stanza. The speaker is a New York Giants fan witnessing the deft double plays executed by the Chicago Cubs' celebrated infield: shortstop Joe Tinker, second baseman Johnny Evers, and first baseman Frank Chance. This trio, whose collaborative play commenced in 1902 and endured until April 1912, was integral to the Cubs' success. The team secured four National League pennants from 1906 to 1910, frequently overcoming the Giants during those championship seasons.

input: Orontid Armenia formally passed to empire of Alexander the Great following his conquest of Persia. Alexander appointed an Orontid named Mithranes to govern Armenia. Armenia later became a vassal state of the Seleucid Empire, but it maintained a considerable degree of autonomy, retaining its native rulers. Towards the end 212 BC the country was divided into two kingdoms, Greater Armenia and Armenia Sophene including Commagene or Armenia Minor. The kingdoms became so independent from Seleucid control that Antiochus III the Great waged war on them during his reign and replaced their rulers.
rewrite: Following its conquest of Persia, the Orontid dynasty of Armenia was formally incorporated into the empire of Alexander the Great, who appointed the Orontid satrap Mithranes as governor. Subsequently a vassal of the Seleucid Empire, Armenia retained significant autonomy under its native rulers. Around 212 BC, the region divided into the kingdoms of Greater Armenia and Sophene (encompassing Commagene, or Lesser Armenia). Their growing independence prompted Seleucid King Antiochus III the Great to launch a military campaign, through which he deposed and replaced their sovereigns.

input: Chopin made his last public appearance on a concert platform at London's Guildhall on 16 November 1848, when, in a final patriotic gesture, he played for the benefit of Polish refugees. By this time he was very seriously ill, weighing under 99 pounds (i.e. less than 45 kg), and his doctors were aware that his sickness was at a terminal stage.
rewrite: Frédéric Chopin's final public performance occurred on 16 November 1848 at London's Guildhall, where he played to support Polish refugees as a last patriotic act. By then, he was gravely ill, weighing less than 45 kilograms, and his physicians recognized his condition as terminal.

input: The first attempts to use standard-frequency single-phase AC were made in Hungary as far back as 1923, by the Hungarian Kálmán Kandó on the line between Budapest-Nyugati and Alag, using 16 kV at 50 Hz. The locomotives carried a four-pole rotating phase converter feeding a single traction motor of the polyphase induction type at 600 to 1,100 V. The number of poles on the 2,500 hp motor could be changed using slip rings to run at one of four synchronous speeds. The tests were a success so, from 1932 until the 1960s, trains on the Budapest-Hegyeshalom line (towards Vienna) regularly used the same system. A few decades after the Second World War, the 16 kV was changed to the Russian and later French 25 kV system.
rewrite: Initial efforts to implement standard-frequency single-phase alternating current for railway electrification occurred in Hungary in 1923. Engineer Kálmán Kandó conducted trials on the Budapest-Nyugati to Alag route, employing a 16 kV, 50 Hz supply. The locomotives featured a four-pole rotary phase converter, which powered a single polyphase induction traction motor operating between 600 and 1,100 V. This 2,500 hp motor utilized slip rings to alter its pole count, enabling operation at one of four synchronous speeds. Following these successful tests, the system was adopted for regular service on the Budapest-Hegyeshalom line (toward Vienna) from 1932 through the 1960s. Decades after the Second World War, the original 16 kV standard was superseded by the 25 kV system, initially Russian and later French in origin.

input: The southern group (South Estonian language) consists of the Tartu, Mulgi, Võru (Võro) and Setu (Seto) dialects. These are sometimes considered either variants of a South Estonian language, or separate languages altogether. Also, Seto and Võro distinguish themselves from each other less by language and more by their culture and their respective Christian confession.

Setu and Võru are differentiated primarily by cultural and religious distinctions rather than linguistic features.

input: The desire to explore, record and systematize knowledge had a meaningful impact on music publications. Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Dictionnaire de musique (published 1767 in Geneva and 1768 in Paris) was a leading text in the late 18th century. This widely available dictionary gave short definitions of words like genius and taste, and was clearly influenced by the Enlightenment movement. Another text influenced by Enlightenment values was Charles Burney's A General History of Music: From the Earliest Ages to the Present Period (1776), which was a historical survey and an attempt to rationalize elements in music systematically over time. Recently, musicologists have shown renewed interest in the ideas and consequences of the Enlightenment. For example, Rose Rosengard Subotnik's Deconstructive Variations (subtitled Music and Reason in Western Society) compares Mozart's Die Zauberflöte (1791) using the Enlightenment and Romantic perspectives, and concludes that the work is "an ideal musical representation of the Enlightenment".
rewrite: The impetus to explore, document, and systematize knowledge significantly influenced musical scholarship in the eighteenth century. A seminal publication of this era was Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s *Dictionnaire de musique* (Geneva 1767, Paris 1768), a widely circulated reference work providing concise entries for terms such as "genius" and "taste," reflecting distinct Enlightenment ideologies. Similarly informed by Enlightenment principles, Charles Burney’s *A General History of Music: From the Earliest Ages to the Present Period* (1776) constitutes both a historical survey and a systematic effort to rationalize musical elements across time. Contemporary musicology demonstrates a revived engagement with Enlightenment thought and its ramifications. For instance, in *Deconstructive Variations: Music and Reason in Western Society*, Rose Rosengard Subotnik analyzes Mozart’s *Die Zauberflöte* (1791) through both Enlightenment and Romantic frameworks, ultimately positing the opera as an ideal musical embodiment of the Enlightenment.

input: In Islam, dogs are viewed as unclean because they are viewed as scavengers. In 2015 city councillor Hasan Küçük of The Hague called for dog ownership to be made illegal in that city. Islamic activists in Lérida, Spain, lobbied for dogs to be kept out of Muslim neighborhoods, saying their presence violated Muslims' religious freedom. In Britain, police sniffer dogs are carefully used, and are not permitted to contact passengers, only their luggage. They are required to wear leather dog booties when searching mosques or Muslim homes.
rewrite: Within Islamic jurisprudence, dogs are frequently deemed ritually impure due to their historical association with scavenging. This perspective has prompted various public initiatives, such as a 2015 proposal by The Hague councillor Hasan Küçük to prohibit dog ownership. Similarly, activists in Lérida, Spain, have argued that dogs in Muslim areas infringe upon religious freedom. Reflecting such sensitivities, British police deploy sniffer dogs with specific protocols, including preventing direct contact with individuals and equipping them with protective booties during searches of mosques or Muslim residences.

input: The Acta Constitutiva de la Federación of January 31, 1824, and the Federal Constitution of October 4, 1824, fixed the political and administrative organization of the United Mexican States after the Mexican War of Independence. In addition, Section XXVIII of Article 50 gave the new Congress the right to choose where the federal government would be located. This location would then be appropriated as federal land, with the federal government acting as the local authority. The two main candidates to become the capital were Mexico City and Querétaro.
rewrite: The Acta Constitutiva de la Federación of January 31, 1824, and the subsequent Federal Constitution of October 4, 1824, established the political and administrative framework for the United Mexican States following independence. Under Article 50, Section XXVIII, the newly formed Congress was granted the authority to designate a permanent seat for the federal government. This designated territory would be appropriated as federal land and administered directly by federal authorities. The primary candidates for this capital were Mexico City and Querétaro.

input: During the late 1980s and early 1990s, Richmond experienced a spike in overall crime, in particular, the city's murder rate. The city had 93 murders for the year of 1985, with a murder rate of 41.9 killings committed per 100,000 residents. Over the next decade, the city saw a major increase in total homicides. In 1990 there were 114 murders, for a murder rate of 56.1 killings per 100,000 residents. There were 120 murders in 1995, resulting in a murder rate of 59.1 killings per 100,000 residents, one of the highest in the United States.
rewrite: From the late 1980s through the early 1990s, Richmond witnessed a significant surge in overall criminal activity, most notably in its homicide rate. In 1985, the city recorded 93 murders, corresponding to a rate of 41.9 per 100,000 residents. This figure rose substantially over the subsequent decade. By 1990, homicides increased to 114, with a rate of 56.1 per 100,000. The peak occurred in 1995, with 120 murders and a rate of 59.1 per 100,000, ranking among the highest nationally.

input: After the first two months of the conflict, South Korean forces were on the point of defeat, forced back to the Pusan Perimeter. In September 1950, an amphibious UN counter-offensive was launched at Inchon, and cut off many of the North Korean attackers. Those that escaped envelopment and capture were rapidly forced back north all the way to the border with China at the Yalu River, or into the mountainous interior. At this point, in October 1950, Chinese forces crossed the Yalu and entered the war. Chinese intervention triggered a retreat of UN forces which continued until mid-1951. After these dramatic reversals of fortune, which saw Seoul change hands four times, the last two years of conflict became a war of attrition, with the front line close to the 38th parallel. The war in the air, however, was never a stalemate. North Korea was subject to a massive bombing campaign. Jet fighters confronted each other in air-to-air combat for the first time in history, and Soviet pilots covertly flew in defense of their Communist allies.
rewrite: Following the initial two months of hostilities, Republic of Korea and allied forces faced imminent defeat, having been pushed back to a defensive position known as the Pusan Perimeter. A decisive United Nations counter-offensive was subsequently initiated in September 1950 with an amphibious landing at Inchon, severing the lines of numerous North Korean units. Those forces that avoided encirclement were compelled into a rapid northward retreat, reaching the Yalu River border with China or dispersing into the mountainous interior. In October 1950, the conflict escalated significantly when Chinese military units crossed the Yalu River to intervene. This action precipitated a sustained withdrawal of UN forces, which persisted until approximately mid-1951. After these profound shifts in momentum, which included the capture and recapture of Seoul on four occasions, the subsequent two years devolved into a static war of attrition, with the stabilized front proximate to the 38th parallel. Conversely, aerial operations never reached a stalemate. United Nations air forces conducted an extensive strategic bombing campaign against North Korea. Furthermore, the conflict witnessed the first historical instances of jet fighter engagements, while Soviet pilots covertly operated in defense of communist assets.

input: Boston's park system is well-reputed nationally. In its 2013 ParkScore ranking, The Trust for Public Land reported that Boston was tied with Sacramento and San Francisco for having the third-best park system among the 50 most populous US cities. ParkScore ranks city park systems by a formula that analyzes the city's median park size, park acres as percent of city area, the percent of residents within a half-mile of a park, spending of park services per resident, and the number of playgrounds per 10,000 residents.
rewrite: Boston’s park system holds national distinction. According to the 2013 ParkScore ranking by The Trust for Public Land, Boston tied with Sacramento and San Francisco for the third-highest rated park system among the fifty most populous U.S. cities. The ParkScore methodology evaluates systems based on median park size, park acreage as a percentage of city area, the proportion of residents within a half-mile of a park, per capita park spending, and playgrounds per 10,000 residents.

input: Music, photos and videos can be played from standard USB mass storage devices, Xbox 360 proprietary storage devices (such as memory cards or Xbox 360 hard drives), and servers or computers with Windows Media Center or Windows XP with Service pack 2 or higher within the local-area network in streaming mode. As the Xbox 360 uses a modified version of the UPnP AV protocol, some alternative UPnP servers such as uShare (part of the GeeXboX project) and MythTV can also stream media to the Xbox 360, allowing for similar functionality from non-Windows servers. This is possible with video files up to HD-resolution and with several codecs (MPEG-2, MPEG-4, WMV) and container formats (WMV, MOV, TS).
rewrite: The Xbox 360 supports playback of music, photographs, and video from several sources. These include standard USB mass storage, proprietary Xbox 360 storage devices (e.g., memory cards and hard drives), and networked computers or servers running Windows Media Center or Windows XP with Service Pack 2 or later, which stream content over a local area network. input: Strasbourg also offers high-class eclecticist buildings in its very extended German district, the Neustadt, being the main memory of Wilhelmian architecture since most of the major cities in Germany proper suffered intensive damage during World War II. Streets, boulevards and avenues are homogeneous, surprisingly high (up to seven stories) and broad examples of German urban lay-out and of this architectural style that summons and mixes up five centuries of European architecture as well as Neo-Egyptian, Neo-Greek and Neo-Babylonian styles. The former imperial palace Palais du Rhin, the most political and thus heavily criticized of all German Strasbourg buildings epitomizes the grand scale and stylistic sturdiness of this period. But the two most handsome and ornate buildings of these times are the École internationale des Pontonniers (the former Höhere Mädchenschule, girls college) with its towers, turrets and multiple round and square angles and the École des Arts décoratifs with its lavishly ornate façade of painted bricks, woodwork and majolica.
rewrite: Strasbourg’s extensive Neustadt district constitutes a significant repository of high-quality eclecticist architecture from the Wilhelmine period. This area preserves a coherent urban fabric largely lost in many major German cities due to extensive Second World War damage. Its streets, boulevards, and avenues present a homogeneous, characteristically German layout, featuring notably broad and tall structures of up to seven stories. The architectural style synthesizes five centuries of European design, incorporating Neo-Egyptian, Neo-Greek, and Neo-Babylonian elements. The Palais du Rhin, the former imperial palace and the most politically contentious German building in Strasbourg, exemplifies the monumental scale and robust stylization of the era. However, the period’s most aesthetically refined and ornate examples are the École internationale des Pontonniers—originally the Höhere Mädchenschule—distinguished by its towers, turrets, and varied angular forms, and the École des Arts décoratifs, with its lavish façade of painted brick, woodwork, and majolica.

input: Models suggest that Neptune's troposphere is banded by clouds of varying compositions depending on altitude. The upper-level clouds lie at pressures below one bar, where the temperature is suitable for methane to condense. For pressures between one and five bars (100 and 500 kPa), clouds of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide are thought to form. Above a pressure of five bars, the clouds may consist of ammonia, ammonium sulfide, hydrogen sulfide and water. Deeper clouds of water ice should be found at pressures of about 50 bars (5.0 MPa), where the temperature reaches 273 K (0 °C). Underneath, clouds of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide may be found.
rewrite: Scientific models indicate that Neptune's troposphere exhibits a banded structure, with cloud composition varying by atmospheric pressure. At pressures below one bar, where temperatures permit methane condensation, upper-level clouds form. Within the one to five bar range (100–500 kPa), clouds are hypothesized to consist of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide. Above five bars, clouds may contain ammonia, ammonium sulfide, hydrogen sulfide, and water. Deeper atmospheric layers, near 50 bars (5.0 MPa) and 273 K (0 °C), are expected to harbor water ice clouds. Beneath these, clouds of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide are also predicted to exist.

input: At a certain temperature, (usually between 1,500 °F (820 °C) and 1,600 °F (870 °C), depending on carbon content), the base metal of steel undergoes a change in the arrangement of the atoms in its crystal matrix, called allotropy. This allows the small carbon atoms to enter the interstices of the iron crystal, diffusing into the iron matrix. When this happens, the carbon atoms are said to be in solution, or mixed with the iron, forming a single, homogeneous, crystalline phase called austenite. If the steel is cooled slowly, the iron will gradually change into its low temperature allotrope. When this happens the carbon atoms will no longer be soluble with the iron, and will be forced to precipitate out of solution, nucleating into the spaces between the crystals. The steel then becomes heterogeneous, being formed of two phases; the carbon (carbide) phase cementite, and ferrite. This type of heat treatment produces steel that is rather soft and bendable. However, if the steel is cooled quickly the carbon atoms will not have time to precipitate. When rapidly cooled, a diffusionless (martensite) transformation occurs, in which the carbon atoms become trapped in solution. This causes the iron crystals to deform intrinsically when the crystal structure tries to change to its low temperature state, making it very hard and brittle.
rewrite:
At a specific elevated temperature, typically within the range of 1,500 °F (820 °C) to 1,600 °F (870 °C) as determined by carbon concentration, the fundamental iron within steel undergoes an allotropic transformation. This involves a rearrangement of atoms within the crystalline lattice. This structural change enables the comparatively small carbon atoms to diffuse into the iron matrix by occupying interstitial sites within the crystal. In this state, the carbon is described as being in solid solution, forming a singular, homogeneous crystalline phase known as austenite.

Subsequent slow cooling permits the iron to revert to its low-temperature allotropic form. During this gradual transformation, the solubility of carbon in iron decreases substantially, forcing the carbon to precipitate from the solid solution. This precipitation results in nucleation, forming a distinct carbide phase (cementite) within a matrix of ferrite. The resultant microstructure is heterogeneous, comprising these two phases, and yields a relatively soft and ductile material.

Conversely, rapid quenching suppresses this precipitation process. The swift cooling instigates a diffusionless, martensitic transformation, wherein the carbon atoms remain trapped interstitially within the iron lattice. As the crystal structure attempts to shift to its low-temperature configuration, the entrapped carbon induces severe lattice strain and intrinsic deformation. This process produces an extremely hard yet brittle microstructure.

input: Namibia extends from 17°S to 25°S: climatically the range of the sub-Tropical High Pressure Belt, arid is the overall climate description descending from the Sub-Humid (mean rain above 500 mm) through Semi-Arid between 300 and 500 mm (embracing most of the waterless Kalahari) and Arid from 150 to 300 mm (these three regions are inland from the western escarpment) to the Hyper-Arid coastal plain with less than a 100 mm mean. Temperature maxima are limited by the overall elevation of the entire region: only in the far south, Warmbad for instance, are mid-40 °C maxima recorded.
rewrite: Namibia spans from 17°S to 25°S, a latitudinal range corresponding to the subtropical high-pressure belt, resulting in a predominantly arid climate. Precipitation decreases from sub-humid conditions (mean above 500 mm) inland, through semi-arid (300–500 mm) and arid (150–300 mm) zones, to the hyper-arid coastal plain with under 100 mm mean. The region's general elevation moderates maximum temperatures, with mid-40°C extremes largely confined to southern areas such as Warmbad.

input: In 1934 the Zagreb Provincial Committee sent Tito to Vienna where all the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia had sought refuge. He was appointed to the Committee and started to appoint allies to him, among them Edvard Kardelj, Milovan Đilas, Aleksandar Ranković and Boris Kidrič. In 1935, Tito travelled to the Soviet Union, working for a year in the Balkans section of Comintern. He was a member of the Soviet Communist Party and the Soviet secret police (NKVD). Tito was also involved in recruiting for the Dimitrov Battalion, a group of volunteers serving in the Spanish Civil War. In 1936, the Comintern sent "Comrade Walter" (i.e. Tito) back to Yugoslavia to purge the Communist Party there. In 1937, Stalin had the Secretary-General of the CPY, Milan Gorkić, murdered in Moscow. Subsequently Tito was appointed Secretary-General of the still-outlawed CPY.
rewrite: In 1934, the Zagreb Provincial Committee dispatched Josip Broz Tito to Vienna, where the entire Central Committee of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia (CPY) was then in exile. There, he was co-opted onto the Committee and began consolidating his position by appointing key allies, including Edvard Kardelj, Milovan Đilas, Aleksandar Ranković, and Boris Kidrič. The following year, Tito traveled to the Soviet Union, where he spent a year working in the Balkans section of the Comintern. During this period, he held membership in both the Soviet Communist Party and the NKVD, the Soviet secret police. He also participated in recruiting volunteers for the International Brigades, specifically the Dimitrov Battalion, during the Spanish Civil War. In 1936, the Comintern directed Tito, operating under the pseudonym "Comrade Walter," to return to Yugoslavia to purge the CPY. Following the 1937 execution in Moscow of the then CPY Secretary-General, Milan Gorkić, on Stalin's orders, Tito was appointed to lead the still-outlawed party as its new Secretary-General.

input: Since the Industrial Revolution some two hundred years ago, the food processing industry has invented many technologies that both help keep foods fresh longer and alter the fresh state of food as they appear in nature. Cooling is the primary technology used to maintain freshness, whereas many more technologies have been invented to allow foods to last longer without becoming spoiled. These latter technologies include pasteurisation, autoclavation, drying, salting, and separation of various components, all of which appearing to alter the original nutritional contents of food. Pasteurisation and autoclavation (heating techniques) have no doubt improved the safety of many common foods, preventing epidemics of bacterial infection. But some of the (new) food processing technologies have downfalls as well.
rewrite: Since the Industrial Revolution approximately two centuries ago, the food processing sector has developed numerous technologies designed to extend shelf life and modify the natural state of foodstuffs. Refrigeration serves as the principal method for preserving freshness, while additional techniques have been devised to prevent spoilage. These include pasteurization, autoclaving, drying, salting, and component separation, all of which appear to transform the inherent nutritional composition. Heating methods such as pasteurization and autoclaving have undoubtedly enhanced the safety of many common foods by averting bacterial epidemics. Nevertheless, certain modern food processing technologies also present significant drawbacks.

input: An early advantage of AC is that the power-wasting resistors used in DC locomotives for speed control were not needed in an AC locomotive: multiple taps on the transformer can supply a range of voltages. Separate low-voltage transformer windings supply lighting and the motors driving auxiliary machinery. More recently, the development of very high power semiconductors has caused the classic "universal" AC/DC motor to be largely replaced with the three-phase induction motor fed by a variable frequency drive, a special inverter that varies both frequency and voltage to control motor speed. These drives can run equally well on DC or AC of any frequency, and many modern electric locomotives are designed to handle different supply voltages and frequencies to simplify cross-border operation.
rewrite: An initial benefit of alternating current (AC) systems was the elimination of the power-wasting resistors required for speed control in direct current (DC) locomotives. Instead, multiple transformer taps provided a range of voltages. Separate low-voltage transformer windings powered lighting and auxiliary machinery motors. Subsequently, the advent of high-power semiconductors has largely supplanted the traditional universal AC/DC motor with the three-phase induction motor. This motor is powered by a variable frequency drive, an inverter that modulates both frequency and voltage to regulate speed. Such drives operate effectively on either DC or AC of any frequency. Consequently, many contemporary electric locomotives are engineered to accommodate various supply voltages and frequencies, facilitating cross-border interoperability.

input: Brigham Young University (often referred to as BYU or, colloquially, The Y) is a private research university located in Provo, Utah, United States. It is owned and operated by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), and, excluding online students, is the largest of any religious university and the third largest private university in the United States, with 29,672 on-campus students. Approximately 99 percent of the students are members of the LDS Church, and one-third of its US students are from Utah.
rewrite: Brigham Young University (BYU) is a private research institution in Provo, Utah, owned and operated by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. With 29,672 on-campus students, it is the largest religious university and the third-largest private university in the United States. Approximately 99 percent of its students are members of the sponsoring church, and one-third of its U.S. student population originates from Utah.

input: Habitat size and numbers of species are systematically related. Physically larger species and those living at lower latitudes or in forests or oceans are more sensitive to reduction in habitat area. Conversion to "trivial" standardized ecosystems (e.g., monoculture following deforestation) effectively destroys habitat for the more diverse species that preceded the conversion. In some countries lack of property rights or lax law/regulatory enforcement necessarily leads to biodiversity loss (degradation costs having to be supported by the community).[citation needed]
rewrite: A systematic relationship exists between habitat area and species richness. Species with larger body sizes and those inhabiting lower latitudes, forests, or marine environments exhibit heightened sensitivity to habitat reduction. The conversion to simplified, standardized ecosystems, such as agricultural monocultures, effectively eliminates habitat for the more diverse pre-existing assemblages. Furthermore, in certain national contexts, inadequate property rights or insufficient regulatory enforcement inevitably precipitate biodiversity loss, thereby externalizing degradation costs onto society.

input: In the 2010s, American jurisdictions have experienced a shortage of lethal injection drugs, due to anti-death penalty advocacy and low production volume. Hospira, the only U.S. manufacturer of sodium thiopental, stopped making the drug in 2011. The European Union has outlawed the export of any product that could be used in an execution; this has prevented executioners from using EU-manufactured anesthetics like propofol which are needed for general medical purposes. Another alternative, pentobarbital, is also only manufactured in the European Union, which has caused the Danish producer to restrict distribution to U.S. government customers.
rewrite: During the 2010s, numerous American jurisdictions encountered shortages of drugs used for lethal injection. This scarcity stemmed from advocacy against capital punishment and limited pharmaceutical production. In 2011, Hospira, the sole U.S. manufacturer of sodium thiopental, ceased its production. Furthermore, a European Union ban on exporting products for executions has prevented access to EU-manufactured anesthetics, such as propofol, which are also essential for general medicine. Similarly, pentobarbital, another alternative, is produced exclusively in the EU, leading its Danish manufacturer to restrict sales to U.S. government entities.

input: The bandolim (Portuguese for "mandolin") was a favourite instrument within the Portuguese bourgeoisie of the 19th century, but its rapid spread took it to other places, joining other instruments. Today you can see mandolins as part of the traditional and folk culture of Portuguese singing groups and the majority of the mandolin scene in Portugal is in Madeira Island. Madeira has over 17 active mandolin Orchestras and Tunas. The mandolin virtuoso Fabio Machado is one of Portugal's most accomplished mandolin players. The Portuguese influence brought the mandolin to Brazil.
rewrite: The bandolim, a term derived from the Portuguese word for mandolin, was a favored instrument among the nineteenth-century Portuguese bourgeoisie. Its subsequent dissemination integrated it into diverse musical contexts. Presently, it features prominently in Portuguese folk traditions, particularly within choral ensembles, with its primary contemporary hub being Madeira Island. Madeira sustains over seventeen active mandolin orchestras and tunas. Virtuoso Fabio Machado ranks among Portugal's most distinguished performers. Portuguese cultural influence also facilitated the instrument's introduction to Brazil.

input: Florida i/ˈflɒrɪdə/ (Spanish for "flowery land") is a state located in the southeastern region of the United States. The state is bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico, to the north by Alabama and Georgia, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean, and to the south by the Straits of Florida and the sovereign state of Cuba. Florida is the 22nd most extensive, the 3rd most populous, and the 8th most densely populated of the United States. Jacksonville is the most populous city in Florida, and the largest city by area in the contiguous United States.
