The Miami metropolitan area is the eighth-largest metropolitan area in the United States. Tallahassee is the state capital.
rewrite: Florida, a state situated in the southeastern United States, derives its name from the Spanish term for "flowery land." Its borders are defined by the Gulf of Mexico to the west, Alabama and Georgia to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the east, and the Straits of Florida and Cuba to the south. Among U.S. states, Florida ranks 22nd in land area, third in population, and eighth in population density. Its most populous city is Jacksonville, which is also the largest city by area within the contiguous United States. The Miami metropolitan area is the nation's eighth largest, while Tallahassee serves as the state capital.

input: Various theories for the decline of the Native American populations emphasize epidemic diseases, conflicts with Europeans, and conflicts among warring tribes. Scholars now believe that, among the various contributing factors, epidemic disease was the overwhelming cause of the population decline of the American natives. Some believe that after first contacts with Europeans and Africans, Old World diseases caused the death of 90 to 95% of the native population of the New World in the following 150 years. Smallpox killed up to one third of the native population of Hispaniola in 1518. By killing the Incan ruler Huayna Capac, smallpox caused the Inca Civil War. Smallpox was only the first epidemic. Typhus (probably) in 1546, influenza and smallpox together in 1558, smallpox again in 1589, diphtheria in 1614, measles in 1618—all ravaged the remains of Inca culture.
rewrite: Scholarly discourse regarding the precipitous demographic decline of Indigenous American populations frequently cites a confluence of factors, including epidemic disease, violent conflict with European colonizers, and intertribal warfare. Contemporary academic consensus, however, identifies the introduction of Old World pathogens as the paramount causal agent. Research indicates that in the century and a half following initial contact, these novel diseases may have precipitated a mortality event affecting 90 to 95 percent of the pre-contact population. The epidemiological impact was profound and sequential. For instance, a smallpox outbreak in 1518 claimed up to one-third of Hispaniola's Indigenous inhabitants, while another, by killing the Incan emperor Huayna Capac, instigated a destabilizing civil war. This initial pandemic was merely the first in a devastating series, which included typhus (c. 1546), concurrent influenza and smallpox (1558), further smallpox (1589), diphtheria (1614), and measles (1618), collectively ravaging the surviving remnants of societies like the Inca.

input: Other common forms include president of the council of ministers (for example in Italy, Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri), President of the Executive Council, or Minister-President. In the Scandinavian countries the prime minister is called statsminister in the native languages (i.e. minister of state). In federations, the head of government of subnational entities such as provinces is most commonly known as the premier, chief minister, governor or minister-president.
rewrite: Alternative designations for the head of government include President of the Council of Ministers, President of the Executive Council, and Minister-President. In Scandinavia, the title statsminister, meaning minister of state, is used. Within federal systems, the leaders of constituent units, such as provinces, are typically titled premier, chief minister, governor, or minister-president.

input: On 7 April 1963, the country changed its official name to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Reforms encouraged private enterprise and greatly relaxed restrictions on freedom of speech and religious expression. Tito subsequently went on a tour of the Americas. In Chile, two government ministers resigned over his visit to that country. In the autumn of 1960 Tito met President Dwight D. Eisenhower at the United Nations General Assembly meeting. Tito and Eisenhower discussed a range of issues from arms control to economic development. When Eisenhower remarked that Yugoslavia's neutralism was "neutral on his side", Tito replied that neutralism did not imply passivity but meant "not taking sides".
rewrite: On 7 April 1963, the state formally adopted the title Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Accompanying reforms promoted limited private enterprise and significantly eased constraints on free speech and religious practice. Subsequently, President Tito embarked on a tour of the Americas. His visit to Chile prompted the resignation of two government ministers. Earlier, in the autumn of 1960, Tito conferred with President Dwight D. Eisenhower during a United Nations General Assembly session. Their discussions encompassed topics from arms control to economic development. When Eisenhower suggested Yugoslav neutralism favored the West, Tito clarified that such a policy denoted active non-alignment rather than passivity.

input: Stout and porter are dark beers made using roasted malts or roast barley, and typically brewed with slow fermenting yeast. There are a number of variations including Baltic porter, dry stout, and Imperial stout. The name Porter was first used in 1721 to describe a dark brown beer popular with the street and river porters of London. This same beer later also became known as stout, though the word stout had been used as early as 1677. The history and development of stout and porter are intertwined.
rewrite: Stout and porter are dark ales produced with roasted malts or barley and slow-fermenting yeast. Variants include Baltic porter, dry stout, and Imperial stout. The term "porter" originated in 1721, denoting a dark brown beer favored by London's porters. This beverage later acquired the name "stout," a descriptor used as early as 1677. Consequently, the historical evolution of stout and porter is fundamentally interconnected.

input: Since 1066, when Harold Godwinson and William the Conqueror were crowned, the coronations of English and British monarchs have been held there. There have been at least 16 royal weddings at the abbey since 1100. Two were of reigning monarchs (Henry I and Richard II), although, before 1919, there had been none for some 500 years.
rewrite: Since 1066, Westminster Abbey has hosted all English and British coronations, beginning with Harold Godwinson and William the Conqueror. It has also been the site of at least sixteen royal weddings since 1100, including those of two reigning monarchs, Henry I and Richard II. Prior to 1919, however, no such ceremony had occurred there for approximately five centuries.

input: After the Communist Party of China took power in 1949, the flag of China became a red flag with a large star symbolizing the Communist Party, and smaller stars symbolizing workers, peasants, the urban middle class and rural middle class. The flag of the Communist Party of China became a red banner with a hammer and sickle, similar to that on the Soviet flag. In the 1950s and 1960s, other Communist regimes such as Vietnam and Laos also adopted red flags. Some Communist countries, such as Cuba, chose to keep their old flags; and other countries used red flags which had nothing to do with Communism or socialism; the red flag of Nepal, for instance, represents the national flower.
rewrite: Following the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the national flag was adopted, featuring a red field with one large star, representing the Communist Party of China, and four smaller stars denoting the four social classes: the working class, the peasantry, the urban petty bourgeoisie, and the national bourgeoisie. Concurrently, the party flag itself became a red banner emblazoned with a hammer and sickle, a design influenced by Soviet symbolism. During the mid-twentieth century, several emerging communist states, including Vietnam and Laos, similarly adopted red flags. However, not all communist nations, such as Cuba, altered their existing banners, while other countries, like Nepal, employ red flags for entirely non-ideological reasons, such as symbolizing a national emblem.

input: In the 1950 parliamentary elections, the Wafd Party of el-Nahhas gained a victory—mostly due to the absence of the Muslim Brotherhood, which boycotted the elections—and was perceived as a threat by the Free Officers as the Wafd had campaigned on demands similar to their own. Accusations of corruption against Wafd politicians began to surface, however, breeding an atmosphere of rumor and suspicion that consequently brought the Free Officers to the forefront of Egyptian politics. By then, the organization had expanded to around ninety members; according to Khaled Mohieddin, "nobody knew all of them and where they belonged in the hierarchy except Nasser". Nasser felt that the Free Officers were not ready to move against the government and, for nearly two years, he did little beyond officer recruitment and underground news bulletins.
rewrite: The Wafd Party, led by Mustafa el-Nahhas, secured a parliamentary victory in the 1950 elections, a success partly attributable to the Muslim Brotherhood's electoral boycott. This outcome was viewed with apprehension by the clandestine Free Officers movement, as the Wafd's platform echoed many of their own reformist demands. Concurrently, allegations of corruption against Wafd officials began to circulate, fostering a climate of public distrust that increasingly positioned the Free Officers as a credible political alternative. The organization had by then grown to approximately ninety members, though, as member Khaled Mohieddin noted, only Gamal Abdel Nasser possessed full knowledge of its complete roster and internal hierarchy. Judging the group unprepared for direct action, Nasser focused for nearly two years on recruitment and the dissemination of underground publications.

input: At the request of the pope, he created an information office for prisoners of war and refugees, which in the years of its existence from 1939 until 1947 received almost ten million (9 891 497) information requests and produced over eleven million (11.293.511) answers about missing persons. Montini was several times openly attacked by Benito Mussolini's government as a politician, and meddling in politics, but each time he found powerful defenses by the Vatican. In 1944, Luigi Maglione died, and Pius XII appointed Tardini and Montini together as heads of the State Department. Montini's admiration was almost filial, when he described Pope Pius XII:
rewrite: At the request of the pontiff, he established an information bureau for prisoners of war and refugees. Operational from 1939 to 1947, this office processed nearly ten million inquiries (9,891,497) and issued over eleven million responses (11,293,511) concerning missing persons. The government of Benito Mussolini repeatedly denounced Montini as a political actor and for alleged interference in state affairs, yet he consistently received robust diplomatic protection from the Vatican. Following the death of Cardinal Luigi Maglione in 1944, Pius XII appointed Domenico Tardini and Montini as joint heads of the Secretariat of State. Montini’s regard for Pius XII was profound, characterized by an almost filial devotion.

input: The Partisan Prohibitions were repealed during the Yellow Turban Rebellion and Five Pecks of Rice Rebellion in 184 AD, largely because the court did not want to continue to alienate a significant portion of the gentry class who might otherwise join the rebellions. The Yellow Turbans and Five-Pecks-of-Rice adherents belonged to two different hierarchical Daoist religious societies led by faith healers Zhang Jue (d. 184 AD) and Zhang Lu (d. 216 AD), respectively. Zhang Lu's rebellion, in modern northern Sichuan and southern Shaanxi, was not quelled until 215 AD. Zhang Jue's massive rebellion across eight provinces was annihilated by Han forces within a year, however the following decades saw much smaller recurrent uprisings. Although the Yellow Turbans were defeated, many generals appointed during the crisis never disbanded their assembled militia forces and used these troops to amass power outside of the collapsing imperial authority.
rewrite: The Partisan Prohibitions were rescinded in 184 AD amid the Yellow Turban and Five Pecks of Rice rebellions. This policy reversal was primarily motivated by the imperial court's desire to avoid further alienating a substantial segment of the gentry, whose potential defection to the rebel causes posed a significant threat. These two concurrent uprisings were distinct hierarchical Daoist movements, led respectively by the faith healers Zhang Jue (d. 184 AD) and Zhang Lu (d. 216 AD). While Zhang Jue's widespread rebellion across eight provinces was crushed by Han forces within a year, followed by decades of sporadic smaller revolts, Zhang Lu's insurrection in modern northern Sichuan and southern Shaanxi persisted until 215 AD. Crucially, although the Yellow Turban movement was militarily defeated, many generals commissioned during the crisis retained their private militias. These forces subsequently became instruments for accumulating autonomous power beyond the control of the disintegrating Han central authority.

input: Tort law covers the entire imaginable spectrum of wrongs which humans can inflict upon each other, and of course, partially overlaps with wrongs also punishable by criminal law. Although the American Law Institute has attempted to standardize tort law through the development of several versions of the Restatement of Torts, many states have chosen to adopt only certain sections of the Restatements and to reject others. Thus, because of its immense size and diversity, American tort law cannot be easily summarized.
rewrite: Tort law encompasses the full range of civil wrongs individuals may commit against one another, with partial overlap to criminal offenses. Despite efforts by the American Law Institute to standardize this area through successive Restatements of Torts, states selectively adopt or reject its provisions. Consequently, due to its extensive scope and variability, American tort law resists concise summarization.

input: In 1578 king Stefan Batory created the Crown Tribunal in order to reduce the enormous pressure on the Royal Court. This placed much of the monarch's juridical power in the hands of the elected szlachta deputies, further strengthening the nobility class. In 1581 the Crown Tribunal was joined by a counterpart in Lithuania, the Lithuanian Tribunal.
rewrite: In 1578, King Stefan Batory established the Crown Tribunal to alleviate the excessive caseload on the Royal Court. This transferred significant judicial authority from the monarch to elected deputies of the szlachta, thereby reinforcing the nobility's power. A corresponding Lithuanian Tribunal was added in 1581.

input: Tucson's largest park, Reid Park, is located in midtown and includes Reid Park Zoo and Hi Corbett Field. Speedway Boulevard, a major east-west arterial road in central Tucson, was named the "ugliest street in America" by Life magazine in the early 1970s, quoting Tucson Mayor James Corbett. Despite this, Speedway Boulevard was awarded "Street of the Year" by Arizona Highways in the late 1990s. According to David Leighton, historical writer for the Arizona Daily Star newspaper, Speedway Boulevard derives its name from an old horse racetrack, known as "The Harlem River Speedway," more commonly called "The Speedway," in New York City. The street was called "The Speedway," from 1904 to about 1906 before the word "The" was taken out.
rewrite: Reid Park, the largest park in Tucson, is situated in the city's midtown area and encompasses both the Reid Park Zoo and Hi Corbett Field. Speedway Boulevard, a principal east-west arterial road in central Tucson, was infamously designated the "ugliest street in America" by Life magazine in the early 1970s, citing then-Mayor James Corbett. However, it later received the "Street of the Year" award from Arizona Highways in the late 1990s. As noted by Arizona Daily Star historian David Leighton, the boulevard's name originates from a former horse racetrack in New York City known as "The Harlem River Speedway," colloquially called "The Speedway." The Tucson street carried the article "The" in its name from 1904 until approximately 1906.

input: The main mode of transportation, however, relies on Seattle's streets, which are laid out in a cardinal directions grid pattern, except in the central business district where early city leaders Arthur Denny and Carson Boren insisted on orienting their plats relative to the shoreline rather than to true North. Only two roads, Interstate 5 and State Route 99 (both limited-access highways), run uninterrupted through the city from north to south. State Route 99 runs through downtown Seattle on the Alaskan Way Viaduct, which was built in 1953. However, due to damage sustained during the 2001 Nisqually earthquake the viaduct will be replaced by a tunnel. The 2-mile (3.2 km) Alaskan Way Viaduct replacement tunnel was originally scheduled to be completed in December 2015 at a cost of US$4.25 billion. Unfortunately, due to issues with the worlds largest tunnel boring machine (TBM), which is nicknamed "Bertha" and is 57 feet (17 m) in diameter, the projected date of completion has been pushed back to 2017. Seattle has the 8th worst traffic congestion of all American cities, and is 10th among all North American cities.
rewrite: Seattle's primary transportation infrastructure is predominantly structured around its street network, which generally follows a cardinal grid pattern. A notable exception exists within the central business district, where the original platting by city founders Arthur Denny and Carson Boren aligned street orientations with the Elliott Bay shoreline rather than true north. Only two limited-access highways provide uninterrupted north-south passage through the city: Interstate 5 and State Route 99. The latter traverses downtown via the Alaskan Way Viaduct, a structure erected in 1953. Following damage incurred during the 2001 Nisqually earthquake, this viaduct is being replaced by a tunnel. The 2-mile (3.2 km) Alaskan Way Viaduct replacement tunnel, initially projected for completion in December 2015 at an estimated cost of US$4.25 billion, has experienced significant delays. These are primarily attributable to mechanical failures of "Bertha," the 57-foot (17 m) diameter tunnel boring machine, the world's largest of its kind. Consequently, the anticipated completion date was postponed to 2017. Traffic congestion remains a considerable challenge, with Seattle ranking 8th among U.S. cities and 10th in North America for peak travel delays.

input: Studio producers Richard D. Zanuck and David Brown offered Spielberg the director's chair for Jaws, a thriller-horror film based on the Peter Benchley novel about an enormous killer shark. Spielberg has often referred to the gruelling shoot as his professional crucible. Despite the film's ultimate, enormous success, it was nearly shut down due to delays and budget over-runs. But Spielberg persevered and finished the film. It was an enormous hit, winning three Academy Awards (for editing, original score and sound) and grossing more than $470 million worldwide at the box office. It also set the domestic record for box office gross, leading to what the press described as "Jawsmania.":248 Jaws made Spielberg a household name and one of America's youngest multi-millionaires, allowing him a great deal of autonomy for his future projects.:250 It was nominated for Best Picture and featured Spielberg's first of three collaborations with actor Richard Dreyfuss.
rewrite: The directorial role for *Jaws*, a thriller-horror adaptation of Peter Benchley's novel concerning a massive predatory shark, was extended to Steven Spielberg by studio producers Richard D. Zanuck and David Brown. Spielberg has frequently characterized the subsequent production as a grueling professional crucible. The project, plagued by delays and budgetary excesses, neared termination despite its eventual and considerable commercial triumph. Spielberg's perseverance resulted in a film that achieved enormous success, earning three Academy Awards (for Film Editing, Original Score, and Sound) and generating over $470 million in global box office revenue. It established a domestic earnings record, spurring a phenomenon termed "Jawsmania" in the press. The film secured Spielberg's status as a household name and provided significant creative autonomy for his subsequent career. Although nominated for Best Picture, it marked the first of his three cinematic collaborations with actor Richard Dreyfuss.

input: In sheer numbers, Kerry had fewer endorsements than Howard Dean, who was far ahead in the superdelegate race going into the Iowa caucuses in January 2004, although Kerry led the endorsement race in Iowa, New Hampshire, Arizona, South Carolina, New Mexico and Nevada. Kerry's main perceived weakness was in his neighboring state of New Hampshire and nearly all national polls. Most other states did not have updated polling numbers to give an accurate placing for the Kerry campaign before Iowa. Heading into the primaries, Kerry's campaign was largely seen as in trouble, particularly after he fired campaign manager Jim Jordan. The key factors enabling it to survive were when fellow Massachusetts Senator Ted Kennedy assigned Mary Beth Cahill to be the campaign manager, as well as Kerry's mortgaging his own home to lend the money to his campaign (while his wife was a billionaire, campaign finance rules prohibited using one's personal fortune). He also brought on the "magical" Michael Whouley who would be credited with helping bring home the Iowa victory the same as he did in New Hampshire for Al Gore in 2000 against Bill Bradley.
rewrite: Heading into the 2004 Iowa caucuses, John Kerry’s campaign was widely perceived as troubled. Although Kerry held endorsement leads in several key states, including Iowa, New Hampshire, and Arizona, he trailed Howard Dean in the overall superdelegate count. National polls and surveys from his neighboring state of New Hampshire consistently highlighted a primary weakness. Furthermore, a lack of updated polling in most other states obscured the campaign’s precise standing. This perception of difficulty intensified following the dismissal of campaign manager Jim Jordan. The campaign’s survival is attributed to several pivotal interventions: Senator Ted Kennedy facilitated the appointment of Mary Beth Cahill as the new campaign manager, and Kerry personally mortgaged his home to provide essential funds, as campaign finance regulations prohibited direct use of his wife’s considerable wealth. Additionally, the recruitment of strategist Michael Whouley proved critical; Whouley, credited with securing Al Gore’s 2000 New Hampshire primary win, was instrumental in orchestrating Kerry’s subsequent Iowa victory.

input: On the other hand, certain financial techniques can reduce the impact of such purchases on the currency. One is sterilisation, in which highly valued assets are sold at the same time that the weaker assets are purchased, which keeps the money supply neutral. Another technique is simply to accept the bad assets as long-term collateral (as opposed to short-term repo swaps) to be held until their market value stabilises. This would imply, as a quid pro quo, adjustments in taxation and expenditure in the economies of the weaker states to improve the perceived value of the assets.
rewrite: Conversely, specific monetary policy interventions can mitigate the exchange rate effects of such acquisitions. Sterilisation, involving the simultaneous sale of high-value assets to offset purchases of weaker ones, maintains a neutral money supply. Alternatively, authorities may accept devalued assets as long-term collateral—rather than through short-term repurchase agreements—retaining them until market prices recover. This approach would necessitate compensatory fiscal adjustments, including tax and expenditure reforms within the affected economies, to enhance the fundamental valuation of the underlying assets.

input: The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi does not release any economic figures specifically for New Delhi but publishes an official economic report on the whole of Delhi annually. According to the Economic Survey of Delhi, the metropolis has a net State Domestic Product (SDP) of Rs. 83,085 crores (for the year 2004–05) and a per capita income of Rs. 53,976($1,200). In the year 2008–09 New Delhi had a Per Capita Income of Rs.1,16,886 ($2,595).It grew by 16.2% to reach Rs.1,35,814 ($3,018) in 2009–10 fiscal. New Delhi's Per Capita GDP (at PPP) was at $6,860 during 2009–10 fiscal, making it one of the richest cities in India. The tertiary sector contributes 78.4% of Delhi's gross SDP followed by secondary and primary sectors with 20.2% and 1.4% contribution respectively.
rewrite: The Government of the National Capital Territory of Delhi does not issue distinct economic statistics for New Delhi independently; however, it produces an annual official economic report encompassing the entire territory. As documented in the Economic Survey of Delhi, the aggregate net State Domestic Product (SDP) was ₹83,085 crore for the 2004–05 period, with a corresponding per capita income of ₹53,976 (approximately US$1,200). By 2008–09, New Delhi's per capita income had risen to ₹1,16,886 (US$2,595), subsequently increasing by 16.2% to ₹1,35,814 (US$3,018) in the 2009–10 fiscal year. During that same fiscal year, the city's per capita GDP in purchasing power parity (PPP) terms reached US$6,860, ranking it among India's most affluent urban centers. The tertiary sector constitutes the predominant share of Delhi's gross SDP at 78.4%, followed by the secondary sector at 20.2% and the primary sector at 1.4%.

input: On October 17, 1987, about 3,000 Armenians demonstrated in Yerevan complaining about the condition of Lake Sevan, the Nairit chemicals plant, and the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant, and air pollution in Yerevan. Police tried to prevent the protest but took no action to stop it once the march was underway. The demonstration was led by Armenian writers such as Silva Kaputikian, Zori Balayan, and Maro Margarian and leaders from the National Survival organization. The march originated at the Opera Plaza after speakers, mainly intellectuals, addressed the crowd.
rewrite: On October 17, 1987, approximately 3,000 Armenians convened in Yerevan to protest environmental concerns, including the degradation of Lake Sevan, pollution from the Nairit chemical plant and Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant, and poor air quality in the capital. Although police initially attempted to prevent the gathering, they did not intervene once the procession commenced. Organized by the National Survival group and led by prominent writers including Silva Kaputikian, Zori Balayan, and Maro Margarian, the demonstration began at Opera Plaza following addresses by several intellectuals.

input: An advantage of the universal motor is that AC supplies may be used on motors which have some characteristics more common in DC motors, specifically high starting torque and very compact design if high running speeds are used. The negative aspect is the maintenance and short life problems caused by the commutator. Such motors are used in devices such as food mixers and power tools which are used only intermittently, and often have high starting-torque demands. Multiple taps on the field coil provide (imprecise) stepped speed control. Household blenders that advertise many speeds frequently combine a field coil with several taps and a diode that can be inserted in series with the motor (causing the motor to run on half-wave rectified AC). Universal motors also lend themselves to electronic speed control and, as such, are an ideal choice for devices like domestic washing machines. The motor can be used to agitate the drum (both forwards and in reverse) by switching the field winding with respect to the armature.
rewrite: A principal advantage of the universal motor is its compatibility with AC power supplies while retaining performance characteristics typical of DC motors, notably high starting torque and a compact design achievable through high operational speeds. The primary disadvantage involves maintenance requirements and reduced longevity due to commutator wear. Consequently, these motors are well-suited for intermittently operated appliances such as food mixers and power tools, which often demand high initial torque. Stepped speed control is commonly achieved through multiple taps on the field coil, albeit with limited precision. For instance, household blenders offering multiple speeds frequently employ a tapped field coil combined with a series diode to enable half-wave rectified AC operation. Furthermore, universal motors adapt readily to electronic speed regulation, making them an optimal selection for applications like domestic washing machines. In such appliances, reversing the drum’s agitation direction is accomplished by switching the field winding relative to the armature.

input: While the largest European-American population in Montana overall is German, pockets of significant Scandinavian ancestry are prevalent in some of the farming-dominated northern and eastern prairie regions, parallel to nearby regions of North Dakota and Minnesota. Farmers of Irish, Scots, and English roots also settled in Montana. The historically mining-oriented communities of western Montana such as Butte have a wider range of European-American ethnicity; Finns, Eastern Europeans and especially Irish settlers left an indelible mark on the area, as well as people originally from British mining regions such as Cornwall, Devon and Wales. The nearby city of Helena, also founded as a mining camp, had a similar mix in addition to a small Chinatown. Many of Montana's historic logging communities originally attracted people of Scottish, Scandinavian, Slavic, English and Scots-Irish descent.[citation needed]
rewrite: Montana’s European-American population exhibits distinct regional settlement patterns. Although those of German ancestry constitute the largest group statewide, areas dominated by agriculture in the northern and eastern prairies show a pronounced concentration of Scandinavian heritage, mirroring adjacent regions of North Dakota and Minnesota. Settlers of Irish, Scots, and English origin also established farming communities. In contrast, the historically mining-focused western region, including Butte, attracted a more diverse array of European ethnicities. Finnish, Eastern European, and notably Irish immigrants profoundly influenced these areas, alongside migrants from British mining districts like Cornwall, Devon, and Wales. Helena, another mining-founded city, shared this ethnic composition and also featured a small historic Chinatown. Furthermore, many early logging communities drew significant numbers of Scottish, Scandinavian, Slavic, English, and Scots-Irish settlers.

input: There are three primary shopping centers in the Bronx: The Hub, Gateway Center and Southern Boulevard. The Hub–Third Avenue Business Improvement District (B.I.D.), in The Hub, is the retail heart of the South Bronx, located where four roads converge: East 149th Street, Willis, Melrose and Third Avenues. It is primarily located inside the neighborhood of Melrose but also lines the northern border of Mott Haven. The Hub has been called "the Broadway of the Bronx", being likened to the real Broadway in Manhattan and the northwestern Bronx. It is the site of both maximum traffic and architectural density. In configuration, it resembles a miniature Times Square, a spatial "bow-tie" created by the geometry of the street. The Hub is part of Bronx Community Board 1.
rewrite: The Bronx contains three principal commercial districts: The Hub, Gateway Center, and Southern Boulevard. The Hub–Third Avenue Business Improvement District (B.I.D.) serves as the central retail core of the South Bronx. Situated at the convergence of East 149th Street, Willis, Melrose, and Third Avenues, it is primarily within Melrose while also bordering Mott Haven to the north. Historically termed "the Broadway of the Bronx," it is analogized to Manhattan's Broadway and its northwestern Bronx counterpart, characterized by peak pedestrian and vehicular traffic alongside high architectural density. Its configuration, resembling a compact Times Square, forms a spatial "bow-tie" shape dictated by the street geometry. The Hub falls within the jurisdiction of Bronx Community Board 1.

input: The economy has been growing quickly in recent years. In both 2010 and 2011, the metro area's gross domestic product (GDP) led 27 other metropolitan areas in the country, according to the Conference Board of Canada, recording growth of 6.6 per cent and 5.8 per cent respectively. At $52,000 the city's per capita GDP is the second highest out of all major Canadian cities. Economic forecasts suggest that the city will continue its strong economic growth in the coming years not only in the "oceanic" industries mentioned above, but also in tourism and new home construction as the population continues to grow. In May 2011, the city's unemployment rate fell to 5.6 per cent, the second lowest unemployment rate for a major city in Canada.
rewrite: The national economy has experienced robust expansion in recent years. According to the Conference Board of Canada, the metropolitan area's gross domestic product (GDP) growth led 27 other major metropolitan areas in both 2010 and 2011, with recorded increases of 6.6 per cent and 5.8 per cent, respectively. With a per capita GDP of $52,000, the city ranks second among all major Canadian urban centers. Economic projections indicate that strong growth will persist, driven not only by established oceanic sectors but also by expanding tourism and residential construction amid ongoing population increases. Furthermore, as of May 2011, the city's unemployment rate declined to 5.6 per cent, representing the second lowest rate for a major Canadian city.

input: The last three years of Eisenhower's second term in office were ones of relatively good health. Eventually after leaving the White House, he suffered several additional and ultimately crippling heart attacks. A severe heart attack in August 1965 largely ended his participation in public affairs. In August 1966 he began to show symptoms of cholecystitis, for which he underwent surgery on December 12, 1966, when his gallbladder was removed, containing 16 gallstones. After Eisenhower's death in 1969 (see below), an autopsy unexpectedly revealed an adrenal pheochromocytoma, a benign adrenaline-secreting tumor that may have made the President more vulnerable to heart disease. Eisenhower suffered seven heart attacks in total from 1955 until his death.
rewrite: During the final three years of his second presidential term, Dwight D. Eisenhower maintained relatively stable health. Following his departure from the White House, however, he experienced a series of debilitating heart attacks. A particularly severe episode in August 1965 effectively concluded his engagement in public life. In August 1966, symptoms of cholecystitis emerged, leading to gallbladder removal surgery on December 12 of that year; the excised organ contained sixteen gallstones. An autopsy conducted after his 1969 death unexpectedly identified an adrenal pheochromocytoma, a benign tumor secreting adrenaline, which may have increased his susceptibility to cardiac illness. From 1955 onward, Eisenhower endured a total of seven myocardial infarctions.

input: Qutb Shahi architecture of the 16th and early 17th centuries followed classical Persian architecture featuring domes and colossal arches. The oldest surviving Qutb Shahi structure in Hyderabad is the ruins of Golconda fort built in the 16th century. The Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Charkaman and Qutb Shahi tombs are other existing structures of this period. Among these the Charminar has become an icon of the city; located in the centre of old Hyderabad, it is a square structure with sides 20 m (66 ft) long and four grand arches each facing a road. At each corner stands a 56 m (184 ft)-high minaret. Most of the historical bazaars that still exist were constructed on the street north of Charminar towards Golconda fort. The Charminar, Qutb Shahi tombs and Golconda fort are considered to be monuments of national importance in India; in 2010 the Indian government proposed that the sites be listed for UNESCO World Heritage status.:11–18
rewrite: The Qutb Shahi architectural style, prominent during the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, was derived from classical Persian precedents, characterized by the extensive use of domes and monumental arches. The earliest extant example within Hyderabad is the sixteenth-century Golconda fort complex. Other surviving structures from this period include the Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Charkaman, and the Qutb Shahi tombs. Among these, the Charminar has achieved iconic status as a symbol of the city. Situated in the historic center of Hyderabad, this square edifice measures twenty meters per side and features four grand arches, each oriented toward a major thoroughfare. A minaret rising fifty-six meters crowns each corner. Many enduring historical bazaars are located along the arterial road extending north from the Charminar toward Golconda fort. The Charminar, Qutb Shahi tombs, and Golconda fort are designated monuments of national importance in India. In 2010, the Indian government nominated these sites for inclusion on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

input: In addition to limiting the total average power used by the device, the USB specification limits the inrush current (i.e., that used to charge decoupling and filter capacitors) when the device is first connected. Otherwise, connecting a device could cause problems with the host's internal power. USB devices are also required to automatically enter ultra low-power suspend mode when the USB host is suspended. Nevertheless, many USB host interfaces do not cut off the power supply to USB devices when they are suspended.
rewrite: Beyond restricting the total average power consumption of a device, the USB specification imposes limits on inrush current—the initial surge required to charge decoupling and filter capacitors upon connection—to prevent potential disruptions to the host's internal power supply. Furthermore, USB devices must automatically enter an ultra-low-power suspend mode when the host is suspended. However, it is notable that many host interfaces fail to deactivate power to USB devices during this suspended state.

input: The Western powers, largely unsatisfied with the Treaty of Nanjing, gave grudging support to the Qing government during the Taiping and Nian Rebellions. China's income fell sharply during the wars as vast areas of farmland were destroyed, millions of lives were lost, and countless armies were raised and equipped to fight the rebels. In 1854, Britain tried to re-negotiate the Treaty of Nanjing, inserting clauses allowing British commercial access to Chinese rivers and the creation of a permanent British embassy at Beijing.
rewrite: The Western powers, dissatisfied with the Treaty of Nanjing, offered only reluctant support to the Qing dynasty against the Taiping and Nian Rebellions. These conflicts precipitated a severe economic decline, characterized by devastated agricultural regions, massive civilian casualties, and the immense cost of mobilizing imperial forces. Subsequently, in 1854, Britain sought to revise the treaty, demanding new provisions for commercial navigation on China's inland waterways and the establishment of a permanent diplomatic legation in Beijing.

input: The introduction of new or equivalent deities coincided with Rome's most significant aggressive and defensive military forays. In 206 BC the Sibylline books commended the introduction of cult to the aniconic Magna Mater (Great Mother) from Pessinus, installed on the Palatine in 191 BC. The mystery cult to Bacchus followed; it was suppressed as subversive and unruly by decree of the Senate in 186 BC. Greek deities were brought within the sacred pomerium: temples were dedicated to Juventas (Hebe) in 191 BC, Diana (Artemis) in 179 BC, Mars (Ares) in 138 BC), and to Bona Dea, equivalent to Fauna, the female counterpart of the rural Faunus, supplemented by the Greek goddess Damia. Further Greek influences on cult images and types represented the Roman Penates as forms of the Greek Dioscuri. The military-political adventurers of the Later Republic introduced the Phrygian goddess Ma (identified with Roman Bellona, the Egyptian mystery-goddess Isis and Persian Mithras.)
rewrite: The incorporation of novel or analogous deities aligned chronologically with Rome's principal military campaigns, both offensive and defensive. In 206 BC, consultation of the Sibylline Books prompted the adoption of the aniconic cult of Magna Mater from Pessinus, formally enshrined on the Palatine by 191 BC. Subsequently, the Bacchic mystery cult, deemed subversive, was suppressed by senatorial decree in 186 BC. Hellenic deities were systematically integrated within the *pomerium*: temples were consecrated to Juventas (Hebe) in 191 BC, Diana (Artemis) in 179 BC, and Mars (Ares) in 138 BC. The cult of Bona Dea, equated with Fauna, was supplemented by the Greek goddess Damia. Further Greek influence manifested in the representation of the Roman Penates as forms of the Dioscuri. During the Later Republic, military-political adventurers introduced deities such as the Phrygian goddess Ma, syncretized with Bellona, alongside the Egyptian Isis and Persian Mithras.

input: These statistics point to the complexities surrounding the lack of health/nutrition literacy and reveal the degree to which they are embedded in the social structure and interconnected with other problems. Among these problems are the lack of information about food choices, a lack of understanding of nutritional information and its application to individual circumstances, limited or difficult access to healthful foods, and a range of cultural influences and socioeconomic constraints such as low levels of education and high levels of poverty that decrease opportunities for healthful eating and living.
rewrite: These data illustrate the multifaceted nature of deficient health and nutrition literacy, demonstrating its deep institutionalization within social structures and its interconnection with systemic challenges. These include insufficient knowledge regarding dietary options, poor comprehension and contextual application of nutritional guidance, constrained access to nutritious foods, and various cultural and socioeconomic factors. Such factors—notably limited educational attainment and prevalent poverty—significantly restrict opportunities for adopting and maintaining healthy dietary and lifestyle practices.

input: By the end of May, drafts were formally presented. In mid-June, the main Tripartite negotiations started. The discussion was focused on potential guarantees to central and east European countries should a German aggression arise. The USSR proposed to consider that a political turn towards Germany by the Baltic states would constitute an "indirect aggression" towards the Soviet Union. Britain opposed such proposals, because they feared the Soviets' proposed language could justify a Soviet intervention in Finland and the Baltic states, or push those countries to seek closer relations with Germany. The discussion about a definition of "indirect aggression" became one of the sticking points between the parties, and by mid-July, the tripartite political negotiations effectively stalled, while the parties agreed to start negotiations on a military agreement, which the Soviets insisted must be entered into simultaneously with any political agreement.
rewrite: By the close of May, formal draft proposals were submitted. Principal negotiations among the three powers commenced in mid-June, centering on potential guarantees for Central and Eastern European nations in the event of German aggression. The Soviet Union advanced a proposal to classify any political reorientation by the Baltic states toward Germany as an act of "indirect aggression" against the USSR. The British delegation opposed this formulation, apprehensive that it could furnish a pretext for Soviet intervention in Finland and the Baltic states or inadvertently drive those nations toward closer alignment with Germany. The debate over defining "indirect aggression" emerged as a principal impediment. Consequently, by mid-July, the political negotiations had effectively reached a stalemate. The parties concurred, however, to initiate parallel discussions on a military agreement, a condition the Soviets insisted must accompany any political pact.

input: The pagan Slavic populations were Christianized between the 6th and 10th centuries. Orthodox Christianity is predominant in the East and South Slavs, while Roman Catholicism is predominant in West Slavs and the western South Slavs. The religious borders are largely comparable to the East–West Schism which began in the 11th century. The majority of contemporary Slavic populations who profess a religion are Orthodox, followed by Catholic, while a small minority are Protestant. There are minor Slavic Muslim groups. Religious delineations by nationality can be very sharp; usually in the Slavic ethnic groups the vast majority of religious people share the same religion. Some Slavs are atheist or agnostic: only 19% of Czechs professed belief in god/s in the 2005 Eurobarometer survey.
rewrite: The Christianization of pagan Slavic peoples occurred from the sixth through the tenth centuries. A predominant religious division persists, with Orthodox Christianity characterizing most Eastern and Southern Slavs, while Roman Catholicism prevails among West Slavs and certain Western South Slavs. These confessional boundaries largely correspond to the historical fault line of the East–West Schism initiated in the eleventh century. Among contemporary religious Slavs, Orthodox adherents constitute the majority, followed by Catholics, with a minor Protestant presence and small Slavic Muslim groups. Religious affiliation frequently aligns sharply with national identity, typically resulting in a single dominant faith within each Slavic ethnicity. Notably, significant portions of some populations, such as the Czechs, profess atheism or agnosticism; a 2005 Eurobarometer survey indicated only 19% of Czechs affirmed belief in a deity.

input: Among all cities in the Mediterranean part of the European Union, Limassol has one of the warmest winters, in the period January – February average temperature is 17–18 °C (63–64 °F) during the day and 7–8 °C (45–46 °F) at night, in other coastal locations in Cyprus is generally 16–17 °C (61–63 °F) during the day and 6–8 °C (43–46 °F) at night. During March, Limassol has average temperatures of 19–20 °C (66–68 °F) during the day and 9–11 °C (48–52 °F) at night, in other coastal locations in Cyprus is generally 17–19 °C (63–66 °F) during the day and 8–10 °C (46–50 °F) at night.
rewrite: Limassol experiences among the mildest winter climates of Mediterranean cities within the European Union. During January and February, its average diurnal temperatures range from 17–18 °C (63–64 °F), with nocturnal lows of 7–8 °C (45–46 °F). This contrasts with other Cypriot coastal areas, which typically see daytime averages of 16–17 °C (61–63 °F) and nighttime lows of 6–8 °C (43–46 °F). In March, Limassol's averages are 19–20 °C (66–68 °F) by day and 9–11 °C (48–52 °F) by night, compared to the broader coastal norm of 17–19 °C (63–66 °F) and 8–10 °C (46–50 °F), respectively.

input: The Ottoman Empire, believed to be about to collapse, was portrayed in the press as the sick man of Europe". The Balkan states, with the partial exception of Bosnia and Albania, were primarily Christian. Starting in 1894 the Ottomans struck at the Armenians on the explicit grounds that they were a non-Muslim people and as such were a potential threat to the Muslim empire within which they resided. The Hamidian Massacres aroused the indignation of the entire Christian world. In the United States the now aging Julia Ward Howe, author of the Battle Hymn of the Republic, leaped into the war of words and joined the Red Cross. Relations of minorities within the Ottoman Empire and the disposition of former Ottoman lands became known as the "Eastern Question," as the Ottomans were on the east of Europe.
rewrite: Portrayed in contemporary press as the "sick man of Europe," the Ottoman Empire was widely perceived to be in a state of terminal decline. Within its borders, the Balkan regions were predominantly Christian, with the partial exceptions of Bosnia and Albania. Beginning in 1894, the Ottoman authorities initiated targeted violence against the Armenian population, explicitly justifying these actions on the grounds that, as a non-Muslim minority, they constituted a potential threat to the empire's Islamic integrity. These Hamidian Massacres provoked widespread condemnation throughout the Christian world. In the United States, figures such as the elderly Julia Ward Howe, author of "The Battle Hymn of the Republic," vocally protested and engaged in humanitarian efforts through the Red Cross. The broader issues of minority relations within the empire and the status of its territories, situated to the east of Europe, were collectively termed the "Eastern Question."

input: On 23 November 1991, in a prepared statement made on his deathbed, Mercury confirmed that he had AIDS. Within 24 hours of the statement, he died of bronchial pneumonia, which was brought on as a complication of AIDS. His funeral service on 27 November in Kensal Green, West London was private, and held in accordance with the Zoroastrian religious faith of his family. "Bohemian Rhapsody" was re-released as a single shortly after Mercury's death, with "These Are the Days of Our Lives" as the double A-side. The music video for "These Are the Days of Our Lives" contains Mercury's final scenes in front of the camera. The single went to number one in the UK, remaining there for five weeks – the only recording to top the Christmas chart twice and the only one to be number one in four different years (1975, 1976, 1991, and 1992). Initial proceeds from the single – approximately £1,000,000 – were donated to the Terrence Higgins Trust.
rewrite: On 23 November 1991, Freddie Mercury issued a prepared statement from his deathbed confirming his diagnosis of AIDS. He succumbed to bronchial pneumonia, a complication of the disease, within twenty-four hours. A private funeral service, conducted in accordance with his family's Zoroastrian faith, was held at Kensal Green in West London on 27 November. In the immediate aftermath of his death, the single "Bohemian Rhapsody" was re-released with "These Are the Days of Our Lives" as a double A-side. The accompanying video for the latter features Mercury's final filmed performance. This release reached the top of the UK charts for a five-week period, achieving the distinction of being the only recording to top the Christmas chart on two separate occasions and to hold the number-one position across four distinct calendar years (1975, 1976, 1991, and 1992). Initial royalties, amounting to approximately one million pounds, were directed to the Terrence Higgins Trust.

input: This article covers numbered east-west streets in Manhattan, New York City. Major streets have their own linked articles; minor streets are discussed here. The streets do not run exactly east–west, because the grid plan is aligned with the Hudson River rather than with the cardinal directions. "West" is approximately 29 degrees north of true west.
rewrite: This article examines the numbered east-west thoroughfares of Manhattan, New York City. While major avenues are detailed elsewhere, the focus here is on minor streets. Their orientation deviates from true east-west, as the grid aligns with the Hudson River. Consequently, "west" corresponds to approximately 29 degrees north of true west.

input: Other important Venetian mosaics can be found in the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta in Torcello from the 12th century, and in the Basilical of Santi Maria e Donato in Murano with a restored apse mosaic from the 12th century and a beautiful mosaic pavement (1140). The apse of the San Cipriano Church in Murano was decorated with an impressive golden mosaic from the early 13th century showing Christ enthroned with Mary, St John and the two patron saints, Cipriano and Cipriana. When the church was demolished in the 19th century, the mosaic was bought by Frederick William IV of Prussia. It was reassembled in the Friedenskirche of Potsdam in the 1840s.
rewrite: Significant Venetian mosaics also exist within the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta on Torcello, dating to the twelfth century, and the Basilica of Santi Maria e Donato on Murano, which features a restored twelfth-century apse mosaic alongside an elaborate pavement from 1140. Furthermore, the apse of Murano's San Cipriano Church originally displayed a notable golden mosaic from the early thirteenth century, depicting Christ enthroned with Mary, Saint John, and the patron saints Cipriano and Cipriana. Following the church's demolition in the nineteenth century, King Frederick William IV of Prussia acquired the mosaic, leading to its reconstruction in Potsdam's Friedenskirche during the 1840s.

input: According to the Quran, God communicated with man and made his will known through signs and revelations. Prophets, or 'Messengers of God', received revelations and delivered them to humanity. The message has been identical and for all humankind. "Nothing is said to you that was not said to the messengers before you, that your lord has at his Command forgiveness as well as a most Grievous Penalty." The revelation does not come directly from God to the prophets. Angels acting as God's messengers deliver the divine revelation to them. This comes out in Quran 42:51, in which it is stated: "It is not for any mortal that God should speak to them, except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger to reveal by his permission whatsoever He will."
rewrite: The Quran delineates a theology of divine communication wherein God conveys His will to humanity through signs and revelations. This transmission is mediated by prophets, designated as 'Messengers of God,' who receive and subsequently deliver these revelations. The core message is described as consistent and universal across all prophetic missions. As one verse asserts, the fundamental warnings and promises remain unchanged. Crucially, the Quran specifies that revelation does not involve direct, unmediated speech from God to a prophet. Instead, divine communication is facilitated through angelic intermediaries, who act as God's messengers. This principle is explicitly articulated in Quran 42:51, which states that God speaks to mortals only via revelation, from behind a veil, or by dispatching a messenger to disclose what He wills.

input: The first visible institution to run into trouble in the United States was the Southern California–based IndyMac, a spin-off of Countrywide Financial. Before its failure, IndyMac Bank was the largest savings and loan association in the Los Angeles market and the seventh largest mortgage originator in the United States. The failure of IndyMac Bank on July 11, 2008, was the fourth largest bank failure in United States history up until the crisis precipitated even larger failures, and the second largest failure of a regulated thrift. IndyMac Bank's parent corporation was IndyMac Bancorp until the FDIC seized IndyMac Bank. IndyMac Bancorp filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in July 2008.
rewrite: The initial institution to manifest distress in the United States was IndyMac, a Southern California-based entity originally spun off from Countrywide Financial. Prior to its collapse, IndyMac Bank functioned as the largest savings and loan association in the Los Angeles area and ranked as the nation's seventh-largest mortgage originator. Its failure on July 11, 2008, constituted the fourth-largest bank failure in U.S. history at that time, and the second-largest failure of a regulated thrift. Following the seizure of IndyMac Bank by the FDIC, its parent holding company, IndyMac Bancorp, subsequently filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in July 2008.

input: In 1896, Patrick and Gilbert observed that during a prolonged period of sleep deprivation, sleepiness increases and decreases with a period of approximately 24 hours. In 1918, J.S. Szymanski showed that animals are capable of maintaining 24-hour activity patterns in the absence of external cues such as light and changes in temperature. In the early 20th century, circadian rhythms were noticed in the rhythmic feeding times of bees. Extensive experiments were done by Auguste Forel, Ingeborg Beling, and Oskar Wahl to see whether this rhythm was due to an endogenous clock.[citation needed] Ron Konopka and Seymour Benzer isolated the first clock mutant in Drosophila in the early 1970s and mapped the "period" gene, the first discovered genetic determinant of behavioral rhythmicity. Joseph Takahashi discovered the first mammalian circadian clock mutation (clockΔ19) using mice in 1994. However, recent studies show that deletion of clock does not lead to a behavioral phenotype (the animals still have normal circadian rhythms), which questions its importance in rhythm generation.
rewrite: The seminal observation by Patrick and Gilbert in 1896 documented that sleepiness during prolonged sleep deprivation oscillates with a periodicity of approximately 24 hours. Subsequently, J.S. Szymanski demonstrated in 1918 that animals sustain 24-hour activity patterns even in the absence of external zeitgebers like light and temperature fluctuations. Concurrently, early 20th-century research noted circadian rhythms in the feeding patterns of bees, prompting extensive investigations by Auguste Forel, Ingeborg Beling, and Oskar Wahl to determine if such rhythms originated from an endogenous clock. A pivotal advance occurred in the early 1970s when Ron Konopka and Seymour Benzer isolated the first circadian clock mutant in *Drosophila*, mapping the "period" gene as the initial genetic determinant of behavioral rhythmicity. Joseph Takahashi identified the first mammalian circadian clock mutation (*clock*Δ19) in mice in 1994. However, subsequent research indicates that deletion of the *clock* gene does not produce a behavioral phenotype, as rhythms persist normally, thereby challenging its presumed central role in rhythm generation.

input: In September 1982, Prime minister Margaret Thatcher travelled to Beijing to negotiate with the Chinese government on the future of Britain's last major and most populous overseas territory, Hong Kong. Under the terms of the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, Hong Kong Island itself had been ceded to Britain in perpetuity, but the vast majority of the colony was constituted by the New Territories, which had been acquired under a 99-year lease in 1898, due to expire in 1997. Thatcher, seeing parallels with the Falkland Islands, initially wished to hold Hong Kong and proposed British administration with Chinese sovereignty, though this was rejected by China. A deal was reached in 1984—under the terms of the Sino-British Joint Declaration, Hong Kong would become a special administrative region of the People's Republic of China, maintaining its way of life for at least 50 years. The handover ceremony in 1997 marked for many, including Charles, Prince of Wales, who was in attendance, "the end of Empire".
rewrite: In September 1982, British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher visited Beijing to negotiate the future of Hong Kong, the United Kingdom's last significant and most populous overseas territory. The legal status of the territory was complex: while Hong Kong Island had been ceded to Britain in perpetuity under the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, the larger New Territories were held under a 99-year lease from 1898, scheduled to expire in 1997. Drawing a parallel with the Falkland Islands, Thatcher initially advocated for continued British administration under Chinese sovereignty, a proposal firmly rejected by the Chinese government. Subsequently, the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration established that Hong Kong would revert to Chinese rule as a Special Administrative Region in 1997, guaranteeing the preservation of its existing social and economic systems for fifty years. The 1997 handover ceremony, attended by Charles, Prince of Wales, was widely perceived as a symbolic conclusion to the British Empire.

input: The relationship between genes can be measured by comparing the sequence alignment of their DNA.:7.6 The degree of sequence similarity between homologous genes is called conserved sequence. Most changes to a gene's sequence do not affect its function and so genes accumulate mutations over time by neutral molecular evolution. Additionally, any selection on a gene will cause its sequence to diverge at a different rate. Genes under stabilizing selection are constrained and so change more slowly whereas genes under directional selection change sequence more rapidly. The sequence differences between genes can be used for phylogenetic analyses to study how those genes have evolved and how the organisms they come from are related.
rewrite: The relationship between genes can be quantified through the alignment of their DNA sequences. The extent of similarity between homologous genes constitutes a conserved sequence. Many alterations to a gene's sequence are functionally neutral, permitting mutations to accumulate over time via neutral molecular evolution. Furthermore, selective pressures influence a gene's rate of sequence divergence. Genes experiencing stabilizing selection are evolutionarily constrained and exhibit slower change, while those under directional selection evolve more rapidly. These sequence differences provide a basis for phylogenetic analysis, enabling the study of gene evolution and the inference of evolutionary relationships among organisms.

input: The CBS Records Group was led very successfully by Clive Davis until his dismissal in 1972, after it was discovered that Davis has used CBS funds to finance his personal life, including an expensive bar mitzvah party for his son. He was replaced first by former head Goddard Lieberson, then in 1975 by the colourful and controversial lawyer Walter Yetnikoff, who led the company until 1990.
rewrite: Clive Davis effectively led the CBS Records Group until his 1972 termination for misappropriating corporate funds to support personal expenses, such as his son's lavish bar mitzvah. His initial successor was former head Goddard Lieberson, followed in 1975 by the flamboyant and contentious lawyer Walter Yetnikoff, who remained in leadership until 1990.

input: According to filings to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) by Thunder Bay Electronics (owner of CBC's Thunder Bay affiliate CKPR-DT) and Bell Media (owner of CBC affiliates CFTK-TV in Terrace and CJDC-TV in Dawson Creek),[citation needed] the CBC informed them that it will not extend its association with any of its private affiliates beyond August 31, 2011. Incidentally, that was also the date for analogue to digital transition in Canada. Given recent practice and the CBC's decision not to convert any retransmitters to digital, even in markets with populations in the hundreds in thousands, it is not expected that the CBC will open new transmitters to replace its affiliates, and indeed may pare back its existing transmitter network. However, in March 2011, CKPR announced that it had come to a programming agreement with the CBC, in which the station will continue to provide CBC programming in Thunder Bay for a period of five years. On March 16, 2012, Astral Media announced the sale of its assets to Bell Media, owners of CTV and CTV Two, for $3.38 billion with CFTK and CJDC included in the acquisition. Whether the stations will remain CBC affiliates or become owned-and-operated stations of CTV or CTV Two following the completion of the merger is undetermined.
rewrite: According to submissions made to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) by Thunder Bay Electronics, the owner of CBC affiliate CKPR-DT, and Bell Media, the owner of affiliates CFTK-TV and CJDC-TV, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) notified these entities that it would not renew its affiliation agreements beyond August 31, 2011. This date coincided with the national deadline for the analog-to-digital television transition. In light of the CBC’s recent operational approach, which has included a decision against converting its retransmitters to digital even in certain mid-sized markets, it is anticipated that the corporation will not establish new transmitters to supplant these affiliates and may instead reduce its existing transmitter infrastructure. Nevertheless, in March 2011, an exception emerged when CKPR-DT announced a five-year programming arrangement with the CBC to continue broadcasting its content in Thunder Bay. Subsequently, on March 16, 2012, Astral Media disclosed an agreement to sell its assets, including CFTK-TV and CJDC-TV, to Bell Media for $3.38 billion. The future status of these stations—whether they will maintain their CBC affiliations or transition to owned-and-operated stations within Bell Media’s CTV or CTV Two networks following the merger’s completion—remains unresolved.

input: Most samurai were bound by a code of honor and were expected to set an example for those below them. A notable part of their code is seppuku (切腹, seppuku?) or hara kiri, which allowed a disgraced samurai to regain his honor by passing into death, where samurai were still beholden to social rules. Whilst there are many romanticized characterizations of samurai behavior such as the writing of Bushido (武士道, Bushidō?) in 1905, studies of Kobudo and traditional Budō indicate that the samurai were as practical on the battlefield as were any other warrior.
rewrite: The samurai were predominantly governed by a strict code of honor, obligating them to model exemplary conduct for their social inferiors. A significant element of this code was seppuku, a ritual suicide permitting a disgraced warrior to restore honor through death, thus remaining subject to societal dictates even in demise. Although modern romanticized portrayals, such as the 1905 text *Bushidō*, are prevalent, historical analyses of Kobudō and traditional Budō reveal the samurai to have been fundamentally pragmatic combatants, comparable to warriors of other traditions.

input: In January 1920, Tito and his wife made a long and difficult journey home to Yugoslavia where he arrived in September. Upon his return, Broz joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. The CPY's influence on the political life of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was growing rapidly. In the 1920 elections the Communists won 59 seats in the parliament and became the third strongest party. Winning numerous local elections, they gained a stronghold in the second largest city of Zagreb, electing Svetozar Delić for mayor. After the assassination of Milorad Drašković, the Yugoslav Minister of the Interior, by a young communist on 2 August 1921, the CPY was declared illegal under the Yugoslav State Security Act of 1921. During 1920 and 1921 all Communist-won mandates were nullified. Broz continued his work underground despite pressure on Communists from the government. As 1921 began he moved to Veliko Trojstvo near Bjelovar and found work as a machinist. In 1925, Broz moved to Kraljevica where he started working at a shipyard. He was elected as a union leader and a year later he led a shipyard strike. He was fired and moved to Belgrade, where he worked in a train coach factory in Smederevska Palanka. He was elected as Workers' Commissary but was fired as soon as his CPY membership was revealed. Broz then moved to Zagreb, where he was appointed secretary of Metal Workers' Union of Croatia. In 1928, he became the Zagreb Branch Secretary of the CPY. In the same year he was arrested, tried in court for his illegal communist activities, and sent to jail. During his five years at Lepoglava prison he met Moša Pijade, who became his ideological mentor. After his release, he lived incognito and assumed numerous noms de guerre, among them "Walter" and "Tito".
rewrite:
In January 1920, Josip Broz, later known as Tito, embarked upon an arduous journey with his wife to return to Yugoslavia, arriving in September of that year. Shortly after his return, Broz became a member of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia (CPY). The party’s influence within the political sphere of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was expanding significantly. During the 1920 parliamentary elections, the CPY secured 59 seats, establishing itself as the third most substantial political force. Its success extended to local governance, most notably in Zagreb, the nation’s second-largest city, where it consolidated power and succeeded in electing Svetozar Delić as mayor.

This period of political ascendancy was abruptly curtailed following the assassination of Yugoslav Interior Minister Milorad Drašković by a young communist on 2 August 1921. In response, the government enacted the Yugoslav State Security Act of 1921, which proscribed the CPY and rendered it an illegal organization. Consequently, all electoral mandates won by communists in 1920 and 1921 were nullified. Forced underground, Broz persisted in his political activities despite increasing state repression. At the beginning of 1921, he relocated to Veliko Trojstvo near Bjelovar, obtaining employment as a machinist.

By 1925, Broz had moved to Kraljevica, where he found work in a shipyard. There, he was elected as a union official and, a year later, led a strike at the facility, resulting in his dismissal. He subsequently moved to Belgrade, working at a railway coach factory in Smederevska Palanka. Although elected as a Workers' Commissary, he was promptly discharged once his affiliation with the banned CPY was discovered. Broz then transferred to Zagreb, where he was appointed secretary of the Metal Workers' Union of Croatia. In 1928, his party responsibilities increased with his appointment as Secretary of the Zagreb branch of the CPY. That same year, however, he was arrested, prosecuted for illegal communist activities, and sentenced to imprisonment.

Broz served five years at Lepoglava prison, where he encountered Moša Pijade, a figure who would become a significant ideological mentor. Following his release, Broz operated clandestinely, adopting several pseudonyms for his covert work, including "Walter" and, ultimately, "Tito."

input: With financial support from Sanders and Hubbard, Bell hired Thomas Watson as his assistant,[N 15] and the two of them experimented with acoustic telegraphy. On June 2, 1875, Watson accidentally plucked one of the reeds and Bell, at the receiving end of the wire, heard the overtones of the reed; overtones that would be necessary for transmitting speech. That demonstrated to Bell that only one reed or armature was necessary, not multiple reeds. This led to the "gallows" sound-powered telephone, which could transmit indistinct, voice-like sounds, but not clear speech.
rewrite: With the financial backing of Sanders and Hubbard, Alexander Graham Bell employed Thomas Watson as his assistant, and together they conducted experiments in acoustic telegraphy. On June 2, 1875, Watson inadvertently plucked a reed. Bell, positioned at the wire's receiving terminus, discerned its overtones, which he recognized as essential for speech transmission. This proved that a single reed, rather than multiple reeds, was sufficient. The insight subsequently yielded the "gallows" telephone, a sound-powered device capable of conveying indistinct, vocal-like sounds, though not intelligible speech.

input: On August 18, 1970, the NAACP filed suit against Michigan state officials, including Governor William Milliken, charging de facto public school segregation. The NAACP argued that although schools were not legally segregated, the city of Detroit and its surrounding counties had enacted policies to maintain racial segregation in public schools. The NAACP also suggested a direct relationship between unfair housing practices and educational segregation, which followed segregated neighborhoods. The District Court held all levels of government accountable for the segregation in its ruling. The Sixth Circuit Court affirmed some of the decision, holding that it was the state's responsibility to integrate across the segregated metropolitan area. The U.S. Supreme Court took up the case February 27, 1974. The subsequent Milliken v. Bradley decision had wide national influence. In a narrow decision, the Court found that schools were a subject of local control and that suburbs could not be forced to solve problems in the city's school district.
rewrite: On August 18, 1970, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) initiated litigation against officials of the state of Michigan, including Governor William Milliken. The suit alleged the maintenance of de facto segregation within public schools, contending that policies enacted by Detroit and surrounding counties perpetuated racial separation despite the absence of de jure mandates. The NAACP further posited a causal linkage between discriminatory housing practices and resultant educational segregation, which mirrored existing residential patterns. The District Court ruling assigned liability for this segregation across multiple governmental levels. While the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed aspects of this judgment, emphasizing a state obligation to pursue integration across the metropolitan area, the U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari on February 27, 1974. Its subsequent ruling in *Milliken v. Bradley* proved nationally consequential. In a narrow decision, the Court determined that educational authority resided primarily with local jurisdictions, thereby precluding the mandatory inclusion of suburban districts in remedies for intra-city school segregation.

input: During his brief majority reign, Murad IV (1612–1640) reasserted central authority and recaptured Iraq (1639) from the Safavids. The resulting Treaty of Zuhab of that same year decisively parted the Caucasus and adjacent regions between the two neighbouring empires as it had already been defined in the 1555 Peace of Amasya. The Sultanate of women (1648–1656) was a period in which the mothers of young sultans exercised power on behalf of their sons. The most prominent women of this period were Kösem Sultan and her daughter-in-law Turhan Hatice, whose political rivalry culminated in Kösem's murder in 1651. During the Köprülü Era (1656–1703), effective control of the Empire was exercised by a sequence of Grand Viziers from the Köprülü family. The Köprülü Vizierate saw renewed military success with authority restored in Transylvania, the conquest of Crete completed in 1669, and expansion into Polish southern Ukraine, with the strongholds of Khotyn and Kamianets-Podilskyi and the territory of Podolia ceding to Ottoman control in 1676.
rewrite: The reign of Murad IV (r. 1623–1640) was marked by a reassertion of central imperial authority, most notably through the reconquest of Iraq from the Safavids in 1639. The subsequent Treaty of Zuhab (1639) formally partitioned the Caucasus and adjacent territories between the Ottoman and Safavid empires, thereby reaffirming the earlier border framework established by the 1555 Peace of Amasya. This was followed by the so-called Sultanate of Women (c. 1648–1656), a period during which queen mothers, principally Kösem Sultan and her daughter-in-law Turhan Hatice, wielded considerable political influence as regents for their sons; their rivalry ended with Kösem’s assassination in 1651. Subsequently, the Köprülü Era (1656–1703) witnessed a series of capable grand viziers from the same family directing imperial administration. This period saw significant military revitalization, including the consolidation of authority in Transylvania, the final conquest of Crete in 1669, and expansion into Polish territory. By 1676, this resulted in the acquisition of the key fortresses of Khotyn and Kamianets-Podilskyi, along with the region of Podolia.

input: The two nations planned a joint mission to dock the last US Apollo craft with a Soyuz, known as the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP). To prepare, the US designed a docking module for the Apollo that was compatible with the Soviet docking system, which allowed any of their craft to dock with any other (e.g. Soyuz/Soyuz as well as Soyuz/Salyut). The module was also necessary as an airlock to allow the men to visit each other's craft, which had incompatible cabin atmospheres. The USSR used the Soyuz 16 mission in December 1974 to prepare for ASTP.
rewrite: The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) constituted a collaborative mission to dock the final U.S. Apollo spacecraft with a Soviet Soyuz. In preparation, the United States developed a specialized docking module for Apollo, engineered to be compatible with the androgynous Soviet docking system, which permitted universal docking among their spacecraft. This module also functioned as an essential airlock, enabling crew transfers between the vessels despite their incompatible cabin atmospheres. Concurrently, the Soviet Union utilized the Soyuz 16 mission in December 1974 as a preparatory test for the ASTP.

input: In Canada, the largest Presbyterian denomination – and indeed the largest Protestant denomination – was the Presbyterian Church in Canada, formed in 1875 with the merger of four regional groups. In 1925, the United Church of Canada was formed by the majority of Presbyterians combining with the Methodist Church, Canada, and the Congregational Union of Canada. A sizable minority of Canadian Presbyterians, primarily in southern Ontario but also throughout the entire nation, withdrew, and reconstituted themselves as a non-concurring continuing Presbyterian body. They regained use of the original name in 1939.
rewrite: In Canada, the principal Presbyterian denomination, which also constituted the largest Protestant group, was the Presbyterian Church in Canada, established in 1875 through the union of four regional bodies. In 1925, a majority of its members united with the Methodist Church, Canada, and the Congregational Union of Canada to form the United Church of Canada. A substantial minority, concentrated in southern Ontario but present nationwide, dissented and reorganized as a continuing Presbyterian church, which reassumed the original name in 1939.

input: Mexico City remains the only Latin American city to host the Olympic Games, having held the Summer Olympics in 1968, winning bids against Buenos Aires, Lyon and Detroit. (This too will change thanks to Rio, 2016 Summer Games host). The city hosted the 1955 and 1975 Pan American Games, the last after Santiago and São Paulo withdrew.
