The ICF Flatwater Racing World Championships were hosted here in 1974 and 1994. Lucha libre is a Mexican style of wrestling, and is one of the more popular sports throughout the country. The main venues in the city are Arena México and Arena Coliseo.
rewrite: Mexico City retains its distinction as the sole Latin American host of the Olympic Games, having staged the Summer Olympics in 1968 after prevailing over bids from Buenos Aires, Lyon, and Detroit. This status will be altered following Rio de Janeiro's hosting of the 2016 Games. The city also organized the Pan American Games in 1955 and 1975, the latter after withdrawals by Santiago and São Paulo. It further hosted the ICF Flatwater Racing World Championships in 1974 and 1994. Lucha libre, a popular Mexican wrestling style, is prominently featured at the city's primary venues, Arena México and Arena Coliseo.

input: The Vietnam War is often regarded as a low point for the U.S. Army due to the use of drafted personnel, the unpopularity of the war with the American public, and frustrating restrictions placed on the military by American political leaders. While American forces had been stationed in the Republic of Vietnam since 1959, in intelligence & advising/training roles, they did not deploy in large numbers until 1965, after the Gulf of Tonkin Incident. American forces effectively established and maintained control of the "traditional" battlefield, however they struggled to counter the guerrilla hit and run tactics of the communist Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese Army. On a tactical level, American soldiers (and the U.S. military as a whole) did not lose a sizable battle.
rewrite: The Vietnam War is frequently characterized as a period of significant challenge for the United States Army, attributable to the reliance on conscripted soldiers, substantial domestic opposition to the conflict, and constraining rules of engagement imposed by political leadership. Although U.S. military advisors had been present in the Republic of Vietnam since 1959, a major conventional deployment commenced only in 1965 following the Gulf of Tonkin Incident. While American forces consistently dominated the conventional battlefield, they encountered persistent difficulties in countering the guerrilla warfare and attritional strategies employed by the Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese Army. Consequently, despite not suffering a single major tactical defeat in a sizable engagement, the overall military effort proved unsuccessful.

input: A second New Haven gastronomical claim to fame is Louis' Lunch, which is located in a small brick building on Crown Street and has been serving fast food since 1895. Though fiercely debated, the restaurant's founder Louis Lassen is credited by the Library of Congress with inventing the hamburger and steak sandwich. Louis' Lunch broils hamburgers, steak sandwiches and hot dogs vertically in original antique 1898 cast iron stoves using gridirons, patented by local resident Luigi Pieragostini in 1939, that hold the meat in place while it cooks.
rewrite: A second notable gastronomic establishment in New Haven is Louis' Lunch, situated in a modest brick building on Crown Street and operating since 1895. While its origins are contested, the Library of Congress credits founder Louis Lassen with inventing the hamburger and steak sandwich. The restaurant employs original 1898 cast iron stoves, broiling hamburgers, steak sandwiches, and hot dogs vertically. This method utilizes patented gridirons from 1939, designed by local resident Luigi Pieragostini, to secure the meat during cooking.

input: Some examples of social and religious transition ceremonies that can be found in the U.S., as well as in other cultures around the world, are Confirmation, Bar and Bat Mitzvahs, Quinceañeras, sweet sixteens, cotillions, and débutante balls. In other countries, initiation ceremonies play an important role, marking the transition into adulthood or the entrance into adolescence. This transition may be accompanied by obvious physical changes, which can vary from a change in clothing to tattoos and scarification. Furthermore, transitions into adulthood may also vary by gender, and specific rituals may be more common for males or for females. This illuminates the extent to which adolescence is, at least in part, a social construction; it takes shape differently depending on the cultural context, and may be enforced more by cultural practices or transitions than by universal chemical or biological physical changes.
rewrite: Various cultures, including that of the United States, employ specific rites of passage to mark social and religious transitions. Examples include Confirmation, Bar and Bat Mitzvahs, Quinceañeras, sweet sixteens, cotillions, and débutante balls. Globally, such initiation ceremonies often signify entry into adolescence or adulthood. These transitions can involve overt physical markers, ranging from altered attire to practices like tattooing or scarification. Furthermore, the rituals frequently differ by gender, with distinct ceremonies more prevalent for males or females. This variation underscores that adolescence is, to a significant degree, a social construct. Its manifestation is contingent upon cultural context, often shaped more powerfully by societal practices and prescribed transitions than by uniform biological or chemical maturation processes.

input: At Maecenas' insistence (according to the tradition) Virgil spent the ensuing years (perhaps 37–29 BC) on the long didactic hexameter poem called the Georgics (from Greek, "On Working the Earth") which he dedicated to Maecenas. The ostensible theme of the Georgics is instruction in the methods of running a farm. In handling this theme, Virgil follows in the didactic ("how to") tradition of the Greek poet Hesiod's Works and Days and several works of the later Hellenistic poets. The four books of the Georgics focus respectively on raising crops and trees (1 and 2), livestock and horses (3), and beekeeping and the qualities of bees (4). Well-known passages include the beloved Laus Italiae of Book 2, the prologue description of the temple in Book 3, and the description of the plague at the end of Book 3. Book 4 concludes with a long mythological narrative, in the form of an epyllion which describes vividly the discovery of beekeeping by Aristaeus and the story of Orpheus' journey to the underworld. Ancient scholars, such as Servius, conjectured that the Aristaeus episode replaced, at the emperor's request, a long section in praise of Virgil's friend, the poet Gallus, who was disgraced by Augustus, and who committed suicide in 26 BC.
rewrite: According to traditional accounts, Virgil composed the *Georgics*—a substantial didactic hexameter poem whose title derives from the Greek for “On Working the Earth”—over the following years (approximately 37–29 BC) at the urging of his patron Maecenas, to whom the work is dedicated. Its overt purpose is to provide instruction in agricultural practice. In treating this subject, Virgil aligns himself with the didactic tradition established by Hesiod’s *Works and Days* and elaborated by later Hellenistic poets. The poem is divided into four books: the first two address crop and arboriculture; the third covers livestock and equine husbandry; and the fourth focuses on apiculture and the nature of bees. Notable sections include the celebrated *Laus Italiae* in Book 2, the proemial temple description in Book 3, and the account of a plague concluding Book 3. Book 4 ends with an extended mythological narrative, an epyllion vividly relating Aristaeus’s discovery of beekeeping and Orpheus’s descent into the underworld. Ancient commentators, such as Servius, speculated that this Aristaeus episode was inserted at the emperor’s behest to replace a lengthy encomium to Virgil’s friend, the poet Gallus, who fell into disgrace under Augustus and died by suicide in 26 BC.

input: At times when a death sentence is affirmed on direct review, it is considered final. Yet, supplemental methods to attack the judgment, though less familiar than a typical appeal, do remain. These supplemental remedies are considered collateral review, that is, an avenue for upsetting judgments that have become otherwise final. Where the prisoner received his death sentence in a state-level trial, as is usually the case, the first step in collateral review is state collateral review. (If the case is a federal death penalty case, it proceeds immediately from direct review to federal habeas corpus.) Although all states have some type of collateral review, the process varies widely from state to state. Generally, the purpose of these collateral proceedings is to permit the prisoner to challenge his sentence on grounds that could not have been raised reasonably at trial or on direct review. Most often these are claims, such as ineffective assistance of counsel, which requires the court to consider new evidence outside the original trial record, something courts may not do in an ordinary appeal. State collateral review, though an important step in that it helps define the scope of subsequent review through federal habeas corpus, is rarely successful in and of itself. Only around 6 percent of death sentences are overturned on state collateral review. In 2010, the death sentences of 53 inmates were overturned as a result of legal appeals or high court reversals.
rewrite: When a death sentence is upheld on direct appeal, it attains finality. Nevertheless, supplementary avenues for challenging the judgment, distinct from the standard appellate process, persist. These supplementary mechanisms are termed collateral review, constituting a procedural route for contesting judgments that have otherwise become final. In instances where a capital sentence originates in a state court—the predominant scenario—the initial phase of collateral review occurs at the state level. (In federal death penalty cases, the process moves directly from direct review to federal habeas corpus proceedings.) While every state maintains some form of collateral review, its specific procedures differ considerably across jurisdictions. The general objective of such collateral proceedings is to allow a prisoner to contest a sentence based on claims that could not reasonably have been advanced during trial or on direct appeal. Typically, these involve allegations such as ineffective assistance of counsel, which necessitate judicial examination of evidence extrinsic to the original trial record—an action generally precluded in ordinary appeals. Although state collateral review serves a critical function in delineating the parameters for subsequent federal habeas corpus review, it is seldom successful in isolation. Approximately six percent of death sentences are vacated during state collateral review. Illustratively, in 2010, the sentences of fifty-three incarcerated individuals were overturned via legal appeals or reversals by higher courts.

input: Among the vast varieties of microorganisms, relatively few cause disease in otherwise healthy individuals. Infectious disease results from the interplay between those few pathogens and the defenses of the hosts they infect. The appearance and severity of disease resulting from any pathogen, depends upon the ability of that pathogen to damage the host as well as the ability of the host to resist the pathogen. However a host's immune system can also cause damage to the host itself in an attempt to control the infection. Clinicians therefore classify infectious microorganisms or microbes according to the status of host defenses - either as primary pathogens or as opportunistic pathogens:
rewrite: Among the diverse array of microorganisms, only a limited number are capable of causing disease in immunocompetent hosts. Infectious disease manifests through a complex interaction between these pathogens and the host's defensive mechanisms. The onset and severity of any resulting illness are determined both by the pathogen's capacity to inflict damage and the host's ability to mount resistance. Notably, the host's immune response can itself contribute to tissue damage while attempting to control the infection. Consequently, clinicians categorize infectious microbes based on host defense status, distinguishing between primary pathogens and opportunistic pathogens.

input: The Somali Telecommunication Association (STA), a watchdog organization that oversees the policy development and regulatory framework of Somalia's ICT sector, reported in 2006 that there were over half a million users of internet services within the territory. There were also 22 established ISPs and 234 cyber cafes, with an annual growth rate of 15.6%.
rewrite: In 2006, the Somali Telecommunication Association (STA), a regulatory body for ICT policy and frameworks, reported over 500,000 internet users in Somalia. The sector also comprised 22 Internet Service Providers and 234 cyber cafes, demonstrating an annual growth rate of 15.6%.

input: The major settlements in the ceremonial county are concentrated on the Fylde coast (the Blackpool Urban Area), and a belt of towns running west-east along the M65: Preston, Blackburn, Accrington, Burnley, Nelson and Colne. South of Preston are the towns of Leyland and Chorley; the three formed part of the Central Lancashire New Town designated in 1970. The north of the county is predominantly rural and sparsely populated, except for the towns of Lancaster and Morecambe which form a large conurbation of almost 100,000 people. Lancashire is home to a significant Asian population, numbering over 70,000 and 6% of the county's population, and concentrated largely in the former cotton mill towns in the south east.
rewrite: The principal settlements within the ceremonial county are primarily located along the Fylde coast, comprising the Blackpool Urban Area, and within a west-east corridor following the M65 motorway, encompassing Preston, Blackburn, Accrington, Burnley, Nelson, and Colne. South of Preston lie Leyland and Chorley; these three towns constituted part of the designated Central Lancashire New Town in 1970. The northern region is largely rural and sparsely populated, with the exception of the Lancaster-Morecambe conurbation, which houses approximately 100,000 residents. Lancashire also contains a substantial Asian population, exceeding 70,000 individuals and constituting six percent of the county's total, predominantly concentrated in the former cotton manufacturing towns of the south-east.

input: Romulus was credited with several religious institutions. He founded the Consualia festival, inviting the neighbouring Sabines to participate; the ensuing rape of the Sabine women by Romulus's men further embedded both violence and cultural assimilation in Rome's myth of origins. As a successful general, Romulus is also supposed to have founded Rome's first temple to Jupiter Feretrius and offered the spolia opima, the prime spoils taken in war, in the celebration of the first Roman triumph. Spared a mortal's death, Romulus was mysteriously spirited away and deified.
rewrite: Romulus is credited with establishing several foundational religious institutions. He instituted the Consualia festival, to which neighboring Sabines were invited; the subsequent abduction of the Sabine women integrated themes of violence and assimilation into Rome's origin myth. As a successful commander, he also reportedly founded the first temple to Jupiter Feretrius and dedicated the *spolia opima*, the foremost spoils of war, during the inaugural Roman triumph. Ultimately, he was spared a mortal death, mysteriously vanished, and was deified.

input: According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Uniform Crime Reports, in 2010 the Raleigh Police Department and other agencies in the city reported 1,740 incidents of violent crime and 12,995 incidents of property crime – far below both the national average and the North Carolina average. Of the violent crimes reported, 14 were murders, 99 were forcible rapes and 643 were robberies. Aggravated assault accounted for 984 of the total violent crimes. Property crimes included burglaries which accounted for 3,021, larcenies for 9,104 and arson for 63 of the total number of incidents. Motor vehicle theft accounted for 870 incidents out of the total.
rewrite: Data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Uniform Crime Reports for 2010 indicate that law enforcement agencies in Raleigh, including the Raleigh Police Department, documented 1,740 violent crimes and 12,995 property crimes. These figures were substantially lower than both the national and North Carolina state averages. The violent crime total comprised 14 murders, 99 forcible rapes, 643 robberies, and 984 aggravated assaults. Among property crimes, 3,021 were burglaries, 9,104 were larcenies, 63 were arsons, and 870 were motor vehicle thefts.

input: The earliest Greek philosophers, known as the pre-Socratics, provided competing answers to the question found in the myths of their neighbors: "How did the ordered cosmos in which we live come to be?" The pre-Socratic philosopher Thales (640-546 BC), dubbed the "father of science", was the first to postulate non-supernatural explanations for natural phenomena, for example, that land floats on water and that earthquakes are caused by the agitation of the water upon which the land floats, rather than the god Poseidon. Thales' student Pythagoras of Samos founded the Pythagorean school, which investigated mathematics for its own sake, and was the first to postulate that the Earth is spherical in shape. Leucippus (5th century BC) introduced atomism, the theory that all matter is made of indivisible, imperishable units called atoms. This was greatly expanded by his pupil Democritus.
rewrite: The earliest Greek philosophers, termed the pre-Socratics, sought to provide rational, competing accounts for a fundamental question inherited from mythological traditions: the origin of the ordered cosmos. Pre-Socratic thinker Thales (c. 640-546 BC), often called the "father of science," pioneered non-mythological explanations for natural phenomena. He proposed, for instance, that land floats on water and that earthquakes result from the agitation of this water, displacing the earlier attribution to the god Poseidon. His student, Pythagoras of Samos, established a school that pursued mathematics intrinsically and first postulated a spherical Earth. Subsequently, Leucippus (5th century BC) introduced atomism, the theory that all matter consists of indivisible, imperishable atoms, a doctrine substantially developed by his pupil Democritus.

Although he avoids the controversial topic of human origins in the rest of the book so as not to prejudice readers against his theory, here he ventures a cautious hint that psychology would be put on a new foundation and that "Light will be thrown on the origin of man". Darwin ends with a passage that became well known and much quoted:
rewrite: In the concluding chapter, Darwin recapitulates key arguments from preceding sections, expressing hope that his theory will instigate transformative shifts across natural history. While deliberately omitting the contentious subject of human origins elsewhere to avoid prejudicing readers, he cautiously suggests that psychology may be established upon a novel foundation and that "light will be thrown on the origin of man." The work closes with a passage that subsequently achieved widespread recognition and frequent citation.

input: Apple was initially reluctant to embrace mice with multiple buttons and scroll wheels. Macs did not natively support pointing devices that featured multiple buttons, even from third parties, until Mac OS X arrived in 2001. Apple continued to offer only single button mice, in both wired and Bluetooth wireless versions, until August 2005, when it introduced the Mighty Mouse. While it looked like a traditional one-button mouse, it actually had four buttons and a scroll ball, capable of independent x- and y-axis movement. A Bluetooth version followed in July 2006. In October 2009, Apple introduced the Magic Mouse, which uses multi-touch gesture recognition (similar to that of the iPhone) instead of a physical scroll wheel or ball. It is available only in a wireless configuration, but the wired Mighty Mouse (re-branded as "Apple Mouse") is still available as an alternative. Since 2010, Apple has also offered the Magic Trackpad as a means to control Macintosh desktop computers in a way similar to laptops.
rewrite: Apple exhibited a prolonged reluctance to adopt multi-button and scroll-wheel mice. Until the release of Mac OS X in 2001, the Macintosh operating system lacked native support for pointing devices featuring multiple buttons, including those from third-party manufacturers. The company persisted in offering exclusively single-button mice, in both wired and Bluetooth wireless forms, until August 2005. At that time, it introduced the Mighty Mouse. Although its design resembled a conventional single-button mouse, it incorporated four buttons and a scroll ball capable of independent movement along the x- and y-axes. A Bluetooth version was released in July 2006. Subsequently, in October 2009, Apple launched the Magic Mouse, which replaced physical scrolling mechanisms with multi-touch gesture recognition technology, akin to that of the iPhone. This model is exclusively wireless, though the wired Mighty Mouse, re-branded as the "Apple Mouse," remains available. Since 2010, Apple has also provided the Magic Trackpad, enabling gesture-based control for Macintosh desktop computers similar to laptop interfaces.

input: The year 1789 brought the French Revolution and with it the first division of Alsace into the départements of Haut- and Bas-Rhin. Alsatians played an active role in the French Revolution. On 21 July 1789, after receiving news of the Storming of the Bastille in Paris, a crowd of people stormed the Strasbourg city hall, forcing the city administrators to flee and putting symbolically an end to the feudal system in Alsace. In 1792, Rouget de Lisle composed in Strasbourg the Revolutionary marching song "La Marseillaise" (as Marching song for the Army of the Rhine), which later became the anthem of France. "La Marseillaise" was played for the first time in April of that year in front of the mayor of Strasbourg Philippe-Frédéric de Dietrich. Some of the most famous generals of the French Revolution also came from Alsace, notably Kellermann, the victor of Valmy, Kléber, who led the armies of the French Republic in Vendée and Westermann, who also fought in the Vendée.
rewrite: The year 1789 marked the onset of the French Revolution and the subsequent initial administrative partition of Alsace into the départements of Haut-Rhin and Bas-Rhin. Alsatian citizens actively participated in the revolutionary events. Following reports of the Storming of the Bastille in Paris, a crowd assailed the Strasbourg city hall on 21 July 1789, compelling municipal authorities to flee and symbolically terminating the feudal regime in the region. In 1792, Rouget de Lisle composed the revolutionary anthem "La Marseillaise" in Strasbourg, originally titled "Chant de guerre pour l'Armée du Rhin." It was first performed in April of that year at the residence of Strasbourg's mayor, Philippe-Frédéric de Dietrich. Furthermore, Alsace produced several distinguished generals of the Revolution, including Kellermann, victor at Valmy; Kléber, who commanded republican armies in the Vendée; and Westermann, who also campaigned there.

input: As with most ancient civilizations, Rome's military served the triple purposes of securing its borders, exploiting peripheral areas through measures such as imposing tribute on conquered peoples, and maintaining internal order. From the outset, Rome's military typified this pattern and the majority of Rome's wars were characterized by one of two types. The first is the foreign war, normally begun as a counter-offensive or defense of an ally. The second is the civil war, which plagued the Roman Republic in its final century. Roman armies were not invincible, despite their formidable reputation and host of victories. Over the centuries the Romans "produced their share of incompetents" who led Roman armies into catastrophic defeats. Nevertheless, it was generally the fate of the greatest of Rome's enemies, such as Pyrrhus and Hannibal, to win early battles but lose the war. The history of Rome's campaigning is, if nothing else, a history of obstinate persistence overcoming appalling losses.
rewrite: The military of ancient Rome, like that of most early civilizations, fulfilled three primary functions: securing territorial frontiers, extracting resources from peripheral regions through mechanisms such as the imposition of tribute, and preserving internal stability. From its origins, the Roman military exemplified this model, and its conflicts predominantly fell into two categories. The first consisted of foreign wars, typically initiated as defensive counter-offensives or interventions on behalf of allies. The second category was civil war, which afflicted the Roman Republic extensively during its final century. Despite their formidable reputation and numerous victories, Roman forces were not invincible. Across centuries, Roman command produced its share of incompetence, leading to catastrophic defeats. However, even Rome's most formidable adversaries, including Pyrrhus and Hannibal, generally met the fate of winning initial battles but ultimately losing the broader conflict. Consequently, the history of Roman military campaigns is, above all, a testament to obstinate persistence triumphing over severe losses.

input: The large magnitude of solar energy available makes it a highly appealing source of electricity. The United Nations Development Programme in its 2000 World Energy Assessment found that the annual potential of solar energy was 1,575–49,837 exajoules (EJ). This is several times larger than the total world energy consumption, which was 559.8 EJ in 2012.
rewrite: Solar energy's substantial potential renders it an attractive electricity source. According to the 2000 UN Development Programme World Energy Assessment, its annual potential ranges from 1,575 to 49,837 exajoules (EJ). This vastly exceeds global consumption, which was 559.8 EJ in 2012.

input: A working group consisting of Leon van de Kerkhof (The Netherlands), Gerhard Stoll (Germany), Leonardo Chiariglione (Italy), Yves-François Dehery (France), Karlheinz Brandenburg (Germany) and James D. Johnston (USA) took ideas from ASPEC, integrated the filter bank from Layer 2, added some of their own ideas and created MP3, which was designed to achieve the same quality at 128 kbit/s as MP2 at 192 kbit/s.
rewrite: An international working group comprising Leon van de Kerkhof (Netherlands), Gerhard Stoll and Karlheinz Brandenburg (Germany), Leonardo Chiariglione (Italy), Yves-François Dehery (France), and James D. Johnston (USA) developed the MP3 format. This synthesis integrated concepts from ASPEC, incorporated the Layer 2 filter bank, and introduced novel contributions. The design objective was to match the audio quality of MP2 at 192 kbit/s using only 128 kbit/s.

input: Chanakya, 4th Century BC Indian political philosopher. The Arthashastra provides an account of the science of politics for a wise ruler, policies for foreign affairs and wars, the system of a spy state and surveillance and economic stability of the state. Chanakya quotes several authorities including Bruhaspati, Ushanas, Prachetasa Manu, Parasara, and Ambi, and described himself as a descendant of a lineage of political philosophers, with his father Chanaka being his immediate predecessor. Another influential extant Indian treatise on political philosophy is the Sukra Neeti. An example of a code of law in ancient India is the Manusmṛti or Laws of Manu.
rewrite: Chanakya, a fourth-century BCE Indian political philosopher, authored the *Arthashastra*. This treatise systematically outlines the science of governance for an effective ruler, encompassing foreign policy, military strategy, the administration of espionage and surveillance, and the maintenance of economic stability. Chanakya references prior authorities such as Brihaspati, Ushanas, and Manu, while identifying himself within a philosophical lineage, noting his father Chanaka as his direct predecessor. Other significant ancient Indian works include the *Sukra Neeti* on statecraft and the *Manusmṛti* (Laws of Manu) as a foundational legal code.

input: Sessions for West's sixth solo effort begin to take shape in early 2013 in his own personal loft's living room at a Paris hotel. Determined to "undermine the commercial", he once again brought together close collaborators and attempted to incorporate Chicago drill, dancehall, acid house, and industrial music. Primarily inspired by architecture, West's perfectionist tendencies led him to contact producer Rick Rubin fifteen days shy of its due date to strip down the record's sound in favor of a more minimalist approach. Initial promotion of his sixth album included worldwide video projections of the album's music and live television performances. Yeezus, West's sixth album, was released June 18, 2013 to rave reviews from critics. It became the rapper's sixth consecutive number one debut, but also marked his lowest solo opening week sales. Def Jam issued "Black Skinhead" to radio in July 2013 as the album's lead single. On September 6, 2013, Kanye West announced he would be headlining his first solo tour in five years, to support Yeezus, with fellow American rapper Kendrick Lamar accompanying him along the way.
rewrite: The initial recording sessions for Kanye West's sixth solo studio album commenced in early 2013, conducted within the living area of his private loft at a Paris hotel. With a stated intent to subvert commercial expectations, West assembled a core group of frequent collaborators, pursuing a sonic amalgamation of Chicago drill, dancehall, acid house, and industrial music. Drawing primary inspiration from architectural concepts, West's perfectionism prompted him to enlist producer Rick Rubin merely two weeks prior to the project's deadline to radically simplify the recordings, adopting a starkly minimalist aesthetic. Promotional activities preceding the album's release included global video projections of its visual content and televised live performances. The album, titled *Yeezus*, was released on June 18, 2013, to widespread critical acclaim. It achieved West's sixth consecutive debut at number one on the Billboard 200 chart, albeit with his lowest first-week sales for a solo project. The lead single, "Black Skinhead," was serviced to radio by Def Jam Recordings in July 2013. Subsequently, on September 6, 2013, West announced a solo concert tour—his first in five years—in support of *Yeezus*, with fellow American rapper Kendrick Lamar scheduled as the supporting act.

input: In addition to the Jazz Festival (described above), New Haven serves as the home city of the annual International Festival of Arts and Ideas. New Haven's Saint Patrick's Day parade, which began in 1842, is New England's oldest St. Patty's Day parade and draws the largest crowds of any one-day spectator event in Connecticut. The St. Andrew the Apostle Italian Festival has taken place in the historic Wooster Square neighborhood every year since 1900. Other parishes in the city celebrate the Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua and a carnival in honor of St. Bernadette Soubirous. New Haven celebrates Powder House Day every April on the New Haven Green to commemorate the city's entrance into the Revolutionary War. The annual Wooster Square Cherry Blossom Festival commemorates the 1973 planting of 72 Yoshino Japanese Cherry Blossom trees by the New Haven Historic Commission in collaboration with the New Haven Parks Department and residents of the neighborhood. The Festival now draws well over 5,000 visitors. The Film Fest New Haven has been held annually since 1995.
rewrite: Beyond the previously noted Jazz Festival, New Haven hosts the annual International Festival of Arts and Ideas. The city’s Saint Patrick’s Day parade, established in 1842, is the oldest such observance in New England and attracts the largest single-day spectator audience in Connecticut. Since 1900, the historic Wooster Square neighborhood has annually held the St. Andrew the Apostle Italian Festival. Additional parish celebrations include the Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua and a carnival honoring St. Bernadette Soubirous. Each April, Powder House Day is observed on the New Haven Green to mark the city’s entry into the Revolutionary War. The Wooster Square Cherry Blossom Festival commemorates the 1973 planting of seventy-two Yoshino cherry trees by the New Haven Historic Commission, in cooperation with the Parks Department and local residents; it now draws upwards of 5,000 attendees. Furthermore, the Film Fest New Haven has occurred annually since 1995.

input: The Palacio Taranco is located in front of the Plaza Zabala, in the heart of Ciudad Vieja. It was erected in the early 20th century as the residence of the Ortiz Taranco brothers on the ruins of Montevideo's first theatre (of 1793), during a period in which the architectural style was influenced by French architecture. The palace was designed by French architects Charles Louis Girault and Jules Chifflot León who also designed the Petit Palais and the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. It passed to the city from the heirs of the Tarancos in 1943, along with its precious collection of Uruguayan furniture and draperies and was deemed by the city as an ideal place for a museum; in 1972 it became the Museum of Decorative Arts of Montevideo and in 1975 it became a National Heritage Site. The Decorative Arts Museum has an important collection of European paintings and decorative arts, ancient Greek and Roman art and Islamic ceramics of the 10th–18th century from the area of present-day Iran. The palace is often used as a meeting place by the Uruguayan government.
rewrite: Situated facing Plaza Zabala in the heart of Montevideo's Ciudad Vieja, the Palacio Taranco was constructed in the early twentieth century as a residence for the Ortiz Taranco brothers. Its site was previously occupied by the city's first theatre, established in 1793. The palace's design reflects the prevailing French architectural influence of the period, conceived by the French architects Charles Louis Girault and Jules Chifflot León, notable for their work on Paris's Petit Palais and Arc de Triomphe. Acquired by the city from the Taranco heirs in 1943, along with its significant collection of Uruguayan furniture and draperies, the building was subsequently repurposed as a museum. It formally opened as the Museum of Decorative Arts of Montevideo in 1972 and was declared a National Heritage Site in 1975. The museum's holdings comprise important European paintings and decorative arts, Greco-Roman antiquities, and Islamic ceramics from the tenth to eighteenth centuries originating in present-day Iran. The palace also frequently serves as a venue for official governmental functions.

input: Mexico City offers an immense and varied consumer retail market, ranging from basic foods to ultra high-end luxury goods. Consumers may buy in fixed indoor markets, mobile markets (tianguis), from street vendors, from downtown shops in a street dedicated to a certain type of good, in convenience stores and traditional neighborhood stores, in modern supermarkets, in warehouse and membership stores and the shopping centers that they anchor, in department stores, big-box stores and in modern shopping malls.
rewrite: Mexico City presents a vast and diverse retail market, encompassing goods from essential foodstuffs to premium luxury items. Consumers access this market through numerous channels, including fixed and mobile markets (tianguis), street vendors, specialized commercial streets, traditional neighborhood shops, convenience stores, supermarkets, warehouse clubs, department stores, big-box retailers, and contemporary shopping malls anchored by these larger establishments.

input: The territory now contained within Bronx County was originally part of Westchester County, one of the 12 original counties of the English Province of New York. The present Bronx County was contained in the town of Westchester and parts of the towns of Yonkers, Eastchester, and Pelham. In 1846, a new town, West Farms, was created by division of Westchester; in turn, in 1855, the town of Morrisania was created from West Farms. In 1873, the town of Kingsbridge (roughly corresponding to the modern Bronx neighborhoods of Kingsbridge, Riverdale, and Woodlawn) was established within the former borders of Yonkers.
rewrite: The area comprising present-day Bronx County was initially situated within Westchester County, one of the twelve original counties of the English Province of New York. This territory was incorporated within the town of Westchester and sections of the towns of Yonkers, Eastchester, and Pelham. In 1846, the town of West Farms was formed from a partition of Westchester; subsequently, the town of Morrisania was created from West Farms in 1855. The town of Kingsbridge, established in 1873 within the prior bounds of Yonkers, corresponds approximately to the contemporary Bronx neighborhoods of Kingsbridge, Riverdale, and Woodlawn.

input: The cuisine of Switzerland is multifaceted. While some dishes such as fondue, raclette or rösti are omnipresent through the country, each region developed its own gastronomy according to the differences of climate and languages.  Traditional Swiss cuisine uses ingredients similar to those in other European countries, as well as unique dairy products and cheeses such as Gruyère or Emmental, produced in the valleys of Gruyères and Emmental. The number of fine-dining establishments is high, particularly in western Switzerland.
rewrite: Swiss cuisine exhibits considerable regional diversity. Although dishes like fondue, raclette, and rösti are nationally recognized, distinct regional gastronomies have evolved, influenced by climatic and linguistic variations. Utilizing common European ingredients alongside unique local dairy products and cheeses—such as Gruyère and Emmental from their eponymous valleys—the cuisine maintains a strong traditional character. Furthermore, Switzerland, especially its western region, hosts a significant concentration of fine-dining establishments.

input: Extensive and diverse public spending is, in itself, inherently at risk of cronyism, kickbacks, and embezzlement. Complicated regulations and arbitrary, unsupervised official conduct exacerbate the problem. This is one argument for privatization and deregulation. Opponents of privatization see the argument as ideological. The argument that corruption necessarily follows from the opportunity is weakened by the existence of countries with low to non-existent corruption but large public sectors, like the Nordic countries. These countries score high on the Ease of Doing Business Index, due to good and often simple regulations, and have rule of law firmly established. Therefore, due to their lack of corruption in the first place, they can run large public sectors without inducing political corruption. Recent evidence that takes both the size of expenditures and regulatory complexity into account has found that high-income democracies with more expansive state sectors do indeed have higher levels of corruption.
rewrite: Extensive and diverse public expenditure inherently presents opportunities for cronyism, kickbacks, and embezzlement. This risk is exacerbated by complex regulatory frameworks and arbitrary, unsupervised administrative conduct, forming a common argument in favor of privatization and deregulation. Critics, however, often dismiss this reasoning as ideological. Its premise—that the mere opportunity for corruption guarantees its occurrence—is challenged by nations, such as the Nordic countries, which maintain large public sectors alongside low to non-existent corruption levels. These states achieve high scores on indices like the Ease of Doing Business Index, underpinned by transparent, often streamlined regulations and a firmly entrenched rule of law. Their established institutional integrity permits expansive public sectors without inducing systemic political corruption. Nonetheless, recent empirical analyses, controlling for both expenditure size and regulatory complexity, indicate that among high-income democracies, more expansive state sectors correlate with higher observed levels of corruption.

input: Notre Dame's conference affiliations for all of its sports except football and fencing changed in July 2013 as a result of major conference realignment, and its fencing affiliation will change in July 2014. The Irish left the Big East for the ACC during a prolonged period of instability in the Big East; while they maintain their football independence, they have committed to play five games per season against ACC opponents. In ice hockey, the Irish were forced to find a new conference home after the Big Ten Conference's decision to add the sport in 2013–14 led to a cascade of conference moves that culminated in the dissolution of the school's former hockey home, the Central Collegiate Hockey Association, after the 2012–13 season. Notre Dame moved its hockey team to Hockey East. After Notre Dame joined the ACC, the conference announced it would add fencing as a sponsored sport beginning in the 2014–15 school year. There are many theories behind the adoption of the athletics moniker but it is known that the Fighting Irish name was used in the early 1920s with respect to the football team and was popularized by alumnus Francis Wallace in his New York Daily News columns. The official colors of Notre Dame are Navy Blue and Gold Rush which are worn in competition by its athletic teams. In addition, the color green is often worn because of the Fighting Irish nickname. The Notre Dame Leprechaun is the mascot of the athletic teams. Created by Theodore W. Drake in 1964, the leprechaun was first used on the football pocket schedule and later on the football program covers. The leprechaun was featured on the cover of Time in November 1964 and gained national exposure.
rewrite:
In July 2013, the University of Notre Dame altered its conference affiliations for all sports except football and fencing, a shift precipitated by widespread conference realignment. Its fencing affiliation subsequently changed in July 2014. This restructuring involved Notre Dame’s departure from the Big East Conference for the Atlantic Coast Conference (ACC), a move undertaken during a period of significant instability within the Big East. While maintaining its historic independence in football, the university committed to scheduling five games per season against ACC opponents. Concurrently, the institution’s ice hockey program was compelled to secure a new conference affiliation. This necessity arose following the Big Ten Conference’s 2013–14 adoption of hockey, which triggered a series of realignments culminating in the dissolution of Notre Dame’s former league, the Central Collegiate Hockey Association, after the 2012–13 season. Consequently, the hockey team relocated to Hockey East. Subsequent to Notre Dame’s ACC membership, the conference announced it would sponsor fencing as an official sport beginning in the 2014–15 academic year.

The athletics program’s identity is deeply rooted in its "Fighting Irish" moniker, a name applied to the football team by the early 1920s and later popularized through the New York Daily News columns of alumnus Francis Wallace. The official university colors are Navy Blue and Gold Rush, which are worn by athletic teams in competition. Reflecting the Irish heritage implied by the nickname, the color green is also frequently incorporated into athletic uniforms. Serving as the official mascot for all athletic teams is the Notre Dame Leprechaun. Designed by Theodore W. Drake in 1964, the leprechaun first appeared on football pocket schedules and later on program covers. The mascot gained national prominence following its feature on the cover of *Time* magazine in November 1964.

input: During colonial times, Edenton served as the state capital beginning in 1722, and New Bern was selected as the capital in 1766. Construction of Tryon Palace, which served as the residence and offices of the provincial governor William Tryon, began in 1767 and was completed in 1771. In 1788 Raleigh was chosen as the site of the new capital, as its central location protected it from attacks from the coast. Officially established in 1792 as both county seat and state capital, the city was named after Sir Walter Raleigh, sponsor of Roanoke, the "lost colony" on Roanoke Island.
rewrite: Edenton functioned as North Carolina’s colonial capital from 1722 until 1766, when New Bern assumed that role. Construction of Tryon Palace, the official residence and administrative headquarters of Provincial Governor William Tryon, commenced in 1767 and concluded in 1771. In 1788, Raleigh was selected as the new capital due to its central, defensible inland location, safe from coastal assault. Formally established in 1792 as both state capital and county seat, the city was named for Sir Walter Raleigh, patron of the Roanoke Island settlement known as the "lost colony."

input: Carnivore and herbivore diets are contrasting, with basic nitrogen and carbon proportions vary for their particular foods. "The nitrogen content of plant tissues averages about 2%, while in fungi, animals, and bacteria it averages about 5% to 10%." Many herbivores rely on bacterial fermentation to create digestible nutrients from indigestible plant cellulose, while obligate carnivores must eat animal meats to obtain certain vitamins or nutrients their bodies cannot otherwise synthesize. All animals' diets must provide sufficient amounts of the basic building blocks they need, up to the point where their particular biology can synthesize the rest. Animal tissue contains chemical compounds, such as water, carbohydrates (sugar, starch, and fiber), amino acids (in proteins), fatty acids (in lipids), and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). These compounds in turn consist of elements such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, manganese, and so on. All of these chemical compounds and elements occur in various forms and combinations (e.g. hormones, vitamins, phospholipids, hydroxyapatite).
rewrite: Carnivorous and herbivorous diets are fundamentally distinct, with differing ratios of nitrogen and carbon reflective of their respective food sources. Notably, plant tissues exhibit an average nitrogen content of approximately 2%, whereas fungi, animals, and bacteria average between 5% and 10%. Herbivores frequently depend on microbial fermentation to derive digestible nutrients from recalcitrant plant cellulose. Conversely, obligate carnivores require animal flesh to procure specific vitamins and nutrients they cannot endogenously synthesize. All animal diets must supply essential biochemical precursors in adequate quantities, complementing the organism's inherent biosynthetic capabilities. Animal tissue comprises compounds including water, carbohydrates (sugars, starches, fiber), amino acids (in proteins), fatty acids (in lipids), and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). These compounds are constituted from elements such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, and manganese. Collectively, these chemicals and elements manifest in diverse forms and combinations—including hormones, vitamins, phospholipids, and hydroxyapatite—to fulfill biological functions.

input: The Theater District is a 17-block area in the center of downtown Houston that is home to the Bayou Place entertainment complex, restaurants, movies, plazas, and parks. Bayou Place is a large multilevel building containing full-service restaurants, bars, live music, billiards, and Sundance Cinema. The Bayou Music Center stages live concerts, stage plays, and stand-up comedy. Space Center Houston is the official visitors' center of NASA's Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center. The Space Center has many interactive exhibits including moon rocks, a shuttle simulator, and presentations about the history of NASA's manned space flight program. Other tourist attractions include the Galleria (Texas's largest shopping mall, located in the Uptown District), Old Market Square, the Downtown Aquarium, and Sam Houston Race Park.
rewrite: Situated within a seventeen-block radius in central downtown Houston, the Theater District encompasses the Bayou Place entertainment complex alongside various dining establishments, cinemas, plazas, and parks. Bayou Place itself is a substantial multilevel structure featuring full-service restaurants, bars, venues for live music, billiard halls, and the Sundance Cinema. The adjacent Bayou Music Center hosts live concerts, theatrical productions, and comedy performances. Nearby, Space Center Houston, the official visitor center for NASA's Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center, presents interactive exhibits such as lunar samples, a shuttle simulator, and historical presentations on manned spaceflight. Additional notable attractions include the Galleria—Texas's largest mall in the Uptown District—Old Market Square, the Downtown Aquarium, and Sam Houston Race Park.

input: During the Age of Enlightenment, philosophers such as John Locke advocated the principle in their writings, whereas others, such as Thomas Hobbes, strongly opposed it. Montesquieu was one of the foremost supporters of separating the legislature, the executive, and the judiciary. His writings considerably influenced the opinions of the framers of the United States Constitution.
rewrite: Enlightenment philosophers debated the separation of powers; Locke advocated for it, while Hobbes opposed it. Montesquieu emerged as a principal proponent of dividing legislative, executive, and judicial authority. His theories substantially influenced the framers of the U.S. Constitution.

input: The strength of the Viking influence on Old English appears from the fact that the indispensable elements of the language - pronouns, modals, comparatives, pronominal adverbs (like "hence" and "together"), conjunctions and prepositions - show the most marked Danish influence; the best evidence of Scandinavian influence appears in the extensive word borrowings for, as Jespersen indicates, no texts exist in either Scandinavia or in Northern England from this time to give certain evidence of an influence on syntax. The change to Old English from Old Norse was substantive, pervasive, and of a democratic character. Old Norse and Old English resembled each other closely like cousins and with some words in common, they roughly understood each other; in time the inflections melted away and the analytic pattern emerged. It is most “important to recognize that in many words the English and Scandinavian language differed chiefly in their inflectional elements. The body of the word was so nearly the same in the two languages that only the endings would put obstacles in the way of mutual understanding. In the mixed population which existed in the Danelaw these endings must have led to much confusion, tending gradually to become obscured and finally lost.” This blending of peoples and languages happily resulted in “simplifying English grammar.”
rewrite: The extent of Viking linguistic influence on Old English is evident in the profound impact upon its core grammatical components, including pronouns, modal verbs, comparative forms, pronominal adverbs (e.g., "hence," "together"), conjunctions, and prepositions. The most definitive evidence of this Scandinavian influence, however, lies in the substantial number of borrowed lexical items. As noted by Jespersen, the absence of contemporaneous texts from either Scandinavia or Northern England precludes definitive conclusions regarding syntactic influence. The shift from Old Norse to Old English was substantive, pervasive, and democratically diffused through population admixture. The two languages bore a close familial resemblance, sharing common vocabulary to a degree that facilitated rudimentary mutual intelligibility. Over time, inflections diminished, giving way to a more analytic structure. Critically, the lexical roots of many words were often nearly identical, with primary differentiation residing in inflectional endings. Within the ethnically mixed Danelaw region, these divergent endings likely generated considerable confusion, progressively leading to their obscuration and eventual loss. This convergence of peoples and languages ultimately precipitated a significant simplification of English grammatical morphology.

input: The teachings on the Four Noble Truths are regarded as central to the teachings of Buddhism, and are said to provide a conceptual framework for Buddhist thought. These four truths explain the nature of dukkha (suffering, anxiety, unsatisfactoriness), its causes, and how it can be overcome. The four truths are:[note 4]
rewrite: The Four Noble Truths constitute a foundational doctrine within Buddhism, offering a conceptual framework for its teachings. They delineate the nature, origin, cessation, and path leading to the cessation of dukkha (suffering or unsatisfactoriness).

input: Another study of dogs' roles in families showed many dogs have set tasks or routines undertaken as family members, the most common of which was helping with the washing-up by licking the plates in the dishwasher, and bringing in the newspaper from the lawn. Increasingly, human family members are engaging in activities centered on the perceived needs and interests of the dog, or in which the dog is an integral partner, such as dog dancing and dog yoga.
rewrite: Research into canine familial roles indicates that many dogs perform designated tasks or routines, most notably assisting with dishwashing by licking plates in the dishwasher and retrieving newspapers from the lawn. Concurrently, human family members are increasingly participating in activities, such as dog dancing and yoga, which are structured around the perceived needs of the dog or in which the dog serves as an integral partner.

input: The Ismailis differ from Twelvers because they had living imams for centuries after the last Twelver Imam went into concealment. They followed Isma'il ibn Jafar, elder brother of Musa al-Kadhim, as the rightful Imam after his father Ja'far al-Sadiq. The Ismailis believe that whether Imam Ismail did or did not die before Imam Ja'far, he had passed on the mantle of the imamate to his son Muḥammad ibn Ismail as the next imam. Thus, their line of imams is as follows (the years of their individual imamats during the Common Era are given in brackets):
rewrite: The Ismaili tradition diverges from Twelver Shi'ism by maintaining a continuous line of living imams following the occultation of the final Twelver Imam. This succession originates from their recognition of Isma'il ibn Jafar, rather than his brother Musa al-Kadhim, as the legitimate successor to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq. Ismaili doctrine holds that the imamate was transmitted from Isma'il to his son Muḥammad ibn Ismail, irrespective of the precise timing of Isma'il's death. input: Chopin's qualities as a pianist and composer were recognized by many of his fellow musicians. Schumann named a piece for him in his suite Carnaval, and Chopin later dedicated his Ballade No. 2 in F major to Schumann. Elements of Chopin's music can be traced in many of Liszt's later works. Liszt later transcribed for piano six of Chopin's Polish songs. A less fraught friendship was with Alkan, with whom he discussed elements of folk music, and who was deeply affected by Chopin's death.
rewrite: Chopin’s stature as both pianist and composer was widely acknowledged by his contemporaries. Schumann honored him with a movement in *Carnaval*, and Chopin reciprocated by dedicating his Ballade No. 2 in F major to Schumann. Liszt incorporated elements of Chopin’s style into later works and transcribed six of his Polish songs. Additionally, Chopin maintained a cordial relationship with Alkan, with whom he explored folk music; Alkan was profoundly moved by Chopin’s passing.

input: Whilst filming in Mexico City, speculation in the media claimed that the script had been altered to accommodate the demands of Mexican authorities—reportedly influencing details of the scene and characters, casting choices, and modifying the script in order to portray the country in a "positive light"—in order to secure tax concessions and financial support worth up to $20 million for the film. This was denied by producer Michael G. Wilson, who stated that the scene had always been intended to be shot in Mexico as production had been attracted to the imagery of the Day of the Dead, and that the script had been developed from there. Production of Skyfall had previously faced similar problems while attempting to secure permits to shoot the film's pre-title sequence in India before moving to Istanbul.
rewrite: During production in Mexico City, media reports alleged that the screenplay was revised to meet the stipulations of Mexican authorities, purportedly to secure tax incentives and financial support valued at approximately $20 million. These alleged modifications included adjustments to specific scenes, character depictions, and casting decisions, all aimed at presenting the nation favorably. Producer Michael G. Wilson refuted these claims, asserting that the sequence was always planned for Mexico, inspired by the visual appeal of the Day of the Dead, and that the script evolved accordingly. This incident echoes prior challenges during the production of *Skyfall*, which encountered difficulties obtaining permits for a sequence initially planned for India before relocating to Istanbul.

input: Brood parasitism, in which an egg-layer leaves her eggs with another individual's brood, is more common among birds than any other type of organism. After a parasitic bird lays her eggs in another bird's nest, they are often accepted and raised by the host at the expense of the host's own brood. Brood parasites may be either obligate brood parasites, which must lay their eggs in the nests of other species because they are incapable of raising their own young, or non-obligate brood parasites, which sometimes lay eggs in the nests of conspecifics to increase their reproductive output even though they could have raised their own young. One hundred bird species, including honeyguides, icterids, and ducks, are obligate parasites, though the most famous are the cuckoos. Some brood parasites are adapted to hatch before their host's young, which allows them to destroy the host's eggs by pushing them out of the nest or to kill the host's chicks; this ensures that all food brought to the nest will be fed to the parasitic chicks.
rewrite: Brood parasitism, a reproductive strategy wherein an individual deposits its eggs in the nest of another, is most prevalent among avian species compared to all other taxonomic groups. Following the deposition of a parasitic egg into a host nest, the host frequently accepts and incubates it, subsequently rearing the foreign offspring, often to the detriment of its own brood. This parasitism exists in two primary forms: obligate, in which species such as honeyguides, icterids, ducks, and notably cuckoos are entirely dependent on hosts to raise their young due to an inability to do so themselves; and non-obligate, wherein individuals, though capable of parental care, may parasitize conspecifics to augment their reproductive success. Approximately one hundred bird species are obligate parasites. Furthermore, many parasitic chicks exhibit adaptive traits, such as earlier hatching, which enables them to eliminate host eggs or chicks through eviction or direct aggression, thereby monopolizing all parental provisioning delivered to the nest.

input: The area near the border with Cameroon close to the coast is rich rainforest and part of the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko coastal forests ecoregion, an important centre for biodiversity. It is habitat for the drill monkey, which is found in the wild only in this area and across the border in Cameroon. The areas surrounding Calabar, Cross River State, also in this forest, are believed to contain the world's largest diversity of butterflies. The area of southern Nigeria between the Niger and the Cross Rivers has lost most of its forest because of development and harvesting by increased population, with it being replaced by grassland (see Cross-Niger transition forests).
rewrite: The coastal region bordering Cameroon comprises dense rainforest within the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko coastal forests ecoregion, a significant biodiversity hotspot. This area serves as critical habitat for the drill monkey, a species whose wild populations are confined to this locality and adjacent parts of Cameroon. Furthermore, the forests surrounding Calabar in Cross River State are considered to possess the world's greatest diversity of butterflies. In contrast, southern Nigeria between the Niger and Cross Rivers has experienced extensive deforestation due to development and resource extraction from a growing population, resulting in widespread grassland replacement, as documented in the Cross-Niger transition forests.

input: Lactase is an enzyme that breaks down the disaccharide lactose to its component parts, glucose and galactose. Glucose and galactose can be absorbed by the small intestine. Approximately 65 percent of the adult population produce only small amounts of lactase and are unable to eat unfermented milk-based foods. This is commonly known as lactose intolerance. Lactose intolerance varies widely by ethnic heritage; more than 90 percent of peoples of east Asian descent are lactose intolerant, in contrast to about 5 percent of people of northern European descent.
rewrite: Lactase is an enzyme responsible for hydrolyzing the disaccharide lactose into its monosaccharide constituents, glucose and galactose, which are subsequently absorbed in the small intestine. An estimated 65% of adults exhibit low lactase production, a condition termed lactose intolerance, which prevents the digestion of unfermented dairy. Prevalence varies significantly by ethnicity, affecting over 90% of individuals of East Asian descent compared to approximately 5% of those of Northern European descent.

input: On August 24, 2006, Apple and Creative announced a broad settlement to end their legal disputes. Apple will pay Creative US$100 million for a paid-up license, to use Creative's awarded patent in all Apple products. As part of the agreement, Apple will recoup part of its payment, if Creative is successful in licensing the patent. Creative then announced its intention to produce iPod accessories by joining the Made for iPod program.
rewrite: On August 24, 2006, Apple Inc. and Creative Technology Ltd. announced a comprehensive settlement to resolve their ongoing legal disputes. Under the terms, Apple will pay Creative US$100 million for a paid-up license to utilize Creative’s patented technology across its product line. Apple is eligible to recoup a portion of this payment should Creative successfully license the patent to other parties. Concurrently, Creative disclosed its plan to develop iPod accessories by enrolling in the "Made for iPod" program.

input: Next, Spielberg teamed with Star Wars creator and friend George Lucas on an action adventure film, Raiders of the Lost Ark, the first of the Indiana Jones films. The archaeologist and adventurer hero Indiana Jones was played by Harrison Ford (whom Lucas had previously cast in his Star Wars films as Han Solo). The film was considered an homage to the cliffhanger serials of the Golden Age of Hollywood. It became the biggest film at the box office in 1981, and the recipient of numerous Oscar nominations including Best Director (Spielberg's second nomination) and Best Picture (the second Spielberg film to be nominated for Best Picture). Raiders is still considered a landmark example of the action-adventure genre. The film also led to Ford's casting in Ridley Scott's Blade Runner.
rewrite: Subsequently, Steven Spielberg collaborated with George Lucas, the creator of *Star Wars* and a personal acquaintance, on the action-adventure film *Raiders of the Lost Ark*, inaugurating the Indiana Jones series. The protagonist, archaeologist and adventurer Indiana Jones, was portrayed by Harrison Ford, an actor previously cast by Lucas as Han Solo in the *Star Wars* franchise. The film functioned as an homage to the cliffhanger serials of Hollywood's Golden Age. It emerged as the highest-grossing film of 1981 and received several Academy Award nominations, including those for Best Director (Spielberg’s second nomination in that category) and Best Picture (marking the second Spielberg film so honored). Widely regarded as a seminal work within the action-adventure genre, *Raiders of the Lost Ark* also precipitated Ford’s casting in Ridley Scott’s *Blade Runner*.

input: The indirect method of applying tesserae is often used for very large projects, projects with repetitive elements or for areas needing site specific shapes. Tiles are applied face-down to a backing paper using an adhesive, and later transferred onto walls, floors or craft projects. This method is most useful for extremely large projects as it gives the maker time to rework areas, allows the cementing of the tiles to the backing panel to be carried out quickly in one operation and helps ensure that the front surfaces of the mosaic tiles and mosaic pieces are flat and in the same plane on the front, even when using tiles and pieces of differing thicknesses. Mosaic murals, benches and tabletops are some of the items usually made using the indirect method, as it results in a smoother and more even surface.
rewrite: The indirect method of tesserae application is frequently employed for extensive projects, those involving repetitive elements, or areas requiring site-specific shaping. In this technique, tiles are affixed face-down to a backing paper with adhesive and subsequently transferred to a permanent substrate, such as a wall, floor, or crafted object. This approach is particularly advantageous for large-scale work, as it permits the artist to rework sections, enables the rapid, single-operation cementing of the entire assembly, and ensures a uniformly flat frontal plane despite variations in individual tile thickness. Consequently, it is the preferred method for producing items like mosaic murals, benches, and tabletops, where it yields a characteristically smooth and even finished surface.

input: Strict separation of powers did not operate in The United Kingdom, the political structure of which served in most instances[citation needed] as a model for the government created by the U.S. Constitution.[citation needed] Under the UK Westminster system, based on parliamentary sovereignty and responsible government, Parliament (consisting of the Sovereign (King-in-Parliament), House of Lords and House of Commons) was the supreme lawmaking authority. The executive branch acted in the name of the King ("His Majesty's Government"), as did the judiciary. The King's Ministers were in most cases members of one of the two Houses of Parliament, and the Government needed to sustain the support of a majority in the House of Commons. One minister, the Lord Chancellor, was at the same time the sole judge in the Court of Chancery and the presiding officer in the House of Lords. Therefore, it may be seen that the three branches of British government often violated the strict principle of separation of powers, even though there were many occasions when the different branches of the government disagreed with each other. Some U.S. states did not observe a strict separation of powers in the 18th century. In New Jersey, the Governor also functioned as a member of the state's highest court and as the presiding officer of one house of the New Jersey Legislature. The President of Delaware was a member of the Court of Appeals; the presiding officers of the two houses of the state legislature also served in the executive department as Vice Presidents. In both Delaware and Pennsylvania, members of the executive council served at the same time as judges. On the other hand, many southern states explicitly required separation of powers. Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina and Georgia all kept the branches of government "separate and distinct."
rewrite:
The United Kingdom did not maintain a strict separation of governmental powers, despite its political structure frequently serving as a model for the framers of the U.S. Constitution. The British Westminster system, founded upon the doctrines of parliamentary sovereignty and responsible government, vested supreme legislative authority in Parliament—comprising the Sovereign (the King-in-Parliament), the House of Lords, and the House of Commons. Both the executive and the judiciary operated under the authority of the Crown, with the executive acting as “His Majesty’s Government.” Notably, ministers were typically drawn from the membership of the two parliamentary houses, and the government was required to retain the confidence of a majority in the House of Commons. The integration of functions was further illustrated by the Lord Chancellor, who simultaneously served as the sole judge in the Court of Chancery and as the presiding officer of the House of Lords. Consequently, while interbranch disagreements occurred, the British system routinely departed from a rigid separation of powers.

Similarly, several early American state governments in the eighteenth century did not adhere strictly to this principle. In New Jersey, the governor also sat as a member of the state’s highest court and presided over one house of the legislature. Delaware’s president served on the Court of Appeals, while the presiding officers of both legislative houses held executive roles as vice presidents. In both Delaware and Pennsylvania, members of the executive council concurrently served as judges. By contrast, many southern states explicitly mandated a separation of powers. The constitutions of Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, and Georgia each contained provisions requiring the branches of government to remain “separate and distinct,” reflecting a deliberate institutional choice distinct from the integrated British model and some of their northern counterparts.

input: The settlement of Plympton, further up the River Plym than the current Plymouth, was also an early trading port, but the river silted up in the early 11th century and forced the mariners and merchants to settle at the current day Barbican near the river mouth. At the time this village was called Sutton, meaning south town in Old English. The name Plym Mouth, meaning "mouth of the River Plym" was first mentioned in a Pipe Roll of 1211. The name Plymouth first officially replaced Sutton in a charter of King Henry VI in 1440. See Plympton for the derivation of the name Plym.
rewrite: The earlier trading port of Plympton, located farther upstream on the River Plym than modern Plymouth, declined when the river silted up in the early eleventh century. This compelled its mariners and merchants to relocate downstream to a settlement near the river’s mouth, then known as Sutton (from the Old English for "south town"). The designation "Plym Mouth," referring to the river's estuary, first appears in the Pipe Roll of 1211. The name Plymouth formally superseded Sutton by the charter of King Henry VI in 1440. (The etymology of "Plym" is addressed in the entry for Plympton.)

input: Through his actions and speeches, and because he was able to symbolize the popular Arab will, Nasser inspired several nationalist revolutions in the Arab world. He defined the politics of his generation and communicated directly with the public masses of the Arab world, bypassing the various heads of states of those countries—an accomplishment not repeated by other Arab leaders. The extent of Nasser's centrality in the region made it a priority for incoming Arab nationalist heads of state to seek good relations with Egypt, in order to gain popular legitimacy from their own citizens.
rewrite: Gamal Abdel Nasser’s capacity to embody the popular Arab will, expressed through his rhetoric and policies, inspired numerous nationalist movements across the region. He uniquely shaped the political discourse of his era, engaging directly with the Arab public and circumventing established state leadership—a feat unmatched by his contemporaries. Consequently, Nasser’s profound regional influence compelled subsequent Arab nationalist leaders to prioritize alliances with Egypt, seeking thereby to derive popular legitimacy and consolidate domestic support.

input: Conversely, most heat-treatable alloys are precipitation hardening alloys, which produce the opposite effects that steel does. When heated to form a solution and then cooled quickly, these alloys become much softer than normal, during the diffusionless transformation, and then harden as they age. The solutes in these alloys will precipitate over time, forming intermetallic phases, which are difficult to discern from the base metal. Unlike steel, in which the solid solution separates to form different crystal phases, precipitation hardening alloys separate to form different phases within the same crystal. These intermetallic alloys appear homogeneous in crystal structure, but tend to behave heterogeneous, becoming hard and somewhat brittle.
rewrite: In contrast, most heat-treatable alloys utilize precipitation hardening, a process producing effects opposite to those in steel. When solution-treated and quenched, these alloys undergo a diffusionless transformation, initially becoming softer before hardening with age. Over time, solutes precipitate out, forming fine intermetallic phases often indistinguishable from the matrix. Unlike steel, where phase separation yields distinct crystal structures, precipitation hardening involves phase formation within a single crystal lattice. Consequently, these alloys retain an ostensibly homogeneous crystal structure yet exhibit heterogeneous mechanical properties, resulting in increased hardness and brittleness.

input: When the Frankish rulers established the system of feudalism, the Bishops of Utrecht came to exercise worldly power as prince-bishops. The territory of the bishopric not only included the modern province of Utrecht (Nedersticht, 'lower Sticht'), but also extended to the northeast. The feudal conflict of the Middle Ages heavily affected Utrecht. The prince-bishopric was involved in almost continuous conflicts with the Counts of Holland and the Dukes of Guelders. The Veluwe region was seized by Guelders, but large areas in the modern province of Overijssel remained as the Oversticht.
rewrite: Under the Frankish establishment of feudalism, the Bishops of Utrecht acquired secular authority, ruling as prince-bishops. Their territory encompassed not only the present-day province of Utrecht (the Nedersticht) but also extended northeastward. Medieval feudal conflicts profoundly impacted the region, engaging the prince-bishopric in near-constant strife with the Counts of Holland and the Dukes of Guelders. Although Guelders annexed the Veluwe, extensive territories in modern Overijssel were retained as the Oversticht.

input: Under the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), the Nanjing area was known as Jiangning (江寧) and served as the seat of government for the Viceroy of Liangjiang. It had been visited by the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors a number of times on their tours of the southern provinces. Nanjing was invaded by British troops during the close of the First Opium War, which was ended by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842. As the capital of the brief-lived rebel Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (founded by the Taiping rebels in the mid-19th century, Nanjing was known as Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital" or "Capital of Heaven").
rewrite: During the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), the region of Nanjing was designated as Jiangning and functioned as the administrative seat of the Viceroy of Liangjiang. It was visited on multiple occasions by the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors during their southern tours. British forces invaded Nanjing near the conclusion of the First Opium War, a conflict formally ended by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842. Subsequently, the city served as the capital of the short-lived Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, a mid-nineteenth century rebellion, during which it was renamed Tianjing, or "Heavenly Capital."

input: General Ridgway was appointed Supreme Commander, Korea; he regrouped the UN forces for successful counterattacks, while General James Van Fleet assumed command of the U.S. Eighth Army. Further attacks slowly depleted the PVA and KPA forces; Operations Courageous (23–28 March 1951) and Tomahawk (23 March 1951) were a joint ground and airborne infilltration meant to trap Chinese forces between Kaesong and Seoul. UN forces advanced to "Line Kansas", north of the 38th parallel. The 187th Airborne Regimental Combat Team's ("Rakkasans") second of two combat jumps was on Easter Sunday, 1951, at Munsan-ni, South Korea, codenamed Operation Tomahawk. The mission was to get behind Chinese forces and block their movement north. The 60th Indian Parachute Field Ambulance provided the medical cover for the operations, dropping an ADS and a surgical team and treating over 400 battle casualties apart from the civilian casualties that formed the core of their objective as the unit was on a humanitarian mission.
rewrite: General Matthew Ridgway was appointed Supreme Commander in Korea, where he reorganized United Nations forces to mount effective counteroffensives, while General James Van Fleet took command of the U.S. Eighth Army. Subsequent UN operations gradually attrited the People’s Volunteer Army and Korean People’s Army. Among these, Operations Courageous (23–28 March 1951) and Tomahawk (23 March 1951) constituted a coordinated ground and airborne infiltration designed to encircle Chinese forces between Kaesong and Seoul. This push enabled UN troops to advance to "Line Kansas," north of the 38th parallel. As part of Operation Tomahawk, the 187th Airborne Regimental Combat Team ("Rakkasans") executed its second combat jump on Easter Sunday 1951 at Munsan-ni, with the objective of establishing a blocking position behind Chinese lines to hinder their northward movement. Medical support was provided by the 60th Indian Parachute Field Ambulance, which deployed an Advanced Dressing Station and a surgical team. The unit treated in excess of 400 battle casualties, in addition to addressing civilian casualties, consistent with its humanitarian mission parameters.

input: The European Revolutions of 1848, known in some countries as the Spring of Nations or the Year of Revolution, were a series of political upheavals throughout the European continent. Described as a revolutionary wave, the period of unrest began in France and then, further propelled by the French Revolution of 1848, soon spread to the rest of Europe. Although most of the revolutions were quickly put down, there was a significant amount of violence in many areas, with tens of thousands of people tortured and killed.
