While the immediate political effects of the revolutions were reversed, the long-term reverberations of the events were far-reaching.
rewrite: The European Revolutions of 1848, also termed the Springtime of Nations, constituted a continent-wide wave of political upheaval. This revolutionary period originated in France, and the subsequent February Revolution there accelerated its diffusion across numerous states. Despite the general suppression of these insurrections, their enactment involved considerable violence, resulting in widespread casualties encompassing tens of thousands of deaths. Although conservative forces restored the immediate pre-revolutionary political order, the events precipitated profound and enduring societal and ideological transformations across Europe.

input: The term "Late Middle Ages" refers to one of the three periods of the Middle Ages, along with the Early Middle Ages and the High Middle Ages. Leonardo Bruni was the first historian to use tripartite periodization in his History of the Florentine People (1442). Flavio Biondo used a similar framework in Decades of History from the Deterioration of the Roman Empire (1439–1453). Tripartite periodization became standard after the German historian Christoph Cellarius published Universal History Divided into an Ancient, Medieval, and New Period (1683).
rewrite: The designation "Late Middle Ages" denotes one of three conventional subdivisions of the medieval era, following the Early and High Middle Ages. Historian Leonardo Bruni first employed this tripartite model in his *History of the Florentine People* (1442), a framework echoed by Flavio Biondo in his *Decades* (1439–1453). The periodization became standard following Christoph Cellarius’s *Universal History Divided into an Ancient, Medieval, and New Period* (1683).

input: The main industries are mineral based, agriculture based, and textile based. Rajasthan is the second largest producer of polyester fibre in India. The Pali and Bhilwara District produces more cloth than Bhiwandi, Maharashtra and the bhilwara is the largest city in suitings production and export and Pali is largest city in cotton and polyster in blouse pieces and rubia production and export. Several prominent chemical and engineering companies are located in the city of Kota, in southern Rajasthan. Rajasthan is pre-eminent in quarrying and mining in India. The Taj Mahal was built from the white marble which was mined from a town called Makrana. The state is the second largest source of cement in India. It has rich salt deposits at Sambhar, copper mines at Khetri, Jhunjhunu, and zinc mines at Dariba, Zawar mines and Rampura Aghucha (opencast) near Bhilwara. Dimensional stone mining is also undertaken in Rajasthan. Jodhpur sandstone is mostly used in monuments, important buildings and residential buildings. This stone is termed as "chittar patthar". Jodhpur leads in Handicraft and Guar Gum industry. Rajasthan is also a part of the Mumbai-Delhi Industrial corridor is set to benefit economically. The State gets 39% of the DMIC, with major districts of Jaipur, Alwar, Kota and Bhilwara benefiting.
rewrite: Rajasthan’s industrial economy is principally structured around mineral-based, agriculture-based, and textile-based sectors. The state holds the position of India’s second-largest producer of polyester fibre. In textiles, the districts of Pali and Bhilwara collectively produce more cloth than Bhiwandi in Maharashtra. Bhilwara is the foremost centre for the production and export of suitings, while Pali leads in the production and export of cotton and polyester blouse pieces and rubia. The southern city of Kota hosts several significant chemical and engineering enterprises. Rajasthan maintains pre-eminence in Indian quarrying and mining; notably, the white marble quarried at Makrana was used in the construction of the Taj Mahal. The state is India’s second-largest cement producer and possesses substantial mineral resources, including salt deposits at Sambhar, copper mines at Khetri and Jhunjhunu, and zinc mines at Dariba, Zawar, and Rampura Aghucha (opencast) near Bhilwara. Dimensional stone mining is also prevalent, with Jodhpur sandstone, locally termed "chittar patthar," being extensively utilized in monuments, significant buildings, and residential structures. Jodhpur is additionally a leader in the handicraft and guar gum industries. Furthermore, Rajasthan’s inclusion in the Mumbai-Delhi Industrial Corridor is anticipated to yield substantial economic benefits, with the state allocated 39% of the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor project, primarily benefiting the districts of Jaipur, Alwar, Kota, and Bhilwara.

input: Valerian's first religious edict singled out Christianity as a particularly self-interested and subversive foreign cult, outlawed its assemblies and urged Christians to sacrifice to Rome's traditional gods. His second edict acknowledged a Christian threat to the Imperial system – not yet at its heart but close to it, among Rome’s equites and Senators. Christian apologists interpreted his disgraceful capture and death as divine judgement. The next forty years were peaceful; the Christian church grew stronger and its literature and theology gained a higher social and intellectual profile, due in part to its own search for political toleration and theological coherence. Origen discussed theological issues with traditionalist elites in a common Neoplatonist frame of reference – he had written to Decius' predecessor Philip the Arab in similar vein – and Hippolytus recognised a “pagan” basis in Christian heresies. The Christian churches were disunited; Paul of Samosata, Bishop of Antioch was deposed by a synod of 268 for "dogmatic reasons – his doctrine on the human nature of Christ was rejected – and for his lifestyle, which reminded his brethren of the habits of the administrative elite". The reasons for his deposition were widely circulated among the churches. Meanwhile, Aurelian (270-75) appealed for harmony among his soldiers (concordia militum), stabilised the Empire and its borders and successfully established an official, Hellenic form of unitary cult to the Palmyrene Sol Invictus in Rome's Campus Martius.
rewrite: The initial religious decree issued by Valerian explicitly targeted Christianity, characterizing it as a particularly self-serving and seditious foreign cult. It prohibited Christian assemblies and compelled adherents to offer sacrifices to the traditional Roman deities. A subsequent edict recognized the Christian threat to the Imperial structure, noting its penetration not at the core, but within proximate and influential orders—the equites and Senators. Christian apologists later construed Valerian’s ignominious capture and demise as divine retribution. The ensuing four decades constituted a period of tranquility, during which the Christian church consolidated its strength. Its literary and theological output attained greater social and intellectual prominence, partly owing to internal efforts to secure political toleration and achieve doctrinal coherence. Origen engaged traditionalist elites in theological discourse within a shared Neoplatonic framework—having previously addressed Philip the Arab, Decius’ predecessor, in like manner—while Hippolytus identified a “pagan” foundation within certain Christian heresies. The Christian churches remained fragmented; for instance, Paul of Samosata, Bishop of Antioch, was deposed by a synod in 268 on both dogmatic grounds—specifically, his doctrine concerning Christ’s human nature—and for his manner of living, which his peers associated with the conduct of the administrative elite. The rationale for his deposition was extensively disseminated among the churches. Concurrently, Aurelian (270–275 CE) appealed for military harmony (concordia militum), stabilized the Empire and its frontiers, and successfully instituted an official, Hellenized version of a unitary cult to Sol Invictus of Palmyra in Rome’s Campus Martius.

input: The United Kingdom has traditionally been governed as a unitary state by the Westminster Parliament in London. Instead of adopting a federal model, the UK has relied on gradual devolution to decentralise political power. Devolution in the UK began with the Government of Ireland Act 1914 which granted home rule to Ireland as a constituent country of the former United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Following the partition of Ireland in 1921 which saw the creation of the sovereign Irish Free State (which eventually evolved into the modern day Republic of Ireland), Northern Ireland retained its devolved government through the Parliament of Northern Ireland, the only part of the UK to have such a body at this time. This body was suspended in 1972 and Northern Ireland was governed by direct rule during the period of conflict known as The Troubles.
rewrite: The United Kingdom has historically functioned as a unitary state, with sovereignty concentrated in the Westminster Parliament in London. Rather than adopting a federal structure, it has pursued a process of incremental devolution to decentralise authority. This process commenced with the Government of Ireland Act 1914, which provided for home rule within Ireland as a constituent part of the then United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Following the partition of Ireland in 1921 and the establishment of the sovereign Irish Free State—later the Republic of Ireland—Northern Ireland maintained a devolved administration via the Parliament of Northern Ireland, uniquely possessing such a legislature within the UK at that time. This institution was suspended in 1972, leading to a period of direct rule from Westminster during the conflict known as The Troubles.

input: During up-peak mode (also called moderate incoming traffic), elevator cars in a group are recalled to the lobby to provide expeditious service to passengers arriving at the building, most typically in the morning as people arrive for work or at the conclusion of a lunch-time period. Elevators are dispatched one-by-one when they reach a pre-determined passenger load, or when they have had their doors opened for a certain period of time. The next elevator to be dispatched usually has its hall lantern or a "this car leaving next" sign illuminated to encourage passengers to make maximum use of the available elevator system capacity. Some elevator banks are programmed so that at least one car will always return to the lobby floor and park whenever it becomes free.
rewrite: During up-peak mode, commonly referred to as moderate incoming traffic, elevator cars within a group are systematically recalled to the main lobby. This operational strategy aims to provide efficient service for passengers entering the building, a pattern most prevalent during morning arrivals or following a lunch period. Dispatching occurs sequentially once a car attains a predetermined passenger load or after its doors remain open for a specified duration. To optimize system capacity utilization, the subsequent car scheduled for departure typically activates a hall lantern or a "this car leaving next" indicator, guiding passengers accordingly. Furthermore, certain elevator groups are configured to ensure at least one car returns and parks at the lobby whenever it is unoccupied.

input: In 1922, Egypt, which had been declared a British protectorate at the outbreak of the First World War, was granted formal independence, though it continued to be a British client state until 1954. British troops remained stationed in Egypt until the signing of the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty in 1936, under which it was agreed that the troops would withdraw but continue to occupy and defend the Suez Canal zone. In return, Egypt was assisted to join the League of Nations. Iraq, a British mandate since 1920, also gained membership of the League in its own right after achieving independence from Britain in 1932. In Palestine, Britain was presented with the problem of mediating between the Arab and Jewish communities. The 1917 Balfour Declaration, which had been incorporated into the terms of the mandate, stated that a national home for the Jewish people would be established in Palestine, and Jewish immigration allowed up to a limit that would be determined by the mandatory power. This led to increasing conflict with the Arab population, who openly revolted in 1936. As the threat of war with Germany increased during the 1930s, Britain judged the support of the Arab population in the Middle East as more important than the establishment of a Jewish homeland, and shifted to a pro-Arab stance, limiting Jewish immigration and in turn triggering a Jewish insurgency.
rewrite:
Following the First World War, during which Egypt had been declared a British protectorate, formal independence was granted in 1922. Nevertheless, the nation effectively remained a British client state until 1954. A continued British military presence was regulated by the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty, which stipulated the withdrawal of forces except from the Suez Canal zone, which they would continue to occupy and defend. As part of this arrangement, Britain facilitated Egypt’s entry into the League of Nations. Similarly, Iraq, under British mandate since 1920, attained independent statehood in 1932 and subsequently gained League membership.

Within its mandate for Palestine, Britain confronted the escalating challenge of mediating between Arab and Jewish national aspirations. The 1917 Balfour Declaration, embedded within the mandate’s terms, endorsed the establishment of a Jewish national home and permitted Jewish immigration, with limits set by the mandatory power. This policy generated mounting Arab opposition, culminating in a major revolt in 1936. As the European crisis deepened in the late 1930s, British strategic calculations shifted. Perceiving the support of the wider Arab world as vital to impending war efforts, Britain adopted a more pro-Arab orientation. This involved imposing strict limits on Jewish immigration, a move that ultimately provoked a Jewish insurgency against British authority.

input: Modern morphology recognizes a continuum between the major morphological categories of root, stem (caulome), leaf (phyllome) and trichome. Furthermore, it emphasizes structural dynamics. Modern systematics aims to reflect and discover phylogenetic relationships between plants. Modern Molecular phylogenetics largely ignores morphological characters, relying on DNA sequences as data. Molecular analysis of DNA sequences from most families of flowering plants enabled the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group to publish in 1998 a phylogeny of flowering plants, answering many of the questions about relationships among angiosperm families and species. The theoretical possibility of a practical method for identification of plant species and commercial varieties by DNA barcoding is the subject of active current research.
rewrite: Contemporary morphology acknowledges a continuum among the principal morphological categories—root, stem (caulome), leaf (phyllome), and trichome—while emphasizing structural dynamics. Modern systematics seeks to elucidate phylogenetic relationships. In contrast, molecular phylogenetics predominantly utilizes DNA sequence data, largely disregarding morphological characters. Through such molecular analyses across numerous flowering plant families, the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group produced a seminal phylogeny in 1998, resolving many questions regarding angiosperm familial and species relationships. Concurrently, the feasibility of employing DNA barcoding for practical identification of plant species and commercial cultivars remains an active area of research.

input: Many television shows and films have been produced which portray in-character professional wrestlers as protagonists, such as Ready to Rumble, ¡Mucha Lucha!, Nacho Libre, and the Santo film series. In the wildly popular Rocky series of films about the fictional boxer Rocky Balboa, Rocky III saw its hero fighting a "boxer vs. wrestler" exhibition match against the enormous and villainous wrestler "Thunderlips", portrayed by real-life soon-to-be wrestling icon Hulk Hogan. At least two stage plays set in the world of pro wrestling have been produced: The Baron is a comedy that retells the life of an actual performer known as Baron von Raschke. From Parts Unknown... is an award-nominated Canadian drama about the rise and fall of a fictional wrestler. The 2009 South Park episode "W.T.F." played on the soap operatic elements of professional wrestling. One of the lead characters on the Disney Channel series Kim Possible was a huge fan of pro wrestling and actually featured it on an episode (with two former WWE wrestlers voicing the two fictitious wrestlers featured in the episode). The 2008 film The Wrestler, about a washed-up professional wrestler, garnered several Oscar nominations.
rewrite: Numerous television programs and films have featured in-character professional wrestlers as central figures, including *Ready to Rumble*, *¡Mucha Lucha!*, *Nacho Libre*, and the Santo film series. The highly successful *Rocky* film franchise, centered on the fictional boxer Rocky Balboa, incorporated this theme in *Rocky III*, wherein the protagonist engages in a "boxer versus wrestler" exhibition match against the villainous wrestler "Thunderlips," portrayed by the future wrestling icon Hulk Hogan. The theatrical realm has also engaged with this subject through at least two stage plays: *The Baron*, a comedic retelling of the life of actual performer Baron von Raschke, and *From Parts Unknown...*, an award-nominated Canadian drama tracing the career of a fictional wrestler. Television narratives have further explored wrestling's dramatic conventions, as seen in the 2009 *South Park* episode "W.T.F.," which satirized its soap-operatic elements, and the *Disney Channel* series *Kim Possible*, which featured a wrestling-enthusiast lead character and included an episode with voice roles performed by former WWE wrestlers. Additionally, the 2008 film *The Wrestler*, depicting a declining professional wrestler, received multiple Academy Award nominations.

input: Some types of energy are a varying mix of both potential and kinetic energy. An example is mechanical energy which is the sum of (usually macroscopic) kinetic and potential energy in a system. Elastic energy in materials is also dependent upon electrical potential energy (among atoms and molecules), as is chemical energy, which is stored and released from a reservoir of electrical potential energy between electrons, and the molecules or atomic nuclei that attract them.[need quotation to verify].The list is also not necessarily complete. Whenever physical scientists discover that a certain phenomenon appears to violate the law of energy conservation, new forms are typically added that account for the discrepancy.
rewrite: Certain forms of energy constitute a composite of potential and kinetic energy. For instance, mechanical energy represents the summation of macroscopic kinetic and potential energies within a system. Similarly, elastic potential energy in materials, as well as chemical energy, fundamentally arise from electrical potential energy at the microscopic level—between atoms and molecules, or between electrons and atomic nuclei. This classification remains provisional; the discovery of phenomena seemingly contravening energy conservation historically necessitates the postulation of novel energy forms to reconcile such discrepancies.

input: Bern was the site of the 1954 Football (Soccer) World Cup Final, a huge upset for the Hungarian Golden Team, who were beaten 3–2 by West Germany. The football team BSC Young Boys is based in Bern at the Stade de Suisse Wankdorf, which also was one of the venues for the European football championship 2008 in which it hosted 3 matches.
rewrite: Bern hosted the 1954 FIFA World Cup Final, notably the site of West Germany's 3–2 upset victory over the favored Hungarian Golden Team. The city is home to BSC Young Boys, whose stadium, the Stade de Suisse Wankdorf, served as a venue for the 2008 UEFA European Championship, hosting three matches.

input: Since the start of the 1994–95 season, the FA Cup has been sponsored. However, to protect the identity of the competition, the sponsored name has always included 'The FA Cup' in addition to the sponsor's name, unlike sponsorship deals for the League Cup where the word 'cup' is preceded by only the sponsor's name. Sponsorship deals run for four years, though – as in the case of E.ON – one-year extensions may be agreed. Emirates airline is the sponsor from 2015 to 2018, renaming the competition as 'The Emirates FA Cup', unlike previous editions, which included 'The FA Cup in association with E.ON' and 'The FA Cup with Budweiser'.
rewrite: Since the 1994–95 season, the Football Association Challenge Cup has operated under commercial sponsorship. To preserve the competition's historic identity, all sponsorship nomenclature has incorporated the official title 'The FA Cup' alongside the sponsor's name. This contrasts with the sponsorship model for the League Cup, wherein the sponsor's name directly precedes the word 'Cup'. Standard sponsorship agreements span four years, subject to occasional one-year extensions, as occurred with E.ON. The current sponsor, Emirates airline, holds the rights from 2015 to 2018, titling the event 'The Emirates FA Cup'. Previous iterations utilized formats such as 'The FA Cup in association with E.ON' and 'The FA Cup with Budweiser'.

input: In July 2013, there were 41,000 non-Germans by citizenship living in Thuringia (1.9% of the population − among the smallest proportions of any state in Germany). Nevertheless, the number rose from 33,000 in July 2011, an increase of 24% in only two years. About 4% of the population are migrants (including persons that already received the German citizenship). The biggest groups of foreigners by citizenship are (as of 2012): Russians (3,100), Poles (3,000), Vietnamese (2,800), Turks (2,100) and Ukrainians (2,000). The amount of foreigners varies between regions: the college towns Erfurt, Jena, Weimar and Ilmenau have the highest rates, whereas there are almost no migrants living in the most rural smaller municipalities.
rewrite: In July 2013, Thuringia was home to 41,000 foreign nationals, constituting 1.9% of its population—one of the smallest such proportions among German states. This figure nonetheless represented a significant increase from 33,000 in July 2011, a rise of 24% within two years. Approximately 4% of the population comprises individuals with a migration background, including naturalized citizens. As of 2012, the largest foreign national groups were Russians (3,100), Poles (3,000), Vietnamese (2,800), Turks (2,100), and Ukrainians (2,000). Geographic distribution is uneven, with the highest concentrations in university cities such as Erfurt, Jena, Weimar, and Ilmenau, while the most rural municipalities have minimal migrant populations.

input: By the early 1970s, softer songs by artists like The Carpenters, Anne Murray, John Denver, Barry Manilow, and even Streisand, began to be played more often on "Top 40" radio and others were added to the mix on many AC stations. Also, some of these stations even played softer songs by Elvis Presley, Linda Ronstadt, Elton John, Rod Stewart, Billy Joel, and other rock-based artists.
rewrite: During the early 1970s, a softer musical style became increasingly prevalent on "Top 40" radio, featuring artists such as The Carpenters, Anne Murray, and Barry Manilow. Concurrently, many Adult Contemporary stations expanded their playlists to include mellower selections from rock-oriented performers, including Elvis Presley, Elton John, and Linda Ronstadt.

input: While no other Timely character would achieve the success of these "big three", some notable heroes—many of which continue to appear in modern-day retcon appearances and flashbacks—include the Whizzer, Miss America, the Destroyer, the original Vision, and the Angel. Timely also published one of humor cartoonist Basil Wolverton's best-known features, "Powerhouse Pepper", as well as a line of children's funny-animal comics featuring popular characters like Super Rabbit and the duo Ziggy Pig and Silly Seal.
rewrite: Although the "big three" remained Timely's most successful characters, other notable heroes such as the Whizzer, Miss America, the Destroyer, the original Vision, and the Angel also appeared, some of whom are referenced in modern retroactive continuity. Additionally, Timely published Basil Wolverton's renowned "Powerhouse Pepper" and a series of humorous animal comics for children, featuring characters like Super Rabbit and Ziggy Pig and Silly Seal.

input: The Second Aliyah (1904–14), began after the Kishinev pogrom; some 40,000 Jews settled in Palestine, although nearly half of them left eventually. Both the first and second waves of migrants were mainly Orthodox Jews, although the Second Aliyah included socialist groups who established the kibbutz movement. During World War I, British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour sent the Balfour Declaration of 1917 to Baron Rothschild (Walter Rothschild, 2nd Baron Rothschild), a leader of the British Jewish community, that stated that Britain intended for the creation of a Jewish "national home" within the Palestinian Mandate.
rewrite: The Second Aliyah (1904–1914), precipitated by the Kishinev pogrom, involved the settlement of approximately 40,000 Jews in Palestine, with nearly half later departing. While both this and the First Aliyah consisted predominantly of Orthodox Jews, the second wave notably included socialist pioneers who founded the kibbutz movement. Subsequently, during World War I, British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour issued the 1917 Balfour Declaration to Baron Walter Rothschild, expressing official British support for establishing a Jewish "national home" within the Mandate for Palestine.

input: Samuel Adelstein described the Lombardi mandolin in 1893 as wider and shorter than the Neapolitan mandolin, with a shallower back and a shorter and wider neck, with six single strings to the regular mandolin's set of 4. The Lombardi was tuned C, D, A, E, B, G. The strings were fastened to the bridge like a guitar's. There were 20 frets, covering three octaves, with an additional 5 notes. When Adelstein wrote, there were no nylon strings, and the gut and single strings "do not vibrate so clearly and sweetly as the double steel string of the Neapolitan."
rewrite: In his 1893 description, Samuel Adelstein characterized the Lombardi mandolin as possessing a broader and shorter form than the Neapolitan variety, featuring a shallower back and a wider, shorter neck. It employed six single strings, tuned to C, D, A, E, B, and G, which were affixed to a guitar-style bridge. The instrument's twenty frets spanned three full octaves plus five additional notes. Adelstein noted that, at the time, the gut strings used did not vibrate with the same clarity and sweetness as the double steel strings of the Neapolitan mandolin.

input: More detail was given in Darwin's 1868 book on The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication, which tried to explain heredity through his hypothesis of pangenesis. Although Darwin had privately questioned blending inheritance, he struggled with the theoretical difficulty that novel individual variations would tend to blend into a population. However, inherited variation could be seen, and Darwin's concept of selection working on a population with a range of small variations was workable. It was not until the modern evolutionary synthesis in the 1930s and 1940s that a model of heredity became completely integrated with a model of variation. This modern evolutionary synthesis had been dubbed Neo Darwinian Evolution because it encompasses Charles Darwin's theories of evolution with Gregor Mendel's theories of genetic inheritance.
rewrite: In his 1868 work, *The Variation of Animals and Plants under Domestication*, Charles Darwin elaborated on these ideas, proposing the hypothesis of pangenesis to explain heredity. While Darwin privately doubted blending inheritance, he grappled with the theoretical problem that novel variations would be diluted within a population. Nevertheless, the observable presence of inherited variation meant his concept of selection acting upon numerous slight variations remained viable. A fully coherent integration of models of heredity and variation was only achieved with the modern evolutionary synthesis during the 1930s and 1940s. This framework, often termed Neo-Darwinian Evolution, successfully merged Darwinian evolutionary theory with Mendelian genetics.

input: An alloy of aluminium and gallium in pellet form added to water can be used to generate hydrogen. The process also produces alumina, but the expensive gallium, which prevents the formation of an oxide skin on the pellets, can be re-used. This has important potential implications for a hydrogen economy, as hydrogen can be produced on-site and does not need to be transported.
rewrite: The introduction of aluminium-gallium alloy pellets to water facilitates hydrogen generation, yielding alumina as a byproduct. The gallium, which inhibits oxide skin formation on the pellets, is recoverable for reuse. This method holds significant potential for a hydrogen economy by enabling on-site production, thereby eliminating the necessity for hydrogen transport.

input: Archaeology confirms the widespread use of binding spells (defixiones), magical papyri and so-called "voodoo dolls" from a very early era. Around 250 defixiones have been recovered just from Roman Britain, in both urban and rural settings. Some seek straightforward, usually gruesome revenge, often for a lover's offense or rejection. Others appeal for divine redress of wrongs, in terms familiar to any Roman magistrate, and promise a portion of the value (usually small) of lost or stolen property in return for its restoration. None of these defixiones seem produced by, or on behalf of the elite, who had more immediate recourse to human law and justice. Similar traditions existed throughout the empire, persisting until around the 7th century AD, well into the Christian era.
rewrite: Archaeological evidence attests to the extensive early use of binding spells (*defixiones*), magical papyri, and figurines commonly termed "voodoo dolls." In Roman Britain alone, approximately 250 *defixiones* have been recovered from both urban and rural contexts. These artifacts exhibit distinct purposes: some invoke direct, often violent, retribution for personal grievances such as romantic rejection, while others formally petition divine intervention to rectify injustices, employing legalistic language and occasionally vowing a small portion of recovered property's value. The *defixiones* appear not to originate from elite social strata, who possessed more direct access to secular legal systems. These parallel traditions persisted across the empire until approximately the seventh century AD, enduring well into the Christian period.

input: BYU accepted 49 percent of the 11,423 people who applied for admission in the summer term and fall semester of 2013. The average GPA for these admitted students was 3.82. U.S. News and World Report describes BYU's selectivity as being "more selective" and compares it with such universities as the University of Texas at Austin and The Ohio State University. In addition, BYU is ranked 26th in colleges with the most freshman Merit Scholars, with 88 in 2006. BYU has one of the highest percentage of accepted applicants that go on to enroll (78 percent in 2010).
rewrite: For the 2013 summer and fall terms, Brigham Young University (BYU) extended offers of admission to 49% of its 11,423 applicants, yielding an entering class with an average GPA of 3.82. U.S. News & World Report categorizes BYU as "more selective," a classification it shares with institutions like the University of Texas at Austin and The Ohio State University. Further, BYU ranked 26th nationally for freshman Merit Scholars in 2006, with 88 scholars, and demonstrates a high yield rate, with 78% of admitted students matriculating in 2010.

input: It seems an oracular cult existed in Delphi from the Mycenaean ages. In historical times, the priests of Delphi were called Labryaden, "the double-axe men", which indicates Minoan origin. The double-axe, labrys, was the holy symbol of the Cretan labyrinth. The Homeric hymn adds that Apollo appeared as a dolphin and carried Cretan priests to Delphi, where they evidently transferred their religious practices. Apollo Delphinios was a sea-god especially worshiped in Crete and in the islands, and his name indicates his connection with Delphi and the holy serpent Delphyne ("womb").[citation needed] Apollo's sister Artemis, who was the Greek goddess of hunting, is identified with Britomartis (Diktynna), the Minoan "Mistress of the animals". In her earliest depictions she is accompanied by the "Mister of the animals", a male god of hunting who had the bow as his attribute. His original name is unknown, but it seems that he was absorbed by the more popular Apollo, who stood by the virgin "Mistress of the Animals", becoming her brother.
rewrite: Evidence suggests the existence of an oracular cult at Delphi dating to the Mycenaean period. In historical times, the presiding priests were known as the Labryaden, or "double-axe men," a title implying Minoan origins, as the labrys was the sacred symbol of the Cretan labyrinth. This connection is reinforced by the Homeric Hymn to Apollo, which recounts the god arriving in the form of a dolphin to transport Cretan priests to Delphi, thereby transplanting their rituals. Apollo Delphinios, a sea deity venerated particularly in Crete and the islands, derives his epithet from Delphi and its associated serpent, Delphyne ("womb"). Furthermore, Apollo’s sister Artemis, the Greek goddess of the hunt, is syncretized with the Minoan Britomartis (Diktynna), the "Mistress of the Animals." Early iconography depicts her alongside a male "Master of the Animals," a hunting deity characterized by a bow. Though his original name is lost, this figure appears to have been assimilated into the more prominent Apollo, who subsequently assumed the role of brother to the virgin Mistress.

input: Anthony Barber and Sree Padma note that "historians of Buddhist thought have been aware for quite some time that such pivotally important Mahayana Buddhist thinkers as Nāgārjuna, Dignaga, Candrakīrti, Āryadeva, and Bhavaviveka, among many others, formulated their theories while living in Buddhist communities in Āndhra." They note that the ancient Buddhist sites in the lower Kṛṣṇa Valley, including Amaravati, Nāgārjunakoṇḍā and Jaggayyapeṭa "can be traced to at least the third century BCE, if not earlier." Akira Hirakawa notes the "evidence suggests that many Early Mahayana scriptures originated in South India."
rewrite: Scholars Anthony Barber and Sree Padma observe that pivotal Mahayana thinkers, including Nāgārjuna, Dignaga, and Candrakīrti, developed their theories within Buddhist communities in Āndhra. They further indicate that major sites in the lower Kṛṣṇa Valley, such as Amaravati and Nāgārjunakoṇḍā, date to at least the third century BCE. This aligns with Akira Hirakawa’s assessment, which posits that considerable evidence points to South India as a place of origin for many Early Mahayana scriptures.

input: Amid preparations for the coronation, Princess Margaret informed her sister that she wished to marry Peter Townsend, a divorcé‚ 16 years Margaret's senior, with two sons from his previous marriage. The Queen asked them to wait for a year; in the words of Martin Charteris, "the Queen was naturally sympathetic towards the Princess, but I think she thought—she hoped—given time, the affair would peter out." Senior politicians were against the match and the Church of England did not permit remarriage after divorce. If Margaret had contracted a civil marriage, she would have been expected to renounce her right of succession. Eventually, she decided to abandon her plans with Townsend. In 1960, she married Antony Armstrong-Jones, who was created Earl of Snowdon the following year. They divorced in 1978; she did not remarry.
rewrite: During the coronation preparations, Princess Margaret expressed her desire to marry Group Captain Peter Townsend, a divorcé sixteen years her senior who had two sons from his prior marriage. The Queen, while personally sympathetic, requested a year’s delay; as Martin Charteris noted, she hoped the attachment would diminish over time. The match faced opposition from senior government figures and was untenable under Church of England doctrine, which prohibited remarriage after divorce. Had Princess Margaret proceeded with a civil ceremony, she would likely have been required to forfeit her place in the line of succession. Consequently, she relinquished her plans with Townsend. In 1960, she married photographer Antony Armstrong-Jones, who was later created Earl of Snowdon. Their marriage ended in divorce in 1978, after which she remained unmarried.

input: On 14 October, the heaviest night attack to date saw 380 German bombers from Luftflotte 3 hit London. Around 200 people were killed and another 2,000 injured. British anti-aircraft defences (General Frederick Alfred Pile) fired 8,326 rounds and shot down only two bombers. On 15 October, the bombers returned and about 900 fires were started by the mix of 415 short tons (376 t) of high explosive and 11 short tons (10.0 t) of incendiaries dropped. Five main rail lines were cut in London and rolling stock damaged.
rewrite: On 14 October, Luftflotte 3 conducted its most intense nocturnal assault to date, deploying 380 bombers against London. The raid resulted in approximately 200 fatalities and 2,000 injuries. Under General Frederick Alfred Pile, anti-aircraft defences expended 8,326 rounds to destroy merely two aircraft. The following night, a force delivering 415 short tons of high explosive and 11 short tons of incendiaries ignited roughly 900 fires. This attack severed five principal railway lines and damaged rolling stock within the city.

input: In 1930, Paul Dirac proposed a model of the vacuum as an infinite sea of particles possessing negative energy, called the Dirac sea. This theory helped refine the predictions of his earlier formulated Dirac equation, and successfully predicted the existence of the positron, confirmed two years later. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle formulated in 1927, predict a fundamental limit within which instantaneous position and momentum, or energy and time can be measured. This has far reaching consequences on the "emptiness" of space between particles. In the late 20th century, so-called virtual particles that arise spontaneously from empty space were confirmed.
rewrite: In 1930, Paul Dirac introduced a model describing the vacuum as an infinite "Dirac sea" of negative-energy particles. This framework refined predictions of the Dirac equation and successfully anticipated the positron, experimentally confirmed in 1932. Separately, Werner Heisenberg's 1927 uncertainty principle established fundamental limits on the simultaneous measurement of conjugate variables, such as position and momentum or energy and time. This principle has profound implications for the conceptual "emptiness" of space. By the late 20th century, the existence of virtual particles, which spontaneously emerge from the vacuum, was substantiated.

input: The great Navicella mosaic (1305–1313) in the atrium of the Old St. Peter's is attributed to Giotto di Bondone. The giant mosaic, commissioned by Cardinal Jacopo Stefaneschi, was originally situated on the eastern porch of the old basilica and occupied the whole wall above the entrance arcade facing the courtyard. It depicted St. Peter walking on the waters. This extraordinary work was mainly destroyed during the construction of the new St. Peter's in the 17th century. Navicella means "little ship" referring to the large boat which dominated the scene, and whose sail, filled by the storm, loomed over the horizon. Such a natural representation of a seascape was known only from ancient works of art.
rewrite: Attributed to Giotto di Bondone, the monumental Navicella mosaic (1305–1313) was originally displayed on the eastern porch of Old St. Peter's Basilica. Commissioned by Cardinal Jacopo Stefaneschi, it occupied the entire wall above the entrance arcade facing the atrium, depicting Saint Peter walking on water. This extraordinary work was largely destroyed during the seventeenth-century construction of the new basilica. Its title, meaning "little ship," references the large vessel that dominated the composition, with its storm-filled sail looming on the horizon. Such a naturalistic rendering of a seascape was unprecedented in the era, having been known only from ancient artistic precedents.

input: Built in 1815, Union Street was at the heart of Plymouth's historical culture. It became known as the servicemen's playground, as it was where sailors from the Royal Navy would seek entertainment of all kinds. During the 1930s, there were 30 pubs and it attracted such performers as Charlie Chaplin to the New Palace Theatre. It is now the late-night hub of Plymouth's entertainment strip, but has a reputation for trouble at closing hours.
rewrite: Constructed in 1815, Union Street formed a central artery of Plymouth's historical and cultural life. It gained renown as a servicemen's playground, frequented by Royal Navy sailors seeking various entertainments. By the 1930s, it housed thirty public houses and attracted notable performers like Charlie Chaplin to the New Palace Theatre. While it remains the city's primary late-night entertainment district, it has developed a reputation for disturbances during closing hours.

input: Eric P. Hamp in his 2012 Indo-European family tree, groups the Armenian language along with Greek and Ancient Macedonian ("Helleno-Macedonian") in the Pontic Indo-European (also called Helleno-Armenian) subgroup. In Hamp's view the homeland of this subgroup is the northeast coast of the Black Sea and its hinterlands. He assumes that they migrated from there southeast through the Caucasus with the Armenians remaining after Batumi while the pre-Greeks proceeded westwards along the southern coast of the Black Sea.
rewrite: In his 2012 Indo-European phylogeny, Eric P. Hamp classifies Armenian within a Pontic Indo-European (or Helleno-Armenian) subgroup alongside Greek and Ancient Macedonian. He posits a homeland for this group on the northeastern Black Sea coast. From there, he proposes a southeastward migration through the Caucasus, with Armenian settling after Batumi and pre-Greek populations moving westward along the southern Black Sea coast.

input: Beer contains ethyl alcohol, the same chemical that is present in wine and distilled spirits and as such, beer consumption has short-term psychological and physiological effects on the user. Different concentrations of alcohol in the human body have different effects on a person. The effects of alcohol depend on the amount an individual has drunk, the percentage of alcohol in the beer and the timespan that the consumption took place, the amount of food eaten and whether an individual has taken other prescription, over-the-counter or street drugs, among other factors. Drinking enough to cause a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.03%-0.12% typically causes an overall improvement in mood and possible euphoria, increased self-confidence and sociability, decreased anxiety, a flushed, red appearance in the face and impaired judgment and fine muscle coordination. A BAC of 0.09% to 0.25% causes lethargy, sedation, balance problems and blurred vision. A BAC from 0.18% to 0.30% causes profound confusion, impaired speech (e.g., slurred speech), staggering, dizziness and vomiting. A BAC from 0.25% to 0.40% causes stupor, unconsciousness, anterograde amnesia, vomiting (death may occur due to inhalation of vomit (pulmonary aspiration) while unconscious and respiratory depression (potentially life-threatening). A BAC from 0.35% to 0.80% causes a coma (unconsciousness), life-threatening respiratory depression and possibly fatal alcohol poisoning. As with all alcoholic drinks, drinking while driving, operating an aircraft or heavy machinery increases the risk of an accident; many countries have penalties against drunk driving.
rewrite: Beer, like wine and distilled spirits, contains ethyl alcohol, and its consumption induces various short-term psychological and physiological effects. These effects are contingent upon several factors, including the quantity of beer ingested, its specific alcohol concentration, the duration of consumption, the presence of food in the stomach, and the concurrent use of other substances, such as prescription medications or illicit drugs. The primary determinant of impairment is the resultant blood alcohol concentration (BAC). A BAC ranging from 0.03% to 0.12% is generally associated with elevated mood, possible euphoria, heightened self-confidence and sociability, reduced anxiety, facial flushing, and diminished judgment and fine motor coordination. At a BAC of 0.09% to 0.25%, symptoms typically progress to include lethargy, sedation, balance impairment, and blurred vision. A BAC between 0.18% and 0.30% often induces profound confusion, slurred speech, staggering, dizziness, and vomiting. Higher concentrations, from 0.25% to 0.40%, may lead to stupor, unconsciousness, anterograde amnesia, and vomiting, with attendant risks of fatal pulmonary aspiration or life-threatening respiratory depression. A BAC of 0.35% to 0.80% can cause coma, severe respiratory depression, and potentially fatal alcohol poisoning. As with all alcoholic beverages, consumption prior to operating a motor vehicle, aircraft, or heavy machinery significantly elevates accident risk, a concern reflected in the legal penalties for drunk driving enacted in many jurisdictions.

input: Fryderyk Chopin was born in Żelazowa Wola, 46 kilometres (29 miles) west of Warsaw, in what was then the Duchy of Warsaw, a Polish state established by Napoleon. The parish baptismal record gives his birthday as 22 February 1810, and cites his given names in the Latin form Fridericus Franciscus (in Polish, he was Fryderyk Franciszek). However, the composer and his family used the birthdate 1 March,[n 2] which is now generally accepted as the correct date.
rewrite: Fryderyk Chopin was born in Żelazowa Wola, 46 kilometres west of Warsaw, within the Napoleonic-era Duchy of Warsaw. His parish baptismal record, dated 22 February 1810, lists the Latin names Fridericus Franciscus. Despite this official documentation, Chopin and his family consistently recognized 1 March as his date of birth, a convention now widely accepted by scholars.

input: Although it is said that the "dog is man's best friend" regarding 17–24% of dogs in the developed countries, in the developing world they are feral, village or community dogs, with pet dogs uncommon. These live their lives as scavengers and have never been owned by humans, with one study showing their most common response when approached by strangers was to run away (52%) or respond with aggression (11%). We know little about these dogs, nor about the dogs that live in developed countries that are feral, stray or are in shelters, yet the great majority of modern research on dog cognition has focused on pet dogs living in human homes.
rewrite: While the adage "dog is man's best friend" applies to the 17–24% of dogs kept as pets in developed nations, the majority in the developing world exist as unowned feral, village, or community dogs, living as scavengers. Research indicates these dogs typically avoid human contact, with one study finding the most common reactions to strangers were flight (52%) or aggression (11%). Despite their prevalence, such free-roaming populations—along with stray and shelter dogs in developed countries—remain understudied. In contrast, the vast majority of contemporary canine cognition research focuses exclusively on pet dogs residing in human households.

input: The common features of passive solar architecture are orientation relative to the Sun, compact proportion (a low surface area to volume ratio), selective shading (overhangs) and thermal mass. When these features are tailored to the local climate and environment they can produce well-lit spaces that stay in a comfortable temperature range. Socrates' Megaron House is a classic example of passive solar design. The most recent approaches to solar design use computer modeling tying together solar lighting, heating and ventilation systems in an integrated solar design package. Active solar equipment such as pumps, fans and switchable windows can complement passive design and improve system performance.
rewrite: Passive solar architecture is characterized by solar orientation, compact proportions to minimize surface area relative to volume, selective shading elements, and integrated thermal mass. When these principles are appropriately adapted to local climatic conditions, they facilitate well-illuminated interior spaces that maintain thermal comfort. A historical exemplar is the Megaron House attributed to Socrates. Contemporary methodologies employ computational modeling to integrate solar lighting, heating, and ventilation into a cohesive design package. Furthermore, active components, including pumps, fans, and switchable glazing, can be incorporated to augment passive strategies and enhance overall system efficacy.

input: In 1814, a secret organization called the Filiki Eteria (Society of Friends) was founded with the aim of liberating Greece. The Filiki Eteria planned to launch revolution in the Peloponnese, the Danubian Principalities and Constantinople. The first of these revolts began on 6 March 1821 in the Danubian Principalities under the leadership of Alexandros Ypsilantis, but it was soon put down by the Ottomans. The events in the north spurred the Greeks of the Peloponnese into action and on 17 March 1821 the Maniots declared war on the Ottomans.
rewrite: Founded in 1814, the clandestine Filiki Eteria (Society of Friends) aimed to secure Greek independence. Its strategy involved instigating coordinated revolts across the Peloponnese, the Danubian Principalities, and Constantinople. The initial uprising commenced on 6 March 1821 in the Principalities under Alexandros Ypsilantis, yet Ottoman forces swiftly suppressed it. This northern insurrection, however, catalyzed the Peloponnesian Greeks. Subsequently, on 17 March 1821, the Maniots formally declared war against the Ottoman Empire.

input: Unicode can be implemented by different character encodings. The most commonly used encodings are UTF-8, UTF-16 and the now-obsolete UCS-2. UTF-8 uses one byte for any ASCII character, all of which have the same code values in both UTF-8 and ASCII encoding, and up to four bytes for other characters. UCS-2 uses a 16-bit code unit (two 8-bit bytes) for each character but cannot encode every character in the current Unicode standard. UTF-16 extends UCS-2, using one 16-bit unit for the characters that were representable in UCS-2 and two 16-bit units (4 × 8 bits) to handle each of the additional characters.
rewrite: Unicode is realized through various character encoding schemes, with UTF-8, UTF-16, and the outdated UCS-2 being the most prevalent. UTF-8 employs a single byte for ASCII characters, maintaining identical code values to ASCII, and utilizes up to four bytes for other symbols. UCS-2 encodes each character with one 16-bit unit but lacks the capacity for all characters in the modern Unicode standard. UTF-16 expands upon UCS-2, using a single 16-bit unit for originally representable characters and two such units (comprising four 8-bit bytes) for the remaining characters.

input: Jehovah's Witnesses believe that God's kingdom is a literal government in heaven, ruled by Jesus Christ and 144,000 "spirit-anointed" Christians drawn from the earth, which they associate with Jesus' reference to a "new covenant". The kingdom is viewed as the means by which God will accomplish his original purpose for the earth, transforming it into a paradise without sickness or death. It is said to have been the focal point of Jesus' ministry on earth. They believe the kingdom was established in heaven in 1914, and that Jehovah's Witnesses serve as representatives of the kingdom on earth.
rewrite: According to Jehovah's Witnesses doctrine, God's kingdom constitutes a literal heavenly government under the sovereignty of Jesus Christ and 144,000 "spirit-anointed" Christians from earth, linked to the biblical "new covenant." This kingdom is understood as the instrument for fulfilling God's original purpose for the earth, ultimately restoring it to a paradisiacal state free from illness and mortality. It is held to have been the central theme of Jesus' earthly ministry, established in heaven in 1914, with Jehovah's Witnesses acting as its earthly representatives.

input: Individual contestants have generated controversy in this competition for their past actions, or for being 'ringers' planted by the producers. A number of contestants had been disqualified for various reasons, such as for having an existing contract or undisclosed criminal records, although the show had been accused of double standard for disqualifying some but not others.
rewrite: This competition has faced controversy due to contestants' past conduct or their status as producer-planted 'ringers.' Several have been disqualified for reasons including pre-existing contracts or undisclosed criminal records. However, the program has been accused of applying a double standard, as not all individuals facing similar allegations have been removed.

input: In the early 21st century, the population of Paris began to increase slowly again, as more young people moved into the city. It reached 2.25 million in 2011. In March 2001, Bertrand Delanoë became the first socialist mayor of Paris. In 2007, in an effort to reduce car traffic in the city, he introduced the Vélib', a system which rents bicycles for the use of local residents and visitors. Bertrand Delanoë also transformed a section of the highway along the left bank of the Seine into an urban promenade and park, the Promenade des Berges de la Seine, which he inaugurated in June 2013.
rewrite: The early 21st century witnessed a gradual resurgence in the population of Paris, driven by an influx of younger residents, culminating in a total of 2.25 million by 2011. Following the March 2001 election of Bertrand Delanoë as the city's first socialist mayor, several key urban initiatives were implemented. To mitigate vehicular congestion, the Vélib' bicycle-sharing scheme was launched in 2007. Furthermore, a segment of the Left Bank expressway was converted into a public park and promenade, the Promenade des Berges de la Seine, inaugurated in June 2013.

input: The Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WSH) program of the Gates Foundation was launched in mid-2005 as a "Learning Initiative," and became a full-fledged program under the Global Development Division in early 2010. The Foundation has since 2005 undertaken a wide range of efforts in the WASH sector involving research, experimentation, reflection, advocacy, and field implementation. In 2009, the Foundation decided to refocus its WASH effort mainly on sustainable sanitation services for the poor, using non-piped sanitation services (i.e. without the use of sewers), and less on water supply. This was because the sanitation sector was generally receiving less attention from other donors and from governments, and because the Foundation believed it had the potential to make a real difference through strategic investments.
rewrite: The Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WSH) initiative of the Gates Foundation commenced in mid-2005 as a "Learning Initiative." It was elevated to a formal program within the Global Development Division in early 2010. Since its inception, the Foundation has engaged in extensive activities within the WASH sector, encompassing research, pilot projects, analysis, advocacy, and on-the-ground implementation. In 2009, a strategic decision was made to concentrate subsequent efforts predominantly on sustainable sanitation services for impoverished populations, specifically emphasizing non-piped, sewerless solutions over water supply. This reorientation was driven by the relative neglect of the sanitation sector by other donors and governments, coupled with the Foundation's conviction that targeted investments could yield substantial impact.

input: Situated in the southern part of Telangana in southeastern India, Hyderabad is 1,566 kilometres (973 mi) south of Delhi, 699 kilometres (434 mi) southeast of Mumbai, and 570 kilometres (350 mi) north of Bangalore by road. It lies on the banks of the Musi River, in the northern part of the Deccan Plateau. Greater Hyderabad covers 650 km2 (250 sq mi), making it one of the largest metropolitan areas in India. With an average altitude of 542 metres (1,778 ft), Hyderabad lies on predominantly sloping terrain of grey and pink granite, dotted with small hills, the highest being Banjara Hills at 672 metres (2,205 ft). The city has numerous lakes referred to as sagar, meaning "sea". Examples include artificial lakes created by dams on the Musi, such as Hussain Sagar (built in 1562 near the city centre), Osman Sagar and Himayat Sagar. As of 1996, the city had 140 lakes and 834 water tanks (ponds).
rewrite: Located in southern Telangana in southeastern India, the city of Hyderabad is positioned 1,566 kilometers south of Delhi, 699 kilometers southeast of Mumbai, and 570 kilometers north of Bangalore by road. It is situated on the banks of the Musi River within the northern Deccan Plateau. The Greater Hyderabad metropolitan region spans 650 square kilometers, ranking it among India's largest urban agglomerations. The city's average elevation is 542 meters, with its terrain consisting largely of sloping grey and pink granite, interspersed with minor hills; Banjara Hills, at 672 meters, is the highest. Hyderabad features numerous lakes, termed *sagar* (meaning "sea"), including artificial reservoirs formed by dams on the Musi River, such as Hussain Sagar (constructed in 1562 near the city center), Osman Sagar, and Himayat Sagar. As of 1996, the urban area contained 140 lakes and 834 water tanks or ponds.

input: Around the beginning of the 20th century, a general dissatisfaction with the emphasis on revivalist architecture and elaborate decoration gave rise to many new lines of thought that served as precursors to Modern Architecture. Notable among these is the Deutscher Werkbund, formed in 1907 to produce better quality machine made objects. The rise of the profession of industrial design is usually placed here. Following this lead, the Bauhaus school, founded in Weimar, Germany in 1919, redefined the architectural bounds prior set throughout history, viewing the creation of a building as the ultimate synthesis—the apex—of art, craft, and technology.
rewrite: The early twentieth century witnessed widespread disillusionment with revivalist architecture and ornate decoration, prompting several ideological movements that prefigured Modernism. A significant precursor was the Deutscher Werkbund, established in 1907 to elevate the quality of industrially manufactured goods, an initiative closely associated with the professional emergence of industrial design. Subsequently, the Bauhaus school, founded in Weimar in 1919, fundamentally redefined architectural principles. It conceived building design as the ultimate synthesis and highest expression of art, craft, and technology.

input: In the oft-cited and oft-criticized Sexual Behavior in the Human Male (1948) and Sexual Behavior in the Human Female (1953), by Alfred C. Kinsey et al., people were asked to rate themselves on a scale from completely heterosexual to completely homosexual. Kinsey reported that when the individuals' behavior as well as their identity are analyzed, most people appeared to be at least somewhat bisexual — i.e., most people have some attraction to either sex, although usually one sex is preferred. According to Kinsey, only a minority (5–10%) can be considered fully heterosexual or homosexual.[citation needed] Conversely, only an even smaller minority can be considered fully bisexual (with an equal attraction to both sexes). Kinsey's methods have been criticized as flawed, particularly with regard to the randomness of his sample population, which included prison inmates, male prostitutes and those who willingly participated in discussion of previously taboo sexual topics. Nevertheless, Paul Gebhard, subsequent director of the Kinsey Institute for Sex Research, reexamined the data in the Kinsey Reports and concluded that removing the prison inmates and prostitutes barely affected the results.
rewrite: In the frequently referenced yet contentious studies *Sexual Behavior in the Human Male* (1948) and *Sexual Behavior in the Human Female* (1953), authored by Alfred C. Kinsey and colleagues, participants were instructed to self-assess their orientation along a continuum from exclusively heterosexual to exclusively homosexual. Kinsey’s analysis, incorporating both behavioral and identity measures, indicated that a majority of individuals exhibited at least some degree of bisexuality—that is, most reported some attraction to both sexes, albeit typically with a preference for one. According to these findings, only a minority, approximately 5–10%, could be classified as entirely heterosexual or homosexual. Conversely, an even smaller proportion demonstrated fully bisexual orientation, characterized by equal attraction to both sexes. Kinsey’s methodology has been subject to significant criticism, particularly concerning the representativeness of his sample, which included prison inmates, male prostitutes, and volunteers comfortable discussing topics then considered taboo. However, Paul Gebhard, a later director of the Kinsey Institute for Sex Research, reanalyzed the data and concluded that excluding the inmate and prostitute subgroups had negligible impact on the overall results.

input: With the growing possibility of an Allied invasion in the Balkans, the Axis began to divert more resources to the destruction of the Partisans main force and its high command. This meant, among other things, a concerted German effort to capture Josip Broz Tito personally. On 25 May 1944, he managed to evade the Germans after the Raid on Drvar (Operation Rösselsprung), an airborne assault outside his Drvar headquarters in Bosnia.
rewrite: As the likelihood of an Allied invasion in the Balkans increased, the Axis redirected greater resources toward eliminating the primary Partisan forces and their leadership. This included a focused German initiative to personally capture Josip Broz Tito. He successfully evaded capture on 25 May 1944 following Operation Rösselsprung, an airborne assault on his headquarters in Drvar, Bosnia.

input: The Multidimensional Pain Inventory (MPI) is a questionnaire designed to assess the psychosocial state of a person with chronic pain. Analysis of MPI results by Turk and Rudy (1988) found three classes of chronic pain patient: "(a) dysfunctional, people who perceived the severity of their pain to be high, reported that pain interfered with much of their lives, reported a higher degree of psychological distress caused by pain, and reported low levels of activity; (b) interpersonally distressed, people with a common perception that significant others were not very supportive of their pain problems; and (c) adaptive copers, patients who reported high levels of social support, relatively low levels of pain and perceived interference, and relatively high levels of activity." Combining the MPI characterization of the person with their IASP five-category pain profile is recommended for deriving the most useful case description.
rewrite: The Multidimensional Pain Inventory (MPI) is a psychometric instrument designed to evaluate the psychosocial condition of individuals experiencing chronic pain. Based on an analysis of MPI outcomes, Turk and Rudy (1988) identified three distinct patient classifications: "(a) dysfunctional, characterized by high perceived pain severity, significant life interference and psychological distress, and low activity levels; (b) interpersonally distressed, marked by a shared perception of inadequate social support for their pain condition; and (c) adaptive copers, who report strong social support, relatively low levels of pain and interference, and relatively high activity." To formulate the most clinically informative case description, it is recommended to integrate this MPI-derived psychosocial classification with the individual's IASP five-axis pain diagnosis.

input: The AEA's work progressed to heavier-than-air machines, applying their knowledge of kites to gliders. Moving to Hammondsport, the group then designed and built the Red Wing, framed in bamboo and covered in red silk and powered by a small air-cooled engine. On March 12, 1908, over Keuka Lake, the biplane lifted off on the first public flight in North America.[N 24] [N 25] The innovations that were incorporated into this design included a cockpit enclosure and tail rudder (later variations on the original design would add ailerons as a means of control). One of the AEA's inventions, a practical wingtip form of the aileron, was to become a standard component on all aircraft. [N 26] The White Wing and June Bug were to follow and by the end of 1908, over 150 flights without mishap had been accomplished. However, the AEA had depleted its initial reserves and only a $15,000 grant from Mrs. Bell allowed it to continue with experiments. Lt. Selfridge had also become the first person killed in a powered heavier-than-air flight in a crash of the Wright Flyer at Fort Myer, Virginia, on September 17, 1908.
rewrite: The Aerial Experiment Association (AEA) advanced its research from kites to heavier-than-air gliders. Upon relocating to Hammondsport, the association designed and constructed the *Red Wing*, a biplane featuring a bamboo frame covered in red silk and propelled by a small air-cooled engine. On March 12, 1908, this aircraft conducted the first public flight in North America over Keuka Lake. Its design incorporated several innovations, including an enclosed cockpit and a tail rudder; subsequent modifications would introduce ailerons for enhanced control. Notably, the AEA developed a practical wingtip aileron, which later became a standard aerodynamic feature on all aircraft. Subsequent models, the *White Wing* and *June Bug*, followed, and by the close of 1908, the AEA had successfully completed over 150 flights without incident. However, the association exhausted its initial funding and was able to continue its experiments only through a $15,000 grant from Mrs. Bell. Concurrently, the field suffered a significant loss when Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge perished in the crash of a Wright Flyer at Fort Myer, Virginia, on September 17, 1908, becoming the first fatality in a powered heavier-than-air flight.

input: There are several major exceptions on tuition fees. In many European countries, it is possible to study without tuition fees. Public universities in Nordic countries were entirely without tuition fees until around 2005. Denmark, Sweden and Finland then moved to put in place tuition fees for foreign students. Citizens of EU and EEA member states and citizens from Switzerland remain exempted from tuition fees, and the amounts of public grants granted to promising foreign students were increased to offset some of the impact.
rewrite: Several significant exceptions exist regarding tuition fees. In numerous European nations, tuition-free higher education remains accessible. Public universities in Nordic countries historically charged no tuition until approximately 2005, when Denmark, Sweden, and Finland introduced fees for non-domestic students. However, citizens of EU and EEA member states and Switzerland continue to be exempt. Concurrently, public grant amounts for qualified international students were augmented to mitigate part of the financial impact.

input: Due to its location at the South Pole, Antarctica receives relatively little solar radiation. This means that it is a very cold continent where water is mostly in the form of ice. Precipitation is low (most of Antarctica is a desert) and almost always in the form of snow, which accumulates and forms a giant ice sheet which covers the land. Parts of this ice sheet form moving glaciers known as ice streams, which flow towards the edges of the continent. Next to the continental shore are many ice shelves. These are floating extensions of outflowing glaciers from the continental ice mass. Offshore, temperatures are also low enough that ice is formed from seawater through most of the year. It is important to understand the various types of Antarctic ice to understand possible effects on sea levels and the implications of global cooling.
rewrite: Antarctica's geographic position at the South Pole results in minimal solar radiation, producing an intensely cold climate where water exists predominantly as ice. Precipitation is scarce, classifying much of the continent as a desert, and falls almost exclusively as snow. This snow accumulates into a vast continental ice sheet. Within this sheet, dynamic ice streams—glaciers in motion—flow toward the periphery. Adjacent to the coastline, these outflows form extensive ice shelves, which are floating extensions of the continental ice mass. In the surrounding ocean, sufficiently low temperatures facilitate the formation of sea ice for much of the year. Comprehending these distinct ice formations is essential for assessing their potential impacts on global sea levels and the broader implications of climatic cooling.

input: In reaction to the emergence of Reform Judaism, a group of traditionalist German Jews emerged in support of some of the values of the Haskalah, but also wanted to defend the classic, traditional interpretation of Jewish law and tradition. This group was led by those who opposed the establishment of a new temple in Hamburg , as reflected in the booklet "Ele Divrei HaBerit". As a group of Reform Rabbis convened in Braunschweig, Rabbi Jacob Ettlinger of Altona published a manifesto entitled "Shlomei Emunei Yisrael" in German and Hebrew, having 177 Rabbis sign on. At this time the first Orthodox Jewish periodical, "Der Treue Zions Waechter", was launched with the Hebrew supplement "Shomer Zion HaNe'eman" [1845 - 1855]. In later years it was Rav Ettlinger's students Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch and Rabbi Azriel Hildesheimer of Berlin who deepened the awareness and strength of Orthodox Jewry. Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch commented in 1854:
rewrite: In response to the rise of Reform Judaism, a traditionalist faction arose among German Jews. While sympathetic to certain Haskalah ideals, this group sought to uphold a classical interpretation of Jewish law and tradition. Its early leadership was galvanized by opposition to a new Reform temple in Hamburg, a stance articulated in the polemical work *Ele Divrei HaBerit*. When Reform rabbis convened in Braunschweig, Rabbi Jacob Ettlinger of Altona issued a counter-manifesto, *Shlomei Emunei Yisrael*, which garnered the signatures of 177 rabbis. Concurrently, the first Orthodox periodical, *Der Treue Zions Waechter* with its Hebrew supplement *Shomer Zion HaNe'eman*, was established (1845–1855). Subsequently, Rabbi Ettlinger’s disciples, notably Rabbi Samson Raphael Hirsch and Rabbi Azriel Hildesheimer of Berlin, significantly expanded the ideological foundation and institutional vigor of Orthodox Jewry. Hirsch himself underscored this development in an 1854 commentary.

input: The Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) oversees the civic infrastructure of the city's 18 "circles", which together encompass 150 municipal wards. Each ward is represented by a corporator, elected by popular vote. The corporators elect the Mayor, who is the titular head of GHMC; executive powers rest with the Municipal Commissioner, appointed by the state government. The GHMC carries out the city's infrastructural work such as building and maintenance of roads and drains, town planning including construction regulation, maintenance of municipal markets and parks, solid waste management, the issuing of birth and death certificates, the issuing of trade licences, collection of property tax, and community welfare services such as mother and child healthcare, and pre-school and non-formal education. The GHMC was formed in April 2007 by merging the Municipal Corporation of Hyderabad (MCH) with 12 municipalities of the Hyderabad, Ranga Reddy and Medak districts covering a total area of 650 km2 (250 sq mi).:3 In the 2016 municipal election, the Telangana Rashtra Samithi formed the majority and the present Mayor is Bonthu Ram Mohan. The Secunderabad Cantonment Board is a civic administration agency overseeing an area of 40.1 km2 (15.5 sq mi),:93 where there are several military camps.:2 The Osmania University campus is administered independently by the university authority.:93
rewrite:
The Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) governs the civic infrastructure across the city's 18 administrative divisions, known as circles, which collectively contain 150 municipal wards. Each ward is represented by a corporator elected through direct popular vote. These corporators, in turn, elect the Mayor, who serves as the ceremonial head of the GHMC. Executive authority is vested in the Municipal Commissioner, an official appointed by the state government. The corporation's responsibilities encompass a broad range of urban services, including the construction and maintenance of roads and drainage systems, town planning and building regulation, upkeep of municipal markets and parks, solid waste management, issuance of birth and death certificates and trade licenses, property tax collection, and the provision of community welfare services such as maternal and child healthcare alongside pre-school and non-formal education.

Established in April 2007, the GHMC was formed through the amalgamation of the former Municipal Corporation of Hyderabad with twelve municipalities from the Hyderabad, Ranga Reddy, and Medak districts, resulting in a total jurisdictional area of 650 square kilometers. Following the 2016 municipal elections, the Telangana Rashtra Samithi party secured a majority, and the incumbent Mayor is Bonthu Ram Mohan. It is noteworthy that certain areas within the metropolitan region operate under separate administrative bodies. The Secunderabad Cantonment Board, for instance, manages civic affairs across 40.1 square kilometers, an area containing several military installations. Similarly, the Osmania University campus is administered autonomously by its own university authority.

input: Religious Ashkenazi Jews living in Israel are obliged to follow the authority of the chief Ashkenazi rabbi in halakhic matters. In this respect, a religiously Ashkenazi Jew is an Israeli who is more likely to support certain religious interests in Israel, including certain political parties. These political parties result from the fact that a portion of the Israeli electorate votes for Jewish religious parties; although the electoral map changes from one election to another, there are generally several small parties associated with the interests of religious Ashkenazi Jews. The role of religious parties, including small religious parties that play important roles as coalition members, results in turn from Israel's composition as a complex society in which competing social, economic, and religious interests stand for election to the Knesset, a unicameral legislature with 120 seats.
rewrite: Within Israel, Ashkenazi Jews adhering to Orthodox religious practice are bound by the halakhic authority of the Ashkenazi Chief Rabbinate. Consequently, these individuals demonstrate a greater propensity to endorse specific religious interests, including particular political parties, within the national context. Such parties emerge from a segment of the electorate that consistently supports Jewish religious factions. While electoral configurations vary, several minor parties typically represent Ashkenazi religious interests. The significant role of these religious parties, including smaller factions that often become pivotal coalition members, stems from Israel's societal composition. The nation constitutes a complex society wherein competing social, economic, and religious interests vie for representation in the Knesset, the 120-seat unicameral legislature.

input: Ecuador, Colombia, Guyana, Peru, and Brazil were the top source countries from South America for legal immigrants to the New York City region in 2013; the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Haiti, and Trinidad and Tobago in the Caribbean; Egypt, Ghana, and Nigeria from Africa; and El Salvador, Honduras, and Guatemala in Central America. Amidst a resurgence of Puerto Rican migration to New York City, this population had increased to approximately 1.3 million in the metropolitan area as of 2013.
rewrite: In 2013, the primary South American sources of legal immigrants to the New York City region were Ecuador, Colombia, Guyana, Peru, and Brazil. Leading Caribbean origins included the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Haiti, and Trinidad and Tobago, while key African sources were Egypt, Ghana, and Nigeria. Central American contributors were El Salvador, Honduras, and Guatemala. Concurrently, renewed Puerto Rican migration elevated this population to roughly 1.3 million within the metropolitan area that year.

input: By the end of the month, the Peloponnese was in open revolt against the Ottomans and by October 1821 the Greeks under Theodoros Kolokotronis had captured Tripolitsa. The Peloponnesian revolt was quickly followed by revolts in Crete, Macedonia and Central Greece, which would soon be suppressed. Meanwhile, the makeshift Greek navy was achieving success against the Ottoman navy in the Aegean Sea and prevented Ottoman reinforcements from arriving by sea. In 1822 and 1824 the Turks and Egyptians ravaged the islands, including Chios and Psara, committing wholesale massacres of the population. This had the effect of galvanizing public opinion in western Europe in favor of the Greek rebels.[page needed]
rewrite: By the close of the month, the Peloponnese had initiated an open revolt against Ottoman authority, culminating in the capture of Tripolitsa by Greek forces under Theodoros Kolokotronis by October 1821. This insurrection swiftly inspired further uprisings in Crete, Macedonia, and Central Greece, though these were subsequently suppressed. Concurrently, the provisional Greek navy attained successes against the Ottoman fleet in the Aegean Sea, obstructing the maritime arrival of Ottoman reinforcements. In 1822 and 1824, Turkish and Egyptian forces devastated several islands, such as Chios and Psara, perpetrating large-scale massacres. These atrocities ultimately served to galvanize Western European public opinion in support of the Greek cause.

input: While Southampton is no longer the base for any cross-channel ferries, it is the terminus for three internal ferry services, all of which operate from terminals at Town Quay.
