input: "The mind-stuff of the world is, of course, something more general than our individual conscious minds.... The mind-stuff is not spread in space and time; these are part of the cyclic scheme ultimately derived out of it.... It is necessary to keep reminding ourselves that all knowledge of our environment from which the world of physics is constructed, has entered in the form of messages transmitted along the nerves to the seat of consciousness.... Consciousness is not sharply defined, but fades into subconsciousness; and beyond that we must postulate something indefinite but yet continuous with our mental nature.... It is difficult for the matter-of-fact physicist to accept the view that the substratum of everything is of mental character. But no one can deny that mind is the first and most direct thing in our experience, and all else is remote inference."
rewrite: The mental substrate of the universe is inherently more general than individual, conscious human minds. This fundamental mind-stuff itself is not extended within space and time; rather, these dimensions constitute part of a cyclical framework ultimately derived from it. One must consistently recall that all knowledge of our environment, from which the physical world is constructed, arrives solely as neural messages transmitted to the locus of consciousness. Consciousness lacks a precise boundary, fading gradually into subconsciousness; beyond this, we must postulate an indefinite domain that remains continuous with our mental nature. While the empirically-oriented physicist may find it challenging to accept that the substratum of all reality is mental in character, none can deny that mind is the primary and most immediate datum of experience, whereas everything else constitutes a remote inference.

input: The first large, diverse lineage of short-tailed avialans to evolve were the enantiornithes, or "opposite birds", so named because the construction of their shoulder bones was in reverse to that of modern birds. Enantiornithes occupied a wide array of ecological niches, from sand-probing shorebirds and fish-eaters to tree-dwelling forms and seed-eaters. While they were the dominant group of avialans during the Cretaceous period, enantiornithes became extinct along with many other dinosaur groups at the end of the Mesozoic era.
rewrite: The Enantiornithes, colloquially termed "opposite birds," constituted the first major and morphologically diverse clade of short-tailed avialans. Their name derives from a shoulder girdle construction reversed relative to modern birds. Occupying a broad spectrum of ecological niches—including shorebirds, piscivores, arboreal forms, and granivores—they were the dominant avialan group throughout the Cretaceous. However, they became extinct alongside numerous other dinosaur lineages at the close of the Mesozoic era.

input: Baden Powell praised "Mr Darwin's masterly volume [supporting] the grand principle of the self-evolving powers of nature". In America, Asa Gray argued that evolution is the secondary effect, or modus operandi, of the first cause, design, and published a pamphlet defending the book in terms of theistic evolution, Natural Selection is not inconsistent with Natural Theology. Theistic evolution became a popular compromise, and St. George Jackson Mivart was among those accepting evolution but attacking Darwin's naturalistic mechanism. Eventually it was realised that supernatural intervention could not be a scientific explanation, and naturalistic mechanisms such as neo-Lamarckism were favoured over natural selection as being more compatible with purpose.
rewrite: Baden Powell commended Charles Darwin’s “masterly volume” for advancing the principle of nature’s self-evolving powers. In the United States, Asa Gray contended that evolution operated as a secondary effect within a designed framework, publishing a pamphlet that reconciled natural selection with natural theology through theistic evolution. This perspective emerged as a popular compromise, endorsed by figures such as St. George Jackson Mivart, who accepted evolution but criticized Darwin’s purely naturalistic mechanism. Ultimately, the scientific community recognized that supernatural intervention could not constitute a scientific explanation, leading to a preference for naturalistic alternatives like neo-Lamarckism, which were viewed as more aligned with teleological purpose than natural selection.

input: The principle of the modern computer was first described by mathematician and pioneering computer scientist Alan Turing, who set out the idea in his seminal 1936 paper, On Computable Numbers. Turing reformulated Kurt Gödel's 1931 results on the limits of proof and computation, replacing Gödel's universal arithmetic-based formal language with the formal and simple hypothetical devices that became known as Turing machines. He proved that some such machine would be capable of performing any conceivable mathematical computation if it were representable as an algorithm. He went on to prove that there was no solution to the Entscheidungsproblem by first showing that the halting problem for Turing machines is undecidable: in general, it is not possible to decide algorithmically whether a given Turing machine will ever halt.
rewrite: The foundational concept of the modern computer was formally established by mathematician and early computer scientist Alan Turing in his seminal 1936 paper, *On Computable Numbers*. Turing reconceptualized Kurt Gödel's 1931 findings concerning the limits of proof and computation. He supplanted Gödel's universal arithmetic-based language with a simplified formal apparatus: the hypothetical Turing machine. Turing demonstrated that such a device could execute any mathematical computation expressible as an algorithm. Furthermore, he resolved the Entscheidungsproblem by proving the undecidability of the halting problem for Turing machines, establishing that no general algorithmic procedure can determine whether an arbitrary Turing machine will halt.

input: The North Korean contributions to the Chinese Communist victory were not forgotten after the creation of the People's Republic of China in 1949. As a token of gratitude, between 50,000 and 70,000 Korean veterans that served in the PLA were sent back along with their weapons, and they later played a significant role in the initial invasion of South Korea. China promised to support the North Koreans in the event of a war against South Korea. The Chinese support created a deep division between the Korean Communists, and Kim Il-sung's authority within the Communist party was challenged by the Chinese faction led by Pak Il-yu, who was later purged by Kim.
rewrite: Following the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the contributions of North Korea to the Communist victory were formally acknowledged. In a gesture of reciprocity, approximately 50,000 to 70,000 Korean veterans of the People's Liberation Army were repatriated with their armaments, subsequently forming a crucial element of the initial offensive against South Korea. China had further committed to supporting North Korea in such a conflict. This patronage, however, exacerbated internal divisions among Korean Communists, challenging Kim Il-sung's authority through a rival faction aligned with China and led by Pak Il-yu, who was later purged.

input: Nishimura's force consisted of two battleships, one cruiser and four destroyers. Because they were observing radio silence, Nishimura was unable to synchronize with Shima and Kurita. Nishimura and Shima had failed to even coordinate their plans before the attacks – they were long-time rivals and neither wished to have anything to do with the other. When he entered the narrow Surigao Strait at about 02:00, Shima was 22 miles (40 km) behind him, and Kurita was still in the Sibuyan Sea, several hours from the beaches at Leyte. As they passed Panaon Island, Nishimura's force ran into a trap set for them by the U.S.-Australian 7th Fleet Support Force. R. Adm. Jesse Oldendorf had six battleships, four heavy cruisers, four light cruisers, 29 destroyers and 39 PT boats. To pass the strait and reach the landings, Nishimura had to run the gauntlet. At about 03:00 the Japanese battleship Fusō and three destroyers were hit by torpedoes and Fusō broke in two. At 03:50 the U.S. battleships opened fire. Radar fire control meant they could hit targets from a much greater distance than the Japanese. The battleship Yamashiro, a cruiser and a destroyer were crippled by 16-inch (406 mm) shells; Yamashiro sank at 04:19. Only one of Nishimura's force of seven ships survived the engagement. At 04:25 Shima's force of two cruisers and eight destroyers reached the battle. Seeing Fusō and believing her to be the wrecks of two battleships, Shima ordered a retreat, ending the last battleship-vs-battleship action in history.
rewrite:
The naval force under Vice Admiral Nishimura comprised two battleships, one cruiser, and four destroyers. Operating under strict radio silence, Nishimura was unable to establish tactical coordination with the fleets of Vice Admirals Shima and Kurita. Furthermore, Nishimura and Shima had neglected to synchronize their operational plans prior to the engagement, a failure attributable to a longstanding professional rivalry and mutual disinclination for cooperation. As Nishimura’s squadron entered the constricted waters of Surigao Strait around 02:00, Shima’s force trailed approximately 22 miles (40 kilometers) astern, while Kurita’s remained in the Sibuyan Sea, several hours distant from the Leyte landing zones. Upon passing Panaon Island, Nishimura encountered a prepared defensive position established by the U.S.-Australian 7th Fleet Support Force under Rear Admiral Jesse Oldendorf. This opposing force disposed six battleships, four heavy and four light cruisers, 29 destroyers, and 39 PT boats. To transit the strait and assail the invasion beachhead, Nishimura was compelled to navigate this formidable gauntlet.

Commencing around 03:00, the Japanese battleship *Fusō* and three destroyers sustained torpedo impacts; the *Fusō* subsequently fractured amidships. At 03:50, the American battleships commenced main battery fire. Their superior radar-directed fire control systems enabled effective engagement at ranges beyond the capabilities of the Japanese vessels. The battleship *Yamashiro*, one cruiser, and one destroyer were incapacitated by 16-inch (406 mm) shellfire; the *Yamashiro* foundered at 04:19. Of Nishimura’s seven warships, only a single destroyer survived the encounter. At 04:25, Shima’s force—two cruisers and eight destroyers—arrived at the scene. Observing the burning halves of the *Fusō*, which he misinterpreted as two distinct battleship wrecks, Shima ordered an immediate withdrawal. This decision concluded the final battleship-versus-battleship engagement in naval history.

input: 187th Street crosses Washington Heights and running from Laurel Hill Terrace in the east to Chittenden Avenue in the west near the George Washington Bridge and Hudson River. The street is interrupted by a long set of stairs east of Fort Washington Avenue leading to the Broadway valley. West of there, it is mostly lined with store fronts and serves as a main shopping district for the Hudson Heights neighborhood.
rewrite: 187th Street traverses Washington Heights, extending from Laurel Hill Terrace in the east to Chittenden Avenue in the west, proximate to the George Washington Bridge and Hudson River. Its path is interrupted by a lengthy staircase east of Fort Washington Avenue, descending into the Broadway valley. To the west, the street is predominantly lined with commercial storefronts, functioning as a primary retail corridor for the Hudson Heights neighborhood.

input: The strongest contribution of the French Academies to the public sphere comes from the concours académiques (roughly translated as 'academic contests') they sponsored throughout France. These academic contests were perhaps the most public of any institution during the Enlightenment. The practice of contests dated back to the Middle Ages, and was revived in the mid-17th century. The subject matter had previously been generally religious and/or monarchical, featuring essays, poetry, and painting. By roughly 1725, however, this subject matter had radically expanded and diversified, including "royal propaganda, philosophical battles, and critical ruminations on the social and political institutions of the Old Regime." Topics of public controversy were also discussed such as the theories of Newton and Descartes, the slave trade, women's education, and justice in France.
rewrite: The most significant contribution of the French Academies to the public sphere emerged from the *concours académiques* (academic contests) they organized nationally. These contests represented arguably the most public institution of the Enlightenment era. Revived in the mid-seventeenth century from a medieval tradition, these competitions initially focused on religious and monarchical themes in essays, poetry, and painting. By approximately 1725, however, their scope had radically expanded and diversified to encompass, as noted, "royal propaganda, philosophical battles, and critical ruminations on the social and political institutions of the Old Regime." They furthermore served as a forum for publicly contentious topics, including Newtonian and Cartesian theories, the slave trade, women's education, and the administration of justice in France.

input: The Jamahiriya's radical direction earned the government many enemies. In February 1978, Gaddafi discovered that his head of military intelligence was plotting to kill him, and began to increasingly entrust security to his Qaddadfa tribe. Many who had seen their wealth and property confiscated turned against the administration, and a number of western-funded opposition groups were founded by exiles. Most prominent was the National Front for the Salvation of Libya (NFSL), founded in 1981 by Mohammed Magariaf, which orchestrated militant attacks against Libya's government, while another, al-Borkan, began killing Libyan diplomats abroad. Following Gaddafi's command to kill these "stray dogs", under Colonel Younis Bilgasim's leadership, the Revolutionary Committees set up overseas branches to suppress counter-revolutionary activity, assassinating various dissidents. Although nearby nations like Syria also used hit squads, Gaddafi was unusual in publicly bragging about his administration's use of them; in June 1980, he ordered all dissidents to return home or be "liquidated wherever you are."
rewrite: The radical orientation of the Jamahiriya generated significant opposition to the regime. In February 1978, upon discovering an assassination plot orchestrated by his head of military intelligence, Muammar Gaddafi increasingly concentrated security responsibilities within his own Qaddadfa tribal network. This alienation was compounded by widespread confiscations of wealth and property, driving many to oppose the administration. Expatriate communities subsequently formed several Western-funded opposition organizations. The most notable, the National Front for the Salvation of Libya (NFSL), founded in 1981 by Mohammed Magariaf, executed militant attacks within Libya. Another group, al-Borkan, targeted Libyan diplomats overseas. In response, Gaddafi issued orders to eliminate these "stray dogs." Under Colonel Younis Bilgasim, the Revolutionary Committees established foreign branches to suppress counter-revolutionary activity, conducting assassinations of dissidents. While other states, such as Syria, employed similar covert squads, Gaddafi was distinctive in his public boasting about their use. His explicit June 1980 ultimatum demanded all dissidents return home or face liquidation abroad.

input: The state of California was admitted to the United States in 1850. That same year San Diego was designated the seat of the newly established San Diego County and was incorporated as a city. Joshua H. Bean, the last alcalde of San Diego, was elected the first mayor. Two years later the city was bankrupt; the California legislature revoked the city's charter and placed it under control of a board of trustees, where it remained until 1889. A city charter was re-established in 1889 and today's city charter was adopted in 1931.
rewrite: California achieved statehood in 1850, the same year San Diego was designated the county seat of its newly formed county and incorporated as a city. Joshua H. Bean, the final alcalde, became its first mayor. Municipal bankruptcy in 1852 prompted the state legislature to revoke the city's charter, placing governance under a board of trustees until 1889. A charter was re-established that year, with the current city charter being formally adopted in 1931.

input: The vast majority of visitors in Greece in 2007 came from the European continent, numbering 12.7 million, while the most visitors from a single nationality were those from the United Kingdom, (2.6 million), followed closely by those from Germany (2.3 million). In 2010, the most visited region of Greece was that of Central Macedonia, with 18% of the country's total tourist flow (amounting to 3.6 million tourists), followed by Attica with 2.6 million and the Peloponnese with 1.8 million. Northern Greece is the country's most-visited geographical region, with 6.5 million tourists, while Central Greece is second with 6.3 million.
rewrite: In 2007, the predominant origin of visitors to Greece was continental Europe, totaling 12.7 million arrivals. The United Kingdom provided the largest single national cohort at 2.6 million, closely followed by Germany with 2.3 million. Regarding domestic distribution in 2010, Central Macedonia was the most frequented region, attracting 18% of the national tourist influx, or 3.6 million visitors. It was succeeded by Attica (2.6 million) and the Peloponnese (1.8 million). Geographically, Northern Greece received the highest volume at 6.5 million tourists, with Central Greece ranking second at 6.3 million.

input: The digital data on a CD begins at the center of the disc and proceeds toward the edge, which allows adaptation to the different size formats available. Standard CDs are available in two sizes. By far, the most common is 120 millimetres (4.7 in) in diameter, with a 74- or 80-minute audio capacity and a 650 or 700 MiB (737,280,000-byte) data capacity. This capacity was reportedly specified by Sony executive Norio Ohga in May 1980 so as to be able to contain the entirety of the London Philharmonic Orchestra's recording of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony on one disc. This is a myth according to Kees Immink, as the code format had not yet been decided in May 1980. The adoption of EFM one month later would have allowed a playing time of 97 minutes for 120 mm diameter or 74 minutes for a disc as small as 100 mm. The 120 mm diameter has been adopted by subsequent formats, including Super Audio CD, DVD, HD DVD, and Blu-ray Disc. Eighty-millimeter discs ("Mini CDs") were originally designed for CD singles and can hold up to 24 minutes of music or 210 MiB of data but never became popular.[citation needed] Today, nearly every single is released on a 120 mm CD, called a Maxi single.[citation needed]
rewrite: The digital data on a compact disc (CD) is encoded in a spiral track originating at the disc’s centre and extending outward toward the periphery. This design permits adaptation to discs of varying physical dimensions. The standard CD exists in two primary sizes. The predominant format is 120 millimetres in diameter, offering either 74 or 80 minutes of audio, corresponding to a data capacity of 650 or 700 mebibytes (MiB), respectively. A widely cited anecdote attributes the specification of the 74-minute capacity to Sony executive Norio Ohga in May 1980, purportedly to accommodate a complete recording of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony by the London Philharmonic Orchestra. However, engineer Kees Immink has contested this account, noting that the coding format was not finalized at that time. The subsequent adoption of Eight-to-Fourteen Modulation (EFM) one month later theoretically enabled a playing time of 97 minutes for a 120 mm disc, or 74 minutes for a disc as small as 100 mm. The 120 mm diameter has since become a standard for subsequent optical media, including Super Audio CD, DVD, HD DVD, and Blu-ray Disc. An alternative eighty-millimeter “Mini CD” format, designed for CD singles with a capacity of up to 24 minutes of audio or 210 MiB, failed to achieve significant market penetration. In contemporary practice, singles are typically released on 120 mm discs, commonly termed Maxi singles.

input: Beyoncé has received praise for her stage presence and voice during live performances. Jarett Wieselman of the New York Post placed her at number one on her list of the Five Best Singer/Dancers. According to Barbara Ellen of The Guardian Beyoncé is the most in-charge female artist she's seen onstage, while Alice Jones of The Independent wrote she "takes her role as entertainer so seriously she's almost too good." The ex-President of Def Jam L.A. Reid has described Beyoncé as the greatest entertainer alive. Jim Farber of the Daily News and Stephanie Classen of Star Phoenix both praised her strong voice and her stage presence.
rewrite: Beyoncé’s live performances have garnered significant acclaim for her commanding stage presence and vocal prowess. Jarett Wieselman of the New York Post ranked her first among the best singer-dancers. Critics, including Barbara Ellen of The Guardian and Alice Jones of The Independent, have highlighted her authoritative control and exceptional dedication as a performer. Former Def Jam president L.A. Reid has declared her the greatest living entertainer. Additionally, reviewers such as Jim Farber of the Daily News and Stephanie Classen of the Star Phoenix have specifically commended the power of her voice and her compelling stage persona.

input: The eastern shoreline of Funafuti Lagoon was modified during World War II when the airfield (what is now Funafuti International Airport) was constructed. The coral base of the atoll was used as fill to create the runway. The resulting borrow pits impacted the fresh-water aquifer. In the low areas of Funafuti the sea water can be seen bubbling up through the porous coral rock to form pools with each high tide. Since 1994 a project has been in development to assess the environmental impact of transporting sand from the lagoon to fill all the borrow pits and low-lying areas on Fongafale. In 2014 the Tuvalu Borrow Pits Remediation (BPR) project was approved in order to fill 10 borrow pits, leaving Tafua Pond, which is a natural pond. The New Zealand Government funded the BPR project. The project was carried out in 2015 with 365,000 sqm of sand being dredged from the lagoon to fill the holes and improve living conditions on the island. This project increase the usable land space on Fongafale by eight per cent.
rewrite: During the Second World War, the construction of an airfield—now Funafuti International Airport—significantly altered the eastern shoreline of Funafuti Lagoon. The runway was built using fill material extracted from the atoll's coral base, a process which created numerous borrow pits. These excavations subsequently compromised the integrity of the island's freshwater aquifer. In low-lying areas of Funafuti, seawater can now be observed percolating upward through the porous coral substrate during high tide, forming saline pools. In response, an initiative to evaluate the environmental implications of using lagoon sand to backfill all borrow pits and low-lying zones on Fongafale has been under consideration since 1994. The Tuvalu Borrow Pits Remediation (BPR) project, approved in 2014 and funded by the New Zealand Government, aimed to fill ten such pits while preserving the natural Tafua Pond. Executed in 2015, the project involved dredging approximately 365,000 square metres of sand from the lagoon to infill the excavations, thereby enhancing local living conditions and augmenting Fongafale's usable land area by eight percent.

input: Rebirth refers to a process whereby beings go through a succession of lifetimes as one of many possible forms of sentient life, each running from conception to death. The doctrine of anattā (Sanskrit anātman) rejects the concepts of a permanent self or an unchanging, eternal soul, as it is called in Hinduism and Christianity. According to Buddhism there ultimately is no such thing as a self independent from the rest of the universe. Buddhists also refer to themselves as the believers of the anatta doctrine—Nairatmyavadin or Anattavadin. Rebirth in subsequent existences must be understood as the continuation of a dynamic, ever-changing process of pratītyasamutpāda ("dependent arising") determined by the laws of cause and effect (karma) rather than that of one being, reincarnating from one existence to the next.
rewrite: Rebirth denotes the cyclical process through which sentient beings experience a succession of lifetimes, each spanning from conception to death across various possible forms. This concept is framed by the doctrine of *anattā* (Sanskrit *anātman*), which denies the existence of a permanent, unchanging self or eternal soul, as posited in traditions such as Hinduism and Christianity. Buddhism asserts that no independent, enduring self exists apart from the interdependent universe. Adherents to this view are termed *Anattavādins* or *Nairātmyavādins*. Crucially, rebirth is not the transmigration of a fixed entity but the continuation of a dynamic, conditioned process—*pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent arising)—governed by the causal laws of karma.

input: New York City is situated in the Northeastern United States, in southeastern New York State, approximately halfway between Washington, D.C. and Boston. The location at the mouth of the Hudson River, which feeds into a naturally sheltered harbor and then into the Atlantic Ocean, has helped the city grow in significance as a trading port. Most of New York City is built on the three islands of Long Island, Manhattan, and Staten Island.
rewrite: New York City is located in the northeastern United States, within southeastern New York State, positioned approximately midway between Washington, D.C. and Boston. Its situation at the Hudson River's mouth, leading to a protected harbor and the Atlantic Ocean, facilitated its historical development as a major commercial port. The city's urban area primarily occupies the islands of Long Island, Manhattan, and Staten Island.

input: In winter, the Piedmont is colder than the coast, with temperatures usually averaging in the upper 40s–lower 50s °F (8–12 °C) during the day and often dropping below the freezing point at night. The region averages around 3–5 in (8–13 cm) of snowfall annually in the Charlotte area, and slightly more north toward the Virginia border. The Piedmont is especially notorious for sleet and freezing rain. Freezing rain can be heavy enough to snarl traffic and break down trees and power lines. Annual precipitation and humidity are lower in the Piedmont than in the mountains or the coast, but even at its lowest, the average is 40 in (1,020 mm) per year.
rewrite: During the winter season, the Piedmont region experiences lower temperatures than the coastal areas, with average daytime temperatures ranging from the upper 40s to lower 50s °F (8–12 °C). Nighttime temperatures frequently fall below freezing. The area receives approximately 3–5 inches (8–13 cm) of annual snowfall near Charlotte, increasing slightly toward the northern border with Virginia. The Piedmont is particularly prone to sleet and freezing rain, the latter of which can accumulate sufficiently to disrupt transportation and damage trees and power infrastructure. While annual precipitation and humidity levels are lower than in the mountains or coast, the region still averages a minimum of 40 inches (1,020 mm) of precipitation per year.

input: The Neolithic 2 (PPNB) began around 8,800 BCE according to the ASPRO chronology in the Levant (Jericho, Israel). As with the PPNA dates, there are two versions from the same laboratories noted above. This system of terminology, however, is not convenient for southeast Anatolia and settlements of the middle Anatolia basin. This era was before the Mesolithic era.[citation needed] A settlement of 3,000 inhabitants was found in the outskirts of Amman, Jordan. Considered to be one of the largest prehistoric settlements in the Near East, called 'Ain Ghazal, it was continuously inhabited from approximately 7,250 – 5,000 B.
rewrite: According to the ASPRO chronology, the Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB) period commenced around 8,800 BCE in the Levant, as evidenced at sites like Jericho. As with the preceding PPNA, two chronological versions from the aforementioned laboratories exist. This terminology, however, proves less suitable for southeast Anatolia and the central Anatolian basin. Preceding the Mesolithic, this era is exemplified by the large settlement of ‘Ain Ghazal near Amman, Jordan. Continuously occupied from circa 7,250 to 5,000 BCE and housing around 3,000 inhabitants, it is regarded as one of the largest prehistoric settlements in the Near East.

input: The American Civil War boosted the local economy with wartime purchases of industrial goods, including that of the New Haven Arms Company, which would later become the Winchester Repeating Arms Company. (Winchester would continue to produce arms in New Haven until 2006, and many of the buildings that were a part of the Winchester plant are now a part of the Winchester Repeating Arms Company Historic District.) After the war, population grew and doubled by the start of the 20th century, most notably due to the influx of immigrants from southern Europe, particularly Italy. Today, roughly half the populations of East Haven, West Haven, and North Haven are Italian-American. Jewish immigration to New Haven has left an enduring mark on the city. Westville was the center of Jewish life in New Haven, though today many have fanned out to suburban communities such as Woodbridge and Cheshire.
rewrite: The American Civil War stimulated the local economy through wartime procurement of industrial products, notably including those manufactured by the New Haven Arms Company, the precursor to the Winchester Repeating Arms Company. (Winchester maintained arms production in New Haven until 2006, with many of its former factory structures now comprising the Winchester Repeating Arms Company Historic District.) In the postwar period, the population expanded significantly, doubling by the turn of the twentieth century, largely attributable to immigration from Southern Europe, especially Italy. Consequently, Italian-Americans now constitute approximately half of the residents in East Haven, West Haven, and North Haven. Furthermore, Jewish immigration has profoundly shaped the city's character. While the Westville neighborhood historically served as the focal point of Jewish communal life, many descendants of these immigrants have since relocated to suburban areas including Woodbridge and Cheshire.

input: Most bacteria have a single circular chromosome that can range in size from only 160,000 base pairs in the endosymbiotic bacteria Candidatus Carsonella ruddii, to 12,200,000 base pairs in the soil-dwelling bacteria Sorangium cellulosum. Spirochaetes of the genus Borrelia are a notable exception to this arrangement, with bacteria such as Borrelia burgdorferi, the cause of Lyme disease, containing a single linear chromosome. The genes in bacterial genomes are usually a single continuous stretch of DNA and although several different types of introns do exist in bacteria, these are much rarer than in eukaryotes.
rewrite: The majority of bacterial species possess a singular circular chromosome, with sizes varying substantially from approximately 160 kilobases in endosymbionts like *Candidatus* Carsonella ruddii to over 12 megabases in soil bacteria such as *Sorangium cellulosum*. A key exception is found in *Borrelia* spirochaetes, which feature a linear chromosome, as exemplified by *Borrelia burgdorferi*, the etiological agent of Lyme disease. Typically, bacterial genes constitute contiguous DNA sequences, and while introns are present, their occurrence is significantly less frequent compared to eukaryotic organisms.

input: Daniel Gralath was the first to combine several jars in parallel into a "battery" to increase the charge storage capacity. Benjamin Franklin investigated the Leyden jar and came to the conclusion that the charge was stored on the glass, not in the water as others had assumed. He also adopted the term "battery", (denoting the increasing of power with a row of similar units as in a battery of cannon), subsequently applied to clusters of electrochemical cells. Leyden jars were later made by coating the inside and outside of jars with metal foil, leaving a space at the mouth to prevent arcing between the foils.[citation needed] The earliest unit of capacitance was the jar, equivalent to about 1.11 nanofarads.
rewrite: Daniel Gralath pioneered the combination of multiple Leyden jars in parallel, forming a "battery" to augment total charge storage capacity. Benjamin Franklin later studied the device, correctly concluding the charge resided on the glass itself rather than in the water, as was previously supposed. Franklin also adopted the military term "battery"—referring to a row of cannon—for such clusters, a designation later extended to groupings of electrochemical cells. Subsequent designs coated the jar's interior and exterior with metal foil, while leaving an uncoated gap at the mouth to prevent electrical arcing. The jar, the earliest unit of capacitance, was equivalent to approximately 1.11 nanofarads.

input: Cara Cusumano, director of the Tribeca Film Festival, stated in April 2014: "Piracy is less about people not wanting to pay and more about just wanting the immediacy – people saying, 'I want to watch Spiderman right now' and downloading it". The statement occurred during the third year that the festival used the Internet to present its content, while it was the first year that it featured a showcase of content producers who work exclusively online. Cusumano further explained that downloading behavior is not merely conducted by people who merely want to obtain content for free:
rewrite: In April 2014, Cara Cusumano, director of the Tribeca Film Festival, asserted that film piracy is driven less by an aversion to payment and more by a demand for immediate access, exemplified by individuals seeking instant viewing. This statement coincided with the festival's third year of online content distribution and its inaugural showcase for digital-exclusive producers. Cusumano elaborated that such downloading practices are not solely attributable to those seeking free content.

input: As of the early 21st century, Christianity has approximately 2.4 billion adherents. The faith represents about a third of the world's population and is the largest religion in the world. Christians have composed about 33 percent of the world's population for around 100 years. The largest Christian denomination is the Roman Catholic Church, with 1.17 billion adherents, representing half of all Christians.
rewrite: Christianity, with approximately 2.4 billion adherents in the early 21st century, constitutes the world's largest religion, representing roughly one-third of the global population—a proportion maintained for about a century. The Roman Catholic Church is the largest denomination, comprising 1.17 billion followers, or half of all Christians.

input: In this respect, the counterpart of Ashkenazi is Sephardic, since most non-Ashkenazi Orthodox Jews follow Sephardic rabbinical authorities, whether or not they are ethnically Sephardic. By tradition, a Sephardic or Mizrahi woman who marries into an Orthodox or Haredi Ashkenazi Jewish family raises her children to be Ashkenazi Jews; conversely an Ashkenazi woman who marries a Sephardi or Mizrahi man is expected to take on Sephardic practice and the children inherit a Sephardic identity, though in practice many families compromise. A convert generally follows the practice of the beth din that converted him or her. With the integration of Jews from around the world in Israel, North America, and other places, the religious definition of an Ashkenazi Jew is blurring, especially outside Orthodox Judaism.
rewrite: In this context, Sephardic Judaism serves as the primary counterpart to Ashkenazi Judaism, as most non-Ashkenazi Orthodox Jews adhere to Sephardic rabbinic authorities irrespective of their ethnic descent. Traditionally, matrimonial unions across these lines dictate communal affiliation: a Sephardic or Mizrahi woman marrying into an Ashkenazi Orthodox family raises children within the Ashkenazi tradition, while an Ashkenazi woman marrying a Sephardic or Mizrahi man typically adopts Sephardic practice, with children assuming a Sephardic identity—though familial compromises frequently occur. Converts generally follow the customs of their officiating rabbinical court. Due to global Jewish integration in Israel, North America, and elsewhere, the religious definition of an Ashkenazi Jew is becoming increasingly fluid, particularly beyond Orthodox circles.

input: Somerset is a rural county of rolling hills such as the Blackdown Hills, Mendip Hills, Quantock Hills and Exmoor National Park, and large flat expanses of land including the Somerset Levels. There is evidence of human occupation from Paleolithic times, and of subsequent settlement in the Roman and Anglo-Saxon periods. The county played a significant part in the consolidation of power and rise of King Alfred the Great, and later in the English Civil War and the Monmouth Rebellion. The city of Bath is famous for its substantial Georgian architecture and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
rewrite: Somerset is a rural county characterized by its undulating terrain, including the Blackdown, Mendip, and Quantock Hills, as well as Exmoor National Park, alongside expansive low-lying areas such as the Somerset Levels. Archaeological evidence indicates human presence from the Paleolithic era, with continued settlement through Roman and Anglo-Saxon periods. The region was significant in the consolidation of power under King Alfred the Great and in later conflicts, including the English Civil War and Monmouth Rebellion. The city of Bath is renowned for its extensive Georgian architecture, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

input: Having initially announced a new album entitled So Help Me God slated for a 2014 release, in March 2015 West announced that the album would instead be tentatively called SWISH. Later that month, West was awarded an honorary doctorate by the School of the Art Institute of Chicago for his contributions to music, fashion, and popular culture, officially making him an honorary DFA. The next month, West headlined at the Glastonbury Festival in the UK, despite a petition signed by almost 135,000 people against his appearance. At one point, he told the audience: "You are now watching the greatest living rock star on the planet." Media outlets, including social media sites such as Twitter, were sharply divided on his performance. NME stated, "The decision to book West for the slot has proved controversial since its announcement, and the show itself appeared to polarise both Glastonbury goers and those who tuned in to watch on their TVs." The publication added that "he's letting his music speak for and prove itself." The Guardian said that "his set has a potent ferocity – but there are gaps and stutters, and he cuts a strangely lone figure in front of the vast crowd."
rewrite: Initially announcing a new album titled *So Help Me God* for a planned 2014 release, Kanye West declared in March 2015 that the project would be tentatively renamed *SWISH*. That same month, the School of the Art Institute of Chicago conferred upon him an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree in recognition of his impact on music, fashion, and popular culture. The following month, West headlined the Glastonbury Festival in the United Kingdom, notwithstanding a petition opposing his appearance that garnered nearly 135,000 signatures. During his performance, he proclaimed to the audience, "You are now watching the greatest living rock star on the planet." Critical reception, including across social media platforms like Twitter, was profoundly divided. *NME* observed that the booking had been controversial and that the performance "appeared to polarise both Glastonbury goers and those who tuned in to watch on their TVs," while also noting West was "letting his music speak for and prove itself." *The Guardian* characterized his set as possessing "a potent ferocity," but critiqued its "gaps and stutters," describing West as "a strangely lone figure in front of the vast crowd."

input: Crystal Bowersox, who has Type-I diabetes, fell ill due to diabetic ketoacidosis on the morning of the girls performance night for the top 20 week and was hospitalized. The schedule was rearranged so the boys performed first and she could perform the following night instead; she later revealed that Ken Warwick, the show producer, wanted to disqualify her but she begged to be allowed to stay on the show.

input: During the Eastern Han, conscription could be avoided if one paid a commutable tax. The Eastern Han court favored the recruitment of a volunteer army. The volunteer army comprised the Southern Army (Nanjun 南軍), while the standing army stationed in and near the capital was the Northern Army (Beijun 北軍). Led by Colonels (Xiaowei 校尉), the Northern Army consisted of five regiments, each composed of several thousand soldiers. When central authority collapsed after 189 AD, wealthy landowners, members of the aristocracy/nobility, and regional military-governors relied upon their retainers to act as their own personal troops (buqu 部曲).
rewrite: During the Eastern Han dynasty, compulsory military service could be commuted through a monetary payment. The imperial court increasingly preferred to recruit a volunteer force, known as the Southern Army (Nanjun). The standing professional garrison stationed in and around the capital, commanded by Colonels (Xiaowei), was the Northern Army (Beijun). This force was organized into five regiments, each numbering several thousand soldiers. Following the collapse of central authority after 189 AD, powerful figures—including wealthy landowners, aristocrats, and regional governors—relied upon their private retainers (buqu) to serve as personal troops.

input: On 12 February 1912, after rounds of negotiations, Longyu issued an imperial edict bringing about the abdication of the child emperor Puyi. This brought an end to over 2,000 years of Imperial China and began an extended period of instability of warlord factionalism. The unorganized political and economic systems combined with a widespread criticism of Chinese culture led to questioning and doubt about the future. In the 1930s, the Empire of Japan invaded Northeast China and founded Manchukuo in 1932, with Puyi, as the emperor. After the invasion by the Soviet Union, Manchukuo collapsed in 1945.
rewrite: On 12 February 1912, following extensive negotiations, Empress Dowager Longyu promulgated an imperial edict effecting the abdication of the child emperor Puyi. This act terminated over two millennia of imperial rule in China, precipitating an extended period of instability characterized by warlord factionalism. Concurrently, disorganized political and economic systems, alongside widespread cultural criticism, fostered profound uncertainty regarding the nation’s future. In the 1930s, Japan invaded Northeast China, establishing the puppet state of Manchukuo in 1932 with Puyi installed as its nominal emperor. This entity collapsed in 1945 following the Soviet Union’s military intervention.

input: Valencia's port is the biggest on the Mediterranean western coast, the first of Spain in container traffic as of 2008 and the second of Spain in total traffic, handling 20% of Spain's exports. The main exports are foodstuffs and beverages. Other exports include oranges, furniture, ceramic tiles, fans, textiles and iron products. Valencia's manufacturing sector focuses on metallurgy, chemicals, textiles, shipbuilding and brewing. Small and medium-sized industries are an important part of the local economy, and before the current crisis unemployment was lower than the Spanish average.
rewrite: Valencia's port is the largest on the western Mediterranean coast, ranking first in Spain for container traffic since 2008 and second in total traffic, managing 20% of the nation's exports. Principal exports comprise foodstuffs and beverages, alongside oranges, furniture, ceramics, textiles, and iron products. The local manufacturing sector specializes in metallurgy, chemicals, textiles, shipbuilding, and brewing. Small and medium-sized enterprises are economically significant, and pre-crisis unemployment rates were historically below the national average.

input: When a tree is very young it is covered with limbs almost, if not entirely, to the ground, but as it grows older some or all of them will eventually die and are either broken off or fall off. Subsequent growth of wood may completely conceal the stubs which will however remain as knots. No matter how smooth and clear a log is on the outside, it is more or less knotty near the middle. Consequently, the sapwood of an old tree, and particularly of a forest-grown tree, will be freer from knots than the inner heartwood. Since in most uses of wood, knots are defects that weaken the timber and interfere with its ease of working and other properties, it follows that a given piece of sapwood, because of its position in the tree, may well be stronger than a piece of heartwood from the same tree.
rewrite: In its juvenile state, a tree is typically covered with branches extending nearly, if not entirely, to the ground. As the tree matures, some or all of these lower limbs eventually die and are shed, either through breakage or abscission. Subsequent radial growth can entirely envelop the remaining stubs, though these persist internally as knots. Consequently, even a log with a smooth, clear exterior will contain knots within its central core. This results in the sapwood of an aged tree, especially one grown in a forest setting, being comparatively freer from knots than the inner heartwood. Given that knots generally constitute defects—weakening timber and impeding its workability and other properties—a section of sapwood, by virtue of its position, can possess greater strength than a section of heartwood from the same specimen.

input: Puritans were blocked from changing the established church from within, and were severely restricted in England by laws controlling the practice of religion. Their beliefs, however, were transported by the emigration of congregations to the Netherlands (and later to New England), and by evangelical clergy to Ireland (and later into Wales), and were spread into lay society and parts of the educational system, particularly certain colleges of the University of Cambridge. They took on distinctive beliefs about clerical dress and in opposition to the episcopal system, particularly after the 1619 conclusions of the Synod of Dort they were resisted by the English bishops. They largely adopted Sabbatarianism in the 17th century, and were influenced by millennialism.
rewrite: Denied the opportunity to reform the established church internally and constrained by restrictive religious legislation in England, Puritans nevertheless propagated their doctrines through multiple channels. Congregational emigration disseminated their beliefs to the Netherlands and subsequently New England, while evangelical clergy carried them to Ireland and Wales. From there, these ideas permeated lay society and educational institutions, notably within several colleges at the University of Cambridge. Adopting distinct positions on clerical vestments and opposing episcopal governance—a stance that intensified following the 1619 Synod of Dort and provoked episcopal resistance—Puritans also widely embraced Sabbatarianism and millennial thought during the seventeenth century.

input: Not all boys who pass the College election examination choose to become King's Scholars. If they choose instead to belong to one of the 24 Oppidan Houses, they are known as Oppidan Scholars. Oppidan scholarships may also be awarded for consistently performing with distinction in School and external examinations. To gain an Oppidan Scholarship, a boy must have either three distinctions in a row or four throughout his career. Within the school, an Oppidan Scholar is entitled to use the letters OS after his name.
rewrite: Not all candidates who succeed in the College election examination elect to become King's Scholars. Those opting for one of the 24 Oppidan Houses are designated Oppidan Scholars. This status may also be conferred for sustained distinguished performance in internal and external examinations, requiring either three consecutive distinctions or four cumulative distinctions during a pupil's tenure. An Oppidan Scholar is accorded the privilege of appending the post-nominal letters OS.

input: Some critiqued Paul VI's decision; the newly created Synod of Bishops had an advisory role only and could not make decisions on their own, although the Council decided exactly that. During the pontificate of Paul VI, five such synods took place, and he is on record of implementing all their decisions. Related questions were raised about the new National Bishop Conferences, which became mandatory after Vatican II. Others questioned his Ostpolitik and contacts with Communism and the deals he engaged in for the faithful.
rewrite: Certain critiques of Pope Paul VI focused on the Synod of Bishops, which was granted a purely consultative function despite the Council's specification, though he implemented all recommendations from its five assemblies during his pontificate. Further questions concerned the post-conciliar imposition of mandatory National Bishop Conferences. Additional criticism addressed his Ostpolitik, specifically his diplomatic engagements with communist regimes and the agreements negotiated on behalf of the faithful.

input: By the late Middle Ages, Buddhism had become virtually extinct in India, although it continued to exist in surrounding countries. It is now again gaining strength worldwide. China and India are now starting to fund Buddhist shrines in various Asian countries as they compete for influence in the region.[web 20]
rewrite: Buddhism had largely disappeared in India by the late medieval period, persisting primarily in neighboring regions. It is currently experiencing a global resurgence. In a competition for regional influence, China and India are now financing Buddhist shrines across Asia.

input: The university's first chancellor was Joseph Gibson Hoyt. Crow secured the university charter from the Missouri General Assembly in 1853, and Eliot was named President of the Board of Trustees. Early on, Eliot solicited support from members of the local business community, including John O'Fallon, but Eliot failed to secure a permanent endowment. Washington University is unusual among major American universities in not having had a prior financial endowment. The institution had no backing of a religious organization, single wealthy patron, or earmarked government support.
rewrite: The inaugural chancellor of the university was Joseph Gibson Hoyt. Following the securing of its charter from the Missouri General Assembly by Crow in 1853, Eliot was appointed President of the Board of Trustees. Eliot initially sought patronage from local business figures such as John O'Fallon, yet he was unsuccessful in establishing a permanent endowment. Consequently, Washington University is distinctive among prominent American institutions for lacking an initial financial endowment, religious affiliation, singular wealthy benefactor, or designated governmental funding.

input: European Dutch remained the literary language until the start of the 1920s, when under pressure of Afrikaner nationalism the local "African" Dutch was preferred over the written, European-based standard. In 1925, section 137 of the 1909 constitution of the Union of South Africa was amended by Act 8 of 1925, stating "the word Dutch in article 137 [...] is hereby declared to include Afrikaans". The constitution of 1983 only listed English and Afrikaans as official languages. It is estimated that between 90% to 95% of Afrikaans vocabulary is ultimately of Dutch origin.
rewrite: European Dutch persisted as the literary standard until the early 1920s, when Afrikaner nationalist sentiment prompted a shift toward the local "African" Dutch vernacular over the European norm. This was formalized in 1925 by Act 8, which amended Section 137 of the 1909 Union constitution to declare that the term "Dutch" therein included Afrikaans. The 1983 constitution subsequently recognized only English and Afrikaans as official languages. An estimated 90 to 95 percent of the Afrikaans lexicon derives ultimately from Dutch origins.

input: Unarmed fox hunting on horseback with hounds is the type of hunting most closely associated with the United Kingdom; in fact, "hunting" without qualification implies fox hunting. What in other countries is called "hunting" is called "shooting" (birds) or "stalking" (deer) in Britain. Originally a form of vermin control to protect livestock, fox hunting became a popular social activity for newly wealthy upper classes in Victorian times and a traditional rural activity for riders and foot followers alike. Similar to fox hunting in many ways is the chasing of hares with hounds. Pairs of Sight hounds (or long-dogs), such as greyhounds, may be used to pursue a hare in coursing, where the greyhounds are marked as to their skill in coursing the hare (but are not intended to actually catch it), or the hare may be pursued with scent hounds such as beagles or harriers. Other sorts of foxhounds may also be used for hunting stags (deer) or mink. Deer stalking with rifles is carried out on foot without hounds, using stealth.
rewrite: The practice of unarmed fox hunting on horseback, employing a pack of hounds, is the form of hunting most quintessentially linked with the United Kingdom; indeed, the unqualified term "hunting" typically denotes this specific pursuit. Activities described as "hunting" elsewhere are distinguished in Britain as "shooting" (for game birds) or "stalking" (for deer). Initially a method of vermin control to safeguard livestock, fox hunting evolved during the Victorian era into a fashionable social pursuit for the emergent upper classes and a customary rural pastime for mounted participants and foot followers. A comparable practice is the pursuit of hares with hounds. This may involve coursing with pairs of sight hounds, such as greyhounds, where the dogs are assessed on skill rather than a capture, or it may utilize scent hounds like beagles. Furthermore, various foxhounds are also employed in the hunting of stag or mink. In contrast, deer stalking is conducted on foot, utilizing rifles and stealth, without the assistance of hounds.

input: The restoration of power to the patriciate was only temporary. After a period of unrest with repeated violent clashes such as the Züriputsch of 1839, civil war (the Sonderbundskrieg) broke out in 1847 when some Catholic cantons tried to set up a separate alliance (the Sonderbund). The war lasted for less than a month, causing fewer than 100 casualties, most of which were through friendly fire. Yet however minor the Sonderbundskrieg appears compared with other European riots and wars in the 19th century, it nevertheless had a major impact on both the psychology and the society of the Swiss and of Switzerland.
rewrite: The patrician class's restoration of authority proved transient. Following a phase of instability marked by recurrent violent disturbances, including the Züriputsch of 1839, civil war—the Sonderbundskrieg—erupted in 1847. This conflict was precipitated by several Catholic cantons forming a separate league, the Sonderbund. Although the war concluded in under a month with fewer than one hundred fatalities, many from friendly fire, its historical significance is substantial. Despite its minor scale relative to other contemporary European conflicts, the Sonderbundskrieg profoundly influenced Swiss collective psychology and societal structures.

input: A common application of a torque motor would be the supply- and take-up reel motors in a tape drive. In this application, driven from a low voltage, the characteristics of these motors allow a relatively constant light tension to be applied to the tape whether or not the capstan is feeding tape past the tape heads. Driven from a higher voltage, (and so delivering a higher torque), the torque motors can also achieve fast-forward and rewind operation without requiring any additional mechanics such as gears or clutches. In the computer gaming world, torque motors are used in force feedback steering wheels.
rewrite: A frequent implementation of torque motors occurs within tape drive systems, specifically in the supply and take-up reel mechanisms. When operated at low voltage, these motors utilize their inherent characteristics to maintain a consistently light tension on the tape, irrespective of the capstan's action in moving the tape across the heads. Conversely, when supplied with higher voltage to produce increased torque, the same motors facilitate rapid fast-forward and rewind functions, eliminating the need for supplementary mechanical components like gears or clutches. Additionally, in computer gaming, torque motors are employed to provide force feedback in steering wheel peripherals.

input: The Korean War was a conflict between the United States and its United Nations allies and the communist powers under influence of the Soviet Union (also a UN member nation) and the People's Republic of China (which later also gained UN membership). The principal combatants were North and South Korea. Principal allies of South Korea included the United States, Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom, although many other nations sent troops under the aegis of the United Nations. Allies of North Korea included the People's Republic of China, which supplied military forces, and the Soviet Union, which supplied combat advisors and aircraft pilots, as well as arms, for the Chinese and North Korean troops.
rewrite: The Korean War constituted a military conflict primarily between North and South Korea, with extensive international involvement. The principal belligerents were supported by opposing global power blocs. South Korea was aided by a United Nations coalition, predominantly led by the United States and including forces from nations such as Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom. Conversely, North Korea received substantial support from the People's Republic of China, which deployed military forces, and the Soviet Union, a fellow communist state. Soviet assistance included the provision of arms, combat advisors, and aircraft pilots, operating in support of both Chinese and North Korean troops.

input: On 3 December, Chopin complained about his bad health and the incompetence of the doctors in Majorca: "Three doctors have visited me ... The first said I was dead; the second said I was dying; and the third said I was about to die." He also had problems having his Pleyel piano sent to him. It finally arrived from Paris in December. Chopin wrote to Pleyel in January 1839: "I am sending you my Preludes [(Op. 28)]. I finished them on your little piano, which arrived in the best possible condition in spite of the sea, the bad weather and the Palma customs." Chopin was also able to undertake work on his Ballade No. 2, Op. 38; two Polonaises, Op. 40; and the Scherzo No. 3, Op. 39.
rewrite: On 3 December, Frédéric Chopin expressed dissatisfaction with both his declining health and the inadequacy of medical practitioners in Majorca, satirically noting, "Three doctors have visited me... The first said I was dead; the second said I was dying; and the third said I was about to die." Concurrently, he encountered logistical difficulties in receiving his Pleyel piano, which ultimately arrived from Paris later that month. In January 1839, Chopin informed Pleyel that he had completed his Preludes, Op. 28, on the instrument, which had survived the maritime transit and customs procedures in good condition. During this period, he also progressed on several major compositions, including the Ballade No. 2, Op. 38; two Polonaises, Op. 40; and the Scherzo No. 3, Op. 39.

input: In the 1960s, Downtown Houston consisted of a collection of mid-rise office structures. Downtown was on the threshold of an energy industry–led boom in 1970. A succession of skyscrapers were built throughout the 1970s—many by real estate developer Gerald D. Hines—culminating with Houston's tallest skyscraper, the 75-floor, 1,002-foot (305 m)-tall JPMorgan Chase Tower (formerly the Texas Commerce Tower), completed in 1982. It is the tallest structure in Texas, 15th tallest building in the United States, and the 85th tallest skyscraper in the world, based on highest architectural feature. In 1983, the 71-floor, 992-foot (302 m)-tall Wells Fargo Plaza (formerly Allied Bank Plaza) was completed, becoming the second-tallest building in Houston and Texas. Based on highest architectural feature, it is the 17th tallest in the United States and the 95th tallest in the world. In 2007, downtown Houston had over 43 million square feet (4,000,000 m²) of office space.
rewrite: During the 1960s, Downtown Houston was characterized by a cluster of mid-rise office buildings. The district stood at the precipice of a significant expansion driven by the energy sector in 1970. The subsequent decade witnessed the construction of a series of skyscrapers, numerous projects of which were developed by Gerald D. Hines. This period culminated in 1982 with the completion of the 75-story, 1,002-foot (305-meter) JPMorgan Chase Tower, originally the Texas Commerce Tower, which remains Houston's tallest building. It ranks as the tallest structure in Texas, the 15th-tallest building in the United States, and the 85th-tallest skyscraper globally, based on its highest architectural feature. In 1983, the 71-story, 992-foot (302-meter) Wells Fargo Plaza, formerly the Allied Bank Plaza, was finished, becoming the second-tallest building in both Houston and Texas. By the metric of highest architectural feature, it is the 17th-tallest in the United States and the 95th-tallest worldwide. By 2007, downtown Houston contained over 43 million square feet (approximately 4 million square meters) of office space.

input: Symmetry groups are groups consisting of symmetries of given mathematical objects—be they of geometric nature, such as the introductory symmetry group of the square, or of algebraic nature, such as polynomial equations and their solutions. Conceptually, group theory can be thought of as the study of symmetry.t[›] Symmetries in mathematics greatly simplify the study of geometrical or analytical objects. A group is said to act on another mathematical object X if every group element performs some operation on X compatibly to the group law. In the rightmost example below, an element of order 7 of the (2,3,7) triangle group acts on the tiling by permuting the highlighted warped triangles (and the other ones, too). By a group action, the group pattern is connected to the structure of the object being acted on.
rewrite: Symmetry groups comprise the sets of symmetries associated with specific mathematical objects, whether geometric, such as the symmetry group of a square, or algebraic, such as the symmetries inherent in polynomial equations and their solutions. Fundamentally, group theory constitutes the systematic study of symmetry. Symmetries serve to substantially simplify the analysis of geometric or analytical structures. A group is defined to act on an object X when each group element performs an operation on X in a manner consistent with the group’s internal law. For instance, in a (2,3,7) triangle group, an element of order 7 acts upon a tiling by permuting the warped triangular regions. Through such group actions, the abstract pattern of the group becomes intrinsically linked to the structure of the object under consideration.

input: Currently, the Regular Force component of the Army consists of three field-ready brigade groups: 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Edmonton and CFB Shilo; 2 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Petawawa and CFB Gagetown; and 5 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Valcartier and Quebec City. Each contains one regiment each of artillery, armour, and combat engineers, three battalions of infantry (all scaled in the British fashion), one battalion for logistics, a squadron for headquarters/signals, and several smaller support organizations. A tactical helicopter squadron and a field ambulance are co-located with each brigade, but do not form part of the brigade's command structure.
rewrite: The Regular Force of the Army presently maintains three field-deployable brigade groups: 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group (CFB Edmonton and CFB Shilo), 2 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group (CFB Petawawa and CFB Gagetown), and 5 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group (CFB Valcartier and Quebec City). Each brigade group is organized with one regiment of artillery, armour, and combat engineers respectively; three British-scaled infantry battalions; one logistics battalion; a headquarters and signals squadron; and various smaller support units. A tactical helicopter squadron and a field ambulance are stationed with each brigade, though they operate outside its formal command hierarchy.

input: The kingdom is mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as an important market place for ivory, which was exported throughout the ancient world. Aksum was at the time ruled by Zoskales, who also governed the port of Adulis. The Aksumite rulers facilitated trade by minting their own Aksumite currency. The state also established its hegemony over the declining Kingdom of Kush and regularly entered the politics of the kingdoms on the Arabian peninsula, eventually extending its rule over the region with the conquest of the Himyarite Kingdom.
rewrite: The kingdom is documented in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as a significant emporium for ivory, a commodity widely exported across the ancient world. Under the rule of Zoskales, who also controlled the port of Adulis, Aksum facilitated commerce by issuing its own currency. The state further asserted hegemony over the declining Kingdom of Kush and actively intervened in the affairs of Arabian polities, ultimately extending its dominion over the region through the conquest of the Himyarite Kingdom.

input: The abbey was restored to the Benedictines under the Catholic Mary I of England, but they were again ejected under Elizabeth I in 1559. In 1560, Elizabeth re-established Westminster as a "Royal Peculiar" – a church of the Church of England responsible directly to the Sovereign, rather than to a diocesan bishop – and made it the Collegiate Church of St Peter (that is, a non-cathedral church with an attached chapter of canons, headed by a dean.) The last of Mary's abbots was made the first dean.
rewrite: The abbey was returned to Benedictine control during the reign of the Catholic monarch Mary I, only to be dissolved again under Elizabeth I in 1559. The following year, Elizabeth re-founded Westminster as a "Royal Peculiar"—a Church of England institution directly subordinate to the Sovereign, bypassing diocesan authority—and designated it the Collegiate Church of St Peter. This status entailed a non-cathedral church governed by a chapter of canons led by a dean, with Mary's final abbot appointed as the inaugural dean.

input: This new approach liberated scientific speculation from the dogmatic restraints of Aristotelian science, and paved the way for new approaches. Particularly within the field of theories of motion great advances were made, when such scholars as Jean Buridan, Nicole Oresme and the Oxford Calculators challenged the work of Aristotle. Buridan developed the theory of impetus as the cause of the motion of projectiles, which was an important step towards the modern concept of inertia. The works of these scholars anticipated the heliocentric worldview of Nicolaus Copernicus.
rewrite: This novel methodology emancipated scientific inquiry from the rigid dogmas of Aristotelian tradition, facilitating innovative intellectual pathways. Significant progress emerged within theories of motion, as scholars including Jean Buridan, Nicole Oresme, and the Oxford Calculators critically engaged Aristotle's work. Buridan's impetus theory, explaining projectile motion, constituted a pivotal advancement toward the modern principle of inertia. Collectively, their scholarship prefigured the heliocentric cosmology later advanced by Nicolaus Copernicus.

input: Nasser remains an iconic figure in the Arab world, particularly for his strides towards social justice and Arab unity, modernization policies, and anti-imperialist efforts. His presidency also encouraged and coincided with an Egyptian cultural boom, and launched large industrial projects, including the Aswan Dam and Helwan City. Nasser's detractors criticize his authoritarianism, his government's human rights violations, his populist relationship with the citizenry, and his failure to establish civil institutions, blaming his legacy for future dictatorial governance in Egypt. Historians describe Nasser as a towering political figure of the Middle East in the 20th century.
rewrite: Gamal Abdel Nasser endures as an iconic figure in the Arab world, celebrated for his pursuit of social justice, Arab nationalism, modernization, and anti-imperialism. His tenure fostered a cultural renaissance and ambitious industrialization, epitomized by the Aswan High Dam and Helwan City. Critics, however, condemn his authoritarian governance, human rights abuses, populist tactics, and failure to build durable civil institutions, linking his legacy to subsequent autocratic rule. Historians broadly regard Nasser as a dominant political force in the twentieth-century Middle East.

input: Motorsport racecourses and events were banned in Switzerland following the 1955 Le Mans disaster with exception to events such as Hillclimbing. During this period, the country still produced successful racing drivers such as Clay Regazzoni, Sebastian Buemi, Jo Siffert, Dominique Aegerter, successful World Touring Car Championship driver Alain Menu, 2014 24 Hours of Le Mans winner Marcel Fässler and 2015 24 Hours Nürburgring winner Nico Müller. Switzerland also won the A1GP World Cup of Motorsport in 2007–08 with driver Neel Jani. Swiss motorcycle racer Thomas Lüthi won the 2005 MotoGP World Championship in the 125cc category. In June 2007 the Swiss National Council, one house of the Federal Assembly of Switzerland, voted to overturn the ban, however the other house, the Swiss Council of States rejected the change and the ban remains in place.
rewrite: Following the 1955 Le Mans disaster, Switzerland instituted a ban on motorsport racecourses and events, with limited exceptions such as hillclimbing competitions. Despite this prohibition, the nation continued to cultivate accomplished competitors. These include Formula One drivers Clay Regazzoni and Jo Siffert, World Touring Car Champion Alain Menu, and endurance racing winners Marcel Fässler (2014 24 Hours of Le Mans) and Nico Müller (2015 24 Hours of Nürburgring). Furthermore, Switzerland secured the A1GP World Cup of Motorsport in 2008 with driver Neel Jani, and motorcycle racer Thomas Lüthi claimed the 2005 125cc MotoGP World Championship. Although the Swiss National Council voted to repeal the ban in June 2007, the Council of States rejected the measure, thereby maintaining the prohibition.

input: While outer space provides the most rarefied example of a naturally occurring partial vacuum, the heavens were originally thought to be seamlessly filled by a rigid indestructible material called aether. Borrowing somewhat from the pneuma of Stoic physics, aether came to be regarded as the rarefied air from which it took its name, (see Aether (mythology)). Early theories of light posited a ubiquitous terrestrial and celestial medium through which light propagated. Additionally, the concept informed Isaac Newton's explanations of both refraction and of radiant heat. 19th century experiments into this luminiferous aether attempted to detect a minute drag on the Earth's orbit. While the Earth does, in fact, move through a relatively dense medium in comparison to that of interstellar space, the drag is so minuscule that it could not be detected. In 1912, astronomer Henry Pickering commented: "While the interstellar absorbing medium may be simply the ether, [it] is characteristic of a gas, and free gaseous molecules are certainly there".
rewrite: While outer space represents the most extreme natural instance of a partial vacuum, the celestial realm was historically conceived as being entirely occupied by a rigid, immutable substance termed the aether. Derived in part from the Stoic concept of pneuma, aether was understood as a rarefied air, as reflected in its etymological origins (see Aether (mythology)). Early optical theories postulated this medium as ubiquitous, permeating both terrestrial and celestial regions to facilitate the propagation of light. This framework also informed Isaac Newton’s accounts of refraction and radiant heat. Nineteenth-century investigations into this luminiferous aether sought to measure a slight drag imposed on Earth’s orbital motion. Although Earth indeed traverses a medium denser than that of interstellar space, the resultant drag proved too negligible for detection. Reflecting on this, astronomer Henry Pickering noted in 1912 that while the interstellar absorbing medium might be identified as the aether, its properties are gaseous in nature, confirming that free gaseous molecules are undoubtedly present.

input: However, some scholars contest the idea of a Proto-Euphratean language or one substrate language. It has been suggested by them and others, that the Sumerian language was originally that of the hunter and fisher peoples, who lived in the marshland and the Eastern Arabia littoral region, and were part of the Arabian bifacial culture. Reliable historical records begin much later; there are none in Sumer of any kind that have been dated before Enmebaragesi (c. 26th century BC). Professor Juris Zarins believes the Sumerians were settled along the coast of Eastern Arabia, today's Persian Gulf region, before it flooded at the end of the Ice Age.
rewrite: The hypothesis of a singular Proto-Euphratean substrate language is contested by some scholars. They, along with others, propose instead that Sumerian originated among hunter-fisher populations associated with the Arabian bifacial culture, inhabiting the marshlands and littoral zone of Eastern Arabia. Substantive historical documentation begins only later, with no Sumerian records reliably dated prior to Enmebaragesi (c. 26th century BC). Supporting a coastal origin, Professor Juris Zarins posits that Sumerians were established along the Eastern Arabian coast, in what is now the Persian Gulf, prior to its inundation following the last Ice Age.

input: In Arabic-speaking cultures, two words are commonly used for Christians: Naṣrānī (نصراني), plural Naṣārā (نصارى) is generally understood to be derived from Nazareth through the Syriac (Aramaic); Masīḥī (مسيحي) means followers of the Messiah. The term Nasara rose to prominence in July 2014, after the Fall of Mosul to the terrorist organization Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. The nun or ن— the first letter of Nasara—was spray-painted on the property of Christians ejected from the city.
rewrite: In Arabic-speaking contexts, two principal terms denote Christians: "Naṣrānī" (نصراني), plural "Naṣārā" (نصارى), typically etymologically traced to Nazareth via Syriac, and "Masīḥī" (مسيحي), signifying followers of the Messiah. The designation "Nasara" gained particular notoriety following the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant's capture of Mosul in July 2014, when the Arabic letter nūn (ن), its initial character, was used to mark properties of displaced Christians.

input: Yet the most impressive aesthetic works were done among the scholars and urban elite. Calligraphy and painting remained a central interest to both court painters and scholar-gentry who considered the Four Arts part of their cultural identity and social standing. The painting of the early years of the dynasty included such painters as the orthodox Four Wangs and the individualists Bada Shanren (1626–1705) and Shitao (1641–1707). The nineteenth century saw such innovations as the Shanghai School and the Lingnan School which used the technical skills of tradition to set the stage for modern painting.
rewrite: The most significant aesthetic achievements emerged from scholarly and urban elite circles. Calligraphy and painting remained central pursuits for both court painters and the scholar-gentry, who viewed the Four Arts as integral to their cultural identity and social status. Early dynastic painting featured orthodox masters such as the Four Wangs, alongside individualists like Bada Shanren (1626–1705) and Shitao (1641–1707). The nineteenth century introduced innovations such as the Shanghai and Lingnan Schools, which employed traditional techniques to lay the groundwork for modern painting.

input: Many solar photovoltaic power stations have been built, mainly in Europe. As of July 2012, the largest photovoltaic (PV) power plants in the world are the Agua Caliente Solar Project (USA, 247 MW), Charanka Solar Park (India, 214 MW), Golmud Solar Park (China, 200 MW), Perovo Solar Park (Russia 100 MW), Sarnia Photovoltaic Power Plant (Canada, 97 MW), Brandenburg-Briest Solarpark (Germany 91 MW), Solarpark Finow Tower (Germany 84.7 MW), Montalto di Castro Photovoltaic Power Station (Italy, 84.2 MW), Eggebek Solar Park (Germany 83.6 MW), Senftenberg Solarpark (Germany 82 MW), Finsterwalde Solar Park (Germany, 80.7 MW), Okhotnykovo Solar Park (Russia, 80 MW), Lopburi Solar Farm (Thailand 73.16 MW), Rovigo Photovoltaic Power Plant (Italy, 72 MW), and the Lieberose Photovoltaic Park (Germany, 71.8 MW).
rewrite: A significant number of utility-scale solar photovoltaic power stations have been constructed globally, with a notable concentration in Europe. According to data current as of July 2012, the world's largest operational photovoltaic plants, ranked by capacity, include the Agua Caliente Solar Project in the United States (247 megawatts), the Charanka Solar Park in India (214 MW), and the Golmud Solar Park in China (200 MW). Other major installations are located in Russia, Canada, Italy, and Thailand. Germany hosts several substantial facilities, such as the Brandenburg-Briest Solarpark (91 MW), Solarpark Finow Tower (84.7 MW), and the Lieberose Photovoltaic Park (71.8 MW).
