input: Under a banner of "reducing public drunkenness" the Beer Act of 1830 introduced a new lower tier of premises permitted to sell alcohol, the Beer Houses. At the time beer was viewed as harmless, nutritious and even healthy. Young children were often given what was described as small beer, which was brewed to have a low alcohol content, as the local water was often unsafe. Even the evangelical church and temperance movements of the day viewed the drinking of beer very much as a secondary evil and a normal accompaniment to a meal. The freely available beer was thus intended to wean the drinkers off the evils of gin, or so the thinking went.
rewrite: The Beer Act of 1830, framed as a measure to diminish public inebriation, established a new class of licensed premises known as Beer Houses. Contemporary perceptions held beer to be a benign, nutritious, and even salutary beverage. Due to frequent water contamination, young children were commonly given "small beer," a brew of minimal alcoholic strength. Notably, even contemporary evangelical and temperance movements largely regarded beer consumption as a lesser vice and a customary complement to dining. The legislation's underlying rationale was that this readily accessible beer would divert drinkers from the more pernicious consumption of gin.

input: Gagarin became a national hero of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc, and a worldwide celebrity. Moscow and other cities in the USSR held mass demonstrations, the scale of which was second only to the World War II Victory Parade of 1945. April 12 was declared Cosmonautics Day in the USSR, and is celebrated today in Russia as one of the official "Commemorative Dates of Russia." In 2011, it was declared the International Day of Human Space Flight by the United Nations.
rewrite: Yuri Gagarin was elevated to the status of a national hero within the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc, achieving global celebrity. Mass demonstrations, unparalleled in scale since the 1945 Victory Parade, ensued across Moscow and other Soviet cities. The date of his flight, April 12, was instituted as Cosmonautics Day in the USSR, remaining an official Russian commemorative date. Furthermore, the United Nations designated it the International Day of Human Space Flight in 2011.

input: In June 1718 Blackbeard, aka Edward Teach, ran his flagship, the Queen Anne's Revenge, aground at Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina, in present-day Carteret County. After the grounding her crew and supplies were transferred to smaller ships. In 1996 Intersal, Inc., a private firm, discovered the remains of a vessel likely to be the Queen Anne's Revenge, which was added to the US National Register of Historic Places. In November, after losing his ship and appealing to the governor of North Carolina who promised safe-haven and a pardon, the notorious pirate, Blackbeard (Edward Teach) was killed in an ambush by troops from Virginia.
rewrite: In June 1718, the notorious pirate Edward Teach, commonly known as Blackbeard, deliberately grounded his flagship, *Queen Anne’s Revenge*, at Beaufort Inlet in present-day Carteret County, North Carolina. Following this event, his crew and supplies were relocated to smaller accompanying vessels. The shipwreck, likely identified as this flagship, was discovered in 1996 by the private firm Intersal, Inc., and was subsequently listed on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places. That November, after having sought a pardon from North Carolina’s governor, Blackbeard was killed in a surprise engagement with a force of Virginia troops.

input: QED vacuum has interesting and complex properties. In QED vacuum, the electric and magnetic fields have zero average values, but their variances are not zero. As a result, QED vacuum contains vacuum fluctuations (virtual particles that hop into and out of existence), and a finite energy called vacuum energy. Vacuum fluctuations are an essential and ubiquitous part of quantum field theory. Some experimentally verified effects of vacuum fluctuations include spontaneous emission and the Lamb shift. Coulomb's law and the electric potential in vacuum near an electric charge are modified.
rewrite: The quantum electrodynamic (QED) vacuum exhibits complex properties. While the expectation values of its electric and magnetic fields are zero, their variances are non-zero. This results in the presence of vacuum fluctuations, comprising virtual particle-antiparticle pairs, and a finite vacuum energy. Such fluctuations are a fundamental component of quantum field theory. Experimentally confirmed manifestations include spontaneous emission and the Lamb shift. Furthermore, Coulomb's law and the electrostatic potential near a charge are modified in this vacuum.

input: Transformation, unlike transduction or conjugation, depends on numerous bacterial gene products that specifically interact to perform this complex process, and thus transformation is clearly a bacterial adaptation for DNA transfer. In order for a bacterium to bind, take up and recombine donor DNA into its own chromosome, it must first enter a special physiological state termed competence (see Natural competence). In Bacillus subtilis, about 40 genes are required for the development of competence. The length of DNA transferred during B. subtilis transformation can be between a third of a chromosome up to the whole chromosome. Transformation appears to be common among bacterial species, and thus far at least 60 species are known to have the natural ability to become competent for transformation. The development of competence in nature is usually associated with stressful environmental conditions, and seems to be an adaptation for facilitating repair of DNA damage in recipient cells.
rewrite: In contrast to transduction or conjugation, transformation is a complex process reliant upon numerous bacterial gene products that interact specifically to facilitate DNA transfer, thereby constituting a clear bacterial adaptation. For a bacterium to bind, internalize, and recombine exogenous DNA into its chromosome, it must first achieve a distinct physiological condition known as competence. In *Bacillus subtilis*, competence development requires approximately 40 genes. The size of DNA transferred during transformation in this species ranges from approximately one-third to an entire chromosome. This mechanism is widespread among bacteria, with at least 60 species currently identified as naturally competent. In natural environments, the induction of competence is typically linked to stressful conditions and is considered an adaptation that promotes the repair of DNA damage in recipient cells.

input: On 1 July 1967, BBC Two became the first television channel in Europe to broadcast regularly in colour, using the West German PAL system that is still in use today although being gradually superseded by digital systems. (BBC One and ITV began 625-line colour broadcasts simultaneously on 15 November 1969). Unlike other terrestrial channels, BBC Two does not have soap opera or standard news programming, but a range of programmes intended to be eclectic and diverse (although if a programme has high audience ratings it is often eventually repositioned to BBC One). The different remit of BBC2 allowed its first controller, Sir David Attenborough to commission the first heavyweight documentaries and documentary series such as Civilisation, The Ascent of Man and Horizon.
rewrite: On 1 July 1967, BBC Two inaugurated regular colour television broadcasting in Europe, employing the West German PAL system. This analogue standard remains in use, albeit being progressively supplanted by digital technologies. Notably, BBC Two has historically maintained a distinct programming remit compared to other terrestrial channels, deliberately eschewing soap operas and conventional news bulletins. Instead, it has focused on an eclectic and diverse schedule, though highly popular programmes are frequently transferred to BBC One. This unique mandate enabled its first Controller, Sir David Attenborough, to commission seminal documentary series such as *Civilisation*, *The Ascent of Man*, and *Horizon*, establishing the channel as a forum for substantive factual content.

input: On August 9, 2015, ESPN reported that the New Orleans VooDoo and Las Vegas Outlaws had ceased operations, effective immediately, a claim which was subsequently validated on the AFL website. On September 1, 2015, the Spokane Shock officially left the AFL and joined the IFL under the new name Spokane Empire, becoming the fifth active AFL/af2 franchise to leave for the IFL since bankruptcy (Iowa Barnstormers, Tri-Cities Fever, Green Bay Blizzard and Arkansas Twisters—now the Texas Revolution—left previously).
rewrite: On August 9, 2015, ESPN reported the immediate cessation of operations for the New Orleans VooDoo and Las Vegas Outlaws, a report later confirmed by the Arena Football League (AFL). Subsequently, on September 1, 2015, the Spokane Shock departed the AFL, rebranding as the Spokane Empire to join the Indoor Football League (IFL). This move represented the fifth such transition of an active AFL/af2 franchise to the IFL following the league's bankruptcy, following the Iowa Barnstormers, Tri-Cities Fever, Green Bay Blizzard, and Arkansas Twisters (now the Texas Revolution).

input: Thousands more employees work in Midtown, north of the central business district. Midtown's anchors are the city's largest single employer Detroit Medical Center, Wayne State University, and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. Midtown is also home to watchmaker Shinola and an array of small and/or startup companies. New Center bases TechTown, a research and business incubator hub that’s part of the WSU system. Like downtown and Corktown, Midtown also has a fast-growing retailing and restaurant scene.
rewrite: Midtown, located north of the central business district, employs thousands of additional workers. Its primary institutions include the Detroit Medical Center, the city's largest single employer, alongside Wayne State University and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. The area also hosts Shinola and numerous small and startup firms. New Center contains TechTown, a Wayne State University-affiliated research and business incubator. Similar to downtown and Corktown, Midtown features a rapidly expanding retail and restaurant sector.

input: The name Anabaptist, meaning "one who baptizes again", was given them by their persecutors in reference to the practice of re-baptizing converts who already had been baptized as infants. Anabaptists required that baptismal candidates be able to make their own confessions of faith and so rejected baptism of infants. The early members of this movement did not accept the name Anabaptist, claiming that since infant baptism was unscriptural and null and void, the baptizing of believers was not a re-baptism but in fact their first real baptism. As a result of their views on the nature of baptism and other issues, Anabaptists were heavily persecuted during the 16th century and into the 17th by both Magisterial Protestants and Roman Catholics.[aa] While most Anabaptists adhered to a literal interpretation of the Sermon on the Mount, which precluded taking oaths, participating in military actions, and participating in civil government, some who practiced re-baptism felt otherwise.[ab] They were thus technically Anabaptists, even though conservative Amish, Mennonites, and Hutterites and some historians tend to consider them as outside of true Anabaptism. Anabaptist reformers of the Radical Reformation are diveded into Radical and the so-called Second Front. Some important Radical Reformation theologians were John of Leiden, Thomas Müntzer, Kaspar Schwenkfeld, Sebastian Franck, Menno Simons. Second Front Reformers included Hans Denck, Conrad Grebel, Balthasar Hubmaier and Felix Manz.
rewrite: The term "Anabaptist," signifying "one who baptizes again," was applied pejoratively by their opponents to denote the practice of re-baptizing adult converts who had undergone infant baptism. Anabaptists insisted that candidates for baptism must be capable of professing their faith personally, thereby rejecting pedobaptism as invalid. The movement's early adherents themselves disputed this designation, arguing that infant baptism, being without scriptural foundation, was illegitimate; consequently, the believer's baptism they practiced constituted not a rebaptism, but a first and true baptism. Due to these heterodox views on sacramentology and other doctrines, Anabaptists endured severe persecution throughout the sixteenth and into the seventeenth century from both Magisterial Protestants and Roman Catholics. Although a majority of Anabaptists adhered to a literal hermeneutic of the Sermon on the Mount—renouncing oaths, military service, and civil office—a minority holding divergent views nevertheless engaged in believer's baptism. This latter group thus falls within the technical definition of Anabaptism, even though conservative traditions like the Amish, Mennonites, and Hutterites, along with some historiography, often exclude them from normative Anabaptist identity. Theologians of the Radical Reformation are frequently categorized into the Radical stream and the so-called Second Front. Prominent figures among the former include John of Leiden, Thomas Müntzer, Kaspar Schwenkfeld, Sebastian Franck, and Menno Simons. Key Second Front reformers encompassed Hans Denck, Conrad Grebel, Balthasar Hubmaier, and Felix Manz.

input: The design architecture of USB is asymmetrical in its topology, consisting of a host, a multitude of downstream USB ports, and multiple peripheral devices connected in a tiered-star topology. Additional USB hubs may be included in the tiers, allowing branching into a tree structure with up to five tier levels. A USB host may implement multiple host controllers and each host controller may provide one or more USB ports. Up to 127 devices, including hub devices if present, may be connected to a single host controller. USB devices are linked in series through hubs. One hub—built into the host controller—is the root hub.
rewrite: The Universal Serial Bus (USB) employs an asymmetrical design architecture based on a tiered-star topology. This structure comprises a host, multiple downstream ports, and numerous peripheral devices. The inclusion of additional USB hubs facilitates branching into a tree-like formation, supporting up to five hierarchical tiers. A single host may incorporate multiple host controllers, each furnishing one or more ports. A maximum of 127 devices, inclusive of any hubs, can be connected to one host controller. All devices are linked in series through these hubs, beginning with the root hub integrated into the host controller.

input: Ozawa's "Northern Force" had four aircraft carriers, two obsolete battleships partly converted to carriers, three cruisers and nine destroyers. The carriers had only 108 planes. The force was not spotted by the Allies until 16:40 on 24 October. At 20:00 Toyoda ordered all remaining Japanese forces to attack. Halsey saw an opportunity to destroy the remnants of the Japanese carrier force. The U.S. Third Fleet was formidable – nine large carriers, eight light carriers, six battleships, 17 cruisers, 63 destroyers and 1,000 planes – and completely outgunned Ozawa's force. Halsey's ships set out in pursuit of Ozawa just after midnight. U.S. commanders ignored reports that Kurita had turned back towards San Bernardino Strait. They had taken the bait set by Ozawa. On the morning of 25 October Ozawa launched 75 planes. Most were shot down by U.S. fighter patrols. By 08:00 U.S. fighters had destroyed the screen of Japanese fighters and were hitting ships. By evening, they had sunk the carriers Zuikaku, Zuihō, and Chiyoda, and a destroyer. The fourth carrier, Chitose, and a cruiser were disabled and later sank.
rewrite: Admiral Ozawa’s “Northern Force” comprised four aircraft carriers, two partially converted battleships of obsolete design, three cruisers, and nine destroyers. Its air complement numbered only 108 aircraft. Allied forces did not detect this formation until 16:40 on 24 October. At 20:00, Admiral Toyoda issued orders for a general attack by all remaining Japanese units. Perceiving an opportunity to eliminate the remnants of Japan’s carrier strength, Admiral Halsey committed the formidable U.S. Third Fleet, which included nine fleet carriers, eight light carriers, six battleships, seventeen cruisers, sixty-three destroyers, and approximately 1,000 aircraft, thereby vastly outgunning Ozawa’s contingent. Pursuit commenced just after midnight. U.S. command discounted subsequent reports that Admiral Kurita had reversed course toward the San Bernardino Strait, having effectively taken Ozawa’s decoy bait. On the morning of 25 October, Ozawa launched seventy-five aircraft, most of which were eliminated by U.S. combat air patrols. By 08:00, American fighters had neutralized the Japanese defensive screen and commenced strikes on naval vessels. By day’s end, U.S. forces had sunk the carriers *Zuikaku*, *Zuihō*, and *Chiyoda*, along with one destroyer. A fourth carrier, *Chitose*, and a cruiser were crippled and subsequently foundered.

input: The Bologna process has been adopted, since 2006, by Portuguese universities and poly-technical institutes. Higher education in state-run educational establishments is provided on a competitive basis, a system of numerus clausus is enforced through a national database on student admissions. However, every higher education institution offers also a number of additional vacant places through other extraordinary admission processes for sportsmen, mature applicants (over 23 years old), international students, foreign students from the Lusosphere, degree owners from other institutions, students from other institutions (academic transfer), former students (readmission), and course change, which are subject to specific standards and regulations set by each institution or course department. Most student costs are supported with public money. However, with the increasing tuition fees a student has to pay to attend a Portuguese state-run higher education institution and the attraction of new types of students (many as part-time students or in evening classes) like employees, businessmen, parents, and pensioners, many departments make a substantial profit from every additional student enrolled in courses, with benefits for the college or university's gross tuition revenue and without loss of educational quality (teacher per student, computer per student, classroom size per student, etc.).
rewrite:
Since its adoption by Portuguese universities and polytechnic institutes in 2006, the Bologna Process has structured higher education within state-run institutions. Admission operates competitively, governed by a *numerus clausus* system administered through a national database for student placements. Nonetheless, each institution reserves a supplementary quota of vacancies allocated through extraordinary admission channels. These cater to specific cohorts, including athletes, mature applicants (aged 23 and above), international students, Lusophone foreign students, holders of degrees from other institutions, transfer students, readmitted former students, and those seeking course changes, with each category subject to distinct criteria established by individual institutions or departments.

While public funding covers the majority of student costs, rising tuition fees and the enrollment of new student demographics—such as employees, entrepreneurs, parents, and pensioners, often attending part-time or evening classes—have altered financial dynamics. Consequently, many departments derive significant marginal revenue from each additional enrollee. This contributes positively to institutional gross tuition income without necessarily compromising educational quality metrics, including student-to-teacher ratios, resource allocation such as computers per student, and classroom sizes.

input: The loss of industrial and working-class jobs in the city has resulted in high rates of poverty and associated problems. From 2000 to 2009, the city's estimated median household income fell from $29,526 to $26,098. As of 2010[update] the mean income of Detroit is below the overall U.S. average by several thousand dollars. Of every three Detroit residents, one lives in poverty. Luke Bergmann, author of Getting Ghost: Two Young Lives and the Struggle for the Soul of an American City, said in 2010, "Detroit is now one of the poorest big cities in the country."
rewrite: The decline of industrial and manufacturing employment in Detroit has precipitated widespread poverty and its attendant social challenges. Between 2000 and 2009, the city's estimated median household income decreased from $29,526 to $26,098. By 2010, Detroit's mean income remained several thousand dollars below the national average, with approximately one in three residents living below the poverty line. Scholar Luke Bergmann, author of *Getting Ghost: Two Young Lives and the Struggle for the Soul of an American City*, noted in 2010 that Detroit had become among the nation's most impoverished major cities.

input: The Bithynians were a Thracian people living in northwest Anatolia. After Alexander's conquests the region of Bithynia came under the rule of the native king Bas, who defeated Calas, a general of Alexander the Great, and maintained the independence of Bithynia. His son, Zipoetes I of Bithynia maintained this autonomy against Lysimachus and Seleucus I, and assumed the title of king (basileus) in 297 BCE. His son and successor, Nicomedes I, founded Nicomedia, which soon rose to great prosperity, and during his long reign (c. 278 – c. 255 BCE), as well as those of his successors, the kingdom of Bithynia held a considerable place among the minor monarchies of Anatolia. Nicomedes also invited the Celtic Galatians into Anatolia as mercenaries, and they later turned on his son Prusias I, who defeated them in battle. Their last king, Nicomedes IV, was unable to maintain himself against Mithridates VI of Pontus, and, after being restored to his throne by the Roman Senate, he bequeathed his kingdom by will to the Roman republic (74 BCE).
rewrite: The Bithynians, a Thracian people inhabiting northwestern Anatolia, established an independent kingdom following the conquests of Alexander the Great. Their autonomy was first secured by the native ruler Bas, who repelled Calas, a general of Alexander. This sovereignty was consolidated by his son, Zipoetes I, who successfully resisted Lysimachus and Seleucus I, formally adopting the title of king (basileus) in 297 BCE. His successor, Nicomedes I, founded Nicomedia, a city which rapidly achieved significant prosperity. Throughout his protracted reign (c. 278–255 BCE) and those of his successors, the Kingdom of Bithynia maintained a position of considerable importance among the minor Anatolian monarchies. Notably, Nicomedes I facilitated the entry of Celtic Galatians into Anatolia as mercenaries; these forces later rebelled against his son, Prusias I, who subsequently defeated them. The final monarch, Nicomedes IV, proved incapable of resisting Mithridates VI of Pontus. Following his restoration by the Roman Senate, he ultimately bequeathed the kingdom to the Roman Republic via testament in 74 BCE.

input: The Space Race was a 20th-century competition between two Cold War rivals, the Soviet Union (USSR) and the United States (US), for supremacy in spaceflight capability. It had its origins in the missile-based nuclear arms race between the two nations that occurred following World War II, enabled by captured German rocket technology and personnel. The technological superiority required for such supremacy was seen as necessary for national security, and symbolic of ideological superiority. The Space Race spawned pioneering efforts to launch artificial satellites, unmanned space probes of the Moon, Venus, and Mars, and human spaceflight in low Earth orbit and to the Moon. The competition began on August 2, 1955, when the Soviet Union responded to the US announcement four days earlier of intent to launch artificial satellites for the International Geophysical Year, by declaring they would also launch a satellite "in the near future". The Soviet Union beat the US to this, with the October 4, 1957 orbiting of Sputnik 1, and later beat the US to the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin, on April 12, 1961. The Space Race peaked with the July 20, 1969 US landing of the first humans on the Moon with Apollo 11. The USSR tried but failed manned lunar missions, and eventually cancelled them and concentrated on Earth orbital space stations. A period of détente followed with the April 1972 agreement on a co-operative Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, resulting in the July 1975 rendezvous in Earth orbit of a US astronaut crew with a Soviet cosmonaut crew.
rewrite:
The Space Race constituted a twentieth-century competition for supremacy in spaceflight capability between the two principal Cold War adversaries, the Soviet Union (USSR) and the United States (US). Its origins lie in the post-World War II missile-based nuclear arms race, facilitated by the appropriation of German rocket technology and personnel. Both nations perceived the requisite technological superiority as integral to national security and as a symbol of ideological preeminence. This rivalry precipitated pioneering endeavors, including the launch of artificial satellites, unmanned probes to the Moon, Venus, and Mars, and human spaceflight within low Earth orbit and to the Moon.

The competition formally commenced on August 2, 1955, when the Soviet Union, responding to a prior US declaration of intent to launch satellites for the International Geophysical Year, announced its own plans to orbit a satellite "in the near future." The USSR achieved several early milestones, successfully orbiting Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, and later launching the first human, Yuri Gagarin, into space on April 12, 1961. The Space Race reached its zenith with the United States' Apollo 11 mission, which landed the first humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Following unsuccessful attempts at manned lunar missions, the Soviet Union redirected its efforts toward developing Earth-orbital space stations.

A subsequent period of détente was marked by the April 1972 agreement on the cooperative Apollo-Soyuz Test Project, culminating in the July 1975 rendezvous and docking in Earth orbit of US astronaut and Soviet cosmonaut crews.

input: The last major building work took place during the reign of King George V when, in 1913, Sir Aston Webb redesigned Blore's 1850 East Front to resemble in part Giacomo Leoni's Lyme Park in Cheshire. This new, refaced principal façade (of Portland stone) was designed to be the backdrop to the Victoria Memorial, a large memorial statue of Queen Victoria, placed outside the main gates. George V, who had succeeded Edward VII in 1910, had a more serious personality than his father; greater emphasis was now placed on official entertaining and royal duties than on lavish parties. He arranged a series of command performances featuring jazz musicians such as the Original Dixieland Jazz Band (1919) – the first jazz performance for a head of state, Sidney Bechet, and Louis Armstrong (1932), which earned the palace a nomination in 2009 for a (Kind of) Blue Plaque by the Brecon Jazz Festival as one of the venues making the greatest contribution to jazz music in the United Kingdom. George V's wife Queen Mary was a connoisseur of the arts, and took a keen interest in the Royal Collection of furniture and art, both restoring and adding to it. Queen Mary also had many new fixtures and fittings installed, such as the pair of marble Empire-style chimneypieces by Benjamin Vulliamy, dating from 1810, which the Queen had installed in the ground floor Bow Room, the huge low room at the centre of the garden façade. Queen Mary was also responsible for the decoration of the Blue Drawing Room. This room, 69 feet (21 metres) long, previously known as the South Drawing Room, has a ceiling designed specially by Nash, coffered with huge gilt console brackets.
rewrite:
The final significant architectural modifications to the structure occurred under the reign of King George V. In 1913, Sir Aston Webb undertook a redesign of Edward Blore’s 1850 East Front, drawing partial inspiration from Giacomo Leoni’s Lyme Park in Cheshire. This newly refaced principal façade, constructed from Portland stone, was conceived to serve as a formal backdrop for the Victoria Memorial, a substantial monument to Queen Victoria situated beyond the principal gates. Having succeeded Edward VII in 1910, George V possessed a more sober disposition than his predecessor; consequently, a heightened emphasis was placed upon official ceremonial functions and royal duties over extravagant social gatherings. His patronage of music included a series of command performances featuring notable jazz musicians, such as the Original Dixieland Jazz Band in 1919—marking the first jazz performance for a head of state—followed by Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong in 1932. This historical association led, in 2009, to the palace being nominated for a (Kind of) Blue Plaque by the Brecon Jazz Festival, recognising it as a venue of major significance to the development of jazz within the United Kingdom.

George V’s consort, Queen Mary, was a noted connoisseur of the arts. She took a profound interest in the Royal Collection, actively restoring existing pieces and acquiring new works of furniture and art. Her direct influence extended to interior renovations, including the installation of numerous new fixtures. Among these were a pair of marble Empire-style chimneypieces crafted by Benjamin Vulliamy in 1810, which she had placed within the ground-floor Bow Room, the expansive, low-ceilinged chamber at the centre of the garden façade. Furthermore, Queen Mary supervised the redecoration of the Blue Drawing Room. This apartment, measuring sixty-nine feet (twenty-one metres) in length and formerly designated the South Drawing Room, features a ceiling specially designed by John Nash, coffered and adorned with substantial gilt console brackets.

input: In 2011, the Aragonese government passed a decree for the establishment of a new language regulator of Catalan in La Franja (the so-called Catalan-speaking areas of Aragon). The new entity, designated as Acadèmia Aragonesa del Català, shall allow a facultative education in Catalan and a standardization of the Catalan language in La Franja.
rewrite: In 2011, the Aragonese government decreed the creation of a new regulatory body for Catalan in La Franja, designated the Acadèmia Aragonesa del Català. This entity is tasked with enabling optional Catalan-language education and standardizing the language's use within the region.

input: An influx of interstate and overseas migrants, particularly Irish, German and Chinese, saw the development of slums including a temporary "tent city" established on the southern banks of the Yarra. Chinese migrants founded the Melbourne Chinatown in 1851, which remains the longest continuous Chinese settlement in the Western World. In the aftermath of the Eureka Stockade, mass public support for the plight of the miners resulted in major political changes to the colony, including changes to working conditions across local industries including mining, agriculture and manufacturing. The nationalities involved in the Eureka revolt and Burke and Wills expedition gave an indication of immigration flows in the second half of the nineteenth century.
rewrite: The arrival of interstate and international migrants, notably Irish, German, and Chinese populations, precipitated the growth of slum districts, including a transient "tent city" on the Yarra River's southern bank. Chinese migrants established Melbourne's Chinatown in 1851, constituting the Western world's oldest continuous Chinese settlement. Following the Eureka Stockade, widespread public sympathy for the miners catalyzed significant political reforms within the colony, improving labor conditions in mining, agriculture, and manufacturing. Furthermore, the nationalities represented in both the Eureka rebellion and the Burke and Wills expedition reflected broader immigration patterns during the latter nineteenth century.

input: In December 1994, after being tipped off by his former FBI handler about a pending indictment under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, Bulger fled Boston and went into hiding. For 16 years, he remained at large. For 12 of those years, Bulger was prominently listed on the FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. Beginning in 1997, the New England media exposed criminal actions by federal, state, and local law enforcement officials tied to Bulger. The revelation caused great embarrassment to the FBI. In 2002, Special Agent John J Connolly was convicted of federal racketeering charges for helping Bulger avoid arrest. In 2008, Special Agent Connolly completed his term on the federal charges and was transferred to Florida where he was convicted of helping plan the murder of John B Callahan, a Bulger rival. In 2014, that conviction was overturned on a technicality. Connolly was the agent leading the investigation of Bulger.
rewrite: In December 1994, having been alerted by his former FBI handler of an imminent Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act indictment, James Bulger fled Boston and entered a prolonged state of concealment. He remained a fugitive for sixteen years, during twelve of which he was featured prominently on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. Commencing in 1997, New England media outlets began exposing criminal conduct by federal, state, and local law enforcement officials connected to Bulger, revelations which significantly embarrassed the FBI. In 2002, Special Agent John J. Connolly, the agent who had led the investigation into Bulger, was convicted on federal racketeering charges for facilitating Bulger’s evasion of arrest. Following the completion of that federal sentence in 2008, Connolly was transferred to Florida, where he was subsequently convicted of aiding in the planning of a murder against Bulger’s rival, John B. Callahan. That latter conviction was overturned on a technicality in 2014.

input: Ecuador was the site of many indigenous cultures, and civilizations of different proportions. An early sedentary culture, known as the Valdivia culture, developed in the coastal region, while the Caras and the Quitus unified to form an elaborate civilization that ended at the birth of the Capital Quito. The Cañaris near Cuenca were the most advanced, and most feared by the Inca, due to their fierce resistance to the Incan expansion. Their architecture remains were later destroyed by Spaniards and the Incas.
rewrite: Ecuador hosted numerous indigenous cultures and civilizations of varying scales. The early sedentary Valdivia culture emerged along the coast. Subsequently, the Caras and Quitus unified, establishing a sophisticated civilization that persisted until the founding of Quito. Near Cuenca, the Cañaris were notably advanced and, owing to their fierce resistance, were the most formidable opponents to Inca expansion. Their architectural remnants were later destroyed by both Inca and Spanish forces.

input: Only the Theravada school does not include the Mahayana scriptures in its canon. As the modern Theravada school is descended from a branch of Buddhism that diverged and established itself in Sri Lanka prior to the emergence of the Mahayana texts, debate exists as to whether the Theravada were historically included in the hinayana designation; in the modern era, this label is seen as derogatory, and is generally avoided.
rewrite: The Theravada tradition excludes Mahayana scriptures from its canon, as it derives from a lineage that diverged and consolidated in Sri Lanka before those texts emerged. Scholarly debate persists regarding its historical classification under the term "Hinayana," a designation now widely regarded as pejorative and consequently avoided in contemporary discourse.

input: In 2006, Jian Li, a Chinese undergraduate at Yale University, filed a civil rights complaint with the Office for Civil Rights against Princeton University, claiming that his race played a role in their decision to reject his application for admission and seeking the suspension of federal financial assistance to the university until it "discontinues discrimination against Asian Americans in all forms" by eliminating race and legacy preferences. Princeton Dean of Admissions Janet Rapelye responded to the claims in the November 30, 2006, issue of the Daily Princetonian by stating that "the numbers don't indicate [discrimination]." She said that Li was not admitted because "many others had far better qualifications." Li's extracurricular activities were described as "not all that outstanding". Li countered in an email, saying that his placement on the waitlist undermines Rapelye's claim. "Princeton had initially waitlisted my application," Li said. "So if it were not for a yield which was higher than expected, the admissions office very well may have admitted a candidate whose "outside activities were not all that outstanding".
rewrite: In 2006, Jian Li, a Chinese undergraduate student at Yale University, submitted a civil rights complaint to the Office for Civil Rights against Princeton University. He alleged that his race was a factor in the university's decision to deny his admission application. Li petitioned for the suspension of federal financial assistance to the institution until it ceased "discrimination against Asian Americans in all forms" by abolishing considerations of race and legacy status in admissions. Janet Rapelye, Princeton's Dean of Admissions, addressed these allegations in the November 30, 2006, edition of the *Daily Princetonian*, asserting that "the numbers don't indicate [discrimination]." She contended that Li was not admitted because "many others had far better qualifications," describing his extracurricular activities as "not all that outstanding." Li rebutted this characterization via email, arguing that his initial placement on the waitlist contradicted Rapelye's claim. He noted that "Princeton had initially waitlisted my application," suggesting that had the admissions yield been lower, the office might have admitted a candidate whose extracurricular profile was deemed unexceptional.

input: The Monreale mosaics constitute the largest decoration of this kind in Italy, covering 0,75 hectares with at least 100 million glass and stone tesserae. This huge work was executed between 1176 and 1186 by the order of King William II of Sicily. The iconography of the mosaics in the presbytery is similar to Cefalu while the pictures in the nave are almost the same as the narrative scenes in the Cappella Palatina. The Martorana mosaic of Roger II blessed by Christ was repeated with the figure of King William II instead of his predecessor. Another panel shows the king offering the model of the cathedral to the Theotokos.
rewrite: The Monreale mosaics represent the most extensive ensemble of their type in Italy, encompassing approximately 0.75 hectares and employing an estimated 100 million glass and stone tesserae. Commissioned by King William II of Sicily, this monumental project was realized between 1176 and 1186. The presbytery's iconography parallels that of Cefalù Cathedral, while the nave's pictorial cycles closely correspond to those in the Cappella Palatina. A notable adaptation is the Martorana mosaic of a ruler blessed by Christ, here featuring William II instead of his predecessor, Roger II. A further panel depicts the king presenting a model of the cathedral to the Theotokos.

input: Following the 2013 emergencies, the Minister of Foreign Affairs Tony de Brum was encouraged by the Obama administration in the United States to turn the crises into an opportunity to promote action against climate change. De Brum demanded new commitment and international leadership to stave off further climate disasters from battering his country and other similarly vulnerable countries. In September 2013, the Marshall Islands hosted the 44th Pacific Islands Forum summit. De Brum proposed a Majuro Declaration for Climate Leadership to galvanize concrete action on climate change.
rewrite: In the wake of the 2013 emergencies, Marshall Islands Foreign Minister Tony de Brum was urged by the Obama administration to leverage the crises as an impetus for climate action. He subsequently called for renewed commitment and international leadership to avert further climate disasters impacting his nation and other vulnerable states. During the 44th Pacific Islands Forum summit hosted by the Marshall Islands in September 2013, de Brum introduced the Majuro Declaration for Climate Leadership to catalyze concrete global measures against climate change.

input: Composers of classical music have often made use of folk music (music created by musicians who are commonly not classically trained, often from a purely oral tradition). Some composers, like Dvořák and Smetana, have used folk themes to impart a nationalist flavor to their work, while others like Bartók have used specific themes lifted whole from their folk-music origins.
rewrite: Classical composers frequently incorporate folk music, which originates from predominantly oral traditions and non-classically trained musicians. Figures such as Dvořák and Smetana employ folk themes to evoke national character, whereas others, like Bartók, directly integrate specific, unaltered folk melodies into their compositions.

input: Ronald Inden writes that by the 8th century CE symbols of Hindu gods "replaced the Buddha at the imperial centre and pinnacle of the cosmo-political system, the image or symbol of the Hindu god comes to be housed in a monumental temple and given increasingly elaborate imperial-style puja worship". Although Buddhism did not disappear from India for several centuries after the eighth, royal proclivities for the cults of Vishnu and Shiva weakened Buddhism's position within the sociopolitical context and helped make possible its decline.
rewrite: Ronald Inden observes that by the eighth century CE, symbols of Hindu deities supplanted the Buddha at the imperial core and cosmological apex. The image of a Hindu god was thereafter enshrined within a monumental temple and accorded increasingly elaborate, imperial-style *puja*. While Buddhism persisted in India for centuries, royal patronage of Vishnu and Shiva cults diminished its sociopolitical standing, thereby facilitating its eventual decline.

input: In fledgling democracies funding can also be provided by foreign aid. International donors provide financing to political parties in developing countries as a means to promote democracy and good governance. Support can be purely financial or otherwise. Frequently it is provided as capacity development activities including the development of party manifestos, party constitutions and campaigning skills. Developing links between ideologically linked parties is another common feature of international support for a party. Sometimes this can be perceived as directly supporting the political aims of a political party, such as the support of the US government to the Georgian party behind the Rose Revolution. Other donors work on a more neutral basis, where multiple donors provide grants in countries accessible by all parties for various aims defined by the recipients. There have been calls by leading development think-tanks, such as the Overseas Development Institute, to increase support to political parties as part of developing the capacity to deal with the demands of interest-driven donors to improve governance.
rewrite: In nascent democratic systems, foreign aid represents an additional source of funding for political parties. International donors extend financial support to parties within developing nations, aiming to foster democratic consolidation and sound governance. This assistance may be purely monetary or may encompass other forms of support. Commonly, it is delivered through capacity-building initiatives, such as aiding in the formulation of party manifestos and constitutions or enhancing campaigning techniques. Another prevalent aspect involves facilitating connections between parties sharing ideological affinities. On occasion, such support can be interpreted as directly advancing a specific party's political objectives, exemplified by U.S. government backing for the Georgian party instrumental in the Rose Revolution. Conversely, other donors operate on a more impartial basis, with multiple entities providing grants for recipient-defined purposes, accessible to all parties within a country. Prominent development policy institutions, including the Overseas Development Institute, have advocated for increased support to political parties. This is viewed as essential for building their capacity to manage the expectations of interest-driven donors and thereby improve overall governance.

input: Swayambhu is a Buddhist stupa atop a hillock at the northwestern part of the city. This is among the oldest religious sites in Nepal. Although the site is considered Buddhist, it is revered by both Buddhists and Hindus. The stupa consists of a dome at the base; above the dome, there is a cubic structure with the eyes of Buddha looking in all four directions.[clarification needed] There are pentagonal Toran above each of the four sides, with statues engraved on them. Behind and above the torana there are thirteen tiers. Above all the tiers, there is a small space above which lies a gajur.
rewrite: Swayambhu is a Buddhist stupa situated on a hillock in the northwestern sector of Kathmandu. It ranks among Nepal's most ancient religious sites. While fundamentally Buddhist, the monument is venerated by both Buddhist and Hindu adherents. The stupa's structure features a hemispherical base, surmounted by a cubic harmika adorned with the all-seeing eyes of the Buddha. Each of the four sides is crowned by a pentagonal torana bearing engraved deities. Above these, a spire of thirteen diminishing tiers ascends to a finial known as a gajur.

input: In 1887, the British Empire celebrated Victoria's Golden Jubilee. Victoria marked the fiftieth anniversary of her accession on 20 June with a banquet to which 50 kings and princes were invited. The following day, she participated in a procession and attended a thanksgiving service in Westminster Abbey. By this time, Victoria was once again extremely popular. Two days later on 23 June, she engaged two Indian Muslims as waiters, one of whom was Abdul Karim. He was soon promoted to "Munshi": teaching her Hindustani, and acting as a clerk. Her family and retainers were appalled, and accused Abdul Karim of spying for the Muslim Patriotic League, and biasing the Queen against the Hindus. Equerry Frederick Ponsonby (the son of Sir Henry) discovered that the Munshi had lied about his parentage, and reported to Lord Elgin, Viceroy of India, "the Munshi occupies very much the same position as John Brown used to do." Victoria dismissed their complaints as racial prejudice. Abdul Karim remained in her service until he returned to India with a pension on her death.
rewrite: In 1887, the British Empire commemorated Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, marking the fiftieth anniversary of her accession. The official celebrations commenced on 20 June with a banquet for fifty foreign kings and princes. The following day, Her Majesty participated in a public procession and a service of thanksgiving at Westminster Abbey, events that reflected her restored popularity. Shortly thereafter, on 23 June, she appointed two Indian Muslims as attendants. One, Abdul Karim, was rapidly promoted to the role of "Munshi," tasked with instructing the Queen in Hindustani and performing clerical duties. This appointment provoked dismay among Victoria's family and household, who accused Karim of espionage for the Muslim Patriotic League and of prejudicing the monarch against Hindus. Equerry Frederick Ponsonby further reported that the Munshi had falsified his ancestry, comparing his influence to that formerly held by the ghillie John Brown. The Queen, however, interpreted such objections as manifestations of racial bias. Abdul Karim remained in royal service until Victoria's death, after which he returned to India with a pension.

input: Some new immigrants arrived as refugees with no possessions and were housed in temporary camps known as ma'abarot; by 1952, over 200,000 immigrants were living in these tent cities. During this period, food, clothes and furniture had to be rationed in what became known as the Austerity Period. The need to solve the crisis led Ben-Gurion to sign a reparations agreement with West Germany that triggered mass protests by Jews angered at the idea that Israel could accept monetary compensation for the Holocaust.
rewrite: A number of new immigrants arrived as destitute refugees, initially accommodated in transient camps called *ma'abarot*; by 1952, these tent cities housed over 200,000 individuals. Concurrently, essential goods including food, clothing, and furniture were subjected to rationing, an era termed the Austerity Period. To address the ensuing crisis, Ben-Gurion pursued a reparations agreement with West Germany. This accord provoked substantial public protests from those who opposed accepting monetary compensation for the Holocaust.

input: Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Environmental factors include exposure to air pollution and allergens. Other potential triggers include medications such as aspirin and beta blockers. Diagnosis is usually based on the pattern of symptoms, response to therapy over time, and spirometry. Asthma is classified according to the frequency of symptoms, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and peak expiratory flow rate. It may also be classified as atopic or non-atopic where atopy refers to a predisposition toward developing a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.
rewrite: Asthma etiology involves a complex interplay of genetic predisposition and environmental exposures, including air pollutants and allergens. Additional triggers encompass certain medications like aspirin and beta blockers. Diagnosis relies on symptomatic patterns, therapeutic response, and spirometric assessment, particularly forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1). The condition is classified by symptom frequency, lung function measures, and as atopic or non-atopic, with atopy denoting a propensity for type 1 hypersensitivity reactions.

input: There are 17 universities of technology in Germany with about 290,000 students enrolled. The four states of Bremen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt and Schleswig-Holstein are not operating a Technische Universität. Saxony and Lower Saxony have the highest counts of TUs, while in Saxony three out of four universities are universities of technology.
rewrite: Germany operates 17 universities of technology, enrolling approximately 290,000 students. The states of Bremen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt, and Schleswig-Holstein lack such institutions. Saxony and Lower Saxony contain the most, with three of Saxony's four universities being technological.

input: At the end of 2004, May and Taylor announced that they would reunite and return to touring in 2005 with Paul Rodgers (founder and former lead singer of Free and Bad Company). Brian May's website also stated that Rodgers would be "featured with" Queen as "Queen + Paul Rodgers", not replacing Mercury. The retired John Deacon would not be participating. In November 2004, Queen were among the inaugural inductees into the UK Music Hall of Fame, and the award ceremony was the first event at which Rodgers joined May and Taylor as vocalist.
rewrite: In late 2004, Brian May and Roger Taylor announced a touring reunion for 2005, featuring Paul Rodgers, founder and former lead vocalist of Free and Bad Company. Officially designated "Queen + Paul Rodgers," this collaboration explicitly did not constitute a replacement for the late Freddie Mercury. Bassist John Deacon, retired, did not participate. That November, Queen was inducted into the inaugural UK Music Hall of Fame; the accompanying ceremony marked the first official performance with Rodgers as vocalist alongside May and Taylor.

input: South West Africa became known as Namibia by the UN when the General Assembly changed the territory's name by Resolution 2372 (XXII) of 12 June 1968. In 1978 the UN Security Council passed UN Resolution 435 which planned a transition toward independence for Namibia. Attempts to persuade South Africa to agree to the plan's implementation were not successful until 1988 when the transition to independence finally started under a diplomatic agreement between South Africa, Angola and Cuba, with the USSR and the USA as observers, under which South Africa agreed to withdraw and demobilise its forces in Namibia. As a result, Cuba agreed to pull back its troops in southern Angola sent to support the MPLA in its war for control of Angola with UNITA.
rewrite: The United Nations General Assembly formally redesignated South West Africa as Namibia through Resolution 2372 (XXII) on 12 June 1968. Subsequently, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 435 in 1978, outlining a framework for Namibian independence. Implementation of this plan was delayed for a decade due to South African non-compliance. A diplomatic settlement was ultimately achieved in 1988, involving South Africa, Angola, and Cuba, with the United States and the Soviet Union acting as observers. This tripartite accord mandated South Africa's withdrawal and demobilization of its forces from Namibia. In a reciprocal measure, Cuba agreed to redeploy its troops from southern Angola, where they had been supporting the MPLA government against the UNITA faction.

input: Von Neumann worked on lattice theory between 1937 and 1939. Von Neumann provided an abstract exploration of dimension in completed complemented modular topological lattices: "Dimension is determined, up to a positive linear transformation, by the following two properties. It is conserved by perspective mappings ("perspectivities") and ordered by inclusion. The deepest part of the proof concerns the equivalence of perspectivity with "projectivity by decomposition"—of which a corollary is the transitivity of perspectivity." Garrett Birkhoff writes: "John von Neumann's brilliant mind blazed over lattice theory like a meteor".
rewrite: Between 1937 and 1939, John von Neumann conducted research in lattice theory. He offered an abstract investigation of dimension within complete complemented modular topological lattices, positing that dimension is uniquely specified, up to a positive linear transformation, by its preservation under perspectivities and its ordering by inclusion. A central proof establishes the equivalence of perspectivity with projectivity by decomposition, yielding the transitivity of perspectivity as a corollary. Garrett Birkhoff later remarked that von Neumann's intellect "blazed over lattice theory like a meteor."

input: From early in its development, ASCII was intended to be just one of several national variants of an international character code standard, ultimately published as ISO/IEC 646 (1972), which would share most characters in common but assign other locally useful characters to several code points reserved for "national use." However, the four years that elapsed between the publication of ASCII-1963 and ISO's first acceptance of an international recommendation during 1967 caused ASCII's choices for the national use characters to seem to be de facto standards for the world, causing confusion and incompatibility once other countries did begin to make their own assignments to these code points.
rewrite: From its inception, ASCII was conceived as a national variant within a broader international character encoding framework, later formalized as ISO/IEC 646 (1972). This standard reserved specific code points for national use, while maintaining a common core of shared characters. However, the four-year interval between ASCII's publication in 1963 and the International Organization for Standardization's initial adoption of an international recommendation in 1967 allowed ASCII's specific assignments for these national code points to become entrenched as de facto global standards. This subsequently led to widespread confusion and incompatibility when other nations eventually implemented their own distinct assignments for these reserved positions.

input: A striking technical innovation of the Komnenian period was the production of very precious, miniature mosaic icons. In these icons the small tesserae (with sides of 1 mm or less) were set on wax or resin on a wooden panel. These products of extraordinary craftmanship were intended for private devotion. The Louvre Transfiguration is a very fine example from the late 12th century. The miniature mosaic of Christ in the Museo Nazionale at Florence illustrates the more gentle, humanistic conception of Christ which appeared in the 12th century.
rewrite: A notable technical innovation during the Komnenian era was the creation of highly precious, miniature mosaic icons. These works employed exceptionally small tesserae, often with sides measuring one millimeter or less, set into wax or resin on a wooden support. Such masterpieces of craftsmanship served private devotional purposes. Exemplary specimens include the late twelfth-century Louvre Transfiguration and the miniature mosaic of Christ in Florence's Museo Nazionale, the latter reflecting the more humane and gentle iconographic conception of Christ emerging in that period.

input: Modern Orthodoxy, as a stream of Orthodox Judaism represented by institutions such as the U.S. National Council for Young Israel, is pro-Zionist and thus places a high national, as well as religious, significance on the State of Israel, and its affiliates are, typically, Zionist in orientation. It also practices involvement with non-Orthodox Jews that extends beyond "outreach (Kiruv)" to continued institutional relations and cooperation; see further under Torah Umadda. Other "core beliefs" are a recognition of the value and importance of secular studies, a commitment to equality of education for both men and women, and a full acceptance of the importance of being able to financially support oneself and one's family.
rewrite: Modern Orthodoxy, a movement within Orthodox Judaism exemplified by organizations like the National Council of Young Israel, is characterized by its pro-Zionist orientation. It ascribes profound national and religious significance to the State of Israel, a stance reflected in its affiliated institutions. Distinctively, it engages with non-Orthodox Judaism through sustained institutional cooperation, exceeding mere outreach. As articulated in the concept of Torah Umadda, its tenets affirm the value of secular scholarship, advocate for equal educational access for men and women, and emphasize the necessity of economic self-sufficiency.

input: Strasbourg is situated on the eastern border of France with Germany. This border is formed by the River Rhine, which also forms the eastern border of the modern city, facing across the river to the German town Kehl. The historic core of Strasbourg however lies on the Grande Île in the River Ill, which here flows parallel to, and roughly 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) from, the Rhine. The natural courses of the two rivers eventually join some distance downstream of Strasbourg, although several artificial waterways now connect them within the city.
rewrite: Strasbourg is located on France's eastern border with Germany, delineated by the River Rhine. The Rhine also constitutes the city's modern eastern boundary, directly opposite the German municipality of Kehl. The historic center lies on the Grande Île in the River Ill, which flows approximately 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) west of and parallel to the Rhine. While the two rivers converge naturally downstream, they are also linked within the city by several artificial canals.

input: As Universal's main product had always been low-budget film, it was one of the last major studios to have a contract with Technicolor. The studio did not make use of the three-strip Technicolor process until Arabian Nights (1942), starring Jon Hall and Maria Montez. The following year, Technicolor was also used in Universal's remake of their 1925 horror melodrama, Phantom of the Opera with Claude Rains and Nelson Eddy. With the success of their first two pictures, a regular schedule of high-budget, Technicolor films followed.
rewrite: Universal Studios, historically focused on low-budget productions, was among the final major studios to adopt a Technicolor contract. It first utilized the three-strip process for *Arabian Nights* (1942), featuring Jon Hall and Maria Montez. The following year saw its application in a remake of the 1925 melodrama *Phantom of the Opera*, starring Claude Rains and Nelson Eddy. The commercial success of these initial films subsequently established a consistent program of high-budget Technicolor features at the studio.

input: Digimon started out as digital pets called "Digital Monsters", similar in style and concept to the Tamagotchi. It was planned by WiZ and released by Bandai on June 26, 1997. The toy began as the simple concept of a Tamagotchi mainly for boys. The V-Pet is similar to its predecessors, with the exceptions of being more difficult and being able to fight other Digimon v-pets. Every owner would start with a Baby Digimon, train it, evolve it, take care of it, and then have battles with other Digimon owners to see who was stronger. The Digimon pet had several evolution capabilities and abilities too, so many owners had different Digimon. In December, the second generation of Digital Monster was released, followed by a third edition in 1998.
rewrite: Originating as a digital pet device titled "Digital Monsters," Digimon was conceptualized by WiZ and commercially launched by Bandai on June 26, 1997. Initially conceived as a counterpart to the Tamagotchi, targeting a predominantly male demographic, the virtual pet (V-Pet) retained core caregiving mechanics while introducing enhanced complexity and competitive battle functions against other devices. Users commenced with a Baby Digimon, engaging in training, evolution, and caretaking processes, ultimately testing their creature's strength through battles. The system featured multiple evolutionary pathways, resulting in varied outcomes among users. A second-generation model was released in December 1997, with a third edition following in 1998.

input: The element was probably named by the alchemist Paracelsus after the German word Zinke (prong, tooth). German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf is credited with discovering pure metallic zinc in 1746. Work by Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta uncovered the electrochemical properties of zinc by 1800. Corrosion-resistant zinc plating of iron (hot-dip galvanizing) is the major application for zinc. Other applications are in batteries, small non-structural castings, and alloys, such as brass. A variety of zinc compounds are commonly used, such as zinc carbonate and zinc gluconate (as dietary supplements), zinc chloride (in deodorants), zinc pyrithione (anti-dandruff shampoos), zinc sulfide (in luminescent paints), and zinc methyl or zinc diethyl in the organic laboratory.
rewrite: The element likely derives its name from the German word *Zinke* (meaning prong or tooth), attributed to the alchemist Paracelsus. Pure metallic zinc was first isolated in 1746 by the German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf. By 1800, Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta had elucidated its electrochemical properties. The primary industrial use of zinc is in corrosion-resistant coatings for iron via hot-dip galvanizing. Additional applications include batteries, small castings, and alloys like brass. Commonly used zinc compounds encompass dietary supplements (e.g., zinc carbonate, zinc gluconate), zinc chloride in deodorants, zinc pyrithione in anti-dandruff shampoos, zinc sulfide in luminescent paints, and zinc methyl or diethyl in organic synthesis.

input: During the 1920s and 1930s, British civil servants and politicians, looking back at the performance of the state during World War I, concluded that there was a need for greater co-ordination between the three Services that made up the armed forces of the United Kingdom—the British Army, the Royal Navy, and the Royal Air Force. The formation of a united ministry of defence was rejected by David Lloyd George's coalition government in 1921; but the Chiefs of Staff Committee was formed in 1923, for the purposes of inter-Service co-ordination. As rearmament became a concern during the 1930s, Stanley Baldwin created the position of Minister for Coordination of Defence. Lord Chatfield held the post until the fall of Neville Chamberlain's government in 1940; his success was limited by his lack of control over the existing Service departments and his limited political influence.
rewrite: In the interwar period of the 1920s and 1930s, British officials and policymakers, reflecting upon the state’s performance during the First World War, determined that enhanced coordination was required among the three branches of the United Kingdom’s armed forces: the Army, the Royal Navy, and the Royal Air Force. Although a unified ministry of defence was rejected by David Lloyd George’s coalition government in 1921, the Chiefs of Staff Committee was established in 1923 to facilitate interservice planning. As rearmament grew urgent in the 1930s, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin instituted the post of Minister for Coordination of Defence. Lord Chatfield occupied this role until the collapse of Neville Chamberlain’s government in 1940, but his effectiveness was constrained by his limited authority over the separate service departments and his insufficient political influence.

input: Under contract from the U.S. Military, Matrox produced a combination computer/LaserDisc player for instructional purposes. The computer was a 286, the LaserDisc player only capable of reading the analog audio tracks. Together they weighed 43 lb (20 kg) and sturdy handles were provided in case two people were required to lift the unit. The computer controlled the player via a 25-pin serial port at the back of the player and a ribbon cable connected to a proprietary port on the motherboard. Many of these were sold as surplus by the military during the 1990s, often without the controller software. Nevertheless, it is possible to control the unit by removing the ribbon cable and connecting a serial cable directly from the computer's serial port to the port on the LaserDisc player.
rewrite: Commissioned by the U.S. Military, Matrox manufactured an integrated computer and LaserDisc player for training applications. The system incorporated a 286-class computer and a LaserDisc player restricted to reading analog audio tracks. With a combined weight of 43 pounds (20 kilograms), the unit featured robust handles to facilitate lifting, potentially by two individuals. System integration was achieved via a 25-pin serial port on the player and a ribbon cable linked to a proprietary motherboard port. Throughout the 1990s, numerous units were decommissioned and sold as military surplus, frequently lacking the original control software. However, direct control remains feasible by disconnecting the ribbon cable and establishing a serial connection from the computer's port to the player's serial interface.

input: In the United Kingdom, a bill is presented for royal assent after it has passed all the required stages in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the House of Commons may, under certain circumstances, direct that a bill be presented for assent despite lack of passage by the House of Lords. Officially, assent is granted by the sovereign or by Lords Commissioners authorised to act by letters patent. It may be granted in parliament or outside parliament; in the latter case, each house must be separately notified before the bill takes effect.
rewrite: In the United Kingdom, a bill is submitted for royal assent following its successful passage through all requisite stages in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Pursuant to the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, the House of Commons may, under specified conditions, invoke a procedure to present a bill for assent without the consent of the Lords. Assent is formally conferred by the sovereign or by Lords Commissioners acting under letters patent. This may occur within or outside of Parliament; in the latter instance, each parliamentary house must be individually notified before the bill acquires legal force.

input: In the late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Germany, three pioneer physical educators – Johann Friedrich GutsMuths (1759–1839) and Friedrich Ludwig Jahn (1778–1852) – created exercises for boys and young men on apparatus they had designed that ultimately led to what is considered modern gymnastics. Don Francisco Amorós y Ondeano, was born on February 19, 1770 in Valence and died on August 8, 1848 in Paris. He was a Spanish colonel, and the first person to introduce educative gymnastic in France. Jahn promoted the use of parallel bars, rings and high bar in international competition.
rewrite: In late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Germany, pioneering physical educators Johann Friedrich GutsMuths (1759–1839) and Friedrich Ludwig Jahn (1778–1852) developed apparatus-based exercises for male youth, establishing the foundations of modern gymnastics. Jahn, in particular, advocated for the inclusion of parallel bars, rings, and the high bar in international competition. Concurrently, the Spanish colonel Don Francisco Amorós y Ondeano (1770–1848) introduced systematic educational gymnastics to France.

input: As the President, Tito had access to extensive (state-owned) property associated with the office, and maintained a lavish lifestyle. In Belgrade he resided in the official residence, the Beli dvor, and maintained a separate private home. The Brijuni islands were the site of the State Summer Residence from 1949 on. The pavilion was designed by Jože Plečnik, and included a zoo. Close to 100 foreign heads of state were to visit Tito at the island residence, along with film stars such as Elizabeth Taylor, Richard Burton, Sophia Loren, Carlo Ponti, and Gina Lollobrigida.
rewrite: President Josip Broz Tito utilized considerable state properties linked to his office, facilitating an opulent standard of living. His official Belgrade residence was the Beli dvor, in addition to a personal household. From 1949, the State Summer Residence was located on the Brijuni islands. Its pavilion, designed by architect Jože Plečnik, incorporated a private zoo. This island compound hosted nearly one hundred visiting heads of state, alongside notable film personalities including Elizabeth Taylor, Richard Burton, Sophia Loren, Carlo Ponti, and Gina Lollobrigida.

input: The tradition holds that Virgil was born in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul. Analysis of his name has led to beliefs that he descended from earlier Roman colonists. Modern speculation ultimately is not supported by narrative evidence either from his own writings or his later biographers. Macrobius says that Virgil's father was of a humble background; however, scholars generally believe that Virgil was from an equestrian landowning family which could afford to give him an education. He attended schools in Cremona, Mediolanum, Rome and Naples. After considering briefly a career in rhetoric and law, the young Virgil turned his talents to poetry.
rewrite: According to tradition, Virgil was born in Andes, a village near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul. Etymological analysis of his name suggests descent from earlier Roman colonists, though such modern speculation lacks direct narrative support from his own works or later biographers. While Macrobius records his father's humble origins, scholarly consensus holds that Virgil came from an equestrian landowning family capable of providing his education. He studied in Cremona, Mediolanum, Rome, and Naples. After briefly considering careers in rhetoric and law, he ultimately devoted himself to poetry.

input: Longstanding political tensions from the 27 year rule of William Tubman resulted in a military coup in 1980 that overthrew the leadership soon after his death, marking the beginning of political instability. Five years of military rule by the People's Redemption Council and five years of civilian rule by the National Democratic Party of Liberia were followed by the First and Second Liberian Civil Wars. These resulted in the deaths and displacement of more than half a million people and devastated Liberia's economy. A peace agreement in 2003 led to democratic elections in 2005. Recovery proceeds but about 85% of the population live below the international poverty line.
rewrite: The extended political tensions stemming from William Tubman's twenty-seven-year rule culminated in a military coup in 1980, which overthrew the government shortly after his death and initiated a prolonged period of instability. This included five years of rule by the military People's Redemption Council and five years under the civilian National Democratic Party of Liberia, preceding the devastating First and Second Liberian Civil Wars. These conflicts caused over half a million casualties and displacements, while crippling the national economy. Although a 2003 peace accord enabled democratic elections in 2005 and a subsequent recovery, approximately 85% of Liberians remain below the international poverty line.

input: The production for sulfidic zinc ores produces large amounts of sulfur dioxide and cadmium vapor. Smelter slag and other residues of process also contain significant amounts of heavy metals. About 1.1 million tonnes of metallic zinc and 130 thousand tonnes of lead were mined and smelted in the Belgian towns of La Calamine and Plombières between 1806 and 1882. The dumps of the past mining operations leach significant amounts of zinc and cadmium, and, as a result, the sediments of the Geul River contain significant amounts of heavy metals. About two thousand years ago emissions of zinc from mining and smelting totaled 10 thousand tonnes a year. After increasing 10-fold from 1850, zinc emissions peaked at 3.4 million tonnes per year in the 1980s and declined to 2.7 million tonnes in the 1990s, although a 2005 study of the Arctic troposphere found that the concentrations there did not reflect the decline. Anthropogenic and natural emissions occur at a ratio of 20 to 1.
rewrite: The smelting of sulfidic zinc ores generates substantial emissions of sulfur dioxide and cadmium vapor. Additionally, smelter slag and other processing residues retain significant concentrations of heavy metals. Historical mining and smelting operations in the Belgian localities of La Calamine and Plombières, active between 1806 and 1882, yielded approximately 1.1 million tonnes of metallic zinc and 130 thousand tonnes of lead. Waste materials from these activities continue to leach considerable quantities of zinc and cadmium, resulting in elevated heavy metal concentrations within the sediments of the Geul River. While annual global zinc emissions from such processes totaled roughly 10 thousand tonnes two millennia ago, they increased tenfold after 1850, reaching a peak of 3.4 million tonnes annually in the 1980s before declining to 2.7 million tonnes in the 1990s. However, a 2005 analysis of the Arctic troposphere indicated that this decline was not reflected in atmospheric concentrations there. Anthropogenic emissions currently exceed natural emissions by a factor of twenty.

input: The first written account of a game played was on October 15, 1862, on the Montreal Cricket Grounds. It was between the First Battalion Grenadier Guards and the Second Battalion Scots Fusilier Guards resulting in a win by the Grenadier Guards 3 goals, 2 rouges to nothing.[citation needed] In 1864, at Trinity College, Toronto, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn, one of the founders of Milton, Massachusetts, devised rules based on rugby football. The game gradually gained a following, with the Hamilton Football Club formed on November 3, 1869, (the oldest football club in Canada). Montreal formed a team April 8, 1872, Toronto was formed on October 4, 1873, and the Ottawa FBC on September 20, 1876.
rewrite: The earliest documented match occurred on October 15, 1862, at the Montreal Cricket Grounds, featuring the First Battalion Grenadier Guards against the Second Battalion Scots Fusilier Guards. The Grenadier Guards prevailed with a score of three goals and two rouges to nil. Subsequently, in 1864, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn—a founder of Milton, Massachusetts—established a codified set of rules derived from rugby football at Trinity College, Toronto. The sport's development continued with the establishment of foundational clubs: the Hamilton Football Club (November 3, 1869), recognized as Canada's oldest; Montreal (April 8, 1872); Toronto (October 4, 1873); and the Ottawa Football Club (September 20, 1876).

input: In 1982, Regis McKenna was brought in to shape the marketing and launch of the Macintosh. Later the Regis McKenna team grew to include Jane Anderson, Katie Cadigan and Andy Cunningham, who eventually led the Apple account for the agency. Cunningham and Anderson were the primary authors of the Macintosh launch plan. The launch of the Macintosh pioneered many different tactics that are used today in launching technology products, including the "multiple exclusive," event marketing (credited to John Sculley, who brought the concept over from Pepsi), creating a mystique around a product and giving an inside look into a product's creation.
rewrite: In 1982, Regis McKenna was engaged to direct the marketing strategy and launch campaign for the Macintosh. His team subsequently expanded to incorporate Jane Anderson, Katie Cadigan, and Andy Cunningham, with Cunningham ultimately assuming leadership of the Apple account for the agency. Cunningham and Anderson served as the principal architects of the Macintosh launch plan. This launch pioneered numerous tactics now standard in technology product introductions, such as the "multiple exclusive," event marketing—a concept attributed to John Sculley, who adapted it from Pepsi—cultivating product mystique, and offering behind-the-scenes insights into product development.

input: As of 2012, renewable energy plays a major role in the energy mix of many countries globally. Renewables are becoming increasingly economic in both developing and developed countries. Prices for renewable energy technologies, primarily wind power and solar power, continued to drop, making renewables competitive with conventional energy sources. Without a level playing field, however, high market penetration of renewables is still dependent on a robust promotional policies.
